# GEORGE KEDRENOS

## A COMPENDIUM OF HISTORIES.
<note>original: "ΣΥΝΟΨΙΣ ΙΣΤΟΡΙΩΝ" (Synopsis Historion). This title suggests a "synopsis" or condensed collection of historical accounts gathered from various earlier sources.</note>

<meta>This page continues from the title page of Volume II. It begins the historical chronicle of the reign of the Byzantine Emperor Constantine V (reigned 741–775 AD), focusing on his religious policies and personal character from the perspective of an orthodox historian. The marginal references "P 459" refer to the Paris edition page number, and "B" refers to the standard sectioning used in the Bonn edition.</meta>

In the year of the World 6236, and the year of the Divine Incarnation 739, <margin>P 459</margin> **Constantine <term>Caballinus</term>**, <note>original: "Καβαλλῖνος" (Kaballinos). A derogatory nickname derived from the Greek word for "horse," mocking the Emperor's obsession with horses and stable-life.</note> the **Iconoclast**, <note>original: "εἰκονομάχος" (eikonomachos), meaning "image-fighter." This refers to those who opposed the use of religious icons.</note> began his reign, which lasted thirty-five years. Appearing as a many-colored leopard born from a most terrible lion, <note>A metaphorical reference to his father, Leo III, who began the Iconoclast movement.</note> and as an asp and a flying serpent from the seed of a snake, he inherited both his father's kingdom and his impiety. <margin>5</margin> He distanced himself even further from God, from the **Mother of God**, <note>original: "θεομήτορος" (Theometoros) / "Deipara."</note> and from all the saints. Consequently, he devoted his time to sorcery, licentiousness, the summoning of demons, the dissection of internal organs <note>likely for divination or "extispicy."</note> and other wicked practices, as well as to hunting and chariot racing. He became a fitting instrument of the **Antichrist**, <margin>B</margin> <margin>10</margin> even to the point of issuing a universal decree that no one at all should be called "holy," <margin>10 "any one"] insert from Suidas: "of the servants of the Lord." margin P</margin> but rather that even the discovered remains of the saints should be treated with contempt, and that no one should seek their intercession. "For they have no power," the foul man would say, adding, "Let no one invoke the intercession of Mary, for she can do nothing." Furthermore, he forbade her from being called the <term>Theotokos</term>. <note>The Greek term for "Mother of God," literally "God-bearer." Denying this title was a major theological flashpoint.</note> <margin>15</margin> For taking a purse full of gold in his hand and showing it...

***

### THE CHRONICLE OF GEORGE CEDRENUS

<margin>C</margin>...to all present, he asked what it was worth. When they replied, "it is worth much," he emptied out the gold and asked again what it was worth. They said, "nothing." "In the same way," he said, "so also was Mary: as long as she had Christ within her, she was honored; but from the moment she gave birth to Him, she differed in nothing from the <margin>5</margin> rest of women." Lord, have mercy on us! <note>The chronicler adds this prayer as a reaction to what he considers a blasphemous statement by the Emperor.</note> Because of this, no small despair seized the Christians, so that he was hated by all, and they turned their support to **Artabasdos**, the <term>Kouropalates</term> <note>original: "κουροπαλάτῃ" (kouropalatai). A high-ranking Byzantine court title, originally the 'guardian of the palace,' usually reserved for members of the imperial family.</note> and his brother-in-law by marriage to his sister.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;When Constantine set out for the regions of the **Opsician Theme** <note>original: "Ὀψικίου" (Opsikiou). One of the major military-administrative districts of the Byzantine Empire, located in northwestern Asia Minor.</note> <margin>10</margin> against the Arabs, he was secretly plotting to harm **Artabasdos**, who was then at **Dorylaeum**. But Artabasdos, realizing this, moved against him and killed the <term>Patrician</term> **Biserus**, Constantine’s close confidant, with a broadsword. **Copronymus** <note>The derogatory nickname for Constantine V.</note>, being terrified, mounted a pack-horse and fled to **Amorium**. He won over **Longinus**, the general of the <margin>15</margin> **Anatolic Theme**, with great promises and was kept safe by him. From this followed the most terrible battles among the subjects, as both men were proclaimed emperors.

<margin>B</margin> Artabasdos entered the City <note>Constantinople.</note> and immediately restored the sacred icons throughout the entire capital, and he was proclaimed Emperor by the <term>Themata</term>. <note>The regional military units/provinces of the Empire.</note> But **Anastasius**, the "falsely-named" Patriarch, <note>The chronicler views him as illegitimate due to his shifting loyalties.</note> <margin>20</margin> holding the precious and life-giving Wood <note>The relic of the True Cross.</note>, swore to the people: "By the One who was nailed upon these, thus did Constantine the Emperor say to me: 'Do not consider the one whom Mary bore—the one called Christ—to be the Son of God, but a mere man; for Mary bore him in such a way...'"

### COMPENDIUM OF HISTORIES

"...for Mary gave birth to Him just as my mother Mary gave birth to me." <note>This completes the blasphemous statement from the previous page, where Emperor Constantine V supposedly equated the Virgin Mary with any common woman.</note> And hearing this, the people rejected him. <note>original: "ἀνέσκαψαν αὐτόν" (aneskapsan auton). Literally "dug him up," a metaphorical expression for deposing or rejecting a ruler's authority.</note>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In the second year of his reign, **Hisham**, the leader of the Arabs, died. <note>Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik, the Umayyad Caliph.</note> This man—even though the most holy Church of **Antioch** <margin>C</margin> <margin>5</margin> had remained without a leader for forty years because the Arabs forbade a Patriarch to be appointed there—had a certain favorite Syrian monk named **Stephen**. Stephen was a simple, unlearned man, distinguished only by his piety. Hisham signaled that if the people of Antioch wished to be granted a Patriarch, they should elect this Stephen. Thinking this was a gift from God, they consecrated him to the throne <margin>10</margin> of **Theopolis**. <note>original: "Θεουπόλεως" (Theoupoleos). Meaning "City of God," the honorary name for the city of Antioch.</note> In this same year, Constantine sent envoys to Hisham, as did **Artabasdos**, both of them requesting a military alliance. There was also a great drought and earthquakes in various places, so severe that mountains were joined to one another in the **Desert of Saba**, and a village was swallowed up by the earth. In that same year, **Cosmas**, the Patriarch of <margin>D</margin> <margin>15</margin> **Alexandria**, returned to the orthodox faith along with his city, renouncing the error of the **Monothelites**. <term>Monothelitism</term> <note>A 7th-century theological doctrine that Christ had two natures but only one "will." It was condemned as heresy by the Church.</note> In this year, a sign appeared in the sky. **Walid**, <note>Al-Walid II, who succeeded Hisham.</note> however, seized **Peter**, the most holy Metropolitan of **Damascus**, because he had rebuked the wicked errors of the Arabs and the <term>Manichaeans</term>. <note>Followers of a dualistic religion that viewed the world as a struggle between light and darkness; here, it is likely used as a general slur for religious opponents.</note> Walid had Peter’s tongue cut out and exiled him to **Arabia Felix**, <note>original: "εὐδαίμονα Ἀραβίαν" (eudaimona Arabian). Literally "Fortunate Arabia," referring to the fertile regions of the southern Arabian Peninsula, modern-day Yemen.</note> <margin>20</margin> where he finished his life, having borne witness for Christ and having clearly recited the divine liturgy <note>despite his tongue being removed</note>. In this year, such civil wars broke out as had not occurred since the foundation of the world.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In the third year, a sign appeared in the north, and dust fell from the sky. <margin>P 461</margin>

# COMPENDIUM OF HISTORIES.

...ordered them to enter the houses and plunder the property of the citizens. As for the falsely named patriarch <note>original: "ψευδώνυμον πατριάρχην" (pseudōnymon patriarchēn). This refers to Patriarch Anastasius, who was viewed as a turncoat for supporting the usurper Artabasdos before returning to Constantine's side.</note>, because he was of the same mind, the Emperor terrified and enslaved him, then restored him once more to the throne of the priesthood.
<margin>5</margin> In the fourth year, a great comet appeared in **Syria**, and **Marwan** <note>original: "Μαρουὰμ" (Marouam). Marwan II, the last Umayyad Caliph.</note> gained power over the **Arabs**. At the request of the Christians in the East, he permitted **Theophylactus of Edessa**, a priest, to be ordained as the Patriarch of **Antioch**, following the death of **Stephen**. The Caliph ordered that he be held in universal honor by the **Arabs** through official letters.
<margin>10</margin> In the fifth year, **Copronymus** <note>original: "Κοπρώνυμος" (Koprōnymos). A derogatory nickname for Emperor Constantine V meaning "dung-named," allegedly because he defiled the baptismal font as an infant.</note>, finding an opportunity in the East while the **Arabs** were fighting amongst themselves <note>A reference to the Third Muslim Civil War or Fitna.</note>, captured **Germanicia** <note>Modern Kahramanmaraş, Turkey.</note> and campaigned against **Dulichia** and **Assyria**. He also took his maternal relatives and resettled them in **Byzantium** <note>Constantinople</note>, and along with them, many Syrian **Monophysites** <note>original: "μονοφυσίτας" (monophysitas). From the 10th to the 15th of **August**, there was a misty darkness.
<margin>P 462</margin> In the sixth year, a great earthquake occurred in **Palestine**, by the **Jordan**, and throughout all of **Syria**, on the 18th day of the month of **January**, at the fourth hour. Countless tens of thousands perished, and churches and <margin>20</margin> monasteries collapsed, especially in the desert regions of the **Holy City** <note>Jerusalem</note>. In the same year, a pestilential death <note>The Bubonic Plague</note> began in **Sicily** and **Calabria**. In the fourth year, a great comet appeared in **Syria**, and **Marwan** began his <margin>5</margin> rule over the **Arabs**. He, persuaded by the exhortations of the Christians who are throughout the East, granted that **Theophylactus of Edessa**, a priest, be designated patriarch of **Antioch**, as **Stephen** had then died; and he ordered by public edict that he be held in honor by the **Arabs**.
In the fifth year, **Copronymus**, having found an opportunity for conducting affairs in the East <margin>10</margin> while a civil war was raging among the **Arabs**, recovered **Germanicia** and led his army to **Dulichia** and into **Assyria**. He also took his mother’s relatives to himself and transferred them to **Byzantium**, and with them many **Syrians** who attribute a single nature to Christ, who are called **Monophysites**. From the 10th until the <margin>15</margin> 15th day of **August**, there were thick, foggy shadows.

In the same year, a plague, <margin>20</margin> taking its beginning from **Sicily** and **Calabria**, seized the nearest places like a fire, spreading itself as far as **Monemvasia** and into **Greece** and the surrounding islands. # GEORGE CEDRENUS

...of the 14th indiction <note>A 15-year cycle used in Byzantine dating; the 14th indiction here corresponds to 745/746 AD.</note>. In the 15th indiction, there began to appear suddenly and invisibly in the Imperial City <note>Constantinople</note>, both upon the garments of men and upon the furnishings of the churches, many oily little crosses. 
<margin>B</margin> Consequently, a great sorrow and despondency came upon the people because of the mystery of such a sign. There also occurred a divine wrath <term>theomēnia</term> <note>original: "θεομηνία" (theomēnia), literally "divine anger," often used to describe natural disasters or plagues viewed as punishment.</note> of various diseases, unsparingly destroying the people, not only those in the city but also in all the surrounding countryside. There were also visions, such that many people, falling into a state of ecstasy, imagined that they were traveling with certain strange and terrifying figures, and those who encountered them would address and speak to them as if they were friends. Recording the things spoken by these apparitions, they later explained that these events came to pass. They even saw these same figures entering houses, hanging some of the inhabitants and wounding others with swords. 
<margin>C</margin> It happened that most of the things said by these figures occurred exactly as they had predicted. In the spring season of the 1st indiction <note>747 AD</note>, the evil intensified greatly. In the summer, it flared up all at once, so that entire households were completely shut up <note>Meaning all residents had died, leaving the house sealed.</note>, and there were not enough people whose duty it was to bury the dead. As a result, there were not enough biers <note>original: "κραββάτους" (krabbatous), refers to the litters or beds used to carry the dead.</note> for their removal; instead, they carried out the deceased on the backs of animals and in wagons. They were buried in the fortifications, the suburbs, in dry cisterns, and in pits. When these were filled, they dug up the vineyards and gardens, and even then they were barely able to cover the bodies. 
<margin>D</margin> Every household having been destroyed because of the impiety of **Copronymus** <note>Constantine V. The historian blames the Emperor’s iconoclastic policies for the divine punishment.</note>, he brought all the wealth of the city’s inhabitants into the palace...

In the 10th year <note>of Constantine's reign, approx. 751 AD</note>, Theophylactus, the most holy Patriarch of Antioch, went to his rest.

In the 11th year, Constantine took Theodosiopolis <note>Modern Erzurum, Turkey</note> along with Melitene, taking all who were there captive. ...was carried out. And so, many martyrs emerged on that day. He also burned as many books of the Fathers and relics of the saints as he could find, together with those in whose possession he found them, treating them as impious. He employed various methods of execution, and set fire to the heads of some after smearing them with pitch and oil. If anyone anywhere was found calling upon the name of the Mother of God <note>original: "deiparae," the Latin equivalent of Theotokos.</note>, or living a holy life, or observing the religious obligation of an oath, he was punished as an enemy of the emperor. Thus it happened that in his entire province, after a short time, there was no monk at all. When the emperor learned of this, he gave him thanks by letter, affirming that he had found him to be a man after his own heart’s desire and one who satisfied his will in all things. Others, imitating this man, acted in the same way. Copronymus handed over the monasteries, which had been built for the honor of God and as a refuge for those who would obtain salvation, to his soldiers who embraced his own opinions, and he took pains to cut off the monastic order. In the same year, Niketas—a patriarch in name only—scraped away the images that were decorated with small stones <note>i.e., mosaics.</note> in the small secretariat of the patriarch’s house, and all the other images throughout the entire house of the patriarch.

In the 29th year, an exchange of men was made in Syria, with individuals given for individuals. In this year, Irene came from Athens, and having been crowned in the temple of Saint Stephen, she was joined in marriage to Emperor Leo, the first-born son of Copronymus.

In the 32nd year, Phadalus made an incursion into the Roman domain and led away five hundred men as captives. The Mopsuestians went out to meet him, and having killed a thousand Arabs, they took back the spoil.

In the 33rd year, when Constantine had made an expedition against the Bulgarians, he returned after a peace was arranged. But when the Bulgarians sent twelve thousand into Berzetia, having learned of the matter, he hastened to Lithosoria and there overwhelmed them; and having killed everyone, he returned to the city. He called this the "noble war" because no Christian had perished in it. Furthermore, Elerich, the prince of the Bulgarians, perceiving that he was being betrayed by his own familiars, wrote to Constantine in this vein: "I have decided to flee and betake myself to you. Therefore, confirm by sent letters that all things will be safe for me; and indicate which friends you have here, so that trusting in their faith, I may reach you together with them." By this fraud, that vain and stolid man was circumvented and wrote out the names of his friends; all of whom Elerich destroyed. When this news was reported, Copronymus tore out his own beard.

In the 35th year, when he had undertaken an expedition against the Bulgarians, by the anger of God, carbuncles attacked his feet, and moreover a vehement fever...

### COMPENDIUM OF HISTORIES

Leo, the son of the Khazar woman <note>original: "ὁ ἐκ τῆς Χαζάρας" / "ex Chazara filius". Leo IV's mother was Irene of Khazaria, a princess from the Turkic Khazar Khaganate.</note>, reigned for five years.

Leo, the son of the Khazar, the son of Constantine Copronymus, ruled for five years. In the first year of his reign, Telerig, King of the Lombards, fled to him at Constantinople; having been received, he was bound to the Emperor by gifts. For some time, the Emperor seemed to cultivate piety and to be a friend of the Mother of God and of the monks; thus, in the earliest times, he even entrusted Metropolitan churches to monks. At the demand of the army, he crowned his son Constantine.

In the second year, Pellerigus, prince of the Bulgarians, fled to Leo, and by him was created a Patrician, with the Emperor even giving his wife's cousin to him in marriage; having been received by him from the sacred font <note>This refers to the Emperor acting as a godfather during Telerig's conversion to Christianity.</note>, he was held as greatly dear and honored by him.

In the third year, the Roman army, having set out for Germanicia, led away a great multitude of Syrian Jacobites as captives; these the Emperor settled in Thrace.

In the fifth year, Niketas, who had attained the dignity of Patriarch despite being a Slav and a eunuch, died. In his place was substituted the venerable Paul the Reader, a Cypriot. In the middle week of the fasts, the Emperor found two images in the pillow of his wife, Irene; when he had diligently examined them, an investigation having been made, he discovered they had been brought in by the palatine <term>Papias</term> and several other high officials, whom he then sentenced to the most grievous tortures and punishments. He also lashed out bitterly against his wife, Irene, and said she was of no account...

<meta>This page continues the history of the Byzantine Empire during the regency of Empress Irene. # BY GEORGE CEDRENUS

In the fourth year [of the reign], Paul, the holy and most saintly patriarch, having fallen ill, left his throne and was tonsured <note>original: "ἀπεκάρη" (apekarē); this refers to the ritual cutting of hair when entering a monastery.</note> in the Monastery of Floros. The Empress [Irene] came to him in grief and said, "Why have you done this?" He, with lamentations, replied, "I wish I had never sat upon the throne of the priesthood while the Church of God was being tyrannized and split off from the other universal <term>catholic</term> thrones <note>The "catholic" or universal thrones refer to the Pentarchy: the major Christian centers of Rome, Alexandria, Antioch, and Jerusalem.</note> and placed under anathema. If an ecumenical council is not held and the errors in our midst corrected, you have no hope of salvation." She said to him, "And why did you sign the document at your ordination promising not to venerate icons?" He replied, "It is for this very reason that I lament and 
<margin>C</margin> take refuge in repentance, begging God not to punish me as a priest for having remained silent until now and for failing to preach the truth for fear of your fury." Amidst these words, he fell asleep in peace. From that time on, the discourse concerning the holy icons began to be spoken of openly by everyone.

In the fifth year, Empress Irene, having gathered the entire Senate and the people, asked who should become patriarch. Everyone cried out for Tarasios, the imperial secretary <term>asekretis</term> <note>original: "ἀσηκρῆτις" (asēkrētis); a high-ranking official in the Byzantine imperial chancery.</note>. He, however, declined, citing the dissension among the people and the churches, and requested that a council be held. When the Empress and the people 
<margin>D</margin> consented to this, on the 25th of the month of December, in the 8th indiction <note>The indiction was a 15-year tax cycle used by the Romans and Byzantines for dating.</note>, our holy father Tarasios was ordained Patriarch of Constantinople. Having sent the synodal letters and his profession of faith to Rome, he was accepted by Pope Hadrian.

---

In the 4th year, Paul, the most holy patriarch, affected by illness, left his throne, shaved his head, and hid himself away in the Monastery of Florus. The saddened Empress met with him, asking the cause of his action. To her, Paul said: "I truly wish I had never sat upon the pontifical throne, since the Church of God is oppressed through tyranny and torn away from the other universal thrones and marked with anathema. Unless an ecumenical council is established and the errors up to now are corrected, there is no salvation for you." When Irene further asked why, when he was designated patriarch, he had signed a document saying he would not adore images, he said, "This is the very thing I mourn, and I flee to penance, praying to God that He might not punish me as a priest who kept silent until now and, through fear of your fury, abstained from the proclamation of the truth." After these things were done, he happily exchanged life for death. From then on, words concerning the sacred images were spoken freely by everyone.

In the 5th year, Irene, having called together the Senate and the people, asked for their opinion on creating a new patriarch. Tarasios the secretary, to whom that office was offered by everyone, refused it, citing the disagreement of the peoples and the churches as his reason, and demanding that a council be assembled. When the Empress and the people had agreed to this, our holy father Tarasios was finally declared Patriarch of Constantinople on the 25th day of December, in the 8th indiction. After letters regarding the council and a confession of his faith were sent to Rome, he was approved by Pope Hadrian.

### COMPENDIUM OF HISTORIES

In the 6th year [of the reign], a council was proclaimed in the Church of the Holy Apostles. However, the servants of the devil <note>The author is referring to the iconoclast soldiers and officials who opposed the restoration of holy images.</note> also gathered there; they entered with swords drawn, causing the assembly to be thrown into turmoil, and the participants retreated.

In the 7th year, the universal <term>catholic</term> church was opened in Nicaea. On the 9th day of <margin>5</margin> September, on the first day of the week <note>Sunday</note>, at the fifth hour, a very great eclipse of the sun occurred.

In the 8th year—122 years having passed since the 6th Council—the 7th Ecumenical Council took place in Nicaea. Through the efforts of the most holy Patriarch Tarasios, the universal <term>catholic</term> <margin>P 471</margin> Church regained its ancient beauty <note>original: "κόσμον" (kosmon); this refers to the "adornment" or "glory" of the church, specifically the holy icons that had been removed or destroyed.</note>. Three hundred and fifty fathers <margin>10</margin> gathered in Nicaea for the second time; they decreed that icons, alongside the form of the cross, should be venerated. They did not dogmatize anything new, but rather commanded that the doctrines of the holy and blessed fathers be kept unshaken. Having renounced the new heresy <note>Iconoclasm.</note>, they excommunicated the three falsely-named patriarchs: I mean Anastasios, Constantine, and Niketas <margin>15</margin> the eunuch <note>These were the patriarchs who had supported the Iconoclast emperors.</note>. Both the Emperor and his mother signed the decree <note>original: "τόμῳ" (tomō); the official volume of the council's acts.</note>, and the Church of God was at peace, even if the enemy <note>Satan</note> does not cease to sow his own weeds <margin>B</margin> through his own workers. Yet the Church of God, by His grace, always triumphs even when under attack.

In the 9th year, Empress Irene broke the agreement <margin>20</margin> with the Franks <note>This refers to the dissolution of the betrothal between Constantine VI and Rotrude, the daughter of Charlemagne.</note>. She brought a young woman from the Armenian region of Amnia, named Marina <note>Historically known as Maria of Amnia; the Greek text here uses "Marina."</note>, and joined her in marriage to her son Constantine against his will, and celebrated the wedding.

In the 10th year, a most terrifying earthquake occurred. Meanwhile, certain individuals <margin>25</margin> among Irene’s close circle, driven by envy and wishing to [seize] the administration of affairs...

She, with a steady and prudent mind, spoke to the man who was yesterday a perjured servant but today a tyrant: "I, O man, acknowledge that it was God who raised me to this imperial throne. I attribute my downfall to my own sins; in all these things, let the name of the Lord be blessed. You are certainly not unaware of the plots against you that were reported to me in the past. Had I yielded to those reports, I could have put you to death without any hindrance. But partly because I trusted your oaths and partly because I wished to spare you, I disregarded everything, leaving you to the judgment of God, through whom kings reign and rulers exercise power. And now, I bow before you as a pious emperor chosen by God, and I ask you to have pity on my weakness and permit me to live in the House of Eleutherios <note>A palace and monastery complex in Constantinople built by Irene herself; its ruins are near the modern Yenikapı district.</note>, which I built, to find some solace for my incomparable misfortune."

He replied, "If you wish this to be done for you, swear to me..."

*Nicephorus the patrician and general logothete ruled 8 years and 9 days. On the day after he received the empire, accompanied by certain patricians, he went to Irene, who was being kept by guards. "...not to hide any of the treasures, and I will take every care of you." <margin>C</margin>
She swore an oath to him and pointed out great wealth. But once he had obtained what he desired, he immediately exiled her to the island of Prinkipo <note>The largest of the Princes' Islands near Constantinople; a common site for the exile of royalty.</note>, to a monastery which she herself had built. Seeing that all the officials were grieved for her sake because of his greed, and fearing that the people—remembering her kind deeds—might attempt to proclaim her Empress again, he showed no mercy. Even though a very harsh winter was setting in, he exiled her to Mitylene <note>The capital of the island of Lesbos.</note>, ordering her to be kept under guard. On the 9th of August, she died on that same island of Lesbos from grief and despair. The Emperor later transferred her body to the monastery in Prinkipo which she had built; <margin>D</margin> for being exceedingly pious and virtuous, she had established many <term>xenodocheia</term> <note>Hostels or hospitals for travelers and the poor.</note>, <term>gerocomia</term> <note>Almshouses or homes for the elderly.</note>, and <term>monasteria</term> <note>Monasteries.</note>, and had achieved tax reductions and many other good works.

As for Constantine her son <note>This is Constantine VI, whom Irene had previously deposed and blinded. Nicephorus kept him close to search for more money.</note>, Nicephorus took him to live at his own table, led more by avarice than by mercy, thinking he might reveal hidden wealth. Being treated kindly by him, and due to his lightness of mind, Constantine showed him the treasure hidden in the Semicircle—which is now called the Sigma <note>The "Sigma" was a famous semi-circular portico in the Great Palace of Constantinople, named for its shape resembling the Greek letter sigma (C).</note>—which was built behind <term>orthomarmarosis</term> <note>From the Greek 'orthos' (straight) and 'marmaros' (marble); a decorative technique where marble slabs are set vertically against a wall.</note>. Having seized this as well, the Emperor neglected Constantine just as he had his mother. <margin>P 476</margin> He also rewarded Nicetas Triphyllius in a manner worthy of his own character: though Nicetas had fought alongside him to seize the throne, Nicephorus killed him with poison—a fine return for his services indeed.

### GEORGIUS CEDRENUS ###

Bardanes <note>original Greek: Βαρδάνιος; also known as Bardanes Turkos.</note>, who was the military commander of the East, deliberated within himself about seizing the imperial power. While he was staying in Philomelion <note>A city in Phrygia, modern-day Akşehir, Turkey.</note>, he shared his plan with a certain monk who was renowned for his gift of prophecy. Accompanying him as a confidant was Leo the Armenian <note>The future Emperor Leo V.</note>. <margin>5</margin> When Bardanes heard from this monk that he would suffer the loss of all his property and the blinding of his eyes if he dared to undertake this rebellion, he turned away in great sorrow. 

As his attendants were bringing his horses to him, the monk gazed intently at them and called Bardanes back. <margin>B</margin> Bardanes, hoping that the monk was about to say something that suited his desires, instead heard: "Let there be no thought in you concerning the throne. For whether you wish it or not, do not dare this. If you try, you will suffer the loss of your eyes and your property, as I said. However, regarding those men who brought your horses: the first and the second among them shall wear the imperial diadem, and the third, though proclaimed emperor, shall quickly perish, failing to achieve what he sought." 

Bardanes then revealed the meaning of this prophecy to Leo, Michael <note>The future Emperor Michael II.</note>, and Thomas <note>Thomas the Slav, a general who later led a massive but unsuccessful civil war.</note>, saying: "You, <margin>C</margin> Leo, shall reign as emperor; and Thomas, though proclaimed, shall be killed by Michael (for so the monk told me); and only Michael shall be preserved in the kingdom." 

Not much time passed before many of the <term>themata</term> <note>original: θεμάτων; the administrative and military districts of the Byzantine Empire.</note>—being forced into rebellion by the harsh tax demands imposed on them by Emperor Nicephorus—revolted and proclaimed Bardanes, surnamed "the Turk," as emperor. # COMPENDIUM OF HISTORIES #

### GEORGIUS CEDRENUS ###

Bardanes <note>original Greek: παρητεῖτο; he was declining or resisting</note> tried to refuse the honor, but being unable to escape, he was forced by his followers and came to Chrysopolis <note>A city on the Asian side of the Bosporus, opposite Constantinople; modern-day Üsküdar.</note>, where he was acclaimed as emperor. When these things had happened, Leo and Michael <note>The future emperors Leo V and Michael II, who had previously been Bardanes' closest associates.</note> deserted to the emperor Nicephorus. One was entrusted with the command of the <term>foederati</term> <note>original: φοιδεράτων; a military division originally composed of foreign mercenaries</note>, while the other was given the command of the <term>Count of the Court</term> <note>original: κόμητος κόρτης; the official responsible for the imperial tent and headquarters</note>. <margin>D</margin> Thomas <note>Thomas the Slav, who later led a famous rebellion of his own.</note>, however, remained devoted to his own master, keeping his faith even in the face of great dangers. 

Then Bardanes, who possessed the fear of God in his heart and was terrified that a civil war might break out on his account, secretly sent messengers to the emperor asking for a promise of safety <note>original: λόγους ἀπαθείας; literally "words of immunity" or "guarantees against harm."</note>. Having received this guarantee, he escaped by ship during the night and went to the Monastery of Heraclius at Catabolium <note>A coastal location in Bithynia.</note>, where he became a monk. The people who were with him then returned to their homes. 

The emperor, pretending that he was bringing Bardanes into the capital, sent a swift warship <note>original: δρόμωνα; a dromon, the primary vessel of the Byzantine navy</note>. When Bardanes arrived at the island of Prote <note>One of the Princes' Islands near Constantinople.</note>, at the monastery he himself had built on his own estate, he was blinded by certain men from Lycaonia, acting on the secret orders of the emperor. <margin>P 477</margin> Consequently, having feigned grief at such an act of hypocrisy, the emperor—who never once kept a sacred oath—assured everyone with many vows that he was innocent of such a tragedy.

In the second year of his reign, he crowned his son Stauracius as emperor, a man who was unremarkable in appearance, character, and physical strength. In that same year, Nicephorus went out on a campaign against the Arabs, but he returned after being shamefully defeated. He was very nearly captured himself, had it not been for some of the most courageous commanders who barely managed to rescue him.

# COMPENDIUM OF HISTORIES #

### GEORGIUS CEDRENUS ###

In the third year of his reign <note>804–805 AD</note>, having found a brief period of peace, the Emperor rebuilt Ancyra in Galatia <note>modern-day Ankara, Turkey</note>, as well as Thebes and Andrasos.

<margin>B</margin> In the fourth year <note>806 AD</note>, the most holy Tarasios, Patriarch of Constantinople, died in glory; he was buried in the monastery he himself had built in the Straits <note>The Bosporus</note>. <margin>5</margin> On the fourth day of the first week of Lent, and on the Great Sunday <note>Easter Sunday</note>, the most holy Nicephorus was ordained as Patriarch. He had previously been an <term>asekretis</term> <note>original: ἀσηκρῆτις; a high-ranking imperial secretary</note>, and was chosen by the vote of all the people, the Emperor, and the clergy. However, Plato and Theodore, the leaders of the Stoudios Monastery <note>The "Studites," a powerful and rigorist monastic community in Constantinople</note>, did not consent to the ordination of Nicephorus. <margin>10</margin> They even caused a schism, using the seemingly reasonable argument that a man should not be promoted suddenly from the rank of a layman to that of a bishop. The Emperor wished to expel them from the city, but he was dissuaded by certain people. <margin>C</margin> Indeed, this practice was neither strange nor newly devised, for many others had been made bishops from the ranks of laymen and had served the priesthood in a manner worthy of God. 

In this same year, Aaron <note>Harun al-Rashid, the Abbasid Caliph</note>, the leader of the Arabs, campaigned <margin>15</margin> against the Roman Empire <note>Byzantium</note> with three hundred thousand men. When he reached Tyana, he built a "house of his blasphemy" <note>original Greek: οἶκον τῆς βλασφημίας αὐτοῦ; a common Byzantine polemical term for a mosque</note> and captured countless fortresses. He sent out a raiding party of sixty thousand men as far as Ancyra, and having destroyed everything in their path, they returned. <margin>20</margin> The Emperor Nicephorus also went out, displaying great courage in the face of despair. After some deliberation, he sent a message to the Caliph seeking peace, declaring the following:

When Aaron learned of this, he sent [an army] again and took Thebes; he also sent a fleet to Cyprus, where he destroyed the churches and deported the Cypriots. ...to act [in this way]? Does not your prophet Muhammad command you to have and recognize every Christian as a brother? By this letter, to which certain gifts were added, the Arab was appeased and sent many wonderful gifts in return to Nicephorus, admiring his sharp wit, and he departed after peace was made. The pact was that the Romans should pay thirty thousand <term>nomismata</term> to the Arabs annually, and three <term>nomismata</term> for the Emperor himself and his son as a head tax, and that the Romans should not repair the forts captured by the Arabs. However, as soon as the Arabs had moved away, Nicephorus immediately restored and fortified them. When Aaron discovered this, he sent his army again and captured Thebes; and having sent a fleet to Cyprus, he overthrew the temples and drove out the Cypriots, and having gained great booty, he tore the peace asunder.

# BY GEORGE CEDRENUS #

In the 6th year <note>roughly 808 AD</note>, the Arabs occupied Rhodes with a fleet, and though they took many captives, they were unable to capture the fortress. On their return, when they arrived at Myra <note>the city in modern-day Turkey where Saint Nicholas served as Bishop</note>, they attempted to shatter the sacred tomb of Saint Nicholas, but instead of his, <margin>C 5</margin> they shattered another lying nearby. Immediately, a great storm of winds and a surge of sea-waves, along with a turbulent display of thunder and lightning, seized the fleet, so that many ships were wrecked. The people themselves recognized the power of the Saint, and against all hope, they escaped their destruction.

<margin>10</margin> In the 7th year <note>809 AD</note>, Theodore, the leader of the Stoudios Monastery <note>Theodore the Studite, a famous monk and defender of icons</note>, and his brother Joseph, the Archbishop of Thessaloniki, along with Plato the recluse and the rest of the monks, broke away from communion with the most holy Patriarch Nicephorus. They did this because of Joseph the steward, on the grounds that he had unlawfully crowned Constantine and Theodote <note>This refers to the "Moechian Controversy," a scandal where Emperor Constantine VI divorced his wife to marry his mistress, Theodote; the "steward" Joseph performed the marriage</note>. The <margin>15</margin> Emperor, seizing this opportunity, gathered many bishops and abbots <margin>D</margin> and ordered a synod to be held against Theodore. Through this council, they were cast out from the monastery and the city and were sent into exile. In the same year, while the payroll was being distributed to the people in Strymon <note>a region and river in modern-day Greece/Bulgaria</note>, the Bulgarians fell upon them and seized it—one thousand one hundred pounds of gold—<margin>20</margin> and they slaughtered the general along with the people. Taking the baggage train <term>touldon</term> <note>original: τοῦλδον; the military's non-combatant support staff and supply train</note>, they retreated. At that same time, Krum, the leader of the Bulgarians, captured Sardica <note>modern-day Sofia, Bulgaria</note> and slaughtered six thousand soldiers. Emperor Nicephorus, supposedly setting out against him, <note>The Latin text adds: "did nothing great or memorable."</note>

### COMPENDIUM OF HISTORIES ###

He performed nothing noteworthy, but when the commanders who had survived the retreat <note>likely referring to a military defeat against the Bulgars or Arabs</note> asked for a guarantee of safety, he refused to grant it, forcing them to flee to the enemy. <margin>P 479</margin> Among these was Euthymius, a **spatharios** <note>original: σπαθάριος; a high-ranking court official and bodyguard</note> and a military engineer. <margin>5</margin> When a rebellion broke out against him, he secretly won over the majority with bribes, but later harmed them by subjecting them to the confiscation of their property and to exile. 

Planning to humble the military forces, what evil did he not devise against the Christians? He ordered Christians from every **theme** <note>original: θέματος; an administrative military district</note> to be relocated to the Slavic lands, and their estates <margin>10</margin> <note>original: στάσεις / hypostaseis; refers here to landed property and holdings</note> to be sold; this matter was no less a tragedy than being taken captive. While everyone was in a state of helplessness, he ordered a second hardship along with this: that the poor should be enrolled in the army and equipped by their neighbors, who were to provide 18 **nomismata** <note>original: νομίσματα; the standard Byzantine gold coins</note> each, and they were held <margin>B</margin> mutually responsible to the treasury for their public taxes <note>This policy of "mutual guarantee" for tax payments was known as the *Allelengyon*</note>. <margin>15</margin> A third malice: that everyone should be audited and their public taxes increased, with them also paying two **keratia** <note>original: κεράτια; small coins, 1/12th of a nomisma</note> for the "paper fee" <note>original: χαρτιατικοῦ / chartiatikon; a fee paid to the tax officials for the paperwork</note>. A fourth plague: he ordered all tax remissions to be cancelled. A fifth calamity: he demanded the **smoke tax** <note>original: καπνικὰ / kapnikon; a tax on every household hearth</note> <margin>20</margin> from the residents of pious houses—including orphanages, hospices, homes for the aged, churches, monasteries, and imperial estates—retroactive to the first year of his tyranny. He also ordered the best of their properties to be seized for the imperial stewardship, while the taxes for those lands were still <margin>C</margin> imposed on those remaining in those same pious houses. Thus, the taxes for many were doubled, while their dwellings were restricted and their villages and...

<meta>This page continues the catalog of "ten vexations" or fiscal burdens imposed by Emperor Nicephorus I (r. 802–811 AD), following his military and administrative reforms. The text lists the final five of these oppressive policies.</meta>

-> ### GEORGIUS CEDRENUS ### <-

...to live abroad. The **sixth tyranny** was his command that the generals keep watch over those who had suddenly risen from poverty to wealth and demand money from them, treating them as if they had discovered hidden treasures. The **seventh affliction** targeted those who, in the last twenty years, had found a jar or any other vessel; they too were forced to pay in cash. The **eighth injustice** was that those who had inherited property from their grandfathers or great-grandfathers—even if it had been divided twenty years prior—were forced to pay back a portion to the public treasury. He also ordered that those who purchased household slaves outside of Abydos <note>a strategic customs station on the Hellespont used to control trade to Constantinople</note> pay two **nomismata** <note>original: νομίσματα; the standard gold coin of the Byzantine Empire</note> each, specifically targeting those living in the Dodecanese <note>literally "the Twelve Islands," an administrative region in the Aegean</note>. 

<margin>D</margin> The **ninth madness** forced the shipowners living along the coasts, especially in Asia Minor, to buy lands he had seized from others against their will. These men had never lived as farmers, yet they were forced to pay the appraised value of these properties. The **tenth godlessness** occurred when he gathered the prominent shipowners in Constantinople and forced them to accept loans of twelve pounds of gold each. They were required to pay an interest rate of four **keratia** <note>original: κεράτια; a unit of currency worth 1/24th of a gold nomisma, making this roughly a 16.6% interest rate</note> per gold coin, while still being forced to pay the usual customs duties <note>original: κομμέρκια / commercia; taxes on trade and transport</note>. 

These are but a few of the many evils I have recorded in summary, demonstrating the many-faceted cunning of his greed in every form. We have omitted the terrible things he inflicted upon the high, middle, and lower classes in the capital <note>Constantinople</note>, as they are too numerous to write. He went so far as to incite wicked servants to bring false accusations against their own masters—specifically those who were wealthy—granting honors to the informers while stripping the accused of their money.

When it was brought, that darkened man <note>meaning the Emperor, portrayed as spiritually blinded by greed</note> <margin>B</margin> said: “Why do you have need of such distractions? Dine with me, and taking one hundred **nomismata** <note>original: νομίσματα; the standard gold coin of the Byzantine Empire</note>, go your way and be content with them.”

In the ninth year of his reign, he intensified his schemes against the Christians, including godless inspections <note>original: ἐποψίας ἀθέους; likely referring to intrusive tax audits of church or private property</note>, the forced purchase of all kinds of irrational beasts and crops, and the <margin>10</margin> unjust confiscations and fines of high-ranking officials. He—who had legislated for everyone else that they must not charge interest—personally practiced **usury on maritime loans**, and devised a myriad of other evils. To describe these in detail would be burdensome for those who seek to learn of events in a summarized history.

Furthermore, he was a fervent friend to the **Manichaeans** <term>followers of a dualistic religion that viewed the world as a struggle between light and dark</term>—those now called **Paulicians** and **Athinganoi** <term>a sect centered in Asia Minor known for ritual seclusion and sometimes associated with magic</term>—who lived in <margin>15</margin> Phrygia and Lycaonia. They were neighbors to him, for he had been born in that region. <margin>C</margin> He delighted in their oracles and secret rites. Under his reign, these groups found the freedom to live without fear, and many of the more frivolous people were corrupted by their lawless doctrines.

In the “outer column” district <note>original: τῷ ἔξω κιονίῳ; a reference to a specific area in Constantinople, possibly near a monumental pillar</note> there was a man named **Nicolaus**, a false hermit. <margin>20</margin> He and his companions blasphemed against the right word of faith and the **venerable icons**. By supporting these men, the Emperor caused great grief to the High Priest <note>the Patriarch of Constantinople</note> and to all those living according to God’s will. For often...

# GEORGE KEDRENOS

...the Patriarch would often rebuke him, but Nicephorus took great pleasure in those who were at odds with one another. He criticized those who, through the ages, had dedicated gold or silver vessels to God, and he decreed that sacred church objects should be put to common use <note>meaning he believed church wealth should be secularized for state or military spending</note>. He blamed all the emperors before him for being incompetent at governing, entirely rejecting the idea of divine providence and claiming that no one can be more powerful than the ruler, provided that the ruler governs with shrewdness <note>original: ἐντρεχῶς (entrechos); meaning with expert skill or agility</note>. <margin>10</margin>

<margin>P 481</margin> Thus, this foolish and God-hated man became vain in his reasonings. He prepared for battle against the Bulgarians along with his son Stauracius. Upon leaving the imperial city, he ordered Niketas—a nobleman and the **General Logothete** <term>the high-ranking official in charge of the empire's treasury and taxation</term>—to increase the public taxes on churches and monasteries, and <margin>20</margin> <margin>B</margin> to demand eight years of **back-taxes** <note>original: ὀπισθοτέλειαν (opisthoteleian); the retroactive collection of unpaid or newly levied taxes</note> from the households of the aristocracy. > “Who will go and entice Ahab? <note>A quote from 1 Kings 22:20, where King Ahab is lured into a battle where he is destined to die</note> For whether it be God or the Adversary <note>the Devil</note>, I am being dragged along against my will.”

After the first skirmishes, thinking himself successful, he proclaimed that the victory was due not to God but to the good fortune of his son Stauracius. He threatened the officials who tried to block his further entry into the country. <margin>D</margin> <margin>20</margin> He ordered that people of every age, even down to infants, be mercilessly slaughtered. He left the dead bodies of his fellow men <note>original: ὁμοφύλων (homophylon); implying either fellow humans or specifically the local inhabitants regardless of age</note> unburied, caring only for the collection of spoils. He placed locks and seals upon Krum’s treasuries, securing them as if they were already his own property. Furthermore, he cut off the ears and other limbs of Christians who had dared to touch the loot.

# THE COMPENDIUM OF HISTORIES BY GEORGE KEDRENOS

...stating that the time was ripe to fulfill his long-desired ambition. The Emperor stated that he had entrusted that care to Leo, the leader of the Easterners, a man most prudent and friendly in spirit toward him. Exabulius said, "You seem to me, O Emperor, to be quite deceived in your judgment of that man's will." Indeed, Michael had not yet entered the palace when it was announced to him that Leo had been declared Emperor. Terrified by this rumor and deliberating on what should be done, some urged him to retain the empire with every effort and to oppose the usurper as much as he was able. 

But Michael, as he was of a peace-loving nature, was unwilling to cast himself into the danger of such a great matter. He sharply rebuked those by whom he was being incited to commit civil slaughter. He sent one of his intimates to Leo with the diadem, the purple, and the scarlet shoes (these are the insignia of the empire), indicating that he was yielding the empire to him, because he judged it better even to lose his life than to see one small drop of Christian blood shed. He commanded him to come without any fear or doubt and occupy the palace. 

But Procopia, the Emperor's wife, strove against this, saying that one should die in the empire. When she could not lead her husband from his purpose, she affirmed it was a thing more unworthy than all unworthiness if the wife of the usurper should be dressed in the imperial <term>modiolus<gloss>crown</gloss></term>. Mocking her name, she called her Barca, and so meditated on what she should decide regarding her own affairs.

# GEORGIUS CEDRENUS

The usurper <note>original: τυραννος (tyrannos); used here to denote one who seized power by rebellion</note>, entering through the Golden Gate while being acclaimed by the army, the people, and the senate, came to the Church of the Forerunner in the Stoudios <note>The Monastery of St. John Stoudios, the most influential monastery in Constantinople</note>. From there, accompanied by his bodyguard, he occupied the palace. As he was about to offer a prayer of arrival to God in the Golden Triclinium <note>The *Chrysotriklinos*, the main ceremonial throne room of the Great Palace</note>, he took off the garment he happened to be wearing and gave it <margin>5</margin> <margin>C</margin> to Michael, the commander of the grooms <note>Michael II, later known as 'the Stammerer'</note>. When Michael immediately put the garment on himself, those who saw it considered the event an omen <note>original: οἰωνὸς (oionos)</note> that he himself would ascend to the throne after Leo. When the Emperor changed into a different garment and departed for the church within the palace, Michael followed behind him; walking carelessly <margin>10</margin> and headlong, he stepped on the edge of the imperial robe. Leo considered this an evil omen and suspected that a revolution <note>original: νεωτερισμὸν (neoterismon)</note> would arise from him.

Nevertheless, once the usurper had entered the palace and seized the sovereignty—which had been yielded to him without a struggle—he held it amidst no small amount of trouble and <margin>15</margin> turmoil. The [former] Emperor Michael and his wife <margin>D</margin> Procopia, together with their own children, took refuge as suppliants in the Church of the Mother of God, which is called the Pharos <note>The "Lighthouse" church, the primary repository for holy relics in the palace</note>. Dragging them from there, the usurper separated them from one another. He sent Michael into exile <margin>20</margin> at the monastery on the island of Prote <note>The nearest of the Princes' Islands to the city</note>, where, having set aside his worldly hair <note>a reference to the tonsure, marking his entry into monastic life</note>, he spent the remainder of his life. He castrated Theophylact, the eldest of Michael’s sons, and sent him into exile along with his mother and brothers <note>Castration was a common Byzantine practice for deposed rivals to ensure they could never claim the throne, as the Emperor was required to be physically "whole."</note>. <margin>23</margin>

Meanwhile, Leo the usurper, having entered through the Golden Gate while the army, people, and senate followed with auspicious acclamations, arrived at the Stoudian Church of John the Baptist, and from there, surrounded by his guards, he invaded the palace. When he wished to return a vow to God in the Golden Triclinium for his successful entry, he set aside the robe he was wearing and handed it to Michael, the prefect of the grooms, who immediately put it on. Those who saw this judged it an omen that Michael would hold power after Leo. And as Leo, dressed in another robe, proceeded to the Palace temple, the same Michael followed from behind; while walking incautiously and rashly, he stepped on the hem of the imperial robe. Leo took this as a sinister omen, foreboding that this man would one day stir up a revolution.

After Leo entered the palace and occupied the empire—which was offered to him peacefully but taken with great business and tumult—Michael Rangabe with his wife Procopia and children betook themselves to the temple of the Mother of God, which is called Pharos, for the sake of supplication. Having torn them from there, Leo separated them, and indeed deported Michael to the monastery of the island of Prote, where, with his hair shorn and bidding farewell to this secular age, he lived out the rest of his life; however, he sent his eldest son Theophylact, now castrated, into exile with his mother and brothers.

<margin>D</margin> ...the aforementioned war was rekindled, and not least because of the reason about to be told. Certain Bulgarians, having left their ancestral lands, came with their whole families into Roman territory. They were welcomed by Emperor Michael <note>Michael I Rangabe, reigned 811–813</note> and settled in various regions. Furthermore, some Romans who had been taken captive in previous wars broke their chains and returned to their own homelands. The leader of the Bulgarians, Krum <note>original: Κροῦμος (Kroumos); the powerful Khan of the Bulgars who was a constant threat to Constantinople</note>, demanded that all these people be handed back to him. To some Romans, this extradition seemed like a good idea; the Emperor himself and certain notable monks agreed to it. They believed that by surrendering the refugees, they would be spared from barbarian raids. <margin>P 487</margin> However, others were displeased by this opinion. The leaders of this opposition were the Patriarch Nicephorus and the *magister* <term>magister</term> <note>original: μάγιστρος (magistros); one of the highest administrative offices in the Byzantine court</note> Theoctistus, who was then pre-eminent in virtue and wisdom, along with many others. They argued that they should commit their safety to God rather than abandon His all-powerful help to appease the barbarian’s arrogance by surrendering refugees. Because Krum’s demand was not met, the war flared up again. This resulted in a retreat and a great slaughter of the Romans, as God was seemingly ordaining a different outcome.

Meanwhile, Leo <note>Leo V, known as 'the Armenian'</note>, having invested himself with the imperial power, promoted Thomas. This Thomas was one of the three men previously mentioned in the story as being with Bardanes <note>Bardanes Turcus, a rebel general who had sought a prophecy about which of his associates would become emperor</note> <margin>B</margin> when he visited the monk in Philomelium <note>A city in Asia Minor where a famous hermit lived</note>. He noticed that the Bulgarians were pursuing the fugitives in a disorganized manner, abandoning all military formation. 

<margin>15</margin> After exhorting those around him to be brave men and pleading with them not to let the glory of the Romans crumble into nothingness, he launched a sudden and violent attack upon the enemy. By the unexpected nature of this assault, he routed those he encountered, and the rest of the Bulgarian army was struck with sudden <margin>20</margin> panic and filled with confusion and fear, so that no one thought of further resistance. Many of them fell in this attack, including the leader of them all, although he was quickly placed upon a swift horse <margin>D</margin> by his own men and secured his safety by flight. Even more were taken prisoner...

...a man of sharp mind, Leo placed him in command of the division of the federated troops. Michael the Stammerer <note>Latin: Balbum (the Mute/Stammerer)</note>, who was also one of those three and whose son Leo had received from the sacred font <note>meaning he was the child's godfather</note>, he created a Patrician and made him Count of the School of the Excubitors. Meanwhile, the Bulgarians, still inflated by their recent victory over the Romans, made incursions into Thrace, devastating and depopulating everything they met with plundering. It seemed best, therefore, to the Emperor to send legates for the sake of arranging a peace with the Bulgarian leader. But as the latter was acting ferociously and proudly refused peace, Leo was compelled to decide the matter by war. Once a great battle had begun, and when the Roman armies were again being defeated and the Bulgarians were giving themselves over to pursuit, Leo stood with his company on an elevated place. Watching the fight, he noticed that the Bulgarians had broken their ranks and were pursuing in a scattered fashion. Then, having encouraged his men and implored them to show themselves brave and strenuous, and not to allow the glory of the Romans to be reduced to nothing, he attacked the enemy with great force. Driving back those in his way by this unforeseen impression, he terrified the entire army of the Bulgarians by this sudden turn of events, and excited such trepidation among them that all courage left their minds. Many Bulgarians fell in that battle, and even the leader himself; but he was quickly placed upon a free horse by his men and achieved safety by flight. Many more were captured than [killed]...

### GEORGE KEDRENOS

Taking him along, he comes to the monk. As the conversation began, the monk—having the Emperor stand very close to him—acted as if he had foreknowledge by divine inspiration of the imperial dignity. 
<margin>P 489</margin> "You do not act rightly, O Emperor," he said, "misleading us 
<margin>5</margin> with this commoner’s cloak, and veiling the Emperor hidden within it. But even if you act this way, the grace of the Holy Spirit has not allowed us to be further outwitted by you." When the Emperor heard this, and saw that he had not succeeded in hiding his imperial status under a humble <gloss>5 "humble" or "cheap"</gloss> appearance, he was struck with awe—as was natural for one unaware of the trickery <note>The Emperor did not know that Theodotus had tipped off the monk about the disguise, so he mistook the monk's performance for a genuine miracle</note>—and he recognized the monk as a divine man. He promised to carry out the monk's instructions obediently and swiftly, and he voted for the destruction of the venerable images <note>This refers to religious icons; Leo V became a leader of the Second Iconoclastic movement</note>. At first, he considered in 
<margin>B</margin> secret how their plan might be carried out, so that no riot might be stirred up within the Church. 
<margin>15</margin> Then he brought the decree out into the open, and of those in power and those of the Church, some willingly and others unwillingly submitted to the command. Even the great and celebrated among patriarchs, the renowned Nicephorus <note>Patriarch Nicephorus I of Constantinople, a staunch defender of icons</note>, was being forced to sign the decree <note>original: τόμῳ (tomō); a formal religious volume or document</note> for the destruction of the holy images. Since he would in no 
<margin>20</margin> way comply, the Emperor sent him into exile to Proconnesus <note>An island in the Sea of Marmara, used frequently as a place of exile</note>. Nicephorus had long before sensed Leo’s perverse character, and how he would stir up and throw the affairs of the Church into confusion. For it seemed to the blessed Nicephorus, at the moment he was placing the imperial crown on Leo’s head, that his hand was pierced by thorns and briars—and this was a sign...

Once the conversation had begun, the monk, standing very near the Emperor, acted as one who felt the presence of the imperial majesty by divine instinct. "It was not rightly done by you, Emperor," he said, "that you deceived us with the clothing of a private citizen, hiding your person within. But though you do this, the grace of the divine spirit has not permitted us to be fooled by you any longer." When the Emperor heard this, and realized he had tried in vain to hide his imperial dignity with a common garment, his soul was struck—as was natural for one ignorant of that machination. Confessing the monk to be a divine man, he promised he would do what was commanded obediently and without delay, and thus he approved with his own vote the destruction of the venerable images commanded by the monk. Then, at first, he considered how he might secretly fulfill his promises, lest that matter should stir up any sedition in the church. But afterward, he also proposed a public decree on the matter, with the leading men and the ecclesiastics obeying, partly of their own will and partly against the conviction of their minds. He also wished to compel the great and famous among patriarchs, Nicephorus, to subscribe to the edict; and when he would in no way obey, he relegated him to Proconnesus. Long before, he had sensed the perversity of Leo, and that the affairs of the church were going to be agitated and disturbed by him. For at the time he placed the crown on his head, it seemed...

### A COMPENDIUM OF HISTORIES

<margin>C</margin> ...and he took it as an omen of the evils that were to happen afterward. As the great man <note>Patriarch Nicephorus I, the head of the church in Constantinople who opposed the Emperor's iconoclasm</note> was being led away into exile, the confessor Theophanes—the superior of the Monastery of the Great Agros <note>Theophanes the Confessor was a famous monk and historian; "Agros" means "The Field"</note>—sensed his passing by divine inspiration. While staying in a certain field, he sent him off with incense and candles as the ship passed by. The Patriarch himself greeted him with the highest reverence, stretching out his hands and offering blessings. They did not see each other with physical eyes, but perceived one another with spiritual eyes, each paying the other the respect they deserved.

When one of those sailing with him asked the Patriarch, <margin>D</margin> "To whom, O Master, are you raising your hands and offering a greeting?" he replied, "To the most holy confessor Theophanes, the superior of Agros, who is welcoming us with torches and incense."

### GEORGE CEDRENUS

...[having obtained] the royal authority, no longer in the dark or in corners, but openly and with full confidence, he published the heresy of the **Iconoclasts** <note>original: "εἰκονομάχων" (eikonomachon). This was a movement in the Byzantine Empire that sought to ban and destroy religious images, or icons.</note>.

The Emperor Leo <note>Leo V, also known as the Armenian, reigned 813–820 AD</note>, puffed up by his previous victory over the <margin>5</margin> **Bulgarians** and having been fortunate against the **Arabs** a short time before, was unrestrained in his arrogance and began to lean toward harshness and cruelty. He became implacable in his anger and a most stern punisher of faults; he was unapproachable to those who wished to speak with him and a poor counselor. For small sins, <margin>10 B</margin> he would impose heavy sentences, cutting off the hands of some, the feet of others, or other vital limbs. These amputated parts he ordered to be hung along the main highway, perhaps to strike terror and fear into those who saw them. 

Because of this, he became hated by all his subjects. But his subsequent actions increased this hatred even further; <margin>15</margin> for he was not only enraged and driven wild against his fellow human beings, but he also raged against the pious faith itself and against God. He found a suitable instrument for this purpose: a certain man notorious for his villainy, who held the leadership of the group of singers in the palace. On the outside, <margin>20 C</margin> this man appeared holy and god-fearing, but within he hid a wolf under a thick fleece <note>A reference to the "wolf in sheep's clothing" from the Gospel of Matthew</note>. This profane man, finding a suitable opportunity when the prophecy of the most "loud-voiced" **Isaiah** was accustomed to be read aloud in the church, which says, "To whom [will you compare the Lord?]" <note>original: "τίνι..." referring to Isaiah 40:18. Iconoclasts used this verse to argue that God cannot be depicted in art.</note>

...[having] help for himself, no longer in shadows and corners but openly and with a full voice, he promulgated the heresy of the **image-destroyers** <note>original: "imaginiperdarum". A Latin translation of the Greek "iconoclast."</note>.

But the impulses of Leo’s mind were altogether unbridled, inflated by the recent victory over the Bulgarians and the matter successfully handled against the Arabs a little while before. And so he began to be harsher and to slide toward cruelty, to carry implacable rages, and to punish crimes most severely. He showed himself difficult to those wishing to meet or consult with him; for small crimes he imposed heavy punishments; he ordered the hands of some, the feet of others, and other more prominent members of the body to be amputated and these to be hung on the royal road, so that he might strike terror and fear into those seeing them. On account of these things, he was hated by every one of his subjects, and he increased the hatred against himself by the crimes that followed. For he was not only carried away and raged against men of the same nature and dignity as himself, but he also raved against piety itself and God. For these things he obtained a most fit instrument: a certain man of notable craftiness, set over the company of those who sang in the palace; who, showing sanctity and piety outwardly, carried a wolf hidden under thick wool. That impure man, having found a favorable time when the prophecy of the most "grand-speaking" Isaiah was practiced to be recited to the ears of the church: "To whom will you liken the Lord?"

### COMPENDIUM OF HISTORIES

> “To whom have you likened the Lord? And to what likeness have you compared Him? Has a craftsman not made an image, or a goldsmith, having melted gold, gilded it, or prepared it with a likeness?” <note>Original: Isaiah 40:18-19. This scriptural passage was frequently used by Iconoclasts to argue that God cannot be represented in art and that icons were therefore idols.</note>

And following the rest of the prophecy, the man <note>The advisor mentioned on the previous page, likely Theodotus Kassiteras.</note> stood beside the King and said: 
> “Understand what is being said, <margin>5</margin> O King, and do not let the truth escape you; hold fast to such worship as the prophet suggests to you.”

By saying such things, he instilled more of the poison of the heresy into the mind of the King. As a result, the form of worship which he had previously been driven to preach with restraint and hesitation, <margin>D</margin> he now began to enforce with an open face and without shame—or more accurately, <margin>10</margin> he compelled people to choose it through threats and dangers. Thus, those who were weak-willed and betrayed the truth lived in safety; however, those who did not obey his most impious decree were handed over to incurable tortures and calamities.

Yet, despite being so full of impiety and lawlessness, <margin>15</margin> he was most vigilant in his management of public affairs, so that he left nothing of necessity or benefit neglected. They say, at least, that after his death, Patriarch Nicephorus <note>Nicephorus I, the Patriarch of Constantinople who was deposed by Leo for opposing Iconoclasm.</note> remarked that the Roman state <note>original: "πολιτεία Ῥωμαίων" (politeia Rhomaion). In addition to managing <margin>20 P 491</margin> public business with care and wakefulness, he was also extremely burdensome to those who committed injustices. For instance, as the King was once leaving the palace, a man approached him complaining that his wife had been abducted by one of the senators. “I,” the man said, “complained of this to both you and the Prefect of the city, but no—”

<header>THE HISTORIES OF GEORGE KEDRENOS</header>

“...one retribution followed.” The King, having listened to the man’s words, immediately ordered that the accused senator should be brought before him face-to-face upon his return. And as the King was returning, there stood before him both the victim seeking justice and the one who had committed the abominable deed, as well as <margin>B</margin> the Eparch <note>The Eparch of the City was the highest administrative official in Constantinople, acting as a sort of mayor and chief justice.</note> himself. At the King’s command for the petitioner to describe what he had suffered, the man recounted everything from beginning to end. The one guilty of the charge, since he was unable to escape the evidence—being caught on all sides by the proofs—confessed to the unholy deed. When the King asked the Eparch why he had not inflicted a fitting punishment for such an atrocity, the official became speechless and unable to offer a defense. Consequently, the King removed him from his office and handed the adulterer over to the penalties of the law.

He conducted most of his business while sitting in the Lausiakos <term>triclinium</term> <note>The Lausiakos was a famous reception hall in the Great Palace of Constantinople; a "triclinium" refers to a formal dining or audience hall.</note>. He appointed generals, soldiers, and officials from among the most distinguished and incorruptible men, being himself a most rigorous despiser of bribes. He was also quite ambitious regarding his own voice, <margin>C</margin> wishing to be rhythmic and musical, even though his nature was not in harmony with this; for he was unmusical and ill-suited to melodic harmony. <margin>C</margin> At that time, a custom prevailed—quite different from the one held now—which began from that very period: that the clergy who sang in the palace church did not reside within the palace itself. Instead, they lived in their own homes, and around the **third watch of the night** <note>Roughly between 2:00 AM and 6:00 AM; the traditional time for the early morning service of Matins.</note> they would gather at the **Elephantine Gate** <term>Elephantine Gate</term> <note>Also known as the Ivory Gate, a specific entrance within the Great Palace complex of Constantinople.</note>. From there, they would proceed to the church to offer their morning prayers to God. The conspirators, mingling with these clergymen, <margin>5</margin> entered with them, carrying daggers hidden under their armpits. They lay in wait in a dark corner of the church, watching for the signal. As the hymn was being completed, the Emperor arrived; he took the lead in the chanting, as was his habit, singing: "Out of love for the King of all, they held cheap..." <note>original: *tō pantanaktos exephaulisan pothō*. A line from the Ninth Ode of the Christmas Canon, referring to the Three Holy Children in the furnace.</note> (for as we mentioned, <margin>10</margin> he had a particularly clear and piercing voice). Just then, the conspirators rushed in <margin>D</margin> all at once. In their first assault, they missed their target, having been led astray toward the **leader of the clergy** <term>Archon of the Clergy</term>, either because he resembled the Emperor in his physical build or because of the similar garment he wore on his head. For the hour was <margin>15</margin> bitter and wintry, and for this reason, everyone was bundled in heavy cloaks, covering their heads with very sharp, pointed caps <term>Pilos</term> <note>A felt cap used in antiquity and the middle ages.</note>. However, the leader of the clergy warded off the danger by snatching the cap from his head and securing his safety by revealing his **baldness** <note>This visual proof confirmed he was not the bearded Emperor Leo.</note>. The Emperor, sensing the plot, <margin>20</margin> retreated into the innermost part of the sanctuary. Grabbing the chain of the **censer** <term>Thurible</term>—or as some say, a **holy cross**—he braced himself against the blows of his attackers. <margin>P 495</margin> But the conspirators, rushing him in a mass rather than one by one, struck him: one on the head, another in the guts.

The Emperor prepared his rule. The custom then was not that which is held now, received from that time, that the clergy who sing in the Palatine temple should live in the palace: but each living in his own home, they gathered at the elephantine or ivory gate around the third watch of the night, and from there, progressing into the temple, they offered morning vows to God. The conspirators then, mixing themselves with these, with daggers hidden under their arms, entered together, and hidden in a dark place of the temple, they waited for the signal. The hymn being finished, the emperor also came, and according to his custom, intoned the song with a louder voice: "they despised all things for the love of the supreme prince." Then the conspirators gave the attack in a body, which at the beginning carried them by error against the master of the clergy, either because he was similar in body to the emperor, or because he had covered his head with a similar garment: for at that time there was a great frost, and therefore everyone did not uncover his head, which was covered by a thick cap. But he indeed, having pulled the cap from his head and shown his baldness, withdrew himself from the danger. The emperor, sensing the snares, withdrew into the inner part of the altar, and having snatched the chain of the thurible, or as others hold, the divine cross, received the blows of the strikers. But they, not one by one but rushing in a formed wedge, one at the head, another at the belly, another at another part of the body...

He had reigned for seven years and five months. He was as cruel as any man who ever lived, <margin>15</margin> and the most impious of all his predecessors; these vices obscured both the diligence he showed in public affairs and his personal bravery in battle. It is said that a voice from heaven also broke forth immediately, announcing the "good news" of his downfall to many. <margin>C</margin> Some sailors who heard it noted the exact time and the night; <margin>20</margin> later, by comparing the facts, they found the sign to have been true.

Once *Leo* had been killed, the assassins—now entirely free of fear because the royal palace was secured on all sides by their own armed men—dragged his corpse mercilessly through the *Skyla* <term>Skyla</term> <note>A specific gate or passage within the Great Palace complex, named after a nearby bronze group of Scylla.</note> and out into the **Hippodrome**. ...to her children: Sabbatios, who was renamed Constantine at his proclamation as co-emperor, as well as Basil, Gregory, and Theodosius. <margin>D</margin> Having placed them in a small boat, they took them away to the island of **Prote** <note>The first of the Princes' Islands near Constantinople, frequently used as a place of exile for deposed royalty.</note>. There, after all of them had been castrated <note>A common Byzantine practice to ensure deposed heirs could never claim the throne, as an emperor was expected to be physically "whole."</note>, it happened that Theodosius ended his life and was buried in the same grave as his father. <margin>5</margin>

But Michael, released from the custody of the **Papias** <term>Papias</term> <note>The high-ranking official in charge of the security and keys of the Great Palace.</note>, still had his feet held fast in iron shackles. This was because the key to the irons was kept hidden in the pocket of Leo’s own robe. Thus, just as he was, with the irons still on his legs, he sat upon the imperial throne; he was proclaimed and shown the traditional act of **proskynesis** <note>original: *prosekunēthē*. A ritual of bowing or prostration before the emperor.</note> by everyone then present in the palace. <margin>10</margin> By midday, as the news had spread everywhere, his bonds were violently smashed apart with a hammer. Without even washing his hands, without taking the fear of God into his mind, and without performing any of the other proper duties, he proceeded to the great temple of **Holy Wisdom** <note>The Hagia Sophia.</note>. He was determined to be crowned by the hand of the Patriarch and <margin>15</margin> was eager to receive the formal public proclamation, trusting only in those <margin>P 496</margin> fellow-conspirators who had carried out the murder. Here, one might marvel at the wicked character of both men: first, the one who had perished [Leo], in that he had not a single person to help him among his many and great flatterers, who had all slunk away into holes like reptiles; <margin>20</margin> and second, the shamelessness and impudence of the man who followed him [Michael]. He entered the church not as a murderer or an executioner with blood-stained hands, but like a prize-athlete or a victor, exulting in what had occurred...
