...The designated emperor had taken the name of Constantine, along with Basil, Gregory, and Theodosius; all of whom were placed in a skiff and carried away to the island of Prota. There all were castrated, and Theodosius, having departed this life, was buried together with his father.

But Michael, freed from the custody of the *papias*, sat upon the imperial throne even as he still had his feet enclosed in iron shackles (for their keys were kept in Leo’s pocket). He was greeted and adored as emperor by all who were then present in the palace. Toward noon, the news having already been spread in every direction, and the shackles having been split open by force with a hammer, he went forth to the great temple of Holy Wisdom. He had neither washed his hands, nor brought the fear of God into his soul, nor performed any other thing that was fitting to be done. He desired to be crowned by the hand of the patriarch and to be greeted as emperor by the whole people, trusting only in his partners in the conspiracy and the slayers of Leo. Here one might marvel at the perversity of both: of Leo, because he had no defender of his own from among so many and such great flatterers, who then had all hidden themselves in holes in the manner of creeping beasts; and the impudence of Michael, who entered the temple not as some murderer or executioner with hands polluted by blood, but as if a victor...

# COMPENDIUM OF HISTORIES

...having spilled the blood of his fellow countrymen, not in just any location, but at the divine altar, where the Lord’s ransom <note>A reference to the Eucharist or the blood of Christ, which the author argues was desecrated by the blood of the murdered Emperor Leo V.</note> is poured out daily for our sins.

<margin>5 B</margin> This Michael was born in the city of **Amorium**, located in Upper Phrygia. From ancient times, a great multitude of Jews, **Athinganoi** <term>Athinganoi</term> <note>original: Ἀθιγγάνων. A religious sect in Asia Minor often accused of mixing Jewish and Christian practices; the name literally means "untouchables."</note>, and other godless people had lived there. From their constant interaction and long-standing social mixing, a certain heresy emerged that possessed a new character and strange doctrines. Michael was himself a participant in this sect, fulfilling the religion handed down by his ancestors. <margin>10</margin> This sect allows those being initiated to participate in the divine and salvific washing <note>The rite of Baptism.</note>, but in all other respects, it maintains everything else by observing the **Mosaic Law** <note>The legal and religious framework of the Old Testament.</note>, with the exception of circumcision. Michael had a teacher and leader who had initiated him into these mysteries—a certain Hebrew man (or perhaps a Hebrew woman) within his own household—who instructed him not only in matters of the soul but <margin>C</margin> <margin>15</margin> also in the management of the house. Being influenced by this person, Michael preserved nothing pure in his faith; rather, he was a gathering-place of unbelief. He corrupted the traditions of the Christians, debased the religion of the Jews, and adulterated all other things. Having become such a person in his faith—diverse and many-formed—he was like those wild beasts said to exist in **Libya**, <margin>20</margin> which are forced together by the scarcity of water and interbreed with one another. When he was finally elevated to the imperial power, he took great pride and adorned himself with the crown and the imperial purple, but...

# GEORGIUS CEDRENUS

...learning, as if it would overturn his own views and be capable of teaching him <margin>D</margin> better things, he rejected and held in contempt. Instead, he honored his own particular skills exceedingly. These skills were: predicting which newborn pigs would be well-nourished and grow to a great size, and which would be the opposite; knowing how to stand near kicking horses and how to skillfully avoid kicking donkeys by staying as far away as possible. He was an excellent judge of mules, discerning which were suitable for carrying burdens and which could carry riders comfortably without throwing them <margin>5</margin> over their heads due to some sudden fright. Furthermore, he could judge horses by their appearance alone, determining which were vigorous and fast for racing and which maintained their endurance for war. He could also judge the fertility of sheep and cattle, and which ones were naturally endowed with <margin>10</margin> an abundance of milk. Among the newborn animals, he could distinguish which offspring belonged to which mother. These were his studies and his proudest boasts during his youth—and, one might say, even until his final days. 

As he reached his prime, while enduring a life of poverty, he strove to shake it off by every possible means. <margin>15</margin> Once, having presented himself to his **General** <note>original: στρατηγῷ (strategō). Upon hearing this, the general’s soul was set on fire with excitement, and seeing the future as if in a mirror—

# BY GEORGE CEDRENUS

Believing what was said, he went in and read with a loud and very clear voice the words: "Once again, my Jesus." <note>original: "πάλιν Ἰησοῦς ὁ ἐμός." He urged the Emperor to restore the veneration of holy icons and to bring about a return to <margin>B</margin> true piety. However, Michael replied that he did not come to power to meddle with the established decrees concerning the faith, nor would he work to attack or abolish any of the traditions already handed down and agreed upon. "Therefore," he said, "let each person do what seems best and desirable to them, remaining free from hardship and untouched by grief." However, he did not maintain this intention to the end, for he had not been a true Christian even from the beginning. Instead, as his hold on the empire grew stronger, his miserable nature and cruelty became more apparent...

### A COMPENDIUM OF HISTORIES

...[Michael] stirred up a most cruel war against the Christians and his own kin, at times spitting upon the monks and surrounding them with all kinds of terrors—inventing punishment upon punishment—and at other times locking the other faithful in prisons or driving them into exile. <margin>C</margin> Among these were **Methodius** <note>Later Patriarch Methodius I (843–847), who eventually ended the Iconoclast controversy.</note>—who shortly thereafter was deemed worthy of the patriarchal throne—and **Euthymius**, who at that time presided over **Sardis** <note>An ancient city in modern-day Turkey, once the capital of the Lydian Empire and one of the Seven Churches of Revelation.</note>. Because they would not yield to his will nor deny the honor due to the holy icons, <margin>5</margin> he drove them from the city. He handed the divine Methodius over to prison on the island of **Akritas** <note>A small island or coastal fortress near the Gulf of Nicomedia, used as a place of exile.</note>, but the blessed Euthymius he handed over to death at the hands of **Theophilus**, his own son, <margin>10</margin> being whipped unsparingly with scourges of ox-sinew.

However much he oppressed the inheritance of Christ, to that same degree he made the **Jews** exempt from taxes and free, loving and cherishing them beyond all other men. <margin>D</margin> He set before himself the life of **Copronymus** <note>original: "Κοπρωνύμου." This was the derogatory nickname for Emperor Constantine V, meaning "the dung-named," because he allegedly defiled the baptismal font as an infant. He was a notorious and fierce Iconoclast.</note> as a sort of goad and <margin>15</margin> archetype of his own life for imitation, and he strove to mimic him to the extreme. Therefore, he reached the very summit of impiety: at one moment legislating that one must fast on the **Sabbath** <note>In the Eastern Church, fasting on Saturdays was generally forbidden, except for Holy Saturday.</note>, at another sharpening his tongue against the holy prophets, and at another rejecting the future resurrection and <margin>20</margin> mocking the good things promised there. He even insisted that the **Devil** does not exist at all, since he was not mentioned by Moses. He embraced debauchery and legislated that one must swear by the God over all, while placing **Judas** [Iscariot] among those who are saved with his unbridled tongue.

...he moved against the Christians and their kin with a wicked and most cruel spirit, now spitting upon the monks and afflicting them in various ways, and setting one punishment after another upon them, now casting other pious men into prison or driving them into exile. Among these, Methodius—who not long after was raised to the throne of the patriarch—and Euthymius, at that time the leader of Sardis, because they would not obey his will nor deny that honor was due to the holy images, he cast out from the city. And Methodius indeed he gave into custody on the island of Akritas, but the blessed Euthymius he killed by the hand of his son Theophilus with whips. However much trouble he gave to the heritage of Christ, by so much did he relieve the Jews with grants of immunity from tribute and liberty, they being beloved by him above all men. For an example to imitate and as a kind of stimulus, he proposed to himself the life of Copronymus, and having emulated it with the greatest zeal, he proceeded to the height of impiety. Thus, now he prescribed a fast on the Sabbath, now he sharpened his tongue against the divine prophets, now he denied the future resurrection and derided the good things promised to us from it, and now he denied that there was any devil, because Moses handed down nothing concerning him. The same man also made much of fornications, and brought a law concerning swearing by the God who is over all, and with an unbridled tongue numbered Judas among the blessed.

### A COMPENDIUM OF HISTORIES

<margin>1</margin>Having found success in his endeavors, Thomas grew from a small figure into a great one, becoming powerful from a state of weakness. Some he led through persuasion and friendship—those who were driven by a love of novelty <note>In a Byzantine context, "novelty" or "new things" often refers to political revolution or social upheaval.</note> and a desire for wealth—while others he brought under his command through necessity and force, namely those who loathed the evils of civil strife. <margin>5</margin> From this beginning, civil wars broke out; like cataracts of a river rushing down, they flooded the earth not with water, but with blood. <margin>D</margin> All of Asia <note>Specifically the Roman province of Asia Minor (modern-day Turkey).</note> suffered a slow and agonizing death as it was plundered and looted. Some cities joined Thomas out of fear, while <margin>10</margin> those that remained loyal to the reigning Emperor were pillaged and their people sold into slavery.

All of Asia became subject to the rebel, with the exception of the Opsician Theme <term>Theme: A military-administrative district of the Byzantine Empire.</term>—for its general, Katakylas, maintained his loyalty to the Emperor until the end—and also the Armeniac Theme, where the general <margin>15</margin> Olbianos likewise remained faithful to the Emperor. As a reward for their service, the Emperor granted these districts the public tax revenue that was usually paid into the imperial treasury, known as the "smoke tax" <term>Smoke tax (kapnikon): A hearth tax paid by households; one of the most basic and universal taxes in the Byzantine Empire.</term>.

When the Agarenes <note>original: "Ἀγαρηνοῖς" — A term used by Byzantine writers for the Arabs, whom they believed to be descendants of Hagar.</note> learned of this civil strife, they were overcome with joy and began to leap with excitement. Taking the order as a stroke of luck <note>original: ἕρμαιόν (hermaion); literally a "gift from Hermes," referring to an unexpected piece of good fortune.</note>, when the trumpet sounded the call to battle and the ranks met in hand-to-hand combat, they did not merely feign a retreat as they had been instructed. Having sat down before Adrianople, he surrounded the city with a palisade and a ditch and conducted the siege with great vigor.

<margin>B</margin> Thomas first drove out of the city everyone of an age useless for war and every animal that was of no service. *Because they had already been away from their wives and children for a long time and had contaminated their hands with the blood of their own race, and at the same time worn out by the delay of time (for already three years had passed), and feeling they had undertaken an effort without an end, serving the insanity and greed of one man, they took that command as a divinely offered advantage. Some also being lowered from the wall by ropes at night, others gave themselves to the emperor, others fled to Bizye to the natural son Anastasius. At length, when the besieged had consumed everything fit for food, and necessity had already driven them to unusual foods and even to the eating of putrefied hides, having spoken secretly with Michael and bargained for a pardon of their crimes, they delivered Thomas in shackles to the emperor. He, observing a custom that had long ago pleased emperors and had been received into habit, first of all ordered him to lie stretched out on the pavement and trampled his neck with his feet; then, having mutilated him in his feet and hands and placed him upon a donkey, he ordered him to be led around the camp as a spectacle, crying out nothing else than "Have mercy on me, you who are the true king." And when the king inquired whether he had also had certain conscious accomplices and partners of his sedition from the court, he would have undoubtedly denounced many, had not John Exabulius the patrician warned the emperor that it was not fitting, but rather entirely repugnant to reason, to have faith in enemies accusing friends. By this word, he cut off the pretexts for many punishments of the wretched citizens and friends of the emperor. Thomas, consumed by slow punishments, at last exhaled his soul in the middle of the month of October; a man who at the beginning indeed attempted great things and was spirited and a strenuous pursuer of his purpose, but in his progress became much worse than himself...

# THE COMPENDIUM OF HISTORIES BY GEORGE CEDRENUS

As soon as they learned of the misfortunes that had befallen Thomas, they did exactly as the people of Adrianople had done: they seized Anastasius <note>Thomas the Slav's adopted son and co-emperor</note> and, <margin>P 503</margin> having bound him hand and foot, they delivered him to the Emperor. Even after the usurpers <note>original: "tyrannoi" — referring to Thomas and Anastasius as illegal claimants to the throne</note> were overthrown, the coastal cities of Thrace—specifically Parium and Heraclea—continued to resist, still favoring the cause of the rebel. This was due to their hatred of Michael and because the Emperor refused to restore the holy icons <note>Michael II was an Iconoclast, part of a movement that opposed the religious use of images. This caused significant friction with the icon-venerating population.</note>. Parium was eventually taken after its walls were brought down by an earthquake, while Heraclea was conquered by an assault from the sea.

Thus the rebellion of Thomas reached its conclusion. The Emperor returned from the cities of Thrace in triumph, <margin>B</margin> but he did not seek severe vengeance against those who had joined Thomas’s revolt and were captured in the war. Instead, during the holding of the chariot races in the Hippodrome, he simply had them paraded around seated upon donkeys and then sent them into exile. However, a "spark" <note>original: "zopyron" — literally a glowing coal that can reignite a fire</note> of the rebellion remained in the fortresses of Kabala and Saniana. These were held by Choereas and Gazarenus, respectively, who used these strongholds as bases for robberies and raids. Yet even these men refused the imperial letters granting them immunity and the high titles offered to them—for the Emperor had even offered to make both of them a <term>magister</term> <note>magister officiorum: one of the highest-ranking administrative and honorary positions in the Byzantine court</note>...

The Emperor sent Damianus—who was the Count of the Imperial Stable and a <term>protospatharios</term> <note>A high-ranking Byzantine court title, literally meaning "first sword-bearer"</note>—with a large force and equipment to aid General Photinus. Freed from civil wars, Emperor Michael did not credit the victory to God, but to his own wisdom and strategy. Consequently, puffed up with pride, he was unrestrained in his leadership.

Therefore, the Emperor sent Damianus, the count of his stable and a *protospatharios*, with great forces and grand equipment to bring relief to Photinus. Photinus escaped with difficulty on a light galley to the Emperor and brought him news of the disaster. The Emperor, because Photinus was held in the highest honor by him, appointed him governor of Sicily instead of Crete. 

While the Saracens were still occupied by cares and disturbances, a certain monk, having descended from the mountains of the island, taught them that they erred if they believed they had settled safely in that place. At the same time, he showed them **Chandax**, an opportunistic place for every convenience. There they founded a city, as if it were a citadel for the whole island, and from there they made incursions into the whole island and even those nearby, having driven the inhabitants into slavery and captured all the cities of Crete, save one. At that time also, Cyril, the Bishop of Gortyna, obtained the crown of martyrdom through execution, because he had been unwilling to deny Christ. In this way, Crete fell into servitude.

Furthermore, Emperor Michael, being freed from civil wars, did not credit the victory to God but to his own prudence and skill. And so, swelling with pride, he was carried away by the unbridled impulses of his mind. Accordingly, his wife having died...

He was intent on fulfilling his own passion, caring nothing for the laws, but looking only to the example of the emperor [Michael II], who had himself dared such a thing <note>Michael II had controversially married a nun named Euphrosyne</note>. <margin>15</margin> At any rate, he seized the maiden from the convent <note>original: askētērion</note> and took her to himself against her will. Therefore, her brothers approached Michael, recounting the events of the drama. <margin>B</margin> The emperor commanded the general <note>The military governor, or strategos, of Sicily</note> that, if he found this to be the truth, he should cut off the nose <note>Slitting or amputating the nose was a standard Byzantine punishment intended to shame the criminal and disqualify them from holding office</note> of the daring Euphemius. Learning of this, Euphemius <margin>20</margin> took as fellow conspirators his subordinates and some of the vice-commanders <note>original: tourmarchai</note>; he drove away the general who had come for this purpose and fled to the ruler of Africa <note>The Aghlabid Emir in North Africa</note>, [promising to deliver] all of Sicily...

# COMPENDIUM OF HISTORIES #

...he was beheaded. And so he paid this penalty for his own madness.

<margin>P 513</margin> From that time on, the Agarenes <term>Agarenes: A medieval Byzantine term for Arabs or Saracens, based on their traditional descent from Hagar</term> became masters not only of Sicily, but also of Calabria and most parts of Italy, <margin>5</margin> overrunning and plundering everything. As for Michael, after holding the throne for nine years and eight months, he ended his life after being seized by the disease of dysentery. He was the cause of so many evils for the Roman state because of his impiety toward God and his wickedness in managing affairs, as has <margin>10</margin> already been mentioned in this account. During his reign, all of Dalmatia also revolted. There was also an ancient oracle being circulated about him, which went like this:

->A beginning of evils shall fall upon the land,<-
->When a dragon shall rule over Babylon,<-
->One of difficult speech <note>A reference to Michael II’s nickname, "the Stammerer"</note> and exceedingly fond of gold.<-

<margin>15</margin> <margin>B</margin> His body was buried in the great mausoleum of Justinian at the Church of the Holy Apostles, in a sarcophagus of green Thessalian stone <note>original: prasinō Thessalikē; likely "Verde Antico," a dark green marble-like stone prized by Byzantine emperors</note>.

After Michael’s death, his son Theophilus, who was already of a man's age, succeeded to his father’s rule in the month of October, during the 8th Indiction <term>Indiction: A 15-year tax cycle used by the Byzantines for dating purposes</term>. In his speech, <margin>20</margin> he wished to be called a fiery lover of justice and a strict guardian of the city’s laws, but in truth, he was simply guarding himself against conspirators, so that no one would dare any bold move against him.

...and as he was held firmly, the other brother cut off his head. Thus Euphemius paid the price for his wickedness.

Furthermore, the Agarenes occupied not only Sicily from then on, but also Calabria and many parts of Italy, infesting everything with their incursions and population raids. Michael, however, having held the empire for 9 years and 8 months, died of dysentery; with his impiety toward God and his perversity in conducting affairs, he brought so many and such great evils upon the Roman Empire as we have recounted. ->this beginning of evils will happen to the earth,<-
->when the Babylonian dragon shall gain power over affairs,<-
->of a hindered tongue and most greedy for gold.<-

His corpse was placed in the great chapel of Justinian, at the temple of the apostles, in a green Thessalian chest.

Upon his death, his son Theophilus, now of manly age, succeeded him in the month of October, in the 8th indiction. He made a show of a most fervent zeal for justice and an accurate custody of the civil laws, though in reality he feigned those things to keep himself safe from treachery, lest any should plot anything against him.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;While these were Theophilus’s opening acts, his subsequent deeds were not unworthy of praise. For by championing the cause of justice, he was fearsome to all the wicked but a source of wonder to the good; to the latter because 
<margin>10</margin> he seemed a hater of evil and a just man, and to the former because he was solemn and <margin>B</margin> austere. Yet it was not possible for him to be entirely pure of all vices. <margin>15</margin> never allowing them to rest throughout the entire duration of his reign. Because of this, he never met with success in wars; he was always defeated and never returned home in a manner befitting an emperor. Nevertheless, adhering to justice and to the faith and zeal he thought he held toward Christ and his Mother, he went out 
<margin>20</margin> each week on horseback through the main thoroughfare to the divine temple of the Mother of God at Blachernae <term>Blachernae: A suburb of Constantinople famous for its imperial palace and the Church of St. Mary, which housed the Virgin's robe</term>, escorted by his bodyguards. He would go out making himself available to everyone, but primarily to those who had been <margin>C</margin> wronged, so that they might have the opportunity to voice their grievances and not be prevented by any of the unjust men who lived in fear of the punishment he would deal out.

<margin>B</margin> Empress Theodora hailed from the region of the Paphlagonians <note>A region on the northern coast of Asia Minor, known for producing many prominent Byzantine families</note>. She boasted of her father Marinus, a man of some renown, and <margin>10</margin> her mother Theoctista, also known as Florina. When Theodora was crowned with the diadem, her mother Theoctista <margin>15</margin> was also honored with the rank of *zoste patricia* <term>Zoste patricia: literally the "Girded Lady of Honor," this was the highest court title for a woman, making her the chief lady-in-waiting to the Empress</term>. She would welcome them with various <margin>C</margin> <margin>20</margin> gifts, the kind that naturally entice the female mind, and taking them aside privately, she would implore them not to be weak or remain merely "female" in spirit—which is what they were—but to act with courage and think thoughts worthy of their mother's milk. She urged them to loathe their father’s heresy <note>The official state policy of Iconoclasm</note> and to embrace the forms of the holy icons. And...

The Augusta’s name was Theodora, her homeland Paphlagonia; her parents were Marinus, a man of noble standing, and Theoctista, surnamed Florina. Both were piously educated and did not renounce the veneration of divine images, but cultivated it with the most ardent zeal. When Theodora was crowned, her mother Theoctista was also decorated with the dignity of *zoste* and *patricia*. She had a house very near to the Gastria. Frequently inviting Theodora’s daughters to her (there were five: Thecla, Anna, Anastasia, Pulcheria, and Maria) and coaxing them with various gifts by which that sex is accustomed to be soothed, she privately exhorted them to be wise beyond their sex, to take up manly spirits worthy of their mother’s fortune, and, having loathed their father’s heresy, to embrace the sacred images. ### GEORGE CEDRENUS ###

...at the same time, placing these [the icons] into their hands (which she kept in a small chest), she would sanctify them by pressing the images against their faces and lips, kindling in the children a love for them. <margin>D</margin> This did not escape the notice of Theophilus, who inquired as to what had been given to them by their grandmother and what worthy favor she had performed. While the other daughters, possessing a steady mind, robustly avoided his questions as if they were traps, Pulcheria—being a mere child in age—recounted the grandmother's kindnesses and the abundance of fruits she gave them. She also added the matter of the veneration of the venerable icons, thinking and speaking so innocently, saying that there were many "dolls" <note>original Greek: *ninia* (νινία), meaning dolls or puppets; the child did not have the vocabulary for "icons"</note> in her grandmother's chest, and "she places these upon our heads and faces after giving us kisses."

This stirred the Emperor into a frenzy of rage, yet he was prevented from taking any drastic action against her [Theoctista]. He was restrained by the respect and reverence he held for his wife, and even more by the boldness with which Theoctista conducted herself. Indeed, she was known for clearly mocking and rebuking him for his daily persecutions of the confessors <note>Those who suffered for their faith during the Iconoclast period</note> and for his adherence to the aforementioned heresy [Iconoclasm]. She was almost the only one who dared to make the universal hatred felt toward him manifest to his face. 
<margin>P 516</margin> Consequently, he merely forbid his daughters from visiting Theoctista in the future.

As she did this repeatedly, so that she might kindle the desire for the worship of the venerable images in her granddaughters, it did not escape Theophilus. For when he eventually questioned his daughters on what gifts they had received from their grandmother, or what clever things they had done, the others constantly declined his questioning as if it were a snare. Pulcheria, led by the simplicity of her tender age, explained how kindly they had been treated and what various fruits they had been given; she also betrayed the adoration of the images, saying that in her grandmother's chest there were many dolls <note>original Latin: *puppas*</note>, which she applied to their heads and faces after kisses. Stirred by fury at these things, the Emperor nevertheless did not dare to decree anything too harsh against his mother-in-law, hindered by reverence for his wife and much more by the freedom of speech used by Theoctista herself (for she openly attacked her son-in-law, and rebuked him on account of the daily vexations of the confessors and his heresy, and alone dared to make the hatred of all men toward him plain). He only forbade his daughters from approaching their grandmother in the future.

A similar case befell the Empress [Theodora]. A foolish little man, much like Homer's Thersites, was raised in the court, Denderis by name, of a hindered tongue...

<note>The following section, found in some versions of the manuscript, describes a famous diplomatic mission to the Abbasid Caliphate.</note>

Wishing also to make the power of his empire manifest to the Saracens <note>A term used by Byzantines for the Arab Muslims</note>, or perhaps wishing to be feared by them, he sent John the Syncellus—his former teacher, a man of great political discipline, a follower of his own heresy <note>John Grammatikos, a brilliant scholar and leading Iconoclast who rejected the use of religious images</note>, and most skilled in debated arguments—to the ruler of Syria. He gave him many other items for which the Emperor of the Romans <note>The Byzantines referred to themselves as "Romans" (Rhomaioi)</note> is admired and which astound foreign nations, and additionally gave him forty *centenaria* of gold. 

While he sent the other items to the Commander of the Faithful <note>original: *amermoumne*, a Greek transliteration of the Arabic *Amir al-Mu'minin*</note> as gifts, the gold was provided so that John might have a supply for his own generosity to show off his wealth. For if the envoy could scatter gold like sand as he pleased, then surely the one who sent him would be worthy of even greater admiration. In addition to these, he gave two vessels made of gold and precious stones, which common speech calls *cherniboxesta* <note>elaborate pitchers and basins used for the ceremonial washing of hands</note>, exalting and adorning his ambassador in every way. 

When John arrived at Babylon—now called Baghdad—he appeared great through the flow of his speech, and great also from the outward wealth that flourished upon him, giving no small amounts to those sent to him or who visited him. He brought great honor to the Emperor of the Romans, was admired by the Saracens, and was held in high esteem. These things took place when he crossed the barbarian borders. When he drew near the ruler and delivered the Emperor’s words, he went to his place of rest. There he displayed his own high-mindedness and skill in all things; for while exalting the affairs of the Romans and magnifying them to those who came to him for whatever reason...

# COMPENDIUM OF HISTORIES

### THE REIGN OF THEOPHILUS

The Emperor also built the palace of Bryas <note>A famous palace on the Asian side of the Bosporus, notable for its non-Byzantine style</note>, constructing it in the likeness of Saracen <note>The Byzantine term for Arab/Muslim</note> dwellings.

In such matters, Theophilus was thought and considered to be magnificent and wonderful; but toward those who venerated the divine and undefiled icons, he was exceedingly harsh and austere, <margin>5</margin> striving to surpass all the tyrants before him in cruelty.

<note>The following passage describes the diplomatic exploits of John the Grammarian, the Emperor's envoy to the Caliph.</note>

Whenever people, both of high and low status, came to him or were sent to him, he would present them with a silver vessel filled with gold. Once, while dining with the barbarians <note>original: *barbarois*; here referring to the Arabs</note>, he ordered the servants to "lose" one of those two aforementioned expensive vessels. When a low-born clamor arose over its loss, and all the barbarians—struck by the beauty of the vessel—were wounded in their souls and made a great search and inquiry so that the stolen item might be found, he then ordered the second vessel to be brought in. Adding that the lost one should be allowed to perish, he struck the Saracens with amazement, thus calmly putting an end to their searching. 

Furthermore, the leader of the Arabs <note>likely the Caliph al-Ma'mun or al-Mu'tasim</note>, competing in generosity and not wishing to be seen as second to him, sought to honor him with other gifts. John was not won over by these, but threw them before his face as if they were dust. The leader then gifted him one hundred captives, having just brought them out of prison and adorned them with decent clothing, stripping away the mournful rags of their captivity. But even so, John praised the great-heartedness of the giver but would by no means accept them, saying that the men should remain for a time in ease and freedom among their own people, until he could work out a fitting compensation and give back an equal number of Saracen captives held in Roman prisons. With this, he astonished the Saracen leader, who no longer treated him as a stranger but as one of his own household, calling upon him constantly and showing him his own treasures and the beauty of his dwellings. He honored him exceptionally until his return to the Romans.

He persuaded the Emperor, and the works were completed according to his description, with only one addition: a church raised in the name of the Mother of God <note>Theotokos</note> right by the bedchamber. <meta>This page continues the account of Emperor Theophilus’s reign, shifting from his diplomatic displays of wealth to his religious policies. # BY GEORGE CEDRENUS

...surpassing them. For his predecessors were Leo <note>Leo III the Isaurian, who started the first Iconoclasm</note> and Constantine Copronymus <note>Constantine V; his nickname "Copronymus" or "Dung-named" was a slur used by his religious opponents</note>, as well as Michael the Stammerer <note>Michael II</note>, who was this man’s [Theophilus’s] father. Michael had decreed that upon none of the painted icons, wherever they might be depicted, should the word **"Holy"** <note>original: *hagios*</note> be inscribed. He claimed <margin>5</margin> that such a title was appropriate for the Divine alone, but he did not strike the mark with his reasoning. For since God shares the very name "God" <note>original: *theos*</note> with men—a title much higher than the address "Holy"—He would surely not deprive them of the much humbler title of "Holy" <note>The author argues that if the Bible calls humans "gods" (Psalm 82:6), it is illogical to forbid calling Saints "holy."</note>. Nevertheless, this is what Michael decreed.

<margin>C</margin> Before him, Leo and his son Constantine had decreed that icons should not be venerated at all. <margin>10</margin> However, Theophilus went further, decreeing that they should not even be given form through colors <note>In other words, he banned the painting of icons entirely, not just their veneration.</note>. He claimed it was a base thing to be excited by such objects, and that one should look only to the truth. Consequently, the divine images were cast down from every church. In their place, <margin>15</margin> images of **wild beasts and birds** were set up <note>Iconoclast emperors often replaced religious scenes with garden or hunting scenes</note>, exposing his own beastly and servile ignorance.

From that time on, the holy and sacred treasures were tossed into the marketplace by profane hands and treated with indignity. The prisons, usually reserved for criminals, <margin>D</margin> were filled with those who held the divine images in honor—monks, bishops, the laity, <margin>20</margin> and those who painted them. The mountains and caves were also filled with people who, treated like villains, perished from hunger and thirst. For Theophilus had commanded that the cities be kept inaccessible to the monks, ordering that they be driven away by every means; or rather, he decreed that they should not even dare to be seen in the countryside...

***

<note>The following section is a Latin translation of the Greek text above, provided in the original manuscript for Western scholars. It summarizes the same events: Michael II's ban on the word "Holy," the total ban on veneration by Leo and Constantine, and Theophilus's prohibition of painting icons, leading to the persecution of monks and the replacement of icons with secular art.</note>

His father [Michael II] had edicted that the name "Holy" should not be impressed upon any painted image, wherever it might be, because he thought it suited nothing but God alone—an error of opinion. For since God gives the name "God" to man, which is a much narrower term than the word "Holy," why would He deny that which is much lowlier? Leo and his son Copronymus had strictly forbidden all adoration of them. Theophilus, however, did not even allow them to be painted in colors, saying that admiration for such things was the mark of an abject mind, and that truth alone should be beheld. Thus, divine images were thrown down in all the temples, and in their place, figures of beasts and birds were fixed, proving the brutish and slavish madness of Theophilus. From then on, sacrosanct gifts were tossed about the forum by impure hands and handled ignominiously; and prisons meant for the guilty were filled with those who worshipped divine images: monks, bishops, subjects, and their painters. The mountains and caves were also filled with those who were killed by hunger and thirst in the place of criminals. For Theophilus had edicted that no monk be allowed to enter any city, and commanded that they be kept away by every means, so much so that it was not safe for them to be seen in that region.

<meta>This page continues the history of the Emperor Theophilus and his intensifying persecution of those who venerated icons (the Iconophiles). While the previous page discussed his ban on the word "Holy" and the painting of images, this page describes the physical destruction of monastic life and the theological defense mounted by defiant monks.</meta>

### COMPENDIUM OF HISTORIES. 111

...[the Emperor] turned the monasteries and famous hermitages into crowded secular dwellings <note>The Greek term *poluandria* suggests he converted quiet religious houses into noisy, public spaces or barracks to humiliate the monks.</note>. Because these holy men did not wish to betray their virtue or their sacred garments <note>The monastic habit, which was a symbol of their commitment to God.</note>, they chose instead to end their lives through hunger and hardships. Some, having become negligent of their clothing <margin>5</margin>, perished because of this. Many others, living more carelessly, embraced a loose and unrestrained life, disregarding the divine hymns, songs, and even the monastic habit itself. For the tyrant did not even allow <margin>P 519</margin> these assemblies to be held—gatherings which are often the only things capable of maintaining discipline and acting as a bridle <margin>10</margin> for those who slide irrationally toward their passions. 

Yet, the spirit of boldness and freedom did not entirely depart from humanity even then. Instead, some of the more fervent individuals—many acting alone, and some in groups—stood their ground. Among these were the monks coming from the Monastery of the Abramites <note>A prominent monastery in Constantinople that became a center of resistance against the Emperor’s policies.</note>. Appearing before him with boldness, they argued logically <margin>15</margin> from the writings of our holy fathers—specifically Dionysius the Great <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, an early Christian theologian</note>, Hierotheus, and Irenaeus <note>Irenaeus of Lyons, a 2nd-century bishop</note>. They <margin>B</margin> demonstrated that the monastic way of life and its establishment were not invented "yesterday or the day before," but were ancient and primordial. Furthermore, they proved that the forms of the divine icons <margin>20</margin> were familiar and common to the Apostles themselves. They noted that the divine apostle Luke depicted the form of the Mother of God <note>original: *Theotokos*</note>, and that Christ our Master and God himself, having imprinted his own likeness upon a cloth <note>The "Mandylion," a famous relic believed to be a cloth miraculously imprinted with the face of Jesus.</note>, left it for us as an image "not made by human hands" <note>original: *acheiroteukton*</note>. These most divine men thus [rebuked] the tyrant's folly...

---

1 "but the" in Manuscript C | "crowded secular dwellings" in Manuscript P 
8 "often" omitted in Manuscript P 
23 "intent" in Manuscript C

---

Indeed, he even turned the monasteries and the buildings founded for sacred quiet into places frequented by profane men. Meanwhile, pious men, who would not betray their virtue and sacred dress, preferred to die of hunger and tortures. Some perished having neglected their habit; many others, who had less zeal for virtue, gave themselves over to a free and loose life, casting aside the sacred hymns, songs, and even the clothing itself. For the Emperor broke up these gatherings, which alone served to restrain the desires of men. Nevertheless, at that time, freedom of speech was not entirely taken away from men; but certain ones of a more heated spirit, either individually or in a formed line, rebuked the prince. The foremost of these were the Abramite monks, who, having come freely into his sight, demonstrated from the sayings of the holy fathers—namely the great Dionysius, Hierotheus, and Irenaeus—that the monastic way of life and institution had not appeared recently, but was very ancient. They also showed that sacred images were familiar to the apostles themselves, since both Luke the divine apostle painted the form of the Mother of God, and Christ our Lord and God left to us his own likeness impressed upon a cloth, produced by no service of a human hand. In this way, these most divine men [confronted] the tyrant's...

Indeed, Theophilus, with a mind most hostile toward icons, decided to remove all painters from our midst, allowing them to keep their lives only if they would spit upon the images and trample them underfoot as profane. He was so mangled by tortures that it was thought he would depart this life, and was cast into prison. When the Emperor heard that he had recovered from his illness and was again painting sacred forms, he ordered glowing iron plates to be applied to his palms, which consumed the flesh until, overcome by the evil, he lay half-dead. Then, because divine mercy wished to preserve him for posterity, the tyrant, hearing he was now breathing his last, was moved by the prayers of his wife and her close associates to release him from prison. Thus he was hidden in the shrine of the Forerunner, which is called "The Terrible," and despite his wounded body, he nevertheless painted an image of the Forerunner; this lasted a long time and [cured] diseases...

# GEORGE CEDRENUS

When the true faith <note>original: "ὀρθοδόξου πίστεως" (orthodoxou pisteōs)</note> shone forth again, he restored the image of the God-man Jesus Christ at the Chalke <term>Chalke Gate: The main ceremonial entrance to the Great Palace of Constantinople, where a famous icon of Christ stood.</term> with his own hands. This blessed Lazarus, when he was begged by the wonderful Empress Theodora to grant forgiveness to her husband <note>The Emperor Theophilus, who had died by the time icons were fully restored.</note> and to pray for God’s mercy upon him, replied:
> “God is not so unjust, O Queen,” he said, “as to forget our love and the labors we endured for His sake, and instead show favor to that man’s hatred and his exceeding madness.”

<margin>D</margin> But these things happened later. The foul tyrant [Theophilus], seeing that the confessor Theophanes and his brother Theodore excelled most men in wisdom, ordered them to appear at the Triclinium of Lausus <term>Triclinium: A formal reception or dining hall; in this context, a hall within the imperial palace.</term> to debate publicly concerning the faith. And he said:
> “Come now, you cursed men, by what passages of Scripture are you persuaded to worship idols?”

(for this was how he referred to the holy icons with his unbridled mind and tongue)
> “And why do you convince so many simple-minded people to do the same?”

He added other blasphemous and harsh words against the holy icon of Christ our God with an increasingly impudent voice. But those blessed men replied:
> “May the mouth be stopped,” they said, “that speaks lawlessness against God.”

The Emperor then hid his “lion’s skin” for a time and put on the "skin of a fox" <note>This is a classical metaphor for switching from brute force to deceptive cunning.</note>; he demanded that they provide prophetic citations and testimonies that permitted the icons to be worshipped.

### A COMPENDIUM OF HISTORIES

Theophilus argued against this, and at the same time, unrolling his own book, he tried to show that his words were trustworthy. But the saintly man <note>Theophanes the Confessor</note> cried out that not only had this book been tampered with by him, but indeed all the books that had happened to come into his hands. He proposed instead that the book kept in the Patriarchal library in the Thomaïtes <term>Thomaïtes: A grand hall or reception room in the Patriarchal palace of Constantinople, known for housing important records and a library.</term>, located in its proper place, should be brought to him <margin>5</margin> to confirm the truth of what was being said. 

Once someone had been sent and brought the book faster than words can tell, the Emperor began unrolling it; however, he deliberately "missed" the passage he was looking for. Out of shame, he skipped over the phrase in question and searched in other places. <margin>10</margin> But when he was instructed by the blessed <margin>B</margin> Theophanes, who pointed with his finger and said, "If you turn three more pages, you will find what is sought," the Emperor could no longer endure the bold rebuke. 

Knowing that the truth was indeed so, he cast off the patience he had shown until then and, revealing the "beast" <note>A classical metaphor for the Emperor's underlying cruelty and rage, contrasting with the "fox" persona he had previously adopted.</note> within, he said, <margin>15</margin> "It is not right for an Emperor to be insulted by such men." 

He then ordered them to be led away to the inner garden of the Lausiakos <term>Lausiakos: A section of the Great Palace of Constantinople, often used for imperial receptions or as a walkway connecting halls.</term> to be beaten with the heaviest of rods, up to two hundred lashes, and to have those nonsensical iambic verses he had composed branded <margin>20</margin> onto their foreheads in a barbarian manner <note>This branding earned the brothers the nickname "the Graptoi" or "The Branded Ones." Theophilus allegedly wrote the verses himself to mock their devotion to Jerusalem.</note>. <margin>C</margin> These were the verses:

->As all people desire to hasten to that city<-

When [Theophanes] brought this up, Theophilus replied that the passage did not say such a thing, and at the same time he opened his own book. There, Theophanes cried out that not only this book, but all that had come into the hands of Theophilus, had been corrupted. He demanded that a codex from the Patriarchal library of the Thomaïtes (while pointing out exactly where it was kept) be brought to investigate the truth of his words. 

A certain man was sent and brought the codex very quickly. The Emperor, unrolling it of his own accord, studiously wandered away from the intended passage out of a sense of shame, and skipping the place in question, he searched elsewhere. But when Theophanes, with a pointed finger, showed him that if he turned three pages he would find the place he was looking for, the Emperor—unable to bear the freedom of this rebuke and knowing the truth—cast aside the patience he had kept until then and revealed the "wild beast." 

Saying it was an unworthy thing for an Emperor to be mocked by such men, he ordered them to be led into the inner garden of the Lausiakos and to be beaten most severely with rods, up to 200 strokes. Furthermore, he ordered that their foreheads be marked in the barbarian fashion with those foolish iambic verses he had composed himself:

# GEORGE KEDRENOS

[The Emperor] did not shrink from directing the music himself, giving the clergy one hundred pounds of gold <note>The Latin version of this text says "silver" (argenti), though the Greek specifies "gold" (chrysiou).</note> for this purpose. They say that the *sticheron* <term>sticheron: A short hymn or verse of Byzantine chant, usually sung between verses of a Psalm.</term> for Palm Sunday, which begins:
> "Go forth, nations; go forth, O peoples,"
was a product of his own soul.

<margin>5</margin> Because he naturally had very little hair on his head, being somewhat balding, he issued a decree throughout the empire that hair must be shorn close to the skin. He would not permit anyone who considered himself a Roman to wear his hair longer than the neck. Anyone who disregarded this decree was to be punished with many lashes; the Emperor boasted that he was restoring the virtue of the ancient Romans <margin>10</margin> through this discipline.

<margin>D</margin> Being the father of five daughters, as our account previously mentioned, and lacking any male offspring, he felt it necessary to marry off the youngest of them all, Maria, whom he loved exceedingly. The groom was from the Krenitai family, from the <margin>15</margin> Armenian region, named Alexios and surnamed Mosele. He was handsome in appearance and in the prime of his youth. First, the Emperor honored him with the rank of Patrician <term>patrician: One of the highest honorary titles in the Byzantine court.</term> and Proconsul; then he made him Magister <term>magister: A high-ranking administrative and military office.</term> and later Caesar <term>Caesar: Usually the rank immediately below the Emperor, often designating an heir or a very close relative.</term>. Providing him with sufficient troops, he sent him to Longobardia <note>original: Λογγιβαρδίαν (Longibardian) - referring to Byzantine-held territories in Southern Italy.</note> for an urgent matter. Alexios departed and performed his duties well, <margin>P 523</margin> <margin>20</margin> exactly as the Emperor desired. Consequently, while the Emperor’s affection for him flourished, human envy grew alongside it. Men began to slander him, claiming that he desired the imperial throne and adding...

Because he naturally had few hairs on his head and was balding, he issued an edict ordering everyone’s hair to be shorn, and that no Roman should wear it hanging below the neck. He sanctioned this edict with the heavy punishment of the lash, striving to recall the virtue of the ancient Romans.

And since he had, as we mentioned above, five daughters and lacked male offspring, he decided to give the youngest of them in marriage—the one he loved more dearly than the others, named Maria. He chose as her husband Alexios, surnamed Mosele, an Armenian by birth from the Krenitai clan, elegant in form and in the flower of his age. To him he first granted the honor of Patrician, then Proconsul; then he made him Magister and finally Caesar. Equipped with a large army, he sent him to Longobardia as circumstances required. Having set out, Alexios managed affairs excellently and according to his father-in-law’s wishes. Thus it happened that as the Emperor's affection grew, envy also increased; some accused him of being greedy for power, adding—

# GEORGIOS KEDRENOS

After the enemy had campaigned, Theophilus also went out to meet them with a competitive spirit, casting aside all fear. Even if some small trace of fear remained, the military experience and nobility of the men accompanying him pushed it far away. These men were Theophobos and Manuel.

<margin>D</margin> Manuel’s bravery was well known even to his enemies; he had commanded the Armies of the East under Emperor Leo <note>Leo V the Armenian (reigned 813–820 AD).</note>, and under Michael <note>Michael I Rangabe (reigned 811–813 AD).</note> before him, he had served as the first of the imperial grooms. They call this office the **Protostrator**. <term>Protostrator: Originally the "first groom" of the imperial stables, by this period it had become a high-ranking military and court title.</term> 

Our account will also explain who Theophobos was: where he came from, how he, being of Persian descent, became known to the Emperor, and how he came to be joined in marriage to the Emperor's sister. Long ago, a certain man of the Persian royal line came to Constantinople as an ambassador. While there, he fathered this boy—not through a legal marriage, but through a secret and hidden union—and then departed. 

Since there is an inviolable law among the Persians that no one may take power over them unless they are of the royal line, and since the royal line had failed because of continuous wars and being driven out by the Agarenes <note>original: "Ἀγαρηνῶν" (Agarenon). A Byzantine term for Arabs or Saracens, referencing the biblical Hagar.</note>, the Persians frequently set out to retrieve this Theophobos from Constantinople so that he might rule over them.

...to send out a search for the one they sought. And indeed, having arrived at our city and searched extensively, they found him living with his mother in the Oxia <note>The Oxia (the "Sharp") was a district and hill in Constantinople, likely named for its steepness.</note> district. Since the man they sought was revealed and recognized not only by his outward appearance but also by the characteristics of his soul and body, and since a neighbor also testified to the union the woman had with the Persian—for nothing is hidden that will not eventually become known to the many—those who had been sent made themselves known to the Emperor and clarified the purpose of their mission. They promised peace, treaties, and the submission of their entire nation if he would not refuse to hand Theophobos over to them. The Emperor was certainly pleased with these promises. And since he found the truth to be exactly so, he took the young man into the palace and provided him with a liberal education and training. 

But another account says that Theophobos was not the seed of an ambassador, but came about through a chance event such as happens in wars. It says his father—whether he was a king or very close to a king by blood—fled from Persia and came to the reigning city <note>Constantinople</note>, living a life of poverty. There, while working for a certain woman who was a tavern-keeper, he was captured by love for her, and through a legal union, she gave birth to Theophobos. But the father passed away. Through some astrology and divination—for they say these sciences still flourish in Persia—the Persians learned concerning Theophobos that there was someone descended from the royal tribe living in Byzantium. When they learned this, they made haste to Byzantium to find the one they sought, and in this way, he became known to the Emperor. 

When his appearance was made known to everyone in Persia by the returning ambassadors, it seemed most pleasant to all of them to plan a revolt against the Agarenes and to join the Roman Empire, so that they might prosper under a leader of their own race. It also happened that the leader of the Persians, Babet <note>This refers to Babak Khorramdin, the leader of a major Iranian uprising against the Abbasid Caliphate.</note>, had already revolted from the Agarenes five years prior with seven thousand men. Driven by both a longing for Theophobos and a fear of the Agarenes, he came to the Roman territory at the city of Sinope and made himself and his entire nation subjects of the Emperor. Because of this, Theophilus elevated Theophobos to the honor of Patrician <term>Patrikios: One of the highest ranks in the Byzantine court, usually reserved for senior governors and generals.</term>

Theophobos <note>A Persian nobleman who converted to Christianity and became a high-ranking Byzantine general.</note> outwitted the Saracens <note>original: "Σαρακηνοὺς" (Sarakenous). A standard Byzantine term for Arab Muslims.</note> by ordering his soldiers to make a great noise and shouting, and to use lyres, stringed instruments, and the sound of trumpets as if a second relief force were suddenly <margin>5</margin> arriving to support them. Having suspected this very thing, the Saracens retreated six miles back, fearing they would be surrounded. From this, the Persians <note>Refers to the "Persian" corps, Khurramite refugees who had settled in the Empire.</note> felt an even greater affection for Theophobos, and they petitioned the Emperor that they alone might serve under him to undertake the war against the Agarenes <note>original: "Ἀγαρηνῶν" (Agarenon). Being impressed by the man's words, the Emperor treated him with kindness and, out of respect for his status as a citizen, gifted him fine robes and garments.

Now, as the first light of spring began to show, <margin>P 526</margin> Theophilus once again gathered his forces and set out against the Saracens <note>original: "Σαρακηνῶν" (Sarakēnōn). A common Byzantine term for the Arab Muslim forces of the Abbasid Caliphate.</note>. Having recalled the holy Methodius <margin>5</margin> from exile, he kept the man with him. It was the Emperor’s habit to do this during his wars, either so that he might use the wisdom inherent in Methodius to explain obscure matters unknown to many, or because he was guarding against any uprisings that Methodius might incite in his absence due to the war over the divine and venerable icons <note>The "war over icons" refers to the Second Iconoclasm (814–843 AD). Theophilus was a staunch Iconoclast, while Methodius—the future Patriarch of Constantinople—was a leader of the Iconophiles who supported the use of religious images.</note>. For the elite of the city and those who loved God held the man in no small honor; <margin>10</margin> for this reason, it did not seem advantageous to the Emperor to leave him behind. Meanwhile, as the armies clashed, and the <margin>B</margin> Ishmaelites <note>original: "Ἰσμαηλιτῶν" (Ismaēlitōn). Another Byzantine term for Arabs, referencing their traditional descent from Ishmael.</note> gained the upper hand, the Emperor found himself surrounded and was on the verge of being captured. When Manuel—the commander of the army—learned of this, <margin>15</margin> he considered it a terrible thing to see a Roman Emperor taken as a prisoner of war. Encouraging those around him, he entered into the danger with great courage. When he found the Emperor exhausted and despairing of his safety, making the excuse that he did not wish to abandon his fleeing people, Manuel said, <margin>20</margin> "Come now, O Emperor, follow me as I lead the way and find a path for you." But as Manuel began to fight his way out, the Emperor, cowering in fear, did not follow, and Manuel was forced to turn back a second time. When he failed again, for the third time... <margin>C</margin>

...however, having respected the man's virtue and showing reverence to his own people, he spoke friendlily to Krateros and presented him with robes as a mark of honor.

With spring begun, Theophilus again moved against the Saracens with gathered troops, having recalled the holy Methodius from exile and joined him to himself. He was accustomed to doing this in wars, either to use his wisdom in explaining many obscure and intricate matters, or to guard against him stirring up some rebellion in his absence due to the removal of the sacred images. For those of the citizens who were prominent and pious toward God held Methodius in great honor; therefore, it did not seem advisable to the Emperor to leave him behind. Indeed, once the battle was joined, the Ishmaelite cause was superior, and the Emperor, having been surrounded, almost fell into the hands of the enemy. Manuel, the leader of the army, sensing this, and having rallied the spirits of his men with a speech because he judged it a most shameful thing if a Roman emperor were captured by the enemy, boldly entered the crisis. And when he had broken through to the emperor, who was now exhausted and despairing of safety, yet pretending he did not want to betray his people by fleeing, Manuel urged him to follow him as he led the way and opened a path. After Manuel himself broke out, the Emperor followed immediately behind...

### GEORGIUS CEDRENUS

...threatened him with death if he would not follow. In this way, at long last and with great difficulty, he rescued the Emperor from the peril. Because of this, Theophilus welcomed him with honors equal to his deeds and cared for him with gifts, calling him his benefactor and savior. However, envy gained power over such a man, and through slander he was accused of high treason <term>High Treason (kathosiōsis): A crime against the majesty of the Emperor or the state, often carrying the penalty of death or mutilation.</term>. <margin>5</margin> Perceiving the significant danger orchestrated against him, he was informed by one of his most faithful followers—a man who had formerly been his servant but was at that time the cupbearer to Emperor Theophilus—that the Emperor intended to have him blinded <note>Blinding was a common Byzantine punishment used to disqualify political rivals from the throne or to punish perceived treachery.</note>. Consequently, he dared to revolt and defected to the Agarenes <note>original: "Ἀγαρηνοὺς" (Agarenous). A Byzantine term for the Arab forces of the Caliphate, referring to their traditional descent from Hagar.</note>. He was held in high regard among them as well, being honored with the greatest distinctions. <margin>D 10</margin> Indeed, he was entrusted with a large army and sent against the neighboring enemies who are called the Karmatians <note>original: "Κερμάται" (Kermatai). These were a radical Ismaili sect that led several uprisings against the Abbasid Caliphate.</note>. Refusing to allow anyone else to follow him except the Romans who were held in the prisons, whom he took as his fellow soldiers, he achieved the greatest and most magnificent victories, even capturing the place called Khorasan <note>original: "Χωροσὰν". A vast historical region in the east of the Abbasid Caliphate, covering parts of modern-day Iran, Afghanistan, and Central Asia.</note>. <margin>15</margin> For it was not only his exceptional courage that stunned his opponents; the strangeness of the language <note>The soldiers spoke Greek rather than Arabic.</note>, the change in their appearance, and the unexpected tactics of their warfare drove the enemy into an extraordinary state of cowardice. He proved himself noble not only against these enemies but also against the wild beasts that were ravaging the land. <margin>20</margin> Having become the cause of great benefits for them, and for himself...

<column-break/>

...was not the case; once again, and since even then Theophilus would not follow, he returned a third time and threatened him with death unless he accompanied him. Thus, he finally snatched him from the present danger. For this reason, the Emperor rewarded him with worthy honors and gifts, acknowledging him as his benefactor and savior. But such was the power of envy that, when Manuel was accused of high treason through calumny, it created the greatest peril for him. Realizing this, and having been informed by a certain faithful man—who had once served him but was then the Emperor’s cupbearer—that he was to be deprived of his eyes, he attempted a defection and went over to the Agarenes. He was also great among them and treated with the highest honors. For the Agarenes sent him, equipped with a large army, against their neighboring enemies called the Karmatians. Manuel refused to lead any others but the Romans who were being kept as captives in the prisons. Having formed an army of these men, he brought back great and illustrious victories, and also captured Khorasan itself (this is the name of a fortified place). For he struck terror into the enemies not only by his remarkable bravery, but also by the foreignness of the speech and dress, and the unexpected change in the form of war, which threw them into no small fear. He conducted himself energetically not only against the enemy, but also against the wild beasts devastating that region. And on account of the many good things which...

->### A COMPENDIUM OF HISTORY<-

Manuel was exceptionally beloved by the leader of the Saracens <note>original: "Σαρακηνῶν" (Sarakenon). In this context, it refers to the Abbasid Caliph in Baghdad.</note> and by their council of elders. Upon learning of this, Emperor Theophilus was, as might be expected, deeply distressed; <margin>P 527</margin> he left no stone unturned in his efforts to recall the man to his service. Consequently, he sent a cross and a chrysobull <term>Chrysobull (chrysoboullon): A formal decree issued by a Byzantine Emperor, authenticated with a golden seal, used here to guarantee Manuel's safety and restoration of rank.</term> by means of a certain wandering monk to Manuel, calling upon him to return and promising him a full amnesty for his past offenses. The messenger, having received these items, delivered them secretly into Manuel’s hands. Manuel accepted them, and his soul was set on fire with a longing for home. Having already gained the Caliph's trust through his prior military successes, he informed the leader of the Saracens that he nurtured a desire to lead a campaign against the Romans <note>original: "Ῥωμαίων" (Rhomaion). The Byzantines called themselves Romans; "Romania" refers to the Empire.</note> to take revenge on the enemies dwelling in Cappadocia who had slandered him to the Emperor. He also requested that the leader's own son be sent with him <margin>B</margin> to further dispel any suspicion of his motives. Ismael <note>original: "Ἰσμαήλ" (Ismael). A name used here to refer to the Caliph or a high Arab commander.</note> granted his requests and gave him permission to begin the expedition. As Manuel approached the Roman borders, he revealed his situation to the military governor of Cappadocia, explaining his impending return to the Empire. At the same time, he gave instructions that an ambush should be laid at a specific location, saying, "When I arrive there, I will cause the Saracen scouts to ride off to another place, while I myself will run back to the Roman territories." And so it happened. For when they approached the designated spot according to the signal, he embraced the son of Ismael many times and said, <margin>C</margin> "Go back safely, my child, to your father; as for me, I am going to my own Emperor."

Having received favor from him, the Saracens held him in the highest esteem, and he was exceedingly dear to their prince and nobles. When Theophilus learned this, he felt a heavy burden of distress, as was natural; and to bring Manuel back to him, he left nothing untried. Finally, through the efforts of a certain monk—the kind who are accustomed to wander here and there through various regions—he sent him a cross and letters, urging him to return and promising forgetfulness of all offenses. Manuel, having these items secretly delivered to him, with his spirit Kindled, and since he had already proven his loyalty to the prince of the Saracens by his deeds, signaled to him that he desired to undertake an expedition against the Romans and to take vengeance on his enemies who had denounced him to the Emperor, those living in Cappadocia. He also asked that the prince’s son be sent with him, the better to hide his true purpose. Prince Ismael assented to his petition. Manuel, approaching the borders of the Roman jurisdiction, informed the prefect of Cappadocia of his affairs; at the same time, he ordered him to place an ambush at a certain spot so that he himself, when he arrived there, could send the Saracen scouts elsewhere and enter the Roman jurisdiction. Therefore, when he reached the place that had been established, having greeted the son of Ismael at length, he told him to return safe to his father, while he himself went to the Emperor...

### BY GEORGE CEDRENUS

...and my lord.” <note>original: "καὶ κύριον" (kai kyrion). This concludes the message Manuel sent to the Roman commanders on the previous page to announce his return.</note> Having escaped safely from there to the reigning city <note>Constantinople</note>, he met with the Emperor at the Church of the Mother of God at Blachernae. <note>Blachernae was a famous imperial palace and church complex at the northern corner of Constantinople's walls.</note> He was honored by him with the rank of *magistros* <term>Magistros: One of the highest administrative and honorary titles in the Byzantine court hierarchy.</term> and from that time on acted as the Emperor's *synteknos*. <term>Synteknos: A spiritual relative, usually the godparent of one's child, implying a very close, almost familial bond with the Emperor.</term> Such was the outcome of the affairs regarding Manuel.

Meanwhile, after Theodotus Melissenus—whom history has also known from earlier as Cassiteras—had occupied the throne of Constantinople <note>The Patriarchal throne</note> for a sufficient time and had just recently ended his life, Iannes, the tutor of Emperor Theophilus, succeeded to that throne. <margin>D</margin> He received the high priesthood as a reward for his unfaithfulness and impiety. <note>original: "ἀπιστίας καὶ ἀσεβείας" (apistias kai asebeias). The author, writing from a pro-icon perspective, views Iannes (John VII Grammatikos) as a heretic for his Iconoclast beliefs.</note>

When the Emperor Theophilus was inquiring searchingly about those who would rule after him, a certain woman was brought before him. She had been captured from the Saracens <note>original: "Ἀγαρηνῶν" (Agarenon), referring to the Hagarenes/Arabs.</note> during one of the previous wars and was naturally gifted in making such prophecies. The Emperor asked her about the things he wished to know, commanding her to declare whose succession to the Empire would be long-lasting. This woman, moved either by a divine trance or by a demonic influence, said: “To you, O Emperor, your son shall be the successor together with his own mother; but after him, the family of the Martinakioi shall prevail over the Empire for a long time.” As soon as he heard this, despite the fact that Martinakios <note>A member of the noble Martinakeioi family.</note> was dear to him, the Emperor had him tonsured as a monk <margin>P 528</margin> and designated his house as a dwelling for monastics <note>Theophilus turned his friend's private estate into a monastery to remove him from the political line of succession.</note>. Not only did this woman speak this prophecy, but she also foretold many other future events...

...she foretold that the Patriarch Iannes would be cast out of the patriarchal throne, and that the venerable icons would receive their fitting honor and worship. From his Iconoclast perspective, the Emperor Theophilus viewed the veneration of icons as the worship of idols.</note> It was not only the little woman who prophesied these things, but Iannes himself, through the use of lecanomancy, <term>Lecanomancy: A method of divination performed by observing the patterns of water or oil in a basin.</term> clearly revealed to him the man who was destined to succeed him in power. 

The little woman did not only resolve the inquiries of the Emperor, but <margin>B</margin> she also made clear what was to happen to Constantine—a man of great influence among the Triphyllios family at that time—telling him that he and his sons were destined to be deprived of their property and to put on the clothing of the clergy. This indeed came to pass later, during the reign of Basil. <note>Emperor Basil I, who reigned 867–886 AD, several decades after the events described here.</note> She also foretold to George the soldier the death that would overtake him in the *sphendone* of the Hippodrome; <term>Sphendone: The curved, U-shaped end of the Hippodrome of Constantinople, which was supported by massive masonry arches.</term> for there later, while Basil was reigning, he was beheaded after being caught in a charge of rebellion.

Now, as the spring was shining forth, both the Agarenes <margin>C</margin> <note>original: "Ἀγαρηνοὶ" (Agarenoi). Upon his return, Theophilus received an embassy from the Khagan <term>Khagan: The title of the supreme ruler of the Khazars, a powerful Turkic nomadic people north of the Black Sea.</term> of Khazaria, who requested that the place named Markel <note>The fortress is more commonly known as Sarkel. Upon his return, Petronas gave his counsel to the Emperor, stating that he would not otherwise hold firm rule over Cherson <note>A vital Byzantine city-state on the Crimean Peninsula.</note> unless he appointed a personal military governor <term>strategos: A high-ranking military commander who also served as the civil governor of a province or "theme."</term> there. From that time on, the custom was established that military governors should be sent to Cherson.

In the following year, when the spring season arrived, Theophilus set out against the Agarenes <note>original: "Ἀγαρηνῶν" (Agarenon). He advanced further into Syria, both shaving the land bare and ravaging it, plundering everything he encountered. By the law of war, he seized and enslaved two cities, and he even besieged and captured the city called Sozopetra, which happened to be the birthplace of the Caliph. <margin>P 529</margin> <note>original: "ἀμερμουμνῆ" (amermoumne). ### A COMPENDIUM OF HISTORIES

This city, once the most distinguished of the eastern cities, was now shown to be nothing more than a deserted ruin. Its people were led away as captives of war, including the commanders of the armies: the patricians Callistus, Constantinus, and Theodorus Craterus, along with many others who were illustrious in their military commands and held the highest honors.

<margin>C</margin> Once the city had been subdued in this manner, the leader of the Saracens <note>The Abbasid Caliph Al-Mu'tasim</note> ordered the Byzantine ambassadors to inspect every detail of what had occurred. Acting as if he were mocking the situation and feasting upon these deeds, he sent them back to the Emperor as messengers to report the disaster themselves. The Emperor <note>Theophilus</note> then sent them back again to the *amermoumne* <note>original: ἀμερμουμνῆν (amermoumnēn). A Greek transliteration of the Arabic title *Amir al-Mu'minin*, meaning "Commander of the Faithful" or Caliph.</note>, requesting the return of the illustrious men captured during the siege, as well as his own kinsmen and the rest of the prisoners. He promised to pay twenty-four *centenaria* <term>centenaria: a Byzantine measurement of weight for gold, where one centenarium equals 100 pounds of gold.</term> as a ransom for them. However, the Caliph received the embassy and dismissed the envoys with insults, declaring that he would be a fool if, after spending a thousand *centenaria* to assemble his own army, he were to return those he had captured for such a small amount of gold.

<margin>D</margin> When the ambassadors returned without success, Theophilus was struck by the overwhelming weight of the calamity. He turned away from all food and drink and became almost entirely unable to eat; accepting nothing else but water squeezed from snow, he was seized by the affliction of dysentery. Yet, despite being in such a wretched state, he could not find rest, nor could he endure the destruction of Amorium with any composure. Instead, he sought a time and a way by which he might take his revenge...

With Amorium captured in this way, the prince of the Saracens, as if insulting the achievements and proudly feasting upon them, sent the emperor’s ambassadors—who had been ordered to inspect everything that had been done—back to their master as messengers of the disaster. # A COMPENDIUM OF HISTORIES

<margin>5</margin> ...showed that those who were slandering Theophobus <note>Theophobus was a commander of Persian origin (a Khurramite) who had converted to Christianity and married into the imperial family; he was seen as a potential rival for the throne.</note> found their opportunity through the aforementioned accusations. As Theophilus recognized that the end of his own life was near, he cast Theophobus into the darkest of dungeons near the Bucoleon <note>The Bucoleon was a seaside palace that formed part of the Great Palace complex of Constantinople.</note>. And as his own end was already approaching, he ordered the beheading of Theophobus and that the head be brought to him. Receiving it and touching the hair with his hands, he uttered his final words: "From this moment, neither am I Theophilus, nor are you Theophobus." <note>original: "ὡς ἀπὸ τοῦ νῦν οὔτε ἐγὼ Θεόφιλος οὔτε σὺ Θεόφοβος" — a grim play on their names meaning "Friend of God" and "Fearer of God," signifying that in death, their earthly ranks and identities were extinguished.</note> Some, however, attribute the <margin>D</margin> slaughter of Theophobus to Oryphas, who happened to be the *drungarius* of the Watch <note>original: δρουγγαρίῳ τῆς βίγλας (droungariō tēs viglas); the commander of one of the elite palace guard units.</note>, claiming he performed the deed of his own <margin>10</margin> volition without anyone having commanded it.

Upon Theophilus’s departure from this life, his son Michael <note>Michael III, known as "the Drunkard" in later hostile sources, though he was only a child at this time.</note> took up the scepters of the empire together with his mother Theodora. He had as guardians and directors those whom his father had appointed for him by testament: Manuel the *magister* <note>A high-ranking administrative and military official.</note>, who had also served as the Domestic of the Schools <note>original: δομέστικον τῶν σχολῶν (domestikon tōn scholōn); the commander-in-chief of the imperial field army.</note>, <margin>15</margin> and the patrician Theoctistus, the Logothete of the Dromos <note>The Logothete of the Dromos was one of the most powerful officials, responsible for the public post, diplomacy, and internal security.</note>. While some were accusing Theophobus before the emperor, Theophilus, feeling his life's end pressing upon him, thrust Theophobus into a most dark prison located near the Bucoleon.
