*From the beginning, through the counsel of pious men, the matters of the heresy of the* ***Iconoclasts*** <note>original: εἰκονομάχων (eikonomakhōn); those who opposed the use of religious images or icons.</note> *were being reconsidered—a heresy that had spread throughout the Roman* <note>The Byzantines referred to themselves as "Romans" (Rhōmaioi), as they saw their empire as the direct continuation of the Roman Empire.</note> *dominions from the reign of Leo the Armenian until the death of Theophilus. Theoctistus also joined in the effort to abolish this heresy. Manuel, however, was hesitant for a time, and no one dared to speak openly or bring the word of this restoration into the light, for the greater part of the Senate, the Council, and even the Patriarch himself* <note>John VII Grammaticus, the last Iconoclast Patriarch of Constantinople.</note> *were held fast by the heresy. Only Manuel, moved by a divine impulse, dared to take this step.*

<margin>B</margin> *For previously, as has been said, he had been in doubt regarding the veneration of the venerable icons, but later he embraced it for the following reason. He was seized by a most grievous illness, and his life was despaired of, all medical art having failed. Certain pious monks from the* ***Stoudios monastery*** <note>The most influential monastery in Constantinople, famous for its resistance to Iconoclasm.</note> *came to him, having heard he had died; but approaching his bed and finding him still living and breathing, they brought him the good news of life and recovery and restoration to his former health. At first, he was distrustful; yet as the holy men persisted, telling him not to doubt the gift and glory of God* <margin>C</margin> *revealed to them, he recovered slightly from the illness and spoke to them with a thin and feeble breath:* "And how shall this be for me, O holy fathers? The powers of my soul have failed, and my body is completely weakened and withered. For I lie..."

Only Manuel dared this, excited by divine power. For although he had hesitated for a while concerning that business, as we have said, he finally took it up in earnest for this reason. He had fallen into a most grave disease, so much so that with all the art of the physicians exhausted, his life was now despaired of. Certain pious monks from the Stoudios monastery approached him, to whom it had been announced that he was dead; and when they approached the bed and perceived him still to be living and breathing, they preached a joyful message to him about the preservation of his life and the recovery of his former health. "...dried up like a mummy and a skeleton, differing in no way from any other of the dead except only for the fact that I still breathe. What hope then, or what reasoning will there be to persuade me that I shall recover my strength and return to my former health?" 

The most holy men, taking up the conversation, said to him: "All things are possible, and nothing is unattainable for God. <margin>D</margin> If you will strive, once you have recovered, to extinguish the wildfire of the **iconoclasts** <note>original: εἰκονομάχων (eikonomakhōn); literally 'image-fighters,' those who opposed the use of religious icons.</note> and to restore the holy icons according to the ancient and ancestral decrees, we herald the news of life to you." They spoke and withdrew. 

And immediately the disease abated and his natural bodily functions were carried out without hindrance; in a short time, he had gained a complete release from his ailment. Having become stronger after the illness, he immediately rode out on horseback to the palace and went in to see the **Empress** <note>Theodora, acting as regent for her young son, Michael III.</note>. He urged her in every way to restore the divine icons. She herself had long been eager to seize an opportunity for this, being constantly encouraged toward it by her own mother and her maternal uncles, who were **patricians** <note>A high-ranking title in the Byzantine court.</note>. 

Nevertheless, Theodora resisted Manuel’s words, either because she was wary of the oaths she had sworn to her late husband <margin>P 535</margin> or, as we have said, because she feared the great number of those who had been caught up in the heresy. As Manuel persisted, Theodora said: "My husband, O **Magister** <note>original: μάγιστρε (magistre); a title for a high-ranking administrative and military official.</note>, was both a man and an emperor who loved precision, and he never did anything without careful consideration. And this doctrine—had it not been forbidden by the sacred laws and the holy scriptures—he would not have cast it out from the Church."

When a certain faithless and savage nation, employing three leaders, was harassing the Roman domain, and that matter held **Theophilus** anxious, as was natural, **Iannes**—having dismissed the sickness of his mind—ordered him to hope for the best regarding affairs, if only he were willing to obey his counsel. This counsel was pleasing to the Emperor, and he ordered it to be so done. Two of them struck off two heads of the statue with very strong blows; the third, striking somewhat more weakly, indeed bent it, but did not pull the whole head away from the body. It was done in the same way with the leaders of that nation: for sedition having arisen, and it having turned into an internal battle...

# THE COMPENDIUM OF HISTORIES BY GEORGE CEDRENUS

...two of the leaders fell, and the third was also struck, though not fatally; nevertheless, he was incapacitated by the wound, and thus the nation, having been weakened, returned home. Such were the results of his sorcery.

This sorcerer, **Iannes** <note>John VII Grammatikos, the iconoclast Patriarch of Constantinople (837–843 AD) often accused of magic by later historians.</note>, had a biological brother named **Arsabir** <margin>5</margin> <note>original: Ἀρσαβήρ</note>, who held the rank of patrician. This man owned a suburban estate on the left side of the **Stenum** <note>The "Stenos" or "Stenum" refers to the Bosphorus Strait, the narrow passage between the Black Sea and the Sea of Marmara.</note>, very near the monastery of Saint Phocas. It featured luxurious buildings, colonnades, baths, and other delightful places for leisure. The sorcerer made frequent visits there, and he constructed a subterranean dwelling similar to that of **Trophonius** <term>Cave of Trophonius: an ancient Greek oracular site known for its dark, narrow underground chambers where seekers supposedly communicated with spirits</term>. <margin>C 10</margin> Having fashioned small hidden gates to usher in those he wished, he received them in that wicked workshop. At times, nuns and other women of exceptional beauty were kept there as concubines, with whom he committed debauchery; at other times, he practiced **hepatoscopy** <term>hepatoscopy: the ancient practice of foretelling the future by inspecting the livers of sacrificed animals</term>, <margin>15</margin> **lecanomancy** <term>lecanomancy: a form of divination involving the observation of ripples or reflections in a basin of water</term>, sorcery, and **necromancy** <term>necromancy: the practice of communicating with the spirits of the dead</term>. Through these means, and often with the assistance of demons, he would predict future events. However, this property later came into the possession of the Emperor’s **chamberlain** <term>parakoimomenos: literally "one who sleeps beside [the imperial bedchamber]," a high-ranking court official, usually a eunuch</term>, who leveled it to the ground and built a monastery dedicated to Phocas the Great Martyr.

And as we have said, although he and his associates were subjected to <margin>20</margin> deposition <note>Being removed from their ecclesiastical offices.</note>, they did not remain quiet. <margin>D</margin> Instead, they continued to act insolently against the holy icons and plotted evil against the pious...

...[the enemy] failing, two of the leaders fell, and the third received a wound, but not a fatal one. Nevertheless, being rendered useless for further action by that event, the nation, deprived of its strength, returned home.

This Iannes had a biological brother named **Arsaverus** <note>The Latinized form of Arsabir.</note>, a patrician by rank. He held a suburban estate on the left side of the Stenum, very near the monastery of Saint Phocas, furnished with sumptuous buildings, colonnades, baths, and other works prepared for luxury. There, Iannes was accustomed to staying frequently; he made a certain subterranean dwelling similar to the Trophonian cave, in the back of which were doors for admitting people. Into that wicked workshop, he sometimes brought nuns and other women of remarkable beauty, and had relations with them; at other times, he practiced inspections of livers, divinations by the basin, and other deceits and the summoning of the dead. Often, with the help of demons, he predicted future things. This suburban estate was later acquired by the Emperor's chamberlain, who leveled it to the ground and built there a monastery named after the great martyr Phocas.

While cakes and pastries were being served, the Empress continuously gazed at the faces of the fathers, noticing the letters branded into their skin, and she began to sigh and weep. One of the fathers, noticing <margin>5</margin> this, asked why she looked at them so frequently. 

When she replied, “I marvel at your endurance, how you endured such letters being carved into your faces, and I lament the cruelty of the one who did this to you,” <margin>C</margin> the blessed Theophanes <note>Theophanes and his brother Theodore were known as the "Grapti" (the Written-Upon) because the iconoclast Emperor Theophilus had twelve lines of insulting verse tattooed onto their foreheads as punishment for their faith.</note> replied, “For this writing, O Lady, <margin>10</margin> we shall seek justice against your husband the Emperor at the incorruptible judgment seat of God.” 

At these words, the Empress was struck to the heart. With tears, she said to the saint, “Is this your promise and your written agreements? That you would not only fail to forgive him, but even call him to trial?” The Patriarch and the rest of the assembly of bishops, <margin>15</margin> calling her back and lightening the weight of her grief, rose and said, “Our agreements and treaties, O Empress, remain firm and <margin>D</margin> unshaken; it is best to ignore his [Theophanes'] slight <note>The bishops are attempting to soothe the Empress, who was terrified that her husband would be eternally damned despite her efforts to reconcile him with the Church.</note>.” 

Thus the Empress’s pain was calmed. At that time, a certain <margin>20</margin> heresy arose called that of the Zilici, named after its leader, Zilic, who served among the imperial secretaries <term>asecretis: A high-ranking official in the Byzantine imperial chancery responsible for drafting state documents.</term>. This heresy was quickly extinguished and vanished, as he and his followers were brought back to true piety and were perfected through anointing with the divine chrism <note>Holy oil used for reconciliation and confirmation.</note>. Such was the state <margin>24</margin> of affairs in the city.

During the banquet, when cakes and delicacies were served, the Empress frequently looked at their foreheads, and reading what was inscribed there, she groaned and wept. About this time a certain heresy called that of the Zilici arose, but together with its leader Zilic, who was of the rank of *a secretis*, it was extinguished and dissipated; he and his followers were converted to the true religion and perfected with the holy ointment. This was the state of affairs in the city.

Bogoris <note>Also known as Boris I, who ruled Bulgaria from 852–889 AD.</note>, the leader of the Bulgarians, having heard that a woman was ruling the Romans <note>Byzantine citizens referred to themselves as "Romans" (Rhomaioi) as the direct successors of the Roman Empire.</note> along with a tender child <note>Her son, the young Emperor Michael III.</note>, was moved to boldness. Once the entire nation had turned toward the worship of God, he wrote to the Empress <note>The Empress Theodora, acting as regent for her son Michael III.</note> requesting that land be given to him, as those under his rule were suffering from lack of space; in return, he <margin>10</margin> promised to unite the nations and establish a peace that would be eternal and unchangeable. # GEORGIUS CEDRENUS #

The men sent to carry out the decree—Leo (the son of Argyrus), Andronicus (the son of Ducas), and Sudalis—carried out their orders not with moderation but with savagery. Some they hung from gallows, others they put to the sword, and still others they consigned to various forms of torment. <margin>5</margin> Through these diverse and manifold methods of punishment, they destroyed approximately one hundred thousand men and confiscated their property. # GEORGE CEDRENUS #

Let us present this account to those who encounter it and trace the story from an earlier point. A certain disagreement arose between Manuel and the Logothete <term>Logothete</term> <note>A high-ranking administrative official, similar to a chancellor or prime minister; specifically the Logothete of the Course, Theoctistus, who managed the empire's internal affairs.</note> Theoctistus. Since both men were guardians of the Emperor and resided <margin>5</margin> within the palace, this dispute subjected Manuel to a charge of treason <note>original: "kathosioseos enklemati" — a crime of violating the sacred majesty of the Emperor.</note>. Manuel, fearing this charge and also dreading the envy of his peers, decided it was necessary to leave the palace and withdraw from constant <margin>D</margin> social interactions and the administration of affairs. He therefore retired to his own house, located near the Cistern of Aspar <note>One of the great open-air water reservoirs of Constantinople, built in the 5th century by the general Aspar.</note>, which he later converted into a monastery and where he was eventually buried <note>original: "ton choun ekeise katetheto" — literally "deposited his dust there."</note>. From there, <margin>10</margin> he would occasionally return to participate in administrative matters. 

Now Bardas <note>The Emperor's uncle and a powerful figure at court.</note>, having pushed Manuel aside—not by his own hand but through the actions of Theoctistus—hastened to seize the opportunity to achieve his own ambitions. Realizing that Theoctistus would naturally be an obstacle, he hurried to put him out of the way as well, especially since Theoctistus reproached him for <margin>15</margin> his secret intimacy with his own daughter-in-law. The beginning of this plot took the following form: Emperor Michael had a tutor who was ill-bred and wicked. The Emperor <margin>P 543</margin> wished to promote this man to high imperial ranks and grant him greater honors, and he urged both his mother and Theoctistus to agree. <margin>20</margin> However, he could not persuade Theoctistus, who said, "The affairs of the Empire should be administered with merit, not by the unworthy." The matter must be recounted from a slightly earlier point, so that it might become clearer to the reader. After the murder of Theoctistus, Bardas took the office of the <term>kanikleios</term> <note>The "Keeper of the Imperial Inkstand," one of the most powerful administrative positions, responsible for the emperor's private seals and the purple ink used for imperial signatures.</note> for himself. Since they could not bear her reproaches, and because Bardas was intent on pursuing his own goals, they decided to put her out of the way as well, so that they might thereafter do as they pleased without fear or hindrance. 

When she detected this (for she was a woman of great insight and foresight), she did not think she should

# A COMPENDIUM OF HISTORIES #

...besides these, there is much other varied wealth. <margin>a</margin> I am displaying this to you now, so that if, after my departure <margin>b</margin> from the palace, my son—who is also your Emperor—should say that I left the royal treasury empty of riches, he might not be easily believed." At the same time she spoke, she brought forward the keepers of the royal funds, who signaled their agreement with what she said. After greeting the Senate and resigning from every official duty and administration, the Empress left the palace.

But the royal wealth, though it was so vast and so great, brought no benefit because of the folly of Michael. For he delighted in horse-racing more than anyone else, and he did not even refuse to drive the chariots there himself. He would act as a godfather <note>The text refers to the Emperor "receiving children from the divine baptism," a spiritual sponsorship that usually involved a significant social and financial bond.</note> to the children of those who played, drove, and competed with him, and would then empty the royal treasury <margin>14 C</margin> by granting each of them one hundred and eighty, or at the very least fifty, pounds of gold. 

Once, he bestowed the rank of <term>patrikios</term> <note>A "Patrician," one of the highest honorary titles in the Byzantine court, usually reserved for the most senior officials and generals.</note> on a man named Himerius. He was given this name by way of irony <note>The name Himerius is derived from the Greek word for "longing" or "pleasantness," making it a cruel joke when applied to a man of such "wild" appearance.</note> because of the ferocity of his face. In flattery, he surpassed the Himerius who lived in the time of the Emperor Tiberius, and he acted as a buffoon at the table, using foul language and shamelessly breaking wind—while the Emperor and the guests were listening—so loudly that he even extinguished a candle with the noise. To this man, Michael gave one hundred pounds of gold. He also acted as godfather to the son of Cheilas, one of his fellow chariot-drivers, and gave him one hundred pounds of gold as well.

# THE COMPENDIUM OF HISTORIES BY GEORGE KEDRENOS #

<margin>D</margin> In this way, that man <note>The Emperor Michael III, known to later historians as "the Drunkard."</note> wasted and consumed the public funds on things of no value. Because he had exhausted such great wealth in a short time through such lawless actions, the time arrived for the distribution of the imperial gifts, but there was no supply of money. He then took the famous <term>Golden Plane Tree</term> <note>A celebrated mechanical marvel of the Byzantine court; it featured golden birds that would sing when air was pumped through the "branches."</note> and the two golden lions and the two <margin>5</margin> griffins—which were also made of beaten gold—as well as the solid gold organs and other works which made the Empire of the Romans an object of wonder, and which weighed no less than two hundred <term>centenaria</term> <note>original: "κεντηναρίων" – A centenarium was a unit of weight equal to 100 pounds of gold.</note>. He had these melted down and ordered the gold to be struck into coins in the royal treasury. He did much the same with the imperial robes; <margin>10</margin> some were made entirely of gold and others were woven with gold. He gave these to the <term>eidikos</term> <note>The "Logothete of the Eidikon," the official in charge of the imperial workshops and the private treasury.</note> so that these too might be melted down. However, he passed away from among men <note>A euphemism for Michael III's assassination in 867 AD.</note> before they could be melted, and <margin>P 545</margin> Basilius <note>Basil I, the founder of the Macedonian dynasty.</note> succeeded to the throne. He recovered the robes, having found nothing left of such vast wealth <margin>15</margin> except for three <term>centenaria</term> of gold and nine bags of <term>miliarisia</term> <note>A "miliarision" (μιλιαρίσιον) was the standard silver coin of the mid-Byzantine period.</note>. When he displayed these before the Senate, he lamented the poverty of the state and wondered how the public needs could ever be met.

<margin>B</margin> It was the custom of the Empress Theodora to visit the divine temple of the <term>Theotokos</term> <note>The "God-bearer" or Virgin Mary.</note> at Blachernae, both for the sake of <margin>20</margin> prayer and to use the bath there with her daughters. When the Emperor and her brother Bardas learned that she had gone there, they sent Petronas—whom history has recorded was her own brother—to forcibly cut her hair and make her a nun along with her daughters.

->10 The imperial robe.<-

---

...wasted the public funds. When he had squandered such vast resources through his wickedness in a short space of time, and the day appointed for the Emperor's donations approached, the means of providing money failed. He ordered the famous golden plane tree, the two golden lions and vultures—these too fashioned from gold with hammers—and other furniture made of solid gold, and other works for which the palace of the Roman Emperor was held in admiration, to be melted down. He commanded that the money struck from these be brought into his treasury. They weighed no less than 200 <term>centenaria</term>. He treated the imperial garments in the same way, of which some were entirely gold and others were interwoven with gold. For he gave these also to be melted down; but he was prevented by death before this could happen, so that Basilius, the successor to the empire, recovered them. Indeed, when Basilius took power, he found nothing remaining of such great riches except three <term>centenaria</term> of gold and nine small bags of <term>miliarisia</term>; having brought these into the Senate, he deplored the poverty and ordered a deliberation on how the public deficits could be repaired.

Besides these things, as Theodora had been accustomed to go to the shrine of the Mother of God at Blachernae, partly for the sake of praying and partly so that she might bathe with her daughters, the Emperor and Bardas, her uncle, noticed that she had betaken herself there at a certain time. They sent Petronas, whom we have shown above was also a brother of Theodora, to cut the hair of her and her daughters...

He supplied them with expenses on a large scale; and as he was a student of the good arts, he often attended the school himself, confirming the eagerness of the learners by his own example. In this way, he raised the liberal arts—which had previously been so completely extinguished that not a trace or a spark of them remained—to great prominence in a short space of time.

The same Bardas, having been made Caesar, frequently visited the judgments which were conducted in the Circus <note>the Hippodrome</note>, and he brought it about that the laws should flourish again, since through the fault of the times their accurate treatment had become obsolete. <margin>10</margin> after, having experienced divine wrath, they returned home. Meanwhile, another fleet from Crete was at one moment devastating the Cyclades islands and at another the entire coastline as far as Proconnesus.

<margin>15</margin> One of the greatest occurred on the day the Ascension of the Lord is celebrated. <meta>This page continues the history of the Byzantine Empire under Michael III (r. 842–867), contrasting his perceived incompetence and obsession with the hippodrome against the strategic wisdom of his predecessors, specifically regarding the "optical telegraph" or beacon system used for defense against the Saracens.</meta>

# GEORGE CEDRENUS

...of the chariot races at the church of the holy martyr *Mamas*, which had been built in the *Stenon* <note>original: "Στενῷ" (Stenon); meaning 'the Narrows,' referring to the Bosphorus strait</note>. It is worth not passing over in silence this particular account, as it serves to demonstrate both the stupidity of this emperor and the diligence of those who came before him.

<margin>5</margin> The emperors of old, wishing to make the incursions of the *Saracens* <note>a medieval term for Arabs or Muslims</note> against the lands of the *Romans* <note>the Byzantines referred to themselves as Romans</note> clearly known—so that they would not fall upon them suddenly, plundering the regions and capturing those living in the villages and fields—built a fortress near 
<margin>C</margin><margin>10</margin> *Tarsus* upon a very high and rugged hill. They gave this fortress the name *Loulon*. Now, whenever the guards in this place perceived a raid, they would light a beacon. Seeing this, those stationed on Mount *Argaeus* <note>a high volcano in central Turkey, modern Erciyes Dağı</note> would light another, and in turn, those on Mount *Isamos*. Seeing this again, those at *Aegialus* would light another, and then those at the place called 
<margin>15</margin> *Mamas*. Then *Kirkos* <note>or Cyrizus</note> would receive the signal, then *Mocillus*, and after that the hill of Saint *Auxentius* would make the raid known to the <term>diaetarioi</term> <note>palace stewards or officials in charge of specific quarters</note> appointed for this purpose in the Great Palace. And so, by this succession of 
<margin>D</margin><margin>20</margin> beacons, they provided knowledge to the emperor in an instant. Thus, the inhabitants of the regions, learning of the danger, would take refuge behind their walls and escape the raids. While such a custom was in effect, it once happened that while *Michael* was about to drive his chariot at the church of the martyr *Mamas*, the beacon from the *Pharos* <note>the lighthouse or signal tower within the palace complex</note> was lit. Wishing the incursions of the *Saracens* into *Roman* territories to be in no way ignored—lest they, rushing in unexpectedly, should devastate the regions and catch the inhabitants in the villages and fields—they had built a certain castle very close to *Tarsus* on a most lofty and naturally fortified hill, named *Lulum*. The guards stationed there, when they perceived the *Saracens* attempting an incursion, gave a signal by lighting a fire. Upon seeing this fire, those who kept watch on the hill of *Argaeus* did the same. Those on the hill of *Isamus* took up the signal from them, followed by those at *Aegialus*, and after them those at *Mamas*, then those at *Circus*, and from these to those at *Mocillus*, and finally, after these, those who held the station on the hill of divine *Auxentius* gave the sign by fire to the watchmen of the Great Palace that an enemy incursion was happening. By this order of fires following one another, the emperor was made certain of the enemy's attempt in a moment of time; and the country folk, having received the news, would shut themselves within their walls and avoid the enemy's attack. While this custom was maintained, it happened once that, while *Michael* was preparing himself to drive horses at the temple of *Mamas*, the fire was signaled from the *Pharos*. Once, having encountered a common woman returning from the bath and carrying a bucket in her hands (he happened to have become the godfather of her child through the holy font), he dismounted from his horse. He sent away the members of the Senate who were following him back to the palace there, but taking along the dissolute and whorish little men whom he had made his companions and was supporting, he went away with the woman. 

He took the bucket from her hands and said, "Come now, woman, be of good heart and receive me into your house, for I have a craving for bran bread and lime-cheese." <note>original: "ἀσβεστοτύρου" (asbestotyrou); literally "unslaked-lime cheese," a term for an extremely hard, dry, and low-quality cheese, emphasizing Michael's preference for "common" or "crude" tastes over imperial luxury.</note> 

When the woman stood frozen at these words, as she had nothing suitable for receiving a guest, Michael—faster than a word—took the linen cloth <note>original: "σινδόνα" (sindona)</note> which the woman had brought from the bath, and which was still soaked, and spread it on the floor instead of a tablecloth. Then, taking the woman’s key, he himself acted as the Emperor, host, cook, table-setter, and guest all at once. 

After dining with the woman, he returned to the palace on foot at a walking pace, condemning the great simplicity and vanity of the Emperors before him who had laid claim to proper decorum. All of these actions made the man hateful, and they justly stirred up everyone's anger against him.

There, either by providence or through simple ignorance, they pitched the Emperor’s pavilion on the flat ground, but they spread the Caesar's <note>Bardas held the title of Caesar, making him the second-most powerful man in the Empire, just below his nephew, the Emperor Michael III.</note> tent on a high, prominent hill. <margin>C</margin> <margin>20</margin> The supporters of Michael, who were hostile to the Caesar, seized upon this as a stroke of luck. They blamed Bardas for the incident, using it to fuel the Emperor's suspicions and incite him to act against his uncle. However, the great power and influence of the Caesar still unnerved them and made them hesitate to carry out their attempt.

For Michael, frequently drinking unmixed wine and becoming intoxicated, would give many absurd orders during his drunken fits—commanding that some have their ears cut off, others their noses, and still others their heads. **Basil** would prevent these things from happening, not so much out of concern for the others as out of fear for his own safety. <margin>5</margin> When Michael realized that Basil was an obstacle to him, he wove a great conspiracy against him. It was this: he instructed someone to hurl a spear, ostensibly aimed at a wild beast, but in reality aimed at Basil. This became clear when the man who had been ordered to do it confessed while he was at the point of death. <margin>10</margin> He did indeed hurl the spear, but he missed, and Basil was saved. <margin>P 557</margin> Having been saved, Basil was more eager to act than to suffer; and so Michael was slaughtered in the palace of **Saint Mamas** <note>An imperial palace and suburb located on the European shore of the Bosporus, favored by Michael III for its stables and hippodrome.</note>, in the year 6376 <note>original: ",ϛτοϛʹ". This is an Anno Mundi date (counting from the creation of the world) which corresponds to September 867 AD.</note>, at the third hour of the night. He had ruled with his mother for 14 years, and as sole monarch for 11 years. <margin>15</margin> Yet, even though he lived so discordantly and lawlessly, he was not entirely lacking in praiseworthy acts; for he presented a **communion set** <term>discopoterium</term> <note>original: "δισκοποτήριον" (diskopoterion). A liturgical set consisting of a paten (the plate for bread) and a chalice (the cup for wine).</note> to the Great Church <note>The Hagia Sophia in Constantinople.</note>, and **candelabra** <term>polycandela</term> <note>original: "πολυκάνδηλα" (polykandela). Elaborate multi-lamp chandeliers used to illuminate grand ecclesiastical spaces.</note> that far surpassed those that came before.

After Michael was killed, as we have said, Basil assumed the power of the empire. As to who this man was and where he had come from, and by what cause he ascended from a <margin>20</margin> humble and obscure fortune to the imperial heights, our account will explain by going back to the beginning. <margin>B</margin>

### COMPENDIUM OF HISTORIES. 189 ###

...that he was destined to bring about the reconstruction and growth of this present monastery. But the abbot, thinking that what he had seen was merely a phantom <note>original: *phantasma*, a dream or apparition</note>, took no account of what had been said, but instead <margin>D</margin> gave himself back over to sleep. Having seen the same vision a second time, and because he did not rouse himself—being somewhat sluggish and sleepy—he sees the martyr <note>Saint Diomedes, the patron of the monastery</note> for a third time, no longer commanding quietly and gently, but threatening him most severely and appearing to strike him with lashes, should he not quickly obey the instructions. 

Then, waking up in terror and shaking off his hesitation, he stands at the gateway and, according to the divine command, called out, "Basil!" And he immediately replied, "Here I am, lord; what do you command your servant?" Leading him inside the monastery, the abbot granted him the necessary care and attention and shared every hospitality with him. Then, having secured his silence and enjoining him not to let the matter be known to anyone but to keep the mystery to himself, he revealed to him the martyr's prophecy; and he begged him that, after the outcome of these events <margin>P 561</margin> he should remember both him and the monastery.

&emsp;&emsp;Basil was occupied with these things, but his mother longed to learn how things had gone for him on his journey and what sort of rest from his labors had received him. In her distress and anxiety, she saw <margin>C</margin> in her sleep a great plant resembling a cypress, standing inside her <margin>15</margin> courtyard, covered with golden leaves and having golden branches and a trunk, upon which her son Basil sat. Awakening, she told the vision to one of the pious women; the woman encouraged her to be of good cheer regarding her son and, interpreting the sight, declared that her son would become the **Emperor of the Romans** <note>The traditional title for the Byzantine Emperor.</note>. ...to have servants, and to adorn them with silk clothes and other distinguished dress. &emsp;&emsp;Meanwhile, his mother, desiring to know how her son’s journey had succeeded and what end to his labors he had obtained, while she was troubled in mind, imagined in a dream that she saw in her courtyard a large plant like a cypress, with a golden trunk, golden branches, and entirely shining with gold, and her son Basil sitting upon it. When she woke, she presented this dream to a certain religious woman. She told her to be of good heart on account of her son, and inferring the power of the dream, she pronounced that he would be the **Emperor of the Romans**. From that point on, Basil’s mother, having added this argument of her son’s future happiness to the previous ones, ceased to be anxious for him and, joyful in mind, nourished the best hopes.

He especially criticized the actions of the emperor's uncle, **Bardas the Caesar**. Eventually, the emperor—who was otherwise quite dull and sluggish in grasping affairs of state—was provoked to take notice, and he overturned or perhaps corrected some of the Caesar’s deeds.

The Caesar, unable to endure this, secretly plotted against Damianus. After that, the office of the **Chamberlain** <term>parakoimomenos</term> <note>original: "παρακοιμωμένου" (*parakoimomenos*); a high-ranking court position, literally "the one who sleeps beside" the imperial bedchamber, usually held by a trusted confidant</note> remained vacant for some time. While the **Caesar** <note>Bardas, the Emperor's uncle and the effective ruler of the state</note> and his faction tried to promote various candidates to this post, the providence of God—invisibly directing affairs as He willed—rendered all their wisdom and cunning useless. For after some time, the Emperor appointed **Basil** as Chamberlain, honoring him with the rank of **Patrician** <note>original: "πατρικιότητι" (*patrikios*); one of the highest honorary titles in the Byzantine hierarchy</note> as well. He also joined him in marriage to a woman who surpassed all her peers in physical grace, beauty, and modesty. 
<margin>D</margin> She was the daughter of **Inger**, a man renowned by all for his wisdom and noble birth, who belonged to the **Martinakios** lineage <note>The woman is Eudokia Ingerina, who remained the Emperor's mistress even after her marriage to Basil, a scandalous arrangement that secured Basil's status</note>. Once this was done, and the Emperor’s love for Basil continued to increase, the Caesar [Bardas] watched these events with a biting envy. Dreading what the future might hold, he frequently said to those who had persuaded him to get rid of **Damianos**:

> “By following your ill-advised plans, I have cast out a fox only to bring in a lion in its place, so that he might devour us all at once.”

Shortly after this, Emperor **Michael** set out on an expedition against the **Cretans** together with his uncle, **Bardas the Caesar**. However, Bardas began to handle affairs with increasing arrogance, gradually offending the Emperor and giving those around him cause for suspicion. When they arrived at **The Gardens** <note>original: "Κήποις" (*Kepoi*); a location on the coast of Asia Minor</note>—
<margin>P 566</margin> a coastal place where the **Maeander River** flows into the sea—it was there that a plot and a plan were devised by those around the Emperor. They intended to act first so that they would not be struck down themselves, and...

---

The office of the chamberlain was vacant: although the Caesar and his associates attempted to put first one man and then another in charge of it, God’s providence, secretly governing affairs by His own judgment, rendered all their cleverness and craftiness ineffectual. Some time later, the Emperor created Basil his chamberlain, also decorating him with the patrician dignity; he joined him to a wife whose beauty of form and modesty excelled all her equals, being the daughter of Inger, a man most famous for his prudence and nobility, of the Martinakios stock. This having been done, and the love of the Emperor for Basil growing ever stronger, Bardas, seeing these things and stung by envy and anxious for the future, often said to those by whose urgings he had removed Damianos:

> “By obeying your wicked counsels, I have driven out a fox and led a lion into its place, who will tear us all to pieces together.”

Afterward, Michael undertook an expedition with his uncle Bardas, and Bardas began to conduct affairs more insolently; by degrees he offended the Emperor and provided the occasion for sinister suspicions about himself. When they came to **Cepi** (which in Latin you would call "The Gardens" <note>original: "hortos"</note>), which is the name of a maritime place where the **Maeander River** flows into the sea, the Emperor and his followers entered into a council, lest they be overwhelmed by being anticipated by Bardas; and the matter having been settled and matured...

<margin>5</margin> broke camp and turned his thoughts toward returning to the **ruling city** <note>Constantinople</note>. Upon his return to **Byzantium**, since he lacked his own offspring, <margin>B</margin> he adopted **Basil** and raised him to the rank of **Magister** <term>magister</term> <note>original: "μαγίστρων" (*magistron*); one of the most prestigious administrative and honorary titles in the Byzantine court, second only to the Emperor and Caesar.</note>. **Symbatios** the **Logothete of the Course** <term>logothetes ton dromou</term> <note>original: "λογοθέτης τῶν δρόμου"; the official responsible for the imperial post, diplomacy, and internal security—effectively the Emperor’s foreign minister.</note>, who was the son-in-law of the Caesar Bardas, could not bear this out of envy. 
<margin>10</margin> Using the excuse that he could no longer live in the capital, he requested the governorship of the **Thracesian Theme** <note>original: "Θρακησίων ἐξαιτεῖ στρατηγίαν"; the Thracesian Theme was a major military province in western Asia Minor (modern Turkey).</note>, and indeed he received it. A short time passed, and the empire was being steered dangerously, since the Emperor Michael focused his mind on other things and 
not on the administration of affairs. The death of Bardas clearly exposed the Emperor’s 
<margin>15</margin> worthlessness and lack of sophistication. For while Bardas had been watchful as a partner in affairs and had held onto the administration as much as possible, the Emperor’s insignificance had been covered by his care and diligence. But when Bardas was slaughtered and the entire care of the empire <margin>C</margin> fell upon the Emperor alone, then his 
<margin>20</margin> unfitness and his negligence toward political actions were clearly exposed. Consequently, there were constant grumblings from the common people against the Emperor; neither the Senate nor the citizenry were pleased with what was being done, and even the army itself happened to be stirred up and agitated. The Emperor heard of these 
things through his closest associates—

Bardas, having embraced the feet of the emperor, was slaughtered; this matter was explained by us above. This was done on the first day of April, in the 14th indiction. After Bardas was killed, the emperor, having abandoned the expedition, immediately returned to Byzantium. Having returned there, since he lacked offspring, he adopted Basil and raised him to the dignity of the mastership (*magisterium*). When Symbatios the logothete of the course, the son-in-law of Bardas, could not endure this because of envy, pretending that he could not live in Constantinople, he sought and obtained the command over the Thracesians. A little time flowed by, when it became sufficiently clear that the empire was being governed dangerously, inasmuch as Michael was intent on matters other than managing the state, and his futility and folly became openly known from the death of Bardas. For indeed Bardas, as one who was a colleague of the emperor, kept watch for the state and was intent on its administration to the best of his ability; by his industry and diligence, he had hidden the laziness of Michael. With Bardas removed, and all the care of the empire leaning upon Michael alone, it appeared clearly what sort of man he was: inept and sluggish at handling the state. Therefore, there were frequent complaints from the subjects about the emperor, and his acts were approved of neither by the senate nor the citizens; and even the armies themselves grew fierce and were driven to unrest. <margin>15</margin> Having just ascended to power, **Basil** first appointed to high offices men who were said to be most resistant to bribes and who were attested to keep their hands clean of any kind of illicit gain. He also appointed judges, elevating them with salaries and various honors, <margin>D</margin> and he commanded them to spend the whole day in court resolving the disputes of those in conflict.

<margin>5</margin> He set aside suitable places for the judges, specifically the Magnaura <term>Magnaura</term> <note>original: "Μαγναύραν"; a grand hall in the Great Palace of Constantinople used for receptions and as a seat of high learning.</note>, the so-called Hippodrome, and the place known as the Chalce <term>Chalce</term> <note>original: "Χαλκῆν"; the "Bronze Gate," which served as the ceremonial main entrance to the imperial palace complex.</note>. This gate, which had suffered from the passage of time and was in danger of collapsing at any moment, he repaired and renovated. He also ordained a provision of food for the poorer litigants so that they would not be forced by the pressure of poverty to abandon their legal cases. He personally devoted himself to this work whenever he was free from military campaigns and from the business of receiving embassies from abroad. He would go down to the so-called *Genikon* <term>Genikon</term> <note>original: "γενικὸν"; the General Treasury, the department responsible for land taxes and general revenue.</note> and examine those from whom the state was collecting taxes, ensuring that no one was being <margin>P 569 10</margin> unfairly exploited; in this way, he came to the aid of those who were being wronged. It is said that once, when he went down to the aforementioned place of study and judicial business <note>original: "διατριβήν" (*diatribēn*); often a place for scholarly or legal discourse.</note>, he found no one bringing a complaint. Suspecting that those in need might be being blocked by certain officials from gaining access to him, he sent several of his bodyguards to various parts of <margin>15</margin> the city to seek out anyone in need of assistance. When they returned saying they had found no one at all, he shed a tear of joy and offered his thanks to God.

Observing also that wicked men found opportunities for injustice in the shorthand symbols used for numbers—I refer to the fractions of a half, a sixth, a twelfth, and the like—where the scribes used the ancient <margin>B 20</margin> notations, he wished to remove this opportunity from those who chose to do wrong. He decreed that such figures must be written out in plain letters, which would be easy for even uneducated country folk to read...

...to judge. For this purpose, he designated suitable locations: the Magnaura, the Circus (Hippodrome), and the Chalce (the Bronze Gate), which he restored and adorned as it was suffering from the fault of time and threatening to fall. He also arranged sustenance for the poorer people who were involved in legal disputes, lest they be forced by want to desert their bail. He himself also gave attention to these matters whenever he was free from war and from hearing ambassadors. Descending to the *Genikon*, where the public taxes and tributes are received, he looked out to see that nothing was unjustly exacted from anyone, and he brought aid to those who suffered injury. They say that once, when he had descended to the *Diatriba* (the name of the place where judgments were exercised) and found no one complaining, he suspected that those who desired to speak with him were being kept away by certain men. He sent his attendants through the city to ask if there were any in need of the emperor's help. When they returned and said they had found no one, he shed tears of joy and gave thanks to God.

### A COMPENDIUM OF HISTORY ###

...ordered signs to be written, personally paying for the cost of the paper, the ink, and the scribes.

He also turned his attention to the affairs of the Church. By means of a convened synod, he removed Photius from the high priesthood—as Photius had jumped into the office <note>original: "ἐπεισπηδήσαντα" (epeispēdēsanta); suggesting an illegal or forceful entry into power</note>—and ordered the seat to remain vacant until God should restore the man who had been rightfully appointed to it. In Photius's place, he brought back Ignatius, who had been wickedly and unlawfully expelled by the Caesar Bardas <note>Bardas was the uncle of the previous Emperor Michael III and a powerful statesman who had clashed with the traditionalist Ignatius.</note>. In this way, he ensured that the churches of God would return to a state of calm. <margin>C</margin>

<margin>10</margin> Furthermore, seeing that the civil laws were full of great obscurity and confusion, he hastened to restore them in a fitting and useful manner. He intended to strip away the useless parts of the laws that had been abolished and to clarify the vast number of those still in force. However, he did not have enough time, as he was overtaken by death. The work was begun by him, but it was Leo, his son, who completed it thereafter. <note>This refers to the *Basilika*, a 60-volume Greek codification of Roman law that replaced the older Latin codes of Justinian.</note>

<margin>15</margin> During the first year of Basil's reign, a plot and conspiracy was formed against him, led by the patricians <term>patricians</term> <note>original: "πατρικίων"; a high-ranking honorary title in the Byzantine court.</note> George and Symbatios. When the crime was discovered and the evidence became manifest, <margin>D</margin> <margin>20</margin> these two were blinded, as they were the primary instigators of the plot. The rest of the multitude of conspirators were paraded in a mocking procession and then sent into exile. To thwart further plots against the crown, Basil crowned his own sons, Constantine and Leo.

# GEORGE CEDRENUS #

In the third year of his reign, he also proclaimed his son Alexander as emperor. His youngest son, Stephen, he enrolled in the holy service of God’s church. <note>Stephen later became the Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople.</note> Since he also had four daughters, he consecrated them as well in the divine sanctuary of the all-praised martyr Euphemia.

Having thus arranged his domestic affairs to his satisfaction, as it seemed, he made haste to lead an expedition against those set in opposition to the Roman Empire <note>original: "Ῥωμανίᾳ" (Romania); the contemporary term for the Byzantine Empire</note>. Indeed, the military rolls had been diminished under the former ruler, <margin>P 570</margin> Michael <note>Michael III, Basil's predecessor.</note>, because their annual pay <term>annual pay</term> <note>original: "ῥόγας" (rhogas); a standard cash salary for Byzantine soldiers and officials</note> and grain rations <term>grain rations</term> <note>original: "σιτηρέσια" (sitēresia)</note> had been cut off. Basil replenished the ranks through a recruitment of new men and led the phalanxes against the barbarians. He first moved against Tephrike <note>Tephrike (modern Divriği, Turkey) was the fortified capital of the Paulicians, a heretical Christian sect that formed a breakaway state allied with the Abbasid Caliphate.</note>, which was led by Chrysocheir, a man considered to excel in courage and intelligence, who had been severely overrunning and plundering the lands of the Romans. The emperor led his army against this man and his city. However, Chrysocheir did not withstand the assault but retreated within the walls. After the emperor had overrun and plundered all the territory under his control, he pitched his camp right at the wall of Tephrike, thinking he could capture the fortress through a long blockade. But when he realized it was <margin>B</margin> heavily fortified on all sides, and that there was no hope of it being taken by siege (since all the necessities in the surrounding countryside had already been consumed), he lifted the siege, having first stormed and destroyed the forts near Tephrike.

*It was no small advantage that they were to launch their attack on the enemy from a high position, as the enemy had made camp in the valley. They divided the entire army into two parts, so that a select group of six hundred soldiers with their leaders would rush the enemy, while the remaining few stood on the heights, feigning a great multitude. They arranged the matter so that when the first group attacked the enemy, the others would immediately let out a terrible shout with great applause and sounding trumpets, with the mountains echoing at the same time. With these things prepared, they reached the enemy's camp secretly through the night, before the sun could light the tops of the mountains. Singing a song of praise with a great voice and shouting "The Cross has conquered," they attacked the enemy, while the rest from the mountain let out a military shout. The barbarians were suddenly terrified by this unhoped-for event; they could neither gather together, nor have time to observe the multitude of enemies rushing upon them, nor could they take any safe counsel at all in that moment, but gave themselves over to flight. The Romans followed them and called upon the absent legions and their leaders, as well as the Domestic of the Schools, just as had been commanded. With the terror and tumult of the fugitives increased, the Romans followed them for thirty miles, covering the intervening space with the countless corpses of the enemy.*

Recognizing the man, he turned to him and said: "What evil have I done to you, wretched Poulades, that you pursue me so furiously, desiring to kill me?" To which Poulades briefly replied: "I trust in God that on this day I shall return thanks to you according to your merits." From there Chrysocheir proceeded, dazed and senseless, with Poulades boldly following until they reached a deep ditch. When Chrysocheir's horse would not permit him to jump across, he was quickly struck in the side with a spear by Poulades and fell from his horse, unable to bear the pain. A certain man named Diaconitzes was present. He immediately leaped from his horse and took up the task of caring for Chrysocheir, placing the head on his own knees and weeping over this misfortune. Meanwhile, Poulades' other companions caught up, and leaping from their horses, they cut off the head of the already failing and dying Chrysocheir; they bound Diaconitzes and placed him among the captives. Immediately, a messenger of the successfully completed matter was sent to the emperor along with the head of Chrysocheir. And with him thus killed, all the vigor and strength of Tephrike withered away. This, therefore, was the end of the Tephrikan matter, and the multitude of Manichaeans, raised to the highest glory, vanished into smoke within the space of a single hour.

**Vocabulary:** George Cedrenus, Tephrike, Chrysocheir, Poulades, Diaconitzes, Manichaeans, Paulicians

When he saw that the besieged bore the attack bravely and undauntedly, he made a truce and asked them what they trusted in, that they were so calm of mind while their country was in imminent danger of destruction. One of the elders replied that they were certain the city would not be conquered by him at present, but by someone else of his lineage named Constantine; therefore, they were not terrified by this siege. And when Basil had shown them his son and said that he was called Constantine, that speaker replied that this was not the Constantine who would be the destroyer of this city, but another who would come much later from Basil's posterity. The Emperor, moved to anger by these words and desiring to show by the deed itself that this prophecy was false, applied himself to the siege with greater force than before. But when he saw that, despite everyone's exhaustion, nothing was being achieved, and at the same time a great frost arose and afflicted those living under the open sky, he broke off the siege and led his men home. While returning, he ordered the multitude of prisoners, who were a burden, to be slaughtered with the sword. Thus, with the army lightened, he continued the march begun toward the city, having struck great terror into the Hagarenes. Since he had foreseen that they would set traps for him in the narrows, he sent his soldiers to favorable places and captured many of the ambushers alive. By these events, the spirit of Abdelomeler, who was in charge of those places, was so broken that he sent legates to seek pardon and peace. The Emperor assented, and thereafter held him as a willing ally.

Because they were few in number due to their previous defeat by Andreas and were not a match for a pitched battle, they gathered many horses and tied dry hides to the horses' tails. <margin>5</margin> At a single command, they let them loose against many parts of the Roman <note>The Byzantines called themselves "Romans" (Rhomaioi).</note> camp. # A COMPENDIUM OF HISTORIES #

<margin>5</margin> The Terbuniotes, Canalites, Diocletians, and Rentani <note>These were Slavic tribes living in the regions of modern-day Montenegro, Herzegovina, and southern Dalmatia.</note>—having shaken off the yoke of the Roman <note>The Byzantines referred to their empire as the Roman Empire and themselves as Romans.</note> sovereignty to which they had long been subject, and having established their own autonomy—were also attacked, as the opportunity arose, by the <term>Agarenes<note>original: "Ἀγαρηνοί" (Agarenoi). A common Byzantine term for Arabs or Saracens, derived from the name of Hagar, the handmaid of Abraham.</note></term> from Carthage. These invaders, having appointed as their leaders Soldanos, Sabas, and Kalphous—men who were attested to surpass their fellow countrymen in military experience— <margin>P 577</margin> dispatched a fleet of thirty-six warships against Dalmatia. Before the ambassadors arrived, however, Emperor Michael [III] died, and the envoys reached Basil [I] <note>Basil I "the Macedonian," who succeeded Michael III in 867 AD.</note>. # GEORGIUS CEDRENUS #

...to experience misfortune, the King granted him freedom of speech and permitted him to live as his companion. But the Sultan, being deceitful and crafty, wove a plot against the <term>King<note>original: "ῥήξ" (rheks), a Greek transliteration of the Latin 'rex'. This refers to the Frankish ruler, likely Louis II.</note></term>, which eventually drove the King from Capua and secured the Sultan’s own return home. For he knew that <margin>5</margin> these two Italian cities, Capua and Benevento, having been only recently acquired by the King, did not maintain a firm loyalty to him, but were always dreaming of their liberty. Knowing also that the King was anxious about how to hold them securely and safely, he approached the King and said: <margin>D</margin> <margin>10</margin> "Seeing you, O King, constantly worried and concerned about how you might safely hold these Italian cities, I come to offer you a plan. Know then, most noble one, that your possession of these cities will never be secure unless you relocate their leading men to the ancestral lands of the <term>Franks<note>original: "Φράγγων" (Phrangon). The Sultan is suggesting the Lombard elites be deported to the Frankish heartlands to prevent rebellion.</note></term>. <margin>15</margin> For by nature, that which is enslaved against its will clings to the hope of freedom, and when it finds an opportunity, it breaks out into the rebellion it has been planning." Pleased by these words and thinking them to his advantage, the King decided to act accordingly. Consequently, iron collars and chains were being forged in secret, as if for some <margin>20</margin> urgent necessity. Having thus cleverly tricked the King, the Sultan then approached the leaders of the citizens (for he had become <margin>P 579</margin> familiar with them as well and spent time in their company constantly) and said to them: "I wish to reveal a secret to you, but I fear that if it is discovered, it will bring destruction to me and danger to you..."

...finding him wise, the King thereafter permitted him to meet and converse with him freely. But the Sultan, a crafty and versatile man, laid a trap for the King, by which he expelled him from Capua and secured his own return to his people. He knew that the two cities of Italy, Capua and Benevento, recently subdued by the King, did not remain constant in their loyalty but still dreamed of liberty; nor was he ignorant that the King was anxious about keeping them surely and safely. Therefore, addressing the King, he said: "I see that you are constantly meditating and taking care how you might keep these two cities surely in your power. Regarding that matter, I bring counsel. Know therefore that your rule over them will not be firm unless you deport their princes into <term>Francia<note>The Frankish kingdom.</note></term>. For it is so arranged by nature that those who serve unwillingly affect liberty, and when an opportunity is seized, they break out to obtain what they desire." The King found this speech pleasing, and thinking it to be to his benefit, he determined to carry it out. And so, bronze shackles and chains were secretly prepared, as if they were required for some other uses. But the Sultan, having mocked the King with this fabrication, approached the leading citizens (for he had prepared for himself a familiarity and frequent social intercourse with them) and showed that he held a secret which he would reveal to them, were it not for the fear that if it were made public, it would bring ruin to them and danger to himself.

...and imploring [help]. These he dismissed insultingly, responding that their destruction would be a joy to him. After the ambassadors returned without success, those under siege, having nowhere to turn and being reduced to the greatest difficulties by the assault, sent a messenger to **Basil**, Emperor of the Romans, demanding that he help them. The Emperor agreed; he immediately sent the messenger back to command his people to be of good cheer, and to announce that a sufficiently strong auxiliary force would soon arrive to rescue them from the danger. 

That messenger was captured by the enemy on his return. The Sultan, having him brought to him, said: “A choice is given to you: choose what is better. If you wish to be safe and to be moved by great gifts, tell those who sent you, so that everyone may hear, that the Roman Emperor has denied them aid; but if you report the truth, you will perish instantly.” The messenger promised that he would do what the Emir had commanded; and when they had approached the walls within the distance of a bowshot, he asked for the leaders of the city to come forward. When they were present, he addressed them thus: “Although, O fathers, certain death hangs over me and the sword is at my throat, I will not hide the truth, and I ask that you show gratitude to my wife and children. I, lords, although now in the hands of the enemy...”

# GEORGII CEDRENI #

He struggled to drive back the defenders from the walls. However, the people of Euripus, filled with courage and zeal, <margin>D</margin> bravely defended themselves from the walls with stone-throwing <term>engines<note>original: "ὀργάνων" (organon). Refers to mechanical artillery such as traction trebuchets or similar siege machinery.</note></term>, catapult bolts, bows, and stones thrown by hand. <margin>5</margin> Every day they killed many of the barbarians. Having observed a favorable wind, they launched their own triremes against the opposing ones and burned many with <term>liquid fire<note>original: "ὑγρῷ πυρὶ" (hygro pyri). Known to history as "Greek Fire," this was a state secret of the Byzantine Empire—a combustible liquid that could be sprayed from tubes and would continue to burn even on the surface of the sea.</note></term>. Faced with this helplessness, and knowing that the longing and love for money makes many men despise death, the barbarian [Esman] <margin>10</margin> placed a large shield in front of the palisade and, having filled it with gold, declared he would give this as a prize—along with a hundred choice captive maidens—to the first man to scale the wall and secure victory for his kinsmen. The people of the city, seeing this and immediately understanding the purpose of what was being done, encouraged one another with exhortations <margin>15</margin> and stirred themselves to valor. At a single signal, they threw open the city gates and bravely rushed out against the barbarians. <margin>P 581</margin> During the first encounter, the <term>Emir<note>original: "ἀμηρᾶ" (amera). A title for a Muslim ruler or military commander, derived from the Arabic 'Amir'.</note></term> received a fatal blow and fell; many others were killed along with him, and the rest turned to flight. <margin>20</margin> As the pursuers pressed upon them, they were slaughtered all the way to the remaining ships, and there was a great massacre of the barbarians. Those who remained filled a few of the ships and fled in shame to their own lands. And such was the end of the fleet from Tarsus.

He intended to repel those who protected the walls with missiles. There, those who were in the garrison of Euripus, filled with strength of mind, fought for the city with machines throwing rocks, ballistae, bows, and stones to be sent by hand; in this way they repeatedly struck down many of the barbarians. Having observed a favorable wind, they sent their triremes against the enemy and burned many of the enemy's ships with Greek fire. Boiling with anger at these things, Esman—knowing meanwhile that many despise death out of a desire for money—placed a great shield full of gold before the rampart. He promised he would give this, and a hundred of the most select captive virgins, as a reward to him who first climbed the wall and was the author of victory for his people. When the townsfolk saw this and immediately sensed what the aim of this matter was, they mutually exhorted each other to bravery. Once the signal was given, they opened all the gates and made a sharp attack upon the barbarians. In the first clash, the <term>Emir<note>original: "ameras". Latinized form of the Arabic title.</note></term> fell, having received a lethal wound, and many were killed with him. The rest, turned to flight while the <term>Romans<note>The Byzantine Greeks referred to themselves as Romans (Rhomaioi), a terminology preserved here in the Latin translation.</note></term> pressed on, hurried with a huge slaughter of their own people all the way to the remaining ships. The survivors of the barbarians, having filled a few ships, fled toward home with disgrace. This misfortune the Tarsian fleet held.

<summary>The defenders of Euripus successfully repel a Saracen siege using Greek Fire and a daring sally from the gates. The Emir of Tarsus is killed in the battle, leading to the total defeat and retreat of his fleet.</summary>

...was plundering **Methone**, **Pylos**, **Patras**, and the regions adjacent to **Corinth**. <note>These were major port cities in the Peloponnese (southern Greece) that were frequent targets for Arab pirate raids from Crete.</note> He [Oryphas] formed a prudent and wise plan. On the other side, however, when the enemy pressed upon **Procopius**, who was leading the **Slavs** and Westerners, and no reinforcements were sent to him by **Leo**—who clung to their discord—it happened that, as the line of his men gave way, he fell while fighting bravely. **Leo**, so that he might wipe out the disaster brought about by the disagreement with a distinguished exploit, took his army along with those **Procopian** soldiers who had escaped the slaughter and captured the fortress of **Tarentum**, which the **Agarenes** still held, taking everyone within as captives. Nevertheless, this did not pacify the Emperor; rather, once he recognized the cause of **Procopius’s** death, he stripped **Leo** of his dignity and banished him to **Cotyaeium**, where he used to live. Thereafter, **Baianus**, who was the chief of **Leo’s** grooms, and some others who were formerly **Leo’s** servants, brought an action of high treason against him. When **Bardas** and **David**, his sons, discovered this, they killed **Baianus**; and fearing for themselves from the angry Emperor because of this deed, they took their father and attempted a flight into **Syria**. The Emperor, informed of this matter, sent the prefect of the guard <note>The Latin "praefectum sodalitatis" corresponds to the Greek commander of the Hetaireia.</note> with certain soldiers, ordering them to pursue and capture them quickly. These men, without delay, overtook them in **Cappadocia**...

Likewise the church of **Philip the Apostle**, and the house of **Luke the Evangelist** which was situated toward the setting sun [the west] from this one, having suffered heavy ruin; and also the great temple of **Mocius the Martyr**, and its inner chamber which was leveled with the ground, even with the sacred table broken, he raised from the ruins. He restored to its original beauty the repaired church of **Andrew the Apostle**, called before the others, which was near those; likewise he reduced from old to new the churches of **Saint Romanus** and **Saint Anna** in the **Deuteron**, and of the great martyr **Demetrius**, and of the martyr **Aemilianus** in **Rhabdos**. He also restored the collapsed house of **Saint Nazarius**; and in the porticoes of the lord he adorned the repaired temple of the **Resurrection of Christ** and of **Anastasia the Martyr** with a roof, which had previously been wooden, now made of stone. He erected the shrine of **Plato**, the renowned martyr, which had collapsed; and nearby to this he established the shrine of the martyrs **Hesperus and Zoe**, distinguished by their noble victory. From the ruin that was threatening, he also rescued the church of **Acacius**...

Sandabarenos, realizing his snares were succeeding, met with the Emperor and indicated that a plot against his life was being stretched by his son. If he did not believe it, he should order Leo’s boots to be pulled off when they went out to hunt: if a knife were then found, he would understand that the monk's warning was correct. 

The monk having said this, Basil immediately announced a hunt and went out with the usual company. When they had come to a certain place, he feigned that he had need of a knife and demanded it quite vehemently. Thereupon Leo, who had known nothing of the suspicion conceived by his father, simply drew out the knife he was carrying with him and offered it to his father. Immediately, therefore, Sandabarenos’s warning was held as true, and Leo’s excuses were judged vain. 

Having returned home, the Emperor, with a hostile mind, despoiled his son of his imperial ornaments and shut him in a certain chamber of the palace named Margarites, and kept him there; and unless the Patriarch and the Senate had forbidden it, he would even have dug out his eyes (for he was being instigated to this by Sandabarenos). A great deal of time passed after this, until...

And although the Senate had many times wished to send an embassy to intercede on this matter, they were prevented in various ways and for various reasons. However, a reasonable pretext was eventually provided, which led them toward the goal of resolving the issues they were so concerned about. <margin>B</margin> There was a certain winged animal in a cage <margin>5</margin> hanging in the palace for the sight and delight of those watching and listening—the animal was called a "parrot" <note>original: "ψιττακὸς" (psittakos)</note>—a creature capable of mimicry and many voices. This bird, whether taught by someone or perhaps just by chance, frequently cried out: "Alas, alas, Lord Leo!" <note>original: "αἲ αἲ κύριε Λέον" (ai ai kyrie Leon)</note>. 

One day, while a banquet was being held for the Emperor and the leading members of the Senate were dining with him, <margin>10</margin> the bird frequently uttered the aforementioned cry. Growing somber, the guests at the banquet stopped eating and sat in deep reflection. Noticing this, the Emperor asked the reason for their abstinence from food. 

With their eyes filling with tears, <margin>15</margin> they said: "O Master <note>original: "δέσποτα" (despota)</note>, what food shall we eat, being thus rebuked by the voice of this unreasoning animal? We, who are considered rational and loyal to our masters, see that even this unreasoning beast calls out for its own master <margin>C</margin>, while we, living in luxury, have forgotten our master who has done no wrong. For if he is proven to be a wrongdoer who has prepared his right hand against his father, <margin>20</margin> we ourselves will be the ones to execute him, never having our fill of his blood. But if he escapes conviction for the crimes he was accused of, how much longer shall the slanderous tongue prevail against him?" 

Softened by such words, the Emperor then told them to sit down...

At length, the Senate having frequently attempted to intercede for Leo, but having been hindered by various other causes, finally such an opportunity for carrying out their proposal presented itself. In the palace, a certain bird that was an imitator of the human voice and of others lived suspended in a cage, by the name of parrot <note>original: "psittacus"</note>, so that it might delight the spectators and listeners. That bird, whether by chance or having been so taught by someone, was accustomed to cry out: "Alas, alas, Lord Leo." 

At a certain time, when the Emperor had invited the leading senators to a banquet and the bird was emitting that cry quite often, a sadness arose and the guests, setting aside their food and drink, sat lost in thought. When the Emperor noticed this and inquired after the cause of the matter, they, their eyes filled with tears, said: "How, O Emperor, can we take food, we who are rebuked by the voice of this beast, we who are believed to be composed of reason and devoted to our masters? This brute bird invokes the name of its master; we, given over to luxury, consign an innocent man to oblivion. For indeed, if Leo is convicted of plots structured against his father, we are all prepared to kill him with our own hands, nor will his blood suffice to satisfy us. But if the crimes charged against him are not demonstrated, how long, finally, shall a slandering tongue oppress him?" 

Softened by these words, the Emperor commanded them to be of good cheer for the present, promising that he would take care of the matter...

The Duke of Lombardy <note>The Greek text uses "Bardias," a common shorthand in this period for Longibardia (Lombardy) in Southern Italy</note>, who was the son-in-law of the King of the Franks, having learned of the death of the Emperor Basil, revolted from his alliance with the Romans <note>The Byzantines continued to refer to themselves as "Romans"</note> and took the whole region under his own control. When the Emperor learned of this, he dispatched the <term>Patrician</term> Constantine, the Master of the Table <note>Greek: "epi tes trapezis," a high-ranking court official responsible for imperial banquets</note>, against him <margin>C</margin> with the Western <term>themes</term> <note>Administrative and military divisions of the Empire</note>. At this time, there was also an eclipse of the sun around the sixth hour of the day <note>Noon</note>, so that the stars were visible; there were also violent blasts of wind, lightning, and terrifying thunder, as well as scorching thunderbolts, by which seven men were struck and killed on the steps of the Column of Saint Constantine in the Forum. Samos was also besieged by the Saracens, and the <term>Strategos</term> <note>Military governor</note> in command there, the <term>Patrician</term> Constantine Paspalas, was taken prisoner. <margin>D</margin> Meanwhile, the Emperor, overcome by his affection for Zoe, the daughter of Zaoutzes, honored her father with the title of <term>Basileopator</term> <note>Literally "Father of the Emperor"</note>; he created this rank himself, as it had not existed before. For Zoe, who was then most radiant in her beauty and elegance, had been married to the <term>Patrician</term> Theodore Guniazitzes; however, after he was treacherously murdered by poison, she became the Emperor’s concubine, even while his own wife was still alive, as has been mentioned.

In the following year, Stephen—the Emperor’s brother and the Patriarch—departed this life, and Antony [Kauleas] was appointed in his place.

The Duke of Lombardy, son-in-law of the King of France, having learned of Basil's death, revolted from the Roman alliance and claimed the entire territory for himself. Then also Samos was besieged by the Saracens, and its governor Constantine the <term>Patrician</term>, surnamed Paspalas, was also shut in and captured. But the Emperor, driven by his love for Zoe, called her father Zaoutzes the "Father of the Emperor," having devised a new dignity. For this Zoe, since she was easily the most outstanding of all women of that age in beauty, had married the <term>Patrician</term> Theodore Guniazitzes; but when her husband was craftily killed by poison, the Emperor kept her as a concubine even while his wife was still surviving, as was already said above.

### THE HISTORIES OF GEORGE CEDRENUS

...at the same time three or even four wives. However, the Patriarch <note>Nicholas I Mystikos, who served as Patriarch of Constantinople during this crisis</note> prevented this with all his effort.

In the month of June, Emperor Leo was invited by Constantine Lips <note>A high-ranking Byzantine official and admiral; the monastery he founded is known today as the Fenari Isa Mosque in Istanbul</note> to the monastery he had recently constructed near the Church of the Holy Apostles, in order to perform its dedication and <margin>5</margin> to dine there. Suddenly, a violent southwest wind <note>original: ἄνεμος λὶψ; there is a linguistic pun here between the name of the host, Lips, and the name of the wind</note> began to blow, shaking many buildings; it so terrified the people that everyone fled from their houses into the open air. However, a falling rain eventually calmed the storm.

When a fleet <margin>D</margin> of the Saracens <term>Agareni</term> <note>original: Ἀγαρηνῶν; a term used by Byzantine writers for Arab forces, suggesting they were descendants of Hagar</note> set out against the Romans <note>The Byzantines referred to themselves as "Romans" (Rhomaioi)</note>, the Emperor <margin>10</margin> appointed Himerius, the Logothete of the Drome <term>Logothete of the Drome</term> <note>original: λογοθέτην τοῦ δρόμου; one of the highest officials in the Empire, responsible for the public post, diplomacy, and internal security</note>, as the commander of the Roman fleet. Andronicus Ducas was also ordered to join him and fight against the Saracens.

But the chamberlain Samonas, being an implacable enemy of the Ducas family because of his previous capture by Constantine <margin>15</margin> <note>Constantine Ducas, the son of Andronicus, had previously captured Samonas when the latter tried to defect to Arab territory</note>, influenced one of Andronicus’s friends. He persuaded this friend to write secretly to Andronicus, warning him not to board the ships because Himerius had received a secret order from the Emperor—at the instigation of Samonas—to blind him.

When Andronicus received this letter, he refused to join Himerius. Because of this, Himerius was forced to engage the enemy alone on the 6th of October. <margin>20</margin> <margin>P 603</margin> Upon joining battle, he decisively routed and destroyed the enemy forces. When Andronicus learned of this victory and realized his own situation was now desperate <note>since his refusal to join the battle could now be seen as treason rather than self-preservation</note>, he gathered his relatives and servants and seized a certain fortress situated above Iconium <note>Modern-day Konya, Turkey</note>...

Many illustrious men were working toward the same end, that it might be permitted for a man to take three or four wives at once. In the month of June, Constantine the African <note>The Latin translator here interprets 'Lips' as 'Afer' (African), though the Greek refers to the name of the official</note> invited the Emperor to his monastery, which he had built near the sanctuary of the apostles, to attend its dedication and lunch. Thus, Himerius was forced to clash with the enemy alone on the sixth day of October, and he defeated and killed them.
