### GEORGE KEDRENOS

<margin>D</margin> [Leo] was the first to be granted the surname of the **Argyroi** <term>Argyrōn</term> <note>original: Ἀργυρῶν; meaning "the Silver Ones," a prominent noble family in Byzantium</note>, whether it was because of the purity of his life, his physical beauty, or the noble character of his nature. For this man so far surpassed the men of the time of *Michael* <note>Referring to Emperor Michael III (r. 842–867)</note> that he alone, with only his household servants, would break the lines of the *Manichaeans* <note>likely referring to the Paulicians, a dualist Christian sect often allied with the Arabs</note> from *Tephrike* and the *Hagarenes* <note>a term used for Muslims/Arabs, claiming descent from Hagar</note> from *Melitene*, easily putting them to flight. Indeed, it is said that the mere mention of his name was enough to strike terror into all his enemies.

For the purpose of an **exchange of prisoners** <term>allagiou</term> <note>original: ἀλλαγίου; a formal diplomatic procedure for swapping captives between the Empire and the Caliphate</note>, envoys were sent from *Tarsus* and *Melitene*: the famous *Abelbakis* and the father of *Samonas*. They arrived at the reigning city [Constantinople]. The Emperor received them by hosting a great banquet and magnificently decorating the *Magnaura* <note>a grand ceremonial hall in the Great Palace of Constantinople used for receiving foreign dignitaries</note>.

<margin>P 605</margin> He also adorned the Great Church [Hagia Sophia] sumptuously and led them inside, showing them all the precious items and the vessels used in the divine liturgy. This act was considered unworthy of a *Christian* state—to make a spectacle for foreigners and unbelievers of those things which are not even to be seen by the pious if they are not living a good life. But when the father of *Samonas* witnessed the freedom of speech his son possessed with the Emperor, and saw his honor and glory, he chose to stay with his son, renouncing his homeland of *Melitene*. However, *Samonas* would not permit this; instead, he advised him to return to his own people and hold to his own faith, and to wait for him there, should he find a favorable opportunity to join him. He also built a monastery for him in Nossiai <note>a district in Constantinople</note> in the name of the Savior, which he dedicated along with the Patriarch Euthymius. Then, the Agarenes <note>original: Ἀγαρηνῶν; a Byzantine term for Arabs, referring to their traditional descent from Hagar</note> set out with three hundred ships, led by Damian, the Emir of Tyre, and Leo of Tripoli. 
<margin>5</margin> Himerius the *logothete* <note>a high-ranking administrative official</note>, who was the admiral of the Romans <note>the Byzantines referred to themselves as Romans</note>, <margin>C</margin> encountered them at Samos in the month of October. Romanos Lekapenos <note>the future Emperor Romanos I</note> was then serving as the governor <note>original: ἐστρατήγει; the strategos or military commander</note> of that region. Engaging in battle with them, Himerius was defeated, and after the ships under his command were scattered, he himself barely escaped safely to Mitylene.

<margin>10</margin> The Emperor was then seized by a bowel ailment <note>original: κοιλιακῷ νοσήματι; likely dysentery or a similar wasting gastric disease</note>, and having been worn down by this affliction for some time and driven to the point of extreme weakness, he was barely able to deliver the customary public address during the season of fasting <note>referring to the Lenten period preceding Easter</note>. When the Senate had assembled, he began his speech to them with these words: 
<margin>15</margin> "My friends, my poor body, wasted by disease, has failed; my strength has left me, and perhaps I shall no longer live among you, nor shall I reach the day of the <margin>D</margin> resurrection of Christ our Lord <note>Easter</note>. Therefore, I ask of you this one final favor: to remember the good-will I had toward you, and in return for this, to maintain your loyalty to my wife 
<margin>20</margin> and to my son." Such was the Emperor's address. The Senate, weeping and with many lamentations, replied that they were consumed by inconsolable grief at being deprived of such a master and emperor, but that they would maintain their loyalty to the Lady <note>Empress Zoe Karbonopsina</note> and to our master and emperor, your son, so that, if...

<margin>P 607</margin>
Upon seeing Alexander, as they say, coming for his final meeting, Leo is said to have remarked: "Behold the evil time after thirteen months." <note>original: ἴδε ὁ κακὸς καιρὸς μετὰ ιγ' μῆνας; this was seen as a prophecy, as Alexander would die after reigning for only thirteen months</note>. Therefore, having handed over the power of the empire as stated, and having strongly urged Alexander to raise his son Constantine and deem him worthy of proper care, and finally to leave him as his successor, he passed away.

<note>The following description of Leo's character and scholarship is found in some manuscript versions of the text:</note>
*This emperor was devoted to learning, especially to predictive astronomy <note>original: ἀποτελεσματικῇ; often referring to astrology or the calculation of celestial influences</note>. His letters and other works also circulate, full of all learning, fashioned after the ancient style. He also read the works of Archimedes accurately, like no other of his time.*

Alexander, the brother of Leo, being already a young man and passing his twentieth year, took up the reins of the empire upon Leo's death, with the boy Constantine, son of Leo, reigning alongside him. As soon as he ascended

# GEORGE CEDRENUS

...those who had been his companions before his reign—ministers and partners in his licentious deeds—he showered with vast amounts of wealth and elevated to the dignity of the patriciate <note>The rank of "Patrician" was one of the highest honorary titles in the Byzantine court, usually reserved for senior governors and high-ranking relatives of the Emperor</note>. It is said that he intended, had God not prevented it, to raise Basilitzas to the imperial throne and to castrate his own nephew, Constantine <note>Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus, the young son of the late Leo VI. Castration would have legally barred him from ever becoming Emperor</note>.
<margin>5</margin> And this would have surely happened, had not God first intervened, as has been said, and then those who remained loyal to Leo, the boy’s father. They obstructed him, at one time saying the boy was a mere infant, and at another that he was sickly.
<margin>P 608</margin> Thus, by gradually leading Alexander astray with such talk, they saved the boy until death overtook the Emperor. During his reign, a comet appeared in the West, which those skilled in such matters call *Xiphias* <note>original: ξιφίαν; literally "sword-shaped." Comets were traditionally viewed as omens of impending doom or change</note>. They said this signified a shedding of blood in the capital.

The Emperor, however, having surrendered himself to charlatans and sorcerers,
<margin>15</margin> inquired whether his reign would be long-lasting.
<margin>B</margin> They promised him a long life if the bronze wild boar standing in the Hippodrome <note>The great stadium of Constantinople, used for chariot racing and public ceremonies</note>—which lacked genitals and teeth—received these parts from him. For they claimed this was clearly his "talisman" <term>stoicheion; an object believed to be magically linked to the destiny or health of a person or city</term>; for it was said to be "fighting against the Lion"—referring to his brother, Leo.
<margin>20</margin> Persuaded by them, the man who truly "lived like a pig" <note>original: χοιρόβιος (choirobios); a pun on his devotion to the bronze boar and his own gluttonous lifestyle</note> restored the missing parts to the swine. Caught up in such madness, he held chariot races, taking the sacred veils from the churches and the holy lamps and candelabra to decorate the Hippodrome.

->8 The word "as" after "but" is omitted in Manuscript C. 10 Manuscript C uses "they saved" (a different verb form). 20 Manuscript C reads "pig-like."<-

Having used the ministers and associates of his lusts, he raised them, enriched by lavish gifts of money, to the patrician dignity. It is reported that he intended to make Basilitzas his successor and to castrate Constantine, the son of his brother Leo. And he would have accomplished this, had not God especially hindered him, and had those who remained faithful to Leo not resisted—saying at one time that Constantine was still just a boy, and at another that he was infirm. Thus, by gradually coaxing Alexander, they stalled him until death intercepted his plans. During this reign, a comet, which is called *Xiphias* from its resemblance to a sword and is said to portend the shedding of blood in the city, appeared from the West.

Furthermore, when Alexander had given himself over to impostors and jugglers, and inquired of them whether his rule would be of long duration, he received the response that he would live a long time if he added the genitals and teeth (for these were missing) to the bronze boar which was in the Circus <note>The Latin term for the Hippodrome</note>. For they claimed that this was undoubtedly the talisman of Alexander, struggling against his brother Leo. This was persuaded to a man truly leading a porcine life, and he restored those parts of the boar. Seized by this folly, when he gave equestrian games, he used ecclesiastical hangings and sacred candelabra for the purpose of adorning the Circus...

<margin>B</margin> They wrote to him that the empire was headless and was being poorly managed, and was in no small danger of falling into a disastrous ruin. With auspicious acclamations following him, he occupies the Chalke; entering through it, he proceeds as far as the station of the Excubitors. Meanwhile, John Eladas the *magistros*, one of the guardians, having selected rowers and companions as the occasion allowed, and having equipped them with whatever weapons chance offered to each, ordered them to confront Ducas. By this event, Ducas was not lightly disturbed; to encourage his men, he spurred his horse to the front lines. But the horse collapsed on the stone slabs with which that place was paved, and someone, seeing him thrown and lying on the ground, deserted by his men who had all been scattered in flight, cut off his head with a sword and brought it with a swift run to the Emperor Constantine. The guardians had also learned of this future end for Ducas from another source. For a certain Nicolaus, a public collector of the Chaldian tax, when he had squandered the tax he had received and had no means to satisfy the public treasury, had fled to Syria; having renounced our religion, he had given himself to astrology. # GEORGE CEDRENUS #

...as he [the young Emperor] did not understand what was being done, how did you dare to commit such deeds without his command? The regents <note>These were the guardians of the child-emperor Constantine VII, led by Patriarch Nicholas Mystikos</note> also tonsured the wife of Ducas <note>Forced her to become a nun</note> and sent her away to her home in Paphlagonia <note>A region on the northern coast of Asia Minor (modern-day Turkey)</note>. They also castrated her son, Stephen.

<margin>5</margin> While these things were being carried out in the city, Simeon, the ruler of Bulgaria, made an invasion against the Romans <note>Byzantine Greeks continued to call themselves "Romans" (Rhomaioi)</note> with a heavy force. Reaching the imperial city, he surrounded it with a fortified camp from Blachernae <note>The northwestern district of Constantinople where a major imperial palace was located</note> as far as the so-called Golden Gate <margin>B</margin> <note>The main ceremonial entrance at the southern end of the city's land walls</note>. <margin>10</margin> He was high in his hopes of easily capturing the city. However, when he learned of the strength of the walls, the multitude of those guarding them, and the abundance of stone-throwing and bow-firing engines, he abandoned his hopes and retreated to the Hebdomon <note>A suburb seven miles from the city center</note>, requesting a peace treaty.

The regents received this proposal most gladly. Simeon sent <margin>15</margin> his own *magistros* <term>magistros: a high-ranking administrative official</term>, Theodore, to discuss peace. After many words had been exchanged, the Patriarch, along with the other regents, took the Emperor to the Palace of Blachernae. After giving notable hostages, they brought Simeon into the palace, and he dined with the Emperor. <margin>20</margin> <margin>C</margin> Simeon bowed his head to the Patriarch and received a prayer from him; the Patriarch, as they say, placed his own *epirrhiptarion* <term>epirrhiptarion: a monastic veil or head-covering</term> upon the barbarian’s head instead of a crown <note>This was a famous diplomatic gesture; Simeon wanted to be recognized as Emperor, but the Patriarch cleverly used his own veil to perform a "blessing" that looked like a coronation to the Bulgarians but carried no legal weight for the Byzantines</note>. After the feast, since they could not reach an agreement on the terms of the peace, Simeon and his sons were sent off to their own country with gifts. And so, these things were done in this manner.

Since the young Emperor Constantine was continually mourning and calling for his mother (for Alexander <note>The Emperor Alexander, brother of Leo VI, who ruled briefly from 912 to 913 and had banished Zoe from the palace</note> had already removed her from the palace), the regents brought her back up, even if they did so reluctantly. Once she had returned and gained control of the government, she brought into her service Constantine the *parakoimomenos* <term>parakoimomenos: literally "the one who sleeps beside" the imperial bedchamber; the highest-ranking eunuch official and often the Emperor's closest advisor</term>, as well as Anastasios and <margin>5</margin> Constantine, the brothers surnamed Gongylios. <margin>D</margin>

On the advice of John Eladas, they dismissed the associates of the late Emperor Alexander: John the *rector* <term>rector: a high-ranking administrative official, often acting as a deputy for the emperor</term>, Gabrielopoulos, Basilitzes, and the others. Zoe <margin>10</margin> *Augusta* <note>Augusta: the title used for the Empress</note> also promoted Dominicus to the rank of *hetaireiarches* <term>hetaireiarches: the commander of the imperial bodyguard, known as the Hetaireia</term>, as he seemed to be an active man and devoted to her commands. On his advice, the Patriarch <note>Nicholas Mystikos, the head of the church who had been leading the regency council</note> was expelled from the palace. The *magistros* <note>original Latin: "magister"</note> John Eladas also left voluntarily, having been seized by a disease from which he later died.

Constantine the *parakoimomenos*, wishing to take all <margin>15</margin> the reins of government into his own hands and to have no one to hinder him, slandered the *hetaireiarches* to the Empress, claiming that <margin>P 612</margin> he was attempting to seize the throne for his own brother. Persuaded by these words, she honored Dominicus with the title of *patrician*, but when he came down to receive his blessing as was customary, she ordered him to remain at home <note>Essentially a polite form of house arrest or forced retirement</note>. <margin>20</margin> In his place, she appointed John Garidas as *hetaireiarches*, and Damian, a newly-appeared eunuch, as the *drungarios* of the watch <term>drungarios of the watch: the commander of the Vigla, an elite regiment responsible for guarding the palace and the emperor on campaign</term>.

While Simeon <note>The powerful Tsar Simeon I of Bulgaria</note> was plundering and carrying off spoils from the regions of Thrace, and while the Empress was deliberating with the high officials on how they might stop his raids, John Bogas, a *patrician*, promised...

A battle was joined between the Romans and the Bulgarians at the fortress of Achelous, and the Bulgarians were pushed back and laid low with great slaughter. There, when the Domestic, dripping with much sweat and fainting in spirit, had dismounted from his horse at a certain spring to wash away the sweat and refresh himself, the horse by chance broke its bond and rushed away, running through the army empty of its rider. When the soldiers recognized it, thinking the Domestic had died, their minds were struck with fear, and they ceased from the pursuit of the enemy; some even turned themselves back. Simeon, seeing this from a high place (for he was not making his flight in a scattered way or with broken ranks), sent his men against the Romans. The Romans, already dejected in spirit and trembling, seeing the enemy suddenly rushing in, immediately turned their backs. That flight was most perilous, some trampling one another, others being slain by the enemy. Leo the Domestic escaped by flight to Mesembria. Not only did a military multitude perish then, but also innumerable leaders and commanders of the ranks. Also killed were Constantine the African and the leader of the Excubitors, John Grapson. Romanos Lakapenos the patrician had been sent, the drungary of naval affairs, with the whole fleet, ordered to hug the shore and be a help to Leo and to the Patzinaks brought by Boga to bring aid to the Romans...

A little later, Leo Phocas, by the persuasion of his kinsmen and the encouragement of the armies, attempted a revolution; and having summoned Constantine the chamberlain, the brothers Constantine and Anastasios Gongylios, and Constantine Malelianus, he strove to persuade everyone that he was bearing arms for the emperor Constantine. But Romanos [issued] a diploma, by which the undertaking of Leo was refuted, written and [signed] by the hand and seal of the emperor...

...whom I no longer consider a subject, but pronounce a deserter and a tyrant; who without my command has devised this rebellion so that he might transfer the empire to himself. When Simeon had reached the camp, and the decree sent to the army had been read and its meaning understood, all began to defect from Leo to Romanos, the father of the emperor. Leo at first tried in vain to block the reading of the decree, but soon seeing himself deserted by his men, he sought safety in flight as the situation became desperate. Accompanied by a few of his most faithful followers, he reached the castle named Ateous. Driven back from there, he occupied the castle named Goeleontos—as if it were the "Lamentation of Leo," surely a bad omen. There he was captured by Michael the Heavy and many others in an organized attack. Men were therefore sent to lead him back to Constantinople: John Tubaces and Leo Pastelas. These men tore out his eyes, whether by a secret order of Romanos, as some say, or by their own accord, as Romanos asserted—who also appeared to take this badly as if it were done against his will. Yet another conspiracy was formed against Romanos by a certain <margin>D</margin> Constantine Ktematenos, David Koumoulianos, and Michael, the curator of the Mangana <term>Mangana: An imperial estate in Constantinople that served as an arsenal, judicial center, and monastery</term>. ### A COMPENDIUM OF HISTORIES ###

On the day of holy <term>Pentecost: A major Christian feast day occurring fifty days after Easter</term>, Romanos crowns <margin>B</margin> his own son, Christopher. This was done through Constantine <note>Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus, the legitimate young emperor</note>, who appeared to willingly accept the act on the surface due to the pressure exerted on him, but in secret, he was distressed and mourning his own misfortune. These two alone <note>Christopher and Constantine VII</note> took part in that imperial procession. In the month of July, during the eighth <term>Indiction: A fifteen-year tax and chronological cycle used in the Byzantine Empire</term>, the union of the Church took place. This reconciled the differing metropolitans and clergy who had been divided since the time of the Patriarchs Nicholas and Euthymios <note>This refers to the "Tomos of Union" in 920 AD, which ended the "Tetragamy" schism caused by Emperor Leo VI's four marriages</note>.

Emperor Romanos then exiled the *magister* <term>Magister: One of the highest-ranking administrative titles in the Byzantine court</term> Stephen to the island of Antigone, suspecting that he was <margin>10</margin> perhaps aiming for the throne. He had Stephen’s hair shorn to make him a monk, and along with him, he exiled Theophanes "the Wall-man" and Paul the *orphanotrophos* <term>Orphanotrophos: An official responsible for the care of orphans and the administration of charitable estates</term>, who were Stephen's closest associates. While a <margin>C</margin> public procession was taking place at the tribunal, the emperors suddenly returned to the palace because a plot had been reported to them. The leaders of the conspiracy were seized—the patrician Arsenios and the *manglabites* <term>Manglabites: A high-ranking member of the imperial bodyguard</term> Paul—and they were blinded, had their property confiscated, and were sent into exile.

In this same year, Emperor Romanos also found a son-in-law for his daughter Agatha: Leo, the son of Argyros. Leo was a noble man, surpassing others in physical beauty and stature, and was further adorned with intelligence and wisdom.

As the banquet <note>original Greek: εὐωχίας (euochias)—meaning a festive meal or symposium</note> was proceeding, a conversation arose concerning the Bulgarians. After the emperor had spoken many persuasive words—arousing their spirits with enthusiasm and exhorting them to go out courageously **C** against their adversaries and to fight for their homeland—<margin>5</margin> everyone readily agreed to go out and fight on behalf of the Christians. At dawn, therefore, having armed himself, Sacticius <term>Sacticius: Identifying John Sacticius, the Drungary of the Watch, a high-ranking military commander</term>, coming up behind the Bulgarians and entering their camp—since most of them had scattered throughout the countryside to plunder spoils—slaughtered everyone who was found in the encampment. <margin>10</margin> When the multitude of Bulgarians learned of what had happened from those who had escaped, they returned to the camp. As a clash occurred, the fresh Bulgarians, fighting against the weary, and the unblemished against men already battered by the preceding battle, **D** turned Sacticius back, who with only a few men had received the assault of the enemy. <margin>15</margin> Having fought nobly and killed many of the enemy, when he was being overpowered, he slackened his horse’s reins and, turning his back, he fled. As the banquet proceeded, a conversation was introduced concerning the Bulgarians; and the emperor, having spoken many things suitable for warming their souls and stirring their courage, and having exhorted them to go bravely against the enemy and fight for their own country, all promised their eager efforts in defending the Christians. At the first light of the following day, the armed Sacticius followed the Bulgarians from the rear; and having entered their camp—while most were wandering through the fields for plunder—he killed all who were in the camp. The Bulgarians, having recognized the situation from those who had escaped, returned to the camp; and when the battle was joined, they themselves, fresh in strength, routed the Romans <note>The Byzantines consistently referred to themselves as "Romans" (Rhomaioi)</note> who were exhausted by the preceding battle, while Sacticius and a few others bravely withstood their attack. And after he had fought excellently for some time and struck down many of the enemy, when he was hard-pressed, he gave his horse the reins and surrendered himself to flight. But in the crossing of a certain river, when his horse had become stuck in the mire, the Bulgarians caught up with him, and he received a mortal wound in the buttocks and thigh. ## 314 ##

“How could an accusation touch one who is innocent? Those who are eager for your deposition put forward only one cause, claiming that you are entirely illiterate. If, therefore, we are able to refute this, those who are plotting against you will certainly be revealed as gaping wolves. If you will take my advice, <margin>5</margin> in the presence of the entire synod <note>A council of high-ranking clergy</note>, write your name and your priestly title on a blank piece of parchment and send it to the Emperor. In this way, he will be fully informed, and having lost this hope, he will cease his plotting against you.” This advice seemed profitable. Immediately, therefore, a synod was gathered, and once it had assembled, the Patriarch spoke to them: <margin>10</margin> “O divine fellow-ministers, those who wish to unjustly cast me down from this throne have set many schemes in motion to find a reasonable cause to ostracize me, but they have found none. Now, they finally attach this charge to me: they say I am unlettered. <margin>15</margin> Therefore, in the sight of you all, I shall scratch out these letters, so that these slanderers, seeing and being fully informed, may cease from unjustly troubling me.” Having said this, he took a blank sheet of parchment and, in the sight of <margin>P 629</margin> everyone, he signed it as follows: “Tryphon, by the mercy of God, Archbishop of Constantinople, New Rome, and Ecumenical Patriarch.” Having written this, he sent it to the Emperor by way of the *protothronos* <note>The "first-throne" bishop, the highest-ranking member of the synod after the Patriarch</note>. <margin>20</margin> Taking this into his hands, the Emperor attached another blank piece of parchment above it and wrote a resignation, stating that Tryphon, being unworthy, was stepping aside for whoever wished to take the throne. When this resignation was produced before the synod, Tryphon was removed from the church.

A certain Basil, a Macedonian, falsely claiming to be Constantine, the son of Doukas <note>A reference to a popular but deceased noble whose identity was often used by pretenders</note>, deceived many and drew them to his cause. Wandering about, he stirred up trouble and threw the cities into turmoil, inciting them to rebellion. However, he was seized by a certain *tourmarches* <term>a commander of a military division</term> <margin>10</margin> named Elephantinos. Brought before the Emperor as a rebel, he was deprived of one of his hands. Later, after he was released, he fitted himself with a hand made of bronze and had a massive sword fashioned for himself. He then began to roam the Opsikion <term>a major military province in northwest Asia Minor</term>, deceiving the simpler folk into believing he was indeed Constantine <margin>C</margin> the son of Doukas. Having gathered a large force, he launched a rebellion. <margin>15</margin> He seized the fortress called Plateia Petra <note>original: *Platēia petra*; meaning "Broad Rock"</note> and stored all kinds of supplies within it. Setting out from there, he plundered and looted the surrounding areas. The Emperor then sent an army against him, capturing both him and his followers. After a long <margin>20</margin> interrogation to discover if any high-ranking officials were his accomplices, and ultimately finding no evidence of any significant conspiracy, the Emperor delivered the man to the fire in the place called Amastrianos <note>A public square in Constantinople often used for public executions</note>. Emperor Romanos also gave Anna, the daughter of Gabalas, as a wife to his son Stephen; along with the wedding wreath, the crown of the Empire was placed upon her <note>She was crowned Augusta, or Empress, at her wedding</note>.

Having been relegated to the island of Prota <note>original: "Protam insulam"</note>, he [Stephen] shaved his [Romanos's] head against his will and imposed the life of a monk. Thereafter, Stephen gave himself to the administration of affairs with greater zeal, with the husband of his sister and his brother as colleagues.

Because, however, the same things were not approved by all, quarrels and offenses arose among them from these dissensions. The **Porphyrogenitus** began to be suspected by Stephen, and the latter by the former, and each thought of removing the other. Indeed, with no small care and effort did Stephen apply himself to this: that by seizing power from his colleagues, he might hold the supreme power alone. 

But just as the poet says there are certain other things hotter than fire, so he also did not so much inflict as suffer a loss; for Constantine, when he sensed the snares being laid for him, granted no time for the deed to be carried out, with even his wife Helena instigating him many times to cast down her brothers. Therefore, having communicated the secret plan with Basil Peteinos (or "the Bird") <note>original: "Volucri," a Latin translation of the Greek "Peteinos"</note>, and by his help having brought Marianus into the alliance, as well as Nicephorus and Leo, the sons of Bardas Phocas, and Nicholas and Leo Tornicius and many others, he ordered Stephen and his brother Constantine to be seized while they were dining with him, during the meal itself, and to be dragged from the palace on the 27th day of January, in the same indiction. Having placed them on ships, he relegated Stephen to the island of Panormus, and Constantine [to the island of Prota]...

Constantine, however, was of a more restless disposition; rising up more heatedly than was proper and having attempted to flee many times, he was himself slaughtered by the remaining guards in the second year after his fall from power, after he had treacherously murdered his own keeper.

...wishing for these [offices] to be directed by the best men and by careful selection—a task worthy of magnificent power—he instead entrusted authority to whoever happened to be present, such as a generalship or a city prefecture, without any scrutiny. <margin>C</margin> Yet Constantine was not entirely without good deeds. For the following story, being worthy of admiration and wonder, was strong enough to overshadow and dim many of his failings. For the sciences—arithmetic, music, astronomy, geometry, stereometry, and philosophy, the leader of them all—which had for a long time perished through the neglect and ignorance of previous rulers, he restored through his own diligence. Because of this, having driven away "unreason" <note>original: "ἀλογίαν," meaning a lack of logic, education, or refinement.</note>, in a short time he transformed the government into a more rational state.

<margin>D</margin> He also took care of the manual and mechanical arts, bringing them to a high state of development. He was also pious and generous toward God, never appearing before God empty-handed or fruitless during his formal visits to the divine temples, but instead bestowing magnificent offerings befitting a **Christ-loving** emperor. Furthermore, Olga, the wife of the prince of the Rhos, who had led a fleet against the Romans, came to Constantinople after her husband's death. Having been baptized, and after demonstrating a great zeal for true piety, she returned home having been treated with honors suitable to her purpose.

The daughter of Hugh, who had been betrothed to Romanos, died as a virgin, as we have mentioned. The Emperor then provided his son with another wife, by no means of noble birth but of the common people, born of tavern-keepers and named Anastasia. However, he himself gave her the name Theophano.

When the Emir of Tarsus, seeking war with the Romans, sent part of his army to the village of Herakles to plunder, a certain priest named Themel was then performing the bloodless sacrifice. Upon learning of the Saracens' arrival, he abandoned the sacrifice and, dressed as he was in his sacred robes, seized the church's sounding-board. With it, he defended against the rushing enemies, wounding many, killing several, and putting the rest to flight. Subsequently excluded from holy orders by the bishop, and unable to obtain readmission, he betook himself to the Agarenes and swore off the Christian religion. Going out with them, he devastated not only Cappadocia and the neighboring regions, but also reached as far as Asia Minor...

But gradually, following the <margin>15</margin> will of the ruler, they made themselves a laughingstock <margin>C</margin> to those who were still undecided.

At that same time, the precious hand of the Forerunner <note>John the Baptist, often called "the Forerunner" (Prodromos) in the Eastern Church.</note> was brought to the imperial city from Antioch, having been stolen by a certain deacon named Job. When it reached <margin>20</margin> Chalcedon <note>A city located directly across the water from Constantinople.</note>, the Emperor sent out the imperial trireme <note>A large warship with three banks of oars.</note>. A distinguished part of the senate went out, along with Patriarch Polyeuctus and the entire clergy with candles, torches, and incense, and brought it into the palace.

<header>GEORGE CEDRENUS</header>

Meanwhile, Bardas, the Domestic of the Schools <term>Domestic of the Schools: The supreme commander of the land forces of the Byzantine Empire, ranking just below the Emperor in military matters.</term>, set out on a campaign against the Eastern Agarenes <term>Agarenes: A historical term used by Byzantine writers for Arabs, referencing their traditional descent from Hagar.</term>. He destroyed everything in his path, capturing many strongholds and taking the famous city of Adapa <note>original Greek: "Ἄδαπα"; the variant "Adana" is noted in some manuscripts.</note> by siege. 

The Emperor, wishing to frighten the Saracens in Crete—who were launching continuous raids and plundering the coastal lands of the Roman <note>The "Romans" here refers to the Byzantines, who identified as the continuation of the Roman Empire.</note> Empire—and hoping to halt their unchecked momentum, gathered a massive army and prepared a formidable fleet. 

<margin>D</margin> He sent this force against the island under the command of Constantine Gongyles, a patrician. Gongyles was an effeminate man who had been "raised in the shade" <note>A Greek idiom for a man of luxury who has not experienced the harsh "sun" of the battlefield.</note>, was entirely unskilled in war, and was one of the chamberlains in the palace. 

Upon crossing to the island, he performed nothing worthy of a general. He failed to establish a secure camp or post lookouts and scouts to watch for barbarian raids. Consequently, he fell into the gravest danger. The islanders, noticing the general's inexperience and negligence, waited for the perfect moment and suddenly attacked the army. 

<margin>P 641</margin> They easily routed the forces, leading to many Romans being taken captive or killed by the sword. They even captured the camp itself, while the Romans fled in total disgrace. Gongyles himself would have been captured had his servants not formed a shield around him, rescued him from captivity, and brought him safely to the flagship.

<margin>B</margin> Now Romanus, the son of Emperor Constantine, having reached maturity...

Meanwhile Bardas, Domestic of the Schools, having made an expedition against the Eastern Agarenes, laid waste to everything in his way, took many castles, and even captured the very famous city of Adapa. Gongyla was an effeminate man, educated in the shade and ignorant of war, one of the palace chamberlains.

This neglect led him into the greatest danger. For the islanders, having detected the laziness and lack of skill of the Roman leader, seized a favorable time and suddenly attacked the Romans, routing them with no effort. Many of them were either captured or killed by the sword, and as the rest fled, the camp was also captured to the great disgrace of our people. Gongylius himself would have fallen into the power of the enemy, had he not been snatched away by a wedge of his servants and placed upon the praetorian ship.

<margin>5</margin> Having now come of age, and being unable to bear seeing the affairs of state still managed by his father, <insert>the young Romanos</insert> planned to do away with him by poison, with the full knowledge and complicity of his own wife, the daughter of a tavern-keeper <note>original Greek: "καπηλίδος" (kapēlidos); Latin: "cauponis filia." [Constantine VII reigned] for a total of fifty-four years and two months. He co-reigned with his father <note>Leo VI the Wise</note>, his uncle Alexander, and his own mother <note>Zoe Karbonopsina</note> for thirteen years; then with Romanos <note>Romanos I Lekapenos</note>, who had usurped the throne, for twenty-six years; and after the latter’s fall from power, he ruled as sole monarch for fifteen years. Until his very last breath, he harbored a grudge against Polyeuctus <note>Patriarch Polyeuctus of Constantinople, known for his stern moral stance and friction with the imperial court</note> and constantly imagined his deposition. 

A few days before his death, for a considerable length of time as evening fell, stones were sent down from above and fell inside his living quarters with a great whirring sound, creating extraordinary loud noises. 
<margin>P 642</margin> Thinking these were being thrown from the upper floors of the Magnaura <term>Magnaura: A grand reception hall in the Great Palace of Constantinople, used for receiving foreign ambassadors and for ceremonial displays of imperial power.</term>, he stationed guards for many nights to see if he could catch any of those daring to do this. But he remained unaware that he was laboring in vain; for what was happening was not the work of men, but was being carried out by a higher power.

After Constantine passed away and moved on to the state of existence beyond, his son Romanos <note>Romanos II, reigned 959–963 AD</note> became master of the government. After appointing officials who were loyal and pleasing to him, and strengthening the empire as best he could, he also crowned his son <note>The future Basil II "the Bulgar-Slayer"</note> as emperor during the feast of Easter in the same third indiction <term>indiction: A 15-year cycle used by the Byzantines for tax accounting and dating; the "third indiction" here corresponds to 960 AD.</term>, through the hands of Patriarch Polyeuctus in the Great Church <note>Hagia Sophia</note>.

...another son [was born] in the Palace of the Springs <note>original: "Πηγῶν παλατίοις" — The Pege Palace, located outside the city walls, famous for its life-giving spring</note>, whom he named Constantine after his father <note>the child's grandfather, Constantine VII</note>. Accordingly, he took a certain cleric named John, who was a eunuch <note>original: "ἐκτομίαν" — a castrated male, common in the Byzantine bureaucracy</note>. This John had been threatened by Emperor Constantine for some shameful deeds and had donned the monastic <margin>10</margin> habit, remaining hidden until the Emperor’s death. As soon as Romanos <margin>C</margin> gained the throne, he stripped John of the monk’s habit, dressed him in the robes of a cleric, and assigned him to his own chamberlains.

Filled with zeal, Polyeuctus <note>The Patriarch of Constantinople, known for his uncompromising morality</note> was very persistent and troubled the Emperor, urging him to <margin>15</margin> cast this man out of his service because he had renounced his monastic profession. But when the Emperor made excuses, claiming that John had not truly embraced the habit or received a prayer from any of the priests, but had only pretended to live the monastic life out of fear of the [late] Emperor, Polyeuctus was deceived and let the matter go—especially since Joseph <margin>20</margin> Bringas also put great effort into this. Thus, John lived until the death of Romanos, living as a layman and following youthful fashions. But after Romanos died, <margin>D</margin> he put the monk's habit back on once more, though he did not change his character.

[The Emperor] was born in the palace, and named Constantine after his father. However, the young emperor, being devoted to pleasures, committed the care of the state to Joseph, his primary chamberlain surnamed Bringas: he himself applied his mind to nothing other than spending an infamous life with dissolute and impure little men, harlots, mimes, and jesters. For that reason, he took a certain John, a eunuch cleric, whom Emperor Constantine had driven out and made a monk on account of certain foul deeds, and who had hidden until his death. Having gained power, Romanos stripped him of his monk's habit, and restoring his clerical dress, received him among his chamberlains. 

But Polyeuctus, moved by just indignation, vehemently urged the Emperor to eject from his household a man who had renounced his monastic vow. Nevertheless, with the Emperor making excuses—denying that he had truly embraced the monastic state or had been consecrated to that kind of life by any priest, but had only feigned it for fear of the Emperor—Polyeuctus, being deceived, dismissed the case, with Joseph also working hard in this matter. Thus that John led a secular life according to his new custom until the death of Romanos; upon his death, he was again veiled in the monastic habit, but he did not change his mind.

In this year, the Emperor sent Nicephorus Phocas—a *magistros* and the *Domestic of the Eastern Schools* appointed by Emperor Constantine, who had established many trophies over the Eastern Saracens and had thoroughly checked the Emirs Karamones of Tarsus, Chabdan of Aleppo, and Izeth of Tripoli—against the Cretan Saracens with a chosen army of soldiers and a well-adorned fleet. And the author of the conspiracy was Basilios "the Bird" <note>original: "Volucris" — Latin for the Greek "Peteinos"</note> the *magistros*, having as his associates from among the illustrious the patrician Paschalios, the patrician Bardas the son of Libis, and Nikolaos Chalkoutzas. And so, before the defined day arrived, they were seized by Joseph, convicted, and cruelly tortured—Basilios alone excepted. On that very day of the equestrian games, they were led in a triumph <note>A public parade of humiliation for defeated enemies or rebels</note>, banished, and made into monks with their heads shaved. Nevertheless, such was the humanity of the emperor toward them that he recalled them after they had experienced the miseries of exile for only a short time. Only Basilios "the Bird," seized by insanity, perished on Proconnesus, and thus paid the penalty for the emperor Stephen, whom he had betrayed to Constantine through fraud.

But indeed the *magistros* Romanos Saronites, the son-in-law of the old man Romanos, seeing what had happened to "the Bird" and the others, and fearing lest the same thing should happen to him—because he was hated and suspected on account of his own splendor—distributed his wealth among his children according to his will, and having bestowed the rest upon the poor, he withdrew himself to the monastery of Elegmon, and there as a monk for many...

When Helena <note>Empress Helena Lekapene, widow of Constantine VII and mother of the reigning Romanos II</note> saw this, she turned to lamentations and curses, and so swayed her son, who deeply feared the curses she might lay upon him. She was carried forth in a royal funeral and buried in the sarcophagus of her father <note>Romanos I Lekapenos</note>.

<margin>10</margin> Now Nikephoros Phocas <note>The brilliant general and future Emperor Nikephoros II</note>, as was mentioned before, was ordered to <margin>B</margin> return from Crete. He was not permitted to enter the reigning city <note>Constantinople</note> but was instead commanded to proceed to the East with the entire army. For Khabdan <note>original: "Χαβδᾶν" — referring to Sayf al-Dawla, the Hamdanid Emir of Aleppo and a major rival of the Byzantines</note>, recovering himself from his previous defeat, began to rise up again; having gathered a battle-worthy army, he was expected to attack the Roman <note>Byzantine</note> officials <margin>15</margin> and their territories. He took great wealth as booty and many captives, while also liberating the <margin>20</margin> Christians held there as prisoners and sending them to their homes.

Helena, turning to wailing and curses, deterred her son from his purpose through fear of her executive power, and she was permitted to remain in the palace. Phocas, when he came into Syria, overcame and routed him in battle, and forced him into interior Syria; he devastated the city of Berrhoea except for the citadel, and carried away great wealth, rich plunder, and many captives, also freeing and sending home the Christians who had been held captive there.

In the year of the world 6471, the Emperor Romanos died, on the 15th day of March.

### ABRIDGMENT OF HISTORIES

Emperor Romanos died at the age of twenty-four, having reigned for thirteen years, four months, and five days <note>Romanos II reigned as sole Emperor for only four years (959–963), but the "thirteen years" likely counts his time as co-emperor alongside his father, Constantine VII</note>. His sons, Basil and Constantine, succeeded to his <margin>5</margin> empire along with their mother, Theophano. A daughter had also been born to him just two days before his death, whom they named Anna <note>Anna Porphyrogenita, who would later marry Vladimir the Great of Kievan Rus', leading to the Christianization of Russia</note>. Romanos was large in stature, though shorter than his father, and possessed a mild and gentle character and a moderate spirit. Although he was young, <margin>10 D</margin> he was quick-witted, sharp, and highly capable of governing the state—if only he had been permitted to do so by his servants. However, his closest attendants, having surrendered him to the impulses of youth so that they might manage public affairs themselves and amass unspeakable wealth, rendered him inactive and unfit for rule.

# GEORGE KEDRENOS

Taking one of his shield-bearers with him, Phocas <note>Nikephoros II Phocas, the celebrated general and future emperor</note> went to the house of Joseph <note>Joseph Bringas, the powerful chief court official</note> around the hour of the midday meal. Taking Joseph aside privately, he showed him a <meta>5</meta> hair shirt <term>hair shirt: a rough garment made of goat hair worn against the skin by ascetics as a form of penance</term> which he was wearing underneath his outer garments. With oaths, he fully convinced Joseph that he had long ago embraced the lifestyle of a monk <margin>B</margin> and would have already donned the monastic habit and withdrawn himself from worldly cares, had he not been held back by his devotion to the emperors Constantine and Romanos. He claimed he was on the verge of fulfilling his personal goal very soon, and he begged Joseph not to harbor <meta>10</meta> vain suspicions against him. Seeing this, Joseph immediately fell at his feet, seeking forgiveness, and assured him that he would never again believe anyone who spoke against him. When Nikephoros, followed by the favorable acclamations of the entire army, had come to Chrysopolis, Joseph [Bringas] thought about designating some other emperor, thinking that by this reasoning he would blunt the attack of the soldiers. After these things were done, Bringas fell in spirit and hesitated in the greatest difficulties. For he was not fit for soothing the multitude in dangerous times; but where it was necessary to soften them by flattering with mild speeches, he instead exasperated and irritated them. Furthermore, a rumor had spread everywhere—which caused no small disturbance in the church—that *Nikephoros* had stood as godfather <margin>C</margin> to one of *Theophano’s* children at their holy baptism. Seizing upon this rumor as a legitimate excuse, *Polyeuktos* fought to demand that the Emperor either separate from his wife according to the church law <note>Spiritual kinship, such as being a godfather, was considered a legal barrier to marriage, much like biological incense</note> or withdraw from the church. *Nikephoros* chose the latter, remaining devoted to *Theophano*. He then summoned the bishops who were present in the city and the distinguished members of the Senate to deliberate on the matter. All these men claimed that the law forbidding such marriages was a creation of *Copronymus* <note>The derogatory nickname for Emperor Constantine V (r. 741–775), meaning "The Dung-named," used by later historians because he was an Iconoclast</note>, and they judged that it should not be observed. They then signed a petition <margin>D</margin> of absolution and presented it to him.

While *Polyeuktos* still hesitated to take communion with the Emperor, the *Caesar* <note>Bardas Phocas, the Emperor's father</note> assured him that *Nikephoros* had not, in fact, been the godfather. # BY GEORGIOS KEDRENOS

Nikephoros was chosen, a patrician and Domestic of the Schools, who bore the surname Phokas, which one of his ancestors had earned through famous deeds. This Nikephoros, the grandfather of Emperor Nikephoros, was a man of noble character, prudent and pious toward God and just toward men. Having set out for Sicily with an army, in a short space of time he expelled the Saracens from Italy and forced them to confine themselves to Sicily. They say the Italians built a shrine to this man for the perpetual memory of his virtue, not only because he had liberated them, but also because of another memorable act. For the Romans, when they were about to return home with their leader, had seized many Italians whom they wanted to lead away with them into slavery. When the matter was discovered, Nikephoros, saying nothing and offering no occasion for suspicion, waited until they reached Brundusium (for from there they were to cross into Illyricum). He himself ordered each of the fleet-men one by one to enter the ship and cross over, and thus he left the Italians in Italy. Thereafter, Italy was at peace until the rule of Constantine Porphyrogenitus and his mother. Then the Saracens, rising up again, infested Italy with no one to stop them. And the emperors, noticing they were not equal to waging war at the same time against the Eastern and Western Saracens, especially since [the peace] was broken...

# GEORGE CEDRENUS

...the patrician advising what was necessary, Landulf accepted the exhortation and

But the leader of the Bulgarians, Simeon, having raised many trophies of victory against the Romans and being emboldened by these successes, even dreamed of seizing the Roman Empire for himself. Simeon promised that he himself would come through Thrace <margin>10</margin> leading a large and formidable army, and that once their forces were united by land and sea, they would take the Imperial City by siege. They would divide its wealth equally, and while Phatloum would return to his home, he would leave the city of Constantinople to Simeon. The Bulgarians thus sailed secretly to Africa <margin>15</margin>, and because it seemed that Simeon was offering useful counsel, the Africans selected certain notable Saracens <term>Saracens: a term used by Byzantines to describe Arab Muslims</term> to confirm the agreements. When the Emperor saw them (it was Romanos the Elder <note>Romanos I Lecapenus, who reigned 920–944 AD</note>) <margin>20</margin> and learned the exact details of the joint plot, he realized that if this plan succeeded, he would face no small amount of trouble. He promised he would arrive at the same place through Thrace with a strong and numerous army: with their forces joined, they would capture the city by land and sea, and divide its riches between them in equal portions; after the Saracens returned home, he would retain Constantinople for himself. When the Saracens returned to their own ruler, they <margin>B</margin> recounted what they had experienced at the hands of the Emperor and praised his kindness. ### THE REIGN OF NICEPHORUS PHOCAS

When they realized the enemy was nearby and they were unprepared, they were seized by a **Panic terror** <note>original: Πανικῷ δείματι, referring to the god Pan, who was believed to cause sudden, irrational fear</note>. Abandoning their own camp, they fled from *Rhegium* <note>Modern Reggio Calabria</note> and crossed over to *Sicily*. While sailing toward *Panormus* <note>Modern Palermo</note>, they were caught in a most violent storm. Their ships were shattered by the surging waves—or rather, by Christ our God, whom they had blasphemed—and they all perished. A treaty was then struck with the *Romans* <note>The Byzantines referred to themselves as Romans</note>, and the peace was maintained until the coronation of *Phocas*. As soon as he was proclaimed Emperor, he considered it a fate worse than death to pay tribute to the *Saracens* <term>Saracens: A medieval term for Arab Muslims</term>. He dispatched *Manuel*, whom we have mentioned before, against them with a large force. Manuel was young in age and fit to be ranked as a soldier, but he was not at all worthy of being a general. He was possessed by many other passions and paid no heed to those <margin>P 654</margin> offering better counsel. In certain rugged and impassable regions of *Sicily*, he was cut off with his entire army and suffered a total destruction. *Nicetas* the patrician <term>Patrician: A high-ranking title of nobility</term> and *drungary* <term>Drungary: A high-ranking naval commander</term> of the fleet, who was a eunuch, was taken alive and sent to *Africa* in chains. As for *Manuel*, he met his end in this catastrophe, having also caused the death of his entire army.

In the meantime, the Emperor sent *John Tzimiskes* to *Cilicia* <note>A region in modern-day southern Turkey</note>. ### A COMPENDIUM OF HISTORY

A massive fleet from *Egypt* arrived to aid *Tarsus*, fully laden with grain and other necessities for survival. However, it was not permitted to approach the land or disembark because of the soldiers stationed by the Emperor to guard the coast. <margin>5</margin> Having no way to use their supplies, they turned back and encountered great shipwrecks caused by unruly winds and the assault <margin>C</margin> of the Emperor’s warships. After laying waste to and burning the remaining cities of *Cilicia*, in the month of *October* of the ninth indiction <term>Indiction: A 15-year cycle used for dating and taxation in the Roman and Byzantine empires</term>, he returned to *Constantinople*. He brought <margin>10</margin> with him the gates of *Tarsus* and the "hearths" <note>original: ἑστίας – likely referring to the city gates of Mopsuestia</note> of *Mopsuestia*. Having decorated these with gold on the outside, he brought them as an offering to the Imperial City; some he set up at the citadel, and others at the wall of the Golden Gate. He also brought a gift for God, a "tithe" of his own campaign: the precious crosses that had been captured <margin>15</margin> when *Stypeiotes*—who was the Domestic of the Schools <term>Domestic of the Schools: The supreme commander of the Byzantine imperial army</term> at the time—was besieging *Tarsus* and, through his own lack of wisdom, subjected his armies to total destruction. These crosses he dedicated in the most venerable sanctuary of the <margin>D</margin> Wisdom of the Word of God <note>original: τοῦ Θεοῦ λόγου σοφίας – refers to the Hagia Sophia</note>.

In the same second year of his reign, *Nicephorus* also <margin>20</margin> brought the entire island of *Cyprus* back under the rule of the *Romans* <note>Byzantine citizens identified as Romans</note>, having driven the *Agarenes* <term>Agarenes: A medieval term for Arab or Muslim forces, referring to their traditional descent from Hagar</term> from there through *Nicetas Chalkoutzes*, the patrician.

After the capture, a massive fleet arrived from **Egypt** to bring help to **Tarsus**, laden with grain and other things necessary for food. But it was not allowed to reach land or make a landing by those soldiers to whom the Emperor had committed the maritime guard; and since they could achieve nothing, they returned, and fell into great shipwrecks by the force of the winds and the attack of the Emperor's warships. Therefore, having burned and consumed the remaining cities of **Cilicia**, in the month of **October**, in the ninth indiction, he returned to **Constantinople**, bringing with him the gates of **Tarsus** and **Mopsuestia**, which, when he had decorated the outside with gold, he brought as a gift to be dedicated to the royal city, some to be placed at the citadel, others at the wall of the golden gate. He also brought a gift to God and a tithe of his army: the venerable crosses, captured when **Stypeiotes**, the Domestic of the Schools, besieging **Tarsus**, was utterly destroyed with his whole army through his own imprudence; these he also dedicated in the sacrosanct temple of Sophia, the Wisdom of the Word of God.

In the same second year of his reign, **Nicephorus** also reduced the whole island of **Cyprus** to the power of the **Romans**, the **Agarenes** being expelled from there by the patrician and praetor **Nicetas Chalkoutzes**.

### THE HISTORY OF GEORGE CEDRENUS

In the third year of his reign, at the onset of spring, the Emperor again made an invasion into *Syria*. When he arrived at *Antioch*, he did not attack it directly, hoping that the people of *Antioch*—terrified by what had happened to the cities of *Cilicia*—would not even withstand the mere report of his coming. Instead, he passed the city by and advanced into the interior parts of *Syria*. After subduing many cities and territories situated near *Mount Lebanon* and the 

<margin>P 656</margin> coast, he returned in the month of *December*. However, because the people of *Antioch* were vigorously preparing for war—since a great multitude from the surrounding districts had entered the city to aid them—and because the Roman <note>original: Ῥωμαϊκῷ – The Byzantines referred to themselves as Romans</note> army had run out of necessary supplies, and an impassable mire had formed due to heavy rain bursting forth from the heavens, the Emperor withdrew without achieving his goal. He reached the Imperial City <note>Constantinople</note>, bringing with him a ceramic tile <note>original: κέραμον / ollam – Known as the *Keramion*, this was a sacred tile believed to have miraculously received the imprint of Christ's face</note> which bore an image of the likeness of Christ our God not made by human hands <note>original: ἀχειρότευκτον / non manu factam</note>. He had found this in *Hierapolis* <note>Modern-day Manbij, Syria</note> after capturing the city. He also brought a single lock of hair from *John the Baptist*, matted with blood.

<margin>B</margin> Such was *Nicephorus*, and such were the strategies he employed; he expanded the Roman state to such a degree that he held more than a hundred cities and fortresses across *Cilicia*, *Syria*, and *Phoenicia Libanisia* <term>Phoenicia Libanisia: An inland Roman/Byzantine province encompassing regions near the Lebanon mountains, including Damascus and Emesa</term>. Among the largest and most famous of these were *Anazarbus*, *Adana*, the "hearth" of *Mopsuestia* <note>original: ἡ Μόψου ἑστία – a poetic way of referring to the city of Mopsuestia</note>, *Tarsus*, *Pagras*, *Synnephium*, *Laodicea*, and *Aleppo*. Furthermore, when a bishop died, he would send a royal official to set a fixed limit on the funeral expenses, and he would seize any surplus funds for the treasury. ...certain decrees he established that exceeded every form of necessity, which to recount in detail would require a person of great eloquence, intellect, and tongue. <margin>D</margin> He was also eager to establish a law that soldiers who die in wars should be deemed worthy of the honors of martyrs, <margin>5</margin> placing the salvation of the soul in war alone and in nothing else. This was a lighter gold coin introduced by Nicephorus II to circulate alongside the full-weight nomisma, effectively devaluing the currency.</term> Since the coinage had become twofold from that time on, the collection of public taxes required the heavier coin, but in expenditures <note>such as state salaries or public works</note>, the small one was distributed. Though it was the law and custom that every coin bearing the image of a sovereign <margin>15</margin>—as long as it was not reduced in weight—should have equal value, he decreed that his own coin should be preferred, while lowering the value of others. For this reason, he caused no small distress to his subjects in the so-called exchanges. <term>allagia: the business of money-changing or the exchange rate between different types of currency.</term> And what was truly the worst part: while the state was being squeezed for this reason, the goods for sale saw no reduction in price. <margin>20</margin> But more than all these other things, even though they were very harsh, the construction of the palace wall distressed the people. For many works that were around the palace, built for beauty and greatness, were [interrupted or enclosed]... <margin>B</margin>

There are also his other constitutions, exceeding every form of necessity, which to relate one by one would require great talent and eloquence. He also wished to pass a law by which soldiers falling in war would be decreed the honors of martyrs, as one who placed the salvation of the soul in nothing else but war; and he attempted to drive the patriarch and the bishops to approve it. He also debased the *nomisma* <note>the standard Byzantine gold coin</note>, having devised the *tetarteron*. And although it was received by law and custom that all coins marked with the image of any emperor should have the same value, provided nothing was missing from the just weight, he himself wished those marked with his own image to be preferred, with the prices of others being depressed. And by that matter, he inconvenienced his subjects in no small way in their exchanges. This was the worst thing: that while the republic was worn down by these matters, there was meanwhile no relief in the price of things for sale. ...he ordered some men to perform a mock battle as if they were enemies, ostensibly for the entertainment of the spectators. When the people saw that he had not stirred, and realized that what had happened was without his consent, they halted <margin>10</margin> their flight.

...they destroyed [the crops] along with the vines and trees themselves, so that as a result, during the twelfth indiction <note>The indiction was a 15-year tax cycle; the 12th indiction here corresponds to the year 968–969 AD.</note>, a most severe famine was brought upon the land. While it was the duty of the Emperor to provide for the safety and welfare of his subjects, he instead sold the imperial grain at a high price <note>original: *glischrōs* (γλίσχρως) – literally "stingily" or "greedily," implying he was price-gouging.</note>, exploiting the misfortune of those under his rule. He even boasted as if he had achieved something great because, while a *modius* <note>A standard Roman/Byzantine unit of dry volume, roughly 8.7 liters.</note> was being sold for a *nomisma* <note>The standard gold coin of the Byzantine Empire, also known as the *solidus*.</note>, he himself ordered that two should be sold for that price. In this, he failed to imitate the Macedonian Emperor, Basil <note>Basil I (r. 867–886), the founder of the Macedonian dynasty.</note>.

<margin>P 661</margin> For that Emperor, when going out on "New Sunday" <note>The first Sunday after Easter, also known as Thomas Sunday.</note> to the Church of the Holy Apostles <note>One of the most important churches in Constantinople, serving as the imperial mausoleum.</note>, observed certain citizens who appeared dignified and respectable in their bearing, yet were otherwise gloomy and downcast. He called them to his side and asked why they were not present at the festival wearing bright garments <note>original: *lamprophoreuntes* (λαμπροφοροῦντες) – a tradition of wearing white or festive clothing during the Easter season.</note>, but were instead grieving as if the city were in the midst of a great disaster. One of the citizens answered him:

"O Master, it is fitting for you and those standing near you to wear bright clothes and to rejoice; but for those who are closely acquainted with the expectation of death, such things are unseemly. Or are you unaware that two *medimnoi* <note>A larger Greek unit of measure; in this context, it emphasizes the scarcity and high cost of food.</note> of grain are being sold for a *nomisma* because of the harshness of the winds?"

<margin>B</margin> Upon hearing this, the Emperor groaned from the depths of his soul and shed a tear of compassion. He comforted these men generously, and after returning to the palace, he summoned those in charge of civil and imperial affairs and subjected them to countless insults and curses because they had not informed him of the grain shortage. Immediately, he ordered the imperial grain to be put up for sale...

### COMPENDIUM OF HISTORIES

It is said that ten days before his death, the Emperor found a document thrown into his bedchamber which warned him to secure himself, as he was being plotted against by Tzimiskes <note>John I Tzimiskes, the Emperor's nephew and leader of the coup</note>. And they say that a certain cleric, on the evening of the assassination, gave
<margin>5</margin> him a letter containing these exact words: “O Emperor, secure yourself; for a danger of no small size is being prepared for you during this night.” Some say that the Emperor, <margin>**B**</margin> assuming the letter was a petition, did not read it; others say that he did read it, but neglected his own guard because fate stood in the way <note>The concept of 'fate' (to chreon) often appears in Byzantine historiography to explain why wise leaders failed to act on clear warnings</note>,
<margin>10</margin> and after he died, the letter was found containing what had been written. Others say that after reading it, he entrusted the search and the guard to the *protovestiarios* <note term="protovestiarios">The head of the imperial wardrobe, one of the most trusted high-ranking court officials</note>, and he also wrote to his brother Leo, who was staying at home, to take an armed force and come as quickly as possible to the palace. When this message was delivered, Leo received it, but did not even unroll it (for he happened
<margin>15</margin> to be playing dice with some men and was passionately occupied with the game); he placed it on his bed under the pillow. Just as the game was breaking up, <margin>**C**</margin> he went to the letter and, realizing the meaning of what was written, he gathered such a force as the moment required and went to the palace. But when he arrived at the *sphendone* <note term="sphendone">The curved, U-shaped end of the Hippodrome of Constantinople, which was adjacent to the Great Palace</note> in the Hippodrome,
<margin>20</margin> he heard some people talking to one another, saying that Emperor Nikephoros had been murdered; he also heard those in the palace and in the narrow streets acclaiming John <note>John I Tzimiskes</note>. Stunned by this unexpected turn...

->4 "they say" omitted in Manuscript C &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 5 "containing" rather than "as" in C &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 6 "is being accomplished in a small way" in C<-

They report that ten days before he was killed, Nikephoros found a small book in his bedroom, by the writing of which he was warned to be careful: for a plot was being made against him by Tzimiskes. They also claim a certain cleric, on the evening of the night he then perished, showed him a letter in which these things were contained: "Fortify yourself, Emperor: for this night a danger hangs over you that is not light." Some relate that the Emperor did not read those letters, thinking a petition was contained therein. Others say he did read them, but took no account of a plan for his own guarding, hindered by fate; and that those letters were found after he himself was slain. There are those who assert that after they were read, the Emperor mandated the inquiry and the duty of the guard to the *protovestiarios*; and at the same time wrote to his brother Leo, residing at his own home, to come to the palace as quickly as possible with an armed hand. Leo, having received the letters, did not open them, because he happened then to be competing at dice with someone and was most intensely delighted by that plaything, but he laid them down on the frame of his bed. The game finished, he immediately read them, and having perceived the meaning, he collected as large a hand as the matter allowed, and hastened to the palace. ### BY GEORGE CEDRENUS
<page-num>378</page-num>

Leo was stunned, and having no noble plan in mind, he fled as fast as he could with his son Nikephoros to the Great Church <note>The Hagia Sophia in Constantinople</note>. These are the reports that have been handed down; whether they are true or false, I cannot say. Regardless, Nikephoros died inside the palace, having been finished off <margin>D</margin> <note>After the word "finished off," Manuscript C adds: "being fifty-seven years old at that time."</note>.

On the evening of that same day, by the command of John <note>John I Tzimiskes, the leader of the coup and the new Emperor</note>, the body was sent for burial in the deep twilight. They wrapped him in a wooden coffin, whatever was at hand, and carried him out at midnight to the divine sanctuary of the Holy Apostles <note>The Church of the Holy Apostles, the traditional burial place of Byzantine Emperors since Constantine the Great</note>. There, in the mausoleum where the body of the divine and celebrated Constantine lies, they laid him to rest in one of the imperial sarcophagi.

Regarding his appearance, he was of the following sort: his complexion leaned more toward dark than fair; he had thick, raven-black hair and black eyes that were deep in thought, sitting beneath bushy eyebrows. His nose was neither thin nor thick, ending in a slight hook. His beard was well-proportioned, with gray hair beginning to show thinly along the jaws. He was stocky in stature and robust, with very broad chest and shoulders. In his courage and strength, he was like the legendary Hercules, while in wisdom and self-control, he far surpassed all the men of his generation. Upon his sarcophagus, John, the Metropolitan of Melitene, inscribed these lines:

Upon the death of Nikephoros, John Tzimiskes <note>John I Tzimiskes (r. 969–976), a brilliant general of Armenian origin who led the conspiracy against his uncle Nikephoros</note> took up the cares of the Roman <note>original: "Ῥωμαίων" — The Byzantines referred to themselves as Romans and their state as the Roman Empire</note> Empire. # A COMPENDIUM OF HISTORIES

Therefore, by means of letters, he quickly transferred the Eastern forces to the West, and placed over them a commander whom he named General of the Forces, the *magistros* <note>A high-ranking court title, often held by senior generals</note> **Bardas Sclerus** <note>original: "Βάρδαν... τὸν Σκληρόν" — Bardas the Tough. The Sclerus family was a powerful Byzantine aristocratic clan</note>. The Emperor, while still a private citizen, had taken Bardas's sister **Maria** as his lawful <margin>D</margin> wife. The Emperor himself intended to set out at the beginning of spring. <margin>10</margin>

When the **Rus** and their leader **Sphendosthlabos** <note>The Greek rendering of Sviatoslav I of Kiev</note> learned of the crossing of the **Roman** <note>Byzantine</note> army, they joined forces with the **Bulgarians**, whom they had already enslaved. They also took as allies the **Patzinaks** <note>The Pechenegs, a semi-nomadic Turkic people of the steppes</note> and the **Turks** <note>In Byzantine sources of this period, "Turks" usually refers to the Magyars (Hungarians)</note> who dwelt toward the west in **Pannonia**. <margin>15</margin> Having gathered a warlike army from all these nations, which reached a peak of three hundred and eight thousand men, they crossed the **Haemus** <note>The Balkan Mountains</note> and began burning and plundering all of **Thrace**. They pitched camp near the walls of **Arcadiopolis** <note>Modern Lüleburgaz in Turkey</note>, and there they waited for the clash of <margin>P 667</margin> war. But the *magistros* **Bardas Sclerus**, perceiving that he was vastly <margin>20</margin> inferior in numbers (for his entire army amounted to only twelve thousand men), decided to use strategic ruses <note>The Byzantines took great pride in "strategikon," the art of winning through deception and tactics rather than brute force</note>.

## Georg. Cedrenus Vol. II. 25

...to circumvent the opponents and by skill and ingenuity to overcome such great numbers. This indeed came to pass. For by shutting himself up with the army inside the walls, although the enemy frequently challenged them to come out and fight for the final victory <note>original: "περὶ τῶν ὅλων διαγωνίσασθαι" (*peri tōn holōn diagonisasthai*) — literally "to struggle for the whole," meaning a decisive battle to settle the war</note>, he did not comply. <margin>5</margin> Instead, he held firm as if he were truly afraid, even as he saw his rivals carrying and driving away everything they came across <note>A Greek idiom describing the plundering of livestock and property</note>. # GEORGII CEDRENI

...to appear to the enemies, and to continue doing so until they had shut them up within <margin>D</margin> these traps and ambushes; then they were to flee in a disorderly fashion and headlong. Now, the barbarians were divided into three parts (for the Bulgarians and the Rus <note>original: "Ῥὼς" (*Rhōs*) — the Varangian-Rus people from the north</note> made up the first division, while the Turks <note>In this era, Byzantine writers often used "Turks" to refer to the Magyars (Hungarians)</note> were by themselves, as were the Patzinaks <note>A nomadic Turkic people from the Central Asian steppes</note>). Thus, as John advanced, he happened by chance to encounter the Patzinaks; and just as he had been instructed, he feigned flight, making his retreat slowly. The Patzinaks pressed upon them, breaking their own ranks in the hope of utterly destroying those who were fleeing. The Romans, now retreating in good order and now turning back to defend themselves, ran toward the ambush sites. Once they were in the midst of these, they then let go of the reins and fled wildly, and the Patzinaks, pouring forth in disorder, gave chase. But when the Magister <note>A high-ranking administrative and military title; here referring to Bardas Sclerus</note> suddenly appeared with the entire army, <margin>P 668</margin> the Patzinaks were stunned by the unexpected sight and halted their pursuit. However, they did not turn to flee, but stood their ground to receive whoever might attack. When the Magister's men fell upon them with a violent charge, and the rest of the phalanx came up from behind in good order and discipline, the most valiant of the Scythians <note>A classicizing term used by Byzantines for any northern nomadic people, in this case referring to the Patzinaks</note> fell immediately. As their phalanx was split deep through the center, the Patzinaks fell into the middle of the ambushes, with the wings of the Roman army closing together and completing the circle. Having resisted for only a short time, they gave way, and nearly all of them were cut down.

...retreating in an organized column, sometimes even turning to fight the enemy on level ground until they could draw them into the traps: then they were to flee in a scattered and disorderly way. The Romans, sometimes fleeing in an organized column and sometimes turning toward the enemy and fighting, held their course toward the traps; when they came into the middle of these, they fled wildly with loosened reins, and the Patzinaks followed them in a scattered fashion and without distinction. But when Bardas suddenly appeared with the whole army, they were terrified by the unexpected event; giving up the pursuit, they prepared themselves not for flight but for defense. With the violent onset of Bardas's army, and with the other phalanx also attacking from the rear in organized ranks, all the bravest of the Scythians fell at once. Their phalanx being deeply scattered, the Patzinaks were caught in the middle as the wings of the Romans joined together, and being surrounded in a circle, they did not hold their strength for long; their line having wavered, nearly all were slain.

...Bardas Phocas <note>original: "Φωκᾶς" (Phokas) — A member of the powerful Phocas military aristocracy; his uncle was the murdered Emperor Nikephoros II</note>, trusting in his resources, put on a diadem and assumed the other symbols of imperial power to stir up a rebellion against the Emperor. His father, Leo the Curopalates <term>Curopalates — "In charge of the palace," a high-ranking Byzantine court title usually reserved for the Emperor's closest relatives</term>, had persuaded some with gifts <margin>C</margin> and others with promises of ranks and estates, using the Bishop of Abydos as his agent for this purpose. <margin>5</margin> Leo himself intended to cross over secretly from Lesbos with his son Nicephorus to the regions toward Thrace. When the Emperor learned of this—because the bishop had been arrested and, unable to escape the evidence, revealed everything openly— <margin>10</margin> the Curopalates was handed over to the judges. By all of them, he and his son were sentenced to death. However, the Emperor acted more leniently: they were both condemned <margin>D</margin> to perpetual exile and the blinding of their eyes <note>Blinding was a common Byzantine punishment for rebels, as a blind man was considered legally and physically unfit to serve as Emperor</note>. It is said that the Emperor secretly instructed <margin>15</margin> the executioners by no means to mutilate their sight, but rather to give the appearance of blinding while in reality leaving their natural light intact. He also told them to hide that this was an imperial command and to take credit for the deed themselves, as if they had acted out of humanity and granted them their sight as a favor. So ended the affairs of the Curopalates. <margin>20</margin> Meanwhile, Sclerus crossed over to Asia and, upon arriving at Dorylaeum <note>original: "Δορυλαίῳ" — A strategic city in Asia Minor, modern Eskişehir, Turkey</note>, first attempted to test Phocas and his supporters to see if he could persuade them to abandon their plans through promises of rewards. For indeed, he had orders from the Emperor to strive as much as possible to keep his hands clean of the blood of his fellow countrymen.
