Using the pursuit, they caught him in the plain just as he was about to reach the foothills of the fortress. One of them, preeminent in daring and nobility, named Constantine—nicknamed **Charon** <note>original: Χάρων — likely a nickname referencing the ferryman of the dead, implying his lethality in battle</note>—left the others behind and with great intensity fell upon Phokas, who was guarding the rear of his own party. Phokas was prepared to receive anyone who attacked him with spirit. 

<margin>D</margin> Seeing him from a distance and recognizing him, Charon hurled unseemly and indecent insults at him, calling him base and unmanly, and ordering him to wait a moment so that he might receive the "rewards" of his rebellion <note>A sarcastic reference to the punishment for treason</note>. "O man," he said, "you ought to have considered the instability of human fortune <note>original: τὸ ἀστάθμητον... τῆς τῶν ἀνθρώπων τύχης</note> rather than hurling insults; you should not trample upon a man forced by fortune’s own spite. Instead, you should pity and have mercy on my misfortune—I, who had a father who was a *kouropalates* <term>Kouropalates: One of the highest Byzantine court dignities, usually reserved for members of the imperial family</term>, a grandfather who was a *Caesar* <term>Caesar: The rank immediately below the Emperor</term>, and an uncle who was an Emperor <note>Referring to Emperor Nikephoros II Phokas</note>. I myself have been a Duke <term>Duke: From 'doux', a high-ranking military governor</term> and was numbered among those of the highest rank, yet now I am subjected to the ultimate evils and

**Latin Translation of the above passage:**
Mounted on horses, they overtake Phokas in the field just as he was approaching the base of the mountain where the fortress was situated. Among them was Constantine Charon, a leader in boldness and character. Leaving the rest behind, he pursued Phokas at a swift gallop, who was closing the line of his men and was prepared to vigorously defend against any force. Charon, seeing him from afar and recognizing him, threw foul insults at him, calling him degenerate and timid, and ordering him to wait a while until he received the reward for his defection. Phokas, hearing the contumelies and not ignorant of who was throwing them, checked his horse and turned toward Charon, saying: "Heed me! It was proper for you, considering the instability of human fortune, not to reproach nor insult a man cast into this necessity by its wickedness, but rather to pity my calamity—I, born of a father who was a *kouropalates*, a grandfather a *Caesar*, and an uncle an Emperor; and I myself, who had been a duke and numbered among the highest, am now pressed by extreme calamities and misfortunes." To this Charon said, "Rightly, you scoundrel, would these things be said to boys who can be played with words; you will not deceive me with these trifles." At the same time, urging his horse with spurs, he attacked more fiercely. Then Phokas seized the club which he carried hanging under his cloak, and meeting him, with a blow struck upon the head...

Because He was accustomed to aid not those who inflict injury, but those who have suffered it, not only those who surpassed others in bravery were moved, but even the more timid were seized by eagerness and daring, and were stirred by a burning desire for the fight. # GEORGE CEDRENUS #

...of the imperial bodyguards, <note>Anemas was a member of the elite "Immortals" and the son of the last Emir of Crete who had converted to Christianity.</note> seeing him <note>Ikmor, a high-ranking Rus commander.</note> fighting with great spirit and urging on the rest, stirring them up and throwing the Roman <note>Byzantine</note> ranks into confusion, was neither terrified by the man’s great size nor cowed by his prowess. Instead, seized by a fervor of heart and maneuvering his horse this way and that, he made an <margin>P 679</margin> unstoppable charge. Drawing the sword that hung at his thigh, he rushed at the Scythian <note>original: "Skythou" — the Greek term used for the Kievan Rus</note> and struck him with his blade upon the left shoulder near the collarbone. He sliced through the neck so completely that the head, falling along with the right arm, dropped to the ground. While the Scythian lay there fallen, Anemas returned unharmed to his own camp. At this deed, a mingled cry arose: the Romans shouted in triumph over the victory, while the Scythians <margin>B</margin> wailed indistinctly and began to lose their resolve. As the Romans pressed their advantage, the enemy turned to flight and escaped ingloriously into the city. Many fell on that day, some trampled by one another in the narrow passage and others slaughtered by the Romans who caught up to them. Sphendosthlabos <note>original: "Sphendosthlabos" — the Greek version of the Slavic name Sviatoslav I of Kiev.</note> himself would have been captured had not the onset of night rescued him. Those who escaped the danger and reached the safety of the walls raised a great lamentation for the death of Ikmor. While the Romans were stripping the fallen barbarians of their gear, they found women lying among the slain, dressed in men’s clothing, who had fought like men against the Romans alongside their husbands.

<margin>C</margin> Since the war was going poorly for the barbarians <note>The Kievan Rus, whom the author often calls "barbarians" or "Scythians."</note> and there was no hope of alliance from anywhere (for their kinsmen were far away, and the neighboring barbarian nations, fearing the Romans <note>The Byzantines, who referred to themselves as Romans.</note>, had refused to provide aid), they were also running out of provisions. <margin>5</margin> It was impossible to bring in supplies from anywhere, as the Roman fleet was strictly guarding the banks of the river <note>The Danube.</note>. Meanwhile, all good things flowed to the Romans every day as if from an abundant spring, and both cavalry and infantry forces were constantly being added to their strength. <margin>10</margin><margin>D</margin> It was not even possible for the barbarians to escape by boarding their own small boats <note>original: "keletiois" — light, fast rowing vessels.</note>, as the exits, as we have said, were strictly guarded.

Having held a council, some advised stealing away in a secret retreat by night; others suggested asking for pledges of safety and terms from the Romans, since a withdrawal was not possible by any other means, and thus they might depart for their own lands. <margin>15</margin> As others offered various advice as the occasion prompted, and while everyone collectively desired to end the war, Sphendosthlabos <note>Sviatoslav I, Grand Prince of Kiev.</note> urged them to fight the Romans one more time. He argued that they should either fight well and prevail over their opponents, or, if defeated, prefer a glorious and blessed death over a most shameful and disgraceful life. <margin>20</margin> For he said that life would be unlivable for them if they secured their safety through flight, since they would then be held in contempt by the neighboring nations who had previously feared them intensely. <margin>P 680</margin> This counsel of Sphendosthlabos pleased them, and they all resolved to undertake this final danger for the sake of their lives...

By now, everything in the war was going against the barbarians, for there was no hope of reinforcements, since their own kinsmen were far away and the neighboring barbarian tribes, fearing for themselves from the Romans, denied them aid. Their provisions were also failing them, because with the Roman fleet guarding the banks most carefully, nothing could be imported to them. This same situation prevented them from escaping in their small boats, while in the meantime all good things flowed to the Romans daily as if from a perennial spring, and cavalry and land forces arrived one after another. Therefore, they called a council. There, some judged that they should flee secretly by night, while others thought they should implore the Romans for peace and protection, and thus return home (for otherwise it was not permitted). To others, different plans seemed best according to the circumstances. Nevertheless, the opinions of everyone tended toward the conclusion that an end must be made to the war. But Sphendosthlabos urged that they should be willing to clash with the Romans yet one more time, and either defeat them by fighting bravely, or if it was not granted to achieve victory, to prefer a glorious and happy death to a most foul and infamous life. For who would endure a life preserved by flight, with the neighboring peoples—to whom they had previously been a terror—hereafter looking down on them? This opinion was pleasing, and they all gave their assent, promising the extreme...

...that they would undergo the supreme struggle for their lives with all their might. Therefore, on the following day, they all exit the city and close the gates, so that no one might be able to reach the city by fleeing. Once battle was joined, they fought sharply. While the barbarians were now fighting with spirit, the Romans began to faint from both the weight of their heavy armor and the burning heat of the sun at clear midday, as well as from thirst. When the Emperor noticed the situation, he brought aid with his own men and placed himself against the vehemence of the enemy; meanwhile, he ordered skins full of water and wine to be brought. From these, those whom the heat and thirst had afflicted were refreshed, and they rushed upon the Scythians with violent force. As the enemy boldly stood their ground, they fought for some time with the "Mars being equal" <note>A Latin idiom meaning the battle was a draw or evenly matched.</note>. Finally, the Emperor, sensing that the narrowness of the place stood in the way of his men's valor and that the Scythians' courage was increased by this, commanded the leaders to lead the men back into the plain far from the city, and to present the appearance of fleeing—not in a scattered way, but by yielding gradually—so that when they had lured the enemy far from the city, they might suddenly attack with their horses turned about. The leaders executed the orders. And the Rus, thinking the yielding Romans were fleeing, exhorted one another and followed them with a great clamor.

However, he placed the Bulgarian royal robes upon the chariot, and above these, he placed an icon of the Mother of God <note>original: "Theomētōr"</note> as the protector of the city, ordering that it should precede him in the procession. When he arrived at the place known as the Forum and had been sufficiently acclaimed, and after offering victory thanks to the Mother of God and her Son, he stripped Boris <note>Boris II, the captured King of Bulgaria</note> of the insignia of the Bulgarian kingship in the sight of the citizens. These items were a crown of gold, a tiara woven from fine linen, and <margin>P 683</margin> red sandals <note>The "red shoes" were a symbol of imperial authority reserved for the Emperor</note>. From there, he visited the Great Church <note>Hagia Sophia</note> and, having given the Bulgarian crown as a dedicated offering to God, and having raised Boris to the dignity of <term>Magistros: one of the highest honorary titles in the Byzantine court</term>, he proceeded to the palace. 

Now Sphendosthlabos <note>Sviatoslav I of Kiev</note>, while returning to his own lands, fell into ambushes that had already been prepared and were waiting for him as he passed through the land of the Patzinaks <note>The Pechenegs, a nomadic Turkic people</note>. He himself and the entire multitude with him were utterly destroyed, as the Patzinaks were enraged with him because of his treaties with the Romans <note>The Byzantines</note>.

The Emperor, rendering thanks for his victories to Christ the Savior, rebuilt from its foundations the church located above the <term>Chalke: the monumental bronze ceremonial gateway to the Great Palace of Constantinople</term>, sparing no expense that would contribute to its luxury and beauty. He also remitted for all the taxpayers of all the <term>Themes: administrative and military provinces of the Empire</term> the so-called <term>Kapnikon: the "smoke tax" or hearth tax, a direct tax on every household</term>. He also commanded that on the coinage...

# A COMPENDIUM OF HISTORIES #

...acquired recently from Emperor Nicephorus, and this one from this Domestic of the Schools <term>Domestic of the Schools: the supreme commander of the Byzantine field army</term>, and this from so-and-so, and this and that from you, and all has been gifted to Basil <note>Basil Lecapenus, the "Parakoimomenos" or Lord Chamberlain, who was the power behind the throne</note>." Seeing that nothing worthy of mention remained for the <margin>5</margin> public treasury from the lands newly acquired, the Emperor was overcome with grief. Groaning from the depths of his soul, he said: "It is a terrible thing, O bystanders, if the public funds are being consumed, and <margin>P 684</margin> the Roman <note>Byzantine</note> armies suffer, and the emperors endure labors beyond the borders, yet the gains from such <margin>10</margin> great toil and effort become the property of a single eunuch."

The Emperor said these things, but one of those present reported the Emperor’s words to Basil, inciting him to anger. From that time on, Basil sought an opportunity to get rid of the Emperor. Having eventually used flattery and gifts to deceive the man who usually poured the wine for the Emperor, he mixed a poison—not one of the most potent <margin>15</margin> or rapidly acting kinds, but one of the slower types that gradually consumes the strength of the person who drinks it—and offered the cup to the Emperor. After drinking it, the Emperor gradually fell ill and his <margin>B</margin> strength failed him. Finally, his shoulders broke out in carbuncles <note>original: "anthrakiasas"; these were likely septic boils or necrotic sores, interpreted by contemporaries as a sign of poisoning</note>, and much blood flowed from his eyes. Having entered the <margin>20</margin> Imperial City <note>Constantinople</note>, he ended his life. He had reigned for six years and as many months, and a little more. He left as successors to the throne Basil and Constantine, the sons of Romanus <note>Romanus II</note>.

The Roman Empire was expanded by Emperor Nicephorus, partly by this man, partly by another Domestic of the Schools, and some by Tzimiskes himself; and all these things were given to Basil. Seeing nothing worthy of mention left for the state from so many acquired goods, he was seized with heavy grief and, drawing a sigh from the depths of his chest, said: "O unworthy thing, comrades, that public money is spent, Roman armies endure hardships, and emperors tolerate labors outside the borders of their empire—and yet, whatever is achieved with so much labor and trouble, all of it falls into the possession of a single eunuch <note>original Latin: "spadonis"</note>."

This speech of the Emperor was reported by someone to Basil. Irritated by this, from that time he sought an opportunity to remove the Emperor. Therefore, with flatteries and gifts, he corrupted the man who was the Emperor's cupbearer. By his hand, he offered the Emperor a poison, not of the most violent kind that would kill immediately, but one that would slowly extinguish the strength of the one who drank it. Having drunk this, he gradually wasted away and his strength failed. At last, carbuncles having broken out over his shoulders and much blood flowing through his eyes, he returned to Constantinople <note>original Latin: "Cpolin"</note> and made an end of living, leaving the empire to Basil and Constantine, the sons of Romanus. He reigned for 6 years, as many months, and a little more.

# GEORGE KEDRENOS #

<margin>C</margin>The end of John’s life occurred in the manner already described, and the power of the empire passed to Basil and Constantine, the sons of Romanus <note>Romanus II</note>, in the year 6484 <note>976 AD</note>, in the fourth indiction, in the month of December. Basil was then in his twentieth year of age, <margin>5</margin> and Constantine was three years younger than him. Only the appearance and the name of emperors were bestowed upon the youths, for the management of affairs was carried out by the *proedros* <term>Proedros: a high-ranking court official, here referring to the eunuch Basil Lecapenus</term> Basil, because of the young age of the emperors and their tender and not yet established intellect. As soon as the power passed to the children of Romanus, he immediately sent out swift messengers to bring <margin>10</margin> their mother <note>The Empress Theophano, who had been exiled</note> from across the border back to the palace. But he was also fearful of uprisings against the empire, especially regarding the *magister* <term>Magister: "Magister officiorum," a high-ranking military and administrative official</term> Bardas Skleros, who was always lying in wait for the throne and...

...on his brow. <note>The text here provides a retrospective physical portrait of the deceased Emperor John Tzimiskes</note> He had manly and cheerful eyes, a nose both thin and well-proportioned, and his upper beard was reddish and hung down somewhat further than the average, while the lower part was well-trimmed, as was fitting, and not at all lacking. In height he was somewhat short, though he had a broad chest and back. He possessed gigantic strength, with great dexterity in his hands and an invincible might; for a heroic soul was mixed within him, fearless and undaunted, demonstrating supernatural courage in such a small body. He did not shrink from charging an entire phalanx alone; after slaying many with lightning speed, he would return to his own men. In jumping, ball games, throwing the javelin, and drawing the bow, he surpassed everyone of that time. Placing four racing horses side by side, he would leap from one side and land on the fifth like a bird. He would shoot an arrow and hit the target through the hole of a ring. Placing a ball made of leather into the bottom of a glass cup, and repeatedly spurring his horse to increase its speed, he would strike the ball with a rod so that it would leap up and fly away, while the cup remained unmoved in its place. He was magnificent and most liberal in giving, and no one who asked of him went away empty-handed, unless Basil the Lord Chamberlain <note>original: "parakoimomenos"</note> restrained him. He had this flaw: that he sometimes caroused in drink beyond what was proper and was distracted by the pleasures of the body. He was forty-five years old when he became emperor, and he died having lived fifty-one years in total.

He also devised a similar scheme against Michael Burtzes, who was also under suspicion. The *proedros* was eager to detach him from his association with Skleros (for Burtzes was also with him, commanding a certain military regiment). After honoring him with the rank of *magister* <term>Magister: one of the highest honorary and administrative titles in the Byzantine court</term>, he appointed him *dux* of Antioch, which lies by the Orontes River. <margin>P 685</margin>

[Bar]das, having now brought his conspiracy into the open, donned the diadem and assumed the other insignia of royalty. <margin>D</margin> He was proclaimed emperor by the entire Roman army present, with the Armenians leading the shouts of acclaim. Since he knew that one who had <margin>5</margin> cast such a die <note>original: "anarripsanti kybon," a Greek idiom meaning to take a great, irrevocable risk, similar to "crossing the Rubicon"</note> required vast sums of money—without which, as the rhetorician <note>This refers to the famous Greek orator Demosthenes, who famously argued that "money is the sinews of war."</note> says somewhere, nothing that must be done can be accomplished—he immediately turned to gathering funds. He detained the collectors of the public taxes, seized communal money, and arrested and <margin>10</margin> punished those who otherwise gave suspicion of wealth. Some, however, voluntarily brought their own livelihoods <note>meaning their personal fortunes or estates</note> to him in the hope of receiving greater rewards later. Thus, in a short <margin>P 686</margin> time, he gathered a great mass of money. 

He seized a fortified stronghold called Charpote <note>Modern Harput in eastern Turkey</note>, located in Mesopotamia. After securing it in every way and placing an <margin>15</margin> adequate guard over it, he deposited the collected wealth there, intending to keep it as a base of operations in case of failure and a "harbor of safety." He also dealt with the neighboring Saracens <note>The Byzantine term for Muslim Arabs</note>: specifically, Apotulph, the emir of Amida (which is called Emet), and Apotagle, the emir of Martyropolis <margin>20</margin> (which they call Miepherkin). As the news spread everywhere, all those who delight in revolution <note>literally "new things"</note> flocked to him. Already, the [summer was approaching...]

When summer arrived, he set out with his whole army and hurried toward the reigning city <note>Constantinople</note>, full of hope and thinking he was all but seated upon the imperial throne. Indeed, a night vision of a certain monk, who laid claim to great virtue, emboldened him and made him more daring in his enterprise. For this man seemed to see men of fire, who took Bardas and led him up to a very high vantage point; 
<margin>C</margin> there he met a woman of a presence more formidable than any human, and she handed him the royal whip. Bardas considered this whip a symbol of kingship, but it was, in truth, God’s wrath against the Romans.

As soon as the rumor reached the capital, the emperors were thrown into great distress, and despondency seized the sensible and upright part of the citizenry; it gladdened only those who take pleasure in the upheaval of affairs and rejoice in looting. Immediately, letters were dispatched to Peter the commander of the camp <term>stratopedarches: a high military rank, often an administrative and field commander</term>, and the loyal portion of the army was quickly assembled at Caesarea <note>Modern Kayseri in central Turkey</note>.

With all his forces he began the march toward Constantinople <note>original: "Cpolin," an abbreviation for Constantinopolin</note>, full of hope and imagining himself all but sitting upon the emperor’s throne. The news of this matter, brought to Constantinople, threw the emperors into great anxiety and affected every good and wise citizen with heavy sorrow; it was a pleasure only to those who delight in changes of fortune and love to live by plunder. ...[how], having been freed from his chains, he arrived safely in the Roman provinces, we shall now narrate.

The Persian race, stripped of their kingdom by the Saracens, never ceased to be angry with them, and silently pondered and looked for an opportunity to cast them down and recover their ancestral power. There was among them a certain man born of a most noble line, Inargus, famous for both eloquence and military matters and full of energy. Feeling that Chosroes was conducting his rule in a dissolved and inept manner, and thinking that the long-sought opportunity for the Persians was now at hand, he incited the entire Achaemenid race to revolt from the Saracens. Hiring about twenty thousand of the eastern Turks for pay, he drove through and plundered the affairs of the Saracens, punishing those he captured with death, and not even sparing the children.

With this man, Chosroes himself and his leaders often fought, but he always succumbed. His situation now desperate, and feeling further that he could not bear arms against the Persians—since his own armies, often cut down, could no longer endure to even hear the name of the Persians—he remembered the Romans whom he held as captives. It occurred to him, reasoning quite prudently, that unless Sclerus <note>The Latin text explicitly names the general Bardas Sclerus, whereas the Greek implies him</note> was one of the illustrious and highest men, and outstanding in the strength of mind and body, he would surely never have risen up against his own master...

# COMPENDIUM OF HISTORIES

### PAGE 441

...having provided them with appropriate and sufficient full armor <note>The Greek term is *panteuchia*, referring to a complete set of weaponry and armor</note>, and having taken guides for the journey, he set out with them against the Persians. When the battle lines were drawn up, Sclerus’s men made a fierce and violent charge against the Persians. The Persians were terrified by the strange nature of the armor, the unfamiliar sound of the language <note>The Romans would have been shouting in Greek or Latin, rather than the local tongues</note>, and the unknown military formation. More than anything, they were stunned by the rapid force and momentum of the Romans. They were utterly routed and fell in such numbers that (to use the common proverb) "not even a messenger" <note>original: ἄγγελον — a classical idiom meaning a defeat so total that no one survives to tell the tale</note> was left of the disaster, for Inargus himself fell during the assault. 

Having seized a great deal of plunder and many horses, the Romans decided not to return to Chosroes. Instead, they took the road leading toward the Roman Empire and, by traveling with great speed, they managed to escape unnoticed and safely reached their own lands. 

However, another account claims that after the victory over the Persians, they returned and were received kindly by Chosroes. When Chosroes reached the end of his life shortly thereafter, he strictly commanded his son and namesake—who was to be king after him—to grant the Romans an alliance and send them home. 

<margin>P 698</margin> In one of these two ways, Sclerus reached Roman territory. There, he found Bardas Phocas already being hailed as Emperor <note>Bardas Phocas was a rival general who had also revolted against the central government in Constantinople</note>, and Sclerus was likewise proclaimed Emperor by his own companions.

<margin>B</margin> Finding the state of affairs in such a condition, his mind was filled with various and conflicting thoughts. He judged himself too weak to sustain and hold onto a rebellion entirely on his own.

...having washed away the filth, he dressed them in new clothes and armed them as each man’s needs required. With guides chosen for the journey, he led this army against the Persians. When the battle began with opposing standards, the Romans made a sharp attack on the Persians. They were terrified by the unknown type of armor, the unusual language, and the strategy of the ranks and battle which they had never seen before; but they were especially shaken by the violence of the charge. They were scattered and all were slaughtered to a man, so that—as the proverb says—not even a messenger was left from the slaughter. Inargus himself fell in the first line of battle. The Romans, having obtained massive spoils and very many horses, judged that they should by no means return to Chosroes. Instead, they entered the road that leads to Roman jurisdiction and escaped the Saracens <note term="Saracens">A medieval term used by Europeans and Byzantines for Arab Muslims</note> by forced marches, arriving safely.

Another story is told: that the Romans, having defeated the Persians, returned to Chosroes and were treated humanely. As he was departing this life a little later, he commanded his son and successor Chosroes to lead the Romans back to their fatherland with a protective escort. # GEORGIUS CEDRENUS

### PAGE 442

He thought that joining either Phocas or the Emperor would be exceedingly ignoble and unmanly. After deliberating much with his companions, he ultimately concluded that being acclaimed as the sole Emperor was precarious and unprofitable because it was currently impossible. On the other hand, he judged that approaching one of these rulers while disregarding the other was dangerous due to the uncertainty of the future.

Therefore, he decided to win over both powers as much as possible, so that if he failed with one, he might find a helper and protector in the other. He himself sent letters to Phocas, requesting a joint venture and a division of the empire, should they be able to overcome the Emperor together. 

<margin>C</margin> But secretly, he sent his son Romanus to the Emperor under the guise of being a defector. He calculated and judged this very shrewdly, so that if Phocas prevailed, Sclerus himself would be the savior of his son; <margin>D</margin> but if the Emperor’s side proved stronger, he might be rescued from danger through his son's intercession.

Romanus, providing the appearance of flight, went to the Emperor. The Emperor received him very kindly and with great joy; he immediately honored him with the rank of magister <note>original: μάγιστρον — a very high-ranking court title in the Byzantine hierarchy</note> and used him as a constant advisor in matters of war. 

Indeed, after Sclerus's retreat into Syria, the Emperor was relieved of these anxieties and began to take up the administration of affairs more forcefully. ...seeing that the empire did not have enough strength, he judged it unworthy and a deed of an effeminate man to join himself either to Phocas or to the Emperor. Secretly, however, he sent his son Romanus to the Emperor, feigning that he had defected. He meditated on this most craftily, so that if Phocas conquered, he might obtain pardon for his son, or if the Emperor’s affairs prevailed, he might avoid danger through his son’s plea. 

Romanus, therefore, went to the Emperor under a feigned refuge and was received by him most kindly and with joy. He was immediately raised to the dignity of the mastership <note>magisterii</note> and was thereafter held in the highest honor as a counselor in wars.

<margin>5</margin> Once the Emperor was freed from the burden and worries of the civil wars, he began to consider how he should settle the affairs concerning Samuel <note>Samuel was the Tsar of the First Bulgarian Empire and a primary antagonist of Basil II’s reign.</note> and the other local rulers <term>toparchs</term>, who, having seized the opportunity while he was occupied with the rebellions, had caused no small amount of damage to the Roman <note>original: Ῥωμαίων (Rhōmaiōn) — though we call it the "Byzantine Empire," they referred to themselves as the Roman Empire.</note> territories.

On his return journey through Cappadocia, the high official <term>magistros</term> Eustathios Maleinos received him as a guest with his entire army and supplied everything in abundance. The Emperor, pretending to approve of this service, took him back to Constantinople and never permitted him to return home again. Instead, providing for all his needs most lavishly in the city, he detained him until his death, treating him like a wild animal kept in a cage. After his death, all his goods were made public property. The Emperor also decreed by law that the more powerful men should not grow even more powerful by multiplying their estates, although this same law had been issued by his grandfather Constantine and his father-in-law Romanos.

# BYZANTINE HISTORIES BY GEORGE CEDRENUS #

<page-num>456</page-num>

<margin>5</margin>...[Since he could not subdue them by flattery or promises], he moved to **Philippopolis** <note>Modern-day Plovdiv, Bulgaria.</note>. From there, he departed and returned to **Constantinople**.

In the same <term>indiction</term> <note>A 15-year administrative cycle used for tax assessment in the Roman and Byzantine Empires.</note>, he issued an edict that the tax burdens of the impoverished poor who had perished or fled should be paid by the **powerful** <note>original: "dynaton." The *Dynatoi* were the wealthy land-owning aristocracy who were expanding their estates at the expense of small farmers.</note>. This tax arrangement was named the **Allelengyon** <note>original: "allelengyuon," meaning "mutual surety." This was a highly controversial policy intended to curb the power of the elite by making them financially responsible for the taxes of their poorer neighbors.</note>. Although **Patriarch Sergius**, along with many high priests and a great number of ascetic monks, <margin>C</margin> pleaded for this unreasonable burden to be removed, the Emperor did not comply.

<margin>10</margin> In the eighth indiction, in the year 6518 <note>This date in the Byzantine calendar corresponds to approximately 1009–1010 AD.</note>, **Azizius** <note>The Fatimid Caliph Al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah, referred to here by a version of his father's name, Al-Aziz.</note>, the ruler of **Egypt**, broke the treaty he had with the Romans for minor reasons and grievances not worth mentioning. # THE HISTORY OF GEORGIUS CEDRENUS #

<header>GEORGIUS CEDRENUS</header>

Thus, **Dometianos the Caucanos** <note>The "Caucanos" or Kavkhan was the second-highest title in the First Bulgarian Empire, often serving as a chief advisor or military commander.</note>, a powerful man and associate of **Gabriel** <note>Gabriel Radomir, the son of Tsar Samuel.</note>, was captured, along with **Elitzes**, the governor of **Moglena**, and many other lords, as well as a significant number of fighting men. <margin>D</margin> Those capable of bearing arms were deported by the Emperor to **Asprakania** <note>original: "Ἀσπρακανίαν" — likely Vaspurakan in Armenia, where Basil II frequently settled Bulgarian captives to secure the eastern frontier.</note>, while he ordered the remaining common rabble <margin>5</margin> to be plundered and the fortress to be burned. Another fortress called **Enotia** <note>Modern Notia.</note>, located near **Moglena**, was also taken.

On the fifth day, the Roman named **Cheirotmetos** <term>Cheirotmetos</term> <note>Literally "The Hand-Cut." The letters promised that he would show the Emperor all due submission and servitude. The Emperor read these, confirmed his response with letters bearing a **golden seal** <term>chrysobull</term> <note>A "chrysobull" was an official decree from the Byzantine Emperor, named for the golden seal (bulla) attached to it.</note>, and sent them back to **John**. <margin>15</margin>

A few days later, the "hand-cut" Roman returned, bringing more writings from **John** and the lords of **Bulgaria**, professing themselves to be the Emperor’s subjects and servants. <margin>P 710</margin> **Caucanos**, the brother of the **Dometianos** who had been captured at **Moglena**, also defected to the Emperor; Basil received him with great honor. However, when the Emperor realized that **John** had written these things with <margin>20</margin> deceit and cunning, and was actually planning the opposite of what he had promised, he returned again to **Bulgaria**. After plundering the surrounding regions of **Ostrobos** and **Soskos** and the plains of **Pelagonia**, he **blinded all the Bulgarians he captured** <note>Basil II is famously known as "the Bulgar-Slayer" for his practice of blinding captured enemy soldiers to destroy their ability to resist.</note>. He then marched as far as the city of **Achris** <note>Modern Ohrid in North Macedonia.</note>, where the palaces of the Bulgarian kings were established. <margin>25</margin>

John’s <note>John Vladislav, the last Tsar of the First Bulgarian Empire.</note> assault against the **Romans** <note>original: "Ῥωμαίων" — the Byzantines' name for themselves.</note> was hindered because the **Patzinaks** <note>original: "Πατζινάκων" — the Pechenegs, a nomadic Turkic people often acting as mercenaries or raiders.</note> did not provide them with an alliance. # COMPENDIUM OF HISTORIES
## BY GEORGIUS CEDRENUS

**David Arianites**, the **Patrician**, surrendered the fortresses of **Stypeion** and **Prosakos** <note>Stypeion is modern Štip in North Macedonia; Prosakos is the fortress of Prosek.</note> to the Emperor. Basil returned through these strongholds, where he was honored and celebrated with hymns and prayers of thanksgiving. Turning again toward the right, he departed for **Ohrid**, where he established his camp. The entire population met him with songs of victory, applause, and cheers. The city of **Ohrid** is situated upon a high hill, very near a massive lake <margin>5</margin> from which the **Drin** river flows. This river runs toward the north, then turns west and empties into the **Ionian Sea** near the fortress of **Elissos** <note>Modern Lezhë in Albania.</note>. Ohrid was the capital of all **Bulgaria**, where the palaces of the Bulgarian kings were established and their treasures were stored. Opening these, the Emperor found vast amounts of money, crowns set with pearls, gold-woven garments, and <margin>B 10</margin> one hundred *centenaria* <term>Centenarium: A Roman/Byzantine unit of weight; 100 centenaria of gold would equal roughly 7,200 pounds.</term> of coined gold. He distributed all of this as pay to his army. After appointing **Eustathius Daphnomeles**, the **Patrician**, as the governor <margin>15</margin> of the city and providing him with a substantial garrison, the Emperor went out to his camp. There he received the widow of **John Vladislav**, who had been brought to him. She arrived with her three sons and six daughters, as well as an illegitimate son of **Samuel** and two daughters of **Radomir**, the son of **Samuel**.

---

<margin>5 variant: "those meeting him" in manuscript C</margin> <margin>6 manuscript C adds: "called **Lychnidos**"</margin> 
The lake is called **Lychnidos**, and the city is named for it; in ancient times, it was called **Dyassarites**. From this lake, an untold multitude of useful fish is harvested. <margin>8 after "runs"</margin> manuscript C adds: "flowing out from the southern parts near **Diabolis**." Ibatzes was also brought forth, having been deprived of his eyes. It is worth the effort to report how he lost them, as the narrative contains something pleasing and admirable.

### GEORGE CEDRENUS. 472

**Eustathius**, having caught **Ibatzes** alone, immediately threw him to the ground and, pressing his knee against his chest—for he was naturally strong in hand-to-hand combat—he began to choke him. The men themselves ran up to a high upper room and, drawing their swords, waited for those who were sure to <margin>10</margin> come. When the deed became known, an untold multitude came rushing together; some held swords in their hands, others spears, some bows, others stones or wooden clubs, and some held burning torches <margin>15</margin> while others brought flammable material. <margin>C</margin> They ran to help, shouting:

...he began. <margin>D</margin> "O assembled men, you yourselves will all testify that I harbored no prior enmity toward your ruler. You know well that he is a Bulgarian while I am a Roman <note>original: Ῥωμαῖος; the Byzantines referred to themselves as Romans, identifying as the continuation of the Roman Empire.</note>. I would not have so madly thrown myself into such obvious danger, nor would I have shown such contempt for my own life, <margin>10</margin> had there not been a powerful reason forcing me to this action.

Know, then, that this deed was the command of the Emperor <note>Basil II, known to history as the 'Bulgar-Slayer'.</note>, and in obeying him, I served only as his instrument. Instead, I will fight for my own life and, along with my men, I will repel those who attack us until death. If we do die—which is the necessary fate of those surrounded by so many—we shall consider our death a happy and blessed one, for we have one who will <margin>20</margin> seek out and avenge our blood. Consider well whether it is possible for you to resist him for long." When those who had gathered heard these words, they were struck with terror of the Emperor; they began to slip away <margin>B</margin> little by little, and were soon scattered in every direction.

...finishing his silence, he addressed them thus: "O multitude, you yourselves can judge that no private feuds existed between me and your prince. So, if you wish to kill me, I am certainly surrounded and in your power; yet you will not finish us without a struggle, nor shall we commit ourselves to your whims by laying down our arms, but we shall fight for our lives to the very last breath. ### COMPENDIUM OF HISTORIES

Through the efforts of **Xiphias** <note>David Xiphias, a prominent Byzantine general.</note>, the Emperor razed all the fortresses in **Servia** and **Soskos** to the ground. He then arrived at the fortress of **Stagoi** <note>Modern Kalabaka, the site of the Meteora monasteries.</note>, where **Elemagus**, the governor of **Belgrade**, met him in the humble dress of a servant along with his fellow officials. 

From there, he set out for **Athens**. While passing through **Zetounion** <margin>P 717</margin>, he beheld the bones of the **Bulgarians** who had fallen there when the *magistros* **Nicephorus Uranus** routed **Samuel** <note>Referring to the Battle of Spercheios in 997 AD.</note>, and he was filled with wonder. He also greatly admired the wall built at **Thermopylae** to keep out the Bulgarians by **Rupenes**, which is now called the **Skelos** <note>Meaning 'The Leg'.</note>. Upon reaching **Athens**, he offered prayers of thanksgiving for his victory to the **Theotokos** <note>The 'Mother of God'. At this time, the Parthenon had been converted into a cathedral dedicated to the Virgin Mary.</note>. After adorning the temple with many splendid and costly offerings, he returned to **Constantinople**. 

He entered through the great doors of the **Golden Gate** <note>The main ceremonial entrance to Constantinople, used for imperial triumphs.</note> in a victory procession, wearing a golden crown topped with a crest. <margin>B</margin> Leading the way were **Maria**, the wife of **Vladislav**, the daughters of **Samuel**, and the other **Bulgarians**. This occurred in the second indiction, in the year 6527 <note>1018/1019 AD.</note>. Having entered the **Great Church** <note>Hagia Sophia.</note> in this manner with trophies and songs of victory, and having sung hymns of thanks to God, he retired to the palace. 

Upon his victorious return, **Patriarch Sergius** repeatedly entreated him to abolish the **allelengyon** <term>Allelengyon: A controversial tax policy introduced by Basil II that forced wealthy landowners to pay the tax debts of their poorer neighbors.</term> (for the Emperor had promised to do this if he prevailed over the Bulgarians), but he could not be persuaded. This **Sergius**, who had shepherded the Church of God for twenty full years, died in the month of July, in the second indiction, in the year...

### THE COMPENDIUM OF HISTORIES BY GEORGE KEDRENOS

In the year 6527 <note>1018/1019 AD</note>, in the month of July, the Patriarch departed to the Lord. **Eustathius**, who was the lead priest <term>Protos</term> <note>The 'Protos' was the highest-ranking priest or administrator within the clergy of the imperial palace.</note> of the church within the imperial palaces, was then appointed Patriarch.

<margin>C</margin> Once Bulgaria had been subjugated to him, the neighboring nation of the **Croats** <note>original: "Chorbatoi"</note> also flocked to the Emperor. <margin>5</margin> They were led by two brothers who, after submitting and receiving high titles and significant estates, brought their entire people into subjection. Only **Sermo**, the ruler of **Sirmium** <note>A strategic city in modern-day Serbia, formerly a Roman provincial capital.</note> and brother of **Nestongos**, refused to obey. Against him, **Constantine Diogenes**, the governor of those border regions, feigned a spirit of friendship and sent an envoy. <margin>10</margin> He declared under oath that he desired to meet with Sermo to discuss urgent common interests. He proposed that if Sermo felt any fear, he should bring only three attendants, and they would meet in the middle of the river that flowed there; Diogenes promised to arrive with only three attendants as well.

<margin>D</margin> Sermo was persuaded and came to the river to meet Diogenes. <margin>15</margin> While they were talking, Diogenes—who was carrying a dagger hidden in the folds of his robe—suddenly drew it and struck Sermo in the side, killing him instantly. While Sermo's companions fled, Diogenes gathered the nearby troops and, with a sufficient force, <margin>20</margin> marched on **Sirmium**. He first intimidated the widow of the deceased and then softened her with great promises, persuading her to surrender and hand Sirmium over to the Emperor. She was sent to **Byzantium** <note>Constantinople</note> and married to one of the city's high-ranking nobles, while Diogenes was appointed governor of the newly acquired territory.

->5 Croats C &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 8 to obey C &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; he desired C<-

***

In the month of July, in the year of the world 6527, he departed to the Lord. In his place was appointed **Eustathius**, the chief of the priests of the palace church. Once Bulgaria was subdued, the neighboring nation of the **Croats** and its leaders, two brothers, also surrendered to the emperor; the emperor granted them honors and ample wealth. Only **Sermo**, the lord of **Sirmium** and brother of **Nestongos**, still rejected his rule. **Constantine Diogenes**, the governor of the neighboring province, sent an envoy to him, affirming by oath that he desired to meet him in person and discuss necessary matters. If he feared an ambush, he would come to the bank of the river flowing there accompanied by only three servants. Sermo should do the same. Sermo complied and met with Diogenes in this manner. There, when they were about to speak, Diogenes suddenly drove a dagger, which he carried hidden in his chest, into Sermo's side and killed him; the servants escaped by flight. Diogenes, having assembled the neighboring armies, set out for **Sirmium** with a strong force and persuaded the terrified widow, with great promises, to surrender herself and Sirmium to the emperor. She was sent to **Byzantium** and there joined in marriage to a leading citizen; Diogenes was placed in charge of the newly captured jurisdiction.

### THE COMPENDIUM OF HISTORIES

<margin>P 718</margin> The Emperor <note>Basil II, reigned 976–1025 AD</note> also restored the aqueduct of the Emperor Valentinian, so that the citizens might have an abundance of water. However, when **George**, the ruler of **Abasgia** <note>original: "Abasgias"; a kingdom in modern-day Georgia</note>, broke his treaties with the Romans and began raiding the neighboring territories, the Emperor set out against him <margin>5</margin> with his entire army. He left behind the patrician **Nikephoros Xiphias** and the patrician **Nikephoros**, the son of **Bardas Phocas** <note>The Phocas family were long-time rivals of Basil II; Nikephoros's father, Bardas, had previously led a major rebellion against the Emperor.</note>. These two were greatly distressed at being left out of the campaign. Gathering a random crowd from **Cappadocia**, **Rodantos**, and the surrounding regions, they stirred up a rebellion. When this was reported to the <margin>10</margin> Emperor, agitation and agony gripped the camp; they feared they might <margin>B</margin> be caught in the middle between the Abasgians and the rebels and suffer an incurable disaster—for a rumor had spread that Xiphias and his followers had sent messengers to the ruler of Abasgia regarding this very matter.

The Emperor wrote letters to both Xiphias and <margin>15</margin> Phocas and sent them out, instructing the messenger to do his best to remain unnoticed and to give the letter to each man without the other knowing. The messenger did as he was ordered and delivered the letters secretly. Phocas immediately read his own letter to Xiphias; but Xiphias, hiding his own letter and utterly denying that he had received one, <margin>20</margin> called Phocas to a private talk one day. <margin>C</margin> When Phocas arrived, Xiphias killed him using ambushes he had prepared in advance. The gathering of rebels was immediately scattered. When the death of Phocas became known to the Emperor, **Theophylaktos**, the son of **Damianos Dalassenos**, was sent; he seized Xiphias and sent him away...

---

<margin>8</margin> *rhogangou* in manuscript C | <margin>19</margin> "his own" added in manuscript C

---

The Emperor Basil also repaired the aqueduct of the Emperor Valentinian, providing the citizens with a wealth of water. Furthermore, when George, the leader of Abasgia, violated the treaty he had with the Romans and harassed the neighboring areas with incursions, Basil led his army against him. He left at home the patrician Nikephoros [Xiphias] and [Nikephoros] the son of Bardas Phocas. But they, bearing it very indignantly that they were not also ordered to go together to that war, stirred up a rebellion after gathering an army from Cappadocia, Rodantos, and other neighboring regions. The news of this matter, brought to the Emperor, struck great anxiety into the army. For they feared lest, being shut in the middle between the Abasgians and the insurgents (since it was reported that Xiphias had dealt with the prince of the Abasgians through intermediaries concerning this matter), they would be forced to suffer the ultimate extremity. Therefore, the Emperor sent letters to both Xiphias and Phocas, commanding the one who carried them to take care to deliver them to the one while the other was as ignorant as possible. When he had accomplished this, Phocas immediately recited to Xiphias the letter written to him; Xiphias, however, denying that anything at all had been written to him, called Phocas to a conference on a certain day, and killed him as he came by means of snares prepared for this purpose. In this way, that conspiracy was immediately dissipated. And the Emperor, having been informed of the death of Phocas, sent Theophylaktos, the son of Damianos Dalassenos, who brought the captured Xiphias to Constantinople in chains.

# GEORGIOS CEDRENOS

Having taken up the entire power, Constantine, <margin>D</margin> <margin>10</margin> and having received the authority to do whatever he wished, and rejoicing in dissolute deeds, became the cause of many evils for the state. He himself did nothing and planned none of the necessary things, but rejoiced in horse races, mimes, and jesters, <margin>14</margin> and spent his nights at dice and **kottabos** <note>original: "kottabois"; an ancient drinking game, though here likely implying gambling or general carousing. He also blinded Romanos Kourkouas—who was Prusian’s <margin>C</margin> brother-in-law by marriage to his sister—as well as Bogdan, Glabas, <margin>15</margin> and Goudeles. Therefore, Emperor Constantine appointed Diogenes—who was then the governor of Sirmium <note>a strategic city in modern-day Serbia</note>—as the **Duke** <note>a military governor with high-level regional authority</note> of Bulgaria. Having engaged them many times while they were dispersed, he routed them and forced them to cross back over the Ister <note>the ancient name for the Danube River</note> and remain at peace.

### THE HISTORIES OF GEORGE KEDRENOS

Furthermore, throughout the entire duration of his reign, there was a massive drought, <margin>D</margin> so severe that even the perennial springs and rivers dried up. While the late Emperor Basil <note>Basil II, known as the "Bulgar-Slayer," who reigned 976–1025</note>, out of compassion for the poor, was not in the habit of collecting public taxes immediately when they were due, but instead granted stays and delays for these demands, it happened that at the time of his death, two years of taxes were still outstanding. Constantine immediately collected these. He also collected the taxes for the following three years (for his reign lasted that long), and so not only the poor and destitute were crushed, but also the wealthy; for in the space of three years, they were forced to pay five years' worth of tax levies. During this time, a fleet of **Agarenes** <note>A term often used by Byzantine writers for Muslim Arabs, claiming descent from Hagar</note> set out against the Cyclades islands. # GEORGE KEDRENOS

He welcomed his subjects, beginning his good deeds first with acts of piety. Because he knew that the income of the **Great Church** <note>Hagia Sophia, the primary cathedral of Constantinople</note> was insufficient—as he had served as its *steward* <term>oikonomos: a high-ranking official responsible for managing the finances and properties of a church or monastery</term> in former times—and knowing the needs of the other churches served by its <margin>5</margin> clergy, he decreed that eighty pounds of gold should be provided to them every year from the imperial treasury as a supplement.

<margin>P 723</margin> He also completely cut out and uprooted the **Mutual Liability tax** <term>allelengyon: a controversial tax introduced by Basil II requiring wealthy landowners to pay the tax arrears of their poorer neighbors</term>, which Constantine had intended to do but did not live to accomplish. He also emptied the prisons of those confined for various financial penalties <margin>10</margin>, forgiving public debts and paying off private ones from his own funds. He ransomed those captives held in the land of the **Pechenegs** <note>original: "Patzinakia" — a nomadic Turkic people who lived north of the Black Sea and frequently raided Byzantine territory</note>. He also honored three *syncelloi* <term>syncellus: a high-ranking cleric who served as a confidential advisor to a patriarch</term> as **Metropolitans** <note>a high-ranking bishop</note>: Cyriacus of Ephesus, as a kinsman of the Patriarch; Demetrius of Cyzicus, as one very much beloved by him even <margin>15</margin> before his reign; and Michael of the people of **Euchaita**, who was a blood relative of the Emperor because he traced his lineage back to the <margin>B</margin> so-called **Radenos** family.

-> 16 Radenos <-

He summoned John—who had been the *chief secretary* <term>protonotarios: a senior administrative official</term> of Emperor Basil and had already shorn his worldly hair <note>original: "tēn kosmikēn keiramenon tricha" — he had already taken monastic vows</note>—honored him as a *syncellus*, and appointed him as a guardian for his wife’s sister, **Theodora**. Many <margin>20</margin> of God's ministers who had fallen into extreme poverty because of the **Mutual Liability taxes** were restored by him, and he granted comfort to others who were suffering and oppressed by lack of resources. He also provided a vast amount of money, more than could be counted, for the salvation of the soul of his father-in-law <note>The deceased Emperor Constantine VIII</note>. Similarly, he showed favor to all those who had suffered at his <margin>25</margin> hands, promoting some to high offices, while enriching others with estates and money.

# OF GEORGE KEDRENOS

...[Emperor Basil II] had devoted himself entirely to the subjugation of the Bulgarian people. This became the occasion for the more powerful cities of the East to cast off the Roman yoke and seek their own freedom. <margin>B</margin>

When the reins of leadership passed to **Spondyles**, **Musaraph** noticed that the man was easily swayed <note>original: "euripiston," literally meaning "blown about like a fan," or fickle</note>. He promised to be of great use to the Romans if he were released from his chains, claiming he would fulfill all their objectives. He promised to harm his own kinsmen...

There, a certain remarkable thing happened: <margin>15</margin> while the generals—who had a great reputation for courage—and the soldiers did not dare to face the danger but fled in a cowardly manner <note>The variant reading in manuscript C says "ingloriously"</note>, a certain **eunuch** <note>Eunuchs often held high administrative and even military positions in the Byzantine court</note> from among the imperial bedchamber servants saw his own baggage and attendants being carried off. Drawing his bow, he struck one and turned the others to flight; <margin>B</margin> having recovered his belongings, he returned rejoicing. The Emperor himself came close to being captured, but he was safely brought to **Antioch**, as his imperial companions fought with all their hearts and saved both themselves and the Emperor.

# GEORGE CEDRENUS

<margin>C</margin> At that time, while **George Maniakes** was serving as **strategos** <term>strategos: the military governor of a "theme" or administrative district</term> of the **theme** of **Telouch** <note>Modern Duluk, near Gaziantep in Turkey</note>, eight hundred **Arabs**, returning from the rout with an arrogant spirit, came to him. They ordered him to yield as quickly as possible and abandon the city, claiming that the Emperor had been captured and the entire **Roman** army <note>The Byzantines referred to themselves as Romans (Rhomaioi)</note> had been utterly <margin>5</margin> destroyed. They told him not to surrender himself to obvious danger, for when the day dawned, he and his men would perish miserably once they were surrounded. He, appearing to quickly accept the advice and leading them to suspect he would do as he was ordered, sent out sufficient food and drink to them <margin>10</margin> and told them to rest themselves, so that at daybreak he might depart with his companions, leaving them as masters of the city of Telouch and all the Roman property. The Arabs, deceived by his words and actions, and believing they would take possession of everything the next day, <margin>15</margin> turned to drinking and intoxication, spending the night in total security and lack of care. Around midnight, while they were wine-soaked <margin>D</term> and sleeping without a care, he attacked them. He slaughtered all of them and seized two hundred and eighty camels, which were loaded and full of all kinds of Roman goods. <margin>20</margin> Cutting off the noses and ears of those who had fallen, he brought them to the Emperor in **Cappadocia**, who had already reached the **house of Phokas** <note>The ancestral estate of the Phokas family, a powerful military dynasty</note> in his flight and was staying there. The Emperor, welcoming him for this deed, appointed him **katepano** <term>katepano: a high-ranking military official, often a provincial governor with expanded powers</term> of **Lower Media** <note>A region in the eastern frontier, near the borders of modern Iran and Armenia</note>.

<margin>C</margin> Having departed and joined forces with **Pinzarach**, Theoktistos set to work. **Tusper**, the commander-in-chief of the **Egyptians** <note>The Fatimid Caliphate forces</note>, was terrified by the suddenness of the assault and the size of the army, and so he retreated homeward. Theoktistos and his men then took possession of the fortress of **Menikos** itself, which was surrendered to them by a nephew of Mousaraph. They also took another fortress situated on a steep precipice called **Argyrocastron** <note>literally "Silver Castle"</note>. Having settled <margin>10</margin> these affairs in this manner, Theoktistos entered the **Queen of Cities** <note>original: βασιλίδα (basilida), referring to Constantinople</note>, bringing with him **Alach**, the son of **Pinzarach**, whom the Emperor <margin>D</margin> honored with the rank of **Patrician** <term>Patrician: a high-ranking title of nobility in the Byzantine court</term>. Afterward, **Pinzarach** himself arrived, escorted and guarded by **Niketas of Mistheia**, who had served as the governor of **Antioch**. The Emperor received him with great kindness <margin>15</margin> and, having welcomed him with gifts and no small favors, sent him home rejoicing. He also ransomed **Choirosphaktes** from captivity and restored him to his kinsmen.

Regarding the **Protospatharios Orestes**—whom the history previously mentioned had been sent to **Sicily** by Emperor **Basil** <note>Basil II, the predecessor of Romanos III</note>—he was <margin>20</margin> inexperienced in matters of war and handled affairs unskillfully. The **Saracens** of Sicily, watching for a favorable opportunity, suddenly attacked the **Romans**, who were already suffering from a bowel disease <note>likely dysentery</note> caused by luxury <note>original: τρυφῆς (tryphes); implies that the soldiers' health suffered from a soft lifestyle or improper diet compared to the rigors of the campaign</note>. They inflicted a disaster of no small proportions.

...and to attempt the fortress of Menikos. This, Theoctistus briskly carried out. And indeed, Tusber, terrified by his sudden arrival and the great number of troops, returned home. The Saracens, seizing the opportunity, suddenly attacked the Romans, most of whom had contracted a bowel disease from luxury, and afflicted them with no small slaughter.

# COMPENDIUM OF HISTORY

## BY GEORGE CEDRENUS, VOLUME II

Seeking to remedy the recent disaster, the Emperor gathered a formidable force <margin>P 729</margin> from both Greece and Macedonia and sent it to Italy. However, the army was unable to perform any noble deed due to the incompetence and malice of its commander.

<margin>5</margin> In this year 6,539 <note>Byzantine calendar year 6539 corresponds to 1031 AD</note>, in the 14th Indiction <term>Indiction: a 15-year cycle used in the Roman and Byzantine empires for tax and dating purposes</term>, **Prusianos** voluntarily received the tonsure to become a monk. His mother was also transferred from the Mantineion monastery in the **Bucellarian theme** <term>Theme: a military and administrative district of the Byzantine Empire</term> to the **Thracian theme**. Furthermore, the Patrician **Constantine Diogenes** was removed from his tower and tonsured as a monk in the **Studion Monastery** <note>One of the most influential and historic monasteries in Constantinople</note>. 

<margin>10</margin> Emperor **Romanos**, having purchased the house of **Triacontaphyllos**, converted it into a monastery dedicated to our Lady the **Mother of God** <note>original: Θεοτόκου (Theotokos)</note>. He spared no expense in its luxury, yet <margin>B</margin> under this pretext, he greatly burdened his subjects and caused much distress through the forced transport of stones and other materials. 

<margin>15</margin> He also adorned the column capitals of the **Great Church** <note>Hagia Sophia</note> and the Church of the Most Holy **Mother of God at Blachernae** with silver and gold. While he was intending to renovate the altar of the Blachernae shrine, he found an old hanging icon and ordered it to be restored. Upon seeing that the silver plating on the wall's plaster was old, he ordered it to be removed and <margin>20</margin> replaced with new silver. When the plaster was stripped away, an icon painted on wood <note>original: ὑλογραφική (hylographike)</note> was discovered—a small tablet held to the breast, showing the **Mother of God** holding our Lord and God. <margin>C</margin> It had remained uncorrupted from the days of **Copronymus** <note>original: Κοπρωνύμου. This refers to Emperor Constantine V (reigned 741–775), an ardent iconoclast whose nickname, meaning "dung-named," was a slur used by his theological enemies</note> until this day, a span of three hundred years.

So that the Emperor might repair the loss, he sent an excellent army collected from Greece and Macedonia into Italy; however, they themselves could also achieve nothing distinguished on account of the commander's ignorance and malice. 

In this very year of the world 6539, in the 14th indiction, **Prusianus** was shaven as a monk, and his mother was transferred from the Mantineion of the Bucellarian monastery into Thrace. He also decorated the capitals of the columns of the Great Temple and the **Blachernae** shrine with gold and silver. # COMPENDIUM OF HISTORY

## BY GEORGE CEDRENUS

In the year 6540 <note>1031/1032 AD</note>, during the 15th indiction <term>Indiction: a 15-year tax and dating cycle</term> in the month of September, the son of the Emir <note>original: Ἄμερ (Amer), a Greek rendering of 'Emir'</note> of Aleppo came to Emperor **Romanos** bearing many gifts. He requested a renewal of the peace treaty and promised to provide the tributes paid in former times. Consequently, **Theophylaktos the Athenian**, a *protospatharios* <term>Protospatharios: literally "First Sword-bearer," a high-ranking court title</term>, was dispatched; he confirmed the treaties and established a joint alliance with the people of Aleppo.

Empress **Zoe**, following the festival of the **Exaltation of the Holy Cross** <note>A major Christian feast celebrated on September 14</note>, suddenly departed for the **Petrion** <note>A fortified monastery on the Golden Horn often used as a place of confinement for royal women</note>. There, she forced her sister **Theodora** to be tonsured as a nun <margin>D</margin>, declaring that it was otherwise impossible to put an end to the plots and scandals.

Emperor **Romanos** also gave his own niece in marriage, along with a large dowry, to the ruler <note>original: ἐξουσιάρχῃ (exousiarchē), a term for a local sovereign or prince</note> of **Greater Armenia**.

Intending to make a second invasion against **Syria**, the Emperor went out to **Mesanakta**. While he was staying there, it was reported to Empress **Zoe** by **Theophanes of Thessaloniki** that **Constantine Diogenes** had plotted with her sister **Theodora** and was planning an escape to **Illyricum** <note>A region in the western Balkans</note>. This was allegedly done with the secret knowledge of the **Metropolitan of Dyrrachium** and the **Bishop of Peritheorium**.

Immediately <margin>P 730</margin>, both the bishops and **Diogenes** were seized. While **Constantine** was being interrogated at the **Palace of Blachernae** by **John the Praepositus** <term>Praepositus: a high-ranking chamberlain, typically a eunuch</term>—who later became the *orphanotrophos* <term>Orphanotrophos: the official head of the Great Orphanage in Constantinople, a powerful administrative role</term> and was the brother of the future Emperor **Michael IV**—he threw himself from the palace wall. He died of a broken neck and was cast away among the suicides. As for the bishops...

There was also a **trailing of a star** <note>original: "chysis asteros"—literally a "pouring out of a star," likely a meteor or a comet</note> on the Sunday after Easter, around the third hour of the night. ## GEORGIUS CEDRENUS

...[Patriarch Alexius said,] “and I shall step down from the throne for anyone who wishes.” Upon receiving this message, those surrounding Demetrius were filled with both shame and fear—for most of them had been ordained into their positions by Alexius himself. They chose to maintain a respectful silence, and consequently, John <note>John the Orphanotrophos, the Emperor’s powerful brother and court eunuch</note> restrained his ambition to <margin>5</margin> seize the patriarchal throne.

In the year 6546 <note>Byzantine calendar year 6546 AM corresponds to 1037–1038 AD</note>, in the 6th <term>indiction<note>A 15-year tax cycle used by the Byzantines for dating; the 6th indiction here confirms the year 1037 AD.</note></term>, on the second day of November, an earthquake occurred around the tenth hour of the day. The earth continued to tremble until the end of the month of January. A famine also broke out across Thrace, Macedonia, the Strymon region, Thessalonica, and as far as Thessaly. At Thessalonica, the <margin>10</margin> clergy raised a great outcry against the <term>Metropolitan<note>A high-ranking bishop in charge of an ecclesiastical province.</note></term> Theophanes, accusing him of withholding their customary grain rations. The Emperor, who was staying in Thessalonica at the time, attempted to advise the bishop with persuasive words, urging him not to <margin>P 741</margin> deprive the people of the church of the rations to which they were legally entitled. <margin>15</margin> However, when the bishop became abrasive and refused to yield, the Emperor decided he must overcome him with a clever ruse to punish his greed. 

He sent one of his ministers to the bishop, requesting a loan of one <term>centenarium<note>A "hundred-weight" of gold, equal to 100 Roman pounds (approx. 32.7 kg).</note></term> until gold could be brought from Byzantium <note>Constantinople</note>. The bishop swore a solemn oath that he possessed no more than thirty pounds of gold. <margin>20</margin> The Emperor then had the bishop removed from the premises and sent men to search his treasuries. They discovered thirty-three *centenaria* of gold <note>Roughly 3,300 pounds of gold—over a hundred times what the bishop claimed to have.</note>. From this hoard, the Emperor paid the clergy all that had been owed to them from the first year of Theophanes’s term as archbishop until that present hour.

In the year 6542 <note>Byzantine calendar, corresponding to 1038 AD</note>, during the sixth <term>indiction<note>A 15-year cycle used in the Roman and Byzantine tax and dating systems.</note></term>, a conspiracy was hatched against the city of **Edessa**. The governor received the leaders with hospitality and held a banquet for them, but he ordered the horsemen and the baggage to remain outside the walls. A certain poor **Armenian** beggar happened to be where the **Saracens** <note>A common medieval term for Arab or Muslim peoples.</note> were camping. Having overheard one of the men inside the crates (for he understood the Saracen language) asking where they were, he ran and reported the matter to the governor.

# THE COMPENDIUM OF HISTORIES BY GEORGE CEDRENUS

<margin>P 744</margin>
...Seeing, then, that not even a single spark of Roman <note>Byzantine</note> power was left hidden on the island, the islanders gathered every man capable of bearing arms, along with a significant allied force of **Carthaginians** <note>original: "Καρχηδονίων" (Karchēdoniōn). By doing so, he created a pretense of cowardice, causing the **Saracens** to look down on them with contempt. Consequently, they scattered without fear, spending day and night in drinking bouts <note>The manuscript variant 'C' uses the word "μέθαις" (methais) meaning 'drunkenness'.</note>, accompanied by flutes and cymbals, believing that the city would surely fall the following morning. 

On the fourth day, when we are accustomed to celebrate **Pentecost** <note>original: "πεντηκοστήν" (pentēkostēn). A major Christian feast day. Manuscript 'C' suggests the "Mid-Pentecost" festival.</note>, **Kekaumenos** observed the negligence and laziness of the Saracens. Seeing that they lived in such total unconcern that they paid no attention to those inside the walls, he encouraged his own people and ordered the priests to perform the **bloodless sacrifice** <note>The Divine Liturgy or Eucharist.</note>. After everyone had partaken in the divine mysteries together, around the hour of the midday meal, he threw open the gates of the city.

<margin>B</margin>
He burst upon the enemy with the greatest force while they were drunk and heavy-headed from wine. He himself was the first to ride out with his men toward the tent of **Apolaphar**, the ruler of the island. Apolaphar was immediately killed, being unsteady due to his intoxication, and his tent was torn to shreds. The other Saracens also fell in heaps, stumbling from drunkenness and unable to offer any resistance due to the unexpected nature of the attack. Thus, the entire camp was put to flight, with the Saracens <note>The manuscript variant 'P' uses the word "στρατηγῶν" (stratēgōn) meaning 'generals'.</note> trampling and killing one another, until the field was covered with corpses...

On the fourth day, when Pentecost is customarily celebrated, **Ambustus** <note>Latin: "Ambustus" (the Burnt One), a literal translation of the Greek name "Kekaumenos".</note>, considering the security and sluggishness of the Saracens—and how they took no account of those they were besieging—strengthened the spirits of his men with a speech. Having commanded the priests to perform the sacred rite, and after he himself and all the rest had shared in the most holy mysteries, he opened the city gates around the hour of lunch and rushed upon the enemy with the greatest impetus while they were drunk and weighed down by their excesses. Ambustus himself, the leader, rode with his horsemen toward the tent of **Apolaphar**, the prefect of the island; they killed him instantly while he was seized by wine and plundered his tent. Indeed, the rest of the Saracens fell in piles, both staggering from drunkenness and thinking nothing of defense because of the unforeseen attack. # A COMPENDIUM OF HISTORIES

...the field, the nearby ravines, and the rivers [were filled] with the dead, <margin>C</margin> so that out of so many tens of thousands, only a very few managed to escape to **Palermo** <note>original: "Πανόρμῳ" (Panormō). Using a grain measure to count jewels emphasizes the staggering amount of loot.</term>. Thus, while all of **Sicily** had been subdued in a short time by **Maniakes** <note>George Maniakes (d. 1043), a physically imposing and brilliant Byzantine general whose recall led to the loss of the island.</note>, it fell once again under the **Saracens** in a brief moment due to the negligence and wickedness of the generals. Only **Messina** remained, in the manner we have described, after **Stephen** and **Pediadites** fled to **Italy** <note>original: "Λογγιβαρδίᾳ" (Longibardia); referring to the Byzantine Theme of Longibardia in Southern Italy.</note>. <margin>10</margin> Such was the course of events in Sicily.

The **Emperor Michael** <note>Michael IV "the Paphlagonian," reigned 1034–1041.</note> spent most of his time in **Thessaloniki**, staying close to the tomb of the triumphant martyr **Demetrius**, <margin>D</margin> yearning to find a cure for his disease <note>The Emperor suffered from worsening epilepsy and dropsy; he sought a miraculous cure from Saint Demetrius, the patron of Thessaloniki.</note>. He did not involve himself in affairs of state in any way unless it was absolutely necessary; instead, <margin>15</margin> the administration and the handling of public affairs were carried out by **John** <note>John the Orphanotrophos, the Emperor’s brother and a powerful eunuch who served as the de facto ruler.</note>. No form of unholy or illegal scheme was omitted that he did not devise for the ruin and affliction of the subjects. To list each of these would be a **Herculean labor** <note>original Greek: "ἆθλος Ἡράκλειος" (athlos Hērakleios); Latin: "Herculea aerumna." An idiom meaning a task of monumental or impossible difficulty.</note>. All the people lived under the weight of this heavy <margin>20</margin> tyranny, constantly calling upon God and begging for deliverance. God also sent frequent earthquakes, and terrors and portents took hold of the world: the appearance of **comets** in the heavens, and in the air, violent winds and torrential rains,

Therefore, the nearby valleys and rivers were filled. Finally, out of so many thousands, very few reached Palermo by flight. The camp was captured, most full of gold, silver, pearls, and gems, which the soldiers are said to have measured out by the bushel. Thus Sicily, reduced in a short time by Maniakes into the power of the Romans <note>The Byzantines referred to themselves as Romans.</note>, returned to the Saracens in a brief space due to the laziness and carelessness of the leaders, with only Messina being saved for the Romans, as we have said. Furthermore, Stephen and Pediadites fled from the island into Italy. 

Meanwhile, Emperor Michael lived mostly at Thessaloniki, staying at the tomb of the martyr Demetrius, seeking from him a driving away of his disease; nor did he undertake the care of any business, unless compelled by the greatest necessity, with the administration of all things and the entire state falling upon John. There was no dishonest or wicked art which this man did not devise and employ to oppress and harass the subjects. And indeed, to report all his outrages would be a Herculean labor. For a long time, worn down by this tyranny, men repeatedly asked for the help and relief of God. But also, from heaven, continuous shakings of the earth were produced, and the world was full of terrible omens: comets in the sky, winds and most vehement rains in the air...

# THE HISTORIES OF GEORGE CEDRENUS

...on land there were tremors and shakings. These portended, I believe, the destruction of the tyrants that was soon to occur.

<margin>P 745</margin>
In the month of May, in the year 6548 <note>original: "͵ςφμηʹ" (6548 from the creation of the world). In the Byzantine calendar, this corresponds to 1040 AD.</note>, the 8th indiction <term>original: "ἰνδικτιῶνος" (indiktiōnos); a 15-year tax cycle used by the Byzantines for dating.</term>, the Emperor’s sister Maria—who was also the mother of the Caesar—departed for **Ephesus** to pay homage to the Beloved <note>original: "ἠγαπημένου" (ēgapēmenou); referring to Saint John the Apostle and Evangelist, whose tomb was a major pilgrimage site in Ephesus.</note>. Along the way, she learned of many illegal and absurd deeds being committed. Upon returning to **Byzantium** <note>Constantinople.</note>, she reported everything to her brother **John** <note>John the Orphanotrophos, the Emperor’s eldest brother and the true power behind the throne, known for his financial ruthlessness.</note> and pleaded for an end to this wickedness. But he dismissed her with a laugh, saying she thought like a woman and was ignorant of what the Roman state required.

While the Emperor was staying in **Thessaloniki**, as we have mentioned, John sent ten **centenaria** <term>original: "κεντηνάρια" (kentenaria); a "centenarium" was a weight of 100 Roman pounds of gold.</term> of gold to him. 

<margin>B</margin>

The gold was seized by **Stephen**, also known as **Boisthlabos** <note>Stefan Vojislav, a Serbian prince who led a successful revolt against Byzantine authority.</note>, the leader of the **Serbs**, who had recently escaped from the City <note>Constantinople.</note> and seized control of the Serbian lands after driving out **Theophilus Erotikos**. Meanwhile, John, by putting government offices up for sale and giving free rein to injustice, filled the world <note>original: "οἰκουμένην" (oikoumenēn); the civilized or Roman world.</note> with countless calamities. The judges and tax collectors plundered the inhabitants without fear, and no one paid any attention to what was happening.

When the Emperor in Thessaloniki learned of the loss of the gold, he wrote to Stephen, demanding that he return what belonged to the treasury and 

<margin>C</margin>
not provoke a war of his own choosing. But since Stephen paid no heed, the Emperor dispatched an army against him...
