...[to] Thessalonica. At that time, the city of Thessalonica was ruled by the Emperor’s nephew, Constantine the patrician. Having arrived there and surrounded the city with a ditch, Alusian applied himself diligently to the siege. For six days,
<margin>B</margin> he tested the city’s defenses with siege engines <note>original: *elepolesi* — literally 'city-takers', a type of heavy mobile siege tower.</note> and machines. However, being repulsed from every side and despairing of a direct assault, he decided to achieve his goal through a blockade <note>original: *prosedreias* — a persistent "sitting-down" before a city to starve it out.</note>. On a certain day, the locals approached the tomb of the great martyr **Demetrius** <note>St. Demetrius is the patron saint of Thessalonica; he was a 4th-century soldier-martyr believed to be the city's supernatural protector.</note>. After performing an all-night prayer and using the myrrh that flows from the holy tomb <note>St. Demetrius is known as 'the Myrrh-streamer' because of the fragrant oil believed to flow miraculously from his relics.</note>, they threw open the gates as if by a single impulse and charged out against the Bulgarians. Accompanying the Thessalonians was the regiment of the **Magnanimous** <note>original: *megathymon* — likely a specific elite military unit stationed in the city.</note>. Emerging with such unexpected force, they struck terror into the Bulgarians and routed them. The rebels had no will to stand for defense or show their strength, for the martyr himself led the Roman <note>The Byzantines referred to themselves as 'Romans' (Rhomaioi), as their empire was the direct continuation of the Roman Empire.</note> army and cleared the way before them. 
<margin>C</margin> This was confirmed under oath by the captured Bulgarians, who claimed they saw a young man on horseback leading the Roman phalanx, and that fire leapt out from him and scorched his enemies. More than fifteen thousand Bulgarians fell in the battle, and no fewer than that were taken captive by the spear. The rest escaped in great shame along with Alusian to join Deleanus.

In this year, during the ninth indiction <note>A 15-year cycle used for dating in the Byzantine Empire.</note>, on the 10th of June, at approximately the 22nd hour of the day <note>Byzantine timekeeping counted hours from sunrise; the Latin text here notes the 12th hour, suggesting the earthquake occurred towards evening.</note>, an earthquake occurred.

After this rout, Deleanus and Alusian were reunited, but they became suspicious of one another—Alusian being deeply ashamed of his defeat...

Alusian began to suspect treachery, and the two leaders plotted against each other, watching for a favorable opportunity. After making preparations with some of his close associates, Alusian <margin>D</margin> prepared a meal and invited Deleanus <note>Also known as Peter Delyan, the leader of the Bulgarian rebellion.</note> to the banquet. While Deleanus was suffering from the effects of heavy drinking and was intoxicated, Alusian seized him and blinded him. This was done so discreetly that the Bulgarians were not even aware of what had happened. Alusian then fled and came to Mosynopolis to meet the Emperor <note>Michael IV "the Paphlagonian" (reigned 1034–1041).</note>. The Emperor promoted him to the high rank of *magister* <term>magister — one of the most senior honorary titles in the Byzantine court</term> and sent him to the Orphanotrophos <note>John the Orphanotrophos, the Emperor’s brother and powerful chief minister, then in Constantinople.</note> in Constantinople. The Emperor himself left Mosynopolis and went to Thessalonica. From there, he passed through and entered Bulgaria. He captured the blinded Deleanus and sent him to Thessalonica. As he moved further into the interior—for Manuel Ibatza had constructed a wooden barricade <term>dema — a defensive timber fortification or wall built to block mountain passes</term> near Prilep <note>A city in modern-day North Macedonia.</note>, thinking he could block the imperial army from advancing further and hold the inner territories—the Emperor arrived there and, faster than words can tell, broke through the wooden wall, scattered the Bulgarian forces, and <margin>P 749</margin> captured Ibatza. After setting all affairs in Bulgaria in order and appointing governors in the military districts <term>themes — the administrative and military provinces of the Byzantine Empire</term>, he returned to the capital city <note>Constantinople (Byzantium).</note>, bringing Deleanus and Ibatza with him as captives. ...bewailing his sin against Emperor Romanos <note>Michael IV had risen to power by marrying Empress Zoe immediately after the suspicious death of her first husband, Romanos III Argyros, in 1034.</note>. He reigned for seven years and eight months; he was a man who, in other respects, was decent and kind and appeared to live a life of piety, except for that crime against Emperor Romanos. However, most people attribute even this deed to the Orphanotrophos <note>John the Orphanotrophos, the Emperor’s elder brother and the powerful, eunuch chief minister who orchestrated the family's rise.</note>.
<margin>B</margin>
When Michael met such an end, the supreme power passed to Empress Zoe as the rightful heir. Consequently, she applied herself to affairs of state with youthful vigor, aided and supported by her father’s eunuchs <note>Zoe was the daughter of Constantine VIII; her "father's eunuchs" were veteran palace officials who provided a power base independent of Michael IV's family.</note>, whom this history has already mentioned several times. 

However, she did not remain in this frame of mind. Observing the massive weight of the empire and realizing that she could never properly manage public affairs on her own—and considering it disadvantageous for such a great domain to be without a king and a leader—she judged it necessary to appoint an emperor capable of handling matters during whatever crises might arise.
<margin>C</margin>
After deliberating on this for three full days, she chose the late emperor’s nephew and namesake <note>Michael V, later nicknamed "the Caulker" (Kalaphates) because of his father’s original trade.</note>, the son of Stephen (the man who had ruined the campaign in Sicily) <note>Stephen had been an admiral whose incompetence led to the loss of Byzantine gains in Sicily to the Arabs.</note>. Though he was already a *Caesar* <term>Caesar — at this time, the highest title below that of Emperor, usually designating the chosen successor</term> and seemed energetic and skilled in administration, she first bound him with the most terrifying oaths. He swore that he would regard her for the rest of his life as his sovereign, mistress, and mother, doing whatever she commanded. Thus, she took him as her adopted son and proclaimed him Emperor of the Romans...

...having prosecuted the crime against the Roman Emperor. He reigned 7 years and 8 months; a man otherwise good and of a proven life, had that outrage not existed; which, however, many impute to the Orphanotrophos.

Yet she did not hold to that plan: but considering the weight of the empire and understanding herself unequal to the correct handling of such great matters, and feeling it would be harmful if she left such a great empire without an emperor, while seeing that the empire must be committed to someone who could protect the state in doubtful and dangerous times: after spending three whole days in that deliberation, she finally adopted as a son and designated as Emperor of the Romans Michael, the son of the sister of the now-deceased emperor, and of that Stephen who lost the matter in Sicily, already then a Caesar, and in the opinion of men industrious and endowed with some dexterity. <margin>D</margin> Zoe crowned him with the imperial diadem, but only after she had first removed the <term>Orphanotrophos</term> <note>John the Orphanotrophos, the powerful eunuch and brother of the late Emperor Michael IV, who had been the real power behind the throne.</note> from the scene and exiled him to the Monastery of the Monobatae. In a similar fashion, she stripped Constantine, the <term>Domestic of the Schools</term> <note>The commander-in-chief of the Byzantine imperial armies.</note>, of his command and confined him to his estates within the <term>Opsikion</term> <note>The Opsikion Theme was a military-administrative district in northwestern Asia Minor, close to the capital.</note> district. Likewise, she sent George the <term>Protovestiarius</term> <note>The high-ranking official in charge of the imperial wardrobe and private treasury.</note> away to his own properties in Paphlagonia. At the very hour Michael was being invested with the diadem, he was seized by such a fit of dizziness and fainting that he nearly fell over. They were barely able to revive him using myrrh, perfumes, and other fragrant substances. Furthermore, the earth was shaken by earthquakes throughout the entire four months of his reign. 

<margin>P 750</margin> Once he was crowned by the Patriarch and established as Emperor, he began to win over the Senate with honors and promotions, and the common people through the distribution of gifts. By appealing to the Empress <note>Zoe, referred to here as "the Mistress" or *Despoina*.</note>, he obtained permission to recall Constantine the Domestic from exile; he then honored him with the rank of <term>nobilissimus</term> <note>One of the highest court titles, usually reserved for members of the imperial family.</note> and kept him by his side. 

But just when Michael appeared to be standing on firm ground, he suddenly fell. He was corrupted by letters from the Orphanotrophos and the advice of the Domestic, who warned him not to trust the Empress too often. They urged him to be on his guard against her, lest he suffer a fate similar to that of his uncle, Emperor Michael, and the man before him, Romanos <note>Romanos III Argyros, Zoe's first husband, whose death was rumored to be a result of Zoe and Michael IV's plotting.</note>. They claimed these men had been brought down by her sorcery, and they advised Michael that, if possible, he should remove her from his path and act quickly before she could act against him.

Zoe crowned him with the imperial honors, having first removed the Orphanotrophos and relegated him to the monastery of the Monobatae. Earthquakes lasted for the entire time he held power (which was four months). 

Indeed, once crowned by the patriarch and designated emperor, he earned the favor of the senate by bestowing honors and the favor of the people through largesse. By pleading with the Empress, he obtained the right to recall Constantine the Domestic from exile; he decorated him with the honor of *nobilissimus* and kept him with him. However, while he seemed to stand in safety, he suddenly collapsed. For he was corrupted by the letters of the Orphanotrophos and the counsels of the Domestic, who urged him not to trust the Empress [Augusta] too much, but to beware lest he be treated in the same manner as his uncle Michael and Romanos, whom they claimed she had removed by poisonings. They persuaded him to remove her by any means possible and to take care that she did not strike first.

Through their constant pressure regarding this same matter, they were eventually strong enough to persuade him to devise a plot against her <note>Empress Zoe</note>. He decided, therefore, to first test the citizens to see what kind of opinion they held of him; if they appeared to maintain a favorable disposition and proper friendship toward him, he would then proceed with the plan, but if the opposite were true, he would remain quiet. On the Sunday following Holy Easter, having announced a public procession to the Church of the Holy Apostles, and judging that he could test the citizens' sentiments through this event, he went out wearing his crown along with the Senate. The entire city gathered for the spectacle. 

<margin>C</margin> Those living along the main thoroughfare <note>The "Mese," the central high street of Constantinople.</note> hung out gold and silver vessels, along with tapestries and other gold-woven fabrics. In their cheers, they seemed eager, if it were possible, to pour out their very souls for him. Deceived by this, the wretched man <note>Michael V</note>—believing these displays arose from genuine goodwill—returned to the Great Palace and sent word to the Patriarch <note>Alexios I Studites</note> to depart for his monastery in Steno <note>Located on the Bosporus.</note> and wait for him there the next day. Through their continuous exhortations regarding this same matter, he was finally driven to the point of preparing a plot against his mother Zoe. He determined first to test the minds of the citizens, so that if he understood they favored him and were steadfastly inclined toward him, he would undertake the deed; if it turned out otherwise, he would abandon the plan. Therefore, on the Sunday nearest to Easter, he commanded a public procession for the people to the Church of the Apostles, intending to explore the citizens' feelings toward him in this way. He came forth, therefore, crowned with the Senate, with all the urban population rushing to the spectacle; and those who lived along the Royal Way hung gold and silver finery from their houses, as well as veils and garments interwoven with gold. 

<margin>C</margin> In their auspicious acclamations, they vied with one another, as if desiring to pour out the very feelings of their souls. Deceived by these things, that wretched man—thinking everything proceeded from the greatest benevolence—as soon as he returned to the Great Palace, ordered the Patriarch to depart to his own monastery, which was in Steno, and to wait for him there until the next day. Empress Zoe, having regained control of the throne, initially wanted to push aside her sister Theodora. Once the Senate had also assembled, Zoe delivered a speech—first to the senators, and then from a high vantage point to the general public. She expressed her gratitude for their loyalty and offered prayers for them, then turned to the matter of what should be done with the [deposed] Emperor...

<margin>C</margin> Empress Zoe sought the people’s opinion on what should be done with him. With one voice, they all cried out:

Zoe, however, shrank from such punishment and began to feel compassion for the unfortunate man. The Prefect set out for the Monastery of Stoudios <note>A famous and powerful monastery in Constantinople often used as a place of refuge.</note>, followed by the entire mob. They snatched them <margin>D</margin> from the sanctuary and dragged them by their feet through the marketplace. They brought them to the place called the Sigma <note>A semi-circular portico in Constantinople named after the Greek letter Σ (Sigma)</note>, located above the Monastery of the Peribleptos, and there they blinded them both. Michael had <margin>15</margin> pleaded piteously that his uncle should be blinded first, as he was the prime mover and cause of all the evils that had occurred; and this was done. After being blinded, they were sent into exile. Michael was sent to the Monastery of the Elegmoi on the twenty-first of the month of April, in the tenth indiction <note>A 15-year tax cycle used for dating; here it corresponds to 1042 AD</note> of the year 6550 <note>This is the Byzantine year dating from the biblical creation of the world.</note>. He had <margin>20</margin> reigned for four months and five days. All of his relatives were scattered in various directions.

Once again, the sovereign power devolved to Zoe, though she was forced—as we have said—to have her sister Theodora as her co-ruler, much against her own will.

The Senate honored Theodora with advancements in rank, while the common people were celebrated with distributions of gifts. The affairs of state received all <margin>P 753</margin> possible care, with letters and edicts being sent out everywhere. These decrees promised that government offices would henceforth be granted without charge <note>original: "apriatên" — meaning without purchase or bribery</note> rather than being sold as they had been <margin>5</margin> previously, and they commanded that every form of injustice be driven out from the midst of society. Along with his subordinate commanders, he was to go against the Triballians and defeat Stephanus in war.

### HISTORICAL COMPENDIUM

35

...[it was] pitiful and worthy of lamentation. Along with them, Michael was also saved, having himself suffered the same fate.

<margin>B</margin> George Maniakes, who held the rank of <term>magister</term> <note>A "magister" was one of the highest-ranking administrative and military titles in the Byzantine court.</note> in Italy, as has been mentioned <note>original: "ὡς εἴρηται" — referring to earlier accounts of the Italian campaigns.</note>, was sent by Empress Zoe to restore matters there. Everything in Italy was in a state of decay and was being managed poorly due to the inexperience and incompetence of the commanders. However, Maniakes turned his mind toward rebellion. It is worth briefly recounting the causes of this so that those who read this book may have accurate knowledge of the events. 

When Maniakes was first sent to Italy by Emperor Michael <note>Michael IV (reigned 1034–1041).</note> to assist Apolaphari Machumet, the ruler of Sicily, who was being attacked by his own brother and by the North Africans, he happened to recruit as allies five hundred Franks <note>The "Franks" here refers to Norman mercenaries from Northern France who were beginning to settle in Southern Italy.</note> who had been summoned from Gaul across the Alps. They were led by a man named Arduin, a ruler of a certain territory who was subject to no one. With these allies, Maniakes achieved great <margin>C</margin> victories over the Saracens.

However, Maniakes was eventually removed from his command because of slanderous accusations; he was brought back to the City <note>The "City" always refers to Constantinople in Byzantine texts.</note> and imprisoned. In his place, Michael Doceanus the <term>protospatharios</term> <note>A high-ranking court title, literally meaning "first sword-bearer."</note> was sent to rule Italy. Doceanus was an unsuitable man and not naturally gifted in the management of affairs; it did not take long for him to throw everything into confusion and ruin. He failed to provide the Franks with their monthly provisions <note>original: "σιτηρέσιον" (sitērēsion), a term for military rations or the cash equivalent paid to soldiers.</note> at the proper time. Furthermore, as they say, he even [insulted] their leader, who had come to him to urge him to treat the soldiers kindly and not deprive them of the reward for their labors...

# GEORGE CEDRENUS

<margin>D</margin> [Doceanus], having insulted and shamefully flogged him [Arduin], forced the men to revolt. When they took up arms, he ought to have gathered all the Roman <note>The Byzantines referred to themselves as "Romans" (Rhomaioi), as they were the direct continuation of the Roman Empire.</note> forces and engaged them, but he did not do this. Instead, taking only the Opsician <term>tagma</term> <note>A "tagma" was a professional standing regiment of the imperial army, usually based near the capital.</note> and a portion of the Thracesians, he clashed with them at Cannae by the Aufidus River, where in ancient times Hannibal slaughtered many tens of thousands of Roman troops. He was defeated and lost the greater part of his army, shamefully escaping to Cannae himself. 

Having been struck so hard, he still did not "gain sense like the fisherman in the proverb" <note>original: "κατὰ τὸν ἐν παροιμίαις ἁλιέα νοῦν ἔσχεν" — This refers to an ancient Greek proverb about a fisherman who only learns to be careful after being stung or bitten by his catch.</note>, nor did he fortify himself and attack the enemy with his whole army. <margin>P 756</margin> Learning of this, Emperor **Michael** <note>Michael IV "the Paphlagonian" (reigned 1034–1041).</note> removed him from command and sent **Boioannes** <note>Exaugustus Boioannes, the new Catepan (governor) of Italy.</note>, who was considered a man of action and distinguished in war. He traced his lineage back to that Boioannes <note>Basil Boioannes, the legendary general who secured Byzantine Italy twenty years earlier.</note> who was sent to **Italy** under Emperor **Basil** and who at that time brought all of **Italy** as far as **Rome** under the Emperor’s control. # COMPENDIUM OF HISTORIES

<margin>B</margin> [Doceanus], having been previously defeated, joined battle with the enemies near **Monopoli**. The enemies had already grown powerful and were holding the land as if it were their own. He was defeated and captured, and the army with him—those who had not been consumed by the sword—was scattered here and there, finding safety in the fortresses that still remained loyal to the **Romans** <note>The Byzantines called themselves "Romans" (Rhomaioi), as their empire was the direct continuation of the Roman Empire.</note>. 

<margin>5</margin> Thereafter, the **Franks** <note>original: "Φράγγοι" (Phrangoi) — In this period, Byzantine writers used this term to refer to the Normans who were conquering Southern Italy.</note> claimed Italy as a possession won by the spear. Of the local inhabitants, some joined them voluntarily, while others did so through force and necessity—except for **Brindisi**, **Otranto**, **Taranto**, and **Bari**. These four cities alone remained steadfast, guarding their loyalty to the Romans. 

<margin>10</margin> After the death of the Emperor **Michael** <note>Michael IV "the Paphlagonian," died 1041.</note> and the expulsion of his successor <note>Michael V "the Caulker," reigned for only a few months in 1041-1042.</note> from the throne, **Maniakes** <note>George Maniakes, a famously towering and successful Byzantine general.</note>, as was mentioned previously, was sent to Italy by the Empress **Zoe**. Even though <margin>C</margin> he did not have a sufficient force, he nevertheless used the resources at hand and, by employing **strategic maneuvers** <term>strategikais mechanais</term>, was able to drive the Franks out of the regions of **Capua**, **Benevento**, and **Naples**, bringing a moderate state of order and calm to affairs. 

<margin>15</margin> This Maniakes had his estates in the **Anatolic theme** <note>A "theme" was a combined military and administrative district of the Empire; the Anatolic theme was in central Asia Minor.</note> and was a neighbor to **Romanos Sclerus**. Because of frequent disputes with him, Maniakes had often attempted to kill him, and Sclerus would have died had he not secured his own safety by fleeing. 

<margin>20</margin> But when the Roman scepter passed to **Constantine Monomachus** <note>Constantine IX, reigned 1042–1055.</note>, Sclerus was raised to a great height of fortune. Having been defeated at Monopoli, he fell alive into the power of the enemy. From then on, the Franks claimed Italy for themselves as if won in war, with the inhabitants either surrendering voluntarily or being subdued by force. Only four cities remained in the faith of the Romans: Brindisi, Otranto, Taranto, and Bari. 

Upon the death of Emperor Michael and the expulsion of his successor Calaphates <note>Michael V was nicknamed "Calaphates" because his father had been a caulker (ship-repairer).</note>, Maniakes was sent to Italy, as we have said. This Maniakes had possessions in the Eastern provinces and had as a neighbor Romanus Durus <note>Latinized version of "Sclerus" (Skleros means "hard" or "tough," as does the Latin "Durus").</note>, with whom he had carried on enmities. In the month of July of the same indiction, **Stephen** the *sebastophoros* <term>Sebastophoros: A high court official, usually a eunuch, who performed ceremonial duties for the emperor.</term> was accused of plotting against the Emperor, intending to make **Leo** the emperor—a patrician and the general of **Melitene**, and the son of **Lampros**. **Stephen** was stripped of his possessions, had his head shorn as a monk, and was exiled. **Lampros** was cruelly tortured, blinded, and paraded through the marketplace; he died shortly thereafter.

# A COMPENDIUM OF HISTORIES

...incinerates seven ships with prepared fire <note>original: "σκευαστῷ ... πυρί" — This refers to the famous 'Greek Fire,' a combustible weapon used by the Byzantine navy that could burn even on water.</note>, and sinks three along with their crews. He also captures one ship himself by leaping onto it; of those inside, he slaughtered some and put others to flight, as they were struck with terror by his daring.

When the **Scythians** <note>The Byzantine term for the Rus' people.</note> saw the Emperor already approaching <margin>5</margin> with the entire fleet, they reasoned—as was likely—that if <margin>D</margin> they suffered such losses against only three triremes, what might they suffer if they were forced to engage with the whole fleet? Consequently, they turned toward flight. Being driven into a place filled with reefs and underwater rocks, they lost most of their vessels. Meanwhile, the soldiers marching along the dry land <margin>10</margin> also attacked them and slaughtered them. As a result, around fifteen thousand dead bodies were later found cast up on the shores.

After the defeat of the Scythians, the Emperor remained there for two full days, and on the third day, he returned to the **Imperial City** <note>Constantinople.</note>. He left behind <margin>15</margin> two regiments <term>Tagmata: Professional standing regiments of the Byzantine army.</term> and the so-called **Hetaireiai** <term>Hetaireiai: The 'Companies' or 'Associations,' which were elite guard units often composed of foreign mercenaries.</term>, placed under the command of **Nicholas** the *parakoimomenos* <term>Parakoimomenos: A high-ranking court official, often a eunuch, who served as the Emperor's chief chamberlain.</term> and **Basil Theodorokanos** the *magistros* <margin>P 760</margin> <term>Magistros: One of the highest honorary titles in the Byzantine court hierarchy.</term>. Aplesphares was a man of great strategic skill—if anyone ever was—and was capable of military feats and of scattering the plans of his enemies. 

<margin>20</margin> <margin>B</margin> Knowing that he was not an equal match for the Roman power in an open fight, he did not draw up his lines against them. Instead, he shut himself inside his walls and diverted the nearby river, flooding the entire plain. By turning the area into a marshy swamp of mud and stagnant pools, he awaited the enemy's approach.

# THE HISTORIES OF GEORGE CEDRENI
## COMPENDIUM OF HISTORIES

...of the enemies. **Aplesphares** <note>The Byzantine name for Abu'l-Aswar Shavur ibn Fadl, the Shaddadid ruler of Dvin.</note> had scattered foot-archers in the vineyards surrounding the city, ordering them to hide and wait until he himself gave the battle signal with the trumpet. The Roman <note>The Byzantines continued to call themselves Romans (Rhomaioi) throughout their history.</note> commanders, judging the enemy’s withdrawal into the city and the flooding of the plain to be acts of cowardice and despair, rushed toward the city in a disorganized and scattered fashion. 

<margin>C</margin> Some dismounted from their horses while others remained mounted, as each individual pleased, intending to take the city at the first shout. But when they were deep within the paths of the vineyards and had reached the city walls, Aplesphares sounded the trumpet and ordered his men to begin the work. The infantry rose from their ambushes; some shot arrows and others threw stones, while still others wounded the Romans from the vineyard fences. The Romans were thus prevented by these obstacles from defending themselves against their enemies. 

A great rout occurred, and a vast multitude of Romans were slaughtered; the horses were unable to flee, falling instead into the mud and the marshes. 

<margin>D</margin> Having barely escaped, **Iasites** <note>Michael Iasites, a Byzantine general.</note> and **Constantine** <note>Constantine, son of Michael, another high-ranking officer.</note> reached **Ani** <note>The former capital of the Armenian Kingdom, recently annexed by Byzantium.</note> and personally reported the disaster to **Nicolaus** <note>Nicolaus, a eunuch and high-ranking official serving as the overall commander in the region.</note>. 

When the news of the misfortune reached the Emperor, Nicolaus and Iasites were stripped of their commands. In place of Iasites, **Kekaumenos** <note>Katakalon Kekaumenos, one of the most famous and successful Byzantine generals of the 11th century.</note> was appointed Duke of **Iberia** <note>original: "δοὺξ Ἰβηρίας"; this refers to the Byzantine province (theme) in the Caucasus, not the Iberian Peninsula of Spain.</note>. This Constantine was a eunuch of **Saracen** <note>A term used by Byzantines to describe Arabs or Muslims.</note> descent who had served the Emperor faithfully before his accession to the throne...

# GEORGII CEDRENI
## COMPENDIUM OF HISTORIES

...Muchumetus <note>Likely Mahmud of Ghazni (r. 998–1030), though the Byzantine sources often conflate various Eastern rulers under this name.</note> was urgent that they [the Turks] should also join him in the struggle against the Indians who were at war with him. However, they requested that they be allowed to return to their own lands and that the guard placed at the bridge of the **Araxes** <note>The Aras River, which today flows through Turkey, Armenia, Iran, and Azerbaijan.</note> be withdrawn for them. Since he [Muchumetus] insisted and even intended to use force against them, 
<margin>5</margin> they became terrified that they might suffer some terrible fate and revolted. They retreated into the **Carbonitis** desert <note>original: "Καρβωνῖτιν" (Karbonitin). A region often identified with the plains or wilderness near the Aras River.</note>, because they did not dare, being so few, to draw up a battle line against so many tens of thousands. Making excursions from that place, they began to plunder and carry off the possessions of the **Saracens** <note>A term the Byzantines used broadly for Muslims, here referring to the subjects of the Ghaznavid Empire.</note>. Muchumetus, deeply frustrated by these events, gathered an army of about **twenty thousand** <note>represented by "κ’" in the Greek text, the numeral for 20.</note> 
<margin>P 763</margin> and sent them against the Turks. He placed ten generals <margin>10</margin> over them, chosen from the most noble, wise, and proven courageous Saracens. These men set out and departed for the war. They considered it unprofitable to enter the desert itself due to the lack <note>variant: "the scarcity of" water in manuscript C</note> of water and provisions; instead, they camped very close to the mouth of the desert and deliberated <margin>15</margin> on what should be done. However, **Tangrolipix** <note>original: "Ταγγρολίπηξ" (Tangrolipex). This is the Byzantine rendering of Tughril Beg, the founder of the Seljuk Empire.</note>, the leader of the Turks, who was encamped deep within the desert, learned of the expedition against him. Having conferred with those with him and deciding it was advantageous to attack the Saracens and Persians by night, he made a rapid march. <margin>20</margin>
<margin>B</margin> In two days’ time, on the third night, he fell upon them while they were resting without a care in their tents and expecting no evil. He routed them faster than words can tell, and having made himself master of many chariots, horses, and riches, he was no longer thereafter a fugitive and a bandit...

...[The ruler] wished the same Turks to be present for him in the fight against the Indians, by whom he was being attacked. The Turks, fearing greater dangers from him, defected and withdrew into the Carbonitis wilderness (for so few did not dare to fight against so many thousands). From there, they repeatedly broke out and plundered the dominion of the Saracens. Muchumetus, bearing this most unfairly, sends about 20,000 men against the Turks, putting ten of the most noble Saracen leaders, noted for their fortitude and prudence, in charge of the army. These men, having set out for war, judged it inconvenient to enter the desert on account of the lack of water and food. The leader of the Turks, having been informed of the arrival of the Saracens, shared the matter with his own men and decided to suddenly attack the Saracens and Persians; and having covered great distances in two days, on the third night he invades them while they were acting securely in their tents and expecting no evil, and he immediately puts them to flight. There, having gained possession of very much money, horses, and chariots, he no longer practiced robberies as a fugitive, but from then on openly...

# THE HISTORIES OF GEORGIOS KEDRENOS

...with such a small force against such a great multitude of barbarians. <note>The Byzantine forces were significantly outnumbered by the arriving Seljuk army.</note> Once the generals had voiced these opinions, the view of **Aaron** <note>Aaron was a member of the Bulgarian royal family serving as a high-ranking Byzantine official and general.</note> prevailed. They departed with the army for **Iberia** <note>A theme or province of the empire located in modern-day Georgia and northeastern Turkey.</note> and remained stationed in the open air at a certain plain known locally as **Osurtru**. First, they gathered all the rural population—women, <margin>B</margin> children, and every valuable thing—and secured them within the fortifications. They also wrote to the **Emperor** <note>Constantine IX Monomachos, who reigned from 1042 to 1055.</note> via a fast courier, making known the approach of the enemy. 

Upon receiving the letter, the Emperor ordered them to hold back until **Liparites** <note>Liparit IV, Duke of Kldekari, a powerful Georgian prince and Byzantine ally.</note> arrived with the Iberian forces to join the Roman <note>The Byzantines referred to themselves as Romans (Rhomaioi).</note> armies. He also sent a letter to Liparites, commanding him to come as quickly as possible—if indeed he considered himself an ally and friend of the Romans—and, having gathered all his people, to join the Roman generals <margin>C</margin> and fight the war against the barbarians alongside them. 

The generals, upon receiving the letter, remained quiet as they were ordered and awaited the arrival of Liparites. He, however, having received the imperial command, gathered and armed his people at his leisure. <note>Kedrenos implies that Liparit’s delay was a significant factor in the coming events.</note> While he was organizing his own forces and time was being wasted, **Abramios** <note>Ibrahim Inal, the half-brother of the Seljuk Sultan Tughril Bey.</note> reached **Vaspurakan** <note>A strategic region in eastern Armenia, transcribed here as Baaspracania.</note>. Learning that the Romans had gathered there and, aware of his approach, had retreated to Iberia, he suspected this was due to cowardice—which was a reasonable assumption. Setting aside all thought of taking plunder or spoils, he pursued them from behind, hurrying to clash with those present before [they could join forces].

...before another force could be gathered. Meanwhile, Abramios <note>Ibrahim Inal, a leader of the Seljuk Turks and half-brother of the Sultan Tughril.</note>, having missed the Roman army, came to the place called **Artze**. Artze was a large, populous town <note>Located near modern-day Erzurum, Turkey.</note> with immense wealth; for there lived native merchants, as well as a great number of Syrians, Armenians, and other nations. Trusting in their own numbers, they refused to take refuge within walls, even though **Theodosiopolis** <note>Modern Erzurum; a major Byzantine frontier fortress.</note> was located nearby—a very large city with a strong and impregnable wall—and despite Kekaumenos having many times through letters both threatened and exhorted them. When the Turks arrived and began their work, those in Artze blocked the entrances, and <margin>P 773</margin> climbing onto the roofs, they warded off the attackers with stones, wood, and bows. They continued fighting for six full days. When this news was brought to the generals, **Kekaumenos** <note>Katakalos Kekaumenos, a celebrated military commander of the era.</note> was insistent, urging them to set out and engage the Turks while they were occupied with the siege, and not to sit idly and waste time waiting for that "fig-tree" help <note>original: συκίνην (sykinen) — a Greek idiom for something weak or unreliable, like the brittle wood of a fig tree.</note> from Liparites, while watching the opportune moment pass by, which would not be easily found again. ...before other forces could be gathered. When the Turks attacked that settlement, the people of Artze, having blocked the streets, climbed the roofs and from there hurled stones, wood, and javelins at the attackers. When the news of the matter was brought to the Romans, Ambustus <note>original Latin: "Ambustus" — a Latin translation of the name "Kekaumenos," both of which mean "the burnt one."</note> was much engaged in urging and exhorting that they should go and join battle with the Turks who were intent on the siege, so that time would not be uselessly wasted by sitting idle and waiting for that "fig-tree" protection <note>original: ficulnum — Latin for "of a fig tree," used here to mean flimsy or useless.</note> of Liparites, and meanwhile neglecting an opportunity such as they would not easily obtain again. ...having inherited its name from its female ancestor and founder. <note>original: "τῆς προγόνου καὶ ἀρχηγοῦ" (tēs progonou kai archēgou). ...commander of [Adrian]ople, Constantine the Magister Arianites, he wrote, so that with the Macedonian forces, and to Basil the Monk, governor of Bulgaria, so that with the Bulgarian army, they might join Michael and Kegenes and fight against the Pechenegs. The Sultan besieged the city for thirty days without any intermission. Basil, a patrician from Capa, a prudent and experienced man, was in command of that city. ### GEORGE KEDRENOS

...fearlessly attacking the foundations, confident that no one would be allowed to peer over the wall due to the sheer volume of arrows being fired. He imagined that in this way he would capture the city. But seeing these maneuvers from the wall, **Apocapes** commanded the wall-guards to remain perfectly still and for no one to look out. Instead, they were to simply have stones the size of a fist <margin>B</margin> ready, along with bows and other long-range machines, and to await the signal from him. The signal was to be "**Lord Christ, help us!**" <note>Original Greek: *Christe boethei*; Latin translation: *Christe iuva*. A common Byzantine battle cry.</note> Once this was given, they were to set to work. He also had at his disposal enormous beams that were sharpened to a point at the base. 

While he was making these arrangements, **Alkan**—as the Turks on the outside sent out arrows like a hailstorm, appearing to drive back those within the walls—gradually pushed the *lessas* <term>lessas: portable wicker sheds or "penthouses" used to shield soldiers as they approached a wall to mine it or use a ram</term> forward until they were pressed against the wall. When the sheds had reached the point of contact and it seemed impossible for them to retreat, **Apocapes** suddenly gave the signal. 

Those stationed at the beams let them drop onto the sheds, and the rest of the defenders rained down stones and arrows. Then, the specific shed <margin>C</margin> containing **Alkan**, having its roof pierced by many of these heavy beams, was overturned by their sheer weight. Once the shed was flipped over, those inside were left completely exposed; they were struck from all sides by stones and arrows, and no one was able to come to their rescue. 

While everyone else perished there, **Alkan** was taken alive, recognizable by the brilliance of his armor. Two brave and noble young men leaped out from the city gates, grabbed him by the hair, and dragged him into the city.

<margin>B</margin> Meanwhile, the **Patzinaks** <term>Patzinaks: a nomadic Turkic people, also known as Pechenegs, who frequently clashed with the Byzantine Empire</term>, having crossed the **Haemus** <note>The Balkan Mountains</note> as we previously mentioned, surveyed the plain lying between these mountains and the **Istrus** <note>The Danube River</note> which stretches all the way to the sea. <margin>5</margin> Finding a place containing glades, groves, thickets of all kinds, water, and pastures—a place the locals call **"Hundred Hills"**—they settled there. From that base, they conducted raids and caused no small amount of distress to the territories under the rule of the Romans <note>The Byzantines referred to themselves as Romans (*Rhomaioi*)</note>.

<margin>10</margin> In response, the Emperor <note>Constantine IX Monomachos</note> summoned **Kegenes** <note>A Pecheneg chieftain who had defected to the Byzantines, converted to Christianity, and served as a frontier guardian</note> to the capital for a consultation. Kegenes arrived immediately with his entire army and set up camp in the plain designated for the Byzantines at a place called **Maitas** <margin>C</margin>. However, before he could meet with the Emperor or even learn the reason for his summons, <margin>15</margin> he was the victim of a plot that very night. Three Patzinaks attacked him with swords while he was sleeping and inflicted wounds upon him, though they were not fatal. They were immediately identified by the bodyguards, and because they were discovered, their strikes were weak. They attempted to flee, but as the crowd rushed to help, they were captured along with **Baltzar**, the son of Kegenes.

<margin>20</margin> At dawn, Baltzar placed his father on a four-wheeled wagon <margin>D</margin> and dragged the conspirators behind the wagon in chains. He did not dare to do anything more to them at that moment because they were calling upon the name of the Emperor <note>By appealing to the Emperor, the assassins were likely claiming they acted on imperial orders or were seeking a formal trial rather than summary execution</note>, and with his entire cavalry force...

### COMPENDIUM OF HISTORIES

Together with his entire cavalry army, he <note>Kegenes</note> arrived to see the Emperor, traveling on foot alongside his brother **Goulinos** and following a carriage drawn by two horses. When he reached the **Hippodrome** <note>The Great Circus of Constantinople, the heart of the city's public life</note>, he brought the carriage to a halt. He then entered the palace to meet the Emperor, as rumors of his arrival had raced ahead and cleared a path for his entry.

<margin>5</margin> Once he was brought inside, the Emperor <note>Constantine IX Monomachos</note> asked him why he had not immediately taken vengeance upon those who had tried to murder him <note>The original Greek uses "father's murderers," which may be a respectful term for Kegenes as a leader or a specific familial reference</note>. Kegenes replied, "Because they constantly invoked **your** name." At this, the Emperor fell into strange suspicions.

<margin>10</margin> Swifter than speech <note>original: *logou dhatton* — a Greek idiom meaning "immediately"</note>, he sent for the prisoners to be brought before him and inquired into the reason they had attempted to kill the **Patrician** <term>Patrician: *Patrikios*, a high-ranking Byzantine court title the Emperor had granted to Kegenes to secure his loyalty</term.

<margin>P 783</margin> The prisoners claimed that Kegenes was ill-disposed toward your sovereignty and the City. They alleged that he planned to enter at dawn <margin>15</margin> to slaughter everyone inside, plunder the City, and then flee back to the **Patzinaks** <note>Pechenegs</note>. Although the Emperor should have investigated these claims to find the truth, he failed to do so. Instead, believing these baseless and unsubstantiated slanders, he brought Kegenes to the palace and—under the pretext of providing him with medical care—imprisoned him in the **Elephantine** <note>The Elephantine was a specific hall or section of the Great Palace used as a high-security prison for noble captives</note>. He then separated Kegenes' sons from him, placing them in different locations.

<margin>20</margin> To maintain an appearance of goodwill, the Emperor attempted to win over the rest of the **Patzinaks** <margin>B</margin> with all kinds of food and drink. His true aim was to find a way to strip them of their weapons and horses and place them under guard. Meanwhile, he ordered that the men who had actually attempted the murder be allowed to live freely and without restraint, going wherever they pleased.

He sought the reason why they were driven to the death of **Kegenes the Patrician**. They offered this excuse: that Kegenes was unfaithful to the Roman Empire and the City, and intended to enter the city at first light, and having slaughtered everyone within, to sack it and return to the **Patzinaks**. Here the Emperor, who ought to have inquired into the words and searched for the truth, neglected that care and gave credit to uncertain and ill-connected calumnies. He brought Kegenes into the palace and, under the guise of care and medicine, shut him in the **Elephantina**. He placed his sons in different locations, torn away from one another. At the same time, with feigned benevolence, he refreshed the multitude of the Patzinaks with every kind of food and drink, seeking a way, if possible, to strip them of their arms and horses and put them into custody. To the murderers, he granted the faculty of living freely wherever they wished.

<margin>C</margin> The Emperor believed that by acting in this manner, he was remaining unnoticed; however, his actions did not escape the attention of the **Patzinaks** <note>original: *Patzinakai* — a nomadic Turkic people known in English as the Pechenegs</note>. They did not consider the detention of their leader or the separation of his sons to be a good omen, and they viewed the freedom granted to the conspirators as a clear sign of ill-will. 

Consequently, while they accepted the gifts sent to them with expressions of gratitude and cheered for the Emperor—acting as if they approved of everything that had been done—they had different plans. Traveling with intense speed throughout the entire night, they crossed the **Haemus** <note>The Balkan Mountains</note> on the third day and reunited with the main body of the Patzinak people. And the Patzinaks, who had so easily repelled the invading army, then plundered the region of the Romans freely and without fear. The Emperor, however, having been informed of the disaster by those who had fled, grieved as is fitting, but again he collected other troops, and those which had survived, and he strived to repair the accepted slaughter in the following year. In the third indiction of the year 6558, the Emperor sent the Hetaeriarch Constantine, declared leader with supreme command, against the Patzinaks. Taking up those troops which had recently been brought across from the East, and collecting those which were wintering in the West, he set out for Adrianople; and there, having constructed a deep rampart, he delayed with the leading men, considering and exploring from where he might further progress. While he was thinking on these things, suddenly on the eighth of the month of June, the Patzinaks, having crossed the Haemus, approached Adrianople. When their arrival was reported to Constantine by explorers, a consultation was proposed, as to whether with them...

Instead, they directed their whole momentum against Macedonia. Selecting all their most valiant men, they overran the villages in Macedonia; they practiced how to receive any coming war with vigor. <margin>10</margin>

<margin>P 788</margin> When Bryennius and Michael learned of this, they set out at night so that no one would perceive where they were going. By forced marches, they arrived at Chariopolis <note>Modern Hayrabolu, Turkey.</note>, and entering it with their army, they awaited the opportune moment. The Patzinaks, having plundered all the fields and suburbs, returned near evening <margin>15</margin> close to Chariopolis and set up camp, completely unaware that an army was stationed there at all. Consequently, they lay down without fear, reveling with pipes and cymbals. When night fell, the men under Bryennius and Michael went out and, finding them sleeping and snoring, killed them <margin>20</margin> all.

# COMPENDIUM OF HISTORIES

During this same time, the sudden rise of the man called Romanus Boilas <note>A member of a prominent Byzantine family of Bulgar origin.</note> occurred. He had been stationed among the *hetaireiai* <note>term: <term>Hetaireiai</term>, the imperial bodyguard or elite military companies consisting of various ranks and nationalities.</note> and was glib of tongue; because of this, he was considered witty and clever. When he once came into the sight of the <margin>5</margin> Emperor <note>Constantine IX Monomachos, reigned 1042–1055.</note> and, having conversed with him, appeared most charming, he became from that moment inseparable from him at all times. The Emperor used him as an advisor, a servant, and a minister for every kind of task. By gradually promoting him with honors, the Emperor <margin>C</margin> raised him to great heights and exalted him so that he held the first rank in the palace. <margin>10</margin> This man, being resourceful and multifaceted, and always harboring a desire for the imperial power, began to test those among the senators who had clashed with the Emperor, and he revealed his "mystery" <note>The "mystery" here refers to his secret plot or conspiracy.</note> to them. Whosoever among them happened to accept the words of the conspiracy, he would gather them together quietly and gently, securing them <margin>15</margin> with oaths. However, to those who were disgusted by the very hearing of the plan, he would pretend to agree with them and admire their loyalty to the Emperor; he would claim the things he said were spoken only for the sake of testing them, and he would swear <margin>D</margin> to speak on their behalf to the Emperor. Finally, after corrupting many of the citizens and preparing a conspiracy, he was caught. All the others who had conspired with him suffered miserably, being tortured, <margin>20</margin> stripped of their private property, and sent into exile. Yet Romanus suffered nothing bad; for after the Emperor had turned away from him for only a little while, he was forgiven again and restored to his former status.

---

Around this same time, Romanus Boilas was suddenly raised to the highest position. While he was serving in the companies <note>original Latin: "sodalitatibus," referring to the Greek *hetaireiai*.</note>, he was a man ready of tongue and considered sophisticated and witty. When he had once come into the presence of the Emperor and was judged most elegant in conversation, he was never thereafter dismissed from his side. Monomachus <note>The Latin text explicitly names the Emperor as Constantine Monomachus.</note> held him as a counselor and a minister in every matter: he gradually elevated him so that he obtained the first place in the court. As he was a man of craft and variety, suffering from a long-standing lust for power, he sounded out the minds of whichever senators were in the Emperor's disfavor by exposing his secret to them. To those by whom the plot was approved, he joined himself gradually and calmly, binding them with oaths. Those, however, who shrank from the matter at the first hearing, he would pretend to approve of—and even admire—their loyalty toward the Emperor, saying he had spoken those things only for the sake of testing their minds; he would then swear that he would praise their integrity to the Emperor. When he had corrupted many citizens and was already plotting against the Emperor, the matter was discovered. While the partners of the conspiracy were harshly treated after an investigation—being despoiled of their resources and driven into exile—Romanus escaped unpunished. For when the Emperor had been turned away from him for only a little while, he soon restored him to his former place.

# GEORGE CEDRENUS

The Sultan <note>Toghrul Beg, the founder of the Seljuk Empire.</note>, nursing a grudge (as was previously mentioned) against his brother Abramius <note>Ibrahim Inal, a prominent Seljuk leader and relative of Toghrul.</note> and constantly plotting against his life, perpetually sought to destroy him. Perceiving this, Abramius fled to his own nephew Kutlumus <note>Kutalmish, a cousin of Toghrul and an ancestor of the later Sultans of Rum.</note> and, together with him, <margin>P 789</margin> undertook a war against the Sultan. However, the Sultan engaged them at a place called Pasar <note>Possibly refers to the region of Pasinler.</note> <margin>5</margin> and turned them to flight. He captured and killed Abramius; but Kutlumus fled with six thousand men and Melech, the son of Abramius. He sent an embassy to the Emperor <note>Constantine IX Monomachos.</note>, entreating to be received and to become an ally and friend of the Romans <note>The Byzantines referred to themselves as Romans (Rhomaioi).</note>. Arriving in Persarmenia <note>The portion of Armenia historically under Persian influence, now a border zone.</note> at the place called Carse <note>The city of Kars.</note>, he awaited the <margin>10</margin> responses to his embassy. In the meantime, he besieged Carse and, with the exception of the citadel, captured the city. Following behind him, the Sultan arrived with his own forces in Iberia <note>The medieval kingdom of Georgia, not the Spanish peninsula.</note>. <margin>B</margin> Learning of this, Kutlumus fled toward Saba <note>Possibly a reference to the desert regions or the direction of Arabia.</note> and Arabia Felix. The Sultan, having arrived in Iberia, <margin>15</margin> plundered whatever happened to be in his path and put things to the torch. Because of this, the Emperor hastily summoned the Acoluth <note>term: <term>Acoluthus</term>, the commander of the Varangian Guard and a high-ranking military officer.</note> Michael from the West and dispatched him to Iberia. Upon arriving there and having gathered the Franks <note>Western European mercenaries, often Norman or French.</note> and Varangians <note>term: <term>Varangians</term>, the elite imperial bodyguards and mercenaries, often of Scandinavian or Anglo-Saxon origin.</note> who were scattered throughout Chaldia <note>A region on the Black Sea coast around Trebizond.</note> and Iberia, he hurried to restrain the Sultan’s raids <margin>20</margin> in whatever way he could. But the Sultan, learning of Michael's rapid approach and that he was hastening to engage him with a gathered army, considered—as was reasonable—that either outcome of the matter would bring him no glory: for if he were victorious, he would have defeated only a servant...

Upon the arrival of the **Romans**, the Pechenegs shut themselves inside the trench and were besieged. However, as the **Romans** wasted time in vain without achieving anything worthy of mention, and as they were gripped by a shortage of basic necessities, they held a council to discuss what should be done. It was the opinion of all that they should retreat. Having ordered silence in the dead of night and throwing open the gates of the camp, they began to withdraw. This did not escape the notice of **Tyrach** <note>The supreme chieftain of the Pechenegs.</note>; learning that they intended to flee, he led a very large multitude out of the camp and sent them to the mountain passes through which the **Romans** were expected to travel. <margin>P 790</margin>

At this very time, **Michaelas**, son of **Stephanus**, who held the principality of the **Triballians** and **Serbs** after his father’s death, <margin>X</margin> struck a treaty with the emperor, and being decorated with the honor of *protospatharios*, he was enrolled in the register of the allies and friends of the **Roman** empire. There was also sent to **Monomachos** from the prince of **Egypt** an elephant and a giraffe. After these things, the emperor, desiring to utterly drive away the **Pechenegs**, gathered forces from everywhere in the East and West, and put **Michael** the *Akolouthos* in charge of them; he also ordered **Basil** the *Syncellus* to rouse the **Bulgarian** armies, and for both to set out against the **Pechenegs**. When this matter was reported to them, the **Pechenegs** located their camp at Great **Preslav**, and fortified it with a wall and a deep trench, and when the **Romans** arrived they shut themselves in it and endured a siege. The **Romans**, since time was being wasted in the siege with no fruit and they were now beginning to suffer from a lack of supplies, consulted what should be done. It was decided to break the siege. And so, having ordered silence in the dead of night, they departed with the gates of the camp opened. Nor did this escape **Tyrachus**, but having been informed that they were attempting flight, he ordered a great multitude sent from the camp to occupy the roads by which the **Romans** were going to pass, and he himself immediately attacked those departing.

# GEORGIUS CEDRENUS

He <note>Referring to the Pecheneg leader.</note> immediately attacked them as they emerged from the mountain passes. A horrific rout of the **Romans** <note>The Byzantines continued to call themselves "Romans" (Rhomaioi) throughout their history.</note> took place. Some were caught from behind and slaughtered, while others were cut down as they were trapped by the difficult terrain. A great multitude fell, and even the **Syncellus** <note>term: Syncellus; a high-ranking official who served as the deputy or advisor to the Patriarch, here acting in a military capacity.</note> himself was killed. The survivors escaped to **Adrianople** <note>A major Byzantine city in Thrace, modern-day Edirne, Turkey.</note> along with **Michael**.

The Emperor, deeply pained by this disaster, took in those who had survived the rout and began recruiting a new army and gathering mercenaries. He considered his life not worth living unless he could utterly wipe out the race of the **Patzinaks** <note>The Pechenegs, a nomadic Turkic people from the Eurasian steppe.</note>. <margin>B</margin> However, when they learned of this through a deserter, they sent ambassadors to the Emperor to ask for peace. He accepted their embassy and made a truce with them for thirty years.

The Emperor then began building a monastery in the district known as **Mangana** <note>A prestigious district in Constantinople near the sea walls.</note> in the name of the holy Great-Martyr **George**. He spent public funds on these buildings without restraint—alternating between building up and tearing down—until he fell into great financial need. Because of this, he devised every kind of "peddling" <note>original: "καπηλείαν" (kapēleian); used here metaphorically to describe the corrupt selling of offices or trading for profit.</note> and invented absurd and cunning methods of tax collection. <margin>C</margin> He appointed godless and cursed public officials to oversee these matters, and through them, he gathered money from unjust sources. He also disbanded the **Iberian army** <note>The frontier forces stationed in the "Theme of Iberia," which covered parts of modern Georgia and Armenia.</note>, which numbered about fifty thousand men, through **Leo Serblios**. In place of these soldiers, he began extracting heavy taxes from those regions. He also devised many other evil and lawless exactions, which it is a shame even to list.

A terrible slaughter of the Romans occurred there; while some were killed by the enemy pursuing from behind, others were slain by those who had occupied the roads. ### A COMPENDIUM OF HISTORIES

I must say this, for it is necessary: since the reign of that emperor and his profligacy and ostentation <note>original: "σαλακωνίας" (salakōnias); a term for pretentious display or boastful extravagance.</note>, the affairs of the **Romans** <note>The Byzantines continued to refer to themselves as Romans (Rhomaioi) and their state as the Roman Empire.</note> began to decline. From that time until the present, retreating little by little, they have reached a state of complete weakness. <margin>5</margin> For by pursuing a misguided sense of "liberality," he drove his extravagance to the absolute extreme. <margin>D</margin> Nevertheless, he was not entirely devoid of good deeds; some of his works are indeed worthy of historical record. For the aforementioned monastery, as well as the homes for the elderly, the hostels, and the poorhouses within it, are not without merit. Furthermore, his contribution to the **Great Church of God** <note>The Hagia Sophia in Constantinople.</note> <margin>10</margin> is worthy of high praise. Until his time, the bloodless sacrifice <note>The Holy Eucharist or Liturgy.</note> was offered to God in that church only on the most prominent feast days, as well as on Saturdays and Sundays; on other days, it was not performed at all. This was due to a lack of revenue. However, by generously setting aside sufficient funds, he ensured that the sacred <margin>15</margin> liturgy would be celebrated every single day—a practice that continues among us to this day. He also dedicated sacred vessels for this service to the church, made of gold <margin>P 791</margin> and precious pearls and stones, which far surpassed all others in size, beauty, and value. He also adorned the church with many other treasures. So much for his deeds.

<column-break/>

Indeed, I cannot remain silent about this: it was through this emperor's luxury and lust that the Roman state began to diminish and, from that point, gradually wasting away, was brought to the final stage of feebleness. For while he ineptly strove to appear generous, he fell into the depths of prodigality. Yet he did not do absolutely nothing good; some of his works are reported that deserve to be recorded in history. For the monastery I mentioned, and the buildings within it for the support of the elderly, strangers, and beggars, merit some praise. Until that time, only on the more solemn festivals in the great temple of God, and on Saturdays and Sundays, was the bloodless sacrifice performed; on the remaining days, not at all, for it was omitted due to a lack of income. Monomachus generously supplied this so that a Mass <note>The Latin text uses "missa" (Mass) to translate the Greek "leitourgia."</note> might be celebrated daily in that temple; a truly laudable institution which continues today. Furthermore, he dedicated vessels pertaining to this sacrament to the temple, made of gold and decorated with precious pearls and gems, which excelled others in size, price, and beauty; and he decorated that temple with many other gifts.

# A COMPENDIUM OF HISTORIES. 615

At the season of Easter, the emperors are accustomed to meet with the Senate. On this occasion, all the leaders of the army, renowned for both their lineage and their courage, entered the palace. Among them were the **Master** <term>Master: originally *magister*, a high-ranking Byzantine court title</term> **Isaac Komnenos** and the **Master Katakalon Kekaumenos**. <note>Katakalon’s surname, Kekaumenos, literally means "the Scorched" or "the Burned."</note> This Katakalon had been the <margin>5</margin> **Duke** of Antioch, but he had been removed from his command and succeeded by **Michael**, the emperor’s nephew. Upon Michael’s appointment, the emperor renamed him **Ouranos**, <note>original: *Ouranos*. The emperor was attempting to link his nephew to the prestigious and ancient Ouranos family line.</note> claiming he was restoring the family to its ancient namesake; he honored him with the rank of Master of Antioch, just as Katakalon had held, and sent him out as his successor. Also present were **Michael Bourtzes**, the **Bestarches**, <term>Bestarches: A high Byzantine court dignity, originally associated with the imperial wardrobe but later a general title of rank.</term> <margin>10</margin> **Constantine** and **John**, descendants of the lineage of the **Duke of the East**, <margin>P 794</margin> and the rest of the elite among the officials. They had all gathered both to see the new emperor and to obtain honors and rewards from him; for word had spread to everyone regarding his generous nature and his magnificent, liberal spirit toward granting favors.

### GEORGE KEDRENOS
<note>original: *GEORGII CEDRENI*</note>

...the regiments of the East attacked the tent of Bryennios, shouting acclamations for Michael as the sole ruler. Having seized Bryennios, they bound him, while also releasing Opsaras from his chains. Handing Bryennios over to him—shackles and all—they ordered Opsaras to deal with the man as he pleased. <margin>D</margin> Once freed from his fetters and now the master of the situation, Opsaras immediately put out Bryennios’s eyes <note>Blinding was a standard Byzantine punishment for rebels; it was intended to be a "merciful" alternative to death that nonetheless disqualified the victim from ever holding the imperial throne.</note> and sent him to the emperor as a prisoner, reporting the attempted revolt. Opsaras himself remained in that place, ostensibly to carry out the remaining distribution of funds to the rest of the people. Thus, Bryennios paid the penalty for his own rashness and arrogance—not to say his madness. 

Meanwhile, the leaders who held estates in the **Anatolic theme** <term>Anatolikon: a major military province in central Asia Minor</term>—the **proedros** <term>proedros: a high-ranking court title, literally "one who sits in front"</term> Romanos Sclerus (for he too was among those who had sworn the oath), Burtzes, Botaneiates, the sons of Basil Argyrus, and the rest of the group—had remained quiet for a time, waiting for the start of the rebellion to come from elsewhere. <margin>P 798</margin> But when they learned what had happened to Bryennios and the insane misfortune he had brought upon himself, they calculated shrewdly. They realized that under interrogation, he would reveal the conspiracy and things would end poorly for the conspirators. Finding him still living quietly, they roused him even against his will. They traveled with him to a certain level place of sufficient width called Gunaria. There, they gathered the people from the surrounding area and the army...

# COMPENDIUM OF HISTORY.

...soldiers, and all those who, having heard of the movement, had arrived as volunteers—together with all of them, they proclaimed this man sovereign and Emperor of the Romans, on the eighth day of the month of June, in the tenth <margin>B</margin> **indiction** <term>indiction: a 15-year tax cycle used in Byzantine dating; the 10th indiction of this cycle corresponds to the year 1057 AD</term> of the year 6565 <note>The Byzantine "Year of the World" 6565 corresponds to 1057 AD.</note>.

Having been proclaimed emperor, he established a fortified camp and remained in that place, waiting for the rest of those who had participated in the conspiracy to assemble. What persuaded him to wait further and not rush forward was the delay of **Kekaumenos** <note>Katakalon Kekaumenos, a famous general whose name literally means "the burnt one" (translated as *Ambustus* in the Latin text below).</note>. While Isaac was considering this and searching for the cause of the delay, a certain messenger arrived from the East. He reported that Kekaumenos, having changed his mind, had disregarded the oaths he had given and was now loyal to the Emperor’s cause, gathering a force with the intention of attacking the rebels. This report threw Komnenos and his followers into no small agony and confusion, fearing they might have such an enemy at their <margin>C</margin> back. For this reason, they remained in their entrenched camp, striving to learn the truth. But while they were in this state, Kekaumenos remained firm in his original intention to support the conspirators; he was holding himself back and delaying for the following reason. When he had left the imperial city <note>Constantinople</note> to return home, he reached **Nicomedia** <note>modern-day İzmit, Turkey</note> and encountered an imperial courier. Through him, he sent a message to the **Logothete of the Dromos** <term>Logothete of the Dromos: essentially the Byzantine Postmaster General and Foreign Minister, responsible for the state postal system and diplomatic affairs</term>, Niketas Xylinites, in plain and soldierly words: “As I see it, brother, your master and emperor has treated Komnenos and me as nothing, and [dismissed] our requests...”

<note>original: "omnia erant militibus..."</note>
...all things were ready for the soldiers, and many others, hearing that a revolution was being stirred, flocked there of their own accord. By the consensus of all, they hailed Isaac Komnenos as emperor on the 8th day of June, in the 10th indiction, in the year of the world 6565.

Having been made emperor, he remained in that place with a fortified camp, awaiting the arrival of the rest of the members of the conspiracy. Lest he should move too quickly, he chose to endure the delay, moved especially by the lateness of **Ambustus** <note>Latin: *Ambustus*, translating the Greek *Kekaumenos* (the Burnt)</note>. While he was debating the cause of this within himself, a messenger came from the East, indicating that the man had changed his mind, scorned his oath, was supporting the Emperor's affairs, and was drawing together an army to defeat his adversaries. This matter brought no small worry and disturbance to Komnenos, understanding that to have such an enemy at his back would be most dangerous. Therefore, he kept to the camp until he could learn something certain. However, as for Ambustus, although he persisted in the same opinion, the cause of his loitering was this: At the time he was traveling home from Byzantium, he happened upon an imperial courier at Nicomedia, and through him, he ordered these things to be told to Niketas Xylinites, the Logothete of the Dromos, in simple and soldierly words: "As far as I can see, brother, your lord the emperor has considered Komnenos and me as nothing..."

<margin>B</margin> Having first revealed the conspiracy to his own servants and relatives, and having already gathered a band of a thousand men around him, he then began to test the loyalty of those who were not entirely reliable. He first approached the more prominent men of the region one by one, <margin>5</margin> and then, little by little, he tested those who were braver and more inclined toward military life. Once he was able to draw the most distinguished men to his side, he finally began to put the masses to the test. He forged imperial letters <note>Forgery was a common tool in Byzantine coups to convince loyalist troops that they were following legitimate orders.</note> claiming that he had been ordered to take three regiments of allies and the two <margin>C</margin> <margin>10</margin> regiments of the people of **Coloneia** <note>original: "Κολωνειατῶν" — a strategic military district (theme) in northeastern Asia Minor.</note> and the **Chaldians** <note>original: "Χαλδίων" — a rugged coastal region on the Black Sea, known for its hardy soldiers.</note> to march against **Samuch** <note>likely a reference to a local Turkic chieftain or an Arab emir whose raids provided a convenient excuse for troop movements.</note>. Each day, feigning a military review <term>adnumium: from the Latin 'ad nomen,' this was a formal roll-call and inspection used to verify the number and readiness of troops.</term>, he would ride out early in the morning and lead the men far away from the others. First, he would call for the commander and reveal his plan, explaining that it was necessary to do one of two things: either agree to his proposals or suffer the removal of his head. Then he would call one unit, then another, and in the same manner, he forced them all to swear an oath, even against their will. First, he won over the two Roman regiments, then his own household troops, <margin>20</margin> and finally, he directed his efforts toward the foreign contingents. <margin>B</margin> As he arrived at **Nicaea** <note>original: "Νίκαιαν"; modern-day İznik, Turkey, a strategic city guarding the approach to Constantinople.</note>, those within slowly withdrew and dispersed. The soldiers each went home, fearing for their wives, children, and other essential concerns. The generals, however, went to the Emperor to act as messengers, informing him of **Komnenos’s** arrival. <margin>5</margin> Among them were **Lycanthes**, the commander of the Eastern regiments, **Theophylaktos Maniakes**, and **Pnyemius the Iberian**, who led the phalanx of the **Charsianites** <note>original: "Χαρσιανιτῶν"; troops from the Charsianon theme in central Anatolia.</note>, along with many others who were not particularly distinguished.

When the patriarch refused to do so, and blocked his doors and the door of the spiral staircase which leads to the upper chambers of the temple, he sent only the brothers Nikephoros and Constantine, his paternal cousins, and ordered that he be consulted through them. Those who had gathered there, now increased by a great crowd (for as the news spread, they rushed together from everywhere—not only those who rejoiced in new things, but also many of the more prudent and many senators who had not been well treated by Stratioticus <note>Emperor Michael VI "the Military" or "the Aged"</note>), seized the patriarch’s cousins, threatening to strangle them unless he himself descended at once. Therefore the patriarch, whether unwillingly (for I do not pronounce judgment) or, as is asserted by the talk of many, willingly and of his own accord, dressed in his pontifical robe and the other garments and insignia of the high priesthood, descended, pretending to be indignant at a grave injury. The event itself showed that all these things were done as if on a stage, through simulation. Soon the agitators of the people seized him, and having brought a chair, placed him at the right side of the sacred seat. And first, but under a pretext, they urged him to go to the emperor as a legate for them, and to demand...

<summary>A mob led by elites and disgruntled senators corners the Patriarch in the Hagia Sophia, forcing (or appearing to force) him to join the rebellion against Michael VI. This marks the moment the church leadership was pulled into the coup that would eventually place Isaac Komnenos on the throne.</summary>

...demanding that the document they had signed <note>This refers to the written oath of loyalty to Emperor Michael VI mentioned on the previous page</note> be returned to them, on the grounds that the Emperor had already come to terms with **Komnenos** <note>Isaac I Komnenos, the leader of the military rebellion</note> and had declared him Emperor. They argued that as long as that document remained intact and valid, one of two impossible situations would necessarily follow: either they would acclaim him as Emperor and thus commit perjury <note>by breaking their original oath to Michael VI</note>, or they would be punished for insulting a sitting Emperor <note>if they refused to acknowledge Isaac’s new status</note>. At first, the **Patriarch** <note>Michael Keroularios</note> welcomed them and promised to fulfill their request. 

<margin>P 805</margin> Then, after a short time had passed, they set aside all other business and proclaimed **Komnenos** as the Sole Ruler and Emperor <note>original: "autokratora basilea"</note>. They declared that whoever did not wish for this was an enemy of the Romans and a rebel; they even authorized the mob to plunder the houses of such people. 

This occurred with the first-ranking Patriarch himself being present and consenting through **Stephen**, the second-in-command of the Church <note>original: "deuteruontos" — likely the Syncellus or Great Steward</note>. Furthermore, **Theodore**, the **Patriarch of Antioch**, joined in the shouting of the imperial acclamations and even encouraged the crowd to dig up and loot the homes of those in high positions who were not pleased with these developments. 

All of these actions took place inside the holy and world-renowned temple <note>The Hagia Sophia in Constantinople</note>. The Patriarch then sent a messenger to **Komnenos**, and others to the "old man" <note>Emperor Michael VI Stratioticus, who was roughly 70–80 years old at the time</note>. 

<margin>B</margin> To the former, he sent word to hurry and not to delay, while simultaneously demanding a reward <note>original: "misthon"</note> for his cooperation, as if Isaac’s desire for the throne had already been fulfilled through his efforts. To the latter <note>Michael VI</note>, he sent orders to depart from the palace, as it no longer belonged to him in any way. Following this...
