### COMPENDIUM OF HISTORIES

<meta>catchword: of the world</meta>

To everyone, it became undeniably clear that the **Patriarch** <note>Michael Keroularios</note> was not only a participant in the rebellion but its primary instigator. When the Emperor <note>Michael VI Stratioticus</note> asked the metropolitans who had been sent to him, "And what does the Patriarch offer me in exchange for the Empire?" they replied, "The Kingdom of Heaven." 
<margin>5</margin> At those words, he immediately cast off the imperial purple and his scarlet-dyed shoes <note>original: "kokkobaphe pedila" — the "tzangia," footwear strictly reserved for the Emperor</note>, and having dressed himself in the clothes of a private citizen, he stepped down from power. 

This abdication surely would have happened exactly as he wished and as the metropolitans promised, <margin>C</margin> if he had left the palace at the very start of the rebellion. But because he held out until it came to war, and allowed himself to <margin>10</margin> witness such a slaughter of his fellow countrymen, and was then only broken and shaken by the citizens—leaving the throne by force—I do not know if he will truly receive the heavenly kingdom as compensation for his earthly one. But this will be as it pleases God. 

After **Stratioticus** had retired to his own house in the Citadel <note>the Akropolis district of Constantinople</note> on Wednesday, the thirty-first of the month of August, <margin>15</margin> in the tenth indiction <note>a 15-year cycle used for dating in the Byzantine Empire</note>, **Kekaumenos** the **Curopalates** <note>a high-ranking court official; the name Kekaumenos literally means "the Burnt One"</note>—who had been honored by **Komnenos**—entered the city with quite a few noblemen. <margin>D</margin> They arrived by way of a dromon <note>a swift Byzantine war galley</note> at five in the morning and, having entered, took control of the palace. **Komnenos** arrived in the late evening and <margin>20</margin> entered the palace himself. On the following day, the first of September, in the eleventh indiction, in the year 6566 <note>this corresponds to 1057 AD in the modern calendar</note>, he made his public...

To everyone it was clear that the patriarch could offer no excuse, so that he was believed not only to be an ally but the author and chief cause of this defection. When Stratioticus asked the metropolitans sent to him what the patriarch would give him in return for the empire, they said he would give him the heavenly kingdom. And he immediately cast aside the purple and the scarlet shoes, and having dressed in the habit of a private citizen, he departed. Truly, what he wanted and what the metropolitans promised, he would have attained without doubt if he had deserted the palace at the first movement of the rebellion. Now, having remained in it until the war, having endured to see the slaughter of so many citizens in an internal war, and afterwards, with his affairs shattered and his subjects overwhelming him, abdicating the empire against his will, I do not know whether he will obtain the eternal empire as compensation for the fleeting one. But in this matter, what pleases God will happen. Stratioticus having departed to his own house, which was in the citadel, on Wednesday, the last day of the month of August, in the tenth indiction, Kekaumenos the curopalates, sent by Komnenos with not a few born of illustrious rank, on Thursday at the first light of morning, arrived at the palace by galley and entered it. In the evening Komnenos also came and entered the palace. On the next day, which was the first of September, of the eleventh indiction, of the year from the beginning of the world...

In the manner already described, Komnenos <note>Isaac I Komnenos, the first emperor of the Komnenian dynasty.</note> assumed the imperial power. Having already established a reputation for manliness and provided proof of his noble courage in war, he was immediately depicted on the imperial coinage holding a sword. This was not because he attributed everything to God, but rather to his own strength and his experience in wars. As <term>autokrator</term> <note>original: "αὐτοκράτωρ." A title for the Byzantine Emperor meaning "sole ruler" or "ruler of himself," emphasizing absolute authority.</note> he began the administration of the empire, first decorating those who had assisted him in his efforts with generous honors. He also granted the common people the appropriate consideration and appointed many overseers for the public assemblies. Furthermore, he dedicated to the Great Church <note>Hagia Sophia in Constantinople.</note> the right to manage its own affairs, completely removing the imperial power from this administration, so that [the state] should not interfere either in the management or in—

---

In the manner which we have mentioned, Komnenos obtained the empire. Since he had provided both an opinion of his virtue and a specimen of his excellence in military affairs, he was immediately engraved on the royal coinage with a drawn sword; he did not refer all that he had received to God, but to his own virtue and skill in military matters. And just as an emperor with supreme power, he approached those things which pertained to the empire, having first decorated with the greatest honors those who had performed work for him in completing his undertakings. Having also held the people in such regard as was fitting, he created many curators of the public colleges. And he permitted the Great Church to administer its own sacred affairs, the administration having been forbidden entirely to the empire, so that neither for the sake of performing sacred duties nor for holding—

# THE HISTORY OF JOHN <term>CUROPALATES</term> <note>original: "Ioannis Curopalatae." Referring to John Scylitzes, who held the high court title of curopalates.</note>

...that someone chosen by the emperor should oversee the care and protection of the sacred treasures, but rather that the whole matter—both the selection of persons and the administration of affairs—should depend upon the authority of the Patriarch. He also brought his wife from the fortress of Pemolissa and proclaimed her <term>Augusta</term> <note>original: "Αὐγοῦσταν." The traditional title for a Byzantine Empress.</note> and <term>Sebaste</term> <note>original: "σεβαστήν." A title of honor, the Greek equivalent of Augusta.</note>. He honored both his brother John and Katakalon Kekaumenos <note>original: "Κατακαλὼν τὸν Κεκαυμένον." A prominent general and key supporter of Isaac during the revolt that brought him to the throne.</note> as <term>curopalates</term>, and appointed his own brother as <term>Grand Domestic</term> <note>original: "μέγαν δομέστικον." The commander-in-chief of the imperial armies.</note>. Having considered the urgent need for money—without which, according to the orator <note>Likely referring to the ancient Greek orator Demosthenes, who famously called money "the sinews of affairs" or the "sinews of war."</note>, nothing can be accomplished—and because the military had become weakened and completely humbled by the prevailing poverty 
<margin>P 808</margin>of the empire, and because everyone on all sides was rising up against the Romans <note>The Byzantines continued to call themselves "Romans" (Rhomaioi) and their empire "the Roman Empire."</note> (which he considered a disgrace and the most grievous of all burdens), he became a harsh tax-collector for those who owed money to the public treasury. He was also the first to cut the payments given for court offices. He concerned himself with thrift and with adding more land to the imperial holdings. Therefore, he deprived many private citizens of many possessions, ignoring their <term>chrysobulls</term> <note>original: "χρυσοβούλλους." Official imperial decrees sealed with a golden bulla, often granting lands, tax exemptions, or titles.</note>. He also struck at some of the monasteries <note>original: "φροντιστηρίων." Literally "places of thought," a term used for monastic houses.</note>; after seizing many of their estates and calculating what was sufficient for the sustenance of the monks, he reassigned the surplus to the public treasury. To those who look upon things superficially 
<margin>B</margin>and without discernment, this act seemed to lean heavily toward impiety and lawlessness, even sacrilege. However, for those who consider matters deeply and spiritually, it brought about no absurd result, since it led back to a state of poverty those who had professed it as a vow, and [curbed] the Sybaritic <note>Refers to the ancient city of Sybaris, proverbial for its extreme luxury and decadence.</note> and luxurious...

<column-break/>

...that someone chosen by the emperor should oversee the accounts of the sacred treasury, but instead all things should hang upon the authority of the patriarch—both the selection of personnel and the management of things. Likewise, summoning his wife from the town of Pemolissa, he declared her Augusta, and created his brother John and Katakalon "the Burnt" <note>original: "Catacalon Combustum." A literal Latin translation of the Greek surname "Kekaumenos," which means "the Burnt."</note> as curopalates, decorating both with honors; he created his brother Grand Domestic. Considering the necessity of money, without which (according to the orator) nothing is perfected, because military affairs were in a bad state, reduced to the narrowest straits by the poverty of the empire, and because all were incited against the Romans from every side (which seemed to him a source of ignominy and the most grievous thing of all), he was a harsh exactor of taxes from those who owed the republic. He himself was the first to prune away the donations of offices. Parsimony was also a concern for him, as was adding fields to the empire; and for that reason, he despoiled many private men of their possessions, their <term>golden bulls</term> <note>original: "aureis bullis." The Latin term for chrysobulls.</note> being neglected. He even took away many possessions from certain monasteries, and having left the monks suitable expenses for their living (which he had ordered to be calculated), he claimed the remainder for the public. This indeed, to those who judge thoughtlessly and rashly, might seem to tend toward sacrilege from impiety and iniquity; yet he performed nothing absurd by that effort, as it seemed to those who considered the matter seriously and spiritually. Namely, in that way, he brought back to poverty those who had professed it, and [the] soft Sybariti[c]...

...cutting back on luxury, yet not depriving them of the things that were suitable and necessary for their use; he also freed the neighboring landowners from the malice and greed of the monks. Would that he had carried this through to the end, not only regarding the monasteries but simply in all ecclesiastical matters. Thus, these things were managed by the Emperor, and the Queen of Cities <note>original: "βασιλὶς... τῶν πόλεων." A standard epithet for Constantinople.</note> was in this state. 

<margin>C</margin>However, the Patriarch <note>Michael Keroularios, the powerful head of the Church who had helped Isaac to the throne.</note>, emboldened by the Emperor's insatiable favor, became arrogant toward him. He no longer used requests and advice whenever he needed something or spoke on someone’s behalf; instead, having frequently failed to get his way due to the constant and burdensome nature of his requests, he began to use threats and absurd censures. If the Emperor would not obey, he even threatened him with the loss of his imperial power, repeating that common and well-worn saying: "**I built you, oven; and I will be the one to tear you down.**" <note>original: "ἐῶ σε ἔκτισα, φοῦρνε· ἐῶ ἵνα σε χαλάσω." A proverbial expression implying that the Patriarch, having "baked" or created the Emperor's authority, had the right to destroy it.</note> He even ventured to wear shoes dyed with kermes <note>original: "κοκκοβαφῆ... πέδιλα." A deep crimson or purple dye. In Byzantium, purple footwear was a strictly guarded imperial prerogative; for a Patriarch to wear them was a revolutionary claim to secular authority.</note>, claiming that such was the custom of the ancient priesthood and that the high priest in the New Order ought to use them as well. For he said there was no difference, or very little, between the <margin>D</margin> priesthood and the empire, and perhaps in more honorable matters, the priesthood was even greater and more to be esteemed. 

The Emperor, hearing these things being muttered under the Patriarch's breath, hastened to act rather than suffer. Therefore, as the Feast of the Archangels <note>November 8th, a major feast day in the Orthodox calendar.</note> approached, the Patriarch went out to a place outside the city, strictly intending to perform the rites of the festival. The Emperor, seizing the moment as a godsend so that there would be no riot or disturbance...

->6 **this [τοῦτον]** according to Goarus; **of this [τούτου]** in manuscript P<- <note>A technical note comparing different versions of the Greek text: the scholar Jacques Goar (1601–1653) suggested one reading, while a specific manuscript (P) contains another.</note>

<meta>The text below is the Latin translation of the Greek text provided above, now rendered into English for continuity.</meta>

...and he took away those luxuries, yet he did not deprive them of those things which were necessary for use; and he freed the neighbors, that is, those who had nearby fields, from the annoyance and greed of the monks. If only he himself had happily led this to a conclusion, not only in the monasteries but in all things altogether looking toward the church. Thus, therefore, matters were administered by the emperor, and the royal city was in this state. But the patriarch, relying on the insatiable benevolence of the emperor, was elated against him, not only using petitions and admonitions if ever he lacked anything or for anyone, but often being far from his wish because of frequent and odious petitions, he employed threats and absurd rebukes, and unless he obeyed, he threatened the loss of the empire, uttering this common and trite saying: "**I founded you, oven, and I will cast you down.**" He also attempted to put on shoes dyed with kermes, asserting this was the custom of the ancient priesthood, and that it was necessary for the new archbishop to use these as well: for he said that between the priesthood and the kingship there was no difference, or very little, and in more precious matters the priesthood was perhaps more and more to be cultivated. <margin>D</margin>...and even the **Eparch** <note>original Greek: ἔπαρχος (eparchos). The Eparch of Constantinople was the highest-ranking administrative and judicial official in the capital city, similar to a Mayor and Chief Justice combined.</note> of that time were caught as conspirators and fell under the charge of high treason. As a result, they were stripped of their family estates and all of their possessions. 

The Emperor <note>Constantine X Doukas (reigned 1059–1067).</note> desired and loved, far above all other things, the increase of public revenue and the personal hearing of private lawsuits. He poured his greatest care for the empire into these matters, while holding other things in lower regard—namely, military advantages and the brave deeds of soldiers. 

<margin>5</margin>Because of this, the **Roman** <note>The Byzantines referred to themselves as Romans (Rhomaioi) and their empire as the Roman State. <margin>10</margin><margin>P 814</margin>It reached such a point that even the soldiers themselves set aside their weapons and their military service to become advocates and lovers of legal questions and disputes. They said a long "farewell" to the sound of war, to martial training, and to the quick maneuvers of the battlefield. 

<margin>15</margin>While he was as pious as any man who ever lived, a friend to monks and the poor, and less concerned with physical discipline <note>original Greek: περὶ τὸ σῶμα ἧττον κολαστικός. However, he was extremely frugal and resourceful in finding ways to increase public funds. 

He also dominated judicial decisions, often changing them depending on the status of the people involved. In this, he showed himself to be harsh and unbearable toward the powerful. 

<margin>B 20</margin>While he was constantly devoted to these pursuits, he neglected and grew indifferent to military affairs. Consequently, the affairs of the East—and especially those regions on the borders of the Roman lands—were carried off and plundered by enemies, and everything there was being destroyed.

# JOHN SCYLITZES #

...[he lived] sixty years and a little more. Consequently, when the Turks attacked, the people of Melitene resisted alone without the professional soldiers; they were easily harassed and wounded by the barbarians, who attacked from a distance <note>Likely referring to the famous horse-archers of the Seljuk Turks.</note>, while the soldiers remained unaffected <note>The soldiers essentially went on strike, refusing to fight alongside the local militia.</note>.

...approaching in the spring to attack and utterly overturn and destroy the **Roman** <note>The Byzantines referred to themselves as Romans, and their state as the Roman Empire</note> state. All these were gathered by imperial decree in **Phrygia**, that is, in the **Theme of the Anatolics**, <note>The "Anatolic Theme" was the largest and most important military province of the middle Byzantine Empire, located in central Asia Minor</note> where one could see a strange and incredible sight. Those world-renowned champions of the **Romans**, who had enslaved both the East and the West, now consisted of only a few men. These men were bent over by <margin>C</margin> poverty and hardship, and were stripped of their heavy armor. Instead of swords and other military weapons—to use the language of Scripture—they carried **javelins and sickles** <note>original: "ζιβύνας καὶ δρέπανα"; a grim reversal of the biblical "swords into plowshares," as these soldiers were reduced to using farm tools as weapons</note> even though it was not a time of peace. They were lacking war-horses and other necessary equipment, as no Emperor had led an expedition for a long time. For this reason, they had been treated as useless and unprofitable; their wages and their ancient grain rations had been taken away. They appeared cowardly, weak, and fit for nothing noble. Even the standards themselves seemed to speak silently of their condition, appearing filthy and looking as if they were darkened by the soot of smoke, <note>original: "ἐξοφωμένας καπνοῦ"; suggesting the flags were old, neglected, and perhaps stored in smoky barracks for years</note> and they were accompanied by followers who were few in number and impoverished. Seeing these things, those who were present felt great despondency and fear, reflecting on how far the **Roman** fortunes had fallen.

# THE HISTORY OF JOHN SCYLITZES #
<note>Header original: IOANNIS CUROPALATAE. John Scylitzes was a high-ranking official known as a "Curopalates" who wrote a vital history of the Byzantine Empire.</note>

684

Upon learning that they <note>the Turkish forces</note> had already departed after laying waste to **Iconium**, fearing his pursuit, he <note>Emperor Romanos IV Diogenes</note> dispatched a portion of the regiments to **Cilicia**. These were to join with **Kataturios**, the **Duke of Antioch** <note>Antioch was a major administrative center; its "Doux" or Duke was a high-ranking military governor</note>, a noble man who had previously demonstrated many superior qualities of virtue. He was ordered to meet them at **Mopsuestia** <note>An ancient city in Cilicia, modern Misis, Turkey</note> as quickly as <margin>5</margin> possible—for it was expected that the Turks would pass through there—and to <margin>D</margin> wait for them there and harass them in every way. 

Having passed through the mountains of **Seleucia**, they <note>the Turks</note> descended into the plain of **Tarsus**, where they were struck by arrows. There, they were intercepted by the **Armenians** and <margin>10</margin> lost almost all of their plunder. When the enemy learned of the Roman <note>original: Ῥωμαίων. The Byzantines called themselves Romans</note> encampment at **Mopsuestia**, they did not delay even for a moment. The Emperor was seized by distress because those at **Mopsuestia** had failed to act. Having himself marched straight for **Claudiopolis** in **Seleucia**, and upon learning of their flight, he gave up hope and turned back toward **Byzantium** <note>Constantinople</note>. He hurried because autumn had already arrived, <margin>20</margin> leaving another army behind because other Turks were also plundering the Roman lands. These were divided into clans and factions, overrunning the land like highwaymen and thieves, destroying and looting everything they encountered. Because of this, [the pursuit] of these...

Where, when he had learned that they, having destroyed **Iconium**, were setting out—fearing lest he should pursue them—he sent a certain part of the legions into **Cilicia**. ...he ordered [the army] to go into **Syria**. By this reasoning, he defrauded the leader of the power that proceeded from those troops. Therefore, with many captured, even more were finished off by the sword. The *curopalates* was captured along with the others, and the entire camp was stormed, captured, and plundered. And unless the nearby city had saved more of them, the entire Roman generation which had gathered for this war would have perished fundamentally. When this report reached the emperor, it affected him with huge grief; and while it was scarcely heard, another report, swifter and much more penetrating, was brought, which announced that the Turks had occupied the state of **Chonae** and the temple of the **Chief of the Heavenly Host**, most famous for its miracles and gifts, by arms. Everything there was filled with slaughter and blood, and many insults were brought upon the temple by those raving in a drunken fury. The most venerable temple itself was made into a stable for horses, and what was most unworthy, they did not even [respect] the sewers of the chasm, where the flowing rivers are diverted through the ancient arrival and divine miracle of the Prince of the Army, as if through a precipice having a flow of such a kind that it cannot stand still...

...[the river], which runs very swiftly, was unable to keep safe those who had fled there or enable them to escape the danger. Instead—something that had never happened before—the water flooded and, as if sucking up the rivers and uprooting everything, it utterly swept away and drowned all those who had fled, making them submerged even upon dry land.
<margin>C</margin>
These events, when recounted in detail, instilled a great despondency in us. We reckoned what had occurred to be a divine sign and the wrath and anger of God, seeing that not only the enemy but even the very elements were fighting against us. Previously, the great onset and uprising of the foreign nations and the slaughter of those subject to the **Romans** <note>The Byzantines continued to call themselves "Romans" (Rhomaioi) and their empire "Romania"</note> was indeed considered the wrath of God, but it was seen as directed against the **heretics** <term>heretics: individuals or groups whose religious beliefs varied from the established "Orthodox" Church</term> who inhabit **Iberia** <note>An ancient kingdom in the Caucasus, roughly modern-day Georgia</note> and **Mesopotamia** as far as **Lycandus** and **Melitene** and the neighboring **Armenia**. These were the people who follow the "Jewish-like" heresy of **Nestorius** <term>Nestorius: a 5th-century bishop whose followers were accused of over-emphasizing Christ’s humanity</term> and the **Acephali** <term>Acephali: meaning "The Headless Ones," a group of Monophysites who had broken away from their Patriarch</term>; for indeed, these regions are full of such "wrong-thinking." 

But when this terrible calamity also touched the **orthodox** <note>Those following the state-sanctioned "right" faith of Constantinople</note>, all those who followed the Roman way of worship were at their wits' end. They reckoned that their own "measure [of sin]" had been filled, just like that of the **Amorites** <note>A biblical reference to Genesis 15:16, implying that God allows a people's sins to accumulate to a certain point before delivering judgment</note>. 
<margin>D</margin>
They believed then that not only is "right faith" required, but also a life that corresponds to that faith. For this reason, both those who stumble in their faith and those who falter and go limp in their conduct are subjected to the same punishment; for only he who both "acts and teaches" is praised and blessed. Having heard these reports, the **Emperor** <note>Romanos IV Diogenes</note> felt a great eagerness to set out immediately and bring aid to his own land...

...[the river], which runs quite rapidly, was not able to save those who had fled there by avoiding the danger: on the contrary, which had never happened before, the water so overflowed—as if the rivers were being swallowed up—that it oppressed all who had fled there with a flood and inundation, and submerged them beneath the earth. Therefore, these things being reported among other news brought great sorrow and torment of mind to us, as we reflected that what had happened was a divine portent and the anger and indignation of God, since not only the enemies but also the elements themselves were fighting against us. For previously, the gathering and excitement of so many nations, and the rebellion of those who owed [allegiance] under the Romans, happened indeed by divine wrath, but against the heretics who inhabit Iberia and Mesopotamia as far as Lycandus and Melitene and neighboring Armenia, and who worship the "Jewish" heresy of Nestorius and the Acephali. For indeed, these regions are full of this kind of perverse opinion. 

But when the calamity also invaded the orthodox, all who were devoted to the Roman worship knew not where to turn, reflecting that their own measure had been filled just as once that of the Amorites was, and then believing that not only a "right faith" is required but also a life responding to that faith; wherefore both, namely those erring in faith and those offending and limping in life, were affected by an equal punishment; for he who has "acted and taught," this man is judged blessed. Having heard these things, the Emperor [was moved] with the greatest zeal and alacrity of mind to depart as soon as possible and...

# JOHN SCYLITZES #

<note>original: "IOANNIS CUROPALATAE" — John Scylitzes was a high-ranking Byzantine official holding the title of *Curopalates* (manager of the palace); his history is a primary source for the 11th century.</note>

...seized by a likely fear toward everyone. Realizing, as it seems, that the constant flow of previous omens was aimed at him, he did not make his camp in a tent or in open fields, but stayed in hills and small houses. It was there that something occurred that was no less an omen of **misfortune**: for a fire, brought from somewhere, consumed the dwellings in which the Emperor was staying. In this fire, horses and imperial saddle-cloths <note>original: "ἐφεστρίδες" (ephestrides)</note> and bridles—far superior to any others—were burnt together, and they became a total loss to the flames. The horses, seen by the army half-burnt, presented a **pitiful sight**.

<margin>10</margin> Having crossed the Sangarius River <note>Modern Sakarya River in Turkey</note>, near which these events occurred, by way of the bridge called **Zompi**, he began to gather his own forces, which had been scattered due to the attacks of the barbarians <note>Refers to the Seljuk Turk raiding parties</note>. After selecting from these as many as he wished, he dismissed the remainder of the soldiers and the captains. The soldiers he sent away because they were already worn out by their previous defeats; but the captains he dismissed because he himself was afraid to lead them with him, suspecting they might side with the faction of the reserves <note>original: "ἐφέδρων" (ephedron) — likely referring to the rival Doukas family who commanded the rearguard and later betrayed him</note>.

<margin>C</margin> If only he had done this with all of them! But while he drove away **Nicephorus Botaniates** <note>A successful general who would later become Emperor Nicephorus III</note> and others like him as "suspicious," he brought along with him those full of guile and malice, as the following account will show. He himself, proceeding in this way and unaware of the evils that were about to overtake him, crossed the river called the **Halys** <note>The modern Kizilirmak, the longest river in Asia Minor, traditionally seen as a boundary into the deeper eastern frontier</note>...

...strangely sparing, and understanding, as is likely, that those frequent premonitory signs pertained to him, he dwelt not in a tent nor in level places, but in hills and small houses, where also another certain prodigy happened, portending no less misfortune. # HISTORY #

<margin>D</margin> Having crossed the river, he took up residence in a newly constructed fortress, for which he had been assigned the task of building. After this, having completed the crossing, he marked out the distribution of private holdings. Passing by Caesarea <note>Modern Kayseri, Turkey</note>, he arrived at the place known as the **Cold Spring** <note>original: "Κρύαν πηγήν" (Kryan pegen)</note>. <margin>5</margin> This location was well-suited for receiving an army, as it was overflowing with all necessary supplies, known for its mix of town-villages and rural cities which provided a constant flow of resources. However, as the countryside was being ravaged and desolated by the soldiers, the Emperor behaved quite harshly toward certain members of the **German** regiment <note>original: "Νεμιτζῶν" (Nemitzon) — The *Nemitzoi* were mercenaries from the Holy Roman Empire, likely from the Bavarian or Saxon regions.</note>. <margin>10</margin> Those who were stung by this treatment rose up in rebellion. When this became known, the Emperor mounted his horse and, summoning the army, terrified the foreign mercenaries <note>original: "ἰδιοξένους" (idioxenous)</note> and once again reduced them to obedience, even against their will. He set their only punishment as being stationed in the very rear of the march, instead of their former position of proximity as his personal bodyguards. <margin>P 837</margin> From there, he proceeded to Sebasteia <note>Modern Sivas, Turkey</note>, <margin>15</margin> hurrying to reach **Iberia** <note>original: "Ἰβηρίαν" (Iberian) — In this context, it refers to the Byzantine theme of Iberia in eastern Anatolia/Georgia.</note>, at which time he also became a spectator to the corpses of those who had fallen with the *Curopalates* **Manuel Komnenos** <note>Manuel was the eldest brother of the future Emperor Alexios I; he had died while campaigning against the Turks shortly before this expedition.</note>. From there, proceeding slowly and at a walking pace, he reached Theodosioupolis <note>Modern Erzurum, Turkey</note>. This city had previously been neglected, but since the siege of **Artze** <note>original: "Ἄρτζε" — A nearby prosperous trading town destroyed by the Turks in 1048; its destruction led to the fortification of Theodosioupolis.</note>, it had been <margin>20</margin> rebuilt and fortified. From this point, he issued a proclamation that every man should carry two months' worth of food, as they were about to march through an uninhabited and desolate region. When everyone had followed the command, he dispatched the mercenary **Ouzoi** <note>original: "Οὔζων" (Ouzon) — A Turkic nomadic people, often serving as Byzantine mercenaries, though they were ethnically related to the Seljuk enemies.</note> and the **Franks** <note>Western European heavy cavalry mercenaries.</note> under **Roussel** <note>original: "Ῥουσελίῳ" (Rouselio) — Roussel de Bailleul, a famous Norman adventurer and mercenary leader.</note>, a man of brave and warlike character, toward **Chliat** <note>Modern Ahlat, on the shores of Lake Van.</note> for foraging...

...in a recently constructed fortress, whose buildings he had overseen, he pitched his tent. Then, having crossed over, he described the division of his own possessions and, passing Caesarea, arrived at a spring named **Crya**. This place was indeed suitable for receiving an army, abounding in everything useful, known to both townspeople and peasants because they frequently visited there. However, since the region was being harassed and desolated by the soldiers, he showed himself to be more hostile toward certain ones from the legion of the **Germans** <note>original: "Nemitzorum"</note>, who, having been rebuked and offended, rebelled. This matter being known, the Emperor mounted his horse and, having called the soldiers together, deterred his own foreign guests and again subjected them to himself under imposed conditions, even against their will. He defined this one penalty: that they should be placed in the furthest part of the army, they who had been in the first part and the closest guards of his person. From there he set out for Sebasteia, hastening to arrive in Iberia, where he was also a spectator of those who had fallen with **Manuel Komnenos**, the *Curopalates*. And from there, progressing gradually and little by little, he betook himself to Theodosioupolis, which was previously neglected but had been restored and fortified since the time **Artze** was captured. From there he ordered that individuals should carry two months' worth of provisions with them, as if they were about to have a journey through an uncultivated and solitary region. When all had done what was commanded, he sent the mercenary **Ouzoi** and **Franks** with **Roussel**, a man brave and warlike, to **Chliat** for plundering, which he had also done before. <margin>B</margin> ...month. He had also done this previously. Moving forward, he arrived at **Manzikert** <note>original: "Ματζικιέρτ" (Matzikiert) — A strategic city in eastern Anatolia, now Malazgirt, Turkey.</note>, which was a Byzantine <note>original: "Ῥωμαϊκὴν" (Rhomaïkēn) — The Byzantines referred to themselves as Romans.</note> city, but it had been captured by the Sultan before this time and was occupied by a Turkish garrison. Viewing these defenders with contempt because they were few in number, the Emperor detached a significant portion of his army and placed it under the command of **Joseph Tarchaniotes**, who held the rank of *Magister* <note>A high-ranking Byzantine court and military title.</note>. He also provided him with a substantial body of infantry, or rather, the most elite and warlike of the cavalry, who always led the way in dangers and fought in the front ranks against the enemy. **Tarchaniotes** then departed for **Chliat** <note>original: "Χλίατ" — Modern Ahlat, on the northern shore of Lake Van.</note> to bring aid to the **Uzoi** <note>original: "Οὔζοις" (Ouzois) — Oghuz Turks serving as Byzantine mercenaries.</note>, the **Franks** <note>Western European mercenaries, often Norman or Germanic.</note>, and the entire mercenary force. <margin>C</margin> For the Emperor had heard that a massive host of ten thousand men was advancing against them. 

The Emperor divided the army, hoping that he would quickly bring Manzikert to terms—which is exactly what happened—and then join those at Chliat; or, if any urgent necessity arose, he could quickly recall them, as the armies were encamped near one another. For he heard that the Sultan was hurrying against him. Indeed, this division of the forces was not without reason, nor was it lacking in strategic logic, were it not that fate—or rather, divine wrath or a plan more hidden from us—turned the outcome to the contrary. Just as the work was nearing its end and the armies were to be reunited on the same day, it brought the Sultan upon the Turks without warning <note>original: "ἀκηρυκτὶ" (akerykti) — literally "without a herald," meaning the Sultan arrived unexpectedly without a formal declaration of war or advance scouting detection.</note> and prevented the intended plans from being completed. <margin>D</margin> For once the Emperor had taken Manzikert, with the Turks being struck with terror and dreading his arrival, they asked for and received a pledge of safety <note>original: "πίστιν" (pistin) — a formal promise of protection or a treaty of surrender.</note>, where—

---

following after, he arrived at **Manzikert**, a Roman city, but one subdued by the Sultan and previously occupied by the Turks. Despising these as few, he handed over another hand of the army, by no means small, to the *Magister* **Joseph Tarchaniotes**, having also added a cohort of infantry that was not to be looked down upon—indeed, even selected cavalry who were the most warlike and, among the enemy, always the first to face dangers and the first to fight. **Tarchaniotes** set out for **Chliat** to bring help to the **Uzoi**, the **Franks**, and the entire mercenary army. For the Emperor had heard that a multitude, infinite in number, was coming against them, and he had divided the army, hoping he would immediately reduce Manzikert into his own power—which also happened—and would then come to those who were in Chliat. But if any necessity urged it, he would immediately recall them, since they had placed the armies in camps nearby. For they heard that the Sultan was striving eagerly against them. 

And certainly, the division of matters and plans did not lack reason, nor was it foreign to a most experienced leader, unless fate—or rather divine wrath or a reason most remote from us—had perverted the outcome of things to the opposite side. At the very conclusion of the matter and the joining of the army on that same day, it also joined the Sultan to the Turks without a herald, and prohibited the decrees from being brought to a conclusion. He failed to notice that, out of arrogance, he was surrendering the victory to his enemies—at least, this is the conclusion of those who examine such matters accurately—by sending him that most victorious of symbols, the cross. <margin>20</margin> The arrival of the ambassadors had not even reached its conclusion or been fully considered when some of those closest to the Emperor persuaded him to reject the peace as being fraudulent and intended more to deceive than to offer any real benefit. ...[They] suspected that the **Sultan** <note>Alp Arslan, leader of the Seljuk Turks.</note> acted as he did because he did not possess a significant force, and was instead waiting for reinforcements to arrive from the rear, using the pretense of peace to stall for time. He feared the **Turks** might attack him while he was unguarded, and he considered that if he went too far, night would fall, at which point the Turks—being skilled **long-range archers** <term>horse-archers</term> <margin>D</margin>—would turn back from their flight and attack. 698 JOHN CUROPALATES

...the soldiers who made up the phalanxes, seeing the standards turned backward, suspected that the Emperor had suffered a defeat. <margin>P 841</margin> The Emperor, seeing this unexpected development, stood his ground and tried to call back his fleeing men, as is the custom. But no one listened. The enemy, standing on the hills and seeing the Romans' sudden and unexpected misfortune, hurried to report what they saw to the **Sultan** <note>Alp Arslan, the Seljuk leader.</note> and urged him to turn back—for he was already fleeing himself and was far from his own camp. 

As soon as the Sultan returned, a fierce and concentrated battle broke out against the Emperor. He ordered those around him not to give in nor to show any weakness, but to prove themselves brave men; he resisted vigorously for a long time. Meanwhile, as the flight of the others overflowed outside the rampart, no clear word could be heard, <margin>B</margin> for different people reported different things—some announcing a defeat, others a victory, and relating obscure and confusing accounts. Eventually, even some of the **Cappadocians** <note>Troops from the Emperor's home region in central Anatolia; their desertion signaled the total collapse of his support.</note> began to desert him in factions and groups. Many of the imperial grooms also retreated with their horses, struggling to get away so as not to see the Emperor's fate. There was a commotion like an earthquake, as well as wailing and an insurmountable fear, and the **Turks**...

<column-break/>

<note>original: "phalanges habebant, conspicati signa retro conversa..."</note>
The soldiers in the phalanxes, seeing the standards turned back, suspected a slaughter suffered by the emperor. Indeed, one of those present, **Andronikos**, son of the Caesar and the emperor’s cousin, having previously meditated on treachery, spread such a rumor himself. With the soldiers he had, he quickly took himself to the camp; the rest followed his example and all to a man fled. The emperor, witnessing what was happening so recklessly, tried to stop the flight of his men, calling them back as is the custom: but no one was obedient. The adversaries, standing on the hillocks, saw the Roman misfortune occurring for no reason and zealously reported it to the Sultan: they urged him to return, as he was already fleeing far from his camp. Immediately, therefore, a sharp battle was joined with the emperor. Although he commanded his men not to yield or act weakly, but to show themselves as strenuous and brave men, he resisted strongly for some time. But meanwhile, as others fled outside the fortification, the reported news was heard less clearly, because some nuntioed one thing and some another—these a slaughter, those a victory—and they discussed obscure and uncertain things; until even some of the **Cappadocians** began to leave by tribes and divisions, and many of the royal grooms returned with the horses themselves, struggling not to see the emperor. And it was like a movement, a mourning, and an incredible fear, with the **Turks** from all sides...

*The Emperor of the Romans, dressed in a cheap and military garment, caused the Sultan to doubt his identity and demand proof. When agreements were made on the condition that **Diogenes** would renounce the empire and live as a private citizen with his hair shorn <note>original: "τὴν τρίχα δὲ καρέντα" — this refers to the monastic tonsure, a common Byzantine method of disqualifying a rival from the throne</note>, he departed from the <margin>C</margin> fortress dressed in black mourning clothes and lamenting his own fate. **Andronikos** <note>Andronikos Doukas, the general who had captured him</note> immediately turned his mind toward the return journey, dragging **Diogenes** along with him. # THE HISTORY OF JOHN SKYLITZES

There was a certain eunuch named **Nicephorus**, whom people called by the nickname **Nicephoritzes** <note>original: "Νικηφορίτζην" — a diminutive meaning "Little Nicephorus," used here with a sense of familiarity or perhaps derision</note>. He was a descendant of the **Bucellarians** <note>a theme, or military district, in north-central Asia Minor</note>. This man was remarkably clever at devising turmoil, weaving together schemes, and raising "great storms in the midst of a calm," bringing instability even where order prevailed. Having served in the office of secretary to **Michael's** father <note>Emperor Constantine X Doukas</note>, he proved himself to be devious, a slanderer, and a cunning "architect of evils" for his own profit. He even whispered a charge of adultery to the Emperor against the Empress <note>Eudokia Makrembolitissa</note>, driven by envy of his fellow officials.

<margin>D</margin> After being appointed Duke of **Antioch** on two separate occasions, he became the cause of countless disturbances and riots in **Syria**. He, who had previously been known as a man of great distinction, remained a prisoner there for some time. 

<margin>B</margin> He was eventually freed upon the proclamation of **Diogenes** <note>the former Emperor Romanos IV</note> as emperor, but was subsequently exiled to an island. By promising large sums of money, he managed to get himself appointed as a judge of **Hellas** and the **Hellespont** <note>the Latin text in the OCR mentions the Peloponnese here instead of the Hellespont</note>, where he took charge of local administration. 

<margin>P 846</margin> To the misfortune of the **Romans** <note>The Byzantines referred to themselves as Romans (Rhomaioi)</note>, Emperor **Michael** summoned this man and placed him in charge of the entire public administration, appointing him to the post of <term>Logothete|the chief administrative minister of the Byzantine Empire, similar to a Prime Minister or Chancellor</term>. The Emperor became a total captive to this man's enchantments and machinations, largely because Michael lacked a manly and stable mind. 

Because of this, **John of Side** <note>the metropolitan bishop mentioned on the previous page</note> was pushed out of power, and Nicephoritzes took everything upon himself. Meanwhile, Michael occupied himself with trivialities and childish games, while the "Consul of Philosophers," **Constantine Psellus** <note>a famous scholar, historian, and advisor</note>, rendered the Emperor unfit for any useful work...

# OF JOHN THE CUROPALATES
<note>original: "Ioannis Curopalatae" — a title belonging to the historian John Scylitzes, meaning "the one in charge of the palace"</note>

The Turks held their prisoners and treated them with respect. When the ransom for the captives was demanded, the Emperor <note>Michael VII Doukas</note> was eager to purchase the Caesar’s release. At that time, **Maleses** <note>A Byzantine official and judge</note>, who had only recently been released by the Caesar, arrived; however, he was immediately sent into exile and his property was confiscated. <margin>5</margin> Thus, he traded his previous captivity—the one he shared with the Emperor **Diogenes** <note>Romanos IV Diogenes, captured at the Battle of Manzikert</note>—for the captivity of **Roussel**, followed by this confiscation and banishment. <margin>B</margin> But **Roussel’s** wife, with great haste and effort, managed to ransom him herself. Consequently, those sent by the Emperor returned having ransomed only the **Caesar** <note>John Doukas</note>.

<margin>10</margin> When the **Caesar** arrived at the **Propontis** <note>The Sea of Marmara</note>, he became fearful. He worried that, because he had been proclaimed emperor by the rebels (even if against his will), he might be viewed as a suspect or a traitor and suffer some terrible, irreversible fate. Therefore, he cast off his worldly clothing, sheared his hair, and donned the robes of a monk. It was in this humble attire that he finally presented himself at the imperial palace.

From all these events, men of sound mind perceived the divine wrath. <margin>15</margin> They concluded that the Divine had become hostile toward them because they had neglected and set aside the holy commandments and precepts. Even though they were conscious of these failings, they continued to lead the Roman forces into great wars and dangers without first seeking to appease God’s favor. Thus, even as they suffered disasters and were mercilessly defeated, <margin>C</margin> they failed to perceive the sense of divine retribution.

<margin>20</margin> The Romans of old did not act in this way; they achieved those fearsome and celebrated victories by laying claim to virtue, justice, love, and truth. By pursuing every good and noble thing to the best of their ability, the Divine was present with them, and they overcame their enemies in every way.

# HISTORY

->**OF JOHN THE CUROPALATES**<-

When the **Caesar** <note>John Doukas, the Emperor's uncle</note> entered the city, it seemed to the ruler <note>Emperor Michael VII Doukas</note> that everything had been successfully resolved. However, he was deeply distressed by the failure to capture **Roussel** <note>Roussel de Bailleul, a Norman mercenary leader who had rebelled and attempted to create his own state in Asia Minor</note>. Indeed, the Emperor considered the destruction of his own kin, the loss of his empire, the slaughter of <margin>D</margin> Christians, the enslavement of villages, and the devastation of the countryside to be matters of secondary importance compared to the threat of **Roussel**.

<margin>5</margin> Meanwhile, **Roussel** set out from the fortress of **Metabole** with his remaining **Frankish** <term>Frankish: In Byzantine texts, this refers generally to Western Europeans, specifically the Normans</term> soldiers, his wife, his children, and his possessions. He marched through the heart of the country without hindrance. Upon reaching the <term>Armeniac Theme: a large military-administrative district in northeastern Asia Minor</term>, he returned to his former strongholds. <margin>10</margin> From there, he launched raids against the **Turks**, preventing them from invading that specific district.

However, when the Emperor heard of this, he believed it was more advantageous for the **Turks** to hold Roman <note>original: "Ῥωμαίων" — the Byzantines continued to call themselves Romans</note> territories than for **Roussel** to be established in any one place. He was urged and provoked into this view by **Nicephorus** <note>Likely Nikephoritzes, the Emperor's powerful and influential chief minister</note>. <margin>P 850</margin> Therefore, the Emperor <margin>15</margin> sent one of the nobles—young in age but otherwise energetic and prudent—the **proedros** <term>proedros: a high-ranking Byzantine court title</term> **Alexios Komnenos** <note>The future Emperor Alexios I, here serving as a young general</note>. Alexios arrived in the city of **Amaseia** and waited to see how events would unfold.

Now, **Roussel** had established a treaty and friendship with the leader of the **Turks**. He met with him without his soldiers, <margin>20</margin> as he had grown accustomed and familiar with him. But one day, while he was dining with them, he was seized and bound. For among the **Turks**, it is an accepted and unquestioned rule to deceive the Romans, even under oath. **Alexios** the **proedros** purchased him for a high price and brought him in chains to the Emperor. The Emperor then handed him over to the torturers to be beaten with <margin>B</margin> <term>ox-sinews: a whip made from dried animal tendons, used for severe corporal punishment</term>.

He tortured him with unbearable blows from ox-hide whips, as if he were some runaway slave, and having shut him in one of the darkest towers, he kept him bound in chains and neglected.

The **Logothete** <note>The Logothete of the Dromos, Nikephoritzes, who became the de facto ruler during Michael VII’s reign</note>, who was very powerful with the Emperor, as previously mentioned, directed and managed everything as he wished. Being more resourceful <margin>10</margin> in vice than any other man, and refraining from no shameful deed for the sake of profit, he established a warehouse <term>Phoundax: A centralized grain exchange or state-controlled warehouse</term> in **Rhaedestos** <note>A port city on the Sea of Marmara, modern-day Tekirdağ</note> and a monopoly. For if anyone says "**Michael**," and does not add "**Parapinakes**," he would not be immediately <margin>D</margin> recognized. This was because at that time a *modios* <term>Modios: A standard Byzantine measure for grain</term> <margin>20</margin> was sold for a gold coin, but was short by one *pinakion* <term>Pinakion: A smaller measure, approximately one-quarter of a modios. The nickname "Parapinakes" literally means "minus a quarter-measure"</term>.

<note>John Scylitzes held the title of Curopalates, a high-ranking court dignity, and wrote a famous synopsis of Byzantine history.</note>

Taking up the thread, I will relate the story. For when Emperor **Basil** <note>Basil II, reigned 976–1025, known as the "Bulgar-Slayer" for his conquest of the Bulgarian Empire</note>, at the time he brought **Bulgaria** under his subjection, did not wish to change any of their customs, but decreed that they should manage their affairs under their own leaders and according to their own habits, just as they had during the time of **Samuel** <note>The Bulgarian Tsar who was Basil II's great rival</note>,
<margin>5</margin> who had been their leader. Now, even before this, the nation had been thrown into turmoil, being unable to bear the greed of the **Orphanotrophos** <term>Orphanotrophos: An official title for the head of the imperial orphanage; here referring to John the Orphanotrophos, the powerful brother of Michael IV</term>, at the time when <margin>P 851</margin> they proclaimed **Doleanus** <note>Peter Delyan, who led a major Bulgarian uprising in 1040</note> as their king—events which have been described in detail earlier in the text. But now, they once again looked toward rebellion. For they could not bear the greed of **Nikephoros** <note>Referring to the minister Nikephoritzes</note> and the schemes he had devised against everyone.
<margin>10</margin> Since the Emperor paid no attention and occupied himself only with childish games, the leading men of Bulgaria asked **Michael** <note>Michael I of Zeta/Duklja, a Serbian ruler</note>, who was their leader, to help and support them. They asked him to give them his son, so that they might proclaim him King of Bulgaria and
<margin>15</margin> be liberated from the oppression and heavy-handedness of the **Romans** <note>The Byzantines called themselves Romans (Rhomaioi)</note>. He gladly listened to them, and having selected three hundred of his own men and handed them over to his son **Constantine**, also called **Bodin**, <margin>B</margin> he dispatched him to Bulgaria. He then went out to **Prisdiana** <note>Modern-day Prizren in Kosovo</note>, where the leading men from **Skopje** gathered—the leader of whom was
<margin>20</margin> **George Boitachos** <note>Georgi Voitech, a Bulgarian noble</note>, descended from the family of the **Komchanoi**. There, they proclaimed him King of the Bulgarians, changing his name to **Peter** <note>original: "Πέτρον" — a name chosen to evoke the memory of the sainted Tsar Peter I of Bulgaria</note> instead of Constantine. When **Nikephoros Karantenos**, who was the Duke governing Skopje, heard of this, along with the leaders under him...

For when Emperor Basil, at the time he conquered Bulgaria, did not want to innovate anything regarding those things that were customary for them, but rather had determined that they should be ruled by their own princes and live by their own customs, just as they had while Samuel was ruling, who was their leader . . . . . . thus already, even earlier, the nation had been disturbed because it could not bear the greed of the **Orphanotrophos**, at the time they declared Doleanus their king, which events were shown in detail above. And now also it looked toward rebellion: for it did not bear the greed of Nikephoros, and the things which he himself had orchestrated against everyone, while the Emperor cared for nothing, being occupied only with childish games. The princes of Bulgaria petitioned their prefect Michael to bring them aid and help, and to hand over his son to them, so that they might declare him King of Bulgaria, and deliver them from the empire and cruelty of the Romans. He, however, willingly complied with them, and having chosen three hundred from his own men, and handed them over to his son Constantine, whose surname was Bodin, he sent him into Bulgaria. He went out, therefore, to Prisdiana, where the nobles who were in Skopje assembled, whose prince was George Boitachos, deriving his origin from the Comchani; they declared him King of the Bulgarians, calling him **Peter** after his name was changed from Constantine. # HISTORY

Robert settled in the cities that belonged to his wife <note>original: "ταῖς πόλεσι ταῖς διαφερούσαις τῇ αὐτοῦ γυναικί"; Robert’s second wife was Sikelgaita, a Lombard princess of Salerno, whose dowry included several cities</note>, the first and greatest of which is named **Salerno**. Of the captives he seized, he cut off the hands of some and mutilated the feet of others; from others he cut off both. Some he sold for great sums of money, terrifying them <margin>C</margin> with the threat that if they did not betray their cities and submit to him, they would suffer not only these punishments but even worse. 

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Because those in the imperial court were suffering from their own internal troubles, no attention was paid to the events occurring in Italy. For shortly after **Monomachos** <note>Emperor Constantine IX Monomachos, died 1055</note> passed away, and the Empress **Theodora** held the throne for about one year, and after **Michael** <note>Michael VI, who reigned briefly from 1056–1057</note> was deposed and **Comnenus** <note>Isaac I Comnenus, who led a military revolt</note> rose up against him, the armies were preoccupied with civil wars. Since there was no one to hinder Robert's momentum, he became great and renowned; he assembled a significant army and became master of horses, money, and weapons. <margin>D</margin> Meanwhile, those appointed by the Emperor to command the cities were unable to march out against him because of a lack of manpower and the poor quality of the troops they did have. 

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;When Comnenus gained control of the empire, the nation of the **Turks** was distressing the East, while the **Patzinaks** <note>Also known as the Pechenegs, a nomadic steppe people</note> were pressing upon the West. ### THE REIGN OF CONSTANTINE IX MONOMACHOS (CONTINUED)

Seeing that what had been done <note>referring to the previous page's mention of administrative shifts and local unrest</note> was pleasing to the locals, he went as a fugitive to the Emperor. Therefore, **Abulchares** <note>original: "Ἀβουλχαρέ"; likely a Byzantine official of Eastern or Armenian descent</note> was sent as the **Duke of Italy**. 

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**Robert** <note>Robert Guiscard, the Norman leader</note>, seeing that the people of **Calabria** were suffering greatly because of the murder of the **Scribones** <note>original: "Σκριβώνων"; a prominent local family in southern Italy</note> and were meditating a rebellion for this very reason, set out as if he would never return. Moving with great speed, he captured **Rhegium** <note>modern-day Reggio Calabria</note>, a large and illustrious city where the Duke of Italy was accustomed <margin>P 855</margin> to reside; for it contained magnificent dwellings and a great abundance of necessary supplies. 

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;When Abulchares reached **Dyrrachium** <note>modern-day Durrës, Albania</note> and from there crossed over to **Bari**, he learned that Rhegium had been captured. He remained in Bari, and from there, as much as he was able, he held onto the cities that still favored the **Romans** <note>the Byzantines, who called themselves Romans</note>, appointing generals and sending an army for their defense. <margin>D</margin>Even so, he had not even scratched the surface of the craft of poetry, but was deceived and led astray by the "Chief of the Philosophers" <note>This refers to Michael Psellos, the famous intellectual and statesman who served as the Emperor's tutor and advisor</note>. <margin>10</margin>Many died every day, to the point that the living were unable to carry out the dead. Every imperial decree and every thought was directed toward wronging their own subjects, outwitting them, and preying upon their livelihoods and the very means of their survival.

# HISTORY

The **Pechenegs** <note>original: "Patzinákoi"; a nomadic Turkic people from the Eurasian steppe who frequently raided Byzantine territory</note> appeared before **Adrianople** <note>modern-day Edirne, Turkey</note> with a massive force. This man was not from the Senate, nor from the high ranks of the Church, nor was he any of the other Byzantines famous and renowned for their eloquence or deeds. ### (IOANNES CUROPALATAE)

However, he chose one of two: either **Eudokia**, the former wife of **Doukas** and later of **Diogenes** <note>Romanos IV Diogenes</note>, or **Maria of Alania**, the wife of the recently reigning **Michael** <note>Michael VII Doukas</note>.

When a certain monk—who was famous at that time for his virtue and was called "The All-Holy" <margin>D</margin> instead of any other name—learned of this, he strove in every way to prevent this impropriety, reminding her of many things that might restrain her eagerness.

Thus, the Emperor shamelessly took **Maria** and was joined to her in a sacred rite; immediately afterward, the priest was deposed for having performed a marriage that was an act of open adultery <note>The marriage was considered adulterous because Maria's husband, the deposed Michael VII, was still alive in a monastery</note>. As for **Michael**, having shorn his hair <note>A sign of entering the monastic life</note>, he was appointed Archbishop of **Ephesus** by the decision of the Patriarch and the metropolitans. However, he visited that city only once; returning, he remained in the **Monastery of Manuel**, working with his own hands. He was later honored exceptionally by the man who became Emperor after these events... <note>Referring to Alexios I Komnenos</note>

...striking him with a foreign sword. The **Varangians** also rose up against the emperor and studied how to kill him. But when the emperor's soldiers opposed them, they turned to prayers and, once the emperor was appeased, they obtained pardon.

The Emperor, his wife **Berdena** (who had been declared queen along with him) having died, took another: for many were betrothed to him, including **Zoe**, the virgin daughter of Emperor **Doukas**, beautiful in form, and many daughters of senators now of marriageable age. He therefore sent those who would lead **Eudokia** to him, who followed with the greatest pleasure. When this was known, a monk who then lived with the highest virtue, and whom they called the "Most Holy" in place of any other name, studied by all means to hinder this absurd deed, bringing many things to her memory which might restrain her from this desire. The emperor therefore took **Maria**, all shame removed, and was joined with her in sacrilege; immediately the priest was removed from office as if for a manifest commission of adultery. **Michael**, however, his hair having been cut, was chosen as Archbishop of **Ephesus** by the sentence of the patriarch and metropolitans. <margin>5</margin> Now the *protoproedros* <term>protoproedros: "first among the presidents," a high-ranking court title</term> **Nikephoros Basilakes**, having seized **Dyrrachium** <note>modern Durrës, Albania, a key strategic port</note>, began gathering an army from all the surrounding regions. He also summoned **Franks** from Italy through **Theodosios**, the Bishop of Diabolis, making ambitious preparations to advance his claims against **Bryennios** <note>Nikephoros Bryennios the Elder, a rival general who had also rebelled</note>. Having assembled a significant army of <margin>10</margin> **Franks**, **Bulgarians**, **Romans** <note>original: "Ῥωμαίων" — the Byzantines continued to refer to themselves as Romans</note>, and **Albanians** <note>original: "Ἀρβανιτῶν"</note>, he set out from there and hurried toward **Thessaloniki**. He also invited the **Pechenegs** <note>Patzinakai, a nomadic Turkic people</note> into an alliance. 

When the Emperor learned of his purpose and intent, he issued a *chrysobull* <term>chrysobull: a high-level imperial decree authenticated with a golden seal</term> <margin>20</margin> to offer him security and sent one of his own associates to him, <margin>C</margin> freeing him from all fear and awarding him the rank of *nobilissimus* <term>nobilissimus: "most noble," one of the highest titles in the imperial court</term>. Thus, when **Basilakes** rode through the whole night—thinking himself unforeseen and undetected—he instead fell into a difficult battle. ...the place has been named the **Spring of Basilakes** <note>original: "βρύσις τοῦ Βασιλακίου" (brysis tou Basilakiou). This likely marks the site of his final capture</note>. After this occurred, he was led away on a wagon—a pitiful burden and a wretched spectacle <note>The Latin text describes this as a "miserable load and an unhappy game/sport"</note>.

While the armies were occupied with the expedition against **Basilakes**, <margin>5</margin> the **Patzinaks** <term>Patzinaks: also known as Pechenegs, a semi-nomadic Turkic people known for their raids into Byzantine territory</term> mixed with the **Cumans** <term>Cumans: another nomadic Turkic group from the steppes</term> and attacked **Adrianople** <margin>B</margin> <note>modern-day Edirne, Turkey</note>. They set a great fire and burned many of the houses there, but having accomplished nothing else worthy of note, they retreated.

In this same year, **Philaretos Brachamios** <margin>10</margin>, a **kuropalates** <term>kuropalates: a high-ranking Byzantine court title, usually granted to important governors or allied princes</term>, also professed his loyalty and servitude to the Emperor. However, when **Botaneiates** <margin>15</margin> <note>Emperor Nikephoros III Botaneiates, who took the throne in 1078</note> was girded with the autocratic power, Philaretos became a servant to him of his own accord.

A certain **Lecas**, a **Paulician** <term>Paulician: a member of a dualist Christian sect often persecuted by the Byzantine state; they were famous for their military skill and frequently lived on the frontiers</term> originating from **Philippopolis** <note>modern-day Plovdiv, Bulgaria</note>, fled from **Epigambria** to the **Patzinaks**. In agreement with them, he issued the most fearsome threats against the Roman <note>original: "Ῥωμαίων" (Rhōmaiōn). The Byzantines continued to call themselves Romans long after the fall of Rome</note> mainland. ### John the Kuropalates

During his reign, many ordinations of metropolitans and other sacred ministers took place, though they were not entirely beyond reproach <note>The Latin translation in the source claims they "lacked all blame," but the Greek text suggests these appointments were controversial or irregular</note>. The Emperor, being accustomed to frugality and simplicity, did not depart from his usual character in any way. He was most generous and liberal, and readily inclined to favor everyone. 

He had two servants, **Borilus** and **Germanus**, who did not obey him like typical servants, but instead carried out whatever they wished without hesitation. Because of them, the Emperor was considered burdensome by the leading members of the Senate, who were stung by the behavior these two displayed toward everyone. 

When, as the preceding account related, the **Logothete** <note>Nikephoritzes, the powerful and often unpopular chief minister under the previous emperor, Michael VII</note> fled to **Roussel** <note>Roussel de Bailleul, a Norman mercenary who had rebelled and carved out a lordship in Asia Minor</note> and stayed with him—being held and guarded by him—he [the Logothete] killed Roussel with poison. However, having been brought to **Botaneiates** by Roussel's associates, the Logothete was kept under guard on the island of **Prote** <note>one of the Princes' Islands near Constantinople</note>. Those around the Emperor knew very well that if the Emperor were only to see him, he would receive mercy and be recruited to manage public affairs due to his vast experience. Since the Emperor was somewhat dull in such matters <note>referring to administrative details or perhaps political cunning</note>, those around the sovereign—calculating that this would not be to their advantage, for he would be a thorn in their side...

# THE HISTORY OF JOHN THE KUROPALATES <note>John Scylitzes, a high-ranking official known as a "Kuropalates," whose historical work is being annotated here.</note>

<margin>P 868</margin>
...fearing for their own safety, they dispatched the **Grand Hetairiarch** <term>Grand Hetairiarch: the commander of the imperial bodyguard, known as the *Hetaireia*</term> **Straboromanos** and put the Logothete to death. Although the Emperor had only commanded him to inquire about the funds belonging to the Empress <note>original: "βασιλίδι" (basilidi), referring here to the royal treasury or the Empress's personal wealth</note> and not to harass him further, Straboromanos, as soon as
<margin>5</margin>
he arrived, bound him in chains and interrogated him with extreme cruelty; it was during this torture that he passed away. This occurred despite the fact that the prisoner had promised that, if he were spared from torture, he would confess everything and hand over the money. But as I have noted, those in power were not so much concerned with the imperial treasures as they were with ensuring he was silenced before he could come before the Emperor’s sight and speak with him directly.
<margin>10</margin>
And so, the events surrounding the execution of the **Logothete** <note>Nikephoritzes, the powerful and controversial chief minister under the former Emperor, Michael VII</note> reached their end.

# ANNOTATIONS BY WILHELM XYLANDER OF AUGSBURG ON CEDRENUS.

## GEORGIUS CEDRENUS EXPLAINED IN HIS OBSCURE PASSAGES; WILHELM XYLANDER, TRANSLATOR AND SCHOLAR, PARTIALLY EMENDED

### WITH NOTES ADDED AFTER THE WORK WAS PUBLISHED BY JACQUES GOAR <note>Jacques Goar (1601–1653) was a French Dominican friar and a significant scholar of Byzantine liturgy and history.</note>.

Page 3, line 3. **Syncellus** <term>Syncellus: an ecclesiastical title in the Byzantine Empire, literally meaning "one who shares a cell."</term> is a title of rank or office. This was the name given to the person who was intended to succeed the deceased patriarch (as they frequently call the high prelate of the Church of Constantinople <note>original: "Cpolitanae," an abbreviation for Constantinopolitanae</note>), acting as a sort of suffragan <note>an assistant bishop who assists the primary bishop or patriarch</note>. Our author mentions this in the *Life of Constantine Monomachus* while discussing the war with the Sultan and the capture of Liparites; the same is found in the works of Zonaras. Furthermore, in the section on Leo the Iconoclast <note>original: "Iconomacho"</note>, our author identifies Anastasius as the syncellus of Germanus; in the section on Leo, son of Basil, he identifies his brother Stephen as the syncellus of Photius; in the section on Romanos Lekapenos, he names his son Theophylact as the syncellus of Stephen of Amaseia; and he identifies others elsewhere. 

From where the word is derived—like many others of that kind—is difficult to guess and not greatly necessary. What if it refers to one who lives in the same cell <note>original: "cella"</note> as the person he is destined to succeed? In the account of Michael Stratiotikos, mention is made of a **protosyncellus** <term>protosyncellus: the "first syncellus," a high-ranking official who often served as a chief aide to the Patriarch</term>, specifically Leo Strabospondylos, who was at that time a leading figure in the administration of the state. This seems to be somewhat different from the others. In these annotations, I have decided to report only those things which seemed most necessary. Fair-minded readers will accept this brevity as an excuse if I do not assist them in every single instance. **XYLANDER**

*In the same place.* In the earliest times, a **Syncellus** was nothing more than a partner in companionship and daily life; he was by no means a designated successor. Indeed, the throne of Constantinople <note>original: "CP," abbreviation for Constantinopolitani</note> was attained by merit of virtue and learning, as seen when Tarasius was removed from the living...

Nikephoros the Confessor <note>Nikephoros I (c. 758–828), Patriarch of Constantinople and a notable historian</note> obtained the succession. More information sought concerning the Syncellus will be explained in their proper places; and what Xylander reported about him—though not entirely clear or complete, yet still worthy of approval—will be inserted more conveniently elsewhere. **GOAR.**

Page 3, verse 4. *Maximian and Maximinus*] The first of these was the colleague of Diocletian, surnamed Herculeus; the latter was adopted as son-in-law and Caesar by the same Emperor Diocletian. Cedrenus calls him Maximian in his own history. Some write the name as Maximianus. His name was Galerius. He calls them tyrants because they were unjust to Christians. **XYL.**

Page 4, verse 1. Theophanes <note>original: "Θεοφάνης"</note>] Following the work of Georgius Syncellus, this man began his history where the other ended. He was the son of Theophilos and Michael <note>Goar likely refers to the era of Emperors Michael II and Theophilos, as Theophanes the Confessor actually lived slightly earlier; he was the superior of the Agros monastery</note> at the time when he died as the superior of the Agros monastery. **GOAR.**

Ibid, verse 2. *of the General [Logothete]* <note>original: "τοῦ ἀπὸ γενικῶν"</note>] Zonaras also calls him by this title in the inscription of his reign, in the third volume, folio 99, shortly before relating the things I have transferred here for the sake of clarity. In Suidas, under the entry *Artemios*, it is noted that the one who calculates the accounts of tributes or revenues is called *genikon*, meaning a "reckoner of taxes" <note>original: "τῶν φόρων λογιστήν"</note>. Our author also mentions him in the life of Basil the Macedonian, and in the same place near the beginning, he shows that *Genikon* was the name of a place where money owed to the public treasury, whether by title of tribute or tax, was collected. Otherwise, it is believed that the word *Logothetes* <term>Logothetes: a high-ranking administrative title in the Byzantine Empire, similar to a chancellor or secretary of state</term> designates a chancellor or a master of petitions or something of that sort; it is certainly a title of office. This Nikephoros <note>Emperor Nikephoros I, who reigned 802–811</note> was a contemporary of Charlemagne. **XYL.**

It is well known that Zonaras is otherwise understood by the name "John the Monk." **XYL.** He is indeed Zonaras to me and several others. His name, profession, and writings prove it. Yet those who hold that Zonaras was later than Cedrenus disagree. On what grounds? Because he drew out the thread of the narrative further. This is a weak argument, for Cedrenus ceased writing while his work was not yet finished. **GOAR.**

Regarding Niketas the Paphlagonian, I have nothing to say, for that Choniates was a Phrygian, by his own testimony. **XYL.** Baronius praises this man, surnamed David, as a most faithful writer of the life of the most holy Patriarch Ignatius and the events of his own time (for he lived in the ninth century). Meursius cites the same man by the surname "the Paphlagonian" in his Lexicon. **GOAR.**

Ibid, verse 3. *the Sicilian* <note>original: "ὁ Σικελιώτης"</note>] I wish to say nothing regarding this Sicilian man without due care. I faithfully transcribe what Possevinus writes in the Heidelberg Library, manuscript 394: *The Chronicle of John the Sicilian, from the creation of the world down to Emperor Michael, son of Theophilos, comprising the principal histories.* Zonaras and Cedrenus make mention of him. These are his words. **GOAR.**

Ibid, verse 4. Psellus <note>original: "Ψελλός"</note>] Who is this Psellus? For there was not just one with the surname Psellus, but several, and they were the *Consuls of the Philosophers* <note>original: "τῶν φιλοσόφων ὕπατοι"</note>—not "consuls" in the Roman sense, as some think, but "supreme," as if "the highest" <note>original: "ὑπέρτατοι"</note>. The first was Michael, the most learned teacher of Leo the Philosopher and "highly honored" <note>original: "ὑπέρτιμος"</note>; in the judgment of Baronius, you will find no one more famous or ancient, of whom the author speaks on page 550. The other was Constantine, mentioned on page 803.
