Possevinus <note>Antonio Possevino (1533–1611), a Jesuit scholar and diplomat</note> adds certain historical details to the former. Since the *Curopalates* <note>A high-ranking court title, here referring to the historian George Kedrenos or John Skylitzes, who held this title</note> testifies that Psellus wrote during his own time, there is no doubt that the author is speaking of the latter Psellus. **GOAR.**

Page 4, line 8. *the rest of the Byzantines* <note>original: "οἱ λοιποὶ Βυζάντιοι"</note>] Those whom the *Curopalates* cites by name: Joseph Genesius and Manuel the Byzantine. **GOAR.**

Ibid. *Leo of Caria* <note>original: "Λέων ὁ Καρίας"</note>] Known by the epithet "the Grammarian," he was a commander of the Roman <note>Byzantine</note> fleet and wrote a history of the deeds of nine emperors who followed Theophanes. This work still lies hidden in the Royal Library. **GOAR.**

Ibid, line 9. *Augustanus*] Born in Sebasteia. For Sebasteia <note>original: "Σεβάστεια"</note> is "Augusta," derived from *Sebastos* <note>original: "Σεβαστός"</note>, which means "Augustus." Just as there were many cities named "Augusta" in the Western regions of the empire, so there were cities with the Greek name "Sebasteia" in the East. For Herod named Samaria "Sebaste," as Strabo testifies, and Pliny (Book 6, Chapter 3) mentions a Sebasteia in Cappadocia. **XYL.** He should never be called *Augustianus* (unless perhaps by Xylander's use of *Augustano*, which is Latin but used improperly here), for he was not born in a city named *Augusta*, but rather held the office of prelate in the church located in *Sebaste*. **GOAR.**

Ibid, line 10. *Demetrius of Cyzicus* <note>original: "ὁ Κυζίκου Δημήτριος"</note>] By common usage, he would be considered the Bishop of Cyzicus. Is this the same Demetrius of Cyzicus of whom the author speaks on pages 723 and 740, and who successfully "sharpened his pen" <note>wrote polemical or scholarly defenses</note> against the Armenian followers of Dioscorus? Since no other writer mentions it, the matter remains uncertain. **GOAR.**

Page 5, line 4. *Protovestiarios* <note>original: "πρωτοβεστιάριος"; literally "First Vestiarist"</note>] I believe he used the letter 'B' in place of the consonant 'V,' just as the Greeks write *Barron* for *Varro* or *Birgilios* for *Virgil*. For writing *Ouarrôn* or *Ouirgilios* is less correct, as the syllable count increases. Furthermore, I do not believe it is the custom for learned men to be placed in charge of beasts <note>original: "bestiis"; a play on the phonetic similarity between "Vestiarios" and "Bestiarios" (beast-handler)</note>; nor indeed are the erudite honored or delighted by command over wild animals. Therefore, I suspect the name *Protovestiarios* is indeed a title of office, but one that designates the person in charge of the royal wardrobe—a duty which today seems to belong to the chamberlains. Nor is it beneath the dignity or convenience of a King to have literate men constantly present for whatever needs may arise. Indeed, mention of the *Vestiarii* <note>wardrobe officers</note>—specifically the *Bestiaritai* <note>original: "βεστιαριτῶν"</note>—is made further down in the 22nd year of Justinian, through whose negligence the Emperor's crown was lost. Often, we read that *Protovestiarii* were assigned to the highest affairs, which would by no means be entrusted to a mere beast-keeper, as can be seen in the marriage of Emperor Lakapenos's granddaughter to Peter, Prince of Bulgaria. Sometimes they were sent to conduct military affairs, as is evident from many passages; indeed, under Basil, son of Romanus, the *Protovestiarios* Leo was appointed dictator with imperial power against Sclerus. Sometimes, as is the role of those most intimate with the ruler, they were used to investigate plots hatched against the Emperor, as our author shows in the case of Leo, son of Basil. And in the time of Constantine, son of Romanus, the dignity of the *Protovestiarios* is shown to be next after the Domestic of the Schools and the *Accubitor*, and superior to the *Drungarios* of the Watch. But if anyone finds the derivation of this name from clothing <note>original: "vestitu"</note> unappealing, let him know that in the works of Choniates, the word *bestiarion* is used instead of "treasury" <note>original: "ταμιείου"</note>—meaning, of course, a private chamber—so that, as I said, for this reason also, they are considered among the most intimate...

# OF XYLANDER AND GOAR

<note>Xylander notes:</note> Which of the administrators he might designate. At the word "to give in" <note>original Greek: ἐνδιδόναι</note>, I believe a participle is missing, such as "wishing" <note>original Greek: βουλόμενος</note> or something similar. **XYL.**

<note>Goar notes:</note> That this John is the same person commonly called the *Curopalates* <note>A high-ranking Byzantine court title; here referring to the historian John Skylitzes</note> is proved by his name, confirmed by his writings, and the author Kedrenos himself suggests it quite clearly. The name is evident: his history begins from the death of Nikephoros—specifically from the reign of Michael, surnamed Rangabe. Nor is there any of the writers mentioned here from whom it can be proved that Kedrenos collected more material than this man, whose concise path he followed. He testifies that he set his hand to writing neither to condemn nor to commend the memory of anyone, which is a quality Kedrenos praises in him. 

Nonetheless, an objection arises that anyone might easily notice: the surname "Skylitzes" and the office of *Curopalates* are separated here by a significant distance from the mentions of "the Thracesian" and the "Protovestiarios" <note>The head of the imperial wardrobe and a high financial official</note>. But if one is a name of his homeland and the other a family name, there is no real contradiction. Indeed, various offices frequently do not prove a difference in persons; for the same man could have begun weaving his history as a *Curopalates*, and in following years be promoted to the dignity of *Protovestiarios*, and thus be honored with that title by Kedrenos. 

I am, in fact, far from the conjecture of those who claim the *Curopalates* lived later than Kedrenos. For since the narrative of both is the same—composed of the same words, if you remove a few—it was necessary for one to borrow his material from the other. Furthermore, while both mention the same historical authors in their prefaces, Kedrenos specifically names the work of John the Thracesian, whereas in the *Curopalates*' work, there is no mention of Kedrenos himself. This is an argument that John—whoever he was—preceded Kedrenos, not the *Curopalates*. Otherwise, how could he have been unknown to the *Curopalates* if he had come before? Or why would the *Curopalates*, when enumerating previous historians, remain silent about both that John (if he were someone else) and Kedrenos himself? If he followed Kedrenos’s words point by point and reviewed all other authors in order, would he have suppressed their names out of envy or laziness? 

Therefore, it is better to say that Kedrenos, being nearly a contemporary of the *Curopalates*, had not yet finished his history, while the *Curopalates* had brought his work further along. From him and others, Kedrenos—like a plagiarist—transferred many things into his own *Synopsis* <note>A summary or general view of a subject</note> in their entirety, without effort and without changing the style of the narrative. **GOAR.**

*page 6, line 2. Little Genesis*] This same book is called the *Apocalypse of Moses*, as Kedrenos notes a little later. It is also mentioned by Theodore Metochites, Zonaras, Glycas, and Syncellus. It is, however, apocryphal <note>A text of doubtful authenticity or not part of the accepted biblical canon</note>. I believe it is no great loss to religion or literature that it has utterly perished, along with the *Apocalypse of Enoch* and other inventions of the same sort. For its quality is clear enough from the fragments cited from it. Zonaras, at the beginning of his annals, wisely rejects it <note>original Greek: ἀποδιοπομπεῖται, literally "expels it like a scapegoat"</note>. The Jews have a *Great Genesis*, a *Great Leviticus*, etc., and in them are wondrous trifles. 

Regarding what follows about "nourishment," I have translated it word for word. It is close to what might be expressed by the common proverb: that he "shoves pre-chewed food into our mouths," by delivering the histories of all ages in a condensed form. In this, however, he promises much more than he was able to perform, as we pointed out in the preface. **XYL.**

# ANNOTATIONS.

<meta>catchword: because</meta>

Page 7, line 4. The twenty-ninth] I felt a religious scruple about changing anything, as I was using only a single manuscript, and one that was quite carelessly written in many places. For no one, to my knowledge, has recorded that the Egyptians had more than twelve months. Plutarch, in his *Life of Numa* and others, as well as Augustine in *The City of God*, book 15, mention that their year was sometimes a single month, and sometimes four months long. But these were ancient customs; it is well established that they later defined the year by twelve months. Furthermore, Theon, in his commentary on the *Aratea* <note>Theon of Alexandria's commentary on the astronomical poem by Aratus</note> where the poet describes the primary circles of the sphere, explicitly testifies that the month of March was called *Phamenoth* by the Egyptians. And Plutarch clearly teaches in his treatise *On Isis and Osiris* that the new moon of the month of Phamenoth is the beginning of spring. <term>XYLANDER</term>

Ibid, line 11. Five thousandth] Nicephorus <note>referring to Patriarch Nikephoros I of Constantinople</note> also, in his *Chronology*, counts five thousand five hundred years from the beginning of the world until Christ. However, a truer calculation, demonstrated by Holy Scripture, teaches that Christ was born in the year 3963 from the beginning of the world, in the 751st year from the founding of Rome <note>original: *u. c.* or *ab urbe condita*</note>, having already entered the 42nd year of the reign of Augustus; a point which Cedrenos also expressed regarding Augustus. <term>XYLANDER</term>

Ibid, line 16. Note] I wanted to indicate that word <term>hoti</term> <note>original Greek: ὅτι; meaning "that" or "because"</note> once in my version, but I shall omit it hereafter. Later Greek writers are accustomed to prefixing that mark to the headings of things collected haphazardly from elsewhere and transferred into their own commentaries, just as we commonly use the word *item*. This is very frequent in the works of Suidas and Eustathius. <term>XYLANDER</term>
The commentator <note>Xylander</note>, having promised to omit more things hereafter, also omits this primary point in his observations: the word <term>hoti</term>—expressed as a contracted character in the manuscript copies and always prefixed to the beginning of haphazardly assembled passages—has a corresponding note in the margin, the word <term>semeiosai</term> <note>original Greek: σημείωσαι; meaning "mark well" or "take note"</note>. This is done so that, whether that marginal word is read or understood, a complete sense is maintained with the following words: "Mark well that..." etc. Whether the translator has erased so many small particles with integrity and faithfulness, the fair reader shall judge. <term>GOAR</term>

Ibid, line 17. The first after the Sabbath] St. Augustine, in his 86th letter to Casulanus, citing the passage regarding the "one of the Sabbath" <note>original Latin: *una sabbati*</note> from Acts 20, says: "That day was then called the 'one of the Sabbath' which is now called the Lord's Day, as is found more clearly in the Gospels." For the day of the Lord’s resurrection is called the "first of the Sabbath" <note>original: *prima sabbati*</note> by Matthew, but "one of the Sabbath" <note>original: *una sabbati*</note> by the other three; it is well established that this is the day which was later called the Lord's Day. Thus he wrote. Before him, Justin Martyr explained the matter in his *Dialogue with Trypho* as follows: "For the first of the sabbaths, remaining the first of all the days, is called the eighth according to the number of the cycle of all the days, yet it remains the first." <note>original Greek: μία γὰρ τῶν σαββάτων πρώτη μένουσα τῶν πασῶν ἡμερῶν, κατὰ τὸν ἀριθμὸν πάλιν τῶν πασῶν ἡμερῶν τὴν κυκλοφορίαν ὀγδόη καλεῖται, καὶ πρώτη οὖσα μένει.</note> To this also belong the notes Eustathius made on line 173 of Book 16 <note>designated by the Greek letter Pi</note> of the *Iliad*: "The first rank was led by Menesthius of the shimmering breastplate." <note>original Greek: τῆς μὲν ἰῆς στίχος ἦρχε Μενέσθιος αἰολοθώρηξ; Xylander is noting that the Greek word for 'one' can mean 'first'</note>. I have noted these things for the sake of the unlearned, and lest I should seem reckless to anyone. <term>XYLANDER</term>

Ibid, line 19. I have translated <term>nychthemeron</term> <note>original Greek: νυχθήμερον; a period of a night and a day</note> as "natural day," which is completed by a full equinoctial revolution. <term>XYLANDER</term>
The learned Leone Allacci, more skillfully and clearly, says in *On the Measurement of Time*, chapter 3: "A similar span is the <term>nychthemeron</term>, which..."

# THE ANNOTATIONS OF XYLANDER AND GOAR

*...that is to say, it elapses in the meantime while the sun, rising or setting or being at the meridian, returns again to the rising, or meridian, or setting.* <term>GOAR</term> <note>Goar is explaining the solar cycle and its measurement of time.</note>

Julius Africanus was an ecclesiastical writer of great renown. Eusebius cites his letter to Aristides regarding the genealogy of Christ in the first book of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 6; Augustine also mentions him in the second book of his *Retractations*, chapter 7, as do others. Godfrey of Viterbo, who compiled histories around the year 1200 AD, asserts that he possesses the *Chronicles* of Julius Africanus written under Marcus Crassus. I believe this claim proceeded from a foolish man who, upon reading "Marcus," added the name "Crassus" by a "crass error" <note>original: *crasso errore*, a pun on the name Crassus and the Latin word for "thick" or "stupid"</note>, as he knew of no other Marcus besides Crassus. For who does not see that this ought to be referred to Marcus Aurelius Antoninus? Indeed, our Kedrenos reports elsewhere that Africanus flourished under the Emperor Commodus. Eusebius, in *Ecclesiastical History* book 6, chapter 31, records that he became known under Maximinus. Eusebius also cites Africanus’s books of *Chronographies* <note>original Greek: *chronographikōn*</note> in the tenth book of his *Preparation for the Gospel*, and elsewhere. Otherwise, the passage is obscure, since Kedrenos sometimes uses the term "intelligible" <note>original: *noēton*</note> to mean that which is perceived by the mind alone, and at other times to mean that which is indicated under the guise of something else. I do not care to philosophize further on these matters, since very learned disputes on this subject by Basil, Ambrose, Augustine, and others already exist. <term>XYLANDER</term>

Page 8, line 1. **firmament**] This word seems to correspond quite well to the Greek word *stereoma*. Kedrenos interprets it as the "sky"; others understand it as "the air," among whom is Abraham ibn Ezra, the most learned of the Jews, as they say, according to the testimony of David Kimchi on Psalm 19. And the Jerusalem Targum <note>an Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible</note> uses "air" for the word to which *stereoma* corresponds, namely *raki’a* <note>original Hebrew: רקיע</note> in Genesis 1, as Elias Levita testifies in his *Thesbite*. But it was not my place to change anything. **furthermore, the dry and parched is named Earth** (line 6) is a common usage. I do not know if an epithet used in place of a noun is found among Latin authors, unless one accepts these lines from Virgil: *until the prows hold the dry [land]* (*Aeneid* book 10), and elsewhere *he leaps onto the dry*. Homer indeed said *over the dry and the moist* (*Iliad* book 14, line 308), noting the land and sea by the terms for moist and dry; for "dry" <note>original Greek: *trapheron*</note> means *that which is solid and compact and thus distinguished from the moist*. Now, there is a received opinion that the sky <note>Latin: *caelum*</note> is named from "seeing" <note>original Greek: *oran*</note>; and we ourselves have observed *uranos* <note>the Greek word for sky/heaven</note> used in the Doric dialect among the poets. <term>XYLANDER</term>

*Ibid.* line 14. **of every beast**] It is **of all flesh** <note>original Greek: *sarkos*</note> in Leviticus 17, not "of every beast" <note>original Greek: *ktēnous*</note> as our author has written. <term>XYLANDER</term>

Page 9, line 10. **of the books with which the Jews**] It is more widely accepted, and still common practice today, to count twenty-four books of the Old Testament; whence the Old Testament, which are the Jewish Bibles, are inscribed and named *The Twenty-Four* <note>original Hebrew: ארבע ועשרים / *arba v’esrim*</note>. Regarding both opinions, the "Helmeted Prologue" of Saint Jerome to the Bible will satisfy the reader who is not overly inquisitive. <term>XYLANDER</term>

*Ibid.* line 22. **beasts and**] I have decided that these should be expressed as a question, so that the author may resolve the problem he has set for himself. For he refutes those who use the speech of the serpent as an argument to prove that beasts were able to speak before the fall of Adam. <term>XYLANDER</term>

# ANNOTATIONS

p. 10 v. 2. *endowed with reason*] or with speech: for the word *logos* <note>original Greek: λόγος</note> signifies both; nor is one ever found without the other, since speech is, as it were, a sensible or audible form of reason. **XYL.** <note>Wilhelm Xylander (1532–1576) was a German classical scholar who provided the Latin translation and notes for this edition of Kedrenos.</note>

p. 16 v. 10. *forty years*] He frequently uses the word "times" <note>original Greek: χρόνους (*chronous*)</note> in place of "years" <note>original Greek: ἐνιαυτῶν (*eniautōn*)</note>, which is easy for anyone to observe. However, something is missing before these words, so I have marked it with an asterisk. In the works of Josephus, there is no "Mount Siridus," but rather "in the region of Syria" <note>original Greek: κατὰ τὴν Συριάδα (*kata tēn Syriada*)</note>. I do not quite grasp what kind of word "Egregores" is meant to be. The matter of Moses’s face shining with light is a fact well known from the Sacred Scriptures, such as Exodus 34:2 and 2 Corinthians 3. **XYL.** George Syncellus calls the "Watchers" <note>original Greek: Ἐγρηγόρους (*Egregorous*), meaning "the wakeful ones"</note>—whom the author calls *Egregoras* <note>original: Ἐγρηγόρας</note>—the sons of Seth. These were men beloved by God, pious, tall, and handsome priests who were seized by desire for the daughters of Cain, and whose children, born from that profane union, were also known by this name because of the beauty of their father Seth. "Seth was pious and very well-formed, and all those descended from him were pious and beautiful." <note>original Greek: εὐσεβὴς ἦν ὁ Σὴϑ καὶ εὐδιάπλαστος σφόδρα, καὶ οἱ ἐξ αὐτοῦ πάντες εὐσεβεῖς καὶ ὡραῖοι ἦσαν.</note> **GOAR.** <note>Jacques Goar (1601–1653) was a French Dominican scholar who provided additional commentary for this edition.</note>

p. 17 v. 10. *to be called by the name of God*] The author intends this to mean that Enos was called by the name of God. But these are silly trifles which—to say nothing of the Hebrew truth of the matter—are refuted by the very usage of the Greek language. For the word *epikaleomai* <note>original Greek: ἐπικαλέομαι</note> is what grammarians call a "middle" verb, meaning "to call upon" or "to invoke," which no one is ignorant of unless they have never read the Greek Bible. Enos, therefore, who takes his name from the miseries of human life (as those learned in Hebrew know, though it is not the time to demonstrate it here), was the first among men to place his hope in God and to invoke Him full of confidence. Furthermore, the passage appears to be corrupted: it is manifestly false that Mahalaleel was the son of Enos, when he was actually his grandson through Kenan. What follows concerning Uriel is ambiguous, as to whether he taught Adam or carries prayers up to God; I have left this ambiguity as I found it. I prefer the former interpretation, because this same Uriel is traditionally said to have taught certain things after the time of Enoch as well. **XYL.**

p. 19 v. 1. *and the name*] Truly, "Giant" <note>original Greek: Γίγας (*Gigas*)</note> seems to be a Greek word; Eustathius likes the idea that it signifies the same as "earth-born" <note>original Greek: γηγενής (*gēgenēs*)</note>, which is a fitting etymology derived from the words "to be born" and "earth" <note>original Greek: γίνεσθαι (*ginesthai*) and γᾷ (*ga*)</note>. He proves this with examples in his commentary on the *Odyssey*, Book 4, at line 159. In Hebrew they are called *Gibborim* <note>original Hebrew: גבורים, meaning "mighty ones"</note> because, as the most learned Jews have written, the hearts of those who see them fail for fear. The Chaldean <note>The Aramaic Targum</note> translated it as *Gabbara* <note>original Aramaic: גבריא</note> because of their strength. But they are also named *Emim* <note>original Hebrew: אימים</note> from "terror," meaning the "terrible ones," as in Deuteronomy 2 and elsewhere. **XYL.**

ibid. v. 15. *and that name for the mountain*] *Cherem* <note>original Hebrew: חרם</note> signifies "anathema," a "curse," or a "devoted thing," as seen in Judges 7, Numbers 18, and elsewhere. Therefore, this etymology is not without merit. You will find a very similar narrative in Hilary’s commentary on Psalm 132, which I will refrain from recounting here. **XYL.**

p. 20 v. 18. *The mountains of Ararat in the Parthian region of Armenia* <note>original Greek: τὰ ὄρη Ἀραρὰτ ἐν Παρϑίᾳ τῆς Ἀρμενίας</note>] While pardon has been granted to other apocryphal stories related by the author, let it be permitted to add this from the written histories and ancestral traditions of the Armenians. Jacob of Nisibis... <note>Jacob of Nisibis, also known as Jacob Mousponoë, was a 4th-century bishop famous for his attempt to find the Ark on Mount Ararat.</note>

The <term>Catholicos</term> <note>A title for the head of the Armenian Apostolic Church.</note> (as they call the patriarch) was driven by a desire to journey to the highest peak of the mountains of **Ararat**, called **Massis**, so that by inspecting the place more carefully and adoring the God who restored the human race, he might carry away a fragment of the wood from the remains of the ark—if such a thing were granted—for the inhabitants believe that Noah’s ark still survives there amidst the heaped-up mounds of snow. Having begun the journey, he was repelled by a secret power from approaching the summit of Massis; however, after pouring out prayers, he received the fragment he had hoped for by the gift of God. This wood was deposited in the town of **Aquiri**, situated at the foot of the mountain, where the Armenians frequently visit it. They preserve among themselves, as they say, the wood by which God once commanded the remnants of the human race to be preserved from destruction. **Zonaras** <note>Joannes Zonaras, a 12th-century Byzantine historian.</note> says: *Josephus says the place is called the "Place of Descent" by the Armenians, and that remnants of the ark are shown there.* <note>original Greek: ἀποβατήριον δὲ τὸν τόπον καλεῖσθαι τοῖς Ἀρμενίοις φησὶν ὁ Ἰώσηππος, καὶ λείψανα δείκνυσθαι τῆς λάρνακος ἐκεῖ</note>. **GOAR.**

p. 20 v. 21. *on the first day*] namely, *of the week*, which is expressed below but was omitted here. Furthermore, **Nicephorus** <note>Nicephorus Callistus Xanthopoulos, a church historian.</note> gives the same year for the flood from the beginning of the world. However, the Hebrew calculation holds it to be 1656, which the learned follow. **Clement of Alexandria**, in the first book of his *Stromata*, counts 2148 years and 4 days from the creation of Adam until the flood. Regarding what follows shortly after—that Noah was called **Xisuthrus** by the Chaldeans—**Eusebius** in his *Preparation for the Gospel*, book 9, cites the Assyrian history of **Abydenus**, in which he is called **Seisither** <note>original Greek: Ζείσιθρος</note>, on Greek page 243 b. For the rest, I have used the <term>stigma</term> <note>A Greek ligature for "st".</note> (ϛ) for the "st" in **Mestrom** and **Mestracae**, following what is clearly true; unless someone prefers the "s" (σ), as it appears in Zonaras. **XYL.**

p. 22 v. 13. *630 years after the flood*] <note>original Greek: μετὰ χλ' ἔτη τοῦ κατακλυσμοῦ</note>. This number is greater than is right; and indeed, there is little agreement among writers concerning the number of years from the flood until the birth of Abraham. The Hebrews hand down that for 2,000 years minus four, there was a single type of language on the earth, and the confusion of tongues occurred 340 years after the flood. Their words are: **"For two thousand years less four, the world had one language"** <note>original Hebrew: ב' אלפים פחות ד' שנה היה העולם לשון אחת</note>. Regarding the time of the flood and the confusion of tongues: **"From Adam to the flood, 1656"** <note>original Hebrew: מאדם עד המבול א וחרגו (The OCR here likely contains a corruption of the Hebrew numerals for 1656).</note> and **"From the flood to the division [of tongues], so many years"** <note>original Hebrew: מן המבול עד הפלגה שם שנה</note>. **Funckius** <note>Johann Funck (1518–1566), a German chronologist.</note> places no more than 132 years in his chronology from the flood until that confusion. A little before, **Eber**, the architect of the tower, is placed here, which is clearly foreign to the matter. And **Mount Lubanus**, on which Noah is later written to have planted a vine, is later read as **Lubarus**; we have noted similar variations of this kind elsewhere. He seems to have collected his catalog of historians from the beginning of **Josephus**.

Furthermore, as far as the marks for numbers are concerned, I have gladly used the ancient ones; and I consider that those who bring such things back into use are by no means to be blamed. Meanwhile, I am not unaware that different people have different views on these very matters. I have followed what I thought to be the simplest and truest. Nor will it cause me any regret, following **Priscian** <note>A 6th-century Latin grammarian.</note> and **Manutius** <note>Paolo Manuzio, a Renaissance scholar and printer.</note> (who explained these things in his most learned commentary on the letters of Cicero to Atticus), to also set forth for the sake of the unlearned what I think. I believe these marks imitate the method of lines, by which we calculate with the help of counters drawn on an abacus. To make this better understood, I will reveal it by setting an example before your eyes.

### ANNOTATIONS

You see how a counter <term>calculus</term> <note>originally: "calculus" – a small stone or pebble used for counting on a calculation board or abacus.</note> placed on an upper line is ten times the value of one placed on the line immediately below it; and one that is placed in the space or interval between lines is worth half of the line immediately above it, and for that same reason, five times the value of the line immediately below. The method of composition is well known: that **lx** is 60, and **xl** is 40, **iix** or **viii** is 8, **iv** or **iiii** is 4, **xc** is 90, **xxc** is 80, and so on; everyone sees this. However, there are various conjectures regarding the origin of these signs. First of all, it is clear that the other numbers between five and ten revolve, as if on hinges, around these two, since each hand has five fingers, which together make ten; **Aristotle** <note>Aristotle (384–322 BC), the Greek philosopher. This refers to a passage in his *Problems*, section 15.</note> also mentions this fact. Common daily use, as well as the reasoning of simple people, demonstrates that fingers were the first and simplest instrument for counting, and from this many proverbs have been derived. Now, I believe the mark **i** for a unit is not a letter, but a small line; and I judge the same for **ii**, **iii**, and **iiii**: it is very well known that single units are marked with single lines even by the unlettered and "idiots," as they are called <note>The author uses the term "idiotis" in the original sense of private individuals or common people lacking formal education.</note>. Furthermore, for the number five, as the first "hinge" point, its own character had to be found, which, when joined with the others, could proceed up to ten. This character is **v**, which is certainly not a letter—for why would it not be **o** instead? Rather, it represents two lines meeting at an acute angle. This mark is likewise used by those ignorant of all letters, though some use it inverted like this: **Λ**. From this mark doubled, or rather from one added to the other by joining their tips, **x** is formed, looking like **X**. Indeed, there seems to be no other reason why the letter **x** should signify ten. As for why **l** is the mark for fifty, **Priscian** <note>Priscian (fl. 500 AD), a famous Latin grammarian.</note> provides a subtle reason, one which in my judgment is far too subtle to have a place in such a common matter. I believe they are simply two small lines joined at a right angle, which, being adopted and accepted "by convention" <note>original Greek: κατὰ συνθήκην</note>—as Aristotle says regarding the names of things—would denote 50, just as **v** denotes 5. From this point up to one hundred, no new mark was needed, since everything could be written by combining the previous marks with this one. However, it was decided that 90 should be expressed not as **lxxxx**, but for the sake of brevity by subtracting ten from a hundred; just as 9 is not **viiii**, but **i** subtracted from **x**. This occurs when a smaller character is placed before a larger one, such as **ix** for 9 or **xc** for 90. Furthermore, **xl** is more common than **xxxx** for 40, to be concise. From this we also get **xxc** for **lxxx** (80), **iv** for **iiii** (4), and **ic** for **xcix** (99), and others of that kind. The mark for a hundred is **c**, which is commonly thought to be the letter **c**...

# BY XYLANDER AND GOAR

...is third in order, as it is the head of the word *centum* <note>Latin: "hundred"</note>; and they feel the same about the letter <term>M</term>, which is the mark for a thousand, because the word *mille* <note>Latin: "thousand"</note> begins with that letter. This has some plausibility; but when we get to the heart of the matter, something else appears. For why is <term>Q</term> not also the mark for five <note>quinarius</note> or fifty <note>quinquagenarius</note>, or <term>D</term> for ten <note>denarius</note>? Why did the letters <term>X</term>, <term>V</term>, and <term>L</term> creep in here, if indeed the first letters of words were taken as marks? For that argument is also very weak—that <term>D</term> signifies 500 because it is the letter closest to <term>C</term>. For by that logic, we would join <term>K</term> to signify ten and <term>L</term> to fifty, such that <term>K</term>, through similarity and affinity, degenerated into <term>X</term>. For we might imagine that <term>Y</term> or <term>Z</term>, as non-Latin letters, did not deserve to be received here; but what will happen to the letters <term>E, F, N, O</term> and others? To me, these inventions do not please me. I believe that once straight lines were used, curved lines were also conveniently added to them, especially as the array of numbers grew. 

Therefore, let the semicircle resembling the letter <term>C</term> be the mark for a hundred; this is easier to believe because the remaining characters, even those for thousands, arise from this, as we shall show. For its opposite, <term>Ↄ</term>, with a small line added, thus <term>IↃ</term>, represents five hundred units—surely half of the thousand-mark, which was expressed in antiquity as <term>CIↃ</term>, with a small line inserted between the earlier characters so they would not merge, as I suppose; this small line was also distorted by scribes in the <term>L</term>, because it was painted a bit long and was thought to be the letter l. These same scribes, so they could write a thousand with a single stroke of the pen, drew <term>∞</term> <note>the infinity symbol used as a shorthand for 1000</note>, just as they changed <term>IↃ</term> into the letter <term>D</term>, which Manutius <note>Aldus Manutius (1449–1515), a famous Venetian printer and scholar who wrote on Latin orthography.</note> has excellently noted. It is well known today that <term>M</term> is used as the mark for a thousand, and the reason has been mentioned. It is easy to see how the rest are born from here. In the meantime, I value our own marks <note>Arabic numerals, which were still being contrasted with Roman numerals in scholarly texts of this era.</note> very highly for the sake of utility and brevity, such as 500, 675, etc. But it seems more dignified to use these capital letters in books. Furthermore, I would think nine thousand (for example) could be written concisely thus: <term>IX CIↃ</term> or <term>IXCIↃ</term>. But enough on these matters here: let each follow what they wish, as long as they do not disparage others. **Xyl.**

p. 24 v. 10. *further regions*] <note>original: "ulteriores regiones"</note> The Greek book has "the regions near Joppa"; what sort of thing that is, let others see. It is clear enough that the nations were described which arose from and were occupied by the sons of Noah. **Xyl.**

ib. <note>short for ibidem, "in the same place"</note> v. 8. *Mastusia of the Thracian Chersonese* is a promontory in the region of Ilium <note>Troy</note>, with the Hellespont flowing between. With this reasoning, the calculation of the Hebrews agrees, who count 52 years from the confusion of languages further up to the birth of Isaac. Therefore, he was born...

# ANNOTATIONS

It was in the year 2048 or 2049, when Abraham was in his hundredth year. A little after verse 8, where I wrote "from the lineage of *Ham*," the Greek text reads *Shem*, but this is clearly a mistake. Soon after, regarding Semiramis <note>A legendary Queen of Assyria</note>, it says she "invented bridles." In the Greek, it is "she surrounded the rivers with mouths" <note>original: ποταμοῖς περιέβαλε στόμια</note>; which is not free from error. I suspect the word "rivers" <note>original: ποταμοῖς</note> is a corruption, whether the author intended "horses" <note>original: ἵπποις</note> or something else, so that the invention of equestrian matters might be attributed to this warlike heroine. Indeed, Virgil, in the 7th book of the *Aeneid*, calls Picus her son—if Cedrenus has reported the truth—a "tamer of horses," perhaps famous for that invention, just as another is mentioned there as a planter of vines. It is well known that "mouths" <note>original: στόμια</note> can signify bridles or bits. They also signify orifices or mouths, as of vessels or veins; but I have not read of them signifying the mouths of rivers, nor does that seem to fit here. Further down, in the section on Heraclius, he calls the "mouths of the desert" <note>original: στόμια ἐρήμου</note> the passes or narrows through which one enters the wilderness. XYL. <note>Wilhelm Xylander, the 16th-century humanist scholar.</note>

page 34 verse 21. **bordered with scarlet**] <note>original: ἐχούσας ταβλία ῥούσια</note>. I have not observed the word "tablets" <note>original: ταβλία / tablia</note> used elsewhere. They seem to be the name for small patches of cloth with which the edges of a cloak were bordered—what we call a *fringe* or *border*. Unless one prefers to see them as "stripes" <note>technical term: clavi</note>, about which I have written elsewhere. I have translated "red" <note>original: ῥούσιον</note> as "scarlet." This was the color of the "Red" faction of chariot drivers, which Xiphilinus, quoting Dio, calls "fire-colored gear" in the time of Nero. Pliny mentions this in Book 7, Chapter 53. Most call this color "rose-colored," and indeed the color of roses is not far from the blood-red of a deep blush. Martial somewhere calls such a charioteer "scarlet-clad." XYL.

There is no doubt that by the word "tablets" <note>original: ταβλίων</note> we should understand the Roman "broad stripe" <note>term: latus clavus</note> and "purple border" <note>term: limbus purpureus</note> which notably decorated a garment. For "red" <note>original: ῥούσιον</note> is a rose or purple color, and is one of those colors which the author writes were displayed by the racing factions during the time of Michael, son of Theophilus. Furthermore, he adds "red" <note>original: ῥούσιον</note> to the Green, Blue, and White factions, which they interpret as rose-colored. GOAR. <note>Jacques Goar, a 17th-century Dominican scholar and editor.</note>

page 36 verse 7. **In the beginning**] The verses are confused in the Greek, but I have attempted to present their meaning. XYL.

page 37 verse 5. **falling into a fertile nature**] <note>original: ἐν γονίμῳ φύσει πεσὼν</note>. In the *Suda* <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> under the entry for "Hermes," these same things are related with a few changes, but there it is incorrectly read as "being a boy and" <note>original: παῖς ὢν καί</note>, just as we previously had the error "to himself" <note>original: ἑαυτῷ</note> instead of "to him" <note>original: αὐτῷ</note>. Moreover, the prayer in the *Suda* varies somewhat. XYL.

page 42 verse 4. **But as for Agenor**] This passage is clearly corrupt; the story is well known, even from Ovid. XYL.

page 47 verse 16. **from his wife**] In our manuscript, it is written "from his daughter" <note>original: θυγατρός</note>, and "from his wife" <note>original: γυναικός</note> is noted above it; I have followed the latter, as the context supports it.

Abram, who was afterwards called Abraham; a distinction which either Cedrenus or the scribe neglected, though it was diligently noted by Moses. XYL.

# THE ANNOTATIONS OF XYLANDER AND GOAR

<margin>page 49 verse 14.</margin> **seventh**] <note>original: septimo</note> Surely this means the year had begun, but was not completed; so that he should be understood to have passed away while in his 75th year. XYL. <note>Wilhelm Xylander, the 16th-century humanist scholar.</note>

<margin>ibid. verse 23.</margin> **Jerusalem**] <note>original: Ierusalemam</note> This is what the Greeks, and the Latins following them, call the city *Hierosolyma*. Our word is closer to the Hebrew. The etymology provided by Cedrenus <note>A 11th-century Byzantine historian</note> for the sacred language does not match. Soon after, **Pentapolis** <note>original: Pentapolis</note> refers to five cities, namely Sodom, Gomorrah, and the three remaining ones, which Cedrenus also lists shortly thereafter. XYL.

<margin>page 51 verse 1.</margin> **Gerar**] <note>original: Geraris</note> See Genesis 20, before Isaac was born; and regarding Keturah, Genesis 25. Cedrenus cites these in a mutilated form. There is a note in the margin stating that these were taken from Africanus <note>Sextus Julius Africanus, a 3rd-century Christian traveler and historian</note>. It is uncertain whether this refers to these notes or to what follows regarding Lot and the Dead Sea. I believe the latter to be true; and that Cedrenus is not reporting miracles he saw himself, but those reported by Africanus. As for what he says about **fruit and smoke**, I do not quite follow his meaning. XYL. <note>This likely refers to the "Apples of Sodom," which were said to look beautiful but crumble into smoke and ash when touched.</note>

<margin>page 59 verse 9.</margin> **edible item**] <note>original: edulio</note> I have retained a general term, as I could not quite grasp what the form of a <term>kollyris</term> <note>original: κολλυρίδος; a roll or small loaf of bread</note> was. Athenaeus, certainly, in book 3 when discussing various kinds of breads, cites a verse from Aristophanes’ *Peace* regarding the *collyra*, which he shows from that source was among the types of bread. The commentators on the poet suggest it was either a tiny morsel of bread or some kind of bread product given to children; thus, it does not seem wrong to translate it as a "twist of bread" in the lexicons. Following them, the same author records that they are called <term>kollaboi</term> <note>original: κολλάβους</note> in the same comedy, as if you were to say "mutilated," that is, tiny breads. Furthermore, a mention of the <term>kollyris</term> and its related verb exists in 2 Samuel 13, in the story of Tamar. And earlier in chapter 6, a <term>kollyris of bread</term> <note>original: κολλυρὶς ἄρτου</note> is named. However, in the Hebrew language, this is called <term>challat lechem</term> <note>original: חַלַּת לֶחֶם; a cake of bread</note>, while the other is called <term>levibah</term> <note>original: לְבִיבָה; a heart-shaped or fried cake</note>. Saint Jerome <note>The 4th-century translator of the Vulgate</note> translated the latter as "broth," while he retained the Greek word for the former. Indeed, they are different words. What is named in chapter 6 seems to have been a cake of bread, based on Leviticus chapters 2 and 8, and can be demonstrated elsewhere. The later passage seems to show they were thin wafers <note>original: lagana</note>, or something cooked from flour paste by whatever method—a food rather than a drink. For indeed, Amnon refused to eat, not to drink, as the words simply state. I would not have noted these things unless the authority of Saint Jerome had, as it ought, cautioned me; and I think that if someone were to say that "broths" are also eaten, they could not be justly criticized. The word is derived from "refreshing the heart," and in the holy language, it seems to signify something "cordial," so to speak. But let others look into this. I had written these things long ago when I saw the published *Adversaria*, a most useful book by Adrien Turnèbe <note>A famous French classical scholar</note>, whom we recently lost to the great expense of the literary world, a man of incomparable learning and skill. Let the diligent reader join the beginning of his 4th book with our notes. XYL.

<margin>ibid. verse 13.</margin> **45**] The sacred scriptures provide only 40, and the names are read slightly differently. See the end of Genesis 26. XYL.

<margin>page 60 verse 10.</margin> **astrology**] This passage is clearly mutilated. I have added an asterisk because I can hardly do anything else at present. A little later, **where the horses run**: in the Greek it is <term>into the hippodrome</term> <note>original: εἰς τὸν ἱππόδρομον; a racecourse</note>. In Genesis 35, it is written that she [Rachel] was buried "on the way." Otherwise, I know the Greek word signifies a "Circus," but it does not fit here. As for the word <term>Euphratha</term> <note>original: εὐφρανθᾶ</note> in our manuscript...

# ANNOTATIONS

[...] say, that in Josephus near the end of the 1st book of *Antiquities* it is read as *Ephrathann* <note>original Greek: κατὰ τὴν ἐφραθάννην</note>. The Hebrew word is correctly rendered in Greek as *Euphratha* <note>original Greek: εὐφραθᾶ</note>, and both here and elsewhere the Complutensian edition <note>The first multi-lingual printed edition of the entire Bible, published 1514–1517</note> reads it thus; and Zonaras <note>Joannes Zonaras, a 12th-century Byzantine chronicler</note> has nearly the same reading. **XYL.** <note>Wilhelm Xylander, the 16th-century humanist scholar</note>

*p. 61 v. 21.* [**Idaeans**] A scribe, to whom the name of the "Jews" <note>original Latin: Iudaeorum</note> was undoubtedly more familiar, wrote "Jews" <note>original Greek: Ἰουδαίων</note> instead of "Idaeans" <note>original Greek: Ἰδαίων</note> in both places; even the word "Dactyls" <note>meaning "fingers"</note> should have been enough to call him back from his error. Concerning the Curetes and the Idaean Dactyls <note>mythical archaic beings associated with the Mother Goddess and metalworking</note>, many have written much: Diodorus Siculus does so excellently in Book 5, Greek page 230, as does the Greek interpreter of Apollonius’s *Argonautica* with great antiquity in the annotations on Book 1, number 42, to name but a few. However, I will not find it burdensome to include here the words of Clement of Alexandria from the first book of the *Stromata*, which explain this passage: *But some say in a more mythical fashion that among those called the Idaean Dactyls, certain wise men were the first to exist, to whom is attributed the discovery of the so-called Ephesian letters and the discovery of musical rhythms. For this reason, the "dactyls" used by musicians have received this name. The Idaean Dactyls were Phrygians and barbarians. Herodorus records that Hercules, having become a seer and a natural philosopher, received the pillars of the world from Atlas, the Phrygian barbarian; the myth hints that he received the science of the heavens through learning.* <note>original Greek: τινὲς δὲ μυθικώτερον... μαθήσει διαδέχεσθαι</note> He is speaking there about the inventors of various arts and philosophy. Regarding the Curetes, those interested in pagan antiquity will also find something in the *Orphic Hymns*. A little earlier, I translated literally as "many-bodied" <note>original Latin: multicorporeos</note> those whom the author names *polysomatas* <note>original Greek: πολυσωμάτους</note>: for they are said not only to have had vast bodies, but to have been monstrous with a multiple abundance of limbs, like Aegaeon <note>a hundred-handed giant</note>, for example. Virgil's poems on this are well known. **XYL.**

*p. 64 v. 9.* [**in tremors**] I was moved to translate this passage thus by the etymology of the word *palmotikon* <note>original Greek: παλμωτικὸν, relating to twitching or throbbing</note>, as well as by the testimony of Suidas <note>a 10th-century Greek encyclopedia</note>, who (quoting from some author or other, for it is not clear to me) explains a "palmic omen" <note>original Greek: παλμικὸν οἰώνισμα</note> as a presage of what a leaping or tremor—for example, of the right eye—might foretell; and he says that Posidonius <note>a Stoic philosopher</note> commented on this matter. Indeed, in Theocritus as well, someone wishing for a good omen in his love says: *My right eye is leaping* <note>original Greek: ἅλλεται ὀφθαλμός μοι ὁ δεξιός</note>. Furthermore, what value should be attributed to such divinations you will best understand from St. Augustine in many places, especially in Book 2 of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 20 and the three following. And there indeed, the presages of leaping limbs are also mentioned. Therefore, I do not think those who translated *palmos* <note>original Greek: παλμόν</note> from Epiphanius’s *Panarion* as "tremor" or "concussion" are rightly criticized, especially since in that passage too, *palmos* is placed among those types of divination which do not seem to have much in common with the doctrine of the haruspices <note>diviners who read animal entrails</note> or the palpitation of organs. Furthermore, I have named Potiphar "prefect of the kitchen," or if you prefer, "chief of the cooks," following the Greek word *archimageiros* <note>original Greek: ἀρχιμάγειρος</note>. For the Hebrew word sounds differently, especially if we believe Onkelos the Chaldean paraphrast <note>the author of the Targum Onkelos, an Aramaic translation of the Torah</note> on chapter 39; who seems strongly to support,

# THE NOTES OF XYLANDER AND GOAR

Jeremiah calls Nebuzardan by this very title, who was sent by the Babylonian king to plunder Jerusalem; for that title—"master of cooks"—is not, in my opinion, very well suited to the duties of a high official. To be sure, Saint Jerome <note>A 4th-century scholar known for translating the Bible into Latin</note> translates it as "master of the soldiers" or "of the army"; and the Hebrew word **tabach** <note>original Hebrew: טבח</note> signifies "to slaughter," a craft in which we know even now that barbaric soldiers take great pleasure. **XYL.** <note>Wilhelm Xylander, the 16th-century translator</note>

*p. 66 v. 4.* [**In the marsh-grass**] This word **achin** <note>original Greek: ἄχιν; a loanword from Egyptian referring to river reeds or meadow grass</note> is also found in the Complutensian edition <note>The first printed polyglot Bible, produced in Spain in the early 1500s</note> in this story from Genesis 41. Others, including the Strasbourg edition (as the Aldine edition was not at hand), have read it as **on the bank** <note>original Greek: ἐν τῇ ὄχθῃ</note>. The scribe of Cedrenus noted in the margin that he found it thus in the manuscript, unless it was a mistake made through negligence: <margin>The word **achin** is found this way in the copy, though it was an error.</margin> Jerome translates it as *in marshy places*, as is still read now in the Complutensian book. For in his version of Job, chapter 8—where hypocrites are most elegantly compared to rushes and that kind of plant living in wet ground—the same word **Achu** <note>original Hebrew: אחו</note> is read and interpreted as a sedge-bed. In that same passage, the Seventy Interpreters <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> substituted **flowering rush** <note>original Greek: βούτομον</note>, a word I shall say nothing of here. Most understand it to be a meadow herb. And the cited passage from Job seems to demonstrate well enough that it is a plant of the type that grows in moist and even watery places, and immediately collapses on its own without liquid; thus it cannot be a sedge, since Columella <note>A Roman writer on agriculture</note> equates sedge with fern and teaches that it should be correctly rooted out in its own time as it grows everywhere (Book 2, Chapter 2). This description does not seem to fit the word *Achu*. Kimchi <note>David Kimchi, a medieval Jewish scholar and grammarian</note>, easily the most learned of the Hebrews, does not disagree with those who take it to mean a place (namely, a damp and grassy one). I have noted this to provide the reasoning for my version: for I do not believe the word **achin** belongs to the Seventy Interpreters. A little earlier, I translated **coarse-ground loaves** <note>original Greek: ἄρτους χονδρίτας</note> as "delicate breads," because I did not sufficiently understand that term. And indeed, neither the Hebrew grammarians regarding the Hebrew **chori** <note>original Hebrew: חורי</note>, nor the Greek grammarians regarding the Greek, are in much agreement. If you wish to interpret them as "wheat-breads" or "baked on hot stones" or in any other way, I do not object. **XYL.**

*p. 74 v. 1.* [**From the great**] I have expressed the meaning of the oracle in hexameter verses. In the Greek, everything is confused, and yet they do not seem to have been **unmetered.** **XYL.**

*p. 78 v. 21.* [**Without command**] The text says **as it was permitted** <note>original Greek: ὡς ἐπετράπη</note>, but it appears it should be read as **until** <note>original Greek: ἕως</note>. On page 75, verse 20, where it is written that Tharbis <note>In legendary history, an Ethiopian princess who fell in love with Moses</note>, captivated by the beauty of Moses, betrayed the city of Saba to the Egyptians, the following is noted in the margin: <margin>If because of Mosaic beauty barbarian cities were betrayed back then, what ought to happen now because of you, O most beautiful Emperor Isaac?</margin> He praises the beauty of Isaac, his emperor, as being worthy for cities to be surrendered to him by barbarians, just as they once were to Moses. Ah, such cleverness! <note>Xylander is likely being sarcastic about the excessive flattery directed at the Byzantine Emperor Isaac II Angelos</note> **XYL.**

*p. 79 v. 10.* [**Of the Corinthians**] This was a slip of memory: for these things are said not of the Corinthians but of the apostates Hymenaeus and Alexander in 1 Timothy 1. To be sure, that same Paul judged that the Corinthian man, who had entered into an incestuous marriage with his stepmother, should be handed over to Satan,

# ANNOTATIONS

*2 Corinthians 5.* Our author confused these passages due to a **lapse of memory** <note>original Greek: ἁμαρτήματι μνημονικῷ</note>. **XYL.** <note>Wilhelm Xylander, the 16th-century scholar and translator</note>

*p. 82 v. 9.* [**one god**] Those who wish to (and what sane person would not?) may read the verses of Sophocles—which are shamefully mutilated in our manuscript—in their entirety in Justin Martyr’s <note>A 2nd-century Christian apologist</note> *On Monarchy* <note>original Greek: περὶ μοναρχίας</note>, which our author alludes to, as well as in the *Exhortation* <note>original Greek: Paraenetico</note>, and in Clement’s *Exhortation* <note>original Greek: προτρεπτικῷ</note> and the 5th book of his *Miscellanies* <note>original Greek: Strōmat.</note>. The following passage is also mutilated, which I have noted by adding an asterisk. **Jannes and Jambres** (the ancient translator reads *Mambres*, as in 2 Timothy 3), the magicians of Pharaoh, are also mentioned by the blessed Augustine in his 119th letter to Januarius. **XYL.**

*p. 91 v. 12.* [**slaughter of God according to David**] This passage is clearly mutilated. The Davidic history follows in its own place, but I do not know what Moses had to do with it, unless perhaps the *Little Genesis* <note>likely a reference to the Book of Jubilees</note> contains something on the matter. For the sake of clarity, I have translated the word **thrausin** <note>original Greek: θραῦσιν</note>—which signifies a "rupture" or "shattering" and rather "attrition"—as **slaughter**. The passage concerns the slaughter of 14,700 Hebrews found at the end of Numbers 16. Furthermore, regarding what is written as "Mount Naban," it is read as **Nabau** <note>original Greek: Ναβαῦ</note> in the Complutensian Bible <note>The first printed polyglot Bible, published in Spain, 1514–1517</note> in Deuteronomy 32 and 34, and in Hebrew it is **Nebo**. Therefore, I have annotated **Nabau** in the margin. **XYL.**

*p. 99 v. 10.* [**manifest things**] **he gives to him clear things** <note>original Greek: δίδωσιν αὐτῷ δήλους</note>. I do not know if Cedrenus expressed it this way. The matter is manifest, and relying on the history, I replace "Elithabor" with **upon Tabor** <note>original Greek: ἐπὶ Θαβώρ; referring to Mount Tabor</note>. **XYL.**

*p. 100 v. 12.* [**barley cake**] **a barley loaf** <note>original Greek: μαγίδα κριθίνην</note>. I will not pronounce for certain what this might be. Truly, I think my interpretation is not far from either the Greek or the Hebrew itself: **a rolling loaf of barley bread** <note>original Hebrew: צלול לחם שעורים; from the story of Gideon in Judges 7</note>. Zonaras <note>A 12th-century Byzantine historian</note> has "barley cake." Josephus adds that it was **inedible to men because of its poor quality** <note>original Greek: ὑπ' εὐτελείας ἀνθρώποις ἄβρωτον</note>—that is, it would not be taken as food by men because of its worthlessness (Book 5, Chapter 8). Furthermore, regarding the number of the Midianites that follows, I have expressed it as I found it: 312,000. However, this exceeds not only all belief but all truth. Indeed, even if you read "thousands" instead of "myriads," making it 312,000 <note>Xylander seems to be debating the scale of units here</note>, it still seems larger than is right. In the Sacred Scripture, the army is not numbered, although the comparison to locusts indicates it was very large. Josephus, indeed, is the authority for the fact that 120,000 fell in the battle against the Midianites. **XYL.**

*p. 101 v. 7.* I omit explaining here what an **Ephod** is and what use it serves, since it is not obscure to those who have read the sacred scriptures diligently, and Cedrenus interprets the word in some fashion a little later in the history of Micah. Afterward, Orpheus is called **Bryosius**, a name entirely unknown to me; however, I ought not to change it. The hexameter verses cited from him are miserably jumbled, yet it is not difficult to write the first one thus:

-> **O King, son of Leto, far-shooting and mighty Phoebus.** <-
<note>original Greek: ὦναξ Λητοῦς υἱ' ἑκατηβόλε Φοῖβε κραταιέ</note>

After this, a complete verse begins with **all-seeing** <note>original Greek: πανδερκές</note>. Likewise from **O Sun** <note>original Greek: ἥλιε</note>, if you write **with golden** <note>original Greek: χρυσείοισιν</note>. There is also a meter consisting of **twelfth** <note>original Greek: δωδεκάτην</note> in some way, which is easy to assist. The last will be **with you speaking, but you**, etc. <note>original Greek: σοῦ φαμένοιο, σὲ δ'</note>. Truly, the rest are weak. It did not seem convenient at present to wish to emend these from my own wit. Many such things certainly exist scattered here and there in Clement and Justin.

<meta>This page continues the philological and historical commentary by Wilhelm Xylander (a 16th-century German humanist) and Jacques Goar (a 17th-century French Dominican) on a Byzantine text. Here, the commentators focus on correcting errors in the transmission of "Orphic" poetry and resolving discrepancies between the biblical accounts and the histories of Josephus regarding the period of the Judges and early Kings.</meta>

<page-num>762</page-num>

<header>XYLANDER AND GOAR</header>

Eusebius and others cite the *Orphic verses*. If anyone should encounter these elsewhere, let them correct the inferior versions from the better ones. Unless I am mistaken, I have brought no harm to the original meaning. The *Orphic verses* that follow these lines are also found in the *Suda* <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedic dictionary</note> under the entry "Orpheus," though they appear slightly differently there. Furthermore, the verses regarding human misery cited below are partly complete, partly mutilated, and partly corrupted. **XYL.** <note>Wilhelm Xylander</note>

p. 104 v. 2. *Tyre*] In the margin, the scribe noted *Tarsus* instead of *Tyre*, like this: <note>original Greek: πότε τὸ Ἴλιον ἐκτίσθη, ἡ Κύζικος καὶ ἡ Ταρσός</note> "when Ilion <note>Troy</note> was founded, along with Kyzikos and Tarsus." I thought this worth noting. **XYL.**

p. 108 v. 3. *seventh*] Unless perhaps the word "in the seventh" <note>original Greek: ἑβδόμῳ</note> should be read instead of "the seventh" <note>original Greek: ἕβδομος</note>, though I do not think so. But just as a certain *Samanes* is named above as the successor of *Samson*—a figure unknown to both *Josephus* <note>Titus Flavius Josephus, the 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian</note> and the Holy Scriptures—it is generally accepted that *Eli* <note>Latin: Elim</note> began to govern the Israelites after the death of Samson. *Josephus* also confirms this in Book 5, chapter 2 of his *Antiquities*. Now, the fact that the first book of *Kingdoms* is cited shortly thereafter—the book we today call the first book of *Samuel* <note>Latin: Samuelicum</note>, or "the first of the Kingdoms" <note>original Greek: ἡ πρώτη τῶν βασιλειῶν</note>—should not seem suspicious to the reader. These books were called the books of *Kingdoms* because they described, in order, the kingdom of *Saul*, the kingdom of *David*, the kingdom of *Solomon*, and so on. For this same reason, they are also called the books of *Kings*. Thus, *Justin Martyr* in his *Exhortation* cites the third book of Kings as the "third history of kingdoms" <note>original Greek: τρίτην βασιλειῶν ἱστορίαν</note>, and the blessed *Augustine* does so several times, referring to the "Scripture of Kingdoms," as in the second book of his *Retractations*, chapters 1 and 55. Likewise, he refers to the "Books of Kingdoms" in his 119th letter to Januarius, as do others. **XYL.**

p. 109 v. 12. *Josephus only two*] Either this passage is corrupt, as I suspect, or the manuscript of *Josephus* is, which records "4 months" <note>original Greek: ποιήσασα παρὰ τοῖς Παλαιστινοῖς μῆνας τέσσαρας; referring to the Ark of the Covenant's time among the Philistines</note>. The Book of *Judges* <note>The author likely means 1 Samuel 6:1</note> clearly states "7 months," with no variation in the reading. Furthermore, the sons of *Jeconiah* are not mentioned by name in the history; it only says they were men of *Beth-shemesh*. **XYL.**

p. 111 v. 11. "having passed through and having exercised self-control" <note>original Greek: διαπορευθεὶς καὶ ἐγκρατευσάμενος</note>; this is a faulty reading. What if you were to read "having been at a loss and not having exercised self-control" <note>original Greek: διαπορηθεὶς καὶ μὴ ἐγκρατευσάμενος</note>? From the Hebrew text and from *Josephus*, the meaning of the passage can be established even more clearly in *Antiquities*, Book 6, chapter 7. *Saul* had sent for *Samuel* as the enemies were attacking, and had summoned him. Samuel replied that he would come on the seventh day, commanding that sacrifices be prepared in the meantime, so they could attack the enemy after the offerings were made. Saul, meanwhile, as his men were slipping away and he was caught in great difficulties, saw that the seventh day had arrived but the prophet was not yet there. Not thinking he should wait any longer, he sacrificed to God himself—certainly doubting the prophet and not yielding to his command as he ought. By this act, he stirred up God’s indignation against himself. *Zonaras* <note>A 12th-century Byzantine historian</note> also wrote to this effect. **XYL.**

The author's meaning having been led astray to the opposite sense, the text is restored to its genuine reading as follows: *When Saul had waited a long time and the expectation had stretched further, and having endured the situation by drawing out the delays, he finally offered a sacrifice to the Lord.* **GOAR.** <note>Jacques Goar argues that the original text should be understood as Saul being patient for a long time before finally giving in to pressure, rather than being immediately impulsive.</note>

<header>ANNOTATIONS.</header>

p. 112 v. 4. [on the broadswords <note>original Greek: ῥομφαίαις</note>] Cedrenus <note>an 11th-century Byzantine historian</note> discusses the *romphaea* <note>a long, heavy sword used by Thracians and later by Byzantine guards</note> a little further down, in the passage where he lists the heroes of David. **XYL.**

ibid. [folded his hands] I have left this as a Hebraism <note>a Greek or Latin phrase that mimics Hebrew grammar or idiom</note> so as not to appear too bold in my editing. The meaning is this: he ordered him to stop handling the ark and the ephod <note>a ceremonial garment worn by high priests</note> for the purpose of prophesying, since there no longer seemed to be any doubt about the outcome of the battle. **XYL.**

ib. v. 9. [but all the land was dining] I have placed an asterisk at this passage because it is both faulty and mutilated. The Hebrew texts state that a multitude, gathered from all parts, followed Saul into a forest where honey was flowing along the ground; however, everyone abstained from it because of the king’s vow, except for Jonathan, who ate some without knowing of the oath, etc. **XYL.**

p. 113 v. 21. [with various musical instruments] "on the lyre, the psaltery, and the harp" <note>original Greek: ἐν κιννύρᾳ, ψαλτηρίῳ καὶ ναύλῃ</note>; because these instruments are unknown to us today, I preferred to use a general term. Josephus <note>a 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian</note> recorded in Book 7 of his *Antiquities* that the *kinnura* <note>lyre</note> consisted of ten strings and was struck with a plectrum <note>a pick</note>, while the *nabla* <note>harp</note> had twelve notes and was plucked with the fingers. You should know in passing that I have often given proper names not as they appear in Cedrenus, or even in the Septuagint <note>the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note>, but as they appear in the Hebrew and as they are commonly accepted, such as Michol, Ramatha, etc. **XYL.**

p. 115 v. 9. [where a statue] These details are from the second book of Samuel, chapter 18, so it is easily apparent that this passage is wonderfully mutilated: for the things that follow shortly after concerning David’s heroes are from chapter 23 of that same book, or 1 Chronicles 11. There is also this note in the margin: "the mighty men of David" <note>original Greek: οἱ δυνατοὶ τοῦ Δαβίδ</note>, meaning the powerful ones, or the brave, who held the highest offices under David because of their exceptional valor. For the rest, the reader should compare these passages with Cedrenus himself, adding those found in Josephus, Book 7, chapter 10. For it is not the purpose of our brief work to note every single discrepancy, nor is it so difficult that our labor should be greatly required. **XYL.**

p. 116 v. 1. Regarding the *romphaea* <note>broadsword</note>, the *spatha* <note>longsword</note>, and the *framea* <note>spear or javelin</note>, see Thomas Dempster <note>a Scottish scholar</note> in his *Roman Antiquities*. **GOAR.**

p. 119 v. 12. [Asa] This is clearly false: for Abijah defeated Jeroboam, as was reported shortly before from 2 Chronicles 13, and it is not written there that Asa was an imitator of Solomon. The remaining parts are also surprisingly confused; I did not wish to spend time clarifying them, since they exist in the Bible and in Josephus and are very well known. **XYL.**

p. 128 v. 6. [Zinaic wilderness] Cedrenus has "Mount Sinai," which is a clear error. **XYL.**

p. 131 v. 14. [and exhausted by flying] This passage in the Greek is mutilated and corrupted, and it troubled me until I found it intact in Josephus's *Antiquities*, Book 3, chapter 1, realizing it had been taken from there. **XYL.**

p. 132 v. 4. [Jethro the father-in-law] Cedrenus notes that he was also called the "relative" <note>original Greek: γαμβρόν</note> of Moses, and indeed it is clear that Moses's wife was the daughter of this Jothore or Jethro. The word *pentheros* <note>original Greek: πενθερός</note> not only signifies a father-in-law, but Herodotus also says that Croesus was the *gambros* <note>relative/brother-in-law</note> of Cyrus, having been joined in marriage to his sister Aryenis. In this same way, Eustathius <note>a 12th-century scholar and archbishop</note> describes Eurylochus...

He writes that **son-in-law** <note>original Greek: γαμβρόν — gambron</note> referred to Ulysses, specifically as the husband of his sister Ctimene. Likewise, in Sophocles' *Oedipus the King*, Oedipus calls **Creon his γαμβρόν**, even though Creon was the brother of Jocasta, making him both Oedipus's **uncle** <note>original Greek: θεῖος — theios</note> and **brother-in-law** <note>original Greek: γυναικάδελφος — gynaikadelphos</note>. Eustathius <note>a 12th-century scholar and archbishop</note> teaches the same thing regarding the *Iliad*, book 5, line 474, saying these are properly called **relatives by marriage** <note>original Greek: κηδεστάς — kēdestas</note>: "**alone with your relatives.**" In that same passage, he cites from a tragedy the phrase "**having married into fine relatives**," where the word **γαμβρός** <note>gambron</note> might signify a "father-in-law." I do not remember observing any other such example. The term **γαμβρός** seems to be derived not so much from "giving" a wife as from "leading" <note>marrying</note> one; from this comes the verb **to marry as a relative** <note>original Greek: ἐπιγαμβρεύειν — epigambrevein</note>, which appears even in the Gospel of Matthew, chapter 22 <note>referring to the Levirate law where a man marries his brother's widow</note>. **XYL.**

p. 132 v. 6. *Zipporah's angel*] In the Greek text, the following is found in the margin: <margin>Note that in the *Little Genesis* <note>The Book of Jubilees, an ancient Jewish religious work</note> it is recorded that the one who met Moses <note>referring to the "bridegroom of blood" incident in Exodus 4</note> was not an angel, but a certain many-named being: Samael, Belial, and Mastelma—who is Satan.</margin> **XYL.**

ib. v. 12. *also by deceptions*] So too says Augustine in his 7th letter to Marcellinus. **XYL.**

p. 137 v. 17. *until the next day*] Regarding the manna, these notes are in the margin: <margin>Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish philosopher</note>, interpreting the manna, says its quality was such that it transformed according to the imagination of the eater; while in itself it was like millet boiled in honey, it provided the taste of bread at one time, and meat at another—meat of either bird or land animal—and at other times vegetables or fish, according to each person's desire, so that the specific characteristic of every kind of food was accurately preserved in the taste of the eater.</margin> Furthermore, I will add the words of St. Augustine from his 118th letter to Januarius. He says it also fits this comparison that among the first people <note>the Israelites</note>, the manna tasted in the mouth of each person according to their own will, etc. Reviewing his own words in *Retractions*, book 2, chapter 20, he says: "it did not occur to me where this could be proven except from the Book of Wisdom, which the Jews do not receive into canonical authority; however, this could have happened for the faithful, but not for those murmuring against God, who surely would not have desired other foods if this manna had tasted like whatever they wanted." The passage in the Book of Wisdom is chapter 16, and it is known even from St. Jerome’s short preface that the book was believed to be by Philo the Hebrew. **XYL.**

p. 138 v. 8. *Osea*] Or *Auses*, **Ause** <note>the original name of Joshua, son of Nun</note>. See Numbers 13 and Eusebius's *Ecclesiastical History*, book 1, chapter 4. **XYL.**

ib. v. 17. I read **Scythopolis**, though the writing seems to have **Synthopolis**. I cannot think of what occasion would cause this city to be mentioned here. Strabo, in book 16, teaches that Scythopolis was a city on the borders of Galilee, where he relates how Pompey the Great took possession of Judea. The words of Stephanus <note>Stephanus of Byzantium, a 6th-century geographer</note> are highly corrupt; yet he records that it was once called **Baison** (perhaps **Bason** or **Basan**) by the barbarians. Pliny, in book 5, chapter 18, places it in the Decapolis near Judea, and says it was previously called Nysa, after the nurse of Bacchus <note>Dionysus</note>. In the 12th chapter of 2 Maccabees, mention is made of the "City of the Scythians"—this very one, no doubt—located 600 stadia from Jerusalem. Therefore, it was formerly Basan, the royal city of Og. See Josephus's *Antiquities*, book 4, chapter 5, and compare them with these: you will easily understand that Scythopolis is Basa—

p. 140 v. 25. *Leviticus*] And yet these things are not read in Leviticus, but at the end of Exodus. **XYL.**

p. 143 v. 6. *Clytaemnestra*] I would prefer *Hypermnestra*. However, I do not wish to pursue all such matters, as they are to be sought from the poets and the books written to aid in understanding them, and are therefore well-known in the schools. **XYL.**

p. 144 v. 17. *failing hands* <note>original Greek: χειρῶν ὀλλυμένων — cheirōn ollymenōn</note>] I have nothing to offer here; nor regarding the ox or Jupiter <note>or "Iove"</note>, which follows. **XYL.**

p. 147 v. 16. *Eglon the Zebulunite*] *Elon* <note>original: Elom</note>. I have corrected and supplemented this from the earlier narrative concerning the Judges, and from Judges 12. **XYL.**

p. 149 v. 10. *by whom the ark*] A most corrupt passage. The history is found in the first seven chapters of the First Book of Samuel. **XYL.**

p. 153 v. 11. This number, **234 myriads** <note>2,340,000</note>, agrees neither with what is said immediately after, nor with what is said not much later, nor indeed with the truth. Josephus, in *Antiquities* Book 7, Chapter 10, has the number of **Israelites as 90 myriads** <note>900,000</note> and the **Jews as 40 myriads** <note>400,000</note>. Zonaras records the number as 500,000 for the latter and 800,000 for the former, which is the <term>biblical sum</term>. Cedrenus often varies, I believe, through the fault of the scribes. Furthermore, I have retained an obvious **Hebraism** <note>a Hebrew idiom translated literally into Greek or Latin</note>, by which men who draw the sword are repeatedly mentioned in Scripture, referring to those who are of military age and strength. **XYL.**

p. 157 v. 14. *the Lord God*] In the margin, another reading is noted: <margin>to the name of the Lord God <note>original Greek: τῷ ὀνόματι κυρίου τοῦ θεοῦ — tō onomati kyriou tou theou</note></margin>, which amounts to the same thing. These words are taken from 1 Chronicles 28. Moreover, the name of **Solomon** is a <term>paronym</term> <note>a word derived from another</note> for "peace" <note>the Hebrew name Shlomo is related to Shalom, meaning peace</note>. **XYL.**

ibid. v. 19. *my poverty*] In the margin, the scribe had smeared <note>added a note</note>—unless perhaps Cedrenus was being witty—<margin>May such poverty also be mine, O divine David!</margin> This was spoken quite charmingly and appropriately to the history. Such was also the annotation above on folio 38 regarding the blessing of Manasseh and Ephraim: <margin>I think that because of this, it has been my lot to be unfortunate, just as it was for Manasseh.</margin> There are other such instances scattered about which I have deliberately omitted, certainly not defrauding the reader by bypassing them; for if the reader wishes, he may easily smear something more useful onto the margin himself. **XYL.**

p. 158 v. 1. *David was, however*] In the margin it says: <margin>missing from the manuscript</margin>. To me, however, it certainly does not seem that anything is missing here, so that I marvel at the "scrupulousness" of the scribe, who, while describing so many mutilated passages as if they were whole, only here finally sensed that something had fallen out. **XYL.**

ibid. v. 6. He wrote *from Sophir* <note>original Greek: ἐκ σωφείρ</note> erroneously for **from Ophir** <note>original Greek: ἐξ Ὠφείρ</note>, the two letters having been incorrectly separated in 1 Chronicles 29. **XYL.**

p. 159 v. 20. *nor should it be thought*] At the margin it is annotated: <margin>Note this; it is a remarkable thing against the now foolish and senseless opinion of the common people. And see what he says.</margin> The sense is that this passage should be observed because it addresses the opinion of the unrefined and ignorant men—of whom there is a great multitude—concerning this...
