<header>ANNOTATIONS OF XYLANDER AND GOAR</header>

...matter, foolish and imprudent, to be refuted. I did not pass over this annotation, as it is true: for indeed, if I have any judgment, the passage is worthy of notice, however much Cedrenus may have taken these things from elsewhere. **XYL.**

**p. 165 v. 19. The Tyrian]** An error for **The Syrian** <note>original Greek: ὁ Σύριος — ho Syrios</note>: for Stephanus <note>Stephanus of Byzantium, a 6th-century geographer</note> testifies that the word for a native of the island of Syros is **Syrios**, unless the manuscript is deceptive; which I do not think at all, since it is read thus in Diogenes Laertius, and Homer in the *Odyssey* (Book 15, verse 401) calls the island of Syros "Syria," with Eustathius and the commentator on Dionysius approving Strabo’s opinion there. The Romans call Pherecydes "the Syrian" <note>original Latin: Syrum</note>, as Cicero does in the first book of the *Tusculan Disputations*, where he says he lived during the reign of Servius Tullius, certainly no fewer than 400 years after Solomon. Syros is one of the Cyclades islands, surrounded by Delos, Rhenaea, and Mykonos. See Strabo toward the end of the tenth book. There Pherecydes is called **The Babian** <note>original Greek: ὁ Βάβιος — ho Babios, referring to his father Babys</note>, as also in Suidas: in Eustathius’s commentary on the cited passage of Homer he is called **Babylonian**, and in Laertius (Book 1, in the biography of Pherecydes) he is called **son of Badys** <note>original Greek: βάδυος — badyos</note>, so that it appears Badys was his father, and the rest of the names should be corrected from this. It has commonly prevailed that he originated from Syria, that noble region of Asia by the Euphrates. Blessed Augustine increased this opinion by calling him an Assyrian in his third letter to Volusianus, and even twisting Virgil’s mention of "Assyrian balsam" <note>original Latin: amomum</note> from the *Pollio* <note>Virgil's Fourth Eclogue</note> to support his discussion on the immortality of the soul. For in the third book of *Against the Academics*, he calls the same man a Syrian. **XYL.**

**p. 180 v. 12. and he rested]** <note>original Latin: et requievit</note> I have marked this place with an asterisk because it is utterly mutilated. I refer these words to Elijah hiding in the cave of Mount Horeb, which some have believed was the same refuge used by Moses. **XYL.**

**p. 182 v. 21. who was third from the king]** <term>Tristaten <note>original Greek: τριστάτην — a term indicating a high-ranking officer or "third man"</note></term>. <term>Shalish <note>original Hebrew: שליש — literally "third," often referring to an officer in a three-man chariot</note></term>: scholars of Hebrew interpret it thus, for the name is derived from the number three. Josephus, in *Antiquities* (Book 9, Chapter 3), translated it as **commander of the third division** <note>original Greek: τρίτης μοίρας ἡγεμόνα — tritēs moiras hēgemona</note>, one placed in charge of a third part of the troops. In Suidas, a **tristates** is a bodyguard or royal attendant who holds three spears in his hand. **XYL.** Xylander speaks improperly and incompletely here. More properly and fully: the king sent a *triarius* (or a member of a triumvirate) on whom he leaned. Sanctius, in his commentary on the Book of Kings, interprets **tristaten** as a *triarius* <note>traditionally the third line of a Roman legion, but here used for a high-ranking attendant</note>, one of three ministers on whom the king was accustomed to lean in turns while standing or walking. **GOAR.**

**p. 184 v. 11. Namesius]** <note>The biblical Nimshi</note> Thus it is in the Bibles. But our manuscript also has the years of the kings noted very differently than the truth of Holy Scripture would allow. Let the histories themselves be read, which are both mutilated here and presented in a poor order, sometimes merely noted and sometimes repeated. **XYL.**

**p. 198 v. 14. when it has rotted]** <note>original Latin: cum computruerit</note> I think it is clear to anyone that the things discussed regarding Judea and the city of Jerusalem are neither true nor even brought up in their proper place. Here, however, I have followed Jerome’s version, since my book had **calculated together** <note>original Greek: συμψηφισθείς — sympsēphistheis</note>, the Complutensian edition at Jeremiah has **consumed** <note>original Greek: συμφιθείς — symphitheis</note>, and the Strasbourg edition has **rubbed away** <note>original Greek: συμψησθείς — sympsēstheis</note>. I could not easily say what these two [latter] words mean; and the passage seems least of all to allow us to translate them as "lamented" or "mourned," even though Hesychius noted that **weeping** <note>original Greek: ψιζομένην — psizomenēn</note> is the same as **crying** <note>original Greek: κλαίουσαν — klaiousan</note>, and **drops** <note>original Greek: ψιάδες — psiades</note> in Homer refer to dripp—

<header>ANNOTATIONS.</header>

...[bloody drops] they might be, the bloody tears of Jupiter <note>Original Latin: sanguineae Iovis lacrymae; Zeus in the *Iliad* Book 16, verse 459, weeps tears of blood for his son Sarpedon</note>, *Iliad* Book 16, line 459. The word *psō* <note>Original Greek: ψῶ</note> signifies "to thin out" <note>Original Greek: λεπτύνω — leptynō</note>, as the Greeks record, that is, to attenuate. The Hebrew *sehub* <note>Original Hebrew: סחוב</note> indicates that something is to be dragged or snatched and thrown away, with no meaning of rot at all; thus I cannot guess what Jerome followed <note>Referring to the Vulgate translation</note>, or how it should be read in the Greek version. For the word used by our Cedrenus is entirely foreign. Let the more skilled look into it. **XYL.**

**p. 199 v. 20. into the abyss]** *borboron* <note>Original Greek: βόρβορον</note>, a word which signifies filth or mire. He was indeed cast into a pit, filled not with water but with mire, as in *Jeremiah* 38. **XYL.**

**p. 214 v. 7. Minos of Crete, the son]** In the margin, "of Europa" <note>Original Greek: τῆς Εὐρώπης — tēs Eurōpēs</note> was marked, indicating it should be inserted after "son." I believe it was originally written "the son of Zeus" <note>Original Greek: ὁ Διός — ho Dios</note>, not just "son" <note>Original Greek: υἱός — huios</note>. Perhaps "Europa" was also added. The story is well known. **XYL.** You may easily restore the inverted order of the phrase by omitting Xylander's conjectures in this way: **Minos, the son of Europa, reigned over Crete.** **GOAR.**

**Ibid. v. 11.** Regarding what I have translated as "scribe," the Greek has *notarios* <note>Original Greek: νοτάριος</note>, a notary. And after *lōron* <note>Original Greek: λῶρον</note>, "strap," just as elsewhere he uses *koubiklon* <note>Original Greek: κουβίκλον</note> for "bedroom" <note>Original Latin: cubiculum</note>. He said *doulidas* <note>Original Greek: δουλίδας</note> for "female slaves," imitating the word *therapainidas* <note>Original Greek: θεραπαινίδας — maidservants</note>. A little further down he mentions a "solemn festival," *kosmikēn* <note>Original Greek: κοσμικήν — worldly or public</note>, though I do not know what he meant by that. **XYL.**

**p. 217 v. 20.** I translated *eustolon* <note>Original Greek: εὔστολον</note> as "slender" <note>Original Latin: gracilem</note>, since nothing else occurred to me, and it is not a question of clothing here. For it is known even from Terence that slenderness in women was praised among the ancients. **XYL.** The word *eustolon* has nothing in common with the slenderness of women praised in antiquity; it refers to someone who is well-groomed and elegant in their dress. **GOAR.**

**p. 220 v. 8.** It is not entirely clear what kind of game the "Table of Palamedes" <note>Palamedes was a mythical Greek hero credited with inventing dice to entertain the army during the Trojan War</note> was. Our author calls it *taula* <note>Original Greek: ταύλαν</note>, "table" or "board," which others call *abakion* <note>Original Greek: ἀβάκιον</note>, "a small table." It is clear from Eustathius <note>A 12th-century scholar and archbishop</note> in his commentary on the first book of the *Odyssey* (line 107) that the verb *taulizein* <note>Original Greek: ταυλίζειν</note> was used for playing dice on such a board. In Suidas, under the entry *tabla* <note>Original Greek: τάβλα</note>, you will find nearly the same information as Cedrenus has here. It seems sufficiently clear that it was a game of pebbles or dice <note>Original Greek: πεσσῶν — pessōn</note>, which were cast through a "little tower" <note>Original Latin: turricula; a device to prevent cheating in dice games</note> into a hollowed tray or board placed beneath, and the various positions of the lines or spaces created the different conditions of the game. Eustathius teaches in the place I mentioned that there were five distinct lines; see him also on *Iliad* Book 2, line 300, and Pollux, Book 9. I translated it as "dice" <note>Original Latin: talos</note>, because I had no other word, though I am well aware that *astragalos* <note>knucklebone</note>, *kybos* <note>cube/die</note>, and *pessos* <note>gaming piece</note> were different things. But I have also observed that the translator of Euripides' *Orestes* indiscriminately attributes the invention of the *kybos* and *petteia* <note>board games</note> to Palamedes. And yet, why should I not translate it as "dice" [*talos*], since Horace <note>Original Latin: Flaccus</note>, the most excellent of poets, supports me? In his *Satires* (2.7), the gout-ridden scoundrel Volanerius kept a hired man at a daily wage to pick up and cast the dice <note>Original Latin: talos</note> into the tower <note>Original Latin: pyrgum</note> for him. Martial translates this *pyrgus* as "little tower" [*turricula*], and *pessous* as "dice" [*talos*], which Cedrenus seems to understand by the word *psēphobolon* <note>Original Greek: ψηφόβολον — pebble-thrower</note>. Suidas uses the word *psēphibolon*. I understand *kokkia* <note>Original Greek: κοκκία</note> as the marks [pips] on the dice; and Suidas has "seven grains" <note>Original Greek: ἑπτὰ κοκκία — hepta kokkia</note>. I myself have seen a board divided into black and white squares, in the manner of a **chessboard**; and hanging above it a funnel, through which the cubes <note>Original German: *die würffel* — the dice</note> were dropped in...

<header>ANNOTATIONS BY XYLANDER AND GOAR</header>

...played on a game board or with a dice box <note>Original Latin: abacum vel fritillum</note>. Cedrenus uses the term *meteōrismon* <note>Original Greek: μετεωρισμόν — a state of being raised up or distracted</note>, whereas Suidas <note>A 10th-century Greek encyclopedist</note> uses the term *diagōgēn* <note>Original Greek: διαγωγήν — a pastime or way of life</note>, which is a more elegant and fitting word. Indeed, I hardly think a reputable writer would use *meteōrismon* in this sense elsewhere. The passage from Martial, which I almost forgot to include, is found in the *Apophoreta* <note>A collection of poems intended as "party favors"</note>, in the couplet from Book 14, 16. **XYL.** Suidas, along with the Greco-Barbaric glosses <note>Medieval Greek dictionaries</note>, writes it as *tablan* <note>Original Greek: τάβλαν</note>; this is the name of a game, the "table" <note>Original Latin: tabula</note>, upon which such games are played. **GOAR.**

**p. 220 v. 11. points]** <note>Original Greek: κάσους — kasous; the spaces on a game board</note> Isaac Porphyrogenitus <note>A Byzantine scholar and prince</note> substitutes "entrenchments" <note>Original Greek: χαρακώματα — charakōmata</note> in his *Additions to Homer*. Discussing the game invented by Palamedes <note>A mythological Greek hero credited with inventing dice and letters during the siege of Troy</note>, he says: "He was the first to have discovered how to play *taulizein*, that is, to play at dice." And further down: "He defined the *taula* <note>Original Greek: ταύλαν — the board</note> or the game-table as the earthly world; and the twelve points or 'entrenchments' <note>Original Greek: δώδεκα κάσους ἤτοι τὰ χαρακώματα</note> as the number of the zodiac." **GOAR.**

**Ibid. a dice-thrower]** <note>Original Greek: ψηφοβόλον — psēphobolon</note> A horn or a small basin from which the dice first fall into a tower or channel, and from the tower onto the board. **GOAR.**

**Ibid. v. 12. pieces]** <note>Original Greek: κοκκία — kokkia; literally "grains" or "pips"</note> These are the dice themselves, or rather the gaming-tokens <note>Original Latin: tesserae</note>. There were seven of them, which entered various small hollows in the board. These manifested various conjunctions of the planets and the stars of the zodiac, and consequently revealed the favorable or unfavorable fate of one's life and the game, according to the rules of the astrologers. **GOAR.**

**Ibid. v. 14.** Regarding the Greek letters, there is another place more suitable for commentary. Otherwise, several subsequent passages are mutilated, which I have therefore marked with an asterisk. **XYL.**

**Ibid. v. 19. a man of Chios]** <note>Original Greek: χῖος — Chios</note> This is incorrectly read for "a man of Ceos" <note>Original Greek: Κεῖος — Keios</note>. At the very least, the author was in error; for it is established from approved authors that he was a native of Iulis, a city on the island of Ceos. This island is the first one after Helena as you head toward Asia from Attica. I would not have noted the error had I not known it was common in other books as well. **XYL.**

**p. 223 v. 5. Dictys]** In the margin: <margin>Dictys, from whom Homer took the starting point and composed the *Iliad*, 109 years after the fall of Troy.</margin> While I do not deny that Dictys and even Dares <note>Legendary historians of the Trojan War who were said to have been eyewitnesses</note> composed a history of the Trojan War, I will never allow myself to be persuaded that the little books circulated today under those titles are genuine, worthy of trust, or even worth reading. **XYL.**

**p. 234 v. 20. of those who love]** <note>Original Greek: ἀγαπώντων — agapōntōn</note> To *agapan* is to love. Therefore, I suspect the original word was "those who hurry" <note>Original Greek: ἐπειγόντων — epeigontōn</note> or something similar. The passage is corrupted, though the history or story is very well known. I have rendered the oracle into iambic trimeter verses <note>A common meter for Greek drama and oracles</note>, pursuing the general meaning. **XYL.**

**p. 236 v. 23. Diabena]** I know that Adiabena <note>An ancient kingdom in Upper Mesopotamia</note> is a region lying between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers. This is what Stephanus calls it, as does Eustathius in his commentary on Dionysius, and elsewhere. Regarding this, one should consult Ammianus Marcellinus, Book 23. In Strabo, Book 11, near the end, it is read as *Diabēnē* <note>Original Greek: διαβηνή</note>, but I think this is an error, since even the summary of his work has *Adibēnē* <note>Original Greek: ἀδιβηνήν</note>. But more on this elsewhere. Regarding Scythopolis <note>A city in modern-day Israel, part of the Decapolis</note>, see the notes above. As for what follows, I did not wish to make any notes, since (to pass over many other writers on these matters) Dionysius of Halicarnassensis in his book...

<header>ANNOTATIONS.</header>

...in the first book of the *Roman Antiquities*, he most extensively pursued the history of Aeneas <note>Referring to the historian Dionysius of Halicarnassus, who wrote about the mythical founder of Rome</note>. **XYL.**

**p. 239 v. 8.** The manuscript has the word *ene* <note>Original Greek: ἕνη — meaning the "old" day</note> with a double *n*. Eustathius <note>A 12th-century Byzantine scholar and archbishop</note> noted that there were some who wrote it with a double *n*, although he prefers the single *n*. But he also indicates that some added an "h" sound <note>Original Latin: aspirari — breath mark/aspiration</note> to the *e*, as in the verse from the *Odyssey* (Book 19, line 307): "as one month wanes and the next begins" <note>Original Greek: τοῦ μὲν φθίνοντος μηνός, τοῦ δ' ἱσταμένοιο</note>, which also appears in Book 14. Plutarch, in his life of Solon, indicates that the term "the old and the new" <note>Original Greek: ἕνην καὶ νέαν — enēn kai nean</note> was used to mark the final day of the month, when the moon meets the sun. It is "old" with respect to the month passing (for *enon* <note>Original Greek: ἑνόv</note> means "the old") and "new" with respect to the month beginning. See also Suidas and others. A verse by Aristophanes exists in *The Clouds*: "immediately after this is the old and the new." One can see there what the commentator <note>Original Latin: scholiastes</note> has to say. The grammarians interpret this line from Hesiod as referring to that day: "nor put it off until tomorrow or the day after" <note>Original Greek: μήτ’ ἀναβάλλεσθαι ἔς τ’ αὔριον ἔς τ’ ἔννηφιν</note>. **XYL.**

**p. 244 v. 4. *parapyleōna*]** <note>Original Greek: παραπυλεῶνα — a side gate or passage</note> This was previously called a *parapylion*. Polybius seems to have used the term *rhinopylēn* <note>Original Greek: ῥινοπύλην — literally "nose-gate"</note> for a similar thing. I did not want to change anything, otherwise I would have translated it as "his side-gate" or "pavilion." However, I am surprised that our author's version of the story varies from the accepted Book of Judith. **XYL.**

**ibid. *parapyliou*]** <note>Original Greek: παραπυλίου — a postern or side-entrance</note> *The context itself warns us that a back door or a more private gate is to be understood by this word. I pass over the sequence of the narrative, which differs from our own.* **GOAR.**

**p. 245 v. 1. *Kētaious*]** <note>Original Greek: Κηταίους — a mysterious people mentioned by Homer</note> All these entries are so corrupted that in trying to correct them, I fear we might "waste our oil and labor" <note>An ancient idiom meaning to work in vain</note>. These things can be sought elsewhere. Certainly, this seems to signify that the Mysians <note>A people from northwest Asia Minor</note> crossed into Italy. For Telephus was a Mysian. Homer himself calls the Mysians *Kēteioi* in the 11th book of the *Odyssey*, speaking of Eurypylus, the son of Telephus: "and many Keteian comrades were killed around him" <note>Original Greek: πολλοὶ d' ἀμφ' αὐτὸν ἑταῖροι Κήτειοι κτείνοντο</note>, as Eustathius also does not conceal. **XYL.**

**p. 257 v. 23. *month from the god*]** This is written in the margin: <margin>I found in other historians that because they wept in that very month for those who died in the war, they called the month *Mortium*; for among them, *mortem* is the name for death.</margin> It is strange that he could conceal the name of the author of such a "sacred" etymology. As for the description of the Circus <note>The Roman stadium for chariot racing</note> which follows, I do not follow it; it tastes of the Greek absurdities of later times. Regarding the four kinds or colors of the charioteers <note>The racing factions: Blue, Green, Red, and White</note>, the matter is well known from Latin writers as to what it was and when it was established. Therefore, I have noted nothing. I have departed freely from the faulty reading whenever it suited the facts. **XYL.**

**p. 258 v. 15. *pelma*]** The *pelma* <note>Original Greek: πέλμα — literally "sole"</note> of the entire Circus is the *area* or *arena*. **GOAR.**

**ibid. v. 16. *Euripon*]** <note>Original Greek: Εὔριπον — a channel or trench</note> Thomas Dempster, in his *Roman Antiquities* (5.4), wrote based on Dionysius that this trench surrounded the floor and arena of the Circus to a depth and width of ten feet to receive water for the staging of naval battles <note>Original Latin: naumachiae</note>. **GOAR.**

**ibid. v. 17. *kampton*]** <note>Original Greek: καμπτόν — the turn</note> Which is also called a *kamptēr*, the *turn* around the goal post <note>Original Latin: metam</note>. **GOAR.**

**ibid. *sphendonē*]** <note>Original Greek: σφενδόνη — literally "slingshot"</note> The *carceres* <note>Starting gates</note> of the circus, from which they are released as if from a sling. Georgius Cedrenus, Volume II.

The previous page discussed ancient Greek calendar terms and the works of Dionysius of Halicarnassus; this page shifts focus to the Roman Circus, the names of the racing factions, and the etymology of the month of February.</meta>

<page-num>770</page-num>
<header>OF XYLANDER AND GOAR</header>

...the stone, from which those competing in the race with horses and chariots burst forth; the author very frequently calls this a "sling" <note>original: σφενδόνην — *sphendonēn*; a term used for the curved end of the hippodrome</note>. **GOAR.**

**p. 258 v. 19.** By the word "air" <note>original: ἀέρος — *aeros*</note> I understand a *veil* or awning, which was used to ward off the harms of inclement weather so that the people might stand in a healthier environment; this was the covering of the *Circus*. For what could more suitably represent the sky in the Circus than a veil of this kind? My basis for this is that even the larger and wider *veil* placed over the sacred elements in the liturgy of Chrysostom and in the explanations of Simeon of Thessalonica, Cabasilas, Germanus, and others is not infrequently called "air" <note>original: ἀὴρ — *aēr*</note>; and when it is spread out, the priest exclaims, "*His glory covered the heavens, and the earth is full of his praise.*" Therefore, the term was transferred from sacred use to the Circus, and the author called its veil, which represents the sky, "air." Regarding the veils of theaters, the previously cited Dempster has written abundantly. **GOAR.**

**ib. v. 22.** "Of the Present" <note>original: Πρεσέντου — *Presentou*</note>] The Greeks heard the master called *in Praesenti* <note>meaning "in the [Emperor's] presence"</note>, who was the leader of the guards constantly *present* with the emperor (who were also called *praesentiales*); from this, they even wanted the Green color, which lasts longer and is easily visible to the eyes, to be called "from the present" <note>original: ἀπὸ τοῦ πρεσέντου — *apo tou presentou*</note>, that is, "green" <note>original: πράσινον — *prasinon*</note>—though this is a very forced etymology. **GOAR.**

**ib. v. 24.** "The Blue from Venice" <note>original: τὸ Βένετον ἀπὸ τῆς Βενετίας — *to Beneton apo tēs Benetias*</note>] He would have successfully found the root of the word, if only the *Venetus* color and its name did not predate the city of *Venice* by several centuries. **GOAR.**

**p. 260 v. 2.** *marked with the letter a*] "from uncoined metal" <note>original: ἀπὸ ἀσημείου — *apo asēmeiou*</note>. I had guessed it was written "from the mark A" <note>original: ἀπὸ Α σημείου — *apo A sēmeiou*</note>, but I would easily change my mind if someone else could explain the passage differently. For I know that Varro says the *as* <note>a Roman coin</note> is named from "bronze" <note>Latin: *aes*</note>. **XYL.** This passage will be settled according to Xylander’s wish, if it is nowhere corrupted and receives an easy interpretation: *He was the first to bestow silver and bronze asses upon the Romans.* For "unmarked" <note>original: ἄσημον — *asēmon*</note> refers to uncoined silver, and as in the present case, when joined to a discussion of money, it indicates the raw material. The author calls it "marked" <note>original: ἐπίσημον — *episēmon*</note> again later on page 178. This latter term refers to what is *struck* and *stamped*, while the former properly refers to *unworked* metal; although in common usage, the two words are sometimes used interchangeably. **GOAR.**

**p. 263 v. 13.** *that the kingdom was being sought by him*] "as one meditating a rebellion" <note>original: ὡς ἀνταρσίαν μελετῶντος — *hōs antarsian meletōntos*</note>. I suspected "absolute power" <note>original: αὐταρχίαν — *autarchian*</note> was written. But in other places too, he expressed the seeking of tyranny in this way. The passage is corrupted, and the narrative is repeated from I know not where. It is indeed far removed from the accepted history of those times. "Originating from the faction of the Gauls" <note>original: τοῦ μέρους τῶν Γάλλων καταγόμενος — *tou merous tōn Gallōn katagomenos*</note>; I do not know what that "originating" means. **XYL.** He will know if he translates it: it was someone drawing his origin from the regions of the Gauls, or someone led away from the opposing side of the Gauls and inclined toward them by affection. **GOAR.**

**p. 264 v. 7.** In the margin it is written: <margin>And I found the things concerning this month differently in other histories, which I cannot write down because of their endlessness. This alone will suffice: that the Romans call great cold *phempre*. They therefore called this month February <note>original: Φεβρουάριον — *Phebrouarion*</note> as it is the coldest.</margin> Thus he wrote. It is not worth the effort to bring other things here from elsewhere. **XYL.** The author will bring forth a different reason from this one later on page 168 C. **GOAR.**

<header>ANNOTATIONS.</header>

**p. 269 v. 23. Seres]** Where these people were and what they were like, we shall discuss elsewhere. <margin>In the margin it read: "I do not know who they are. It is a wonder if any such people exist anywhere." <note>original: οὐκ οἶδα τίνες εἰσί. θαυμαστὸν δὲ εἴ τινές που τοιοῦτοί εἰσίν.</note></margin> As for what the **Cabes** are on p. 270 v. 9, I do not know, unless perhaps it is the name of a man-eating Indian tribe. Nor do I know of the **Agelaeos** by that specific proper name. History also suggests that something regarding a certain "marsh" has fallen out of the text before these words on p. 271 v. 2. **XYL.**

**p. 277 v. 9. animalia]** The Greek is "small figures" <note>original: ζῴδια — *zōdia*</note>, which I suspect he intended to be understood as the signs of the Zodiac. Otherwise, I would rather the reader seek out what pertains to this from Diogenes Laertius, Plutarch’s *Opinions of the Philosophers*, Cicero, and others, than for me to be troublesome to him by annotating those things here. Indeed, I have not even undertaken to correct all the errors here, such as those regarding the shape of the earth—"its shape is fluid, round, snowy, and similar to a stone" <note>original: τὸ σχῆμα αὐτῆς ὑγρὸν στρογγύλον χιονῶδες λίθῳ παραπλήσιον</note> on p. 276 v. 21—which I have marked with an asterisk. The verses concerning Anaxagoras are from Diogenes Laertius, but the latter couplet has been omitted. Not far from the end of the *Phaedo*, Plato depicts Socrates complaining about him <note>Anaxagoras</note> for not holding to his opinion regarding the Mind. But these matters belong elsewhere. The passage from Plato which Cedrenus cites from the *Laws* is found two pages from the beginning of the fourth book of the *Laws* (p. 716 in the Stephanus edition). The passage concerning the "gods of gods" and the progeny of Heaven is in the *Timaeus*. The passage about Jupiter driving a "winged chariot" is on the fourth page of the *Phaedrus*. **XYL.**

**p. 291 v. 8. He favored Hyrcanus]** Anyone can see that these things hold together very poorly. I am satisfied to refer the reader to Josephus for study. See Book 14 of the *Antiquities* from the beginning. **XYL.**

**p. 294 v. 18. and of December]** It is exactly so in the Greek, and the months are counted in such a way on both sides that it cannot be seen as an error. It is well known today that six Nones are assigned not to December but to October; an opinion which is also written out below. **A. D.** signifies "before the day" <note>original: *ante diem*</note>. Even the Greeks, imitating this, say "three days before," "one day before," etc. <note>original: πρὸ τριῶν, πρὸ μιᾶς</note>; about which I will speak elsewhere. I have also left the etymologies of our author in the balance; if I had wished to pursue them, either by confirming or refuting them, I would have had to be more prolific, and at times would have needed to be an Oedipus <note>A solver of riddles</note>. **XYL.**

**p. 296 v. 17. Tenes]** In the Greek it is "Teles" <note>original: τέλης</note>. But I have followed the historical account. The affairs of Bellerophon and Hippolytus are too well known for anything to be annotated regarding them. However, Tenes, from whom the island of Tenedos takes its name, is said to have been the son of Cycnus and the grandson of Neptune. He refused to comply with his stepmother when she propositioned him for an illicit affair; therefore, having been exposed in a chest in the sea by his father (who falsely believed the stepmother's accusation), he was carried unharmed to the island of Leucophrys. He gave the island its name and reigned there. This account is found in Tzetzes’ commentary on Lycophron, and in Eustathius’ commentary on the *Iliad* (Book 1, 38). Eustathius shows that this stepmother, called Philonome by some, is called Polyboea by others, even in his commentary on Dionysius. And so it is also found in the Scholiast of Homer at the cited passage. Diodorus Siculus also mentions him at the end of Book 5, but with the stepmother's name omitted. Our author calls her Alphesiboea. If this writing is correct, there is nothing absurd about it; for as to his statement that Peleus abstained from Astydamea, Pindar in the *Nemean Odes* calls her Hippolyta the daughter of Cretheus.

p. 297 v. 14. ***kamelyka***] Modern writers write this as *kamelaukia* <note>original: καμηλαύχια</note>, and they give this name to small caps made of camel hair that cling only to the crown of the head and "flow down toward the neck" <note>original: καὶ πρὸς αὐχένα — *kai pros auchena*</note>. In Greek it might be said to come from 'driving away the heat'" <note>original: παρὰ τὸ καῦμα ἐλαύνειν — *para to kauma elaunein*</note>. GOAR.

ib. v. 20. Instead of "not spaces" <note>original: οὐ σπάτια — *ou spatia*</note>, I have written "those spaces" <note>original: οὓς σπάτια — *hous spatia*</note>. However, what **misos** <note>original: μίσος</note> means in this passage, I do not know. "Misthos" <note>original: μισθός</note> means a reward, which is a word closer to **prize** <note>original: τῷ ἄθλῳ — *tō athlō*</note>. Although in spectacles and contests of this kind, there was also the use of "missiles" <note>objects thrown as gifts to a crowd</note>, which were thrown into the crowd like donations. The custom of throwing cloths <note>mappae</note> is mentioned by Suetonius in chapter 22 of his life of *Nero* and in various places in Martial; Tertullian also mentions it elsewhere and as a kind of proverb at the end of his book *Against the Valentinians*. XYL. Xylander admits he does not know what "misos" means here; he should have also admitted he did not understand "athlon." Now, "athlon" <note>original: ἆθλον</note> is a contest. Dempster calls it an "exercise" in *Roman Antiquities* 5.4. Specifically, it was called a "commission" <note>Latin: *commissio*</note> in technical language. Suetonius says in his life of *Augustus*, chapter 89: "he warned the praetors not to allow their names to become worn out by commissions"; from this comes "to commit" <note>Latin: *committere*</note> meaning to fight, to contend, etc., examples of which are beyond number. Therefore, the **misos** <note>original: μίσος</note> of those competing in the Circus is a "commission," a word written "instead of prize" <note>original: ἀντὶ τοῦ ἄθλου — *anti tou athlou*</note>. GOAR.

p. 298 v. 2. ***repurgamenta*** <note>refuse or elemental waste</note>] He calls elemental and material things "matter" <note>original: ὕλην — *hylēn*</note>. "Skubalon" <note>original: σκύβαλον</note> is excrement, which is considered worthless and filthy so as to be cast away, just as Saint Paul calls human and fleeting things in his letter to the Philippians; and in Phocylides, the "table-scraps" <note>original: σκυβαλίσματα τραπέζης — *skybalismata trapezēs*</note> are what are given to flatterers and those living off another's plate. The "oracle" mentioned here has been lost. As for what **bixilationes** are, I do not know: I know of "bigae" <note>two-horse chariots</note> and "bigarii" <note>charioteers</note>, which I would think he was talking about, were it not for the fact that he mentions them separately soon after. I have boldly rendered "bixila" <note>original: βίξιλα</note> as "vexilla" <note>military banners or standards</note>, as the description supports it. Anyone can see how great Cedrenus's knowledge of Roman antiquity was. I could have translated "bixilationes" as "vexillationes" <note>military detachments named after their standards</note>, but I leave it be. XYL. Vexillationes are "squadrons of Roman horsemen." The *Register of Offices* <note>Latin: *Notitia Imperii*</note> says the same. GOAR.

ib. v. 9. ***the one among the Greeks*** <note>original: ἡ παρ' Ἕλλησιν — *hē par’ Hellēsin*</note>] Xylander is as overly literal as he is ridiculous: the Greeks call a fired brick a "plinthos" <note>original: πλίνθον</note>. Who doesn't know this? But what does a Greek "plinthos" or a Latin "fired brick" have to do with Cedrenus's point? Leaving Xylander's bricks behind, Pancirollus learnedly explains **laterculum** <note>literally "little brick," but used to mean an administrative register</note> in the *Notitia Imperii*, chapter 92. There was a treasury in the Temple of Saturn where the decrees of the plebs and the senate were kept. This was later called a "laterculum." For mathematicians call a square shape that rises in some resemblance to a brick a "plinthion" <note>original: πλινθίον</note>, that is, a "little brick," and a book <note>codex</note> similar to this was called a "laterculum." In this way, architects name a squared stone, and Aelianus names a battle formation. Cedrenus thinks this "laterculum" is derived from that. <header>ANNOTATIONS</header>

It is called a *laterculum* <note>original: "laterculum"—literally "a small brick," used here to mean a register or list</note> by the Romans. However, this is a public register in which the names of senators and legions were written. **GOAR.**

p. 306 v. 14. **now if we wish**] this whole section is corrupted. Perhaps we would not lack conjectures for mending it if it had been our intention to examine the whole ecclesiastical computation (as they call it) and apply it here. Therefore, because that seemed foreign to our purpose for this passage, we have rendered the author's words as they are. **XYL.**

p. 312 v. 5. **during the reign** <note>original: ἐπὶ τῆς βασιλείας — *epi tēs basileias*</note>] and a gap follows in the text. However, it is clear even from Cedrenus himself that these words have fallen out: **of Justinian the Great** <note>original: Ἰουστινιανοῦ τοῦ μεγάλου — *Ioustinianou tou megalou*</note>; for the event occurred during the empire of Justinian the Great. **XYL.**

p. 314 v. 14. **greeting** <note>original: ἀσπασμός — *aspasmos*</note>] where there is talk of sacred images, this term also implies a kiss joined to the act. This is found in six hundred places in the Greek liturgical offices. **GOAR.**

p. 320 v. 10. This oracle is written erroneously, like all other oracles. I would read the first verse thus: **A Hebrew boy commands me, ruling over the blessed** <note>original: Ἑβραῖος κέλεταί με παῖς μακάρεσσιν ἀνάσσων — *Hebraios keletai me pais makaressin anassōn*</note>. But the rest are in a bad state. You can also see Suidas under the entry *Augustus*, where for **singer** <note>original: ἀοιδόν — *aoidon*</note> one should read **of Hades** <note>original: ἀΐδος — *aidos*</note>; so that it seems both can be read: **to leave this house and arrive again at Hades** <note>original: τόνδε δόμον προλιπεῖν καὶ ἀΐδος αὖθις ἱκέσθαι — *tonde domon prolipein kai aidos authis hikesthai*</note>. The third verse is defective. **XYL.**

p. 325 v. 19. **in the seventh month, according to the Hebrews the tenth** <note>original: ἑβδόμῳ μηνí, καθ᾿ Ἑβραíους δεκάτῳ — *hebdomō mēni, kath’ Hebraious dekatō*</note>] the last word is faulty, and I do not see how to restore it. For the Hebrews, September is altogether the seventh month, at least in its primary part. They call it *Tishrei* and *Ethanim*: but to guess that it was written **but Ethan** <note>original: δὲ ἔθαν — *de ethan*</note> or **Ethan** <note>original: ἔθαν</note> is difficult. **XYL.**

p. 326 v. 10. **wheat-colored** <note>original: σιτόχροος — *sitochroos*</note>] literally, with the color of grain. I do not quite see what color that word denotes, since the color of grain is not always the same. If someone teaches me, I will learn. **XYL.**

p. 328 v. 7. **before the times of Christ's presence** <note>original: πρὸ χρόνων τῆς Χριστοῦ παρουσίας — *pro chronōn tēs Christou parousias*</note>] the number of years seems to have fallen out. It could in no way be less than 250, as chronological calculations demonstrate. **XYL.**

ibid. v. 21. **two years later, Herod**] what if you read "two days after his departure, Herod," since in the margin it is written: <margin>that the slaughter of the infants occurred around Herod **two days after the flight of Christ into Egypt** <note>original: ὅτι μετὰ δύο ἡμέρας τῆς εἰς Αἴγυπτον φυγῆς τοῦ Χριστοῦ γέγονε περὶ Ἡρώδην ἡ βρεφοκτονία</note></margin>. Otherwise, it is well known that two-year-olds were killed. But this other reading has something specific about it. **XYL.**

p. 330 v. 22. **Tertullian**] the passage exists not so far from the beginning of the *Apologeticus*, and it is set out in Greek in Eusebius’s *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 2, Chapter 2, from where Cedrenus seems to have borrowed it. Moreover, it is also established from there that it should have been read **having learned that he had entered into the world** <note>original: εἰς τὸν κόσμον εἰσελήλυθεν, μαθών — *eis ton kosmon eiselēlythen, mathōn*</note>. After Herodias, Cleopatra is named; I do not know if this is without error. **XYL.**

p. 332 v. 13. **by John**] clearly false. In Luke 3, mention is made of the 15th year of Tiberius. That Christ taught for three years is not expressly stated in the Holy Scriptures: for if it were, the Church Fathers would not have disputed about it. Clement of Alexandria, in the first book of the *Stromata*, affirms that the Gospel was preached for only one year; and for this, he brings forward the prophecy about the "year of grace," which is recited from Isaiah chapter 61. Regarding the distribution of Judea among the sons of Herod...

<header>774 ANNOTATIONS BY XYLANDER AND GOAR</header>

Regarding this account, see Josephus near the end of Book 17; for we will explain the geographical matters elsewhere. However, the calculation of years from Adam to Christ which follows on page 333, line 20, is erroneous and does not agree with itself if you read **from the 41st year of Cyrus** <note>original: ἀπὸ τοῦ μα' ἔτους Κύρου — *apo tou ma' etous Kyrou*</note>. Indeed, Cyrus did not hold the kingdom for that many years; therefore, instead of 41 <note>original: μα'</note>, we should restore it to the 1st year <note>original: α'</note>. **XYL.**

p. 343 v. 22. **for eight times eleven**] This passage is slippery. Although the whole matter is discussed far more correctly elsewhere. The signs which the Greeks use for designating numbers are partly obscure to most people, and partly all too subject to the corruption of unskilled books. **29 1/2** <note>original: ϰ\theta' \frac{1}{2}</note> is twenty-nine and a half. And the letter **Delta** <note>original: Δ</note> must, by the nature of the matter, designate a **quadrant** <note>original: *quadrantem*—a quarter, or 1/4</note>. But truly, 8 multiplied by 11 1/4 results in 90 days, which is a period of 11 1/2 days beyond three lunar months. Otherwise, it is well established that a lunar month was 29 1/2 days, a lunar year 354 days, and a solar year 365 1/4 days at the time to which these things refer; thus the precise calculation entered here can by no means be seen as accurate. I thought this should be mentioned so that no one would think I was concealing something, for the rest of this passage is not entirely intact. **XYL.**

p. 344 v. 2. Concerning Thrasyllus <note>a famous astrologer to the Emperor Tiberius</note>, see Tacitus Book 5 and our own Dio <note>Dio Cassius</note> Book 55. What **climacterics** <note>original: $\chi\lambda\iota\mu\alpha\chi\tau\tilde{\eta}\varrho\varepsilon\varsigma$ — *klimaktēres*; refers to "critical years" in a person's life, often multiples of 7 or 9</note> are, or what they are called in Latin, I leave for others to explain. Having imitated Pliny (see Book 7, chapter 49) and history, I have attempted to express them. **XYL.**

p. 346 v. 19. **An element-worker** <note>original: $\sigma\tau o\iota\chi\varepsilon\iota\omega\mu\alpha\tau\iota\chi\acute{o}\varsigma$ — *stoicheiōmatikos*</note>: one who achieves miraculous things by means of magical signs, little images, and other deceptions. The deeds of Apollonius <note>Apollonius of Tyana, a famous ancient wonder-worker</note> are well known from Philostratus. Below, concerning the tricks of the patriarch Jannis during the reign of Michael, son of Theophilus, there are **elemental discourses** <note>original: $\sigma\tau o\iota\chi\varepsilon\iota\omega\tau\iota\chi o\grave{\iota}$ $\lambda\acute{o}\gamma o\iota$ — *stoicheiōtikoi logoi*</note>. And we have said more about this word elsewhere. **XYL.** A spirit <note>original: *genius*</note> devoted to familiars and employing their services. A **stoicheion** <note>original: $\sigma\tau o\iota\chi\varepsilon\tilde{\iota}o\nu$</note> is also a spirit and a familiar demon; about which I speak in another place. **GOAR.**

p. 347 v. 3. **The Egyptian robber**] He seems to be speaking of the one mentioned in Acts chapter 21 <note>referring to a messianic rebel mentioned in the New Testament</note>. Eusebius (Ecclesiastical History 2.20) and Nicephorus Xanthopulus (2.26) repeat that history from Josephus's Book 2, chapter 23, on the *Destruction of Jerusalem*. **XYL.**

ibid. v. 7. **between Thera**] See the tenth year of Leo the Iconoclast. Furthermore, Pliny writes (2.87) that among the Cyclades, in the 4th year of the 135th Olympiad, the islands of **Thera and Therasia** were born <note>emerged from volcanic activity</note>. This was in the year 516 **from the founding of the City** <note>original: *ab u. c.* — *ab urbe condita* (753 BC)</note>, five years after the end of the First Punic War. The same Pliny writes in the same place that 130 years later (that is, in the year 646 from the founding of the City, two years before Cicero was born, at the end of the Jugurthine War) **Hiera** was born, which is also called **Automate**. And from it, he says, at a distance of two stadia and after 110 years—in our own age, during the consulship of Marcus Junius Silanus and Lucius Balbus, on the **8th day before the Ides of July** <note>July 8th</note>—**Thia** was born. These consuls are placed in the year 771 from the founding of the City, the fifth year of Tiberius. Therefore, Pliny's passage, if it were not faulty, would disagree with the common calculation by a full 15 years. This is consistent neither with his own diligence nor with the agreement of other writers with him. Dio Cocceius says in Book 60 that an island was born near Thera in the 4th consulship of Claudius and the 3rd of Lucius Vitellius, which year was 800 from the founding of the City.

...as it seemed to others, 779. However, he undoubtedly speaks about this matter and about that island of Thia. Therefore, we must see whether Pliny did not write *after 150 years* <note>original: "post annos 150"</note> where "130" is now read: for it is not a new thing for 150 to be put in place of 153, when numbers are not recorded exactly or precisely. Furthermore, you will easily understand from Pliny (Book 4, Chapter 12) that Thera and Therasia are two islands, not one (I am not speaking here of the one that was among the Aeolian islands, mentioned in Pliny Book 3, Chapter 9); there he writes that Therasia was torn away from Thera, and between them first Automate, and later also Thia, emerged. The same author reports in Book 5, Chapter 24, that Claudiopolis (on page 347, line 10) is a city of Cappadocia. Xiphilinus, drawing from Dio’s account of Hadrian, names Cithynis as a city of Bithynia which is otherwise called Claudiopolis. And regarding the uprising of the Jews under Claudius, see Josephus' *Antiquities of the Jews* (Book 20, Chapter 4) and Eusebius' *Ecclesiastical History* (Book 2, Chapter 19). In Josephus, one reads that only "two myriads" perished, meaning 20,000 <note>original: "δύο μυριάδες" — duo myriades</note>. But Eusebius has the same figure as our author. **XYL.** <note>Wilhelm Xylander, the 16th-century humanist scholar.</note>

p. 347 v. 16. **atrocities throughout the world** <note>original: "atroces per orbem"</note>] In the margin is written: *I too ponder that calamity of old; for the slave is by nature an enemy to the masters.* <note>original Greek: "ἀναλογίζομαι καὶ αὐτὸς τὴν τότε συμφοράν· φύσει γὰρ ἐχθρὸν τὸ δοῦλον τοῖς δεσπόταις"</note> Nerva abolished this edict. **XYL.**

p. 348 v. 15. **from Jonadab** <note>original: "a Ionadabo"</note>] See Jeremiah 35. Regarding the Essenes, read Josephus' *Antiquities* (Book 18, Chapter 2), and many more things in *The Jewish War* (Book 2, Chapter 12), from which our author <note>Cedrenus</note> transferred several items. **XYL.**

p. 356 v. 1. **toward forgiveness for lack of self-control** <note>original: "ad veniam incontinentia"</note>] This passage is mutilated, and I have expressed it word for word; for I did not have the time to look through the works of Basil for the sake of this matter, which someone who delights in this debate and has leisure may do. But the Platonic sections are also mutilated, and thus it is written in the margin: *Almost all these things of Plato are obscure because we do not know his book in which these things are placed.* <note>original Greek: "ἀσαφῆ ταῦτα πάντα σχεδὸν τὰ τοῦ Πλάτωνος διὰ τὸ μὴ εἰδέναι ἡμᾶς τὸ αὐτοῦ βιβλίον ἐν ᾧ ταῦτα κεῖται"</note> They are, however, taken from the second book of the *Republic*, and a verse of Aeschylus from the siege of Thebes is cited there; we translated that passage in Plutarch’s *Life of Aristides*. I did not think it worth the effort to weary myself by correcting this here, since Plato's book is at hand. **XYL.** Nothing here is mutilated or cut short, even for Xylander, if only a fair judge would look more deeply into the author's words. For when he had spoken about the obedience shown to the Gospel words in which chastity is especially praised, he said that those bound by marriage, just like monks, would receive judgment from those words. He asserted that those who could prove they were driven to lawful marriage by an inability to restrain their lust, or by affection for a wife, or by the intimacy of living together, should be declared free from having violated the Lord’s counsel and would obtain forgiveness. This sense, being Catholic, is also complete and perfect. **GOAR.** <note>Jacques Goar, a 17th-century Dominican friar and scholar of Byzantine liturgy.</note>

p. 361 v. 7. **Oblias**] I do not understand what language this word belongs to or what it signifies. I have rendered "enclosure of the people" <note>original: "περιοχὴν λαοῦ" — perichēn laou</note> word for word as "the surrounding of the people." Our author either copied this narrative from Nicephorus or from Hegesippus himself, from whom Nicephorus reports it in his *Ecclesiastical History* (Book 2, Chapter 38). If I had possessed the Greek text of that work, I could have used it in many places to correct Cedrenus. **XYL.** Epiphanius in *Against Heresies* (Heresy 78, section 7): *Joseph, therefore, had as his firstborn James, who was called Oblias...* <note>original Greek: "ἔσχε μὲν οὖν ὁ Ἰωσὴφ πρωτότοκον τὸν Ἰάκωβον τὸν ἐπικληθέντα Ὀβλίαν"</note>

<page-num>776</page-num>
<header>ANNOTATIONS OF XYLANDER AND GOAR</header>

...translated as "wall," and having been surnamed "the Just," and being a Nazirite, which is translated as "holy." <note>original: "ἅγιος" — hagios</note> **GOAR.** <note>Jacques Goar, the 17th-century French Dominican scholar and liturgist.</note>

p. 373 v. 4. *under Constantius*] I have boldly restored the name "Constantius" in place of "Constantine," since Zonaras agrees with me in his *Life of Constantius*, as do Nicephorus (10.2), Theodoret (3.18), and the fragment of Dorotheus the Martyr which is usually prefixed to the Gospel of Luke. However, even in that fragment, "Constantine" is incorrectly read instead of "Constantius," and he is claimed to be the son of Constantine the Great. For Constantine the Great’s son died too early for any of these events to have occurred during his reign. Moreover, in Sophronius’s writing on the fragment regarding St. Luke, it is written that his relics were brought to Constantinople in the twentieth year of Constantine; this is entirely erroneous, both in the name and in the year. **XYL.** <note>Wilhelm Xylander, the 16th-century German humanist.</note>

p. 378 v. 7. *Flavius*] It seemed that one should read *Balbius* or *Balbus*, or perhaps *Flavius Blabius*. But when I consulted the fifteenth book of P. Cornelius Tacitus, I found that "Flavius" is correct. That saying reported there belongs to the tribune Subrius Flavius; indeed, Xiphilinus, drawing from Dio, names the same man in this very history, indicating that he was in command of the bodyguards. However, the claim that Cincinnatus was called from the plow to manage the state during the reign of Nero is a peak example of historical ignorance. <note>original: "ἀνιστορησίας" — anistoresias; a lack of historical knowledge.</note> **XYL.**

p. 384 v. 5. *calls her his mother*] <margin>From this you can well understand the hymn <note>original: "τροπάριον" — troparion, a short hymn in Eastern Orthodox liturgy.</note> which says: "The thorn-bearing synagogue of the Hebrews, not preserving a motherly affection for you, her benefactor."</margin> More will be said about these hymns below. The passage cited shortly thereafter from Lamentations 4 is read somewhat differently there and in the works of Eusebius, Justin, and others: but I did not wish to dwell on this dispute. **XYL.**

p. 429 v. 16. *an excellent administration*] <note>original: "ἄριστον πολιτείαν" — ariston politeian</note> Look here for a fair law of empire and a praised skill in managing public affairs, rather than private morals. **GOAR.**

*ib. v. 22. appropriately — having received*] <note>original: "εἰκότως — κομισάμενος"</note> Word for word: *He received the well-earned rewards for the ferocity that had been innate to him from of old.* **GOAR.**

p. 431 v. 5. *you shall not kill me*] This verse is from the beginning of the 22nd book of Homer’s *Iliad*, where Apollo discourages Achilles from pursuing him. Regarding Apollonius, there exists a proper work by Philostratus, and this story is in Book 8. It is also sufficiently clear from that work, from Suidas, and from others, that one should read "Damis" and not "Damantus." **XYL.**

p. 434 v. 17. *having worn the petal*] <note>original: "τὸ πέταλον πεφορηκώς" — to petalon pephorēkōs</note> This is also read in Eusebius, from whom it appears Cedrenus copied these things. However, I do not yet fully know what it means "to wear the <term>petalon</term>," <note>The *petalon* refers to a golden leaf or plate worn on the forehead; in a Christian context, it was sometimes attributed to Apostles like John or James to signify priestly authority.</note> except that I suspect from the collections of Suidas that it was a woolen cap used as a mark of a teacher, worn for the sake of honor and authority by a primary teacher of the Church, similar to the <term>apices</term> <note>The *apex* was a pointed cap worn by the Roman Flamines (priests).</note> of the ancient priests. **XYL.** Xylander believed that he wore it as a teacher, adorned with the insignia of a teacher, and that he wore the <term>petalon</term> as a "woolen cap in the manner of the priests." Thus he compensates for gold with wool, and grants the Apostle—inspired by the Holy Spirit and a preeminent teacher of the Church—the honor of the Roman priests. But does it not rather signify the dignity of the ancient priesthood...

<meta>This page continues the philological commentary by Jacques Goar and Wilhelm Xylander on the historical chronicle of Georgius Cedrenus. <page-num>777</page-num>
<header>ANNOTATIONS. 777</header>

...wanted the apostle <note>referring to John the Evangelist</note> to be equated with some title of honor and manifested with a new majesty by assuming a certain insignia of his, when he placed before his forehead a *petalon* <note>original: πέταλον — a thin leaf or plate of gold</note> or a *golden plate or thin blade*? Jerome, in his work *On Illustrious Men*, quoting Polycrates, says: "John, who leaned upon the breast of the Lord and became His priest, wearing a golden plate <note>original: χρυσοῦν πέταλον — chrysoun petalon</note> on his forehead, died a witness and teacher in Ephesus." <note>original: Ἰωάννης ὃς ἐπὶ τὸ στῆθος τοῦ κυρίου ἀνεκλίθη καὶ ἱερεὺς αὐτοῦ γέγονε, χρυσοῦν πέταλον ἐν τῷ μετώπῳ βαστάζων μάρτυς καὶ διδάσκαλος ἐν Ἐφέσῳ ἐκοιμήθη.</note> Epiphanius relates a similar thing about James, the brother of the Lord, in *Against Heresies* (78): "This James also wore a plate [petalon] upon his head." <note>original: οὗτος ὁ Ἰάκωβος καὶ πέταλον ἐπὶ τῆς κεφαλῆς ἐφόρεσε.</note> His translator adds: "That James wore a gold blade on his head." <note>original: Iacobus iste bracteam in capite gessit.</note> **GOAR.**

p. 435 v. 4. *Caesarius, brother of the great Gregory*] Suidas and others say the same. As for what follows in the Greek, "at the senate" <note>original: ἐπὶ σενάτου — epi senatou</note>, I do not know how to read it: perhaps it is "in the senate." Nicephorus (12.44) states that this Caesarius was the master of the palace under Theodosius I. This greatly disagrees with what Gregory of Nyssa says in his *Life of Gregory of Nazianzus*, namely that Caesarius departed from the living while Constantius was still reigning. **XYL.** Regarding the note found in the old printed editions of Cedrenus, joined by the two letters *se* <note>original: σε*</note>, I guess it indicates "of the secret council" <note>original: σεκρέτου — sekretou</note> or, as Xylander thinks, "of the senate," or finally—unless the letter *e* stands in the way—"of the synod." Let the reader choose whichever is pleasing, or let another offer a more certain conjecture. **GOAR.**

p. 437 v. 17. *Hadrian’s Hunts* <note>original: Ἀδριανοῦ θήρας — Adrianou theras</note>] This not-unknown author confuses this place with Hadrianopolis in Thrace. But this is a city of Mysia, not Thrace; and it is called "Hadrian’s hunting enclosures" by Cuspinianus, following Dio and Suetonius. **GOAR.**

ib. v. 18. *in the Mitata*] What this might be, I could not easily say. In Xiphilinus (following Dio), the city is simply called "Hadrian’s Hunts," which Merula translates as "Hadrian’s hunting enclosures." Zonaras has it the same way. Spartianus says: "He established the town of Adrianotheras in a certain place because he had hunted there successfully and had killed a bear." What if "in the mitata" <note>original: μιτάτοις — mitatois</note> was meant to signify "boundaries" <note>original: metatis</note>, so that it designates Hadrian’s hunt as being enclosed within certain markers and limits of the city? **XYL.** I interpret *mitata*, or if you prefer the more Latin form *metata*, as the "encampments" of the army, in which the army would stand or rest for a short while during a long march. Hence the "surveyors" <note>original: metatores</note>, about whom Vegetius writes (2.7). **GOAR.**

p. 438 v. 8. *having attained many years of age*] I have followed Xiphilinus here, and indeed that which was clearly true. For that phrase "having lived six years" <note>original: βιώσας μὲν ἔτη Ϛ</note> was placed there by someone who did not understand the elegance of the inscription. It should have been written "having lived many years" <note>original: βιώσας μὲν ἔτη πολλά</note> or (as Xiphilinus has it) "so many years" <note>original: τόσα</note>. For a life lacking in leisure and tranquility, since it would have been unpleasant, he did not consider worthy of the name "life." And it is well enough known that *zen* <note>original: ζῆν</note>, "to live," is used to mean "to live sweetly and pleasantly," even from the epigram about the hours of the day, in which it is said: "The letter Zeta bids one live after those hours." <note>A reference to the Greek numbering system where the letters Alpha through Zeta represent the first six hours of the day—work hours—after which "Zeta" (7) begins the time for living/leisure.</note> **XYL.**

ib. v. 9. where Cedrenus reports that Hadrian remitted the debts owed by cities and citizens: <margin>This too my Emperor Isaac did upon his accession.</margin> **XYL.**

# THE ANNOTATIONS OF XYLANDER AND GOAR

p. 438 line 18. \* *For Trajan*] These matters can neither be accepted as referring to Antoninus, nor do they belong here at all; rather, they refer to Hadrian, who was adopted by Trajan through letters forged by Plotina Augusta <note>Plotina was the wife of Trajan; some historians alleged she faked Trajan's adoption of Hadrian on his deathbed</note>. This is well-established by Xiphilinus, Spartianus, Zonaras, and others. **XYLANDER.**

p. 439 line 4. *Bardesanes*] The name of Bardesanes is clearly inserted here in error, for he was a Syrian man, to say nothing more. One should read "Priscilla among the Phrygians," etc. Regarding Bardesanes, see Eusebius at the end of the fourth book of his *Ecclesiastical History*. Regarding the Cataphrygian heresy <note>The Montanist movement</note> of Montanus and the false prophetesses Priscilla and Maximilla, see the same author at 5.16 and elsewhere. **XYLANDER.**

*ib. line 15. he when against*] These notes stood in the margin: *The most wise Themistius writes that this happened under the Antoninus who came before him, but others say differently and not in this way.* <note>original: ἐπὶ τοῦ πρὸ αὐτοῦ Ἀντωνίνου τοῦτο γενέσθαι ὁ σοφώτατος γράφει Θεμίστιος, ἄλλως δὲ καὶ οὐχ οὕτως.</note> A letter from Antoninus himself on this matter is joined to the second *Apology* of Justin Martyr; however, it is debated which Antoninus it belongs to—Pius or the Philosopher <note>Marcus Aurelius</note>. From Orosius (7.15), it is sufficiently clear that this occurred under the Philosopher, as it is from the order of Eusebius’s narratives, and because he says Marcus, the brother of the other Antoninus (namely Verus), waged the German war and obtained water through the prayers of the Christians (5.5). Furthermore, Melito, cited by the same author shortly before, calls him the grandson of Hadrian (4.26). Xiphilinus and Zonaras also relate the event under the reign of the Philosopher, drawing from Dio. Likewise, Julius Capitolinus expressly indicates that the German and Marcomannic wars were waged by him, and records that he summoned a lightning bolt against the enemy's siege engines and water for his men who were suffering from thirst. **XYLANDER.**

p. 440 line 16. *unto repentance* <note>original: εἰς μετάνοιαν — eis metanoian</note>] *A heretic interprets this as "coming to one's senses," while an orthodox person interprets it as "penitence."* **GOAR.**

*ib. line 19.* The story concerning the man who was baptized with sand is from the end of the third volume of Nicephorus. But what these words—*therefore because nothing* etc.—mean, I do not know. **XYLANDER.** Thus, he does not understand himself. Yet the sense of the words is plain. *Therefore, because this "baptism" of sand was none of these things—as it could not be reduced to the figurative baptism of Moses, the penitential baptism of John, the sacramental baptism of Christ, nor the blood of martyrs—it was rightly not accepted for the Hebrew man who had received it.* **GOAR.**

p. 442 line 6. I do not know why *Severus* should be the same as "heretic." I believe these words were added by some amateur scholar <note>original: sciolo</note> who knew of the heretic Severus; Cedrenus will speak of him later under the reign of Aurelian. **XYLANDER.** I do not think anything here was corrupted by some amateur, as Xylander does. For since *Severus* sounds to the Latins like *grim, rigid, or avenging*, it can also be taken to mean *destructive, ruinous*, and, as Apuleius says, *deadly* <note>original: peremptorio</note>—which is what the Greek word *heretical* (or if you prefer, *destructive* <note>original: ἀναιρετικός — anairetikos</note>) signifies. **GOAR.**

*ib. line 17. kynegion* <note>original: κυνήγιον</note>] *The hunt* is how you will translate this in the author's section on Antoninus. Here and elsewhere, it should not be translated as *cynegium* (as many do), but as *the arena*, the place designated for undergoing combat with beasts (the western region of the city is still called the "Hunter" <note>original: κυνηγός — kynegos</note> today). In this place, the animals were nourished in cages and pits at public expense: Suidas writes that in this place, *those who died a violent death* <note>original: βιοθάνατοι — biothanatoi</note> were thrown. In which...

# ANNOTATIONS

...criminals, as well as the most noble men, were sometimes punished with death <note>original: "capite multatos," literally "punished by the head," usually referring to beheading or capital punishment</note> out of contempt for the laws. **GOAR.**

p. 446 line 3. *unholy* <note>original: "ἀνόσιοι" (anosioi)</note>] This signifies impious heretics. I did not wish to sacrifice clarity for the sake of the text, and it is possible that Cedrenus actually wrote *Anomoeans* <note>original: "ἀνομοούσιοι" (anomooousioi). This refers to a radical Arian sect that believed the Son was of a "dissimilar" substance to the Father</note>. **XYLANDER.** Yet who would have written that, if the word had not yet been coined by Xylander? I would say with more certainty that it is possible he wrote *unequal* or *unjust* <note>original: "ἄνισοι" (anisoi) or "ἀνίσιοι" (anisioi)</note>; these words, among both the ancients and the more recent Easterners, refer to those *affected and led by inequality*; so that these "unjust" ones were indeed the same as the "Anomoeans" <note>original: "ἀνόμοιοι" (anomoioi), meaning "the dissimilar ones"</note>. **GOAR.**

ib. line 16. *to have taken up a life* <note>original: "ἐπανῃρῆσθαι βίον"</note>] *He took up*, *he attempted*, *he chose*. *Having taken up*, *having preferred*, *wishing*. Thus says the Suda <note>A massive 10th-century Greek encyclopedia, often referred to as "Suidas"</note>. The ascetic life is that which is accustomed to subduing the body and devoting itself to piety alone. Monks were devoted to that practice, and from this they were called <term>ascetics</term> <note>from "asketes," meaning one who practices or exercises, like an athlete</note>, as if they were "exercisers." Furthermore, all these matters are read in the Suda somewhat more fully and completely than here under the entry *Origen*, whom I have followed in the appropriate places. See also Nicephorus, book 5, chapters 32 and 33. **XYLANDER.**

p. 449 line 12. *Maurus the Cappadocian*] In Xiphilinus, drawing from Dio—whom Zonaras also followed—it is read that Maurus was from "Sicilia Caesarea"; what that might be, I do not see. Certainly, if he was a <term>Maurus</term> <note>A Moor, or a person from North Africa</note>, he could be neither a Cappadocian nor a Sicilian. It is probable that he was from <term>Mauretania Caesariensis</term> <note>A Roman province in what is now Algeria; its capital was Caesarea</note>. **XYLANDER.**

p. 450 line 21. Those who held Roman power from Maximinus up to Philip are recounted here in a very obscure and confused manner. However, since the works of Herodian, Capitolinus, Zonaras, and others are at hand, I prefer to send the reader to them rather than transcribe those details here. In place of "Puplianus" (p. 451 line 5), I have restored "Pupienus" from the historical record. But what he means by that "Junior" (ibid. line 2) <note>referring to a younger co-emperor or title holder</note>, I cannot guess. Indeed, mention of the <term>protectores</term> <note>bodyguards or elite staff officers</note> as a rank is very frequent in Ammianus Marcellinus. He indicates in book 15 that he himself was among the "domestic protectors" under Constantius, and from book 30 of the same author, it appears this was a rank very close to the dignity of a tribune. In our author, they are called <term>protectors</term> <note>original: "προτίκτωρες" (protiktores)</note>. He says Jovian was also a protector under Constantius. In the same Marcellinus, mention of the <term>palatine schools</term> <note>original: "scholae palatinae," elite guard units</note> is not rare. I think it is clear enough that the name of "schools" was given to the legions that were maintained on a permanent salary; the prefect of these is thereafter repeatedly referred to by the title of <term>domesticus</term>, and sometimes he is called the *leader of the schools* <note>original: "ἐξηγούμενος τῶν σχολῶν"</note>. **XYLANDER.** Marcellinus, in books 25 and 31, lists the <term>Candidati</term> <note>The "Candidates," a select group of the imperial bodyguard named for their white tunics</note> as a military troop. He mentions them serving under Julian and Valens when they were about to perish by violent deaths in nearly the same circumstances. The same author also mentions <term>Protectores</term> as well as <term>Scholares</term> <note>Guardsmen of the Scholae</note>; Henry Valesius <note>Henri Valois, a 17th-century French scholar</note> has shown with great erudition in his annotations that all these were the emperor's bodyguards and attendants. In most places, Graeco-Roman law calls these same men <term>spatharocandidati</term> <note>A high-ranking palace official, literally "sword-bearing candidate"</note>. **GOAR.**

*ibid.* However, it is entirely false that Marcus, who was chosen after Gordian, reigned for three years (ibid. line 16), since it is established even from Zonaras that he died before he had even received the imperial power. To him, Severus Hostilianus...

He succeeded him, and his rule was of the same condition. He is called Justinianus by the scribe of Cedrenus, but is correctly named Hostilianus by Zonaras <note>Joannes Zonaras was a 12th-century Byzantine chronicler</note>. I certainly think that "days" should be read instead of "years" <note>original: "pro ἔτη ἡμέρας, pro annis dies"</note>. This is what appears above (ibid, verse 1). He was the father of the holy martyr Eugenia; you will learn the nature of this story from Zonaras's account of Philip. **XYL.**

p. 450 line 22. *Of the Bostrans* <note>original: "Βόστρων" (Bostron)</note>] This is also found in Zonaras; the rest of the historians record that this man was an Arab and that his city was Bostra in Arabia. Indeed, Ammianus Marcellinus, a most diligent writer, mentions Bostra in Armenia as a vast and fortified city in Book 14. **XYL.**

p. 452 line 1. *He on account of his body*] It is ambiguous whether this should be understood as referring to Sapor <note>The Sassanid King Sapor I</note> or to Philip. Zonaras interprets it as Sapor. Valerian, however, is not relevant here. But even Zonaras will clarify this for the reader. **XYL.**

p. 454 line 9. *The wonderful Gregory*] The Bishop of Neocaesarea <note>Gregory Thaumaturgus, a 3rd-century bishop famous for his reported miracles</note>. See Nicephorus, Book 6, Chapter 17. The things that follow regarding Mani <note>The founder of Manichaeism</note> are also in the collections of the Suda; we have followed those versions where we judged our own manuscript to be less accurate. **XYL.**

p. 464 line 4. *To a banquet at Perinthus*] This passage is mutilated. A little earlier, I translated "subject to certain destruction" what our author calls *with climacterics* <note>original: "μετὰ κλιμακτήρων" (meta klimakteron)</note>. **XYL.** I interpret *climacterics* as the uncertain outcomes of affairs, which, while sometimes remaining stable or even improving, are more frequently accustomed to being driven headlong into ruin. This is a metaphor taken from the completed cycle of seven-year periods <note>In ancient medicine and astrology, the "climacteric" was a critical year in a person's life, believed to occur in multiples of seven</note>, in which, just as there is a change from one bodily temperament to another, so a shift from life to death occurs more often than usual. **GOAR.**

ibid. line 23. *The heresy of the Quartodecimans*] Specifically, the practice of celebrating Easter according to the Jewish custom and on the fourteenth day of the moon <note>From the Latin "quarta decima" (fourteenth). This was a major controversy in the early Church regarding the date of Easter</note>. **XYL.**

p. 470 line 8. *Adaktos* <note>original: "Ἄδακτον"</note>] I read this as *Adauctus* <note>original: "Ἄδαυκτον"</note>, which is found in Eusebius, Book 8, Chapter 11. The letter 'u' was erased by a scribe's error; the name is Latin, and thus fits well for an Italian, just like the names Honoratus, Consentius, Innocentius, and others. However, regarding what he reports about his wife and daughters, Eusebius in the following chapter by no means attributes these things to them, but to others near Antioch who escaped sexual violation in this manner. Furthermore, one can gather the nature of the dignity of the title <term>Magister</term> <note>A high-ranking administrative or military official, such as the "Master of Offices"</note> from Eusebius's account of Adauctus and from other sources. Even today, there are "Masters" of either the court or the cavalry in royal courts. And the history of Xyluntas regarding Leo the Iconoclast shows that these Masters were extremely wealthy. As for the question at hand, Augustine in *The City of God* (Book 1, Chapter 26) says he dares not pronounce anything rashly concerning those who had similar ends. But those are the concerns of others. **XYL.** Eusebius writes of this illustrious martyr in Book 8, Chapter 23: *A certain man who had attained Roman dignities, Adaucus by name, descended from a noble family among the Italians, a man who advanced through every degree of honor granted by emperors, so that he obtained the leadership of what they call the Mastership and general administration.* <note>original Greek: "Ῥωμαϊκῆς ἀξίας ἐπειλημμένος Ἄδαυκος ὄνομα... μαγιστρότητός τε καὶ καθολικότητος"</note>. The Greek text was provided intentionally...

# ANNOTATIONS. 781

I did not present this according to Christophorson’s version <note>John Christophorson was a 16th-century Bishop of Chichester known for translating Greek patristic texts into Latin</note>, in which he rendered the final words as *having performed the duties of the master of offices and general quaestor with integrity and without corruption* <note>original Latin: "magistri officiorum et quaestoris generalis munera integre et incorrupte exsecutus"</note>. He believed that the "prefecture of the mastership" indicated the dignity of the **master of offices** <term>Magister officiorum: one of the most senior administrative officials in the late Roman and Byzantine Empires, overseeing the palace bureaucracy and foreign embassies</term>. I have remained silent regarding the "general quaestor" as an office distinct from the master of offices, for in an empire of such magnitude and weight as it was then, a single man could not have managed both. Nor should the "generality" <note>Greek: καθολικότης (katholikotēs)</note> be separated from the "mastership" <note>Greek: μαγιστρότητος (magistrotētos)</note>, as Eusebius intended them to be connected by a conjunction. Thus, the mastership of Adaucus was "general," extending over many departments (as must be distinguished from the masters of private affairs). As Pancirollus says in his *Notes on the Eastern Empire* (chapter 62), he commanded not only the palatines and the ministers of the prince, nor only the palace schools <note>Elite guard units</note> bearing arms, but also the factories and the frontier dukes and counts. This is discussed at length regarding the Master, a dignity with which Cedrenus records many were honored. Liutprand <note>A 10th-century diplomat and historian</note> counted twenty-four of them by sight during the time of his embassy, as he left witnessed in Book 6, the final chapter; all of them possessed the highest authority as well as dignity during the centuries of the declining empire. **GOAR.**

p. 472 line 23. In the description of the appearance of **Constantine the Great**, it is said that he was called *trachēlas* <note>Greek: τραχηλᾶν</note>, which I have translated as **thick-necked** <note>original Latin: "cervicosum"</note>. In Aurelius Victor, it is noted that he was nicknamed *Traculla*, but for another reason. **XYL.** 
Away with such an infamous word as "thick-necked"—which Xylander here devises—for so noble and venerable a prince! Constantine, who was "like a god in face and shoulders," was called *trachēlas* as one conspicuous for a **broad and upright neck** <note>original Latin: "lata erectaque cervice"</note>, which are **signs of bodily strength and a great soul** <note>original Latin: "corporeae fortitudinis et ingentis animi signis"</note>. Let him receive praise that is perhaps unequal to his highness through a common abundance of words, rather than suffer insult and offense from a single, less-happily invented term. **GOAR.**

p. 473 line 16. *He ruled the Gauls* <note>Greek: ἐβασίλευσε Γαλλιῶν</note>] This carries with it a happy omen for the Kingdom of the Gauls <note>France</note>, that a king given from heaven to himself and the church, just as he holds the first place among faithful princes, so too should he attain the name of **Most Christian** <note>original Latin: "Christianissimi"</note>, and be proclaimed as the one most holy and **most divine** <note>original Latin: "divinissimus"</note> above all others. **GOAR.**

p. 491 line 22. *To receive this name* <note>Greek: ὑποδέξασθαι τοῦτο τὸ ὄνομα</note>] The Greeks themselves adhere to a fabled Jewish tradition where, having composed a prayer in the name of Trypho against various insects devastating the fields, they pronounce: *I adjure you by the great name inscribed upon the rock, which did not hold firm but broke apart like wax before the face of fire* <note>original Greek: "ὁρκίζω ὑμᾶς κατὰ τοῦ μεγάλου ὀνόματος τοῦ ἐπὶ τῆς πέτρας ἐπιγραφέντος, καὶ μὴ βαστασάσης ἀλλὰ διαρραγείσης ὡσεὶ κηρὸς ἀπὸ προσώπου πυρός"</note>. **GOAR.**

p. 495 v. 21. *Kodroubes* <note>Greek: Κοδρούβης</note>] Write, *Kordoubes* <note>Greek: Κορδούβης</note>. He is speaking of **Hosius of Corduba**, a bishop of great authority at that time, as is known from Eusebius and other ecclesiastical writers. See on this matter Socrates (1:7 and 9), Sozomen (1:16), and Theodoret (Book 1). **XYL.** 
Theophanes also uses *Kodroubes* instead of *Kordoubes*, following a custom of transposing letters accepted by modern Greeks. Thus they pronounce and write *kradia* and *amyglada* in place of *kardia* <note>heart</note> and *amygdala* <note>almonds</note>. **GOAR.**
