# THE ANNOTATIONS OF XYLANDER AND GOAR

**p. 496 v. 1. *to build a city for the Mother of God*]** <note>original Greek: οἰκοδομῆσαι τῇ θεοτόκῳ πόλιν (oikodomēsai tē theotokō polin)</note> From this phrase, the city is sometimes referred to as the "City of the Mother of God" <note>original Greek: Θεοτόκου πόλις (Theotokou polis)</note>, just as it is read as "Constantinople." So it appears in the *Menaion* <term>Menaion: a set of twelve liturgical books, one for each month, used in the Eastern Orthodox Church</term> for May 2nd, the anniversary of which is celebrated throughout the East as the *Encaenia* <term>Encaenia: a festival commemorating the dedication of a city or church, specifically the dedication of Constantinople in 330 AD</term>. The history of this festival is presented in the *Synaxarion* <term>Synaxarion: a compilation of hagiographies or short accounts of saints and feasts</term> for that same day, and the historian Zonaras also mentions it in his account of Constantine. **GOAR.**

**p. 497 v. 6. *a year and eight months*]** Indeed, it is clear from the history of this war that it was long-lasting. However, exactly how many months it took to complete is not entirely apparent. In the Greek text, it is said to have lasted "eleven and eight months," a quite unusual number, unless perhaps the fighting first lasted eleven months, and then after a broken treaty, a rebellion occurred which was suppressed in eight months. **XYL.**

**ibid. v. 7. *Licinnius*]** I have written this with two 'n's, following the Greek manuscript. Others have "Licinius" with a single 'n'. However, the poet Horace treated that very syllable "ci" as both long and short in his *Odes*. **XYL.**

**ibid. v. 12. *to be cut off*]** <note>original Greek: ἀποτμηθῆναι (apotmēthēnai)</note> That is to say, *the head*, if indeed the word is used correctly; for the rest of the historians simply record that he was killed. I have translated the word *kyriakas* <note>original Greek: κυριακάς</note> as "temples," with the implied noun being "houses." It is much more probable that our German word *kirchen* <note>the root of the English "church"</note> is derived from this than from the word *ecclesia*. **XYL.** Understand this to mean "houses," called *dominica* <note>the Lord's house</note> by the Latins; these are also written as *kyriaka* in the neuter. **GOAR.**

**ibid. v. 18. *it was organized into a theme*]** <note>original Greek: ἐθεματίσθη (ethemathisthē)</note> Following modern usage, we explain *thema* <term>Thema: originally an administrative and military district of the Byzantine Empire; also used in astrology</term> as a *legion, province, building, or position*. From this also comes the order of the wandering stars <note>the planets</note> as well as the fixed stars, the placement of the heavens, the "mansions" of the constellations (as they say), and their relationship to one another; these are called *thema*, or by Zonaras, a *themation*. Others call this in common speech a "horoscope" <note>original Latin: horoscopium</note>; if you were to compose a chart of this for yourself, you would be said to "thematize" <note>original Greek: θεματίζειν (thematizein)</note> in the words of the historian Cedrenus. **GOAR.**

**ibid. v. 20. *in the third indiction*]** <note>original Latin: indictione tertia</note> Regarding the sign that appears before the numeral "3" in my manuscript, I have discovered that this sign denotes an **indiction** <term>Indiction: a 15-year cycle used in the Roman and Byzantine tax and calendar systems</term> <note>original Greek: ἐπινέμησιν (epinemēsin)</note>. I found this from the eleventh year of Justinian, where the restoration of the Great Temple <note>the Hagia Sophia</note> is discussed, and Zonaras clearly uses "indiction" in place of this sign. The attentive reader will observe this in other places as well. Furthermore, I have rendered everything word-for-word so that no one might accuse me of rashness. In Zonaras, it is written that the Emperor Valens predicted Constantinople would last 696 years, and he judged this from the *thema* or the position of the stars at the birth of the city. From this, you can understand the words of our author. Regarding what is said about the death of Crispus <note>Constantine the Great's eldest son, executed in 326 AD</note>, it does not seem to be free of error. It is well established from historians that he was falsely accused by his stepmother Fausta of a crime—as if he had attempted to violate her chastity—and was condemned to death. And what the phrase "crowned through a vision" <note>original Greek: στεφθεῖσα δι’ ὀπτασίας (stephtheisa di’ optasias)</note> is intended to mean is not entirely clear. See Nicephorus, book 8, chapter 29. And what our author reports obscurely and concisely regarding the Armenians and Tiridates, you will understand from the same author in chapter 35. The same regarding the Persians is found at length in the following chapter, where the man named Usthazanes is the one our author calls Outhazades. **XYL.**

**p. 498 v. 5. *of the chief commander*]** <note>original Greek: τοῦ ἀρχιστρατήγου (tou archistratēgou)</note> Xylander translated this as "of the prefect of the troops." Of which troops? He would have spoken more correctly had he said: "of the Prince of the Heavenly Host" <note>a title for the Archangel Michael</note>.

<meta>This page continues the scholarly commentary on the historical work of George Cedrenus, specifically focusing on the events and urban development under the reign of Constantine the Great and his successors. The previous page detailed the dedication of Constantinople and its festivals. This page examines specific Greek terms for city features—such as forums and porticos—and provides corrections to historical errors regarding Constantine’s sons and the physical description of Emperor Justinian.</meta>

# ANNOTATIONS

**[p. 783]**

**[unlabeled]** That is, of Michael the Archangel. From this, observe the ancient devotion toward the blessed spirits <note>the angels</note> that existed from that time. **GOAR.**

**p. 500 v. 6. *co-without-beginning***] <note>original Greek: συνάναρχον (synanarchon)</note> Is the Son "without beginning" <note>original: ἄναρχος (anarchos)</note> in the same way as the Father? Not exactly; yet the Son is also without beginning, because although he acknowledges a principle of origin <note>the Father</note>, he does not acknowledge a beginning in time or through creation. Gregory the Theologian <note>Gregory of Nazianzus, a 4th-century Church Father</note>. **GOAR.**

**p. 504 v. 1. *to establish by canon***] <note>original Greek: κανονίσαι (kanonisai)</note> To decree by an issued rule. This refers to the saying of Paphnutius <note>a 4th-century bishop famous for his stance on clerical marriage at the Council of Nicaea</note>; while some treat his story as a fable, Cedrenus offers testimony as if it were the truest history. **GOAR.**

**p. 518 v. 1. *forum***] <note>original Greek: φόρον (phoron)</note> Simocatta <note>Theophylact Simocatta, a 7th-century historian</note> says: "The forum is a bright and illustrious place in the city." It also enjoys a name derived from the Latin <note>Latin: *forum*</note>. **GOAR.**

***ibid.*** Here and there, porticos <note>original Greek: ἔμβολοι (emboloi)</note> crowded the forum. According to Allatius <note>Leone Allacci, a 17th-century scholar</note>, these are walkways built with various joined planks and roofed with tiles to ward off the discomforts of heat and sudden rain, as well as for the sake of shade and strolling; they are named from the word "to enter" <note>original Greek: ἐμβάλλω (emballo)</note>, because an entrance lies open to them and through them. Asconius calls them "protruding floorings." This is a fine description, provided you add that the porticos built by Constantine were constructed of stone, supported by marble columns, and covered with vaulted work, providing a most delightful sight for those walking, as well as an ample space for those seeking shelter in them. **GOAR.**

**p. 519 v. 4. *of the Senate***] <note>original Greek: Σενάτου (Senatou)</note> So that the New Rome <note>Constantinople</note> might imitate the Old, a senate house <note>Latin: *curia*</note> was established on the side of the great forum in both cities. This was called the *Sinatus* or *Senatus* of Constantinople, which Zonaras <note>a 12th-century Byzantine chronicler</note> describes as the "greatest house called the Senate." **GOAR.**

***ib.*** **v. 18. *natural hot springs***] <note>original Greek: αὐτομάτοις θερμοῖς (automatois thermois)</note> Understand these to be waters prepared for baths by the spontaneous benefit of nature, without any human industry. **GOAR.**

**p. 520 v. 10. *but that these were destroyed***] <note>original Greek: τὸ δὲ τούτους ἀναιρεθῆναι (to de toutous anairethēnai)</note> The sense would be more complete without these words, if you instead began with: "but since he was thoughtless." **GOAR.**

***ib.*** **v. 17. *to his brother Constantius***] This is false and against the truth of history. For Constantine <note>Constantine II</note>, while bringing war against the absent Constans <note>his other brother</note>, was killed by his army near Aquileia and perished. It is read correctly in this way a little later. **XYL.** <note>Wilhelm Xylander, a 16th-century humanist scholar</note>

**p. 521 v. 1. *bright-eyed***] <note>original Greek: χαροπός (charopos)</note> Here, as in the description of Justinian, the translator rendered "bright-eyed in appearance" as "fierce in appearance." However, it is well known that Justinian’s physical traits, like his character, displayed the greatest mildness. Therefore, I more correctly translate it—following Giambattista della Porta in his *Physiognomy*—as "with bluish-gray eyes" <note>Latin: *caesiis oculis*</note>, such as those of a lion. Suidas <note>a 10th-century Greek encyclopedist</note>, along with an anonymous dictionary in the Royal Library, interprets this same look as "twinkling and beautiful-eyed." **GOAR.**

***ib.*** **v. 8. *heterodoxy***] <note>original Greek: κακοδοξίᾳ (kakodoxia)</note> For he favored the Arian impiety <note>Arianism, a belief that Christ was not co-eternal with God the Father</note>. And it is correctly added in the margin: "Woe, for he was the last of all." He laments that the emperor suffered from this one vice, which is the greatest of all. **XYL.**

***ib.*** **v. 22. *Macelium***] This is a corrupted spelling. Ammianus <note>the Roman historian Ammianus Marcellinus</note>, not far from the beginning of Book 15, calls it "Marcellus' estate": I would therefore read it as *Marcellio* <note>Greek: Μαρκελλίῳ</note>.

<meta>This page continues the philological and historical commentary on the works of George Cedrenus, focusing on specific terminology and potential errors in earlier translations. It follows the previous page's pattern of providing corrections by the scholars Wilhelm Xylander (Xyl.) and Jacques Goar (Goar), particularly regarding ecclesiastical terms and historical figures from the 4th and 5th centuries.</meta>

# THE ANNOTATIONS OF XYLANDER AND GOAR

**[p. 784]**

In the writings of Sozomen <note>a 5th-century church historian</note>, the name is read as "to Marcellus" <note>original Greek: μαρκέλλῳ</note> at book 5, chapter 2; but it is nothing new for proper names to be corrupted in that writer. **XYLANDER.**

**p. 522 line 12. *from the eyes***] <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ ὀμμάτων</note> It was not "from the eyes"—meaning his eyesight was extinguished—that Didymus <note>Didymus the Blind, a famous 4th-century theologian in Alexandria</note> became known, but because he had "departed from seeing." This uses the same phrasing as when a man is called an *ex-consul* <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ ὑπάτων</note> or an *ex-scribe* <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ γραμματέων</note>. **GOAR.**

**p. 524 line 19. *the island of Thalamon***] In Sozomen it is read as "the island of Flavona" <note>original Greek: φλάβωνα νῆσον</note>, book 4, chapter 7. In that author, these and other matters are narrated more extensively. Marcellinus <note>the historian Ammianus Marcellinus</note> says that Gallus was killed at Pola in Istria near the end of book 14. **XYLANDER.**

**p. 525 line 20. *whatever in Macellum***] In the margin: "But regarding the following apostolic saying, what were you going to say, most wise Cedrenus? For the great Paul says further down: 'But if someone says to you, this is food offered to idols, do not touch it.'" This is truly a great question and contains much difficulty. See Augustine’s letter 154 to Poplicola. **XYLANDER.**

**p. 526 line 7. *shovels***] <note>original Greek: ἄμας</note> Let the translator explain, if he can, why he rendered this word as "urns." To the Greeks, it means "shovels" <note>original Latin: batillos</note>, which are instruments for moving earth out, just as *mattocks* <note>original Greek: σκαπάναι</note> are for digging. **GOAR.**

***ibid.*** **line 24. *proven***] <note>original Greek: δόκιμος</note> When this word is used of monks, it does not refer to someone who, having already been tested by the ascetic life, shines with advanced virtues. Rather, it properly refers to one whose strength, purpose, and spirit are currently being tested and shaped toward virtue. In a word, he is not a "distinguished monk" according to Xylander, but according to the common usage in monasteries, he is a "novice." **GOAR.**

**p. 529 line 10. *omophorion***] <note>original Greek: ὠμοφόρῳ</note> The translator rendered this literally as "shoulder-garment" <note>original Latin: humerale</note>. You should understand this as a band of honor encircling the shoulders of bishops, hanging down at the ends in both front and back, which the Latins call a *pallium* <note>the distinctive vestment of an archbishop</note>. The author calls it an *epomis* <note>original Greek: ἐπωμίδα</note> more frequently. **GOAR.**

**p. 530 line 10. *the well of the martyrium***] <note>original Greek: τὸ φρέαρ τοῦ μαρτυρίου</note> The translator thought this should be rendered "the well of the testimony," which is an error. For a *martyrium* <note>original Greek: μαρτύριον</note> is a church dedicated to a martyr, as John Chrysostom holds in homily 31, volume 5, right at the beginning. Here too, open mention is made of the temple of the martyr Acacius; and furthermore, in the time of Emperor Marcian, the house of Euphemia is written as a *martyrium* on page 303. **GOAR.**

***ibid.*** **line 23. *the myrrh***] <note>original Greek: τὸ μύρον</note> He understands the "sacred chrism" <note>anointing oil</note> established for anointing those initiated through baptism, the consecration of which—the subject of this discussion—is found in the *Euchologion* <note>the service book of the Eastern Church</note>. **GOAR.**

**p. 531 line 1. *at the Theophanies***] <note>original Greek: θεοφανίοις</note> The Greeks formerly used to confer baptism solemnly on the feast of Theophany <note>Epiphany</note>, just as they did at Easter and Pentecost. Following an old custom, they still consecrate its water today on the eve of the festival; Cedrenus assigns the institution of this custom to Peter the Fuller <note>a 5th-century Patriarch of Antioch</note>. **GOAR.**

***ibid.*** **line 3. *on Great Friday***] <note>original Greek: τῇ μεγάλῃ παρασκευῇ</note> The drowsy Xylander put "on the great vigil," where he could have written without difficulty "the Great Preparation" <note>Good Friday</note>, meaning the celebration of the Passion. **GOAR.**

<meta>This page continues the philological commentary on the historian George Cedrenus, focusing on the terminology of the imperial court and the Byzantine church. Scholars Jacques Goar and Wilhelm Xylander debate the meanings of hybrid Latin-Greek terms and provide historical context for imperial burials and administrative offices.</meta>

# ANNOTATIONS

**p. 531 line 11. *protector***] <note>original Greek: προτίκτωρ</note> This office is poorly described in the works of Meursius, but is treated most extensively by Pancirollus in his *Notices of the Empire*, chapter 89. This officer personally guarded the Emperor's side. **GOAR.**

**ib. line 12. *monument***] <note>original Greek: ἡρῶον</note> The tombs of the earlier emperors, placed by Constantius at the threshold of the Church of the Holy Apostles, are called "hero-monuments" <note>original Latin: heroum loca et heroicarum cinerum loculi</note>. Specifically, they were arranged "in a separate portico" <note>original Greek: ἐν ἰδιαζούσῃ μέντοι στοᾷ</note>—that is, in a specific portico constructed by the aforementioned Constantius. See the writings of Zonaras on Constantine, near the end. **GOAR.**

**ib. line 15. *trulla***] <note>meaning a dome or vaulted ceiling</note> So as not to hinder myself or others, I have rendered these words literally. It is indeed extremely difficult to correctly express these "hybrid" words, which the Greeks adopted poorly from the Latins and made their own by corrupting them. From Evagrius (Book 4, chapter 31), it appears that a *trulla* is a "tholos" <note>original Greek: θόλον</note>, which is to say, a rounded roof or dome. The Persian tree, whose miracle is mentioned there, is called a "peach tree" <note>original Greek: ῥοδακινέα</note> in the margin; this seemed worth noting in passing. **XYLANDER.**

**ibid. *vaulted, pulpit, soleas***] <note>original Greek: φουρνική, ἄμβωνα, σολέας</note> Xylander asserts these are hybrid words and fears he might hinder himself and others in interpreting them. But is it truly so difficult, as he thinks, to interpret "vaulted" <note>original Greek: τὸ φουρνική</note>? It refers to a church or a dome "adorned with arches" <note>original Latin: fornicibus laqueatam</note>, or as Meursius writes, "vaulted in the likeness of an oven" <note>original Latin: instar furni concameratam</note>; for the Greeks call an oven a *phournos* <note>original Greek: φοῦρνον</note>. The "pulpit" <note>original Greek: τὸν ἄμβωνα</note> is a "raised platform" <note>original Latin: suggestum altiorem</note> located in the middle of the church, which one ascends by steps from the east and west, and from which the Word of God is both read and announced. The "soleas" <note>original Greek: τὰς σολέας</note> are the "steps closest to the altar" <note>original Latin: gradus altari viciniores</note> where the subdeacons have their place, and from which—as if from the throne of Christ the King—the body of Christ is distributed to the faithful people. **GOAR.**

**p. 532 line 19. *tonsurers***] <note>original Greek: κουρίσκους</note> The translator is being childish here, suspecting this word refers to "little boys" <note>original Latin: puerulos</note>, whereas it actually refers to "barbers" in a diminutive sense. See Paul the Deacon's writings on Julian. **GOAR.**

**p. 534 line 6. *roga***] <note>original Greek: ῥόγαν</note> This refers to "military wages" <note>original Latin: stipendia militum</note> or "gifts" from the emperors given on the Calends of January, or on the birthdays of the princes and the royal cities, as Paul the Deacon narrates here. The word is derived from "distributing" <note>original Latin: erogando</note>. **GOAR.**

**p. 536 line 14. *priest-martyr***] <note>original Greek: ἱερομάρτυρος</note> The Greek Church gives the name "hieromartyrs" to those who were both bishops and martyrs. **GOAR.**

**p. 539 line 4. *and inscribed upon it***] The passage is mutilated. For this epitaph was made for him at Tarsus, which even the mention of the Cydnus river might show, even if we were not moved by the authority of Zonaras. **XYLANDER.**

**p. 541 line 5. *and so many***] <margin>Such a man did our time recognize you to be, thrice-august Isaac, even if you possess an incomparable advantage over others in your good qualities.</margin> He is speaking, of course, about Isaac Comnenus, who was a contemporary of Henry IV, approximately five hundred years ago. I have noted this so that—since it is clear enough that these words do not belong to Cedrenus himself but to a scribe—it might be apparent that this manuscript was not many years more recent than the original copy itself. **XYLANDER.**

**p. 542 line 16. *Anatolia***] This is the name given to that part of Asia which is separated from Europe by the Propontis <note>the Sea of Marmara</note> and the Hellespont, in which Bithynia is also located.

<sig>50</sig>

->George Cedrenus, Volume II.<-

<meta>This page continues the philological and historical commentary by Jacques Goar and Wilhelm Xylander on the work of George Cedrenus. The discussion shifts from architectural terms to geographical corrections, the naming of traitors, the nature of public buildings like the Nymphaeum, and the persistence of pagan New Year rituals during the reign of Emperor Valens.</meta>

# 786 XYLANDER AND GOAR

**XYLANDER** thinks that "Asia Minor" is incorrectly understood here. What the Greeks call *anatole* <note>original Greek: ἀνατολή, meaning "the East"</note> and the Turks call *Anatolai* (corrupted by others into *Natolia*), was likely a scribal error. The mistake arose from a similarity between the words; it should be corrected to read *Nacolia* <note>original Greek: Νακωλίας</note> instead of *Natolia*. It was at this city in Phrygia, situated on the Sangaris River, that Procopius met the Emperor Valens, and where the two armies engaged in battle. As Ammianus Marcellinus writes in Book 26: *Valens moved his camp toward Phrygia, and joined battle near Nacolia.* See also Leunclavius’s *Onomasticon* under the entry "Enagiol." **GOAR.**

**p. 543 line 16.** Along with these accounts, one should compare the histories of Marcellinus and other non-Christian authors with what Sozomen writes in Book 6 of his *Ecclesiastical History*. In his work, the traitors who betrayed Procopius are named Agelon and Gomarius (spelled with a long 'o' or omega); see 6:8. See also Nicephorus, Book 11, and Socrates, Book 4. I have corrected the oracle concerning Chalcedon using Zonaras; this oracle also appears in Socrates, 4:20. Cuspinianus discusses the nature of the *Nymphaeum* in his life of Valens; he cites a passage from Zonaras that matches Cedrenus, and in my judgment, he refutes those who hold different views. **XYLANDER** defines a *nymphaion* <note>original Greek: νυμφαῖον</note> as a public house dedicated to celebrating wedding feasts and games. Our author later says: *a nymphaeum, in which the weddings of those who did not have their own houses were held.* **GOAR.**

**ibid. line 17. *performed a festival***] <note>original Greek: ἱερομηνίαν ἐπετέλεσεν</note> Xylander translates this as "he kept a feast day." But which one? By what ritual? For what reason? I shall explain briefly. The City Prefect performed a celebration for the start of the New Year. Although pagan rituals had been suppressed, they were not extinguished during the too-brief reign of Jovian; indeed, they were now being renewed and stirred up again. Taking the opportunity of the completion of the Nymphaeum and the aqueduct, the Prefect held a dedication for both according to ancient custom, superstitiously praying for the permanence of these works and distributing a large gift of money <note>term: congiarium; a traditional Roman imperial distribution of cash or goods to the citizens</note> to the people. I am led to this unfavorable interpretation by the malicious spirit Valens showed toward the Christian religion and the liberty he granted to pagans. As Theodoret writes in 4:22, *those enslaved to error performed Hellenic rites.* Our author also mocks this same practice later in the entry for year 7. I am further moved by the specific meaning of the word *hieromenia* <note>meaning a "holy month" or "festival time"</note>, which has no Christian flavor. Stephanus teaches that this term carries more weight than *noumenia* <note>New Moon festival</note> or *Kalends*, both of which were outlawed by the Council in Trullo (Canons 62 and 65), citing a significant heap of authorities. Finally, Herodian admits that these are performed according to ancient and therefore profane ritual during the Saturnalia: *they celebrate the beginning of the month as a festival according to the custom of the Italians.* **GOAR.**

**p. 544 line 11. *provost***] <note>original Greek: πραιπόσιτον; from the Latin *praepositus*, a high-ranking official or chamberlain</note> Simocatta (4:15) writes: *He sent out a eunuch, the most distinguished of those assigned to the royal bodyguard, whom the Romans were accustomed to call a praepositus.* **GOAR.**

**ibid. *with the very robes***] <note>original Greek: αὐτοῖς τοῖς ἀμφίοις</note> That is to say, wearing the official garments that served as the insignia of their office. **GOAR.**

**ibid. line 19. *Dacibyza***] Sozomen (6:14) writes that legates came to Nicomedia to see Valens; he notes that their ship was set on fire while they were sailing across the middle of the Astacian Gulf, and the fire lasted until they reached Dacida, a coastal village of Bithynia. See also Suidas <note>a massive 10th-century Greek encyclopedia</note> under the entry "Valens."

### 787 ANNOTATIONS

**as far as Dakibiza.** In Nicephorus, this is read the same way as it is in Sozomen. **XYL.**

**p. 545 line 11. *which had occurred to Basil the Great***] In the Greek, the passage is corrupted, and the name of Julian—which is completely irrelevant to the context—has been forced in. I have followed the history provided by Sozomen (Book 6, chapter 15) and Nicephorus (Book 11, chapter 18). **XYL.**

**p. 546 line 8. *council in Illyricum***] At Sirmium <note>An important Roman city in Pannonia, modern-day Serbia, where several church councils were held</note>. **XYL.**

**p. 548 line 2. *Dominica***] In Zonaras, her name is Domnina. Our author calls her Dominica <note>original Greek: Δομνίκαν</note>, and others more correctly call her Dominica. However, where Valens is said to have been of a "two-thirds" <note>original Greek: διμοιραίᾳ</note> stature, I truly do not know what is meant to be understood. "Two-thirds" <note>original Greek: δίμοιρον</note> signifies a *bes* <note>A Roman unit representing two-thirds of a whole, such as eight ounces of a pound</note>. And if you translate *helikia* <note>original Greek: ἡλικίαν</note> as "age" (which seems out of place here), it is not clear why an age of 50 years would be called "two-thirds," unless perhaps 75 years is considered the full span of a man's life. **XYL.** Xylander seeks obstacles on a flat road here, and in his *Observations* he applies a term to age that he ought to have taken as referring to *stature*. But the words do not say "Valens was of mediocre stature"; rather, they suggest he was *so tall that he seemed to equal two-thirds [of some larger measure]* <note>Goar is arguing that Valens was exceptionally tall, rather than short or middle-aged</note>. Nor is this surprising: for his brother Valentinian was "great of body" <note>original Greek: εὐμεγέθης</note>, and nature could have granted an equal physical height to one who was quite different in terms of piety. **GOAR.**

**p. 550 line 12. *heretic*** <note>original Greek: αἱρετικός</note>] At the start of Gratian's reign, this word is entirely superfluous and contrary to the truth. Moreover, what is said about Theodosius is shown to be false by other historians. And the one who arranged for him to be killed is named by others as Maximus, not Maximianus (as our author has it). Indeed, our author also calls him Maximus later in the seventh year of Theodosius. **XYL.**

**p. 553 line 20. *valedictory oration*** <note>original Greek: συντακτήριον λόγον</note>] Most people, along with Xylander, believe this refers to the speech bearing this title delivered by Gregory the Theologian to settle the disputes among the bishops. Billius, in *Sacred Observations* 1.22, thinks it should rather be called a *farewell speech* <note>original Greek: ἀποτακτήριον</note>, by which one bids others be well. His conjecture is supported mainly by the words of Damascene (or the author of the pamphlet *That the dead are helped by the good deeds of the living*), in which those condemned and separated from the righteous are said "to lament the valedictory" <note>original Greek: θρηνεῖν τὸ συντακτήριον</note>—that is, "to mourn at the final departure and complain of the future eternal separation." The author also writes below on page 555 "to fulfill the valedictory" <note>original Greek: συντακτήριον ἐκπληροῦν</note>, meaning to commend the departure to God with formal prayers. An anonymous Lexicon states: "Valedictory orations are farewells given upon departure to officials, such as the valedictory of the great father Gregory the Theologian." The author relates that Bardas, the uncle of Michael, being about to set out to sea, "fulfilled the valedictory"—that is, he commended his journey to God with formal prayers before his departure. **GOAR.**

**p. 556 line 10. *for certain reasons***] This is "for some causes" <note>original Greek: δι' αἰτίας τινάς</note> in Zonaras. Our author has "because of *mitata*" <note>original Greek: διὰ μιτάτα; this term usually refers to the forced billeting of soldiers or official lodgings</note>, the meaning of which I do not grasp. This history is found in, among others, Theodorit's *Ecclesiastical History* 5:17, Sozomen 7:24, and Nicephorus 12:40. But "mitata" fits nowhere. Unless he calls a chariot race a *mitaton*, from the *metae* <note>the turning posts in a Roman circus</note> by which it was enclosed. **XYL.** Xylander lies here struck against the *meta* <note>A pun by Goar, suggesting Xylander has tripped up on his own interpretation</note>, unaware that the contests of charioteers driving their cars toward the *meta*...

### 788 NOTES BY XYLANDER AND GOAR

In the Circus Games, they are called **lodgings** <note>original: μιτάτα (mitata)</note>, and these gave the occasion for the sedition of the Thessalonians, about which Sozomen writes in Book 7, Chapter 24: <note>original: ἦν τῆς ἁμαρτίας πρόφασις τοιάδε. Βωτερίχου τότε τοῦ ἡγουμένου τῶν Ἰλλυριῶν στρατιωτῶν ἡνίοχος τὸν οἰνοχόον αἰσχρῶς ἰδὼν ἐπείρασε, καὶ συλληφθεὶς ἐν φρουρᾷ ἦν. ἐπισήμου δὲ ἱπποδρομίας ἐπιτελεῖσθαι μελλούσης, ὡς ἀναγκαῖον εἰς τὴν ἀγωνίαν ὁ Θεσσαλονικέων δῆμος ἐζήτει ἀφίεσθαι· ὡς δὲ οὐκ ἤνυεν, εἰς χαλεπὴν κατέστη στάσιν.</note> "The occasion for the crime was this: A charioteer attempted to shamefully seduce a cupbearer belonging to Boterichus, who was then the commander of the troops in Illyria. The charioteer was arrested and held in custody. When a famous horse race was about to be held, the common people of Thessalonica demanded he be released as he was necessary for the competition; when they did not succeed, they fell into a severe rebellion." I admit, however, that the term **lodgings** <note>original: τὰ μιτάτα</note> is derived from **military encampments** <note>original: metationibus</note>, where troops would stay while on the march. Theophanes also writes that the people were moved to sedition **because of the military lodgings** <note>original: διὰ τὰ μιτάτα τοῦ στρατοῦ; Goar's Latin: propter castrorum metationes</note>. **GOAR.**

It is not a slave-quarters <note>original: mancipium</note>, but a baker's workshop—a mill. Because of this, you should restore the unfaithful translation as follows: "And he abolished the custom by which animals that happened to wander into the public mill, or were found there by chance, were forced to drive the millstones until old age." **GOAR.**

page 572, line 2. *certain few things*] In the margin: "He spoke indeed before kings, and was not ashamed." <note>original: ὄντως ἐλάλησεν ἐναντίον βασιλέων, καὶ οὐκ ἠσχύνετο</note> He alludes to Psalm 118 <note>Psalm 119:46 in modern Bibles.</note>. But what follows concerning the origin of the word "indiction" <note>A 15-year cycle used in Roman accounting and dating.</note> is ridiculous. **XYL.**

page 575, line 18. *preconception* <note>original: προλήψει (prolepsei)</note>, that is, an opinion held not by certain and investigated reason, but by the authority of accepted custom. Justin Martyr used it this way in his letter to Zenas, and our author used it above. This Theophilus was the bishop of Alexandria. See Nicephorus Book 13, Chapter 4, and Sozomen Book 8, which book should be read alongside these histories. **XYL.**

page 578, line 3. *arrogant in conversation*] In the margin: "The anger of a righteous man is better than the honor of a wicked one." <note>original: θυμὸς δικαίου κρείσσων ἢ τιμὴ κακοῦ</note> This is a six-foot verse, indicating it is better for an upright man to be angry with you than for a wicked man to honor you. Likewise: "For he was truthful for the most part, because the mouth of the wise shall speak truth." <note>original: ἀληθευτικὸς γὰρ ἦν τὰ πολλά, ὅτι καὶ στόμα σοφοῦ λαλήσει ἀλήθειαν</note> For he cherished the truth, according to the saying: the mouth of the wise will speak truth. **XYL.**

page 581, line 5. *at the oak*] This was a suburb of Chalcedon <note>The site of the infamous "Synod of the Oak" in 403 AD where John Chrysostom was deposed.</note>. Sozomen 8.17. But even toward the end of Leo the Iconoclast, it is again written as *Praenetum* in our text. **XYL.** It was a suburb of the city of Constantinople, not of Chalcedon as Xylander imagines: for histories reveal that the Rufinianum palace was in Constantinople. Chrysostom himself, in his first letter to Innocent, complains at length about Theophilus, because having entered the great city of Constantinople, which is devoted to divine worship, he did not go to the church according to the custom prescribed for clerics. Instead, having bypassed its entrances, he disembarked from his ship and immediately hurried outside the city to that place where he later delivered a wicked sentence against John [Chrysostom]. That sacred custom, by which a bishop entering a city should first go to the church, [was practiced by] his sister Macrina, who was in failing health—

page 586, line 6. *pounds of gold* <note>original: χρυσίου λίτρας (chrysiou litras)</note>] A "libra" (pound) of gold, writes Budaeus <note>Guillaume Budé, a famous French humanist scholar of the 16th century.</note> in *De Asse* Book 5, can be valued at no less than one hundred gold *solidi* <note>The standard gold coin of the later Roman/Byzantine Empire.</note>. The author of the *Legal Lexicon* testifies that it weighed seventy-two. As the Empire declined, it was counted as only ten. For where Paul the Deacon writes "ten pounds," Theophanes puts "one hundred coins." In the final times, it was valued at only eight, according to Blastares in chapter 7 of the letter T: "The pound as we reckon it contains eight coins." Furthermore, the word for "gold," not "silver," should be read in the text. **GOAR.**

page 589, line 4. *Galba*] I do not see what just cause he had for numbering Galba among the wicked. The word in the codex is "Gallas" <note>original: γάλλας</note>, and I had no closer fit than "Galbas" <note>original: Γάλβας</note>. **XYL.**

page 590, line 19. *diptychs* <note>original: διπτύχοις (diptychis)</note>] These are twin tablets; from one, the names of the living are read, and from the other, the names of the dead among the communicants of the church are read during the solemnities of the Mass. **GOAR.**

page 591, line 4. *regarding the apple*] As for the apple given as a gift to Paulinus by Eudocia, in Nicephorus 14.23 one reads not "apple" but "sheep." And truly, the word *melon* <note>original: μῆλον</note> signifies both. However, the account of Cedrenus, in all its circumstances, seems more likely to be about an apple than a sheep. As for what is read in Nicephorus—that Eudocia replied to her husband that his gift was "sweetly feeding" at her home—if it is so in the Greek, it must certainly be understood as a sheep. How the Greek stands there, I do not know. <note>In Greek, the word "melon" (μῆλον) can mean apple, but with a different vowel length or context, it refers to a sheep or goat. This led to historical confusion in the famous story of Empress Eudocia's gift, which triggered her husband's fatal jealousy.</note>

### ANNOTATIONS.

Certainly Zonaras, just like our author, says that Eudocia replied that she had eaten the apple <note>original: "τὸ μῆλον" (to melon). This refers to a famous legend where Empress Eudocia was accused of adultery after an oversized apple she received from the Emperor was later found in the possession of a courtier.</note>. Who would believe a response about a sheep? <note>There is a linguistic confusion here: in Greek, "melon" can mean both "apple" and "sheep." Xylander is arguing the "apple" reading makes more sense.</note> And in Nicephorus, after chapter 49, this very thing is called the "apple of discord" <note>original: "μῆλον ἔριδος" (melon eridos)</note>, as is noted in the margin; and it is well known that an apple was proposed by Eris <note>The goddess of Strife</note> at the wedding of Peleus. It does not seem very probable that the author played on an ambiguity from "sheep" to "apple." I thought the reader should be warned of this, lest they think I wrote something different from the Latin Nicephorus without reason. **XYL.**

page 593 line 3. *his own syncellus*] This was, unless I am mistaken, Anastasius the priest, who is mentioned shortly. What a <term>syncellus</term> <note>Literally "cell-mate." A high-ranking clergyman who lived in the same quarters as a Patriarch to act as a witness to his character and a close confidential advisor.</note> is, I explained in the first annotation. However, this history in the manuscript is quite confused and concise. You will read it usefully in Socrates [Scholasticus] 7.32 and following, and in Evagrius, Book 1. **XYL.** Lest anything be rashly forced in here regarding the *syncellus* (leaving more important matters for another place), I remind you that the word "syncellus" <note>original: "σύγκελλος"</note> is a mark of dignity and honor, not of office. Patriarchs distinguished with this title those whom they admitted into their fellowship as companions of private life, confidants of their mind, mediators in business, directors of spirit, fathers for confessions, and thus sharers of the same hearth and "cell-mates" <note>original: "concellaneum"; for "kellion" <gloss>original: "κελλίον"</gloss>, as you will read, is a cell</note>. Hence, this Anastasius the priest, the *syncellus* of Nestorius, is described by Evagrius (6.2) as his fiercest supporter and joined to him as a companion when he set out for his bishopric; and as a *syncellus* thereafter, according to Socrates (7.32): *Anastasius the priest remained with him, having been sent from Antioch with him. He held this man in great honor and used him as a counselor in affairs.* <note>original Greek: "συνῆν αὐτῷ Ἀναστάσιος πρεσβύτερος, ἅμα αὐτῷ ἐκ τῆς Ἀντιοχείας σταλείς. τοῦτον διὰ τιμῆς εἶχε πολλῆς, καὶ ἐν τοῖς πράγμασι συμβούλῳ ἐχρῆτο."</note> The things Xylander notes he observed elsewhere about the *syncellus* are superfluous and out of place here. For by what reasoning would a man be designated as the successor to the patriarch who did not succeed him, and who at that time was usually announced as the heir to the pontifical throne not by the patriarch, but by the emperor? **GOAR.**

ibid line 7. *scholasticus of the Augusta*] A rhetorician according to Nicephorus (14.32). **XYL.** One of the guards <note>original: "scholaribus"</note> of the Augusta’s <note>The title for the Empress.</note> household. Regarding the "Scholae" <note>Elite imperial guard units.</note>, see Pancirollus on the *Notitia Imperii*, chapter 63. **GOAR.**

ibid line 11. *Proclus*] He was the bishop of Cyzicus, and (I think) for the sake of honor delivered a sacred sermon to the people at Byzantium, with Nestorius presiding. See Nicephorus. The same is said of Eusebius, bishop of Dorylaeum (14.47) and Evagrius (1.9). **XYL.**

page 594 line 4. *sacred letter*] This is how imperial edicts concerning church matters are sometimes called. I have observed that in ecclesiastical histories, they are called "divine sacred letters" <note>original: "divales sacras"</note>. **XYL.**

page 595 line 16. *Oasis* is in Arabia. Zonaras. **XYL.**

page 598 line 14. *in Anaplo*] A place in Constantinople so named. **GOAR.** The translator of Nicephorus translates *Anaplous* <note>original: "ἀνάπλους"</note> as "crossing" (15.22). It appears to have been a suburb of Constantinople. **XYL.**

page 599 line 9. *of the foederati* <note>original: "φοιδεράτων" (phoideratōn). Federated troops, usually barbarian allies serving under their own leaders within the Roman army.</note>] "Foederati" means "under treaty," <note>original: "ὑπόσπονδοι" (hypospondoi)</note> writes Harmenopulus (Book 4, title 12). # XYLANDER AND GOAR

When Constantine founded the city in his own name, the Goths participated in the work, *who, having entered into a treaty with the emperor, offered forty thousand of their men to him as support against various nations.* <note>original: "qui foedere inito cum imperatore quadraginta suorum milia illi in solatia contra gentes varias obtulere."</note> This number and these thousands are still named in the state today as the *foederati* <note>treaty-allies</note>. And as far as the current topic regarding Theodosius is concerned, it is added below: the entire army remained in the service of the Emperor Theodosius, submitting to the Roman Empire and forming one body with the soldiery; those thousands of treaty-allies, formerly established under Prince Constantine, were renewed, and they themselves were called *foederati*. **GOAR.**

page 600 line 12. *and his own baiulus*] <note>original: "suumque baiulum"</note> indeed, this is the word used literally in the Greek, and perhaps it denotes the person to whom the emperor had committed all his affairs, *the one who was the "factotum" or do-it-all.* <note>original German: "der das fac totum were"</note> **XYL.** A <term>baiulus</term> <note>original: "βαΐουλος" (baioulos)</note> is one who is called a steward <note>original: "ἐπίτροπος" (epitropos)</note>, according to Gregoras 4.9. However, Moschopulus says a tutor and physical trainer <note>original: "παιδαγωγὸς καὶ παιδοτρίβης" (paidagogos kai paidotribes)</note> is what is called a *baiulus*. An author writing about this same Antiochus on folio 334 says: "Having sent a certain Antiochus, a wonderful and most learned man, as steward and tutor." Leunclavius says: The Grand Baiulus of the emperor is the moderator and arbiter of his counsels and actions, or even the guardian of an emperor who is still a minor. **GOAR.**

*ibid.* The word "Papa" here signifies a cleric, or *a priest*; <note>original German: "ain Pfaffen"</note> a term Augustine and others often use in their letters. Zonaras explicitly writes that Euphemianus was made a cleric of the college at Chalcedon. The narratives that follow are in poor condition in the Greek text. **XYL.** There is a difference between a *pápas* <note>original: "πάπας"</note> and a *papás*: <note>original: "παπᾶς"</note> the latter is a priest or private cleric, though living in the secular world; the former is the Pope, the Roman Pontiff. An author recently mentioned the former on folio 339: "Cyril of Alexandria, who held the place of Pope Celestine of Rome." Allatius and Codinus also write about this. Choniates even asks, "Where is the priest?" <note>original: "ποῦ ποτὲ ὁ παπᾶς;" (pou pote ho papas?)</note> Theophanes writes: "Cyrus, having fled to the church, became a priest." **GOAR.**

*ibid. line 17. papers*] <note>original: "χάρτους" (chartous)</note> however, the more common word is *chartes*: <note>original: "χάρτης"</note> from which, I believe, come the old French words *charte* and *chartre*. An anonymous lexicon in the Royal Library derives it from the word "to contain." <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ χωρῶ" (apo tou choro)</note> **GOAR.**

page 601 line 2. *Hypogotthos*] Perhaps the Visigoths. **XYL.**

*ibid. line 3. Abaris*] From this comes the "Avares" <note>the Avars</note>, just as "Serbi" is used for "Servi" and other such examples. **XYL.**

*ibid. line 6. Keeper of the Vessels*] <note>original: "σκευοφύλαξ" (skeuophylax)</note> The translator of Nicephorus identifies this as the keeper of the sacred offerings, 14.47. **XYL.**

*ibid. line 14. Zumnas*] In the selections of Theodore Anagnostes, right at the beginning, a man named Tzumas is said to have been killed by Pulcheria. **XYL.**

page 603 line 2. *he sends for the patriarch*] <note>original: "μεταστέλλεται τὸν πατριάρχην"</note> Marcian was the first of the Christian princes to receive the insignia of the empire from a high priest. **GOAR.**

*ibid. line 12. of the number*] <note>original: "νουμέρου" (noumerou)</note> Nothing is more common among the Latins than using the word *numerus* <note>number</note> for a cohort of soldiers. From them, the word was transferred to the Greeks. Having rejected the borrowed term, the Greeks used a word from their own storehouse, *arithmon*, <note>original: "ἀριθμόν"</note> which was discussed above. Oecumenius on Acts chapter 15 says: "a 'band' <note>original: "σπεῖρα" (speira)</note> is what we call..."

# ANNOTATIONS. 793

Now a *number* <note>original: "νούμερον", a late Roman military unit</note>. But what indeed are *cohorts* <note>original: "σπεῖραι"</note>? Suidas says: "multitudes of armies, phalanxes, units." **GOAR.**

page 606 line 18. *ancestral* <note>original: "avitus"</note>] *abibos* <note>original: "ἄβιβος"</note>. But I have followed the more corrected writers. **XYL.**

*ib. line 22. Symeon the stylite of the monastery* <note>original: "ὁ τῆς μάνδρας στυλίτης Συμεών"</note>] Rosweidius, in the notes published on the life of this elder, demonstrates that there were three Simeons, and those same three were stylites <note>saints who lived atop pillars</note>. He recounts that one lived as a *priest and archimandrite* <note>original: "πρεσβύτερον καὶ ἀρχιμανδρίτην", a superior of a monastery</note>, and another lived on the *Wonderful Mountain* <note>original: "ἐν Θαυμαστῷ ὄρει"</note>, a very high mountain so named. This one, who was the first of all, is more frequently described by the author as having ascended the column *at Anaplus* <note>original: "ἐν Ἀνάπλῳ"</note>, coming from the monastery <note>original: "τῆς μάνδρας"</note> where he spent some of his youth. **GOAR.**

page 607 line 2. The name of Eudoxia is placed here instead of Eudocia, a confusion encountered elsewhere as well. And what is said shortly after—that Anatolius succeeded Atticus—is clearly erroneous: for after Chrysostom, the succession was Arsacius, then Atticus, Sisinnius, Nestorius, Maximian, Proclus, Flavian, and then Anatolius. Later, mention is made of Timothy Aelurus. In the margin it says, *the thrice-cursed one confirmed his nickname by his deeds* <note>original: "ἐβεβαίωσε τὴν ἐπωνυμίαν τοῖς ἔργοις ὁ τρισκατάρατος"</note>. Now, *aelurus* <note>original: "aelurus"</note> signifies a cat, as we commonly call it; and the tricks and nature of that animal are well known. Regarding the fire in Constantinople, consult Evagrius book 2, chapter 13. In the *Eclogues* of Theodore, one reads *Thomas, the son of Amantius* <note>original: "Θωμᾶ τῶν Ἀμαντίου"</note>. **XYL.**

page 611 line 12. *cleric* <note>original: "κληρικῷ"</note>] The name of "cleric" among the Greeks is not obtained by everyone admitted to the clergy, but only by the one who holds a dignity or office in the church. From this, you can perceive who the patriarch's clerics are—namely, those who perform some office around him. Every monk is excluded from this group; for although the more learned Greeks number them among the clergy, they never allow a monk to be or be called a "cleric." **GOAR.**

*ib. line 21. general of the entire East* <note>original: "στρατηγὸν τῆς ἑῴας ἁπάσης"</note>] He who, as the empire aged, would be called by the author the *Domestic of the East, of the Easterners, of the Dawn, or of the Themes of the East* <note>original: "δομέστικος τῆς ἀνατολῆς, τῶν ἀνατολικῶν, τῶν ἑῴων, τῶν θεμάτων τῆς ἀνατολῆς"</note>, is the same person who is called the "Praetorian Prefect of the East" by the Latins, if I guess correctly. See Pancirolus in the *Notitia Imperii* <note>a document detailing the administrative organization of the Roman Empire</note>. **GOAR.**

page 612 line 16. *of troparia* <note>original: "tropariorum"</note>] That is, of sacred hymns or songs. Likewise below. **XYL.** The Greeks sing various types of hymns in the churches, produced by various authors and designated by different names; many of these they call *troparia* <note>original: "τροπάρια"</note>, *from the word "to turn"* <note>original: "παρὰ τοῦ τρέπεσθαι"</note>, because they are to be "turned"—or more aptly put, sung—in imitation of others that serve as models for their melody. I called them *melodic measures* in my *Euchologion* <note>the primary prayer book of the Eastern Orthodox Church</note>, as being *composed in meters according to the manner of others and intended for singing.* Originally, they were produced as poems, and elegant ones at that; but later, while the number of syllables was preserved and the vowel quantity was neglected, there emerged a plain, unrefined, and austere composition *of troparia* <note>original: "τῶν τροπαρίων"</note>. Nevertheless, the authors of these never declared themselves stripped of the distinguished title of "poets." Allatius and Arcudius have discussed troparia and their poets at greater length. **GOAR.**

page 613 line 12. *65 [units] of gold* <note>original: "χρυσίου ρρξε"</note>] The doubled letter rho <note>ρρ</note> is placed as a sign for a <term>centenarium</term> <note>a Roman unit of weight equivalent to 100 pounds</note>; thus it should have been translated as 65 centenaria of gold and [X] centenaria of silver—

# ANNOTATIONS BY XYLANDER AND GOAR

70 centenaria <note>a *centenarium* was a unit of weight, usually representing 100 pounds of gold</note>. This is discovered both by the matter itself and from the repetition of this mark further down in the section on Michael the Paphlagonian, concerning the greed of Theophanes, the Metropolitan of Thessalonica; where it appears the same amount was a pound. Nor is it unknown that a pound was also a *mina* <note>an ancient unit of weight and currency</note>. It is repeated later during the reign of Zoe after the death of Calaphates, where 53 centenaria are expressly mentioned as fifty-three <note>original: "πεντήκοντα τρία"</note>. In Procopius, it is said that Leo spent three hundred thousand on this war (Book 3 of *The Vandalic War*); in Nicephorus (15.27), it is twelve hundred centenaria—weights of gold. How these agree with each other and with Cedrenus, I do not know. But if I had been permitted to hear either of these writers in the original Greek, it might have been easier for me to divine the truth. **XYL.**

Xylander thinks that two *rho* characters <note>original: "ρ' ρ'"</note>, with a transverse line added and an accent placed over both, signify a centenarium <note>original: "κεντηνάριον"</note>, which he estimates at a thousand gold pieces according to the calculation of Johann Kahl. This is indeed learned. But where he counts only 65 centenaria of gold, and 70 of silver, let him see how small a sum that is—hardly enough for an army exceeding one hundred thousand men and for exhausting the royal treasuries. Theophanes clearly writes that the amount rose to 1300 centenaria, with whom Procopius (cited by Xylander himself) agrees; nor does Nicephorus differ from the calculation of both except by 100 centenaria. Hence it is clear to me that Xylander erred from the true number by 1225 centenaria, or perhaps misread the arithmetic symbols. **GOAR.**

page 613 line 18. What follows concerning the son of Aspar accords poorly with the narration of other historians, especially Zonaras and Nicephorus; it seems to be something stitched together from mutilated verses. Euthymius was a monk, and it is established from Nicephorus (14.52) that Cedrenus is speaking of him here. **XYL.**

page 614 line 4. *having crowned the emperor* <note>original: "στέψας βασιλέα"</note>] from which perhaps the custom flowed, so that those whom later princes created as colleagues in the empire, they also crowned with their own hand. See Codinus, chapter 17. **GOAR.**

ib. line 8. *to her temple* <note>original: "τῷ ναῷ αὐτῆς"</note>] this temple bore the name of Anastasia for a threefold reason: the author reports one here, and you will find two others mentioned on page 315. **GOAR.**

ib. line 9. In writing *Augustulus* instead of *Augustalius*, I followed the more corrected authors, just as I used *Verina* for *Berenice*. **XYL.**

page 615 line 8. The statement that Zeno is said to have held the empire for 27 years is not true; instead of 27 <note>original: "κζ"</note>, one should write 17 <note>original: "ιζ"</note>. The historical witnesses, and specifically Evagrius (3.29), confirm this. **XYL.**

page 617 line 11. *with types* <note>original: "cum typis"</note>] that is, by a universal edict, which naturally pertained to everyone. Theodorus the Reader calls it a *general type* <note>original: "τύπον γενικόν"</note> in this very history. Cedrenus uses this word quite often, and sometimes employs *to type* <note>original: "τυποῦν"</note> instead of "to decree." Nicephorus, as I found noted in the margin of the version, uses *encyclical syllables* <note>original: "ἐγκυκλίους συλλαβάς"</note>, of which he also provides an example (15.3). Later I called it a general edict. Evagrius also calls circular letters *encyclical epistles* <note>original: "ἐγκυκλίους ἐπιστολάς"</note>; consult his third book. **XYL.**

# ANNOTATIONS.

p. 617 v. 14. *papa* <note>meaning "father" or "pope"</note>: although the Greeks are accustomed to attach this name to any priest without distinction, they nevertheless attribute "the Papa" <note>original: "τοῦ πάπα"</note> only to the Roman and Alexandrian pontiffs. And lest we seek external witnesses, we read the bishop of Rome written this way in our author on pages 421, 435, and elsewhere throughout. That the Alexandrian bishop was also called this is demonstrated by the address made to Timothy Aelurus <note>a 5th-century Patriarch of Alexandria</note> by the inhabitants of that city: *You have fed your enemies, Papa* <note>original: "ἐψώμισας τοὺς ἐχθρούς σου πάπα"</note>. This is also shown by the titles of documents issuing from the Alexandrian see, ever since Celestine wrote to Cyril so that he might hold his place in the Synod of Ephesus. *From which time it is said*, writes Nicephorus (14.34), *that he also received the wearing of the miter, took the title of Papa, and was named the judge of the world.* **GOAR.**

p. 618 v. 19. *the sphere of the statue of the Forum* <note>original: "ἡ σφαῖρα τοῦ ἀνδριάντος τοῦ φόρου"</note>] That is certainly the *globe* which the statue of Constantine, erected in the Forum, held in its hand; it was not a *globe of a column*, as Xylander wrongly has it—unless by the word "column" he understands the statue placed on the Porphyry Column, of which the author already spoke on folio 265. **GOAR.**

*ibid. v. 20. of the Taurus* <note>original: "τοῦ Ταύρου"</note>] A square <note>the Forum Tauri</note> of the city so named. **GOAR.**

p. 619 v. 8. *defender* <note>original: "ἔκδικον" (ekdikon)</note>] Xylander is far from fulfilling the duty of a Latin translator, as he translates *ekdikon* not as *defender* <note>original: "defensorem"</note> but as *executor* <note>original: "exsecutorem"</note>. What was he executing, pray tell? A *defender* certainly devoted himself to the causes of the poor and the churches; the martyr Sebastian held this title. The Greek Church reckons the same office—indeed several, and a primate over them all—among the officials mentioned by Codinus. Regarding these, see the Council of Carthage in Balsamon, canon 78. **GOAR.**

p. 620 v. 3. "*Oasis* <note>original: "Ὄασιν"</note>] A "Great" one, to be sure, located near Abydos; sterile, uncultivated, and uninhabited, into which criminals were deported. Pancirollus says more on this in chapter 140. **GOAR.**

*ibid. v. 7. with the Trisagion* <note>original: "τρισαγίῳ"</note>] This is a prayer than which nothing is more frequent on the lips of the Greeks: *Holy God, Holy Mighty, Holy Immortal, have mercy on us.* Before the final words of this prayer, the followers of Peter the Fuller <note>a 5th-century Patriarch of Antioch</note> wanted these others inserted: *who was crucified for us.* Furthermore, this hymn is not called "most holy" in any general sense, as Xylander suggests, but *thrice holy* <note>original: "ter sanctus"</note> in the Greek Church, because of the word "holy" being repeated three times. **GOAR.**

*ibid. v. 17. Euthymius*] One should read Euphemius, according to Nicephorus, Zonaras, Theodore, Suidas, and Evagrius, even though further down under Anastasius it is read this way again. Moreover, Zonaras advises at the beginning of the reign of Anastasius that having been a *silentiary* <note>original: "silentiarium"</note> was not an office of great dignity. Cuspinian translates it as *minister of quiet*, and thinks it is what the legal experts call a "most distinguished man of the sacred palace"; and so it is read in Procopius (Book 2 of the *Persian War*) that Adolius the Armenian was the emperor's *minister for matters of quiet* in the palace, a duty which the Romans call *silentiarius*. But it would be useful to know what the Greek texts have. Others, in my judgment not ineptly, think he was a *courtly scribe*, that is, one who is now called a secretary. I think it is more correctly written *silentiarios* <note>original: "σιλεντιάριος"</note> than *silentarios*. Certainly, in the time of Leo the Iconoclast, *to make a silentium* <note>original: "σιλέντιον ποιεῖν"</note> means to write a decree, where the acts of Leo with...

# THE ANNOTATIONS OF XYLANDER AND GOAR

The deeds are attributed to Germanus. **XYLANDER.** The school of the silentiaries <term>Silentiarii: a prestigious group of court officials tasked with maintaining order and silence in the imperial palace</term> was the most distinguished among the emperor's bodyguards, to which Anastasius was appointed. Evagrius writes in his *Ecclesiastical History* (3.29): *He placed the crown upon Anastasius, who had not yet entered the Senate, but was enrolled in the so-called school of the silentiaries.* <note>original: "Ἀναστασίῳ τὸν στέφανον περιτίθησιν οὔπω μὲν ἥκοντι εἰς γερουσίαν, ἐν δὲ τῇ λεγομένῃ τῶν σιλεντιαρίων σχολῇ καταλεγομένῳ"</note>. These officials are called "makers of quiet" <note>original: "ἡσυχοποιοί"</note> by the Greeks; according to Agathias, they are those who command silence and peace at the emperor's side, being "overseers of the silence surrounding the king" <note>original: "ἐπιστάται τῆς ἀμφὶ τὸν βασιλέα σιγῆς"</note>. They are numbered among the most illustrious by Dorotheus: for their service is, as he says, a "splendid army" <note>original: "λαμπρὰ στρατιά"</note>, although Zonaras writes that this Anastasius held one of the "lowly dignities" <note>original: "τῶν χαμαιζήλων ἀξιωμάτων"</note> or bottom-tier ranks; he was certainly famous among the courtiers, yet he seemed to have been placed far from any hope of seeking the imperial purple. **GOAR.**

p. 622 v. 19. *kalegia* <note>original: "καλήγια"</note>] Xylander thinks this is an allusion to the Latin *caligae* <note>heavy military boots</note>. But how could Zeno have gnawed on and "devoured" linen, wool, or silk? It is certainly easier to imagine him eating shoes, which the word *kalegia* refers to. The *Euchologium* <note>a Greek Orthodox prayer book</note> removes all doubt; there, a candidate for the religious life about to receive the monk's habit—a rite I once attended—is ordered to cast off the "kalegia on his feet" <note>original: "τὰ ἐν ποσὶ καλήγια"</note>, baring his feet not of military boots, but of shoes. **GOAR.**

ibid. v. 22. *whence—from then on* <note>original: "ὅθεν— ἔκτοτε"</note>] Xylander translated this in a mutilated and ignorant fashion. I restore it as: "from which time, by his command, so that Zeno would not be shut in again, guards of the royal tombs were established." **GOAR.**

p. 623 v. 2. *who are called Nephthalitae*] Judging the preceding text to be mutilated, I have marked it with an asterisk. These are the Huns who are neighbors to the Persians; they are called Euthalitae <note>the Hephthalites or "White Huns"</note> by Procopius in Book 1 of the *Persian War*, at least as read in Volaterranus's version. For they are also called Nephthalitae in Nicephorus (16.36), and a people living in the East is mentioned in Suidas, citing Josephus. **XYLANDER.**

p. 626 v. 3. *a confession is demanded from Euthymius* <note>original: "ἀπαιτεῖται ὁμολογίαν παρὰ Εὐθυμίου"</note>] From this event, it later became the custom for emperors and princes to publish their faith and confirm it with a written oath. Indeed, Zeno professed his faith in writing when he later sought to return and reclaimed his power by force (see page 358 and page 403). **GOAR.**

p. 627 v. 6. *folles* <note>original: "φόλλεις"</note>] Small coins. Other authors also mention this currency; read about the end of Conon the Iconoclast in our author. Moreover, Suidas teaches that a *follis* is an obol <note>a small silver or copper coin</note>. He also testifies that Timotheus of Gaza, the grammarian, produced a tragedy against Anastasius because of this tax (see under the entry *Timotheus*). **XYLANDER.**

ibid. v. 19. *of John Scethis*] This is read as "the Scythian" <note>original: "Scythae"</note> in Evagrius (3.35) and in the second book of the *Excerpts* of Theodore the Reader. He is speaking of Longinus, the brother of Zeno, and his associate Theodore, who were rebelling by stirring up the Isaurians <note>a people from the rugged mountainous region of southern Asia Minor</note>; although Zonaras considers this Longinus to be different from Zeno's brother. **XYLANDER.**

p. 628 v. 14. *Arethas*] I believe this refers to a Persian leader, who is called Zarethos in Nicephorus (16.35). Amida is a city in Mesopotamia. Procopius writes at length about this Persian war in Book 1. **XYLANDER.**

Regarding Anastasiopolis, which is located 98 stadia <note>about 11 miles</note> from Nisibis, see the cited passage in Procopius. As for what *opheia* <note>original: "ὠφεῖα"</note> are, Suidas seems to teach us when he interprets the word as a "storehouse" <note>original: "ταμιεῖον"</note>; in Greek, it is also used in the *Pandects* <note>a compendium of Roman law</note> to mean a granary. Otherwise, I would have thought it should be written as *odea* <note>original: "ὠδεῖα"</note>, meaning concert halls. **XYLANDER.**

ib. v. 21. *Barbarum*] In Nicephorus, the name is read as "Barba" (16.35). Euchaita is a city near the Black Sea, as is clear from what follows. **XYLANDER.**

p. 631 v. 14. I have used the word "dwellings" <note>original: "mansiones"</note> literally for those places commonly called monasteries or cloisters, from which the "enclosed monks" <note>original: "ἔγκλειστοι"</note> take their name. In some places in the margin, "monastery" <note>original: "μονή"</note> is written where the text has "temple" <note>original: "ναός"</note>. On the Monastery of Stoudios and its sanctuary, see also Suidas. **XYLANDER.** On the enclosed monks, see Balsamon's commentary on Canon 41 of the Council of Trullo. **GOAR.**

p. 632 v. 8. *had cut them down with hooked swords*] <note>original: "ἠγκυλοκόπησεν"</note> In Nicephorus, it is said that they continued to speak even after their tongues were cut out (16.36). **XYLANDER.** I provide a more accurate interpretation: Cabades <note>a Persian King</note> had tortured certain Christians in Persia with spiked "scorpions" <note>a type of whip or hook</note>, but they nevertheless walked afterward. For the Greek root "to strike" <note>original: "κόπτω"</note>, when joined with another word in later Greek usage, never indicates a single cutting, but rather the frequency of a repeated action. Thus, "to strike with a rod" means to beat repeatedly with sticks, and "to strike with a hammer" means to pound again and again. Therefore, "hook-striking" <note>original: "ἀγκυλοκόπῶ"</note> should be understood as a tearing of the legs and feet performed with hooked spikes rather than a cutting with swords. **GOAR.**

p. 636 v. 14. *Acyntian* <note>original: "Ἀκυντιανῇ"</note>] Made of yellow Acyntian marble, brought from Mount Acyntius on the shore of Chalcedon. I interpret *larnax* <note>original: "λάρνακα"</note> as a chest or a tomb, not a mere box. Constantine was laid in porphyry (that is, red marble); this person in yellow; Justin in Proconnesian (that is, white); and Tiberius in prasin (that is, green) marble. **GOAR.**

p. 637 v. 1. *He crowned Lupicia* <note>original: "Λουππικίαν ἔστεψεν"</note>] Justin is the first recorded to have crowned his wife with such a famous ceremony. You can find the ritual for the coronation in Codinus (chapter 17) and at the end of our *Euchologion* <note>a prayer book of the Greek Church</note>. **GOAR.**

ib. v. 2. *the factions* <note>original: "δῆμοι"</note>] In the plural, this does not mean the common people as a mass, but the various factions and parties of the people in the games, processions, and public assemblies. They were distinguished by the different colors they wore, and they were often divided by their different loyalties. I have discussed this somewhat above and will do so more extensively below. **GOAR.**

ib. v. 13. *concerning the one who did not die*] See Nicephorus (18.45). **XYLANDER.**

p. 638 v. 6. *the Blue faction held dominant power* <note>original: "ἐδημοκράτει τὸ Βένετον μέρος"</note>] That is, the Blue party stood out in power above the other three, and it devastated the Green party—its constant rival—with violence, looting, rioting, and slaughter. He calls the Blue faction...

<meta>This page continues the scholarly commentary by Wilhelm Xylander and Jacques Goar on Byzantine history, focusing on the reign of Emperor Justinian, the culture of the chariot racing factions in Constantinople, and the origins of religious festivals.</meta>

# BY XYLANDER AND GOAR

one part was to be distinguished by its conspicuous Blue color <note>original: "Veneto"</note> from the Green color <note>original: "Prasina"</note>. Of the two remaining parts, one used White and the other Rose-colored insignia. These factions, as we have recently stated, were each known by their own names; they were forged from the differing passions of those competing in chariot races and the speed of the runners. From these opposing rivalries in the games, even more serious dissensions were born throughout the city, which drove the citizens to arms, seditions, and all manner of wicked crimes. The author will provide examples from the 22nd year of Justinian (p. 375), the 35th year (p. 387), and the final year of Maurice (p. 403). Simocatta <note>Theophylact Simocatta, a 7th-century Byzantine historian</note> mentions this in many places in his history. The <term>demarchs: leaders of the people</term> <note>original: "δήμαρχοι"</note> were their heads and leaders, whom you might call "tribunes" in our own tongue, and the <term>demoteuontes: faction members</term> <note>original: "δημοτεύοντες"</note> were those individuals assigned and enrolled in a specific part. See the aforementioned Simocatta (8.7). Hence, what the author calls "world-wide democracies" <note>original: "κοσμικὰς δημοκρατίας"</note> in the 31st year of Justinian (p. 386) actually refers to the **general conflicts** of one faction against another, occurring not only in Constantinople but everywhere. And his use of the word <term>demoteuein: to enroll</term> <note>original: "δημοτεύειν"</note> means **to review the people by tribes and factions and then to number them among the rest of the military**. One should certainly consult Balsamon on Canon 24 of the Council in Trullo. **GOAR.**

p. 639 v. 9. Regarding the Homerites <note>The Himyarite Kingdom in modern-day Yemen</note>, one should consult Nicephorus (8.35 and 17.32), who has a more detailed description of the history of Arethas and Elesbaas (17.6). But where "agitators of the people" is translated, these are the <term>demoi: the factions</term> <note>original: "δήμοι"</note>: I think he is speaking of the Blue faction. Procopius also mentions the Homerites in Book 1 of the *Persian War*: and our author mentions them below in the section on Muhammad. **XYLANDER.**

ib. v. 23. *The Scirtus river shall leap*] In Nicephorus (17.3), a Greek hexameter is written in the margin: "The Scirtus shall leap a leap of evil for the citizens." <note>original: "Σκίρτος σκιρτήσει τε κακὸν σκίρτημα πολίταις"</note> I would have written *something* <note>original: "τι"</note> instead of *and* <note>original: "τε"</note>, unless perhaps this is one verse out of many where a conjunction is appropriate: **the leaping of the Scirtus shall afflict the wretched citizens.** <note>The Scirtus river was known for its sudden, violent flooding; its name literally means "The Leaper."</note> **XYLANDER.**

p. 641 v. 5. *Holding over* <note>original: "ἐπέχον"</note>] I read this as *being distant* <note>original: "ἀπέχον"</note>. That plain is called "The Seventh" <note>original: "Ἕβδομος"</note> because it is seven miles away. I have discussed this above. **GOAR.**

ib. v. 20. *Hypapante* <note>The Feast of the Presentation of Jesus at the Temple</note>] This name was given because the people went out, as it were, to meet Christ in the dedication of the Temple. It is the solemnity we usually call the Purification. I first learned this from the Chronicles of Martinus Polonus, though he says it was instituted under Justinian the Great because of a plague; Nicephorus says the same (17.28). Sigebert agrees, stating this was in the year 542 AD, a time when Justin had already died, even by Cedrenus's own testimony. Paul the Deacon mentions it in Book 16 of his *Roman History*. I believe the "Stay of the Augusta" refers to the monastery founded by Pulcheria. **XYLANDER.**

p. 642 v. 8. *Euphraemius of Amida*] It is clear enough from Evagrius (4.6) and Nicephorus (17.3) that he was the Prefect of the East (who is here called a *count* <note>original: "κόμης"</note>). **XYLANDER.**

ib. v. 13. *Bright-eyed* <note>original: "χαροπόν"</note>] Xylander translated this as "with a fierce face," but the word is far from that meaning; it should be interpreted only regarding the eyes, commending Justinian as notable for his **gleaming and lively blue eyes.** **GOAR.**

ib. v. 15. *Consulship* <note>original: "ὑπατείαν"</note>] I thought this meant a banquet, or perhaps gifts thrown to the people according to custom, or games. See below. **XYLANDER.**

# ANNOTATIONS.

*p. 642 v. 20. in the church of Sergius and Bacchus]* The passage is mutilated, so it is no wonder if I have not guessed perfectly. However, Procopius, in Book 1 of his work *On the Buildings of Justinian*, does not seem to contradict our version. **Xyl.**

*p. 643 v. 1. a monastery of illustrious men <note>original: "μοναστήριον περιφανῶν ἀνδρῶν"</note>]* A place into which noble and famous men might retire. **Goar.**

*ib. v. 8. commander <note>original: "στρατηλάτην"</note>]* Rigaltius calls him the <term>Master of Soldiers: a high-ranking military official in the late Roman and Byzantine Empire</term> <note>original: "magistrum militum"</note>, about whom Pancirollus writes extensively in the *Register of Dignities* <note>original: "notitiam imperii"</note>. **Goar.**

*ib. v. 11. of the Heruli]* You should know that these people are more correctly called "Heruli" than "Eluri." In the works of Evagrius they are called <note>original: "ἕρουλοι"</note>, citing also a passage from Procopius (4.20). The same spelling is found in Nicephorus (17.13). Therefore, I have dared to strike out the incorrect spelling used by Zonaras, even though it is well-established, although I know the names of nations are corrupted in various ways. But I believe no improvement can be hoped for from this source. **Xyl.**

*ib. v. 18. For Armenia did not have <note>original: "οὐ γὰρ εἶχεν 'Αρμενία"</note>]* Pancirollus, chapter 131: 
> *Justinian, having subdued the neighboring barbarians, created a new province called Greater and Inner Armenia (Final Law, Code "On the Office of the Master of Soldiers"), which he entrusted to Zeta, the Master of Soldiers (the author calls him Tzytas <note>original: "Τζίταν"</note>). He states: "We have entrusted to your care, along with their leaders, Greater Armenia—which used to be called Inner—and the tribes of Antizena, Angilena, Astyanea, Sophena, Sophonena (where Martyropolis is located), Belabitena, as well as First and Second Armenia and Pontus Polemoniacus. For the generals and counts were subject to the Master of Soldiers."* 

Pancirollus says the same in chapter 139. **Goar.**

*p. 644 v. 2. Of the Huns called the Sabiri <note>original: "Οὔννων τῶν λεγομένων Σαβήρ"</note>]* These are recognized from Constantine Porphyrogenitus's *On Administering the Empire* as being situated toward the Dnieper and Dniester rivers, quite near to Cherson <note>a Byzantine city in the Crimea</note>. **Goar.**

*ib. v. 13. of the Bosporus <note>original: "Βοσπόρου"</note>]* This is not the Thracian Bosporus <note>the strait at Constantinople</note>, but the Maeotic one <note>the Cimmerian Bosporus near the Sea of Azov</note>, whose neighbors are the <term>Pechenegs: a nomadic Turkic people</term> <note>original: "Patzinacae"</note>; about whom and that Bosporus, Constantine Porphyrogenitus writes in *On Administering the Empire*, chapter 42. **Goar.**

*p. 645 v. 8. the Exokionitai <note>original: "ἐξωκιονιτῶν"</note>]* I do not quite follow this. I suspect that he perhaps allowed the Arians <note>a Christian sect deemed heretical</note> to have churches outside the city and something like private assemblies. Indeed, later in the history by Nicephorus the Patriarch, mention is made of a certain wicked hermit named Nicholas, who lived in the Exokionion and aided the emperor's impiety. The word literally signifies <note>original: "ἔξω κίονιον"</note> "the pillar that is outside," or "a small column." **Xyl.** Outside the royal city at the column called "the pillar outside" <note>original: "ἔξω κίονιον"</note>, from which the neighbors were called "Exokionitai," the Arians stayed, having been permitted to keep a church. The author mentions this below on page 552. **Goar.**

*ib. v. 14. He filled — he made <note>original: "πληροῖ — ἐποίησε"</note>]* This version fits the truth of the text more faithfully. He also finished the upper area of the royal Cistern of Illus and made it larger. Now, Illus lived under Emperors Leo and Zeno and served as a Master of Soldiers. **Goar.**

*p. 647 v. 11. The rebellion called the Nika <note>original: "ἡ ἀνταρσία τοῦ λεγομένου Νίκα"</note>]* The sequence of events is gathered from the corrupted and obscure words of Theophanes. At the races in the Circus, whenever Justinian went out, the people used to shout, among other acclamations, <note>original: "τοῦ βίκας"</note> "May you conquer!" <note>original: "tu vincas" in Latin, "νίκα" in Greek</note>; and immediately [they called] a certain Calepodius to account for the grievances inflicted on them...

**p. 649 v. 20. having held the consulship <note>original: "ὑπατείαν ποιήσας"</note>]** I noted above that <term>consulship <note>original: "ὑπατείαν"</note>: the high office of consul</term> is used for the games or gifts a consul would give to the people; at the beginning of Justinian's reign, it meant "to give a consulship." However, you will understand how that does or does not apply here. Zonaras says of this matter: "Belisarius was also deemed worthy of the consulship." In Procopius, who described this business of Gelimer in the first book of the *Vandalic War*, it reads as follows, in the translation by Volaterranus:

> "Shortly after, a triumph was decreed for Belisarius in the ancient manner. For he was made consul, carried on a silver <term>curule chair <note>original: "curuli sella"</note>: a traditional seat of high-ranking Roman magistrates</term> upon the shoulders of captives; he dispersed golden belts and other riches from the Vandal spoils to the people, even though he seemed to be doing something new."

**XYL.** He held the consulship in the city, as Xylander expressed; hence he acts poorly as a translator. According to the author’s intent: *he distributed a bounty to the soldiers and a gift to the people, or according to the ancient custom of consuls, he scattered money among the people*. For regarding his <term>Victoriati <note>original: "nummis eius Victoriatis"</note>: ancient silver coins stamped with the figure of Victory</term>. "So that Justinian," etc. **GOAR.**

**ib. v. 24. truly envy]** It is not inelegantly written in the margin: <margin>This has been the destruction of men from the beginning. **p. 650 v. 14. song]** A <term>troparion <note>original: "τροπάριον"</note>: a short hymn of one stanza</term>. This is noted in its entirety in Nicephorus (17.28). **XYL.** Out of hatred for the Arian heresy, Justinian published a hymn of this kind in praise of the incarnate Word of God, to be sung at various times and especially at the very beginning of the Mass, after the first two antiphons have been completed:

> Only-begotten Son and Word of God, being immortal, and deigning for our salvation to become incarnate of the holy Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, without change becoming man, and being crucified, O Christ our God, trampling down death by death, being one of the Holy Trinity, glorified together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, save us. <note>original Greek: "ὁ μονογενὴς υἱὸς καὶ λόγος τοῦ θεοῦ..."</note>

**GOAR.**
