...where Menas, acting as prefect, focused on receiving wandering poor people. **GOAR.**

*ibid.* v. 9. [**having lived for one period** <note>original: "ζήσας χρόνον ἕνα"</note>] This Silvester is named Silverius by others who have described the Roman pontiffs. Silverius succeeded Agapetus, but at the order of Empress Theodora—who hated him because of Anthimus the <term>Theopaschite <note>original: "Theopaschitam": a follower of the belief that God suffered on the cross, often associated with Miaphysitism</note></term> who had been deposed by Agapetus—he was trapped by a false charge of betraying Rome. This plot was carried out by Antonina, the wife of the general Belisarius. Silverius was stripped of the papacy and exiled to the island of Pontia, having been pope for a little over a year. See Paul the Deacon (Book 16), Marianus Scotus, and Martinus Polonus. I wonder why Nicephorus names Agatho as the successor to Agapetus; I do not quite understand why his interpreter thinks it was Boniface. Vigilius was substituted for Silverius; Nicephorus also reports this from Procopius (17.13), though he elsewhere writes (17.26) that Silverius succeeded Agatho. Furthermore, Procopius writes in Book 1 of the *Gothic War*, near the end, that Silverius was sent to Greece by Belisarius because he was suspected of defecting to the Goths, and Vigilius was substituted in his place. See also *Novel 42*. **XYLANDER.**

*ibid.* v. 11. ***procession***] I have used this common word to denote the crowd of people who follow the pontiffs during a solemnity or public prayer. The Greek term is *litē* <note>original: "λιτὴ"</note>. **XYLANDER.** "**The procession went out from the Holy Resurrection**" <note>original: "ἐξῆλθεν λιτὴ ἀπὸ τῆς ἁγίας ἀναστάσεως"</note>. The final and most important rite in the dedication of a sacred building is the deposition of holy relics within it. Once the preliminary dedication ceremonies are finished, the Greeks bring these relics from a neighboring church in a solemn processional order into the newly consecrated one. Therefore, in the dedication of the Temple of **Saint Sophia**, the processional pomp set out with the relics from the Church of **Saint Anastasia**, which was mentioned above. **GOAR.**

*ibid.* v. 14. Regarding the number of years, perhaps we should read sixty-forty (6040) with Zonaras instead of sixty-eight (6008)—that is, forty years rather than eight years above the 6,000-year mark. **XYLANDER.**

*p. 652 v. 6.* "**General of Illyricum**" <note>original: "στρατηλάτην τοῦ Ἰλλυρικοῦ"</note>] Not a prefect, but a <term>Master of Soldiers <note>original: "magister militum"</note>: a high-ranking Roman military official</term> in Illyricum. **GOAR.**

*ibid.* v. 18. **Euphratesia**] This refers to Commagene. Thus Procopius says in this very history in Book 2 of the *Persian War*: "after Chosroes reached the region of the Commagenians, which they call Euphratesia," etc. Following this same sense, I previously read "having come" <note>original: "ἐλθών"</note> for "of those having come" <note>original: "ἐλθόντων"</note>. **XYLANDER.**

*p. 656 v. 16.* "**Axumites**"] Nicephorus (17.32) speaks of the "Axumite Indians," and Domnus of the **Homerites** <note>original: "Homeritarum": the Himyarite Kingdom in modern-day Yemen</note> as a prince of the Indians, instead of Damian, king of the Hebrews. **XYLANDER.** Paul the Deacon calls them the Azumitenses in Book 16. Procopius writes about these Homerites in Book 1 of the *Persian War*. **GOAR.**

*p. 658 v. 15.* ***procensus***] I believe this was a public assembly where the emperor would come out to meet the people. We see this also below regarding Justin the <term>Curopalates <note>original: "curopalata": a high court official, usually a member of the imperial family</note></term>. **XYLANDER.** A *prokensos* <note>original: "πρόκενσος"</note> is a "processus" or procession, also called a *litē*. Meursius has written learnedly on this word. Furthermore, we read of another such solemn procession to the **Hebdomon** <note>original: "septimum lapidem", the Seventh Milestone</note> held in the ninth year of Justin. **GOAR.**

*p. 659 v. 23.* "**of Jerusalem**"] I have omitted the name of Eutychius, which was forced into the text. The passage is suspect because of the phrase "**but the representatives**" <note>original: "τοποτηρηταὶ δέ"</note>. Eustochius was there.

# THE ANNOTATIONS OF XYLANDER AND GOAR

At that time he was the bishop of Jerusalem. See Evagrius, Book 4, Chapter 38, and Nicephorus, Book 17, Chapter 27. <term>XYLANDER.</term>

page 660, line 3. [**blind**] “from the eyes” <note>original: "ἀπὸ ὀμμάτων"</note>. See Nicephorus, Book 9, Chapter 17. <term>XYLANDER.</term>

page 674, line 10. [**Lord, have mercy**] <note>original: "κύριε ἐλέησον"</note> This is a phrase commonly uttered by the Greeks, not so much for the sake of seeking mercy as for expressing wonder at an unusual or shocking event. <term>GOAR.</term>

page 675, line 7. [**he impaled/hanged**] <note>original: "ἐφούλκισε"</note> I am not certain what this means, unless perhaps it means “to send to the gallows” <note>original: "sub furcam mittere"</note>. The same term is used later regarding the Emperor Pogonatus, stating he “hanged them at Sycae.” Zonaras records that these people were simply killed. I might have believed they were “suspended from fig trees,” <note>The Latin word for fig tree is *ficus*</note> had I not learned from the writings of Leontius that “The Fig Trees” <note>original: "Ficus"</note> is actually the name of a suburb of Constantinople. <term>XYLANDER.</term> *He did not kill them with just any punishment, as the wavering interpreter suggests, but specifically executed them by hanging or the gallows.* <term>GOAR.</term>

*ibid.* line 17. [**with cruelty**] <note>original: "μετὰ φιλανίας"</note> This is undoubtedly a corrupted reading, as are many of the things that follow, which are very difficult to interpret. This is partly because they are full of errors, and partly because they lack clarity due to the mixture of "barbaric" <note>Byzantine Greek</note> and semi-Latin words, as noted just a moment ago. <term>XYLANDER.</term>

*ibid.* line 19. [**invitation-banquets**] <note>original: "κλητόρια"</note> I truly do not know what these are. It appears they were festival days, perhaps intended for the beginning of a reign or another event, which were celebrated at great expense. I do not remember reading about them elsewhere. <term>XYLANDER.</term> *These are the "Banquets of the Twelve Days" <note>original: "κλητόρια τοῦ δωδεκαημέρου"</note>, which are signs of joy and feasting to be celebrated for twelve days starting from the birth of Christ. Meursius judges that "kletoria" is the correct reading, and I agree with him, guided by the authority of Paul the Deacon: "He brought to an end the luncheons which are customarily held at the Nineteen Couches." Theophanes first called these "breakfasts"; Liutprand of Cremona (Book 6, Chapter 3) describes them more fully: "There is a house near the Hippodrome, facing north, of wonderful height and beauty, which is called the Nineteen Couches <note>original: "deca ennea cubita"</note>. This name was chosen for obvious reasons: 'deka' in Greek is 'ten' in Latin, 'ennea' is 'nine,' and 'cubita' we can call 'couches' for reclining or leaning. This is because nineteen tables are set out there on the feast of the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ; at these tables, the Emperor and his guests feast not by sitting, as on other days, but by reclining. On these days, they are served not with silver vessels, but only with gold ones," etc. See also Leunclavius.* <term>GOAR.</term>

page 676, line 16. [**worldly democracies**] <note>original: "κοσμικαὶ δημοκρατίαι"</note> I think he uses this term to describe when the people rise up against a magistrate. There is a well-known saying of a man who, when someone was advocating for democracy, replied that the advocate should first establish a democracy in his own home if he truly approved of that form of government. <term>XYLANDER.</term> *This refers to the slaughter resulting from the factions and parties—mentioned above—clashing and rioting against one another.* <term>GOAR.</term>

*ibid.* line 21. [**Justinian beautifying the dome**] <note>original: "Ἰουστινιανοῦ φιλοκαλουμένου τοῦ τρούλου"</note> Perhaps this refers to when Justinian was about to repair the dome. <term>XYLANDER.</term> *This means the dome had already been finished and perfectly adorned with paintings, carvings, and mosaic work. The previous interpreter omitted these details. Regarding the word "trullos" <note>dome</note>, some double the letter 'l'.* <term>GOAR.</term>

*ibid.* line 23. [**ciborium**] <note>original: "κιβώριον"</note> A dome-like canopy resting on four columns over the altar—

<meta>This page continues the scholarly commentary by Wilhelm Xylander (XYL.) and Jacques Goar (GOAR.) on Byzantine history and architecture. Having previously discussed ecclesiastical politics and the punishment of criminals, the focus now shifts to technical architectural terms regarding the Hagia Sophia and the military defenses of Constantinople, specifically correcting previous translations of Greek architectural and military vocabulary.</meta>

# ANNOTATIONS

Supported on four corners, covering and surrounding the altar—the kind that most ancient Roman churches still preserve—this is the **ciborium** <note>original: κιβώριον; a canopy-like structure over an altar</note>. Germanus in his *Mystagogia*, Codinus in his work on the Church of Saint Sophia, and we ourselves have written more on this in our descriptions of Greek churches. <term>GOAR.</term>

page 677, line 5. I have also left out the rest, so as not to trouble myself and others to no benefit. I translated **pinnacles** <note>original: πινσοὺς; pinsous</note> as "small spires" <note>original: pinnacula</note>. In the lexicon of Suidas, it appears as *pisos* or *pinsos*, but as *pesos* in the writings of Procopius. From the historian Zonaras, it is clear that after the Great Temple [Hagia Sophia] had been finished by the emperor (to which the word "decorated with beauty" <note>original: φιλοκαλουμένου</note> refers), this specific collapse occurred. <term>XYLANDER.</term>

*ibid.* line 2. [**pillars**] <note>original: πινσοὺς</note> Meursius ridiculously leads readers away from the truth by deriving this from "peas and legumes" <note>original: a pisis et leguminibus</note>, where he replaces the word *pinsos* with *pinsum* and *pisum*. Xylander also foolishly rendered it as "pinnacles"; in fact, these are the supports, namely the massive square pillars or columns that hold up the vaulted roof. To prevent a similar accident in the Holy House of Loreto—repairing it in a way similar to what happened in Constantinople—Tursellinus describes the care taken in the third book, chapter 7 of his *History of Loreto*: *The dome of the basilica stood resting on eight brick pillars. However, either due to the height of the walls built above or the excessive weight of the lead roof pressing down, it began to give way under the burden and suddenly developed cracks, threatening a foul ruin to the new decoration of the chamber and the chamber over which it hung. (The sacred chamber is located under the dome, where the Constantinople-style ciborium and the altar placed beneath it were erected). From here, after some deliberation: immediately by common consensus (the architect Sangallo along with Nerucio) proceeded with intense care to fortify and strengthen the pillars that were unequal to such a burden. Therefore, he immediately propped up the dome with strong beams, and having vigorously excavated the foundations around them, he busily encased the pillars with squared stone; he strengthened them by constructing four smaller arches between the alternating pillars to be sufficient for the weight placed above. In a word, our author says: **he raised other pillars and supported the dome.** <note>original: ἤγειρεν ἄλλους πινσοὺς καὶ ἐδέξατο τὸν τροῦλλον</note>* <term>GOAR.</term>

*ibid.* line 5. [**spiral stairs**] <note>original: κοχλίαι; literally "snails"</note> These are round steps ascending in a spiral, the exterior structure of which reinforced the interior pillars and supported the dome. <term>GOAR.</term>

*ibid.* line 6. [**of the arches**] <note>original: τῶν ἀψίδων</note> Namely, the four arches connecting the four pillars together and placed under the vaulted cupola or dome to support it. <term>GOAR.</term>

*ibid.* line 20. [**Huns**] <note>original: Οὖννοι</note> Agathias calls these people the "Cotrigur Huns," whom he reports broke into Europe under their leader Zabergan in his fifth book. <term>GOAR.</term>

*ibid.* line 23. [**The Walls of Anastasius**] This is the same wall soon referred to as the "Long Wall." It was built by the Emperor Anastasius Dicorus. Whoever wishes for a description of it should seek it from Anastasius the Silentiary in Suidas, and from Nicephorus, Book 16, Chapter 39. <term>XYLANDER.</term> They were built by Anastasius at the isthmus of the Chersonese to check the incursions of barbarians. As Agathias is quoted: *on this isthmus a longer wall was built, extended to both seas.* Throughout this history, it is frequently called **the Long Wall** <note>original: μακρὸν τεῖχος</note>. <term>GOAR.</term>

page 678, line 5. [**to muster an army**] <note>original: ποιῆσαι φοσσάτον</note> This means nothing less than "to dig a ditch" according to Xylander, but it actually means **to gather forces or to pitch camp.** <term>GOAR.</term>

<meta>This page continues the scholarly annotations by Wilhelm Xylander and Jacques Goar on Byzantine terminology. The focus shifts from the architectural details of the Hagia Sophia to broader military, naval, and administrative vocabulary found in the historical manuscripts of authors like Procopius and Zonaras.</meta>

-># XYLANDER AND GOAR<-

**Fossaton** <note>original: φοσσάτον</note> is an **army** <note>original: στρατός</note>, as the "Greeko-Barbarian Glossaries" <note>Late Medieval Greek lexicons</note> teach; it is also used to refer to a **camp** fortified with a rampart. <term>GOAR.</term>

page 678, line 10. **double-sterned ships** <note>original: πλοῖα δίπρυμνα</note>] Agathias writes that these are fast-sailing vessels <note>original: actuarias naves</note> with multiple banks of oars, and are themselves "double-prowed" <note>original: amphiproras</note>. Fast vessels are those driven by oars; double-prowed vessels have a prow at both ends, just like **double-sterned ships** <note>original: δίπρυμναι</note> have a stern at both ends. These are sometimes without a single fixed rudder and can be driven in either direction without turning. Zonaras describes such double-prowed ships accurately in his account of Constantine: *Most of the ships were single-banked, but some were double-banked. On some of them, rudders were fitted both at the prow and at the stern, and they had double sets of helmsmen and sailors, so that whether they sailed forward or withdrew, they would not need to turn around, thus deceiving the enemy both in their approach and their departure.* <term>GOAR.</term>

*ibid.* line 13. **Curopalates** <note>original: Curopalatam</note>] This is a compound word. It is a title of high rank, as you may learn from Zonaras. Evagrius, at the beginning of volume 5, interprets it when he says that Justin was entrusted with the "guardianship of the court," that is, the **care of the palace** <note>original: palatii curam</note>; those performing this duty are called "Curopalates" by the Romans. Nicephorus says the same in book 17, chapter 33. Moreover, a "Curopalates of Iberia" <note>referring to a kingdom in the Caucasus, modern-day Georgia</note> is mentioned elsewhere. <term>XYLANDER.</term> Named from the "care of the palace" undertaken, as Cassiodorus speaks in his *Variae* and Marcellinus in books 26 and 31. Because he **cares for the palace** <note>original: curat palatium</note>, he is called the **Caretaker of the Palace** <note>original: cura palatii</note> in Latin. <term>GOAR.</term>

*ibid.* line 15. [of the] **Sangarios** <note>original: Σαγγαρέως; a major river in Anatolia</note>] Procopius calls it the "Sarus" in Book 5 of *On the Buildings of Justinian*, oration 5, and in his narrative, he traces its source from the mountains of Armenia. Paulus Diaconus gives it the name "Agoreos" and speaks briefly of it: *The emperor,* he says, *began to build a bridge over the Agoreos river, diverting the same stream into another channel; he desired five marvelous arches and made it passable, whereas before it had been made of wood.* Others call it the Sagaris, upon which the Phrygian city of Nacolia is situated. Today, the Turks call it the **Sakarya** <note>original: Zacarim</note>, according to Leunclavius. <term>GOAR.</term>

*ibid.* line 16. [of] **arches** <note>original: καμαρῶν</note>] This word denotes something curved or bent. As the poet says: *shaggy ears under curved horns* <note>original: hirtae camaris sub cornibus aures</note>. <term>XYLANDER.</term> *Kamara* <note>original: καμάρα</note>, or *kamera* <note>original: καμέρα</note> to others, is a **vault**, an arch, or a domed ceiling. <term>GOAR.</term>

*ibid.* line 21. **projections** or **displays** <note>original: προβολάς</note>] Perhaps it should be written as **stalls** or **front-shops** <note>original: προπωλάς</note>. <term>XYLANDER.</term> It has already been suggested above that the term for **bakeries** <note>original: μαγκιπεῖα; mankipeia</note> is far from meaning "legal ownership" <note>original: mancipio</note>. For it is a flour-mill or a shop where bread is set out for sale. A **probole** <note>original: προβολή</note>, however, is indeed a shop, but one where goods are displayed, though no work is actually done there. Finally, an **ergasterion** <note>original: ἐργαστήριον</note> is a workshop of craftsmen, where any kind of work can be produced by human industry. The author mentions this below in the final year of Justinian. <term>GOAR.</term>

page 679, line 14. **Viriam and Brincas**] These names are corrupted. It is difficult to guess what should be restored. The deeds of Narses against the Goths are found in Procopius, in the final book of the *Gothic War*. <term>XYLANDER.</term>

*ibid.* line 21. **inner courtyard** <note>original: μεσίαυλον; mesiaulon</note>] Xylander notes the allusion rather than the literal sense regarding the *mesiaulon*, which indicates an open area, an atrium, or a space open to the sky but enclosed by walls; we have already discussed this above. Here, however, it suggests a roofed building, specifically a place located in the middle of the courtyard. <term>GOAR.</term>

# ANNOTATIONS

page 679, line 21. **concerning the word** <note>original: ad vocem</note> **Garsonustasion** <note>original: Γαρσονυστάσιον</note>, it is noted in the margin: "It seems to me to be a **paidostasion** <note>original: παιδοστάσιον - a place for servants or youths</note>; for *gartzounion* among the Latins means a boy." Furthermore, this word is not Latin, but is French even today <note>original: garcon</note>. <term>XYLANDER.</term> Theophanes writes the same thing; the word is a blend of Italian and Greek, and means a **station for footmen** <note>original: pedissequorum statio</note>, the courtyard of the boys, or lackeys. <term>GOAR.</term>

page 680, line 18. **movables** <note>original: ἔπιπλα</note> **hangings, rugs, and veils are properly garments** <note>original: aulaea, stragulae, vela proprie sunt pepla</note>, **not tools** <note>original: instrumenta</note>, as the translator corruptly has it. <term>GOAR.</term>

page 684, line 17. **Avars** <note>original: Ἄβαρες</note>] Simocatta, book 1, chapter 3: *These Huns, who live near the Ister [Danube], are a most untrustworthy and greedy nation.* <term>GOAR.</term>

*ibid.* line 18. **Artabanus**] Zonaras calls this man Ardamanees; Evagrius, in book 5, calls him Adaarman. <term>XYLANDER.</term>

*ibid.* line 22. **Hormisdas**] King of the Persians according to Zonaras; for Evagrius makes this man out to be Chosroes. <term>XYLANDER.</term>

*ibid.* line 23. **on the Great 5th** <note>original: τῇ μεγάλῃ ε</note>] Thus he calls the fifth day of the week, or **Maundy Thursday** <note>original: diem Iovis malis</note>, which is the day immediately before Easter, celebrated for the institution of the Holy Supper; in German, **the High or Green Thursday** <note>original: der hoch oder grünen donnerstag</note>. Zonaras uses the same term in his account of the later reign of Constantine, son of Leo. <term>XYLANDER.</term>

page 685, line 1. **of thy mystical supper** <note>original: τοῦ δείπνου σου τοῦ μυστικοῦ</note>] This is a musical measure in the Liturgy of Basil, to be sung at the time of communion. <term>GOAR.</term>

*ibid.* I do not know which image he speaks of, unless one thinks it refers to the image of himself impressed upon a linen cloth by Christ and sent to Abgar of Edessa <note>A reference to the Mandylion, a famous miraculous relic</note>. <term>XYLANDER.</term>

*ibid.* line 4. **Cherubic Hymn** <note>original: Χερουβικὸς ὕμνος</note>] This is chanted daily among the holy liturgical hymns when the sacred gifts—that is, the bread and wine—are carried in solemn procession from the table of preparation to the altar. See Arcudius in his work *On the Agreement of Both Churches*, and the *Euchologion* <note>Prayer book</note> in the notes to the liturgy of Chrysostom. <term>GOAR.</term>

*ibid.* line 6. **Excubitors** <note>original: ἐξκουβιτώρων</note>] These men kept watch at the doors of the palace and observed the entrance. The "Glosses on the Basilica" <note>Byzantine law code notes</note> say: *Excubitors are guards stationed at the side-exits of the palace.* Simocatta, acting as if he were a commentator on Cedrenus, writes in book 3, chapter 11 concerning our Tiberius: *Justin, having honored Tiberius with adoption and made him a partner in the kingdom, proclaimed him Caesar. He happened to be the leader of the King’s bodyguards and shield-bearers, whom it is the custom of the Romans to call the "Count of the Excubitors" in their usual tongue.* He is perhaps the same person whom Marcellinus, in book 20, lists as the "Count of the Household Excubitors" after mentioning the guards. <term>GOAR.</term>

*ibid.* line 7. **afflicted in his feet** <note>original: στυφόμενος τοὺς πόδας</note>] Zonaras says that he suffered from a foot ailment <note>likely gout</note>. <term>XYLANDER.</term>

*ibid.* line 15. **Archistrategos** <note>original: ἀρχιστρατήγου</note>] Xylander is ignorant of the name of Michael, the prince of the celestial militia, and childishly calls him the "Chief of Leaders." <term>GOAR.</term>

*ibid.* line 18. **Eutyches**] This should be read as "Eutychius," following Zonaras and Nicephorus, book 17, chapter 36. And a little later, Cedrenus has it this way himself. <term>XYLANDER.</term>

# THE ANNOTATIONS OF XYLANDER AND GOAR

page 806

page 686, line 16. **falling at his feet** <note>original: ἐν τοῖς ποσὶν αὐτοῦ πεσόντος</note>] The liturgical rite in the *Euchologion* <note>The primary prayer book of the Byzantine Church</note> teaches that those being adopted should prostrate themselves at the feet of those adopting them; Tiberius performs this for Justin, and he acknowledges Sophia, Justin's wife, no longer as "Mistress" <note>original: δέσποινα - an imperial title</note> or Empress, but as a mother entrusted to him. Theophylact Simocatta reports the same in the cited passage; he also relates that the Patriarch himself read the prayers of adoption from the *Euchologion*, to whose prayers those standing by also added their blessings. <term>GOAR.</term>

*ibid.* line 21. **Proconnesian** <note>original: Προικοννησίῳ</note>] Referring to the white stone praised by Strabo in Book 13, quarried from Proconnesus, an island in the Propontis <note>The Sea of Marmara</note>. <term>GOAR.</term>

page 688, line 10. **and he declared** <note>original: ὁ δὲ ἐδήλωσεν</note>] Because the name "Anastasia" was common to both that temple and the Empress <note>Anastasia was the wife of Emperor Tiberius II</note>. We have already discussed more regarding the temple alongside the author. <term>GOAR.</term>

*ibid.* line 20. **channeled or fluted** <note>original: imbricatas / σωληνωτάς</note>] Here the translator [Xylander] guessed; and he left the word **ornas** <note>original: ὄρνας - borders or hems</note> alone because he did not understand it. <term>XYLANDER.</term> Here the translator affirms he was guessing: and why not, since prophets too can be mistaken? Yet there is no room for guessing or deception here, since **channeled robes** <note>original: σωληνωταί στολαί</note> are nothing other than garments variegated with a many-layered arrangement of woven ribbons, which, whether they shine with straight channels or oblique spirals, nevertheless proclaim luxury, lightness, and extravagance by their appearance. For a **solen** <note>original: σωλήν</note> is a channel or a small pipe, from which the Greeks call any channeled or hollowed work *solenoton*, which the French pronounce as **canellé** <note>ribbed fabric</note>. <term>GOAR.</term>

*ibid.* **from silk** <note>original: ἀπὸ βλατίου</note>] The text refers to **blation** <note>original: τὸ βλατίον</note> as a fine-woven or any silk cloth: for where one reading in Book 3 of Nicetas Choniates' *Life of Alexios Komnenos* has "without the *blatia*," another puts "except for the silk threads." Thus, the comments that Jacob Gretser spreads throughout his work on Codinus—regarding the color **blatteus** (that is, rosy or purple) and the Greek word *blattion* based on a similarity of names, as if speaking from the Delphic tripod—are trifles and of no significance. <term>GOAR.</term>

*ibid.* line 21. **sharply** <note>original: ὀξέως</note>] One would say this word is an indication of a violet color according to modern Greeks, rather than "sharp" or "vivid" as the cited Gretser has it; and if you wish to examine the author more closely, you will assert that the cloaks of the competitors in the Circus games were of this violet sort, which were not entirely different from purple: namely, **cloaks very similar to the royal ones** <note>original: χλάμυδας nempe παραπλησίας τοῦ βασιλικοῦ</note>: understand this as referring to either the color or the style. <term>GOAR.</term>

*ibid.* line 23. **two-finger-wide borders** <note>original: διδακτυλίους ὄρνας</note>] Hems or borders the width of two fingers. It is called an **orna** because it is the hem or ornament of a garment; and for that reason, the place in the Circus where those about to compete stood or adorned themselves is called the **ornatorium** <note>dressing room</note> in Theophanes. He reports that a certain Rufus was led by Emperor Philippikos to the "ornatorium of the Greens" <note>The Green faction of the Hippodrome</note>; Paul the Deacon says this same place was the "oratory" <note>original: oratorium</note> of the Greens, where they certainly adorned themselves with "oras" <note>hems</note> and "limbs" <note>borders</note> woven onto their clothes; we shall observe that Cedrenus called this same place the **armatorium** <note>armory/equipment room</note>. <term>GOAR.</term>

page 689, line 3. **consulship** <note>original: ὑπατείαν</note>] I understand this as consular coinage: for the Emperors also held the consulship and commemorated it in their titles—

*ibid.* line 20. **The Persian tuldum**] This appears again below. I believe it was a specific sign or a primary standard, just as further down under Heraclius it is used for a troop or squadron, "a banner" <note>original German: ein fanen</note>. <term>XYLANDER.</term> Xylander is dreaming here regarding the **tuldum** <note>original: τοὺλδον</note> and imagines it refers to a "standard," from which it was entirely distinct. While a standard was carried into battle, the *tuldum* refers to the baggage, pack animals, supplies, and young servants—things that are either unnecessary or a hindrance in a conflict. Suidas <note>A 10th-century Greek encyclopedic lexicon</note> says: "The pack animals which we call the *tuldum* carry the baggage and transport the necessities." <term>GOAR.</term>

page 690, line 9. **by contracts** <note>original: συμβολαίοις</note>] It would be more accurate here to translate this as **diplomas** or **letters** rather than Xylander’s "formulas for contracts." <term>GOAR.</term>

page 691, line 2. **mulberries** <note>original: συκάμινα</note>] My word! *ibid.* line 6. **having returned to his own bed** <note>original: ὑποστρέψας ἐν τῇ ἰδίᾳ κλίνῃ</note>] Tiberius returned to his own bed to die, after he had addressed the senate, the army, and the patriarch regarding the naming of Maurice as successor to the empire. He was carried on a litter "to the open-air courtyard of the palace, which is adjacent to the much-trodden royal residence, a conspicuous forecourt and glorious stage." Pontanus <note>Jacob Pontanus, a Jesuit scholar and translator</note> rendered these words from Simocatta (Book 1, Chapter 1) somewhat improperly. For the "much-trodden house" <note>original: πολυστιβάς οἰκία</note> refers to a crowded complex of buildings and dwellings, not a bed made of grass and leaves. <term>GOAR.</term>

page 692, line 14. **into Romania**] Into the jurisdiction of the Romans; "into the lands of the Romans" <note>original: εἰς τὰ Ῥωμαίων</note> in the historian Zonaras. <term>XYLANDER.</term>

page 693, line 1. **with a switch** <note>original: βεργίῳ</note>] In Nicetas (18:37) we read "with a willow-twig." <term>XYLANDER.</term> A "willow rod," called a *lygos* by the commentator on Theocritus: "to bind with switches, that is, with willow rods." <term>GOAR.</term>

*ibid.* line 10. **Martyropolis**] A city in Armenia famous for the martyrdom of forty soldiers. <term>GOAR.</term>

page 694, line 18. **by the banners** <note>original: βάνδοις</note>] Standards, I believe military ones, which we call a **banner** <note>original: baner</note>. Suidas, under the entry "Bandos," says: "This is what the Romans call the sign used in war." <term>XYLANDER.</term>

*ibid.* line 21. **public prayer**] This is clearly a "litany," here called a "suppliant embassy" <note>original: λιτὴ πρεσβεία</note>. In Suidas as well, a *litē* is an entreaty. Therefore, he seems to have instituted that litany which is performed from one shrine to another, with a crowd of people and priests processing. Previously, the word was read as *letē*, which was incorrect. The word *litai* [prayers] is a well-known term, even from Homer, as to what it denotes. <term>XYLANDER.</term>

*ibid.* line 22. **on the day of preparation** <note>original: κατὰ παρασκευήν</note>] On every "Parasceue," which is to say, on the sixth day of the week [Friday]. <term>GOAR.</term>

page 695, line 24. **Daonium**] A place in Thrace. <term>GOAR.</term>

page 808

...the nickname of Theophylact the Sophist <note>Theophylact Simocatta, an 8th-century historian</note>. Otherwise, this prediction regarding Chosroes <note>The Persian King Chosroes II</note> is generally clearer in the works of Zonaras and Nicephorus, Book 18, chapter 27. **XYLANDER.**

page 698, line 22. **Magnaura** <note>original: Μαγναύρας</note>] Liutprand <note>Liutprand of Cremona, a 10th-century diplomat and historian</note> writes in Book 6, chapter 2: "It is a building in Constantinople adjacent to the palace of wonderful size and beauty, which is called *Magnaura* by the Greeks—substituting the letter 'r' for 'l'—as if it meant 'great air' <note>original: magna aura</note>, instead of 'great hall' <note>original: magna aula</note>." **GOAR.**

*ibid.* line 23. **The armory of public weapons** <note>original: ἀρμαμέντον δημοσίων ὅπλων</note>] A specific place. See Justinian, *Novellae* 85. **GOAR.**

*ibid.* line 24. **diseased old men** <note>original: senes morbosi</note>] Our author <note>Cedrenus</note> often uses the term **mutilation** <note>original: λωβήν</note> to mean leprosy, as we also noted in the section on Constantine. Therefore, you could translate this as "leprous old men and brothers." However, because these matters were obscure, I have translated them word for word so that more skilled scholars might have material for conjecture. One should read this as **of the lepers**. **GOAR.**

page 699, line 1. **the provision of the necessities of life** <note>original: τοῦ ζωτικοῦ ἐγχορήγον</note>] *A storehouse of the expenses necessary for living*. **GOAR.**

*ibid.* line 8. The temples of **Areobindus and the Deaconess** are also mentioned by Nicephorus, Book 18, chapter 42. **XYLANDER.**

page 700, line 9. **four keratia** <note>original: κεράτια τέσσαρα</note>] These are a sixth part of a coin. For a coin is valued at 24 *keratia* <note>carats</note>, but 12 *miliarisia*. From this, a *keration* is half of a *miliarisium*, or 12 *folles*. The Scholiast on the *Basilica* <note>a collection of Byzantine laws</note>, *Eclogue* 23, says: "One must know that one *keration* is twelve *folles*, which is half of a *miliarisium*. Therefore, twelve *keratia* are half a coin; thus a whole coin <note>a gold nomisma or solidus</note> contains 12 *miliarisia* or 24 *keratia*." **GOAR.**

*ibid.* line 12. **two miliarisia for each**] I do not understand this passage at all, because it is neither sufficiently clear what the coin was worth, nor what the marks **ί' ί' θ λ δ'** mean. Suidas <note>A 10th-century Greek encyclopedia</note> noted that a *miliarisium* makes up a tenth part of a coin, but that does not explain the matter. You may see more on this below at the end of the section on Leo the Iconoclast. **XYLANDER.**

*ibid.* line 16. **at the silentium** <note>original: τῷ σιλεντίῳ</note>] A *silentium* <note>original: σελέντιον or σιλέντιον</note> is a council, assembly, court, or consultation. An author writing on Leo the Isaurian says: "a *silentium* against the holy icons." Paul the Deacon also used the Latin word *silentium* regarding the same Leo: "he celebrated a *silentium* against the holy and venerable icons." Zonaras relates that the other Leo, the Philosopher, was so gripped by intestinal pain "that he was not even able to discuss with the Senate the usual discourse regarding the fast, which is called a *silentium*." **GOAR.**

*ibid.* line 19. The account which follows concerning a **monster seen in the river Nile** seems to be taken from Nicephorus, Book 18, chapter 36. **XYLANDER.**

page 703, line 6. **a broadsword** <note>original: σπάθην</note>] Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville</note>, Book 18, chapter 6: "The *framea* is a sword sharp on both sides, which they commonly call a *spatha*; it is the same as a *romphaea*." **GOAR.**

*ibid.* line 15. **he produced children like wooden bells** <note>original: ἐποίησε παιδία ὡς τὰ ξυλοκώδωνα</note>] The people would have mocked Maurice quite foolishly and clumsily if, according to Xylander’s interpretation, they had babbled that he had fathered sons like wooden bells <note>original: nolarum lignearum</note>. Therefore, the word **wooden-bell** <note>original: ξυλοκώδωνon</note>—which Theophanes writes as **wooden-cuckoo** <note>original: ξυλοκούκουδον</note>—is nothing other than a wooden rattle or a little ball...

# ANNOTATIONS

### page 809

...a hollow wooden object, perforated all over, in which seeds or little bells are enclosed so that children may be amused by its clattering sound. When the people proclaim that they hold the sons of Maurice as if they were playthings of this sort, they demonstrate the greatest contempt for them and their father Maurice, threatening that they will consider their deaths a game and their groans as a playful noise. Furthermore, a **rattle-seed** <note>original: κούκουδον</note> is a seed or a small ball, and a **wooden-rattle** <note>original: ξυλοκούκουδον</note> is a piece of wood full of these types of noisy balls. Is not Xylander himself a wooden man and a **wooden-bell** <note>original: ξυλοκάδωνον</note> for children? **GOAR.**

page 704, verse 15. **the navel-stone** <note>original: ὀμφαλίῳ</note>] a round marker fixed in the middle of an open area. **GOAR.**

*ibid.* verse 22. **he requested to share in communion** <note>original: ἠτήσατο κοινωνῆσαι</note>] I will not hide the fact that I have followed nothing but conjecture here, nor did anything else occur to my mind at the time. If I do not satisfy anyone, let them devise something more suitable. Certainly, later on, Theodosius (the son of Maurice), when he was being led to execution by the order of Phocas, **requested first to partake of the divine mysteries** <note>the Eucharist</note>. **XYLANDER.** Xylander is afraid to acknowledge in his notes the piety of a man who, despairing of his life, asks for the Eucharist. **GOAR.**

page 705, verse 14. **magistrianos:** <note>an official of the Master of Offices</note>] This official is elsewhere called a **master's man** <note>original: μαγιστεριανός</note>, and in the writings of Theophanes a **chief-scout** <note>original: πρωτοκουρσώρ</note>; in the glosses of the *Basilica* <note>a code of Byzantine law</note> he is called a **messenger** <note>original: μανδάτωρ</note> and a **day-runner** <note>original: ἡμεροδρόμος</note>. The anonymous Lexicon of the Royal Library states: "The sun is called a day-runner, as is a foot-runner, and those who serve the imperial decrees with the greatest speed because of the North wind <note>meaning they run as fast as the wind</note>." Leo's *Constitution 3* states: "Messengers are those who carry the mandates from the officials to the soldiers with speed." Hence Maurice sought out those who were experienced, vigilant, and skilled in various languages, adding also that they should be endowed with a sonorous voice for bringing all commands to the public. For this reason, in the accounts of Theophanes, a messenger speaks as an interpreter and mediator for both sides between Justinian and the factions; here, however, he is sent and carries responses to the Emperor. The author mentions this again in the section on Justinian "the Slit-Nosed" <note>Justinian II, known as Rinotmetos</note> right at the beginning. **GOAR.**

*ibid.* verse 21. **they put forward a leader** <note>original: προβάλλονται ἔξαρχον</note>] Simocatta <note>the historian Theophylact Simocatta</note> had previously used similar words in Book 8, Chapter 7: "the multitudes set forward the centurion Phocas as their leader <note>exarch</note>." This was because they had not yet conferred the title or insignia of the Empire upon him, but, as happens in a riot, they had placed him over themselves as a head and guide, given the hope of seizing imperial power. **GOAR.**

page 706, verse 2. **dromon** <note>original: δρόμων</note>] As this word is also used below, it refers to a ship fit for the "course"—that is, for the fastest navigation. For a **dromos** is a "run" or "course." It appears from Nonius Marcellus and the passages of writers he cites that these were what the Latins call **swift-ships** <note>original: celoces</note>; this is also supported by the length of the first syllable. See what Nicephorus writes regarding this history in Book 18, Chapter 40. **XYLANDER.**

*ibid.* verse 6. **Rhegion**] A city of Thrace on the Propontis <note>the Sea of Marmara</note>, further south than the Hebdomon, in which Leon the Philosopher built a bridge; regarding this city, see Constantine's *On the Administration of the Empire*, chapter 51. **GOAR.**

page 707, verse 8. **in the Field of the Tribunal** <note>original: κάμπῳ τοῦ τριβουναλίου</note>] That is, of the city...

# THE ANNOTATIONS OF XYLANDER AND GOAR

->...in the field where the palace called the *Tribunal of the Nineteen Couches* <note>A famous dining hall in the Great Palace of Constantinople used for imperial banquets</note> was built. **GOAR.**<-

page 707, verse 12. [**the Wooden-tailed Gate** <note>original: τῆς ξυλοκέρκου πόρτης</note>] Toward the lowest part of the bay, facing west, is the Xylokerkos gate, named after the wooden stakes fixed into its foundation. Leunclavius. **GOAR.**

page 709, verse 5. [**Arise** <note>original: ἀνάτειλον</note>] "Step forward." This is used similarly in Cicero’s *On the Nature of the Gods*, book 1:
> "when suddenly Roscius arises from the left." **XYLANDER.**

*ibid.* verse 15. [**to partake of the divine mysteries** <note>original: μεταλαβεῖν τῶν θείων μυστηρίων</note>] Xylander looks for the sun at high noon <note>meaning he is looking for something obvious but missing it</note>; he wavers on whether these words indicate the holy communion of the Eucharist. **GOAR.**

page 710, verse 1. [***Calligraphus***] If it is not a proper name, it signifies a painter. Nicephorus (18:41) relates the history slightly differently. In the margin of our manuscript, it was written that these things were announced at Alexandria by **spirits traveling through the air** <note>original: ἐναερίων πνευμάτων</note>. **XYLANDER.** It is neither a proper name, nor does it mean "painter," as Xylander suggests. The historian Simocatta (8:13) explains: "a certain man among those who write with beauty, whom the masses call a 'Calligrapher' <note>literally: beautiful-writer</note> in a compound word." See the Church histories of Origen regarding **tachygraphers** <note>shorthand writers</note> and **calligraphers**. The former were notaries and wrote quickly but with less beauty; the latter wrote more slowly, but with the greatest elegance, and distinguished the letters with colors and gold; for this reason, you will sometimes find them called **chrysographers** <note>literally: gold-writers</note>. **GOAR.**

*ibid.* [**the all-night vigil** <note>original: παννυχίδος</note>] This can also refer to a sacred nocturnal banquet. **XYLANDER.** The Calligrapher was returning home not from just any night watch, but from one he had spent with friends as a night-guest. Simocatta, mentioning this Alexandrian custom, says: "for male children, they celebrate the seventh day as a solemnity, passing the entire long night in luxury and feasting." The *Euchologium* <note>the service book of the Greek Church</note> mentions this regarding the office following baptism. **GOAR.**

*ibid.* verse 2. [**from the altars** <note>original: ἐκ τῶν βωμῶν</note>] The previous translator says "from the altars." This is foolish: for the idols were not *inside* the altars so that they could speak from them. Nor did every idol have its own altar. I correct this to **from their bases**. For a *bomos* <note>original: βωμός</note> signifies an **altar**, but also the **base** of a statue, because it shares the shape of an altar. Simocatta supports this. **GOAR.**

*ibid.* verse 5. [**the Augustal**] I believe the prefect of the city, sent by the Augustus <note>the Emperor</note>, is meant here. **XYLANDER.**

*ibid.* verse 12. [**having increased the pact** <note>original: τὸ πάκτον ἐπαυξήσας</note>] "By increasing the tribute." For the word *pakton* <note>original: πάκτον</note> indicates not only "agreements and contracts," but also the tribute and the money paid for the sake of the agreed-upon tax. The author says regarding the Emperor Phocas in his fourth year: "to decree and receive the *pakta* <note>tributes</note>." **GOAR.**

page 711, verse 10. [**Sakellarios** <note>original: σακελλάριος</note>] The official in charge of the **sacristy** <note>sacella</note> and of the church's treasury. **GOAR.**

*ibid.* verse 14. [**at the mole** <note>original: ἐν τῷ μόλῳ</note>] Not in the harbor itself, but near the harbor; that is, on the embankment surrounding the port where its entrances are too open, which beats back the waves and the winds that break in too violently. **GOAR.**

*ibid.* verse 19. [**Crispus**] Called **Priscus** by Zonaras, Nicephorus, and others.

# ANNOTATIONS. 811

...although Zonaras, in his history of Heraclius, calls Crispus the son-in-law of Phocas, as it is indeed read. **XYLANDER.**

page 711, verse 21. [**General of Africa** <note>original: στρατηγὸν Ἀφρικῆς</note>] I interpret "General" here as *prefect*. For when Africa—having been governed first by vicars—passed into the power of the Vandals in the year 439, and they were finally defeated 95 years later by Justinian, the office of vicar was abolished and it received its own *prefect* from the emperor. The **sub-general** <note>original: ὑποστράτηγος</note> mentioned here could be the one who formerly governed, the *vicar*. Pancirollus in the *Notitia of the Western Empire*. **GOAR.**

page 712, verse 13. [**Count of the East** <note>original: κόμητα ἀνατολῆς</note>] The Count of the East had under his authority the provinces of the East as recorded by Marcellinus and the *Notitia of the Empire*. Ambrose (Letter 29 to Theodosius) establishes his military rank, while Valesius (on Marcellinus, book 24) establishes his civil rank. Zosimus, cited by the same author, leans toward this, and our author especially favors it when narrating that civil affairs were handled by him and that he suppressed the sedition of the Jews of Antioch by inflicting punishments. **GOAR.**

*ibid.* verse 18. [**the image not made by hands** <note>original: τὴν ἀχειροποίητον εἰκόνα</note>] Gretserus (in *Short Works on Images Not Made by Hands*, chapter 15) writes that this was not the Edessa image found later, but the Camuliana image or another miraculously produced or copied by a painter from a prototype not made by hand, and thus also called **not made by hands** <note>original: ἀχειροποίητον</note>. Damascenus Studites also writes of this in his *Treasury*. **GOAR.**

*ibid.* verse 19. [**into the Port of Sophia** <note>original: εἰς τὸν λιμένα τῆς Σοφίας</note>] This is a part of the very large port of Constantinople on the Galata side, named **Sophia** by Justin after his wife's name. See the author under the second year of Justin. **GOAR.**

page 713, verse 22. [**the oratory of Saint Stephen** <note>original: τῷ εὐκτηρίῳ τοῦ ἁγίου Στεφάνου</note>] Theodosius built that sacred oratory after the relics of St. Stephen were translated. The author mentions this in his life. **GOAR.**

page 714, verse 6. [**in imperial fashion** <note>original: βασιλικῷ σχήματι</note>] His predecessor Maurice sought to renew that ancient custom. The author mentions this in the first year of his life. **GOAR.**

*ibid.* verse 20. [**Epiphania was crowned** <note>original: ἐστέφθη Ἐπιφανία</note>] She was the first of the emperors' daughters to be crowned Augusta due to the death of her mother, the Empress. **GOAR.**

page 715, verse 5. [**Sergius crowning her** <note>original: στέψαντος αὐτὴν Σεργίου</note>] The Augusta was crowned not only by the emperor himself, as the author says was first practiced by Justin I, but also by the patriarch. **GOAR.**

page 717, verse 12. [*in the year 60*] The passage is mutilated and requires a diviner <note>meaning a scholar who can guess the missing content based on context</note>. **XYLANDER.**

*ibid.* verse 16. [*as far as* * ] The scribe wrote in the margin: <margin>One must inquire "until when," because nothing concerning this was in the copy.</margin> **XYLANDER.**

page 718, verse 2. [***Bonus*** <note>original: Bono</note>] This is also found in Zonaras. And in the margin of our manuscript, **Bonus** <note>original: Βόνῳ</note> was annotated instead of **Bonosus** <note>original: Βονόσῳ</note>. **XYLANDER.**

page 719, verse 8. [**Turks** <note>original: Τούρκων</note>] Here the name of the Turks is first read in the author; regarding them, see already page 341: "The Turks of the East, whom they also call Khazars." **GOAR.**

*ibid.* verse 10. [**Themes** <note>original: θεμάτων</note>] The name of the <term>theme</term> <note>The administrative and military districts of the middle Byzantine Empire</note> has until now been unknown to the author—

<meta>This page continues the philological commentary by scholars Wilhelm Xylander (XYL.) and Jacques Goar (GOAR.). # THE COMMENTARIES OF XYLANDER AND GOAR. 812

...unknown to the ancients in the sense it is now understood. It signifies, first of all, a legion assigned to a certain province or people. Constantine, in *The Themes of the East* <note>Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus, a 10th-century Emperor known for his scholarly works</note>: <note>original: πρώην καὶ κατ’ ἀρχὰς τάγματά τινα καὶ λεγεῶνες ὑπῆρχον ἀναγεγραμμένα κατ’ ἔθνος</note> "formerly and in the beginning there were certain ranks and legions enrolled by nation." In the process of time, the provinces themselves were called **themes** <term>Thema: a military-administrative district of the Byzantine Empire</term>; and so we do not have to look far for evidence, for this author writes: "passing through the Roman themes." More on this can be found in Rigaltius and Meursius. **GOAR.**

page 720, verse 14. [**the moon emerged**] where I wrote that the moon emerged, the Greek word was *stood still* <note>original: ὑπέστη</note>: but I made a conjecture based on the circumstances. **XYLANDER.**

page 721, verse 13. [**at Gazakos** <note>original: ἐν Γαζακῷ</note>] the text is mutilated here. **XYLANDER.**

*ibid.* verse 14. [**Vigla** <note>original: βίγλα</note>] a Latin word <note>from *vigilia*, meaning 'watch'</note> used in a Greek manner. This is often the case in the writings of Nicetas. **XYLANDER.** *Vigla* refers to military watches. Simocatta (2.9) called it *oversight* <note>original: ἐπισκοπήν</note>, meaning an exploration or a secret and hidden investigation of the enemy; Cedrenus, in his account of Maurice, calls it *reconnaissance* <note>original: κατασκοπήν</note>. **GOAR.**

page 722, verse 9. [***with the Gospels***] namely, so that he might take "lots" from them <note>The practice of *Sortes Sanctorum*, or opening the Bible at random to find divine guidance</note>. This type of fortune-telling is superstitious and impious, which Saint Augustine also mentions and disapproves of at the end of his 119th Letter to Januarius. In the same way, the pagans used to consult the *Virgilian lots*, an example of which is found in Spartianus regarding Hadrian, and elsewhere. **XYLANDER.**

*ibid.* verse 12. [***moved by pity***] <margin>But my Emperor, Isaac Angelus, even those whom he caught red-handed plotting against him, he both favored and elevated to the heights of dignity.</margin> **XYLANDER.**

page 723, verse 7. [**he pitched camp** <note>original: ἠπλήκευσε</note>] I have deduced that this is the meaning of this word from its frequent use by our author, where the context of the events explains this "barbarous" <note>meaning non-Classical Greek</note> vocabulary. **XYLANDER.** <margin>*to measure out a camp.*</margin> [**he pitched camp**] he applied, moved, placed, or fixed the camp. So says Paul the Deacon. The verb is derived from the Latin language, *to apply* <note>original: τὰ ἀπληκεύω</note>. **GOAR.**

page 726, verse 19. [**Magarite** <note>original: μαγαρίτην</note>] whom modern Greeks call a **faith-denier** <note>original: ἀρνόπιστον</note>; this is one who, having renounced the faith, has stained and polluted himself with the foul rite of heathendom. For "to magarize" <note>original: μαγαρίζω</note> means to *defile, contaminate, or fill with filth*, and metaphorically to *violate the law* and to foul the Christian religion through shameful desertion. Theophanes writes: "Umar forbade wine in the cities and forced the Christians to apostatize <note>original: μαγαρίζειν</note>." Paul the Deacon summarized it in one word: *to apostatize*. Hence a *Magarite* is one who has denied the faith; the Greek Church also extends this term to one who pollutes himself with profane and forbidden food. **GOAR.**

page 727, verse 6. [***of the Nestorian religion***] That a Persian was an ally and patron of the Nestorian error is something no one would believe if they recalled what was said previously regarding his superstition. However, further down in the 19th year of Heraclius, our author writes that the church of Edessa was occupied by Nestorians under Chosroes. **XYLANDER.**

page 728, verse 18. [**of carved boats** <note>original: σκαφῶν γλυπτῶν</note>] small river boats prepared in a hurry from a single hollowed-out log, called **monoxyla** <note>literally 'single-wood'</note>; *carved boats*, namely those sculpted and formed from a trunk with a rough chisel.

### ANNOTATIONS. 813

The author speaks of these in "six hundred places" <note>a Latin idiom meaning "countless places"</note> where he mentions the Russians and the Pechenegs <note>original: Patzinacis</note>. Constantine Porphyrogenitus, in *On the Administration of the Empire* (chapter 8), describes most extensively their use, and the method by which they are usually dragged over land or carried on men's shoulders, regarding the Pechenegs' navigation *in dugouts* <note>original: ἐν μονοξύλοις; boats carved from a single tree trunk</note>. **GOAR.**

**page 728, verse 18.** [**the gulf of the horn** <note>original: τὸν κόλπον τοῦ κέρατος</note>] the port of Constantinople <note>the Golden Horn</note>. Leunclavius. **GOAR.**

**page 729, verse 9.** [**at the place called the Old Rock** <note>original: κατὰ τόπον τὸν λεγόμενον τῆς παλαιᾶς πέτρας</note>] From that point to that place, a procession was held according to the ancient pattern <note>original: typum</note>, the ritual and prayers of which are shown in the recently published *Euchologion* <term>Euchologion: a primary service book of the Eastern Orthodox Church containing the liturgies and prayers</term>. That rock is very large, located toward the gate called the Adrianople Gate. **GOAR.**

**page 730, verse 19.** It is easy for anyone reading Simocatta (3.6) to recognize that **bandon** <note>original: βάνδον</note> signifies a military standard <note>original: vexillum</note>. Paul the Deacon calls it this in Latin. Rigaltius adds that it also indicates a *tagma* <note>original: τάγμα; a military unit</note>, meaning a "band" or "troop." I would agree, provided he understands it as that cohort or line of march that serves under one *bandon* or standard, from which it takes its name—a "company." **GOAR.**

**page 731, verse 15.** [**lorion** <note>original: λωρίον</note>] This is never a breastplate <note>original: lorica</note>, but a belt from which a shield or sword hangs; a thong <note>original: lorum</note>. Germanus in the *Mystagogia*. **GOAR.**

*ibid.* [**the brachionia** <note>original: τὰ βραχιόνια</note>] Theophanes reads this with the more common word *brachiolia*, which are armlets or bracelets for the arms. Xylander refers to them as "arm-coverings for tailors" <note>original: sartores brachiorum indumenta</note>. **GOAR.**

*ibid. verse 16.* I think what a **Scaramangium** is can be learned from those who are skilled in the "corrupted" Greek language <note>referring to Medieval or Vernacular Greek</note>. I hear that Homer’s *Iliad* has been published in that language; I wish I could obtain it. Indeed, I wish a lexicon of that language would be published, so that knowledge of later times might become clearer. **XYL.** [**the skaramangion** <note>original: τὸ σκαραμάγγιον</note>] Achmes (chapter 131) interprets this as a *kabbadion*. A *kabbadion* <note>original: καββάδιον</note> is an outer tunic, tight and clinging to the body, but shorter and joined with buttons <note>original: globis</note> at the chest; it is not entirely unlike a military cloak. **GOAR.**

**page 732, verse 11.** [**large pieces of aloe wood** <note>original: ξύλα μεγάλα ἀλόης</note>] commonly called *xylaloe*, but called *Agallochon* by physicians. For where the Greek manuscript of Dioscorides discusses *Agallochon*, a marginal note writes "now called *xylaloe*." Mattioli adds that the Portuguese bring the best kind from the market of Calicut, which, when set on fire, wafts a most sweet scent. **GOAR.**

*ibid. verse 12.* **Metaxa** is a type of silk cloth. See the notes by Lang in Nicephorus (17.32). **XYL.** [**metaxa** <note>original: μέταξαν</note>] This signifies silk threads or raw silk, not a cloth woven from it. **GOAR.**

*ibid.* [**cotton shirts** <note>original: καρβάσια καμίσια</note>] Xylander interprets these as "fine linen shirts." Successfully so. However, I would want these to be understood here as the finer linen and cotton garments that were usually worn by Orientals for elegance, luxury, and display. **GOAR.**

*ibid. verse 13.* I do not know what **asemum** is, unless perhaps it signifies silver that is not marked or (as Maro <note>the poet Virgil</note> says) "unwrought" <note>original: infectum</note>. **XYL.** Silver that has not yet been struck and stamped with any character <note>i.e., uncoined bullion</note>. **GOAR.**

*ibid. verse 14.* [**nakotapeta** <note>original: νακοτάπητα</note>] *Nakos* indeed refers to a fleece, but not...

<meta>This page continues the philological and historical commentary on the Byzantine chronicles, primarily focusing on the reigns of the Persian King Chosroes II and the Byzantine Emperor Constans II. It clarifies technical terms regarding textiles, military titles, and theological disputes of the 7th century.</meta>

### XYLANDER AND GOAR

Therefore, a **shaggy rug** <note>original: νακοτάπητα (nakotapeta)</note> is a leather garment or coverlet, as Xylander conjectures; however, it is more likely a hanging or a rug made of shaggy silk or wool, commonly called a Persian or Armenian rug, whose pile resembles a fleece in some way. **GOAR.**

**page 732, verse 18.** [**Theophany** <note>original: Theophania</note>] These are what people today call Epiphany, **the feast of the Holy Three Kings** <note>original German: der heiligen drey Künig tag</note>. It is named this because, at the baptism of Christ, the Father offered Himself to be heard and the Holy Spirit offered Himself to be seen in the form of a dove. **Dastagerdum** and **Dystagerda** are the same place. **XYLANDER.**

**page 733, verse 5.** [**attendant** <note>original: satellitem</note>] A **sword-bearer** <note>original: σπαθάριον (spatharion)</note>. A little earlier, regarding Razastes, I translated this as "armor-bearer." It is named from the *spatha*, which is a long sword or dagger. **XYLANDER.**

**ibid., verse 11.** [**Kardarikas** <note>original: καρδαρίχαν</note>] Theophanes reads this as *Kardaregas* and writes: "Kardaregas is not a proper name, but a high rank among the Persians, signifying the General of the Persians." **GOAR.**

**page 734, verse 13.** [**Chosroes the patricide** <note>original: Chosroen patricidam</note>] For he is said to have obtained the kingdom after his father Hormisdas was captured and killed in chains. **XYLANDER.**

**page 736, verse 5.** [**of the Jacobites** <note>original: τῶν Ἰακωβιτῶν</note>] These were the followers of a certain Syrian monk named Jacob; they were also adherents of Eutyches and Dioscorus in most matters. However, read this as the 20th year, not the 25th, so that the sequence of years is not disturbed. **GOAR.**

**ibid., verse 14.** [**of Phasis** <note>original: Phasidis</note>] Paul the Deacon (Book 18) has *Phaselis*, as cited in the 7th century of the *New Ecclesiastical History*. Phaselis is a maritime city of Pamphylia, near Lycia. I prefer this reading, even though Zonaras also has *Phasis*. **XYLANDER.** In these notes, Xylander wanders the whole distance from Phasis, a city and river of the Lazi in Colchis <note>modern Georgia</note>, to Phaselis in Pamphylia. **GOAR.**

**ibid., verse 18.** [**Pharan** <note>original: Φαράν</note>] This is a city located midway between Egypt and Arabia. **GOAR.**

**ibid., verse 19.** [**to be submerged in water** <note>original: aqua submergendam</note>] **Water-dyed** <note>original: ὑδροβαφῆ (hydrobaphe)</note>. Perhaps it means "diluted" and "unfit" or "worthless." **XYLANDER.** More correctly, it means "lightly tinted"; one might more accurately call it "futile" or "counterfeit" rather than "submerged in water." **GOAR.**

**page 737, verse 3.** [**he ordains by edict**] In the margin it says: **an un-dogmatic decree upon a decree** <note>original: δόγμα ἐπὶ δόγματι ἀδογμάτιστον</note>. I believe he meant this: that a foolish edict was made for the sake of defending a foolish opinion. But these things are also noted in the same place: "See how this most manly Emperor fell among the heretics; I do not know if he did so even of his own will." **XYLANDER.**

**ibid., verse 12.** St. Maximus was an abbot in Africa. Emperor Constans, the grandson of Heraclius, killed him and his two disciples because they opposed the **Monothelites** <term>Monothelites: heretics who believed Christ had two natures but only one will</term>, as is clear from Zonaras; our author did not hide this in the 16th year of his reign. The passage is confused. Others (Paul the Deacon, Books 18 and 19) make Theodore the Bishop of Constantinople. **XYLANDER.** If the particle **and** <note>original: καί</note> is placed before the words "the disciples," the historical truth and the author's legitimate meaning are preserved. For Pyrrhus and Maximus were not disciples of Theodore, the Pope of Rome; rather, the events concerning Pyrrhus, Maximus, and Maximus's disciples occurred during the time of Theodore. **GOAR.**

**ibid. [and Martin]** The order of history is inverted here so that many things can be presented in summary. **GOAR.**

# ANNOTATIONS. 815

**page 737, verse 16. [the Amalek of the desert]** Muhammad. **XYLANDER.** <note>original: ὁ ἐρημικὸς Ἀμαλήκ (ho eremikos Amalek)</note>

**ibid., verse 18.** The defeats at Gabitha and the Yarmuk are mentioned a little further down. Gabitha is a city in Syria. Concerning the battle fought there, see below under the 24th year of Heraclius. **GOAR.**

**ibid. [the Yarmuk]** The author reads this as "Iermochthan" <note>original: Ἱερμοχθᾶν</note> in year 25, and demonstrates that it is a river in Syria. **GOAR.** <note>original: ὁ Ἱερμουχάν (ho Iermouchan)</note>

**page 738, verse 1. [persecutor of the church]** This was Constans, the grandson of Heraclius. **XYLANDER.**

**page 751, verse 7. [stipend]** The word "roga" <note>original: ῥόγαν</note> is in the text; but I have learned from Choniates <note>Niketas Choniates, a 12th-century Byzantine historian</note> that this is what the Greeks call a **wage**. It is much clearer in our author's section on Leo the Iconoclast near the end, where the verb "to be paid a roga" <note>original: ῥογεύεσθαι (rogeuesthai)</note> is used. Also, near the end of Nicephorus's work, the Saracens intercept the soldiers' stipends "from the general funds," specifically a "roga" of 13 centenaria. Furthermore, in the section on Constantine, the son of Leo, the "roga" is explained as the **usual distribution** to the armies. Finally, at the end of Romanos Argyros, the "roga" of the senators is recorded as a **distribution**. Lastly, Suidas <note>a 10th-century Greek encyclopedia</note> also interprets "roga" as the **piety and generosity** of kings. A little earlier I conjectured that the word "suncharia" <note>original: συγχάρια</note> comes from the word for "rejoicing together," meaning **congratulations** <note>original German: glückwünschung</note> or congratulatory gifts. **XYLANDER.**

**page 754, verse 8. [12 years]** The same is found in Zonaras regarding Constans, the grandson of Heraclius. In the Chronology of Nicephorus, Archbishop of Constantinople, it reads 2 years and 26 days. I have not seen the Greek version of that myself; it was published in Latin, translated by Camerarius, that exceptional ornament of Germany and pillar of fine literature, whom I name with honor. **XYLANDER.**

**page 755, verse 15. [Colossians]** He follows an error propagated by ignorance of geography and names, about which I have written elsewhere. The Colossians are listed with the Asians a little later, where he speaks of the Paulician heresy. **XYLANDER.** Not only the Rhodians, but also the Phrygians of Chonae (who are also called Passalenses) are Colossians; Xylander ought to have noted this so as not to stumble. **GOAR.**

**page 756, verse 12. [of the bugler]** "Boukenator" <note>original: βουκηνάτωρος</note>; for I did not think it was a proper name. It is a small matter. **XYLANDER.** A "bukinon" or "boukinon" <note>original: βύκινον</note> is a **bugle** <note>original Latin: buccina</note>, a curved instrument made of horn, to be blown with the breath in wars. It differs from the **trumpet** <note>original Latin: tuba</note>, which is smaller, and in Leo's *Constitution 7* it is called a "small bugle." However, according to Nicetas in his work on Manuel Comnenus, the "buccina" is an **elongated pipe**, and therefore he wrote in book 6 "long like bugles." Hence, you may often read the "salpinx" <note>original: σάλπιγγα</note> or "tuba" as being distinct from the "buccina," although the aforementioned Leo confuses the two when he says the signal is given by the "tuba," which they now call a "boukinon." **GOAR.**

**page 757, verse 16. [named Simeon]** The passage is mutilated, and as is clear from what follows, it should be read thus: "one named Simeon, but who wanted to be called Titus. After him, Genesius, who nonetheless called himself Timothy," etc. **XYLANDER.**

**page 761, verse 6. [elsewhere]** I believe he is hinting at some theological book he wrote; which perhaps perished without a great loss to history. What if it was the *Dogmatic Panoply* <note>original: δογματικὴ πανοπλία (Dogmatike Panoplia)</note>, a defense (I think) against wicked opinions on sacred matters, which I mentioned above when discussing the delusions of Muhammad—

**page 766, verse 6. [ten thousand]** Zonaras has three. The symbols for the numbers 10 <note>represented by the Greek letter iota</note> and 3 <note>represented by the Greek letter gamma</note> have similar shapes. He also has only 8 servants. **XYLANDER.**

# 818 XYLANDER AND GOAR

...built so that the people might receive the emperor there; this is not inconsistent with this opinion. For I suppose even the barbarians know what the **Saximodeximum** <note>original: σαξιμοδέξιον; a ceremonial area near the palace</note> is. **XYLANDER.** **Near the palace** <note>original: πλησίον δὲ τοῦ παλατίου</note>] From the description of the Royal City of Constantinople, it is clear that after passing through the gate of the first wall one encounters a very large courtyard, fortified by a most faithful bodyguard but open and granted to the common crowds. Here, Justinian [II] was laboring to build stone seats for the **Blue faction** <note>The "Blues" (Venetae) and "Greens" (Prasini) were the two primary sports and political factions in Constantinople, often involved in riots and imperial successions.</note>, toward whom the emperors were more favorably inclined because of the rebellions frequently stirred up by the **Greens** as the more powerful party. These seats were for the faction to stand and welcome him with auspicious cheers upon his return or departure. Nevertheless, deterred by the sanctity of a neighboring temple [church] and wanting to avoid public complaints, he sought the prayers of Patriarch Callinicus to assist his undertaking. The Patriarch first responded that the Church had established prayers for dedicating temples, not for tearing them down; however, soon overcome by the Emperor’s authority, he made the forced consent and the violently extorted agreement more clearly manifest by inventing a new proclamation of God. The **stone benches far from the Blues** <note>original: βάθρα πόρρω τῶν Βενέτων</note> were stone seats to be prepared for the Blue faction, and as Paul the Deacon says, "bases for the people were to be constructed," so that they might receive the emperor there. For I gather that the Greens stood in the same place or nearby from Leo the Grammarian, who writes in his account of [Emperor] Theophilus: **the steps where the factions stand** <note>original: τὰς ἀναβάθρας ἔνθα οἱ δῆμοι ἵστανται</note>. Simocatta writes in Book 8, Chapter 2, that the Blues nevertheless chose a different place from the Greens regarding the coronation of Leontia, the wife of the tyrant Phocas. **GOAR.**

**page 774, verse 4. The Phiala** <note>original: τὴν φιάλην; typically a ceremonial fountain</note>] A mechanism from which water is poured from marble or metal statues through open tubes or pipes, sprayed, or vibrated high into the air. Once the desire of the eyes is satisfied, the water is preserved and freely offered to relieve the thirst and extinguish the heat of the gathering people; it is called a **phiala**, as if a "phial," a vessel suitable for displaying waters. Public buildings, temples, and even palaces always sought to abound in phialas of this kind; the *Euchologion* <note>The primary liturgical service book of the Greek Church.</note> and the most learned Allatius have written about these. **GOAR.**

**ibid., verse 5. To perform the Saximodeximum there** <note>original: τελεῖσθαι ἐκεῖ τὸ σαξιμοδέξιμον</note>] But how was this **Saximodeximum** celebrated such that a church location would be necessary for its completion? Leo the Grammarian briefly explains this obscure and difficult term in his account of Theophilus. The **phiala** (perhaps *phialin*) is the place where the so-called *Saximodeximum* takes place, with the horses of both factions passing through covered in **golden saddlecloths** <note>original: σαγισμάτων; ornate ceremonial coverings</note>. Thus, the factions about to compete in the Circus [the Hippodrome], or those about to accompany the emperor in a **procession** <note>original: προελεύσει or προόδῳ; a formal imperial progress</note>—events celebrated so often in the histories—would show off horses covered in golden rugs at the *Saximodeximum*, and having departed from there, they would take their path. The place was perhaps named so because it was the **introduction of the factions who were to receive [the emperor]** <note>original: εἴσαξις δήμων δεξομένων</note>. **GOAR.**

**ibid., verse 12. At the Petrion church** <note>original: εἰς τὸ Πετρὶν ἐκκλησίαν</note>] Built to compensate for the destroyed one. The **Petrion** <note>A district in the northern part of Constantinople near the Golden Horn.</note> is frequently named in this work. **GOAR.**

**ibid., verse 19. General of the Anatolics** <note>original: στρατηγὸς τῶν ἀνατολικῶν</note>] This is the **Count of the East**, regarding whom see the *Notitia Imperii* <note>A late Roman document listing all administrative and military posts.</note>; the **General of Hellas** <note>original: στρατηγὸς τῆς Ἑλλάδος</note> stands for the **Proconsul of Achaia**.

# 819 ANNOTATIONS

...is either of Greece, or was formerly subject to the Prefect of Illyricum <note>A major administrative prefecture of the Roman Empire covering much of the Balkans</note>. See the *Notitia Imperii* [Register of Dignitaries], and Pancirollus’s commentary on chapter 103. **GOAR.**

**Page 775, line 4. *Callistratici***] Zonaras <note>A 12th-century Byzantine chronicler</note> mentions them in his account of the Emperor Philippicus. **XYLANDER.**

**Ibid., line 10. *With his armed men***] <note>original: μετὰ ἀρμάτων</note>. I do not see how **chariots** <note>original: currus</note> would have been useful in this context. Perhaps it should be "arms" <note>original: ἄρμων</note>, as is common in many Latin translations. However, later in the history of Emperor Monomachus, in the account of the Pecheneg leader Catalin, the word **arms** <note>original: ἅρματα</note> is clearly used to mean weapons or military equipment, and not just once. **XYLANDER.**

**Ibid., line 19. *The basin***] <note>original: λουτῆρα</note>; the **baptistery** <note>original: baptisterium</note> of the Great Church [Hagia Sophia], otherwise called a bath <note>original: λουτρόν</note>, a pool <note>original: κολυμβήθρα</note>, or a baptistery <note>original: βαπτιστήρ</note>. **GOAR.**

**Ibid., line 21. *That they be dug up***] <note>original: ἀνασκαφῇ</note>. It is obscure what this phrase intends. I believe, however, that these words signify the deposition of this Justinian **Rhinotmetus** <note>Justinian II, nicknamed "the Slit-nosed" after his facial mutilation upon being deposed in 695 AD</note> from the empire. I did not want to change anything, even though it is almost certain a mistake lurks in the text, and it is not clear what it means for the "bones of a living man to be dug up." Certainly, the same phrase appears later regarding his second reign, used twice: "they dug up Justinian" <note>original: ἀνέσκαψαν τὸν Ἰουστινιανόν</note>, meaning they revoked his imperial authority. I believe this was carried out in such a way that the statues erected to the emperor were overturned at the same time. The same occurs regarding the Emperors Artemius and Calaphates. And here, a little later, the noun for "digging up" <note>original: ἀνασκαφῆς</note> is used as a synonym for the revocation of imperial power. **XYLANDER.**

**Page 776, line 3. *At the Ox***] <note>original: ad Bovem</note>. The manuscript mistakenly has "the hill" <note>original: βουνόν</note> instead of "the ox" <note>original: βοῦν</note>, as is clear from Zonaras. Our author also mentions this forum—the **Forum of the Ox** in Constantinople—frequently above. See Zonaras at the end of the reign of Phocas. **XYLANDER.** "The Hill" <note>original: βουνόν</note> refers to **The Mount**, a place in Constantinople so named. Paul the Deacon writes "Vaurum," and Xylander writes "The Ox," but he does so out of ignorance: although in the neuter gender among modern Greeks the word "the hill" <note>original: βουνόν</note> sounds like **beef**. **GOAR.**

**Ibid., line 9. *Of Alis***] <note>original: Ἀλιδí</note>. Paul the Deacon says "Senalidus." And for "Rome" <note>original: Ῥώμην</note>, one should undoubtedly read **Romania** <note>a common term for the Byzantine Empire</note>, or at least understand the former as meaning the latter, as seen later in the account of Apsimar. Instead of "Patriarch" <note>original: πατριάρχης</note>, write **Patrician** <note>original: πατρίκιος</note> following the same author. **XYLANDER.** **Of Lazica**] <note>original: Λαζικῆς</note>; the region of **Colchis** <note>An ancient region on the Black Sea, modern-day Georgia</note>. **GOAR.**

**Ibid., line 16. *Leaving behind a taxation***] <note>original: ταξατίωνα καταλιπών</note>. I have not yet learned what this means. **XYLANDER.** Legal experts interpret this word as **assessment** <note>original: taxationem</note>; but Meursius says there is another interpretation of the word here. Certainly, he adds, Xylander did not translate it well: he should have instead used "garrison" <note>original: praesidium</note>, specifically a **personal detachment** <note>original: ταξατίωνα ἴδιον</note> granted to John for his protection. Thus, in Constantine Porphyrogenitus's *On Administering the Empire*: "While Abimelech held power, the Arabs marched against Africa and seized it, and from their own army they established a **detachment** <note>original: ταξατίωνα</note> within it." **GOAR.**

**Ibid., line 17. *Protosymbolus***] <note>A high-ranking official title</note>. In Zonaras, it is read as *protosymbulus* [chief counselor], which I think is a mistake. **XYLANDER.**

**Ibid., line 19. *He camps in military fashion***] <note>original: φοσσατικῶς ἀπληκεύει</note>. I interpret this as: "He moves his army and all his forces according to the laws of warfare." **GOAR.**

**Ibid., line 21. <term>Drungarius</term>** <note>A high-ranking military or naval commander in the Byzantine hierarchy</note>. He is a **tribune of the soldiers**, as Wolfius noted from Aelian and the booklet *On the Offices of the Palace*. See also Turnebus, book 24, chapter 25 of his *Adversaria*. The Cibyrratae are in Cilicia. **XYLANDER.** **Drungary of the Cibyrraeotae**] <note>original: δρουγγάριον τῶν Κιβυρραιωτῶν</note>. In the Roman [Byzantine] army, there were naval squadrons just as there were land forces, named after their specific provinces. The most famous was that of the **Cibyrraeotae**, named for the great city of **Cibyra** in Caria mentioned by Strabo.
