# 820 COMMENTARIES OF XYLANDER AND GOAR

...called, over which a commander known as a **drungarius** <note>original: δρουγγάριος</note> ruled. A **drungos** <note>original: δροῦγγος</note> was a third or fourth part of the whole fleet, and the **drungarius** was the leader of such a body of soldiers. From this, just as Maurice writes in Book 1 of his *Strategic Works* <note>The *Strategikon*, a manual of war traditionally attributed to the Emperor Maurice</note> that it is "a part composed of three gathered parts" <note>original: μέρος ἐστί, τὸ ἐκ τριῶν μερῶν συγκειμένων ἄθροισμα</note>, it follows that there were as many **drungarii**. Leo [the Wise] in his *Naval Battles* <note>The *Naumachica*</note> says: "The naval generals of the other districts <note>The Byzantine "themes" or administrative-military regions</note> were once called **drungarii** in ancient times" <note>original: οἱ τῶν ἄλλων θεμάτων πλώϊμοι στρατηγοὶ δρουγγάριοι ἐκαλοῦντο ποτὲ τοῖς ἄνω χρόνοις</note>. Theophanes mentions the fleet of the **Cibyrrhaeots** <note>A major naval district on the southern coast of Asia Minor</note> during the reign of [Constantine V] Copronymus. **GOAR.**

**Page 777, line 2. *In Sycae***] <note>original: ἐν Συκαῖς</note> in the place now called **Galata** <note>A district of modern Istanbul</note>, about which Stephanus speaks. "Sycae," he says, "is a city opposite New Rome" <note>Constantinople</note>. Socrates says the same in Book 2, chapter 30. **GOAR.**

**Ibid., line 6. *Sole-general***] <note>original: μονοστράτηγον</note> here this is contrasted with the **drungarius**, as he alone commands the battle line. **GOAR.**

**Ibid. *On foot and on horseback***] <note>original: τῶν ἐξωκαβαλλαρικῶν; literally "the external cavalrymen"</note>. From the chronicler Zonaras, it seems the reading should be "of the infantry and cavalry" <note>original: τῶν πεζῶν καὶ καβαλλ.</note>, which is what I have followed. **XYLANDER.**

**Ibid., line 22. *Abdelas***] It is also read as **Abderas** <note>original: Ἀβδερᾶς</note>. But I preferred the former, since [Paul] the Deacon calls him **Habdalla** <note>Abdullah</note>, the leader of the Saracens, in Book 20. However, the claim there that he besieged Tarentum is clearly erroneous; it should be read, as our author correctly has it—and as found in others—as **Antaradus** <note>A city and island on the coast of Syria, modern Tartus</note>, which is an island situated between Cyprus and Syria. Our author provides the rest more fully, and it is useful to compare him with others. **XYLANDER.**

**Page 778, line 23.** The **Khazars** <note>A powerful Turkic nomadic people of the Steppe</note> are a people near the Danube and the **Pechenegs**, whose prince is called **khagan** and **pech**. Constantine [Porphyrogenitus] says in *On the Administration of the Empire*, chapter 42: "For that **khagan** and **pech** of Khazaria" <note>original: ὁ γὰρ χαγάνος ἐκεῖνος καὶ πὲχ Χαζαρίας</note>. **GOAR.**

**Page 779, line 2. *Phanagoraea***] "Phagouria" <note>original: φαγουρίαν</note> is a poor reading, and the version written above is better. It is a city at the Cimmerian Bosporus <note>The modern Strait of Kerch</note>. **XYLANDER.**

**Page 780, line 11. *Apolloniada***] a city on Parnassus near Delphi. Stephanus. **GOAR.**

**Ibid., line 20. *He impaled/suspended on the wall***] <note>original: ἐν τῷ τείχει ἐφούλκισεν</note>. In Zonaras it is written "he hung them on timbers by the walls" <note>original: ἐν ξύλοις παρὰ τοῦ τείχεσιν ἀπηώρησε</note>. From this passage, it can be conjectured that **phoulkizein** <note>term: *phoulkizein* (φουλκίζειν); a rare verb possibly derived from military context, here interpreted as a form of execution</note> means to put on a cross or a gallows: that is, to hang from wood <note>German: *hencken*</note>. **XYLANDER.**

**Page 781, line 1.** That **baia** are **branches** <note>specifically palm branches</note> is known even from the Gospel of St. John, chapter 12. I think it signifies the first part of the games, and that a signal was given with a branch to those competing in each race. **XYLANDER.** The end and dismissal of any work, and especially of a celebration, is an **apolysis** <note>original: ἀπόλυσις</note>; here, however, the **baion** <note>original: βαϊον</note> is the laurel given to the victor of the contest. Therefore, until the first contest was completed, Justinian [II] trampled the necks of **Leontius** and **Apsimar** with his feet. It was a shameful thing that those who had worn the imperial purple then suffered punishment in the Circus, in which the disgrace was not delayed—even before the spectacles had begun, we read in Livy, Book 2, that slaves were once punished: "A certain father of a family had driven a slave through the middle of the Circus while being beaten under a yoke <note>original: *furca*</note>, before the show had even commenced." Also in Cicero—

# ANNOTATIONS. 821

...Cicero's *On Divination*, Book 1: "a slave was beaten with rods through the Circus." <note>original: "servus per Circum cum virgis caederetur"</note> In the works of Lactantius <note>An early Christian author (c. 250–325 AD)</note>, Book 1, Chapter 7: "Autronius Maximus had driven a beaten slave under a yoke through the middle of the Circus to his execution." <note>original: "Autronius Maximus diverberatum servum sub furca medio Circo ad supplicium egerat"</note> I return to the word <term>baion</term> <note>original: βαῖον; likely referring to a palm branch or prize</note>. An anonymous lexicon from the Royal Library explains the word <term>pribeion</term> <note>original: πριβήϊον</note> as "that which is given for the sake of honor, a <term>brabeion</term> <note>original: βραβεῖον; a prize or award in a contest</note>." Certainly, the first term, <term>baion</term>, is not far removed from it. **GOAR.**

**Page 782, line 10. *Added custody***] <term>familikos</term> <note>original: φαμιλικῶς</note>. I think this means "with servants" or "slaves." <note>From the Latin *familia*, meaning household slaves</note> Cuspinianus <note>Johannes Cuspinian, a 16th-century humanist</note> thinks the same on page 199. Perhaps <term>soublai</term> <note>original: σοῦβλαι</note> are foundation piles. **XYL.** You would more aptly translate <term>soublas</term> <note>original: σούβλας</note> as "spits" or "stakes" <note>original: "verva vel palos"</note> rather than "piles." Hesychius <note>A 5th-century grammarian</note> acts as a commentator here: "on stakes as if for roasting; for in ancient times they used to impale criminals, sharpening a piece of wood and driving it through the spine and the back, just like fish being roasted on spits." <note>original: σκόλοψιν ὡς ὄπτησιν· τοὺς γὰρ παλαιοὺς κακουργοῦντας ἀνεσκολόπιζον ὀξύνοντες ξύλον διὰ ῥάχεως καὶ τοῦ νώτου, καθάπερ τοὺς ὀπτωμένους ἰχθῦς ἐπὶ ὀβελίσκων</note> **GOAR.**

**Ibid., line 22. *The foremost of them***] I have great doubt about the meaning of this passage. I understood <term>kephalas</term> <note>original: κεφαλάς; literally 'heads'</note> to mean "captains," as the saying goes. **XYL.**

**Page 783, line 20.** <term>Damatrya</term> <note>original: Δαματρύα</note>] A city in Bithynia <note>A region in modern-day Turkey</note>; the author mentions it again in *Monomachos*, page 643. **GOAR.**

**Page 784, line 4.** <term>paraportio</term> <note>original: παραπορτίῳ</note>] The author wrote <term>parapylion</term> <note>original: παραπύλιον</note> on page 143, which clearly means a "postern" or a smaller gate located at the side of a larger one. In the same way, a <term>parekklesion</term> <note>original: παρεκκλήσιον</note> is a "minor church" or "chapel" situated next to a larger one, and a <term>paralaurion</term> <note>original: παραλαύριον</note> is a "minor monastery" next to a larger one and dependent upon it. **GOAR.**

**Page 785, line 6. *Under the leader Philea***] <term>dia tou Philea</term> <note>original: διὰ τοῦ Φιλέα</note>. Either "through Philea," as if it were the name of a place: I have nothing certain to say. Certainly, Suidas mentions a place by this name, but its location is not recorded. **XYL.** The construction of the phrase itself requires us to interpret <term>tou Philea</term> as a place, not a person: it is a town at the side of the Royal City <note>Constantinople</note>, halfway between the city and the mouth of the Euxine Sea <note>The Black Sea</note>. **GOAR.**

**Ibid., line 14.** Nor do I know well enough what an "armatorium" is, whether it comes from "arms" <note>weapons</note> or from <term>harma</term> <note>original: ἅρμα; a chariot</note>. I found it written unclearly. **XYL.** Paul the Deacon <note>An 8th-century historian</note> writes it as the "oratory of the Greens" <note>The "Greens" were one of the major chariot racing factions</note>. Theophanes more aptly calls it the <term>ornatorion</term> <note>original: ὀρνατούριον</note>, which is clearly a place in the Circus where the Greens, about to compete, adorned themselves with clothing and arms. Cedrenus calls it the <term>armatorion</term> <note>original: ἀρματώριον</note> from the taking up of arms there. **GOAR.**

**Ibid., line 17. *The prince of secretaries***] <term>ho protoasekretis</term> <note>original: ὁ πρωτοασηκρῆτις; a high-ranking official in the Byzantine court</note>. **XYL.** Paul the Deacon translates <term>protoasekretis</term> as "first of the secrets." <note>original: "primum a secretis"</note> Codinus, in the *Origins of Constantinople*, refers to him as a "letter-writer" or "amanuensis." <note>original: ἐπιστολογράφον</note> The same author again assigns to him the supreme power of administering justice in *On Offices*, chapter 5: "The service of the <term>protasekretis</term> (for so he writes it) is clear even from the name itself: for he is called the 'first of the secrets' <note>original: πρῶτος τῶν σεκρέτων; or 'first of the secretaries'</note>." (Another reading in Meursius has "first of the judges"). <note>original: τῶν κριτῶν</note> "And there are times when others more honorable than him are joined with him by royal decree." <note>original: ἔστι δὲ ὅτε συγκρίνουσι μετ᾿ αὐτοῦ βασιλικῷ ὁρισμῷ καὶ ἕτεροι ἐντιμότεροι τούτου</note> **GOAR.**

**Ibid., line 18. *To the heretic***] <term>hairetiko</term> <note>original: αἱρετικός</note>. I read this in the genitive case <term>haeretikou</term>: for Zonaras <note>A 12th-century historian</note> and others sufficiently show that he was pious. **XYL.**

**Page 786, line 7.** <term>koitatorion</term> <note>original: κοιτατώριον</note> is the tablet from which the installation of a high priest is read by the one consecrating him. See the *Euchologion* <note>A primary service book of the Eastern Orthodox Church</note>. **GOAR.**

# XYLANDER AND GOAR. 822

**Page 786, line 8. *The divine grace, etc.***] <note>original: "ἡ θεία χάρις etc"</note> These are the words used by the Greeks when appointing a bishop or when transferring a prelate to another see. **GOAR.**

**Ibid., line 13. *into Phoenicia***] <note>original: "in Phoeniciam"</note> Thus says Zonaras <note>A 12th-century Byzantine chronicler</note>. Our author, however, says "to Phoenix" <note>original: "εἰς τὴν Φοίνικα"</note>. **XYL.**

**Page 787, line 7. *general of the Easterners***] <note>original: "τῶν ἀνατολικῶν στρατηγὸς"</note> Recently called "the general for the cavalry" <note>original: "στρατηγὸς εἰς τὰ καβαλλαρικά"</note>, and formerly called a <term>spatharios</term> <note>original: σπαθάριος</note>, which means a bodyguard <note>original: "σωματοφύλαξ"</note>. **GOAR.**

**Ibid., line 19. *service***] <note>original: "ὑπηρεσίᾳ"</note> Zonaras calls this "baggage" or "equipment" <note>original: "ἀποσκευῇ"</note>. **GOAR.**

**Ibid., line 22. *scribe of gold***] <note>original: "auri scriptor"</note> Taken literally, these things are obscure. Zonaras indeed says that before his reign, he was a collector of public taxes. But here I believe something else is being noted. **XYL.**

**Page 789, line 11. *spatharios***] <note>original: "spatharius"</note> It appears that here this does not signify a simple armor-bearer, but a different dignity and military rank. For mention of "first-swordsmen" <note>original: "protospathariorum"</note> appears repeatedly, and Sergius, who led the revolt against Leo the Isaurian in Sicily, is called a <term>protospatharios</term> <note>original: πρωτοσπαθάριος</note> below. In the reign of Michael the Stammerer <note>original: "Michaelo Balbo"</note>, there are two <term>protospatharioi</term>, Photinus and Damianus, and others elsewhere. Those called <term>Ameras</term> or <term>Amerades</term> <note>likely referring to "Emirs"</note> seem to be the same as those they now call <term>Vaaschas</term> <note>Pashas</note>, meaning governors. **XYL.**

**Page 790, line 1. *emperor with favorable [omens/shouts]***] <note>original: "imperatorem faustis"</note> An obscure passage. One may gather what it means from Book 21 of Paul the Deacon <note>An 8th-century historian of the Lombards</note>. He writes that the Egyptian fleets fled to Constantinople with grain. It seems something is missing from the text. **XYL.**

**Ibid. *from Hiereia all the way to the City***] <note>original: "ἀπὸ τῆς Ἱερείας μέχρι τῆς πόλεως"</note> This refers to the area from the mouth of the Propontis <note>The Sea of Marmara</note> above the city, called "the Sacred Place" <note>original: "Ἱερόν"</note> by Strabo in Book 7 and the "Sacred Mouth," a distance of six miles leading right up to the city itself. **GOAR.**

**Ibid., line 23. *protospatharios***] <note>original: "πρωτοσπαθάριος"</note> Codinus, in *On the Offices of the Court of Constantinople*, Chapter 5, says: "In ancient times, the first of the sword-bearing guards" <note>original: "τὸ παλαιὸν πρῶτος τῶν σπαθαρίων παραμονῶν"</note>. He was the one who girded the sword onto the emperor. **GOAR.**

**Page 791, line 3. *Onomagoulos***] <note>original: "Ὀνομαγούλου"</note> Meaning "having the jaw of an ass." This is how the common phrasing has it. **GOAR.**

**Ibid., line 4. *magistrates and governors***] <note>original: "magistratus et praefectos"</note> The Greek is <term>probolas kai archontas</term> <note>original: προβολὰς καὶ ἄρχοντας</note>. Above, near the end of the section on Justinian, I suspected we should read <term>propōlas</term> <note>original: προπωλάς; meaning "retailers" or "sellers"</note> instead of <term>probolas</term>. But if we wish to take a guess from this passage that "probolas" was written by Cedrenus to mean "magistrates," then that previous passage should perhaps be understood such that, during the riot, not only slaves but also the private property of the nobles suffered plundering. **XYL.**

**Ibid., line 15. *apostrophos***] <note>original: "apostrophos"</note> I think this is the proper name of some promontory or shore, named from the word for "turning away" or "bending back." **XYL.** This does not indicate a mountain or promontory, but rather the winding and twisted bays. **GOAR.**

**Page 792, line 2. *to magarize***] <note>original: "μαγαρίζειν"</note> I have understood this word from Paul the Deacon and indeed from the reality of the events <note>The term usually refers to defilement, or specifically to Christians converting to Islam/becoming "renegades"</note>. **XYL.**

**Ibid., line 4. *Caballinus***] <note>original: "Caballinus"</note> This is the one whom others call "Copronymus" <note>meaning "Name of Dung"</note>, so-called from the excrement he passed into the baptismal font. **XYL.**

**Ibid., line 6. *in the dining room of the Augusteus***] <note>original: "τῷ τρικλίνῳ τοῦ Αὐγουστέως"</note> This dining room <note>triclinium</note>, where...

<meta>This page continues the philological and historical commentary on the Byzantine Empire by Jacques Goar and Xylander. # ANNOTATIONS.

Simocatta <note>Theophylact Simocatta, a 7th-century Byzantine historian</note> depicts the celebration of the marriage of Maurice and Constantina in Book 10, Chapter 1. The *Euchologium* <note>A primary liturgical book of the Eastern Orthodox Church</note> uses the title **Augustalion** <note>original: Αὐγουστάλιον</note> during the coronation of an empress. **GOAR**.

**page 792, line 7. *the great baptizer***] <note>original: "τὸν μέγαν βαπτιστῆρα"</note> This is said in respect to a "lesser" one. The *Euchologium* mentions both. **GOAR**.

**ibid. line 13. *they received***] <note>original: "susceperunt"</note> Namely, they received them from the rite of baptism. He calls the leaders of the orders the **heads of the themes** <note>original: "θεμάτων προύχοντας"; the "themes" were the administrative and military districts of the Empire</note>, because below it is said that the **themes** <note>original: "θέματα"</note> appointed Artabasdus as emperor instead of Copronymus <note>A derogatory nickname for Emperor Constantine V</note>. This word is also used for the armies, so that it may be understood to mean the commanders. **XYL**.

**page 793, line 4. *in the tribunal***] <note>original: "ἐν τῷ τριβουναλίῳ"</note> The translator rendered this as "before the tribunal," but he is mistaken, being misled by the word's similarity to the Latin. For the "Tribunalium" was a most majestic palace. Himerius supports this and explains Cedrenus: "in the Palace of the Tribunal of Eudocia, the wife of Theodosius, the grandson of Theodosius." This was the same as the Palace of the **Nineteen Couches** <note>original: "novemdecim Accubitorum," a famous dining hall in the Great Palace of Constantinople</note>, mentioned on page 307. **GOAR**.

**page 794, line 8. *prooikon***] <note>original: "πρόοικον"</note> You will find this called the **mayor of the royal house** <note>original: "domus regiae maiorem"</note> in Gregory of Tours, and the **master of soldiers** <note>original: "magistrum militum"</note> in Paul Aemilius; the Greeks had an office equal to this in name, though not in function, called the **phaiktor** <note>original: "φαίκτωρα"</note>. Liutprand calls him the **rector of the house** in the final chapter of his *History*. **GOAR**.

**ibid. *torrent***] <note>original: "torrens"</note> The Greek is <note>original: "ὁ χείμαρος"</note>. Or perhaps it is a proper name, Chimarus. That torrents can bring great destruction via their flooding—not only to small or poorly built villages, but even to cities that are by no means insignificant—is a fact that even the city of Basel can demonstrate. I have translated the "dogmatic" letter of the Pope literally as **decretal**. **XYL**.

**page 795, line 20.** I think he is called an **Ecumenical Master** as if he were one whose teaching illuminated the whole world, or whose authority flourished throughout all of Christendom. **XYL**.

**page 796, line 18. *strator***] <note>original: "στράτωρ"</note> A **groom** <note>original: "ἱπποκόμος"</note>, one who performs the care of horses, a stable-master. **GOAR**.

**page 797, line 1. *by a stone of the engine***] <note>original: "tormenti lapide"</note> From the Greek <note>original: "ἐκ τοῦ μαγγανικοῦ"</note>. It appears he calls the machine this, which would hurl a large stone by means of tightened ropes. Paul the Deacon calls this a **mango** in Book 21, relating this word almost literally, as he does with many things. **XYL**.

**page 798, line 10. *seditious***] <note>original: "φατριαστήν"</note>. It appears from Suidas and other sources that a **phatry** <note>original: "φατριάν"</note> is something similar to a tribe or a court division. I have followed this conjecture. **XYL**.

**ibid. line 12. *syncellus***] <note>original: "σύγκελλον"</note> What Xylander wrote regarding the **syncellus** <note>A high-ranking office in the Byzantine Church, literally "one who shares a cell"</note> in the first of his annotations is consistent with this passage. For certain priests were sometimes admitted by the Patriarch into a partnership of shared living and family-like intimacy; upon his death, the dignity of the Patriarchate was often conferred upon them. In the course of time, he was adorned with the honor and name of **syncellus** or "cell-mate"—not as a specific office, which Xylander imagines, but as the designated successor of the Patriarch. One should read the author's notes on Michael, the son of Theophilus, where he discusses Iannes. One should also note the words of Theophanes: "Leo, having in this matter a helper and participant, Anastasius, his disciple and **syncellus**, having made an agreement with him as a fellow-minded person in impiety, and..."

# XYLANDER AND GOAR

...to become an adulterer and successor to the throne. Hence, **Stephen, the son of Basil**, who was educated with **Photius** and promoted to the dignity of **syncellus** <note>A high-ranking administrative aide and confidential advisor to a Patriarch, often seen as his heir apparent</note>, was substituted into his place without any dispute. The author mentions this shortly hereafter at the beginning of the section on Leo; likewise further down, where he relates that **Euthymius**, who was also the **syncellus** of Nicholas, was later promoted to Patriarch. Finally, the author explains in the section on **Constantine Monomachus** (page 775) that it was at one time a settled custom for the person serving as **syncellus** to later become the Patriarch. **GOAR**.

**page 798, line 16. *Diippus***] This seems to have been an addition to the Circus. **Zonaras** <note>A 12th-century Byzantine chronicler and canonist</note> uses the term *diippion*. It appears to signify a place intended for equestrian maneuvers. **XYL**. It is the stadium of the Circus, from which two-horse or four-horse chariots race out. **Paul the Deacon** rendered this as *duppim*, but erroneously. **GOAR**.

**page 799, line 1. *fighting wild beasts***] <note>original: θηριομαχῶν</note> Xylander thinks the author alludes to what Paul commemorates about himself in 2 Corinthians 11. **XYL**. Rather, the author alludes to the name of the ferocious Emperor **Leo** <note>"Leo" means Lion</note>, not to the words of Paul as Xylander writes. **GOAR**.

**ibid. line 4. *He was called Dialogos***] <note>original: Διάλογος ἐκλήθη</note> Some depart from the author's opinion, writing that **Gregory the Great** <note>Pope Gregory I</note>, the first of this name, was commonly called **The Dialogist** <note>original: Διάλογον</note> because of the *Dialogues* he authored. **GOAR**.

**ibid. line 10. *Chrysorroas***] <note>original: Χρυσορρόας</note> This means "flowing with gold," that is, pouring forth a golden river of eloquence—praise which **Cicero** also attributed to **Aristotle**. **Paul the Deacon** seems to call him *Chrysaoram* less aptly, meaning "armed with a golden sword," though he might seem honored with this title due to his sharp defense of icons. However, what *Lentrabus* means to the Greeks, I can no more see than what *Manzur* means. Something might be conjectured about the latter if **Lentrabus** <note>original: λέντραβος</note> were a Greek word. **Manzer** is perhaps **Mamser** <note>original: ממזר</note>, which in the Sacred Scriptures and the Aramaic language signifies a **bastard**; and that word has been retained in the Spanish idiom. I believe he is called the "son of Mansur." In the acts of the Synod of Constantinople, it is recorded that he was called **Manzur** by the Fathers there as a mark of disgrace. **XYL**. **Paul the Deacon** writes: *And instead of Mansur, which is his ancestral name and signifies "redeemed," he called him—in the Jewish sense and by changing the name—Manseron (meaning bastard), the new teacher of the Church.* Among holy men, he is called **Chrysorroas** after the name of the river that flows past his homeland of Damascus. **GOAR**.

**ibid. line 12. *melodist***] <note>original: μελῳδός</note> An author of ecclesiastical hymns among the Greeks. **GOAR**.

**ibid. line 14. *the written ones***] <note>original: τῶν γραπτῶν</note> I thought this was a proper name and made him the "Bishop of Graptene," though I was very doubtful. But it is no great matter. **XYL**. Indeed, it is no great matter that Xylander erred; according to the reach of his understanding, he established **Theodore** as the Bishop of the "Graptoi," taking the title to mean "inscribed" because of the iambic verses branded onto the foreheads of both brothers by the impious **Theophilus**. The author discusses that dreadful branding in the section on Theophilus. **GOAR**.

**page 801, line 8. *Hieracitae***] I do not yet know who these people were. I know there were "woman-hawks" <note>original: γυναιοϊέρακας</note> in Italy at that time, but they have nothing to do with this. **XYL**. **The Hieron** <note>The Sacred Place</note> is the throat of the Propontis <note>The Sea of Marmara</note>, from which the **Hieracitae** take their name. **GOAR**.

**ibid. line 13. *Xerolophos***] <note>original: Ξηρολόφῳ; "The Dry Hill"</note> This is a column like that of Trajan or Antoninus in Rome, made from a single stone, and therefore called **monopetra** <note>original: μονόπετρα; "single-stone"</note> by the inhabitants.

# ANNOTATIONS

...from whose roots a spiral staircase <note>Latin: *gradus cochlearis*, literally "snail-shell steps"</note> ascends through the middle to its summit. 
**Xerolophos** <note>original: Ξηρολόφος; meaning "Dry Hill," one of the seven hills of Constantinople</note> is so named as a sort of "dry mound." Suidas and Codinus write more about it in the *Origins of Constantinople*. **GOAR.**

**page 801, line 18. *to proclaim***] <note>original: διαλαλεῖν</note> This does not mean *to address the citizens*, but rather *to promulgate an edict* or *to command by the voice of a herald*. **GOAR.**

**ibid. line 19. *To our Quaestors***] Those who would demand tribute from each of the social classes. The word **canon** <note>original: κάνονος; here referring to a fixed tax or assessment</note> is still commonly used today for a set amount of money that is paid annually. **XYL.** It refers to *a poll tax to be paid following the issuance of an edict*. **GOAR.**

**volume II, page 3, line 10. *lest anyone***] I have restored this passage from Suidas. **XYL.**

**volume II, page 4, line 5. *spare us, Lord***] These are the words of Cedrenus <note>A 11th-century Byzantine historian</note> as he detests a monstrous blasphemy. However, in the margin is written: *If someone puts precious ointment into an alabaster jar, O most swinish one, and then empties it, does not the fragrance of the ointment still remain in the vessel?* <note>original: ἐὰν δέ τις μύρον πολύτιμον εἰς ἀλάβαστρον ἐμβάλῃ, χοιρωδέστατε... This marginal note uses a metaphor to argue that the sanctity of a person or place remains even after the physical presence is gone</note> **XYL.**

**ibid. line 14.** I do not sufficiently know what a **parippion** <note>original: παρίππιον</note> might be. I believe it was a carriage or a vehicle suitable for racing, which a single horseman would accompany. What if it is a "post-horse" <note>Latin: *veredus*</note> being called by this name? **XYL.** Pancirolus, writing on the public post, says: *when a travel permit was granted, one or two horses were considered allowed; but when a third horse was granted, it was called a parippus or paraveredus.* Therefore, a **parippus** is a horse of the public postal service. **GOAR.**

**volume II, page 5, line 10. *Theopolis***] <note>original: Θεούπολις; "City of God"</note> This is the surname of Great Antioch, used by our author and others. **XYL.** The author wrote why Antioch was called *Theopolis* in the second year of Justinian. **GOAR.**

**ibid. line 16. *a sign in the sky***] Doubtless the sign of the Cross, such as had appeared to Constantine the Great. **XYL.**

**ibid. *Validus***] <note>original: οὐαλίδ</note> He is called **Al-Walid** here by the Deacon (Book 22) and others; he was a prince of the Saracens. And **Izidus** is **Yazid**. The one who is read a little later as **Baktagmos** is **Baktaggios** in the works of Zonaras. **XYL.**

**volume II, page 6, line 12. *Chrysopolis***] A city in Asia across the Propontis <note>The Sea of Marmara</note>, directly opposite Constantinople; it is now called **Scutari** <note>Modern-day Üsküdar</note> by the Turks. It is incorrectly confused by some with Chalcedon. **GOAR.**

**volume II, page 7, line 12. *Germanikeia***] A city of Syria, according to Ptolemy. **GOAR.**

**ibid. line 13. *Dulichia***] Another city of Syria, called Doliche by Ptolemy. **GOAR.**

**volume II, page 8, line 3. *with sacred coverings***] <note>original: ἐπίπλοις</note> With peplos-cloths and sacred veils. Simeon of Thessalonica, in his work on the temple, calls the covering of the altar a *sacred cloth of the holy table*, that is, an **altar cloth**. **GOAR.**

**volume II, page 9, line 7. *Chrysarontiae***] The Deacon in Book 22 calls them **Khorasanites**, a people of eastern Persia. **XYL.**

**volume II, page 10, line 12. *the teacher***] I think this refers to **Germanus**, whose **syncellus** <note>A confidential advisor or high-ranking secretary</note> he was. **XYL.**

**ibid. line 15. *the palace of Syria***] This was undoubtedly a place in Constantinople. The acts of this council, which is called the 7th Council of Constantinople, read "the Palace of **Hieria**." <note>Xylander is correcting a likely scribal error where "Hieria" was misread as "Syria"</note> **XYL.**

# ANNOTATIONS BY XYLANDER AND GOAR

**volume II, page 11, line 7. *apocrisiarius***] <note>original: ἀποκρισιάριον</note> This word is also familiar to the Latins as a term for a legate <note>original: *legato*; a representative or envoy</note> who carries decrees or responses back and forth. **GOAR.**

**volume II, page 12, line 2. *Zicchia***] It appears to be the name of a river, **Zikchias** <note>original: ζικχίας</note>. I believe this is a much more accurate reading than **Lycia** found in Deacon <note>Paul the Deacon, an 8th-century historian</note>, who relates this same history in almost the same words in book 22. Furthermore, from this passage, the reader can come to know many proper names by which places near Constantinople are designated, which occur throughout these histories. The same author has **Euphra** instead of **Cupha**. Mention was made above of **Danastris** and **Danapris** in the section on **Rhinotmetus** <note>original: *Rhinotmeto*; a nickname for Emperor Justinian II, meaning "the slit-nosed"</note>: it is clear from there that they were not far from the **Euxine Sea** <note>original: *Euxino Ponto*; the Black Sea</note>. I have taken **Masia** in turn from Deacon, since my manuscript has **Media** <note>original: Μηδίας</note>. **XYLANDER.**

*ibid. line 12.* **Galata** is a most famous city directly across from the port of Constantinople. On that side were the Sophian palaces, and from them—when the sea was frozen solid—there was an easy crossing, just as there was from Chrysopolis in Asia, all the way to **Saint Mamas** <note>original: *D. Mamantis*; a monastery and district</note> situated in the inner corner of Constantinople. **GOAR.**

*ibid. line 14.* **skala** <note>original: σκάλα</note> sometimes signifies a ladder <note>original: *climacem*</note> or any kind of steps; here, however, the word must be stripped of its sense as a staircase and applied to a naval site or a place in a port where goods are brought off ships and sailors disembark. **Moschopulus** <note>A 14th-century Byzantine grammarian</note> properly calls it a **harbor** <note>original: ὅρμον</note>, defining it as *the part of the port to which ships are drawn and tied, which the common people call a skala.* Regarding the maritime "scales" of Constantinople, **Pancirollus** <note>Guido Panciroli, a 16th-century jurist and antiquarian</note> writes at greater length in his short work on the 14 regions of that city. **GOAR.**

**volume II, page 13, line 11. *Tumtzam***] Deacon has **Zitas**, and relates these things a bit more expansively. Where it reads *fire having been sent into the cohorts*, there is an error: for what does it mean to cast fire into cohorts? However, it can be corrected if you read **courts** <note>original: *cortes*; yards or enclosures</note> instead of **cohorts** <note>original: *cohortes*; military units</note>: for our author calls them **courts** <note>original: αὐλάς</note>, which we call huts. He calls **Stephen the Monk** **"the New"** <note>original: νέον</note>, an epithet which is absent in other authors. **XYLANDER.**

**volume II, page 14, line 1. *stephaniten***] <note>original: στεφανίτην</note> I do not know what this is. **XYLANDER.** This means that, having sent away the announcement of his monastic life, the Emperor persuaded him to take a wife. The historians **Theophanes**, **Paul the Deacon**, our author, and others shrank from openly publishing such a foul crime, and decided to describe it only through a metaphor, veiled in the honorable symbols of marriage. Since the Greeks do not celebrate betrothals without crowns, for them **to be crowned** <note>original: *coronari*</note> is the same as **to contract a marriage**, for marriages themselves are called **stephanoma** <note>original: στεφάνωμα; literally "crowning"</note>; a clear view of this rite and the crowning of the spouses can be seen in the recent **Euchologion** <note>A prayer book of the Eastern Orthodox Church</note>. Therefore, when the Patriarch came forward "crowned" instead of as a monk, he demonstrated that he was submitting himself to the yoke of marriage, and at the same time the rigor of fasting was relaxed for him, nor was there any further pleasure from which he considered himself obliged to abstain. This interpretation is confirmed by the Emperor's hideous deed, which the author records: for he both shamefully ridiculed the habit or devotion of the monks and exposed them to public insult in the Circus, ordering each of them to come forward into the middle leading a common woman by the hand. **Lachanodrakon** <note>Michael Lachanodrakon, a Byzantine general and fierce advocate of Iconoclasm</note>, a rival in impiety, proclaimed by his command in the province entrusted to him, as [it follows] below...

# ANNOTATIONS

*He who lies there, who wishes to obey me and the Emperor, let him put on worldly clothing and take a wife this very hour.* <note>original Latin: "iacet, qui mihi et imperatori vult obsequi..." This quote refers to the forced secularization of monks during the Iconoclast period, where they were often coerced into marriage and abandoning their vows.</note> **GOAR.**

**volume II, page 14, line 1.** *As for the lute-players,* <note>original: "citharoedos"</note> *others maintain that the Patriarch permitted the Emperor to have them at his table. However, as I have translated it, the words themselves seem to require it; and the meaning is better.* For I would not believe that the use of music was forbidden to Emperors: but for a monk, lute-players—as they provoke luxury and excess—were certainly not to be heard. **XYLANDER.**

*ibid.* **to partake of meat** <note>original Greek: κρεῶν μεταλαμβάνειν</note>] In the case of the removal from office of Cyril, recently the Patriarch of Constantinople, one crime among many was that he had **defiled** <note>original Greek: ἐμαγάρισεν</note> the patriarchate by the forbidden eating of meat. **GOAR.**

*ibid. line 9. had put into custody*] I have translated the word **having secured** <note>original Greek: ἀσφαλισάμενος</note> in this way. It is not unlike that passage in *Acts 16:* **he secured their feet in the stocks.** <note>original Latin/Greek reference: τοὺς πόδας αὐτῶν ἠσφαλίσατο εἰς τὸ ξύλον.</note> **XYLANDER.**

*ibid. line 17. Pelagiae*] Zonaras <note>a 12th-century Byzantine chronicler</note> identifies this person as a male. **XYLANDER.**

**volume II, page 15, line 6. *chelandia*** <note>term: chelandia; a type of Byzantine warship or transport vessel similar to a galley.</note>] Zonaras describes these as triremes and writes that they suffered shipwreck near Mesembria. **XYLANDER.** A smaller vessel, numbered among skiffs and boats by Paul the Deacon. *All the ships,* he says regarding Justinian, *namely dromons, triremes, skiffs, chimaeras, and boats, he gathered together down to the chelandia.* **GOAR.**

*ibid. line 17.* The name of the heretic **Mani** <note>original: "Manetis"; founder of Manichaeism</note> is deservedly infamous; Cedrenus <note>an 11th-century historian</note> hints in volume 3, folio 96, that this name was almost an omen of perversity. Paul the Deacon mentions a certain Mani, a leader of the **Cybioreots** <note>a Byzantine naval district/theme</note>, under his father. **XYLANDER.**

*ibid. line 18.* I do not know what the office of the **buccellarius** <note>term: buccellarius; originally a private soldier or guardsman, later giving his name to the "Buccellarian Theme," an administrative district in Asia Minor.</note> is. Indeed, in this passage, it seems rather to be a place name. In the account of Romanos Argyros, a monastery is named Mantineum, located in the **Buccellarian district**. Also, a chasm that followed an earthquake is reported in the time of Michael the Paphlagonian as being in the Buccellarian lands. Compare these with what Suidas <note>a 10th-century Greek encyclopedia</note> has, and Turnebus in his *Adversaria* 24.16, where it is taught that Buccellarius was the name of an office. Mention of a "Prefect of the Buccellarians," besides our author, is also found in Zonaras in the section on Irene. **XYLANDER.** No one would deny that the word indicates a region. According to Suidas, it is Galatia and Gallograecia: *The Buccellarians are the Greco-Galatians, and the land of the Buccellarians is Gallograecia.* Rigaltius treats the subject of the Buccellarians with great learning, but his findings do not overturn the sense attributed to the word here. **GOAR.**

**volume II, page 16, line 18.** Regarding what follows about the idols in the house of the patriarch, I have rendered it word for word. I believe he removed the **gems** or **mosaics** (by which I understand the Greek word *psephidas*) with which those things had been adorned. **XYLANDER.**

*ibid. line 23.* **the patriarch having performed a prayer** <note>original Greek: τοῦ πατριάρχου ποιήσαντος εὐχήν</note>] The Greeks undertake no office or dignity without a preceding prayer: the appropriate prayer for creating a Caesar, which is discussed here, is found near the end of the recently printed **Euchologion** <note>term: Euchologion; the primary service book of the Eastern Orthodox Church containing the prayers for the sacraments and various blessings.</note>. **GOAR.**

**volume II, page 17, line 1.** What is reported concerning the **Syrian exchange** is obscure due to its brevity. It is certain, however, that the Syrians were delighted...

# THE ANNOTATIONS OF XYLANDER AND GOAR

...a pronoun, so that perhaps he summoned certain people from Syria into Thrace, having sent others into their places. **XYLANDER.**

**Volume II, page 17, line 3.** The translator imperfectly rendered this as *crowned* <note>original Latin: "coronata"</note>; he should have written it as *crowned for the sake of contracting a marriage*, since empresses were adorned with crowns twice: once as partners of the marriage bed, and a second time as partners in the rule of the empire. The author has counted these second coronations in several places; here he lists the first ones, and Simocatta <note>Theophylact Simocatta, a 7th-century Byzantine historian</note> describes them very extensively in book 1, chapter 10. **GOAR.**

*ibid. in the Church of St. Stephen*] or rather "in the holy crown" <note>original Greek: ἐν τῷ ἁγίῳ στεφάνῳ</note>. However, what that "holy crown" might be is uncertain. There was a certain crown dedicated by Maurice which his son Leo <note>Emperor Leo IV</note>, to his own misfortune, took for himself; I do not know whether it was used for other purposes of this kind. **XYLANDER.** In the Palace Oratory. **GOAR.**

*ibid. line 5. the Roman dominion*] Rome <note>original Greek: Ῥώμην</note>. Thus also in other places. **XYLANDER.**

*ibid. line 10. Berzetia*] The Deacon <note>likely referring to a specific chronicler or scribe</note> has "Beritia," and for "Lithosoraea" he has "Lithsoria." It appears our versions are more correctly emended. The same source has "Teleric" instead of "Elerichus." **XYLANDER.**

*ibid. line 20.* **the beard** <note>original Greek: τὴν γενειάδα</note>] Even today, Eastern men pull out their beards and women their hair in the face of misfortune. **GOAR.**

*ibid. line 22.* **having developed carbuncles on the legs** <note>original Greek: κατὰ τῶν σκελῶν ἀνθρακωθείς</note>] *Fiery boils swelled up and burned in his groin.* This is how the author should properly be rendered, according to the writings of Theophanes <note>Theophanes the Confessor, a Byzantine chronicler</note>. **GOAR.**

**Volume II, page 18, line 6.** **be saved** <note>original Greek: σώζου</note>] I render this more correctly as *farewell* <note>original Latin: "vale"</note> rather than *be unharmed*. **GOAR.**

*ibid. line 8.* **at the copper-markets** <note>original Greek: τοῖς χαλκοπρατείοις</note>] Where all sorts of bronze or copper furniture and household items were put out for sale. **GOAR.**

*ibid. line 16.* Those who followed the Caesar (the eldest son) were adorned with the title of **The Most Noble** <note>original Latin: "Nobilissimorum"</note>. This is according to Dempster in his *Roman Antiquities*. **GOAR.**

**Volume II, page 19, line 2.** *Teleric of the Lombards*] I believe this is false, and was forced in by a Bulgarian, whom the text follows next: for the Lombard situation at that time was far too distant for them to have implored the help of Byzantium. **XYLANDER.**

*ibid. line 6.* **he appointed monks as metropolitans** <note>original Greek: μοναχοὺς προεβάλετο μητροπολίτας</note>] Since ancient times, the Greeks have elevated monks to be high priests, and others only very rarely. **GOAR.**

*ibid. line 19.* The **papias** <note>a high-ranking palace official</note> was the first among the palace priests and the guardian of the palace; because of his religious standing and authority, it was easy for him to provide sacred images to the Empress. We shall speak of the *papias* more conveniently elsewhere. **GOAR.**

*ibid. line 20.* I judge these to be **primicerii** <note>a title meaning "first in the list" or head of a department</note> of the church, not of the palace, whom the matters of religion and faith did not touch quite so closely. Concerning the palace officials, see the *Notitia of the Empire*; concerning the church officials, see Codinus, chapter 1, and the *Euchologion* on the offices of the Church of Constantinople. An anonymous lexicon in the Royal Library defines the *primicerius* in a single word as the "first of the rank" <note>original Greek: πρωτοταξώτην</note>, the head of any order. These men, whom I judge to be ecclesiastical, would be counted as the first of the singers in the choir. **GOAR.**

<meta>This page continues the scholarly commentary by Wilhelm Xylander and Jacques Goar on the history of the Byzantine Empire. # THE ANNOTATIONS

**Volume II, page 22, line 21. *by the indiction*]** This is how I interpret that sign here, as discussed above: for the Deacon <note>likely the chronicler Theophanes the Confessor or a similar Byzantine source</note> clearly seems to call the next year, in which the synod at Constantinople was attempted, a "new indiction" <note>an "indiction" was a 15-year tax cycle used by the Byzantines to track time</note> in line 23. However, our manuscript is damaged at the passage concerning the armed men who disrupted it. **XYLANDER.**

**Volume II, page 23, line 4. *catholic church*]** I believe this refers to the cathedral where people gathered to celebrate the synod. The records of the synod show this took place in the Hagia Sophia. **XYLANDER.**

**Volume II, page 24, line 21. *of the father*]** I would prefer "of the mother." We must investigate what kind of places Atroa and Quaestoria are. **XYLANDER.**

**ibid. line 22. *the shaven ones*]** <note>a derogatory or descriptive term for monks, referring to the tonsure</note> He often speaks this way. **XYLANDER.**

**Volume II, page 25, line 11. *to be acclaimed* <note>original Greek: εὐφημεῖσθαι</note>]** So that they might pray for many years for her in both popular and ecclesiastical assemblies, and that her name would be celebrated everywhere alongside the name of the emperor's son. **GOAR.**

**ibid. line 18. *the kourtē* <note>original Greek: κόρτην</note>]** I have learned from other passages that this means a "cohort" <note>a military unit</note>, as in Nicephorus’s writings on Bardanius. I believe, therefore, that the Praetorian Guard or another noble unit is noted here. **XYLANDER.** **the kourtē]** The translator often makes mistakes here, and thinks *kourtē* is a "cohort." Codinus <note>George Codinus, a Byzantine author on court protocol</note> corrects this error in *On the Offices of the Court of Constantinople*, writing: *into the emperor's tent, which is called the kourtē.* Thus, the *kourtē* is the emperor's tent, not a military cohort. **GOAR.**

**Volume II, page 26, line 23. *as was fitting*]** Zonaras <note>Joannes Zonaras, a 12th-century chronicler</note> records that Constantine sent animal dung to the Bulgarian ruler instead of the required tribute. **XYLANDER.**

**Volume II, page 27, line 6. *at Bursa* <note>original Greek: Προύσῃ</note>]** A city in Asia Minor not far from Nicomedia. **GOAR.**

**ibid. line 14. *the Porphyra*]** This is a place in the palace famous for the births of the emperors, especially the "Constantines," who took their surname from it, being called the "Porphyrogeniti" <note>literally "born in the purple"</note>. **XYLANDER.** From which we get "born in the purple." Liutprand <note>Liutprand of Cremona, a 10th-century diplomat</note> writes in book 1, chapter 2: *I call him Porphyrogenitus not because he was born in purple clothing, but in the house called the Porphyra. For Constantine ordered this house to be built and gave it the name Porphyra, wishing that the future offspring of his noble lineage should come into the light there, so that those born of his stock might be called by this illustrious title of Porphyrogeniti.* He wrote this as an eyewitness to Greek affairs during his embassy. **GOAR.**

**Volume II, page 28, line 1. *the lineage of Copronymus was extinguished*]** For Leo, the son of Constantine, had already died before then. According to Zonaras. **XYLANDER.**

**ibid. line 11. *the customs duties of Abydos and of the Hieron* <note>original Greek: τῆς δὲ Ἀβύδου καὶ τοῦ Ἱεροῦ κομμέρκια</note>]** The straits of the Propontis <note>the Sea of Marmara</note> are below, toward the Aegean Sea, at Sestos and Abydos; and above, toward the Euxine Sea <note>the Black Sea</note>, is "the Hieron," on the Thracian side. In these straits, to ensure Constantinople is not defrauded, a tax is paid, which the author records was reduced by Irene. **GOAR.**

**ibid. line 20. *this one fault*]** As if anything more atrocious, more wicked, or more impious could have been devised! And so a scribe noted quite aptly: *Cedrenus, you are talking nonsense; what could be worse than this? For what wild beast plots against its own offspring?* <note>original Greek: ταλάντα τε Κεδρηνέ, καὶ τί τούτου χεῖρον; ποῖον γὰρ θηρίον ἐπιβουλεύει τοῖς ἑαυτοῦ ἐγγόνοις;</note> He means: "Most foolish Cedrenus, what is worse than this very act? For what even of the wild beasts [plots against] its own...

...plots against the offspring? And again, when Cedrenus says this was done "justly" regarding the second marriage of Michael the Stammerer <note>Michael II, who reigned 820–829</note>, Xylander noted: Why do you say this was done justly, cruel Cedrenus? <note>original Greek: πῶς λέγεις δικαίως, ἄγριε Κεδρηνέ;</note> The same commenter wrote regarding Chrysaorius’s opinion on eunuchs: "If only everyone followed your advice, Chrysaorius, regarding those utterly profane eunuchs." <note>original Greek: εἶθε πάντες ἐποίουν κατὰ τὴν σὴν παραίνεσιν, Χρυσαόριε, εἰς τοὺς παμβεβήλους εὐνούχους.</note> This means: "Would that all had obeyed your counsel, Chrysaorius, concerning your most shameful eunuchs." There must have been two men named Stauracios, or the name is incorrect in one of the passages. **XYLANDER.**

**Volume II, page 31, line 3. *in the Prince's island* <note>original Greek: ἐν τῇ Πριγκήπῳ</note>]** I have followed Zonaras <note>a 12th-century Byzantine historian</note>, even though our author frequently calls it by this name. **XYLANDER.** ***Prinkēpos***] An island in the Propontis <note>the Sea of Marmara</note> below Constantinople, in the Gulf of Astacus. **GOAR.**

**ibid. line 18. *upright marble cladding* <note>original Greek: ὀρθομαρμάρωσιν</note>]** This refers to the semicircle of a building's arch which resembles the ancient shape of the letter sigma (written as C); it is constructed with marbles joined together. The description of a wall built under upright marbles in Xylander's notes is a clumsy architectural interpretation. **GOAR.**

**Volume II, page 32, line 22. *army*]** From the word <term>themata</term>, which also designates other provinces <note>the "themes" were the administrative and military divisions of the middle Byzantine Empire</note>. However, Zonaras writes "the Eastern regiments" <note>original Greek: ἑῷα τάγματα</note>, stating that they proclaimed him emperor. **XYLANDER.**

**Volume II, page 33, line 3.** Instead of *phoiberatōn* <note>original Greek: φοιβεράτων</note>, which I believe means nothing, I have read it as *phoideratōn* <note>original Greek: φοιδεράτων</note> by conjecture—referring to the "Federates" <note>allied barbarian troops</note>—although *phoiberatōn* appears again in the section on Leo the Armenian. Yet in that instance, Zonaras uses *phoideratōn*. **XYLANDER.**

**ibid. line 4. *of the count of the court* <note>original Greek: τοῦ κόμητος κόρτης</note>]** He is called the <term>Count of the Cortinarii</term> by George Codinus. The *cortinarii* serve in the emperor's tent <note>the term comes from *cortina*, meaning a curtain or tent-wall</note>. And again: "There are also *cortinarii* who have their own official in charge, who is called a count." **GOAR.**

**ibid. line 9. *Catabolio*]** If this is not a proper name, it seems to denote a port or a station for ships. **XYLANDER.** It is a city in Cilicia, mentioned by Antoninus. **GOAR.**

**ibid. line 13. *Prōtē* <note>original Greek: Πρώτη, meaning "First"</note>]** An island in the Propontis near the city of Constantinople. **GOAR.**

**ibid. line 18. *unmade* <note>original Greek: ἀποίητον</note>]** Inept, of no value—"unmade" or "uncreated," as we say in German <note>original German: ungemacht oder ungeschaffen</note>. Zonaras explained the matter more clearly. **XYLANDER.** It means fatuous and sluggish, one who is unable to do or accomplish anything. **GOAR.**

**Volume II, page 34, line 18. *koursos* <note>original Greek: κοῦρσος</note>]** A naval pirate raid. **GOAR.**

**Volume II, page 35, line 18. *kephalētiōnos* <note>original Greek: κεφαλητίωνος</note>]** Let the author be consulted on page 457 regarding the 16th year of the reign of Leo the Isaurian <note>this refers to a "capitation" or poll tax</note>. **GOAR.**

**Volume II, page 36, line 14. *because he, against the laws*]** Something has undoubtedly been lost from the text before these words. For it was not Joseph the steward nor Patriarch Nicephorus, but his predecessor, Patriarch Tarasius, who crowned Theodota after Constantine VI divorced Maria. But the chronicler writes that even then, Plato <note>Abbot of Sakkudion and a famous monk</note> began to abstain from communion with Tarasius, and later disapproved of the choice of Nicephorus as patriarch, undoubtedly driven by ambition—a fact that Zonaras does not hide. Therefore the emperor, knowing that this Plato had previously been imprisoned by Constantine due to a disagreement with Tarasius (as the author noted), finally took the opportunity to deal with him and his companions regarding their exile. However, it is not clear what role Joseph the steward played in that matter. **XYLANDER.** Strictly speaking: "Because he, opposing the right of the sacred laws, having placed the wedding crowns upon them..." **GOAR.**

-># ANNOTATIONS.<-

...had joined Constantine and Theodota in marriage. However, it was not Nicephorus <note>Nicephorus I, Patriarch of Constantinople from 806–815</note> himself who attended or blessed the nuptials, but Joseph—called a *steward* <note>original Latin: oeconomus</note> by the author, and by Theophanes identified as a monk and abbot of the Concarata monastery—who, by order of Tarasius and under compulsion from Constantine, performed the rite of the nuptial blessing. Because Nicephorus, as the successor and supporter of Tarasius, protected Joseph and allowed him into church communion, the monk Plato and the Studite monks <note>Followers of Theodore the Studite, known for their strict adherence to church law</note>—who were perpetual adversaries of that shameful union—regarded Nicephorus as a violator of ecclesiastical law. Consequently, they decreed that they would hold no further sacramental fellowship with him or with Nicephorus. Once these facts are considered, all of Xylander’s doubts are dispelled, and it becomes clear what role Joseph played in that marriage. Furthermore, the manner of speaking about weddings using the term "coronation" should be noted again. **GOAR.**

**Vol. II, p. 37, line 7.** A little later, when Cedrenus records the ten calamities brought upon the empire by Nicephorus, a scribe noted that under him, ten plagues were sent upon the Roman Empire, clearly alluding to the plagues of Egypt: *See also the ten-fold plague brought upon the Roman Empire by Nicephorus.* <note>original Greek: ὅρα καὶ ὑπὸ Νικηφόρου τῇ Ῥωμανίᾳ ἐπενεχθεῖσαν δεκάπληγον</note> **XYLANDER.**

**ibid. line 15. *Chartiaticum***] What this is, I truly do not know. Perhaps it was a tax for the support of the scribes and the "chancery," as they call it. <note>A fee likely related to the preparation of official paper or documents, from the Greek 'chartes' (paper)</note> **XYLANDER.**

**ibid. line 19. *hearth tax*** <note>original Latin: fumarium tributum</note>] *smoke tax*. <note>original German: rauchsteur</note> I believe this was a tax exacted from every individual hearth in which a fire was made. All these matters are certainly obscure. Regarding the eighth point, I guess that he wanted anyone to be assessed according to the status of their grandfather or great-grandfather, paying as much tribute as they had, even if their estates had been divided among various heirs, leaving each with a much smaller valuation. From the history of the Cerularius <note>an official in charge of wax or perhaps a specific administrator</note>, who returned home with a tenth part of his gold after the rest was taken away—if compared with Zonaras—it would seem that a gold piece or a gold *nomisma* was a tenth part of a pound; this should be noted. But also in the accounts of John Tzimiskes <note>Byzantine Emperor, r. 969–976</note>, where the *smoke tax* <note>original Greek: kapnicon</note> is said to have been abolished by him, one may notice that the *obol* was silver and the *nomisma* was gold. I have translated *perispasmon* <note>original Greek: περισπασμόν</note> as "anxiety"; for the most kind emperor, not being ignorant that cares increase with wealth and that the rich are in great distress, presumably wanted to free that Cerularius from his burden by relieving him of the gold he possessed so anxiously as a private citizen. **XYLANDER.**

**ibid. line 20.** I interpret the *imperial curatorship* <note>original Greek: τὴν βασιλικὴν κουρατωρείαν</note> not as the *treasury* or *fisc* in a general sense, but as the *private property and domain of the prince*. The prefect of this was the *curator*, whom Harmenopolus calls a *logothete*. Regarding this, Agathias says in Book 5: *It happened that only Anatolius perished, a man honored with the rank of consul, who had received the office of taking care of and overseeing the houses and possessions of the emperor. The Romans call these men 'curators'.* <note>original Greek: Ἀνατόλιον μόνον φθαρῆναι ξυνέβη, ἄνδρα τῇ τε τῶν ὑπάτων ἀξίᾳ τετιμημένον, καὶ πρός γε τὸ φροντίδα τίθεσθαι καὶ ἐπιμέλειαν τῶν βασιλέως οἴκων τε καὶ κτημάτων ἀρχὴν εἰληχότα. κουράτωρας δὲ τούτους καλοῦσι Ῥωμαῖοι.</note> And so we do not depart from our author: he himself clearly relates that Nicephorus transferred the richer fields and more fertile possessions of the monasteries—the "better parts of the estates"—into his own royal curatorship and domain. Theophanes also mentions a curator under Justinian...

Here, the focus shifts to specific administrative titles, geographical designations, and various court customs found in the chronicles of historians like Cedrenus and Theophanes.</meta>

-># ANNOTATIONS BY XYLANDER AND GOAR<-

...curatorships <note>original Greek: κουρατωρειῶν</note>, and under Emperor Maurice, he mentions Aristobulus as the *curator of the royal houses* <note>original Greek: κουράτωρα τῶν βασιλικῶν οἴκων</note>. **GOAR.**

**Vol. II, p. 38, line 9. The Dodecanese]** <note>original Greek: Δωδεκάννησον</note> Here, the "fictional state of the twelve islands" from Xylander’s version collapses, if you interpret "Dodecanese" as the *twelve Cyclades islands* (which constituted a single administrative district and arrangement). Strabo also counted twelve in this group, though he asserts in Book 10 that others were added to them. **GOAR.**

**Ibid., line 15. Commercial taxes]** <note>original Greek: κομμέρκια</note> These are *customs duties on commerce*, and any tributes to be paid to the treasury for the transport of goods. Our author mentioned above, during the reign of Empress Irene: *She lightened the commercial taxes of Abydos and the Hieron.* **GOAR.**

**Vol. II, p. 39, line 19. On an outer small column]** <note>original Greek: ἔξω κιονίῳ</note> I have set forth my conjecture above. However, one may also suspect that this individual, feigning a withdrawal from the world, stood upon a column in some suburb outside the city—much like Daniel the Stylite <note>A famous 5th-century "pillar-saint" who lived on a platform atop a column for 33 years</note> and others mentioned previously. In the original manuscript, the word "outer" <note>original Greek: ἔξω</note> is written without an accent, as if it were linked and merged into a single word with "column." The passages that follow are utterly confused. **XYLANDER.**

**Vol. II, p. 40, line 14. Euchaita]** <note>original Greek: τὰ Εὐχάϊτα</note> This city in Asia Minor was called Hellenopolis by the ancients, and finally Theodoropolis. It was restored by Emperor John Tzimiskes because the body of the martyr St. Theodore was enshrined there. **GOAR.**

**Ibid., line 19. General Logothete]** <note>original Greek: γενικὸν λογοθέτην</note> From the present passage, it is clear that this "General Logothete" cannot be taken for the official we call a *chancellor*. Rather, it concerns the prefect of the public treasury <note>the *Genikon*</note>, who here carries out the task of *increasing the public taxes* and *demanding* other revenues falling to the treasury. See the author later on page 568, and also the writings of the Curopalata <note>A high-ranking palace official</note> at the very end. **GOAR.**

**Vol. II, p. 41, line 20. Bodies of the Bulgarians]** <note>original Greek: τῶν ὁμοφύλων, literally "those of the same race"</note> If you refer this to the Christians, the meaning would be that the leader was so intent on gathering spoils that he did not even grant time for his own men to be buried. **XYLANDER.**

**Ibid., line 22. Storehouses]** <note>original Greek: ταμιεῖα</note> Specifically, those in which the goods of Krum <note>The Khan of the Bulgars, 803–814 AD</note> were stored. According to the historian Zonaras, the "court" signifies the residence of the prince. **XYLANDER.**

**Vol. II, p. 47, line 22. In the imperial modiolus]** <note>The *modiolus* was a unit of measure, but here refers to a specific type of headgear or garment</note> It appears this was the attire of the Empress. **XYLANDER.** The text itself makes it certain that the *modiolus* was a type of feminine and royal garment; its shape, if I have correctly understood ancient depictions of empresses, was not unlike the masculine imperial sack <note>possibly referring to the *akakia*, a cylindrical pouch</note>. For the garment was stretched tight on all sides, stiff and without folds, cinched at the loins, and somewhat wider at the feet, having a nearly unsightly shape. I will say nothing of the sleeves, which were so loose they flowed down to the ground: it is enough to have called that unlovely thing a *modiolus*, as it was fashioned in imitation of the *modiolus* drinking vessel, which Vitruvius <note>A famous Roman architect and engineer</note> describes as being wide at the top and narrowing again at the bottom. Whether the Greek empresses decided to claim the *modiolus* for themselves because a "modimperator" was the one who dictated the rules of a banquet among drinkers, I do not know. Others interpret it as a miter—

...they announce: but since "to clothe" <note>original Greek: περιβάλλειν</note> refers not to the head but to the body, I do not depart from the opinion previously offered regarding the garment. **GOAR.**

**Vol. II, p. 47, line 23.** I do not understand the joke regarding the name *Barce* with which he branded the wife of Leo. **XYLANDER.** The author does not explain with what insults the Empress Procopia attacked Leo’s wife; he only suggests that he played on her name in many ways. This was not a difficult task, for her proper name was shared with *barca* <note>original Latin: barca; understand this as a type of ship or small boat</note>. **GOAR.**

**Vol. II, p. 48, line 4. An inaugural prayer]** <note>original Greek: ἐπιβατήριον εὐχήν</note> Xylander writes this as *a vow for a happy entry into the city*, a prayer which the Patriarch Nicephorus offered for the assumption of the empire and the ascending of the royal throne. This can be taken in a negative sense regarding one who seizes what belongs to another, or it can be taken in a positive sense. In this way, those about to board ships and offer sacrifice were said "to offer inaugural sacrifices" <note>original Greek: ἐπιβατήρια θῦσαι</note>. Indeed, Leo—as Paul the Deacon tells us—had written to Nicephorus regarding his faith, even requesting that he might take up the empire with his prayer and approval. **GOAR.**

**Ibid., line 6. Michael of the horses]** This is Michael the Stammerer <note>original Latin: Michaelus Balbus; Emperor Michael II, who rose from a military background</note>. **XYLANDER.**

**Vol. II, p. 52, line 24.** Some think "of the federate" <note>original Greek: φοιδεράτου</note> should be read; I retain "of the phoiberati" <note>original Greek: φοιβεράτου</note>, spoken of a troop distinct from the *federates* <note>original Latin: foederatis; foreign mercenary troops</note>; regarding which the author speaks on page 755 D, as do we in that same place. **GOAR.**

**Vol. II, p. 54, line 11. In the cell]** <note>original Greek: τῇ κέλλῃ</note> The cells of Greek monks are small huts joined to one another around a central courtyard, in the very middle of which is a church. Thus, he was occupying the cell of another who had died. **GOAR.**

**Vol. II, p. 60, line 23. Of the heirmos]** <note>original Greek: εἱρμοῦ</note> This passage composed in iambic verse is found in the office of Morning Lauds on the day consecrated to the birth of Christ. Regarding the meaning of the *heirmos* <note>The model stanza that provides the rhythm and melody for a Byzantine hymn</note>, see the commentators on ecclesiastical rites: Arcudius, Allatius, and the *Euchologium* <note>The "Book of Prayers" in the Eastern Orthodox Church</note>. **GOAR.**

**Vol. II, p. 61, line 5. Of treason]** <note>original Greek: καθοσιώσεως</note> A word which I have learned from many other passages signifies either a crime against majesty or the plotting of snares against the emperor. And what follows concerning the threat to Balbus regarding his wife’s marriage is obscure, perhaps due to the ambiguity of the phrase "of the same" <note>original Greek: τοῦ αὐτοῦ</note>. Perhaps he <note>the Emperor Leo V</note> decided to marry Theodosia after Leo was slain. What he says concerning a "disease of the tongue" alludes to Tantalus in the *Orestes* of Euripides. Shortly after, where it is written how Theodosia rescued Balbus from imminent punishment, there is a note in the margin: <margin>See how God does not lack a method when He wishes to preserve someone.</margin> This is indeed a memorable example of an "unexpected salvation" <note>original Greek: παραδόξου σωτηρίας</note>. **XYLANDER.**

**Vol. II, p. 62, line 9. In the secretariats]** <note>original Greek: ἐν τοῖς ἀσηκρητείοις</note> In a narrower palace designated for the administration of justice, built near the Hippodrome. "Toward the Hippodrome, near the secretariats" <note>original Greek: πρὸς τὸν ἱππόδρομον κατὰ τὰ ἀσηκρητεῖα</note>. For at that time, the quarters of the *asekreteis* <note>imperial secretaries, from the Latin *a secretis*</note> were located there. Over time, as is clear from this, it was moved elsewhere. **GOAR.**

**Vol. II, p. 65, line 15.** What the dignity of the *kanikleios* <note>original Greek: κανικλείου; the keeper of the imperial inkstand who held the red ink for the emperor's signature</note> might be, I do not know. Mention is also made of it in Nicetas regarding Manuel Comnenus. **XYLANDER.** Regarding the prefect of the inkstand <note>The *kanikleios*</note>, after Meursius, Gretserus has written extensively, as has Georgius Cedrenus in Volume II of his commentary on Codinus. **GOAR.**

<meta>This page continues the philological and historical commentary by Wilhelm Xylander and Jacques Goar on the Byzantine chronicles. Having previously discussed imperial titles and court ceremonies, the scholars now turn to the specific office of the "Keeper of the Inkstand" (kanikleios), the timing of night watches, and the identification of various sects and geographical locations mentioned in the text.</meta>

-># ANNOTATIONS BY XYLANDER AND GOAR<-

...even in the additions, there is nothing that explains the name or the office of the *kanikleios* <note>The Keeper of the Imperial Inkstand</note>. I will briefly address both. The "Graeco-barbarous" Glossaries <note>Reference to medieval Greek dictionaries</note> explain *kanion* <note>original Greek: κανίον</note> as an *alabastron* <note>perfume flask</note>, a *phokadion*, or a *myrotheke* <note>a scent-box</note>; that is, a **vessel for storing ointments** made from alabaster, precious pottery, or metal. Since *kleos* <note>original Greek: κλέος</note> signifies glory, the *kanikleion* would be the most noble of such vessels. This was the container in which the red liquid, or cinnabar, was kept and brought forth for the emperor when he was about to sign "golden bulls" <note>term: chrysobulla; official imperial decrees with a golden seal</note>. The guardian of this vessel was "the one over the *kanikleion*" <note>original Greek: ὁ ἐπὶ τοῦ κανικλείου</note>. Nicetas provides authority for these statements in his history of Manuel Comnenus (Book 1, Chapter 4), where he asserts that a certain Theodore, son of Stypiotes, was promoted to the "magnificent honor of the *kanikleion*." He later adds (Book 3, Chapter 4) that John Hagiotheodorites was moved by envy because "the jeweled golden vessel of red dye" <note>original Greek: δοχεῖον ἐρυθροδάνου διάλιθον χρύσεον</note> had been given to Stypiotes, and that he was set in charge of the official oaths. **GOAR.**

**Vol. II, p. 66, line 3. The third watch of the night]** The author notes a little further down: "it was about the tenth hour of the night." This numbering is drawn from the system of hours and watches of the night, of which the third watch ends around the tenth hour. **GOAR.**

**Vol. II, p. 67, line 21. Through the *Skyla*]** This word is suspect. It is a proper name of a place and should not have been translated <note>Xylander originally likely translated this as "spoils," which is the literal meaning of the Greek *skyla*</note>. Below, where the death of Theoctistus is described during the reign of Michael (son of Theophilus), the same word is repeated. **XYLANDER.** In the present passage, you should never understand this as "spoils" as Xylander does, but as a place of custody and a public prison, to which the corpse of the murdered Leo was ignominiously dragged for the sake of greater infamy. The author narrates below (p. 543) that Theoctistus, when he was about to be put to death, was led there and held: "He was therefore led to the *Skyla* <note>original Greek: πρὸς τὰ σκῦλα</note>, to be delivered for a time to the guard." **GOAR.**

**Vol. II, p. 69, line 14. Matters of the soul]** <note>original Greek: ψυχικά</note> This does not pertain to religion alone, but to the soul in a universal sense. **GOAR.**

**Vol. II, p. 71, line 11. The Athinganoi]** Balsamon, in his commentary on the 61st Canon of the Council of Trullo, numbers the *Athinganoi* <note>A sect often associated with magic or divination</note> among the "palm-readers," "bowl-diviners," "cloud-chasers," and "sorcerers." In Canon 65, he adds "bird-watchers," "soothsayers," and "ventriloquists," as if they were devoted to profane prophecies and superstitious divinations. He reports that they carry snakes in their bosoms, predict the future, and engage in much nonsense that is not even worthy of being recorded in writing. **GOAR.**

**Ibid., line 17. Having adopted him through holy baptism]** He had received him from the font and adopted him. Xylander omitted the second part, the ecclesiastical rite of which is contained in the *Euchologion* <note>The Eastern Orthodox prayer book</note>. **GOAR.**

**Vol. II, p. 73, line 1. To their kinsmen]** Or "to his own kinsmen": for it is clear from what follows that this cannot be understood as referring to the Jews. **XYLANDER.**

**Ibid., line 9. The island of Akritos]** Located in the Propontis <note>The Sea of Marmara</note>, near the island called Prote. **GOAR.**

**Ibid., line 17. To fast on the Sabbath]** The Greeks consider it a sin to fast on Saturday <note>the Sabbath</note> based on the 66th of the so-called Apostolic Canons. **GOAR.**

**Ibid., line 22. Concerning God, who is above all]** I understand this to mean that he did not want Christ or the saints to be named in the formula of the oath, but...

# ANNOTATIONS
835

...that according to the Jewish custom, the creator of the world did not wish an oath to be taken by him, as he is uncircumscribed <note>original Latin: "illo circumscripto"; referring to the theological idea that the Infinite God cannot be "bounded" or "contained" by a formal oath in the same way human matters are.</note>. **XYLANDER.**

**Vol. II, p. 75, line 11. *structuring a fraud***] I have added these words on my own authority for the sake of connecting the narrative. For it seems—provided that nothing has fallen out and the narration is complete—that Thomas's goal was either to be appointed supreme commander of their army by the Romans, or to betray their cities and provinces to the Hagarenes <note>term: Hagarenes; a common Byzantine term for Arabs or Muslims, asserting they were descendants of Hagar.</note>. **XYLANDER.** Xylander is in error here: *and would subject the Roman Empire to them, that is, to the Hagarenes*. For over whom would the Roman then rule, or by what advantage would he be led to subject himself to the Saracens? It is more truthfully corrected as follows: *Thomas promised that after the Roman borders were betrayed to the Saracens, the tyrant of the Saracens would leave a private sovereignty to Thomas's faction, subjected only to them, so that they might not suffer any trouble from the Romans in the future*. **GOAR.**

**Vol. II, p. 78, line 12. *Zichians*** <note>original Greek: Ζίγχων</note>] Ptolemy, in his *Geography* (5.9), counts the *Zinchi* among the Asiatic Sarmatians. Constantine <note>Emperor Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus</note> (Chapter 6) locates them as neighbors to the Russians, Khazars, and the Pechenegs of the Chersonese, and he calls them the *Zichoi*. **GOAR.**

***Ibid.* *Kabari*** <note>original Greek: Καβήρων</note>] Stephanus <note>Stephanus of Byzantium</note>, following the opinion of Eudoxus, joins these people to the Scythians. Constantine calls them *Kabaroi* in Chapters 39 and 40. **GOAR.**

***Ibid.* line 15. *him having been adopted as a son***] Whom exactly? Indeed, mention is soon made of this adopted son again. But not even Zonaras names him. He does say this much: that Balbus <note>Emperor Michael II, known as "the Stammerer" or Balbus</note> took the name of Constantine for himself. **XYLANDER.**

**Vol. II, p. 81, line 3. *Gregory***] This man seems to have been the cousin of Leo <note>Emperor Leo V the Armenian</note>, who was then living in exile on Scyros. For thus I translate *adelphidoun* <note>original Greek: ἀδελφιδοῦν</note>, a word used variously for different relatives. Shortly hereafter, this opinion is clearly confirmed. **XYLANDER.**

***Ibid.* line 9. *Unmercenaries*** <note>original Greek: Ἀναργύρων</note>] Many "Unmercenaries" are venerated by the Greeks; these were physicians who were averse to taking payment. The most famous are Cosmas and Damian, whose temple is located "in the district of Paulinus." **GOAR.**

***Ibid.* line 20. *the garment of the All-Holy Mother of God*** <note>original Greek: τὴν ἐσθῆτα τῆς πανάγνου θεοτόκου</note>] Concerning which, see the author on the 17th year of Leo. **GOAR.**

**Vol. II, p. 87, line 14. *the companies*** <note>original Greek: τὰς ἑταιρείας</note>] *Foreign allies of war*. **GOAR.**

**Vol. II, p. 88, line 10. *a fraudulent and illegitimate son*** <note>original Greek: παράγραπτος καὶ νόθος υἱός</note>] *Added to Thomas’s household through an illegal adoption*. **GOAR.**

**Vol. II, p. 91, line 20. *Amermumnes*** <note>original Greek: ἀμερμούμνην</note>] Leunclavius, in his *Onomasticon* (2), says: *The "Emir Mumini," he says, is the master of ceremonies or the prince of sacred rites among the Saracens. By the Greeks, it is written "Amermumnes" in their histories. The same author says elsewhere: "Amermumnes," the "Amermumnes" of the Greek histories, is formed from "Emir" and "Mumini"; of which the former signifies "lord" or "prince," and the latter "rites" or "ceremonies" or "worship" and "religions"* <note>original Greek: θρησκείας</note>. *For those nearest in rank after the Caliphs* <note>original Latin: "Haliphas"</note> *were so named, as if they were princes of sacred things or kings of sacred things, in the Roman fashion. Giovio* <note>Latin: Iovius; referring to Paolo Giovio</note> *interprets this best as "princes of the believers in religion," but he ought rather to have said: "princes of the right religion" or "orthodoxy"* <note>original Greek: ὀρθοδοξίας</note> *or "princes of the holy men."* **GOAR.**
