# THE ANNOTATIONS OF XYLANDER AND GOAR
836

**Vol. II, p. 93, line 17. *Called Chandax*** <note>original Greek: Χάνδαξ ὀνομαζόμενος</note>] This is the same as the word *chandakion* in modern Greek, or more correctly *chandax*. It corresponds to what the ancients called a *charax*, meaning a **ditch** or **rampart**. It is from this word that the name of the entire island of **Candia** <note>The old Venetian name for Crete, derived from the Arabic word 'al-khandaq' meaning 'the moat'.</note> was subsequently derived. **GOAR.**

**Ibid, line 19. *report of the matter to Photinus*** <note>original Latin: "fama rei ad Photinum"</note>] I have translated these words in this way so that the meaning of the sentence would remain coherent, for the text in the Greek source is mutilated. **XYLANDER.** We have supplied the missing text from the historian Scylitzes. **GOAR.**

**Vol. II, p. 94, line 1. *count of the imperial stable*** <note>original Greek: κόμητα τοῦ βασιλικοῦ ἱπποστασίου</note>] We can easily understand this title to be the "Count of the Stable," as the ancient Franks used to say. Later Greeks called this official the <term>kontostaulos</term>, while our own people used the terms **constable** and **constabulary**. **GOAR.**

**Ibid, line 10. *Saracens***] He uses the terms "Agarenes" and "Saracens" interchangeably, as do other writers. However, the details provided about Chandax previously and those that follow are entirely contradictory, unless a portion of the history has been lost in the middle, or there is an error in the names. For why would they be ordered to pitch camp in Chandax, when they were already established there? **XYLANDER.**

**Vol. II, p. 97, line 20. *joint-tourmarchs*** <note>original Greek: συντουρμαρχῶν</note>] A <term>tourma</term> <note>original Greek: τοῦρμα</note> is a military unit consisting of three ranks: specifically, archers, light infantry, and spearmen. These units could number as few as one hundred, while others rose to three hundred or even five hundred men. They were presided over by a <term>tourmarches</term> <note>original Greek: τουρμάρχης</note>, a commander subordinate to the general of the army. These few details are among the many learnedly collected by Rigaltius. **GOAR.**

**Vol. II, p. 100, line 5. *five-towers*** <note>original Greek: πενταπύργιον</note>] A structure built with four round towers at the four corners and one square tower in the middle. **GOAR.**

**Vol. II, p. 103, line 14. *Theoctista, both girded and patricia*** <note>original Greek: Θεοκτίστη ζωστή τε καὶ πατρικία</note>] Theoctista, the mother of Empress Theodora, was elevated by the privilege of being a <term>zostē</term> <note>original: "zostes" or "cinctae"; a high-ranking lady-in-waiting, literally the "Girded Lady"</note> and by the title of <term>patricia</term> <note>A noblewoman of the highest rank.</note>. For even women sought the titles of the loftier dignities usually granted only to men. And why should they not also seek the insignia? In men, such honors might not imply actual legal power, but simply indicate high status and honor. The dignity of the "patriciate," when held as a title alone, lacks legal jurisdiction; it is essentially the highest step of glory. Emperors could therefore elevate the women closely related to them to this rank, and even adorn them with the male insignia of the patriciate—specifically, the belt. 

Cassiodorus reveals himself as the source of this interpretation in his *Variae* (6.2), where he writes: *“Hence it is that the honor of the patriciate is itself a ‘girding’ [cinctus], even when it is a vacant office, having no jurisdiction yet not setting aside the judge’s belt: for an honor of this kind is not extinguished by death.”* He adds further: *“It is an inseparable ornament, a faithful belt, which knows not how to leave its wearer before they depart from the world; it yields only to the brilliance of the crown, which we sometimes assume ourselves.”* This is the official formula spoken from the person of the prince. From these words, it is not difficult to gather how close the honor bestowed on Theoctista (as the Emperor's mother-in-law) was to the imperial rank itself. You may read of a second <term>zostē</term> on page 580, and a third on page 591. The "excellence of the belt" <note>indicating high rank</note>, as well as the "removal" of the belt for a crime, is mentioned in the law book of the Emperors Leo and Constantine, Title 7, Volume 2 of *Greco-Roman Law*. **GOAR.**

**Vol. II, p. 104, line 23. *maimed*** <note>original Greek: παρακεκομμένος</note>] This term can mean **foolish**, as well as **maimed in the whole body**, a **dwarf**, and even one whose manhood has been removed: a **eunuch**.

# ANNOTATIONS. 837

Otherwise, no matter how foolish, he would not have been admitted into the company of women. **GOAR.**

**Vol. II, p. 105, line 1. *Denderis*** <note>original Greek: Δένδερις</note>] A Turkish expression; it refers to a man who is, as the Greeks say, a *tremouliarēn* <note>original Greek: τρεμουλιάρην</note>—one who jerks his shoulders and head, and acts in a **trembling** manner. **GOAR.**

**Ibid, line 7. *his beautiful dolls*** <note>original Latin: "suas pulchras puppas"</note>] From this passage, it is easy to correct the text of Cuspinianus, who I believe read *kalamos* <note>original Greek: καλάμου, meaning "reed"</note> in Zonaras as a single word <note>Reading "kalamou" as part of a compound rather than a separate word.</note>, whereas *mou* <note>original Greek: μου</note> is actually an enclitic pronoun <note>A short word, like "of me," that joins in pronunciation with the word before it.</note>; one might rightly ask what "reed-like things" are, and (in my opinion) not without reason what "excessive chambers" might be. There are many such instances in Cuspinianus which, by comparing our text and Zonaras, can easily be restored to their original integrity. **XYLANDER.**

**Ibid, line 10. *manan*** <note>original Greek: μάναν</note>] "**mother**," using a term from the common dialect. **GOAR.**

**Vol. II, p. 106, line 8. *accused of cowardice before the emperor*** <note>original Latin: "timiditatis accusatum apud imperatorem"</note>] This is how I have reconstructed the sense: "attaching a charge of unmanliness to the emperor" <note>original Greek: ἀνανδρίας ἔγκλημα προσάψας εἰς βασιλέα</note>. **XYLANDER.**

**Vol. II, p. 111, line 4. *some having neglected*** <note>original Latin: "nonnulli neglecto"</note>] Literally, the passage is obscure. For the rest, Hierotheus—who is mentioned shortly after—was a companion of **Dionysius the Areopagite** <note>A 1st-century judge converted by St. Paul, later associated with influential mystical theology.</note>; you may see Nicephorus, Book 2, Chapter 20, regarding him. **XYLANDER.**

**Vol. II, p. 114, line 1. *Chalke*** <note>original Greek: Χαλκῆ, meaning "Bronze"</note>] There were two places called "Chalke" in Constantinople, named for their bronze gates: one belonged to the palace, the other to the forum. The latter was the church at the forum according to Zonaras’s account of Monomachus; the former was the entrance to the palace. Over both was painted an image of the Savior to stir the devotion of the people and the palace officials. **GOAR.**

**Ibid, line 5. *he is not God*** <note>original Latin: "non est deus"</note>] The monk seems to be alluding to the words of the Apostle in the **Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 6**, and adapting them to himself. **Prodromus** is an epithet for Saint John the Baptist, because he was the "forerunner" of Christ. As for which passage of Isaiah those **confessors** <note>Those who suffered for their faith, specifically during the Iconoclast controversy mentioned here.</note> (whom Cedrenus praises shortly after) brought forward to confirm the use and veneration of images, I have truly not been able to guess. The iambic verses of Theophilus seem to indicate that they, having previously been ordered into exile from Jerusalem, had come to Byzantium. **XYLANDER.**

**Vol. II, p. 117, line 15. *he also strove for the honor of being a melodist*** <note>original Greek: ἐφιλοτιμεῖτο δὲ καὶ μελῳδὸς εἶναι</note>] I translate this as: "**he also sought the reputation of a sacred poet.**" For among the Greeks, <term>melodoi</term> are not those who occupy themselves with singing, but with **sacred poetry**, such as Cosmas of Maiuma, John of Damascus, Timocles, Theophanes, and others. **GOAR.**

**Ibid, line 16. *stichera*** <note>original Greek: στιχηρά</note>] "**Verses**," literally. A type of hymn intended to be sung in the church. **GOAR.**

**Vol. II, p. 118, line 1. *he did not refuse to lead with his hands*** <note>original Greek: οὐ παρῃτήσατο τὸ χειρονομεῖν</note>] I understand this to mean that he directed the singing with the movement of his hands, and prescribed the "measure," as they call it, so that the timing of the hymn being sung would correspond to the motion of his hands. Thus Horace wants the young women to celebrate Apollo and Diana in Sapphic verse, with himself leading the way, in Odes, Book 4, Ode 6: "*Observe the Lesbian foot, and the beat of my thumb.*" The <term>sticheron</term> <note>original Greek: τὸ στιχηρόν</note> is the hymn; the **palm-bearing** <note>original Greek: βαϊοφόρον</note> is the feast of Palms (as it is called). A scribe added the note: "I do not think so," meaning he did not believe this person was the author. **XYLANDER.**

# COMMENTARY BY XYLANDER AND GOAR

**Vol. II, p. 118, line 3. *Come forth, nations*** <note>original: ἐξέλθετε ἔθνη</note>] regarding these words, one should consult the Greek *Triodion* <note>The liturgical book used by the Eastern Orthodox Church during the season of Great Lent</note>. **GOAR.**

**Ibid., line 14. *Krenitai*** <note>original: Κρηνιτῶν</note>] in the works of Zonaras this is read with an 'i', *Krinitai* <note>original: Κρινιτῶν</note>, referring to the *Crinites* or "the long-haired ones." **XYLANDER.**

**Vol. II, p. 119, line 2. *A. on Th.*** <note>original: Alexius in Theophilum</note>] Alexius’s account regarding the Emperor Theophilus. **XYLANDER.**

**Vol. II, p. 122, line 16. *of the Domestic*** <note>original: τοῦ δομεστίκου</note>] Since there were many different types of "domestics" <note>a high-ranking official or commander</note> among the Greeks in later centuries, it is uncertain which one is meant here. For although in the earliest times the word *domestic* indicated the same thing as *oikeiakos*—*referring to the household, or as if part of the family*—it was later *transferred to signify a presiding leader or the head of any order*. This is attested by John, Bishop of Kitros, in the volume on Graeco-Roman Law: "the title of 'domestic' among the Latins signifies the exarch, the leader, or the overseer." 

Hence, in the Church, there is a domestic for the right choir and likewise for the left, among others. Regarding military service, there were domestics of the Eastern themes <note>administrative and military districts of the Byzantine Empire</note>, as well as of the Western themes, and likewise domestics of the *Scholae* <note>the elite imperial guard units</note>. Finally, there was the supreme official of all, the *Grand Domestic* <note>Megas Domestikos</note>, as described by Codinus in *On the Offices of the Palace of Constantinople, chapter 1 and following*, which is relevant to this topic. 

One would not assert that the author here uses the word "domestic" for the prefect of the Eastern or Western themes, if one observes that all the *Scholae* units together yielded in conflict to this single domestic. Therefore, the term must be explained as either referring to the Grand Domestic, who was the commander of the entire army under the Emperor, or the prefect of the imperial guards alone, called the "Domestic of the Schools" by Codinus. As Codinus asserts in chapter 5, number 42, the power of this official was almost equal to that of the Grand Domestic; while the latter commanded the whole army, the former led only the Roman units of the guards. However, the *foederati* <note>foreign allies or mercenaries bound by treaty</note>—namely, the foreign partners in war, such as the Persian leader Theophobus mentioned here—were kept under the command of the "Count of the Foederati," to use the language of the *Notitia Dignitatum* <note>a document from late antiquity detailing imperial administrative and military roles</note>. See below where Theophilus subjects the federated Persians and their ranks to Roman leaders once suspicion arose regarding Theophobus. **GOAR.**

**Vol. II, p. 123, line 3. *strings*** <note>original: χορδαῖς</note>] I believe the "strings" mentioned here refer to smaller lutes <note>citharas</note> with a small soundbox but a long neck, equipped with three or five strings. They produce a harsh sound, not unsuited for military life, such as the Turks still play today in their camps to cheer their spirits—perhaps having originally adopted them from the Greeks. **GOAR.**

**Vol. II, p. 124, line 10. *leader of the phalanx*** <note>original: φάλαγγος ἀρχηγός</note>] known by another name as a *tourmarches* <note>a commander of a 'tourma', a division of a Byzantine theme</note>, about whom Rigaltius has written. This specific group of forty-two martyrs, however, was composed of Armenians. **GOAR.**

**Vol. II, p. 127, line 4. *stron*** <note>original: στρόν</note>] although this is sometimes used as an abbreviation for *straton* <note>"army"</note>, that does not fit the context here. I have read it as *stauron* <note>"cross"</note>. But what the custom regarding it was, I have not yet learned. **XYLANDER.**

***the cross*** <note>original: σταυρόν</note>] "He sends him a cross," says Xylander. But what cross? For what purpose? He remains silent. I shall reveal the mystery to the public. In former times, when sending letters to reveal secrets or when confirming promises and pacts with an added oath, people were accustomed to prefix a cross to the document as a testimony of the sacred vow. Pontanus, drawing from the Greek text of Phranzes, states: *“He is called into the presence of the Emperor of Constantinople, who had come as an envoy from Iberia with me. And the emperor...”*

# ANNOTATIONS

...with his own hand, while the envoy watched, he marked three crosses in cinnabar <note>original: cinnabari — a bright red pigment used exclusively by the Emperor for signing documents</note> on the front of the bull <note>the metal seal attached to a decree</note> as a confirmation according to custom, and delivered the golden bull <note>term: <term>chrysobull</term> — a high-level state document or decree from the Byzantine Emperor, named after its golden seal</note> into the hands of the legate. **Leo Grammaticus:** <note>original: ὁ βασιλεὺς καὶ ὁ Βασίλειος τοὺς τιμίους ὑπέγραψαν σταυροὺς ὅρκῳ βεβαιούντες</note> "The emperor and Basil signed the venerable crosses, confirming the oath." Theophilus, using the services of a wandering and begging monk so that a pretense of religion would not be lacking, sent a similar document to Manuel, so that greater faith might be added to the sacred items, or rather to the golden bull. From this, modern Greeks call violators of such an oath *stauropatas* <note>original: σταυροπάτας — "cross-tramplers"</note>, for they trample the cross; that is, they are not afraid to break an oath that was first made sacred when it was written on a paper tablet and signed with a cross. The most learned *de Marca* discusses similar matters in his national Annals. **GOAR.**

**Vol. II, p. 127, line 13. *Prince Ishmael*** <note>original: princeps Ismaelus</note>] I do not know whether this is a proper name, or if it truly signifies an "Ishmaelite" <note>a common medieval term for a Muslim or Arab</note> as a tribal designation. It is used again in this way shortly after. **XYLANDER.**

**Vol. II, p. 128, line 3. *Godfather*** <note>original: compater</note>] <note>original: σύντεκνος / syntenos</note>. I learned this from the context and from Zonaras, who writes that Michael, the son of Theophilus, was sponsored at his baptism by the returning Manuel. *Godfather* <note>original: Gevatter</note>. **XYLANDER.** For this reason, Zonaras wrote: <note>original: ἐκ τοῦ ἁγίου βαπτίσματος τὸν τοῦ βασιλέως υἱὸν Μιχαὴλ ἐδέξατο</note> "he received the emperor's son Michael from holy baptism." Hence he shares the common name of "godfather" with the father, Theophilus. **GOAR.**

**Vol. II, p. 129, line 1. *Patriarch*** <note>original: πατριάρχην</note>] The author thought that Jannes <note>a derogatory nickname for Patriarch John VII Grammatikos, comparing him to the biblical magician Jannes who opposed Moses</note> should be called "patriarch" as if he were the leader of the lost and the rebellious. Xylander, having become a patron of the iconoclasts <note>those who opposed the use of religious images</note>, reads the word "patriarch" and treats it with religious respect. **GOAR.**

**Ibid., line 4. *Logothete of the Dromos*** <note>original: δρόμου λογοθέτην</note>] A logothete <note>term: <term>logothete</term> — a high-ranking administrative official, similar to a chancellor</note> is a chancellor, as we call it, or a master of petitions, or the head of the archives. For *Dromos* <note>literally "the way" or "the race"</note> I would read, if it were permitted, *Domos* <note>the House</note>, so that you might understand him to be the Emperor's domestic and intimate secretary. However, I did not wish to change it based on conjecture, especially since it is read this way again at the beginning of the reign of Michael, son of Theophilus, and frequently elsewhere; and Wolf cites from the *Book of Palace Offices* that this duty was already unknown by the time that book was written. Meanwhile, I will not hide that Himerius—who performed excellently against the Saracens under Leo, the son of Basil (whom they also call "the Philosopher")—is called "first-secretary" <note>original: protoasecretis</note> by our author, but "Logothete of the Dromos" by Zonaras. Whether the writers disagreed, or whether these two names signify the same office, is not for me to decide. Certainly, Zonaras calls this Theoctistus the "Prefect of the Inkstand" <note>original: τὸν ἐπὶ τοῦ κανικλείου — the keeper of the imperial red ink</note> at the end of this account of Theophilus; and our author, where he records the death of Logothete Theoctistus, says that after he was removed, Bardas took the dignity of the *kanikleion* upon himself. **XYLANDER.** Some modern Greeks, informed by Turkish customs which they believe were inherited from their ancestors, understand this to mean the prefect of the war treasury, or the one who would calculate the expenses of the Emperor's journey and pay out the money for necessary supplies. But because in the time of Codinus, when neither wars nor journeys by emperors had ceased, this type of logothete's ministry had become obsolete, they instead think of the one who kept the accounts for the spectacles of the Hippodrome—or as they spoke in shorthand, the *Dromos*—and who, according to Turnebus, is listed in ancient inscriptions as the "Procurator of the Dromos," or the one in charge of the public post...

It also clarifies the term 'godfather' as a diplomatic bond formed through baptismal sponsorship.</summary>

# THE ANNOTATIONS OF XYLANDER AND GOAR

...he provided for the expenses; consequently, since the empire had been diminished on all sides, his office was of no use, which should be understood as applying to any other such official. **GOAR.**

**Vol. II, p. 129, line 6. *Jannin***] <note>original: Ἰαννῆν</note> A diminutive form in place of "John." Even today, the Greeks play with names in this way, so that they express the name *Maria* in nine different ways: Maria, Marou, Maroula, Maroulou, Marietou, Marietoula, Materneta, Loulou, and Loula. **GOAR.**

**Ibid., line 15. *to the prefect of the military***] <note>original: militiae praefecto; στρατιωτικῷ</note> Military. The "sling" <note>original: funda; σφενδόνη — sphendone</note> is a location in the Circus <note>the Hippodrome of Constantinople</note>, which is mentioned elsewhere by our author and by Zonaras <note>a 12th-century Byzantine chronicler</note>. **XYLANDER.**

**Vol. II, p. 131, line 2. *stipends***] <note>original: stipendia; σιτηρέσια — siteresia</note> It is well known among historians that the pay of soldiers is called this because the greatest part of their compensation consisted of food rations. **XYLANDER.**

**Vol. II, p. 132, line 17. *of the 42 martyrs***] <note>original: τῶν μβ' μαρτύρων</note> **Zonaras:** "Those who completed the course of martyrdom among the Hagarenes <note>term: <term>Hagarenes</term> — a medieval Byzantine term for Arabs or Muslims, referencing descent from Hagar</note>, being forty-two in total." Their feast is celebrated by both the Eastern and Western Churches on March 6. **GOAR.**

**Ibid., line 20. *and having practiced divination***] <note>original: καὶ μαντευσάμενος</note> Perhaps this implies that he not only consulted with his own people about the matter at hand, but also used soothsayers and divinations, as the impious were accustomed to do. **XYLANDER.**

**Vol. II, p. 133, line 5. *Archon of Archons***] <note>original: ἄρχοντα τῶν ἀρχόντων — ruler of rulers</note> The supreme praetor. However, who he was or what rank and office he held among the Saracens is not expressed here. **XYLANDER.** Leunclavius <note>a German historian of the Ottoman Empire</note> says in his *Onomasticon 2*: *This man is called by the Greeks what the Turks in their kingdom name the Beglerbeg <note>term: <term>Beglerbeg</term> — literally "Lord of Lords," a high-ranking provincial governor</note>, who acts as a lord of lords, having other magistrates and presidents, both civil and military, under him.* This man was a Saracen and served a higher Saracen, whose name and the glory of his son are mentioned below on page 612. Those learned in Greek and Turkish matters lean toward this opinion. In which provinces this prince exercised power, however, remains unknown to this day. **GOAR.**

**Ibid., line 6. *of the Daxymeni***] <note>original: Δαξυμηνῶν</note> Strabo <note>the ancient geographer</note> mentions in Book 12 the fertile territory of Daximonitis in Pontus <note>a region on the southern coast of the Black Sea</note> near the Thermodon River, from which the location of the Saracen expedition and the name of the place written by the author is not inconsistent. **GOAR.**

**Ibid., line 16. *reed-bed***] <note>original: καλαμῶνα — kalamona</note> For it seems to me he used this word in the collective form (such as *ampelon* for vineyard, *daphnon* for laurel grove, and similar terms) to mean a "thicket of stalks" collectively: a multitude of spears. This is because a battle line armed with spears, when they are held upright, is in some way similar to many stalks standing erect in a grain field; we know that poets have also drawn comparisons from this. Therefore, Manuel seems to have warned the emperor that perhaps not so many soldiers would survive or enter battle in such a vast multitude. **XYLANDER.** I take *kalamona* to mean a place planted with reeds, a reed-thicket; a dense abundance of spears can seem more like this than Xylander's comparison to a ripe grain field. **GOAR.**

It also features a philological debate between Xylander and Goar regarding whether a "reed-bed" is a literal landscape feature or a metaphor for a forest of spears.</summary>

### ANNOTATIONS

**Vol. II, p. 134, line 17. *those who remained because of me and perished***] <note>original: τῶν δι' ἐμὲ προσμεινάντων καὶ ἀπολομένων</note> I interpret this more suitably as: *since those who bravely stood in the battle line for my sake have already died.* Unless you prefer to read *to perish* <note>original: ἀπολέσθαι — apolestai</note> and translate it: *those who showed themselves ready to sustain the conflict for my sake even to the point of complete slaughter.* **GOAR.**

**Ibid., line 21. *Chiliokomon***] <note>original: Χιλιόκωμον</note> Strabo identifies the *Plain of Chiliokomon* <note>literally "the plain of a thousand villages"</note> in Pontus, and the penultimate note confirms this conjecture. **GOAR.**

**Vol. II, p. 138, line 1. *the king of Francia***] <note>original: τὸν ῥῆγα τῆς Φραγγίας — ton rega tes Phrangias</note> The Greeks always loathed calling the Western emperors or kings "Emperors" <note>term: <term>Basileus</term> — the supreme title used by Byzantine emperors; they denied this title to Western rulers to assert they were the sole heirs of Rome</note>, except for the nearby and hostile Bulgarian prince; they were content to address them as "Kings" <note>term: <term>Rhygas</term> — a Greek transliteration of the Latin "Rex" (King)</note>. Thus, this embassy was sent to Emperor Louis the Pious <note>son of Charlemagne, reigned 814–840</note> as "the King," not "the Emperor of Francia." This is perhaps the embassy of which an anonymous author, writing on the life and deeds of that Louis, says in the year 833: *At Compiègne, an embassy from the Emperor of Constantinople met him, consisting of Marcus, the Archbishop of Ephesus, and the Emperor’s Protospatharius <note>term: <term>Protospatharius</term> — a high-ranking Byzantine court official, literally "first sword-bearer"</note>. Lothair <note>Louis's son</note> offered the gifts given to himself but withheld those sent to his father. Although the embassy was sent to his father, Louis received them as they came to him, heard them, and sent them back reporting a nearly unheard-of tragedy.* **GOAR.**

**Ibid., line 9. *the remaining visible part of the city***] <note>original: τὸ λοιπὸν ἐμφανὲς μέρος τῆς πόλεως</note> This refers to the leaders of the people, the faction leaders <note>term: <term>Demarchs</term> — leaders of the city factions, like the Blues and Greens, who held significant political power</note>, the patriarch, and the chief clergy, whom the historian Simocatta describes the Emperor Maurice as having summoned in a similar case at the beginning of his history. **GOAR.**

**Vol. II, p. 139, line 8. *Drungarius***] <note>original: δρουγγάριος</note> **The commander of a *Drungus*** <note>a military unit</note>. ***Vigla*** <note>original: βίγλα</note> **refers to watches, guards, or scouting the enemy**, which Simocatta calls by the purer Greek terms *episkope* <note>supervision</note> and *kataskope* <note>scouting</note> in most places. The one who went to scout the enemy, set guards in the army, and commanded those on guard was the *Drungarius of the Vigla* <note>a high-ranking officer in the Byzantine central army</note>. Regarding him, the scholar Codinus says: *Before the army dismounts, the Great Drungarius of the Vigla goes out and sets the so-called "day-watch," as commanded by the Great Domestic <note>term: <term>Great Domestic</term> — the commander-in-chief of the Byzantine army</note>.* Thus he describes the day-watches; then he describes the night-watches: *And to those who are to keep watch during that time of night, this Great Drungarius goes before the hour of sunset and says: "Lords, get ready, eat your dinner, and feed your horses." And when the appointed and proper time for the watch arrives, he leads them out of the camp.* Leunclavius states: *A Drungarius is a military tribune; among the Italians, French, and Germans he is called a "colonel," and among the Greeks a "chiliarch" <note>commander of a thousand</note>; he says the name comes from "drungus," a staff and sign of command.* **GOAR.**

**Vol. II, p. 140, line 8. *of the synod***] <note>original: συνόδου</note> A little further on, it is used again in this way. I believe the ecclesiastical order is understood by this word. **XYLANDER.** He means the leaders of the ecclesiastical and senatorial orders. For commonly, the bishops found in Constantinople, along with the clergy of that same church, are called to form a "synod." **GOAR.**

**Vol. II, p. 142, line 18. *Phratriarch***] <note>original: φατριάρχης — phratriarches</note> This is the correct reading, not *Patriarch*. <note>A "phratriarch" was a leader of a "phratry" or clan-based division, a term often used archaically or for specific social groupings, whereas a "patriarch" is a high church official.</note> **GOAR.**

It also provides geographical and philological corrections to historical transcriptions.</summary>

# THE ANNOTATIONS OF XYLANDRUS AND GOAR

**Vol. II, p. 144, line 8. *two hundred leather thongs***] <note>original: λώρων διακοσίων — loron diakosian</note> *This was the highest number of leather thongs, which you have already seen listed in the previous sections.* **GOAR.**

**Ibid. *Great City***] <note>original: μεγαλόπολις — megalopolis</note> *The city of Constantine [Constantinople] was called this because of its size;* ***City of God*** <note>original: Θεούπολις — Theoupolis</note> *was the name given to Antioch because of a miracle that occurred during the second year of Justinian’s reign;* ***Holy City*** <note>original: Ἁγιόπολις — Hagiopolis</note> *was Jerusalem, consecrated by the death of Christ.* **GOAR.**

**Ibid., line 9. *Jannes was born***] *A scribe noted here—as he correctly did in many other places, and much more appropriately than here—that Cedrenus* <note>George Cedrenus, an 11th-century historian</note> *recorded these things simply because he lacked better material to write about: "It seems you had nothing to write, you foolish Cedrenus."* **XYLANDRUS.**

**Ibid., line 12. *the monastery of Sergius and Bacchus***] <note>original: ἡ μονὴ Σεργίου καὶ Βάκχου</note> *This was a building of Justinian’s, mentioned immediately at the start of his reign.* **GOAR.**

**Vol. II, p. 145, line 1. *a faithless and harsh nation***] <note>original: ἔθνος ἄπιστον καὶ σκληρόν</note> *I believe these are the Avars, whom Simocatta* <note>Theophylact Simocatta, a 7th-century historian</note> *similarly called the "most faithless and greediest nation" in Book 3.* **GOAR.**

**Ibid., line 16. *elemental words***] <note>original: στοιχειωτικούς λόγους — stoicheiotikous logous</note> *In the modern Greek language, they use the word* element <note>term: <term>stoicheion</term> — originally meaning "element" or "letter," in later Greek folklore it referred to the indwelling spirit of a place, a ghost, or a person’s natural disposition</note> *to describe a secret natural inclination or aptitude for a specific thing. More frequently, they use it to refer to ghosts and specters appearing at night and haunting houses, and finally for evil spirits who serve as the masters of sorcerers and witches. Hence,* ***elemental words*** *are the incantations used for summoning such demons.* **GOAR.**

**Vol. II, p. 146, line 12. *kept in the bedchambers***] <note>original: θαλαμηπολούμεναι — thalamypoloumenai</note> *Noble virgins and brides who are kept guarded in the more private inner chambers.* **GOAR.**

**Vol. II, p. 147, line 14. *she paraded/triumphed***] <note>original: ἐθριάμβευεν — ethriambeven</note> *The clearly shameless woman was publicizing the infamy of her crime within everyone’s hearing. The anonymous Lexicon in the Royal Library states:* ***to parade*** <note>original: θριαμβεύω — thriambeuo</note> *means to make clearly known.* **GOAR.**

**Vol. II, p. 149, line 12. *the festival of Orthodoxy***] <note>original: τὴν τῆς ὀρθοδοξίας πανήγυριν</note> *With a famous assembly of clergy and people, the solemnity of* Orthodoxy <note>term: <term>Feast of Orthodoxy</term> — celebrated on the first Sunday of Lent to mark the final defeat of Iconoclasm and the restoration of icons in 843 AD</note> *is held every year on the first Sunday of Lent. It was first established by the most religious Patriarch Methodius under Michael (the son of Theophilus) and Theodora, after the icons were restored. During this feast, all heretics are cursed, especially those hostile to the sacred icons; their names are pronounced and immediately followed by an anathema, and thanks are paid to God the Best and Greatest for the defeat of every heresy. An anonymous manuscript in the Royal Library narrates the event slightly differently from our author:* 

"She [Empress Theodora] sent word to the most holy Patriarch Methodius to make it known and to gather every Orthodox person—Metropolitans, Archbishops, abbots, clergy, and laypeople—so they might arrive at the Great Church of God [Hagia Sophia] with precious crosses and holy icons on the first Sunday of the Holy Fasts. When all this had been done, and an innumerable multitude had gathered in the Great Church of God, the Emperor Michael himself arrived with his holy and Orthodox mother and the entire Senate, each of them carrying a royal wax candle. And having joined with the most holy Patriarch, they all set out together in a procession from the holy altar with the holy icons and the..." <note>The text cuts off here at the end of the page</note> **GOAR.**

### ANNOTATIONS

[They carried] the **precious cross** and the **holy gospel**, and went down in procession as far as the royal gates known as the **Ktenarion**. And indeed, after an intensive prayer was made, and after they had said the "Lord have mercy" <note>original: κύριε ἐλέησον — Kyrie eleison</note> with much contrition, many tears, and groans, they returned to the holy church with great joy and splendor to perform the divine and mystical liturgy. And thus were the holy and venerable icons restored in the house of God to be honored, revered, and worshiped by all the faithful. Therefore, those who held power in piety, together with the venerable and most holy Patriarch **Methodius** and the metropolitans and holy ascetics with him, decreed at that time to celebrate this holy and venerable feast annually with splendor in the **Great Church of God** <note>Hagia Sophia</note> on the first Sunday of the **Holy Fasts** <note>Great Lent</note>, which continues to be celebrated until this day. **GOAR.**

**Vol. II, p. 149, line 20. *the fullness of the church*** <note>original: τὸ πλήρωμα τῆς ἐκκλησίας — to pleroma tēs ekklēsias</note>] *This refers to all the ranks of bishops, clergy, and monks.* **GOAR.**

**Ibid., line 21. *of the Karianos*** <note>original: τοῦ Καριανοῦ — tou Karianou</note>] *The place where the daughters of Empress Theodora lived and where Emperor Maurice had built a palace.* **GOAR.**

The Augusta <note>Empress Theodora</note> therefore reminds them of those promises. They respond that they will stand by them, even though **Theophanes**—caring little for this—threatens to pursue the injuries done to him before God as judge. It seems the heresy of the **Zilici** <note>A minor heretical sect</note> despised the holy **chrism** <note>anointing oil</note>, as far as can be gathered from this short account; and I have used the word "to perfect," which in the Greek is <term>teleiousthai</term> <note>original: τελειοῦσθαι; to be initiated or perfected in a religious sense</note>, a term they apply to the sacraments. **XYLANDER.** Regarding these Zilici and any other heretics who must be reconciled through chrism, the *Euchologium* <note>A prayer book of the Eastern Church</note> treats this theologically in its illustrated notes. **GOAR.**

**Vol. II, p. 153, line 14. *Zagora*** <note>original: Ζαγοράν</note>] *Lower Mysia near Mount Haemus, a region which is still called **Zagoria** by its inhabitants.* Zonaras holds the same view. **GOAR.**

**Vol. II, p. 154, line 10. *chief messenger*** <note>original: πρωτομανδάτωρος — protomandatōros</note>] *The prefect of the officers and heralds,* about whom I have spoken above. **GOAR.**

**Ibid., line 14. *Amer***] *This is a proper name,* but **Amēras** <note>original: Ἀμηρᾶς</note> *is a Saracen title of dignity, meaning a leader or Duke;* **amermoumnēs** <note>original: ἀμερμουμνῆς; from the Arabic "Emir al-Mu'minin"</note> *is the title for the "Prince of the Faithful," which is not a proper name but a descriptive title.* **GOAR.**

**Vol. II, p. 155, line 14. *being the general of the Thracesians*** <note>original: στρατηγὸς τυγχάνων τῶν Θρακησίων</note>] *A leader lower than the Domestic of the Schools,* who would command only a portion of the army, namely the **Thracian Theme** <note>a military administrative district</note>. **GOAR.**

**Vol. II, p. 156, line 9. *he laid his dust there*** <note>original: τὸν χοῦν ἐκεῖσε κατέθετο</note>] *I believe this should be understood to mean that **Manuel** wished to be buried there.* **XYLANDER.**

**Vol. II, p. 157, line 9. *after the management of the reports*** <note>original: μετὰ τὴν τῶν ἀναφόρων διοίκησιν</note>] *I read this as "reports" (anaphorōn): things that had been conducted in the Senate or elsewhere, which **Theoctistus** was to report to Theodora. Zonaras says the same; although "report" (anaphora) perhaps—*

<meta>This page continues the philological and historical commentary by scholars Wilhelm Xylander and Jacques Goar on the Byzantine Empire's administrative history. It follows the previous discussion of Empress Theodora's reign, moving specifically into the financial administration of the logothete Theoctistus and the various military and court titles mentioned in the historical chronicles.</meta>

<page-num>844</page-num>

<header>OF XYLANDER AND GOAR</header>

The word might signify something else, namely the public revenues; it is clear from the same source that **Theodora** took diligent care of these, which was beneficial to the state. However, I prefer the former meaning because when the death of **Bardas** <note>Theodora's brother and a powerful official</note> is discussed later, the same word is used in that way. **XYLANDER** translates it as "for the sake of reporting the acts." But which acts? He does not explain. Furthermore, death was prepared for **Theoctistus** the <term>logothete</term> <note>a high-ranking administrative official, specifically the treasurer</note> as he was about to depart for the Lausiakos palace: but it says *after the administration of his duty*, not as if he were still about to report *acts* in the Lausiakos in the future. I would more aptly say that this Theoctistus, as the <term>logothete of the treasury</term>, managed the public funds, and therefore had to discuss the proper administration of the royal revenues and taxes <note>original: περὶ τῆς τῶν ἀναφορῶν διοικήσεως — peri tēs tōn anaphorōn dioikēseōs</note> before the emperor or his council; having completed this, *after the administration of the revenues*, he was about to set out for the Lausiakos; it was on this journey that his death was being prepared. Here I read <term>anaphorōn</term> <note>original: ἀναφορῶν</note> as coming from the word for "revenue." For the other word, *anaphoron*, and its plural *anaphorōn*, can make no sense in this context. See the author on page 555. **GOAR.**

---

**Vol. II, p. 157, line 14. *the asekretia*** <note>original: ἀσηκρήτεια — asēkrēteia</note>] Where the secretaries <note>imperial chancellors</note> used to meet. **XYLANDER.**

**Ibid., line 20. *of the company*** <note>original: ἑταιρείας — hetaireias</note>] Perhaps from his own men, who had conspired in the death of Theoctistus. Otherwise, the *hetaireiai* are fellowships, that is, a certain group of soldiers or court attendants, of which mention is not infrequent. **XYLANDER.** Xylander says "from the fellowship," but I say from the "confederates serving the Emperor." **GOAR.**

---

**Vol. II, p. 159, line 5. *he stood as the guardian of the royal funds*** <note>original: τῶν βασιλικῶν χρημάτων ταμίας παρίστη — tōn basilikōn chrēmatōn tamias paristē</note>] From this I further confirm that the <term>logothete</term> is the supreme prefect of the treasury. For when Theoctistus was killed while performing that duty, why would Theodora order those <term>quaestors</term> <note>legal officials</note> to be present, unless so that she could provide proof from another source? Since the aforementioned prefect had been removed from the living, the people and the Senate could not otherwise have knowledge of the treasury, which her son **Michael** <note>Michael III</note> was squandering on useless expenses; she did this through the quaestors, the subordinate guardians of the treasury and assistants at hand. **GOAR.**

---

**Vol. II, p. 160, line 11. *having given to the private [department] so that it might even melt these down*** <note>original: δεδωκὼς τῷ ἰδικῷ ὥστε καὶ ταύτας χωνεῦσαι — dedōkōs tō idikō hōste kai tautas chōneusai</note>] Perhaps it is this: he gave them to private men, who, since it was not permitted or fitting for them to wear such things, thought about melting them down and turning the gold to their own uses, so that "to the private" <note>original: τῷ ἰδικῷ — tō idikō</note> stands for "to private individuals." But what if he perhaps wrote "to the specific" <note>original: εἰδικῷ — eidikō</note>? Is the minter of coins, who impresses the form upon the gold, called by this name? I do not know. **XYLANDER.** *The private treasury.* **GOAR.**

**Vol. II, p. 163, line 23. *Lalakaion*** <note>original: Λαλακαίωνα</note>] The places enumerated here are near **Melitene** and **Armenia**. **GOAR.**

**Vol. II, p. 164, line 6. *Ptosontis*]** Based on **Zonaras**, I read *ptōsonta* <note>about to fall</note> instead of *piōsonta* <note>about to drink</note>. He also has *Lalakaōn*. It seems that in this name he alluded to the words for "people" and "to burn." **XYLANDER.**

**Ibid., line 9. *to be turned back*** <note>original: γυρισθῆναι — gyristhēnai</note>] The modern use of this word fits this passage, by which it signifies not only to enclose in a circle, but also to turn to flight, to send back, and similar things. **GOAR.**

**Vol. II, p. 168, line 2. *Mamoum*** <note>original: Μαμούμ</note>] This is the same man who was just called by his title of dignity, the **Amermunnis** <note>Al-Ma'mun, the Abbasid Caliph; "Amermunnis" is a corruption of "Amir al-Mu'minin," Commander of the Faithful</note>. **GOAR.**

**Volume II, page 171, line 16. [the courts of the Hippodrome]** <note>original: τοῖς τοῦ ἱπποδρόμου δικαστηρίοις — tois tou hippodromou dikastēriois</note> We read above on page 543, from the same author, that the **secretarial offices** <note>original: ἀσηκρήτεια — asēkrēteia</note> were located in the same place. Regarding the term **Sekreton** <note>original: Σέκρετον</note>—or as Eusebius writes in book 7, chapter 30, *Sekrētou*—I believe it should be understood as the **court** or bench of the judges themselves, rather than as a room for secretaries as the previous translator rendered it. To set aside other examples, the testimony of Nicetas regarding Alexios, the son of Manuel, is sufficient: "the beautiful house of Theodore, who was the prefect of the city and managed the **secretariat of the households** <note>original: τὸ τῶν οἰκειακῶν διέποντος σέκρετον</note>, and who brought honor to the seat of justice." Emperor Basil I also later renovated the Hippodrome as a place for the judges. **GOAR**.

**Volume II, page 172, line 5. [leader]** <note>original: καθηγεμών — kathēgemōn</note> used improperly to mean **prince**, but more properly meaning **superior** or **overseer**. **GOAR**.

**Same page, line 7. [and by the embrace of his own daughter-in-law]** <note>original: τῇ δὲ τῆς οἰκείας νύμφης περιπλοκῇ — tē de tēs oikeias nymphēs periplokē</note> And so it was mentioned above, where **Bardas** <note>a powerful Byzantine regent</note> is said to have thought about removing Theoctistus. Bardas had a son, Antigonus, who was the <term>Domestic of the Schools</term> <note>a high-ranking military commander</note>. **XYLANDER**.

**Volume II, page 173, line 18. [an established victory]** <note>original: ἱδρυμένην νίκην — hidrymenēn nikēn</note> At the same gate, sculptures of the labors of **Hercules** can still be seen today. **Leunclavius**. **GOAR**.

**Same page, line 19. [Deuteron]** <note>original: Δεύτερον</note> This is the name of a place, much like the *Hebdomon*. Xylander would translate it as "the Second," or like the *Stenum* which follows shortly after, as "the Narrows," unless it is better to retain the proper Greek name. Perhaps the word for **fixed structures** <note>original: πάγιαι — pagiai</note> refers to **scaffoldings** <note>original: πήγματα — pēgmata</note>. **XYLANDER**. Obelisks and pyramids were erected at the Deuteron. The manuscript lexicon from the Royal Library defines **crags** <note>original: πάγοι — pagoi</note> as "the protrusions of mountains and rocks." **GOAR**.

**Same page. [chamberlains]** <note>original: διαιταρίοις — diaitariois</note> those **keeping a perpetual watch**. **GOAR**.

**Volume II, page 175, line 9. [The Blue]** <note>original: τὸ Βένετον — to Beneton</note> Here are the four colors of the factions in the chariot races: **blue**, **green**, **white**, and **rose**. Other authors like Simocatta and Zonaras call them by different names: **sky-blue**, **greenish**, **purple**, and **white** <note>original: ἠεράνεον, χλοάζον, πορφυροῦν καὶ ἄσπρον — ēeraneon, chloazon, porphyroun kai aspron</note>. **GOAR**.

**Same page, line 13. [protonotary]** <note>original: πρωτονοτάριος</note> the **first of the under-scribes**, as the Subdeacon Damascene calls him. **GOAR**.

**Volume II, page 176, line 8. [of bread]** <note>original: ψωμοῦ — psomou</note> From this word, the Greeks now name their common bread **psomi** <note>original: ψωμί</note>. Xylander translated this as "broth," but foolishly so. **GOAR**.

**Same page, line 9. [asbestotyrum]** <note>original: ἀσβεστότυρον</note> Literally sounds like **unextinguished cheese**: what this actually is, I prefer to let others judge. It certainly appears that it was a raw cheese of very little value. **XYLANDER**. It is a curd similar to thick diluted lime, hence the name **lime-cheese** <note>original: ἀσβεστότυρον — asbestotyron</note>. Xylander explains it as "unextinguished cheese": did he think the curd was on fire? I wish he understood the proverb: "He who was burned by sour milk, blows even on his porridge." He who has been scorched by curdled milk blows on his soup; if he wanders on the plains, he should not try to cross the rough terrain—in a word, he should have more sense. **GOAR**.

**Volume II, page 177, line 4. [President of Koloneia]** <note>original: Κολωνείας πρόεδρος — Kolōneias proedros</note> Grillus was alluding to his homeland, **Koloneia**, a city in Asia Minor, which currently holds the 68th place among the bishoprics according to Codinus. **GOAR**.

**Same page, line 8. [exclamations]** <note>original: ἐκφωνήσεις — ekphōnēseis</note> After the prayers (which we call "collects") are read in a low voice, the conclusions delivered by the priest in a loud and rhythmic voice are called **ekphōnēseis**. **GOAR**.

**Same page, line 14. [lifting up his phelonion to use percussion]** <note>original: φελώνην ἀναστείλας κρούμασι χρῆσθαι — phelōnēn anasteilas kroumasi chrēsthai</note> obscure...

<header>ANNOTATIONS BY XYLANDER AND GOAR</header>

...to me. **XVI.** [This refers to] the priestly chasuble <note>a liturgical vestment, the phelonion</note> that surrounds the whole person, which he is folding back over his arms. **GOAR.**

**Volume II, page 178, line 16.** [The text mentions] "the latticed partition, or wooden screen separating the people from the sanctuary"; these are the **lattices of the altar** <note>original: κιγκλίδες τοῦ θυσιαστηρίου — kinklidēs tou thysiastēriou</note>. **Allatius. GOAR.**

**Volume II, page 179, line 6. [fulfilling the farewell]** <note>original: τὸν συντακτήριον ἐκπληρῶν — ton syntaktērion ekplērōn</note> Zonaras writes, "bidding farewell to the Mother of God," which is clearer. But above, Saint Gregory the Theologian is said to have departed from the government of the Church after delivering a "syntactic" <note>a formal farewell oration</note> speech; this seems to have been intended to establish the peace and safety of the Church. **XYL.**

**Same page, line 14. [space]** <note>original: χῶρον — chōron</note> This means almost the same thing as "place" <note>original: τόπος — topos</note>. However, this term did not seem as suitable to be taken as a proper noun as the other word did. **XYL.**

**Volume II, page 180, line 15. [parakoimōmenos]** <note>original: παρακοιμώμενος — literally, "one who sleeps beside [the Emperor's bed]"</note> This is the official who, in previous centuries, was called the **Count of the Excubitors** <note>original: κόμης τῶν ἐξκουβίτων — komēs tōn exkoubitōn; the commander of the palace guards</note>. This Roman title ceased to be used in the court of Constantinople once its name was rendered into Greek. Liutprand <note>a 10th-century historian and bishop</note> says in Book 3, Chapter 7, that this official’s duties involved guarding the palace and protecting private property. But he could not carry this out unless he were a permanent guard of the palace or the chief of the guards. Should we, along with Xylander, assert that he was a chamberlain as well as a guard? I do not think so. For in the later centuries, the chamberlains <note>original: κουβικουλάριοι — koubikoularioi</note> were always eunuchs, whereas Basil the *parakoimōmenos* was a "whole man" <note>not a eunuch</note>. The chamberlains stayed in the inner rooms, while this official stood at the doors. Finally, the former were called "chamber-attendants" <note>original: κοιτωνῖται — koitōnitai</note>, chamberlains, or by any other name, but this official's title sounds nothing like those. Indeed, the guards subject to him are shown below on page 567 to have a different name and a different duty, where they are called **bed-attendants** <note>original: παρακοῖται — parakoitai</note> and **members of the household of the parakoimōmenos**, meaning familiar servants assigned to him, or in a word, under his command. **GOAR.**

**Volume II, page 181, line 15. [of the Imperial dromon]** <note>original: Βασιλικοῦ δρόμωνος — Basilikou dromōnos; a fast Byzantine war galley</note> Up until the time of this Basil, the emperors hardly ever used dromons, but rather **Agrarian ships**. Constantine [Porphyrogenitus] discusses both types very extensively in *On Administering the Empire*, Chapter 51; Cassiodorus also mentions them in his *Variae*, Book 5, Letter 16. **GOAR.**

**Same page, line 22.** The first line is a six-foot verse from Euripides; the middle is complete if you read "and secondly" <note>original: καὶ δεύτερον δέ — kai deuteron de</note>. He seems to be alluding to the name of Basilicinus. Otherwise, I do not see why we should believe he was a rower from the imperial family. **XYL.**

**Volume II, page 182, line 17.** I am not certain what kind of cup a **discopoterium** might be. What a **discus** <note>the paten, or plate for the bread</note> is has been explained elsewhere. And I suspect that **polycandyla** is a word corrupted from a semi-Latin form, meaning **polykandēla** <note>original: πολυκάνδηλα</note>, which are candelabras designed to hold many candles. I would easily accept a more solid explanation if one is shown. **XYL.** A *discus* for holding the Eucharistic bread, and a *chalice* for receiving the consecrated wine, together are called a **diskopotērion** <note>original: δισκοποτήριον</note>. **GOAR.**

**Same page, line 18. [polykandyla]** Based on several authors cited in the *Euchologion* <note>a primary liturgical book of the Greek Church</note>, I restore the spelling to **polykandēla** <note>original: πολυκάνδηλα</note>. This is a chandelier decorated with various lamps, hanging from the paneled ceiling of the church and illuminating the whole building with its lights. **GOAR.**

# ANNOTATIONS.

**Volume II, page 192, line 12. [of the spiritual brotherhood]** <note>original: τῆς πνευματικῆς ἀδελφότητος — tēs pneumatikēs adelphotētos</note> In the manner of an adoption where one is enrolled as another’s son, the Greeks devised **ritual brotherhood** <note>original: ἀδελφοποίησιν — adelphopoiesin</note>. Through this, they bind an unrelated person to themselves in a perpetual bond of friendship, to be treated thereafter with brotherly love, sharing in each other’s fortune and acting as a source of counsel and aid. However, since this was unknown to ancient laws, harmful to families, a source of wicked conspiracies, and a helper in unspeakable crimes, it was later proscribed and condemned by the laws of both the Church and the Empire. Nevertheless, the *Euchologium* <note>the primary prayer book of the Greek Church</note> preserves the ancient ritual for celebrating it in the Church; the Greco-Roman Law, Blastares <note>Matthew Blastares, a 14th-century monk and legal scholar</note>, and other Greek legal experts provide clear evidence of its condemnation. **GOAR.**

**Volume II, page 194, line 23. [with the rod]** <note>original: τῇ ῥάβδῳ — tē rhabdō</note> I believe this refers to an arrow, or perhaps a thrown dart. Indeed, it has been observed among Latin poets that "reed" <note>Latin: calamum</note> is also used to mean an arrow, surely because arrows were made from reeds. Virgil writes: "*when you broke Daphnis's bow and his reeds.*" Horace writes: "*the arrows of a Cretan reed.*" **XYL.**

**Volume II, page 195, line 11. [on account of the royal cloak]** <note>original: διὰ τὴν βασιλικὴν ἐφεστρίδα — dia tēn basilikēn ephestrida</note> This was done out of reverence for all things royal, or perhaps lest by sitting upon the purple <note>the color reserved for the Emperor</note> he might give others the impression he was aiming at tyranny, thereby bringing danger upon himself. **GOAR.**

**Same page, line 19. [stabling]** <note>original: στράτωσιν — stratōsin</note> This refers to the **grooms** <note>original: ἱπποκόμοις — hippokomois</note>. These men were led by the **Protostrator** <note>original: πρωτοστράτωρα — literally, "First Groom"</note>, the chief of the grooms. They held this position not to tend to horses in lowly service, but to hold a more noble governorship of the stables and to attend to the Emperor if he happened to travel on horseback. Codinus <note>a reference to Pseudo-Kodinos, the author of a treatise on Byzantine offices</note> writes about them. **GOAR.**

**Volume II, page 196, line 3.** I am uncertain what a **bardoukion** <note>original: βαρδούκιον</note> is. I believe it was a ballista or some kind of weapon or javelin. **XYL.** Meursius <note>Johannes Meursius, a Dutch classical scholar</note> interprets the *bardoukion* as a small axe. By what argument? Because it is hung from the belt, can be thrown, and can split the head of a wild beast. He is guessing, and produces nothing relevant to the matter. *I tortured myself for a long time before I could track down the meaning of this word*, writes Leunclavius in his second *Onomasticon*. He says in that same place: *A "Bardac" is a pitcher or jar made of pottery, crafted for carrying water. He who carries the Emperor's bardoukion is understood to be the horseman who carried a jar full of water for the Emperor's use. The Turks have also retained this office: for among those three youths who are the Sultan’s intimate chamberlains, one is the "kinptar," who cares for the Sultan's drink and always travels on horseback carrying water for the Sultan in a jar, just as it used to be carried for the Greek Emperor in a bardoukion.* **GOAR.**

**Volume II, page 203, line 7. [in the Eidixo]** <note>original: in Eidixo</note> This word seems to signify a place, perhaps one in which the Emperor would store his personal property or "peculium." **XYL.** Where Curopalates <note>an imperial title/author</note> reads *Eidixo* <note>original: Εἰδίξῳ</note>, he reads *Eidikon* <note>original: εἰδικῷ</note>; a previous author on page 544 used *Idikon* <note>original: ἰδικῷ</note>. From these, I gather a significant conjecture that it should be restored as **Eidikon**; it should be understood as a private, yet royal treasury, in which money is not so much kept as it is minted and stamped. Nothing is more common than the public or common treasury, through which public taxes are collected—as the author is about to narrate—and the common returns of all rev-

<meta>The text ends mid-word (revenues/red-).</meta>

# THE ANNOTATIONS OF XYLANDER AND GOAR

<meta>catchword: captured-</meta>

...the accounts are divided, it is called the **General** <note>original: γενικόν — genikon; refers to the general or public treasury</note>. Therefore, the **Special** <note>original: εἰδικόν — eidikon; refers to the private or "special" imperial treasury</note> must correspond to the General, just as a species corresponds to its genus, or the private to the communal. But, you might say, such insight is trivial when authority or historical evidence is lacking. I shall produce both to confirm my statement. 

In their laws inserted into the second volume of the *Greco-Roman Law*, Emperors Leo and Constantine, when instructing the ministers of the treasury, mention the chief officials in Title 7: the **Quaestor**, and **the most glorious Count of the Sacred Incomes** <note>original: τὸν ἐνδοξότατον κόμητα τῶν θείων εἰσοδίων; Latin: gloriosissimum comitem sacrarum largitionum</note>, who is the **Logothete of the General Treasury** <note>original: λογοθέτης τοῦ γενικοῦ</note>. Immediately following, they add **the most glorious Count of the Sacred Private Funds** <note>original: τὸν ἐνδοξότατον κόμητα τῶν θείων εἰδικῶν; Latin: gloriosissimum comitem sacrarum privatarum</note>, who is the very official currently under discussion. 

The extravagant Emperor **Michael** <note>Michael III, r. 842–867</note> had found solid gold machines, trees, animals, and various furnishings hidden away in the treasuries; intending to melt them down for coins, **he gave them to the royal treasury to be struck** <note>original: χαράξαι δέδωκεν τῷ βασιλικῷ ταμιείῳ</note>. Our author says on page 556 that **he did similarly with the royal robes, some of which were made of solid gold and others woven with gold, giving them to the Special Treasury** <note>original: τῷ εἰδικῷ</note> **so that these too might be melted down.** To whom did he give them? Surely to the same office he just mentioned—the **royal treasury**—so that the word "similarly" maintains the same meaning. However, these items were not actually minted, and **Basilius** <note>Basil I, r. 867–886</note> found them upon ascending to the throne. 

Where? **Cedrenus** <note>an 11th-century historian</note> writes that they were **in the Special Treasury** <note>original: ἐν εἰδίξῳ</note>, or as written above, **in the Special** <note>original: ἐν ἰδικῷ</note>; **Curopalates** <note>a high Byzantine title, here referring to the historian Scylitzes</note> also says **in the Special** <note>original: ἐν εἰδικῷ</note>. In a word, they were in the private treasury or the minting-house where the **form** <note>original: εἶδος — eidos</note> and face of the prince is impressed upon the coinage. **Zonaras** <note>a 12th-century chronicler</note> explains it in a few words: **he gave them over to be cut into coinage, which, after he was destroyed, were recovered by the king who reigned after him, Basilius.** **GOAR.**

**Volume II, page 203, line 10. [instrument]** I think this refers to a musical instrument, an **organ** <note>original: ὄργανον — organon</note>, *an organ or instrument.* Note has been made concerning the **General Treasury** at the beginning of the work. **XYL.**

**Volume II, page 204, line 8. [the so-called General Treasury]** The place in which **the public taxes are collected.** **GOAR.**

**Ibid., line 9. [from the public]** <note>original: παρὰ τοῦ δημοσίου</note> meaning **from a public tax-collector.** **GOAR.**

**Ibid., line 11. [to the mentioned residence]** <note>original: εἰς τὴν εἰρημένην διατριβήν — eis tēn eirēmenēn diatribēn</note> There is no proper name here for Xylander to translate literally; he notes it as a **place of judgment** <note>the word "diatribe" can mean a place of stay, a school, or a court</note> without a formal legal trial, in a fictionalized Discourse. The author's meaning is plain: **to the mentioned place**, specifically the **General Treasury**, of which he was speaking. **GOAR.**

**Volume II, page 206, line 11. [Tephrike]** This city, and all the locations mentioned in the following sections, are situated toward **Cilicia** near **Armenia**, and are places in **Armenia Minor**. **GOAR.**

**Volume II, page 209, line 13. [bound with crowns]** The Emperor was crowned once upon taking up the empire, and a second time whenever he celebrated a **triumph**. The insignia of the first coronation is the **crown** <note>original: στέμμα — stemma</note> according to Codinus; the sign of the second is the **trophy-bearing** <note>original: τροπαιουχία — tropaiouchia</note> as described in Chapter 6. Georgius Coresius says the same in his *Letters*. **GOAR.**

**Volume II, page 210, line 4. [of Charsianon]** This is a location in **Cappadocia**. **GOAR.**

**Volume II, page 212, line 6.** I did not quite grasp what that **patron** <note>original: πάτρων — patrōn</note> meant—whether it referred to parents or ancestors (which hardly fits, since **Pulades** is said to have been captured by **Chrysochires** himself), or if it signified a legal patron, and he was thus calling him that **sarcastically**. Therefore, I have omitted it. **XYL.** The captured of Chrysochires once...

# ANNOTATIONS

Pylades correctly calls him **patron** <note>original: πάτρωνα — patrona</note>: for using this word, which is derived from the Italian *patrone* <note>meaning "boss" or "master"</note>, Eastern captives still address their masters today. *Elsewhere*, Hesychius states: **patrons** are the first of those deemed worthy of Roman citizenship. — GOAR.

vol. II, p. 213, line 7. **Doulon** <note>original: Δοῦλον</note>] A very strongly fortified castle near Tarsus; the author discusses its location and advantages above on page 552 C. — GOAR.

ibid, line 14. **To Argaeus** <note>original: τῷ Ἀργαίῳ</note>] Ptolemy (Book 5, Chapter 6) says: remarkable mountains pass through Cappadocia, including Mount **Argaeus** <note>The highest mountain in central Anatolia, modern Mount Erciyes</note>. — GOAR.

vol. II, p. 214, line 16. **Adapam**] In the works of Zonaras, this is called Adata. However, our author calls it Adapam in his account of Constantine, son of Leo, where he records its capture by Bardas Phocas. A little earlier, I read **Anazarbus** <note>original: Ἀναξάρβης</note> instead of **Anabarzes** <note>original: Ἀναβάρξης</note>; this is the homeland of the physician Dioscorides, a well-known city in Cilicia, and I was moved to make this correction because the author mentions it elsewhere in a similar context. — XYLANDER.

vol. II, p. 216, line 4. **Kourton** <note>original: Κουρτῶν</note>] Perhaps he means the **Cretans**: for it is clear that the Saracens <note>original: Agarenos — descendants of Hagar</note> held Crete at that time. Unless it refers to something else: for the "Turks" would fit the spelling of the letters better, though the historical facts do not match. — XYLANDER. The **Kourton** are the **Kurti**, a people living toward Colonia and Mesopotamia; following a victory, they were relocated to Cappadocia. They are located far from the Cretans, whom Xylander imagines here based on a thin and meager word-play. — GOAR.

vol. II, p. 218, line 23. **Chrobatae** <note>original: Χρωβάτων — Croats</note>] I believe these are the people called **Crabatae**, from which comes the name **Croatia** or **Crabatia**. A little further down, all these Scythians are called **Slavs** <note>original: Σλαβίνων — Slavini</note>. **Rhaousion** <note>original: Ῥαούσιον</note> is **Ragusa** <note>modern-day Dubrovnik</note>, according to Zonaras as well. — XYLANDER. **I speak of the Chrobatae and Serbs** <note>original: Χρωβάτων φημὶ καὶ Σέρβων</note>] The Emperor Constantine Porphyrogenitus provides a long history of each of these peoples and their rebellion from the Romans throughout his entire commentary *On the Administration of the Empire*. — GOAR.

vol. II, p. 219, line 21. **Drungary of the Fleet** <note>original: δρουγγάριον τῶν πλωΐμων — droungarion ton ploimon</note>] Leo, in his *Naval Warfare* <note>Naumachica</note>, says: Following the model of the Imperial Fleet, the naval commanders <note>strategoi</note> of the other administrative districts <note>themes</note> were formerly called **Drungaries** in earlier times. — GOAR.

vol. II, p. 220, line 4. **Longobardia** <note>original: Λογγιβαρδία</note>] Ever since the Eastern Emperors resided in Ravenna and exercised sovereignty in Lombardy, they called any other place remaining to them in Italy—namely Calabria, Campania, and Apulia (or Great Greece), of which **Bari** (the city mentioned here) is a part—**Longobardia**. See Constantine, *On the Administration of the Empire*, chapter 27. — GOAR.

ibid, line 19. I did not wish to change **Dolichos** <note>original: Δολῖχον</note>. It is a corruption of **Louis** <note>original: Λοδοῖχον — Lodoichon</note> or something similar: for historical records show that **Louis II** was then the Emperor of the West. Our author, wishing to attribute more status to his own people <note>the Byzantines</note>, calls him merely "King of France," just as he did with **Charlemagne**, his grandfather, mentioned above. — XYLANDER. The Greeks call all Latins **Franks** <note>original: Φράγγους — Phrangous</note>, as the Franks were more familiar to them; and at that time, when Germans could hardly be distinguished from Franks, it was easy for the author to celebrate **Louis II**, King of Germany and successor to Lothair, as the **King of Francia**. Furthermore, regarding the embassy of Basil, the Chronicle edited by Pithoeus states: In the said year (873), in the month of January, around Epiphany, of Basil the Emperor of the Greeks...

### THE ANNOTATIONS OF XYLANDER AND GOAR

The ambassadors of the emperor arrived at Ratisbon <note>Modern-day Regensburg, Germany</note> to meet King Louis <note>Louis the German, r. 843–876</note> with gifts and letters. Among the various tokens of friendship, they offered him a crystal of marvelous size, adorned with gold and precious gems, along with a significant portion of the **Life-Giving Cross** <note>original: salutiferae crucis — a relic of the True Cross</note>. Having been honorably received and given a suitable response, they returned to their own lands. — GOAR.

vol. II, p. 221, line 4. **The ruler of Francia** <note>original: ὁ ἄρχων Φραγγίας</note>] Louis, joining his forces with those of his brother Lothair, seized Capua and Benevento, and then Bari, from the Saracens. Their prince, Seodas, was also captured and is reported to have been slaughtered along with his men by Louis, according to Leo of Ostia (Book 1, chapters 37 and 38). In Leo’s account, there is deep silence regarding any Saracen prince mocking the tricks of fortune. Seek the historical truth on page 142. — GOAR.

vol. II, p. 225, line 10. **Very large ships** <note>original: πλοῖα μέγιστα</note>] These were called **koumbaria** <note>original: κουμπάρια — large Byzantine transport ships</note> by the Saracens, as he says, and further down he notes that they are "accustomed to name them **galleys**" <note>original: γαλέας</note>. — GOAR.

vol. II, p. 228, line 18. ***because of their baptism***] I have inferred this by interpreting even these obscure words. I believe that because they had renounced their baptism to become Saracens and were **circumcised** <note>original: recutiti — literally "skinned back," a term used for the circumcised</note>, the author meant to say that their skin was no longer their own but had been consecrated to their religion. In the second line above, I translated **through the islands** <note>original: κατὰ νῆσον</note>: for Crete had not yet been recovered. Nasar is called Narsas in the works of Zonaras. — XYLANDER.

vol. II, p. 231, line 5. **Protovestiarios** <note>original: πρωτοβεστιάριος — "First Wardrobe-Master"</note>] This official was in charge of the imperial wardrobe above all others. Meursius writes about him clearly, learnedly, and at length under the entry *vestiarios*. — GOAR.

vol. II, p. 232, line 16. **First of the grooms** <note>original: πρώτου τῶν ἱπποκόμων</note>] This is the **Protostrator** <note>An important court official, originally the head of the imperial stables</note>, about whom I have written elsewhere. — GOAR.

*ibid, line 22.* **Leader of the company** <note>original: ἑταιρείας ἄρχοντα</note>] Codinus calls this official by the single word **Hetairiarches** <note>The commander of the imperial bodyguard, often composed of foreign mercenaries</note>, the **leader of the confederates**, of whom much has already been said above. — GOAR.

vol. II, p. 233, line 14. **Nor did he keep a blind watch** <note>original: οὐδ' ἀλαοσκοπιὴν εἶχε</note>] In the margin, it reads "blind-watching" <note>original: τυφλοσκοπιήν</note>. This is a Homeric expression from the *Iliad*, Book 10, regarding Apollo, and elsewhere. — XYLANDER.

*ibid, line 21.* **Of the chief commanders** <note>original: τῶν ἀρχιστρατήγων</note>] Referring to Michael and Gabriel, the leaders of the heavenly host, who are worshipped by the Greeks with particular veneration. — GOAR.

vol. II, p. 236, line 11. **Diaconitzes**] I believe this was the son of Chrysochir, who is shown above to have been killed. Otherwise, the word signifies a servant, being a diminutive form of **deacon**, just as *Theophilitzes* is used for *Theophilus*. — XYLANDER.

*ibid, line 19.* **Diomedes**] The *Euchologium* <note>A liturgical book of the Eastern Orthodox Church</note> shows that his temple was **outside the gates** <note>original: ἐξώπορτα — Exoporta</note>, outside the city. — GOAR.

*ibid, line 23.* **Of the Protospatharioi** <note>original: τῶν πρωτοσπαθαρίων</note>] The **Spatharioi** are attendants or guards, specifically those armed with a sword <note>original: spatha</note>. The one who leads them is the **Protospatharios** <note>First Sword-bearer</note>, who also used to gird the emperor with his sword. — GOAR.

vol. II, p. 238, line 11. ***a temple, as the poet says, in its prime***] original: **neon hebonta** <note>νεὼν ἡβώοντα</note>. It should certainly be written as **hebonta** <note>ἡβώωντα</note>. This error reminds me that instead of "temple" <note>original: νεών — neon</note>, perhaps I should think the author meant "new" <note>original: νέον — neon</note>, as is found in the poet; Cedrenus wrote it this way, as some might suspect. However, I think he was merely alluding to... — XYLANDER.

### ANNOTATIONS

I suspect this is a passage from Homer, and that the author did not intend to name the temple after a "young man" <note>adolescentis</note>. Rather, he used the word **neōn** <note>original: νεών — meaning "temple" in certain Greek dialects</note> (which is to say, **naon** <note>original: ναόν</note>) by a similar sounding name. This is a matter of minor importance, and the wordplay is not entirely elegant. However, he alluded to the words of Phoenix in the *Iliad*, book 9: "not even if a god himself would promise to me to strip away my old age and make me a young man in my prime" <note>original: οὐδ᾽ εἴ κέν μοι ὑποσταίη θεὸς αὐτὸς γῆρας ἀποξύσας θήσειν νέον ἡβώωντα</note>. I note this for the sake of the less experienced readers.

vol. II, p. 233, line 11. ***at the Spring***] <note>original: ἐν τῇ πηγῇ</note>: I think this is a proper name, or used as a title of distinction <note>original: κατ’ ἐξοχήν</note>. A little further on, I translated the plural form "at the springs" <note>original: ἐν πηγαῖς</note>. A bit later, I translated the word **doxologountas** <note>original: δοξολογοῦντας — those offering praise or glory</note> as "teachers" [doctores], following a conjecture, because it is just as probable that their stipends were increased or established as it was for the singers. — XYL. <note>Wilhelm Xylander, 1532–1576, a German classical scholar</note>

vol. II, p. 243, line 24. ***the general***] <note>original: ὁ γενικὸς — ho genikos</note>: understand this to mean the **logothete** <note>original: λογοθέτην — specifically the Logothete of the Genikon, the official in charge of the empire's general treasury</note>. — GOAR. <note>Jacques Goar, 1601–1653, a French Dominican scholar of Byzantine liturgy</note>

vol. II, p. 244, line 8. ***the masters of the state***] <note>original: τοῖς πολιτείας μαγίστροις — tois politeias magistrois</note>: Since many throughout this history are distinguished by the title of "master" [magister], whether of the administrative offices or of the military, etc., a question can arise as to how the word should be understood wherever it occurs. Certainly, since Liutprand <note>Liutprand of Cremona, a 10th-century diplomat and historian</note> (mentioned elsewhere) reports that those who were distinguished by this dignity in the last twenty-four centuries were called "masters of the state" [politeias magistrous] by the author, I have always thought they should be understood as assessors of the royal consistory and the secret council. He who is not pleased by this conjecture may, if he can, twist the author's words into another meaning, just as in these other words of Constantine in *On the Administration of the Empire* <note>original: De Admin. Imp.</note>, chapter 51: "Emperor Leo, being somewhat more liberally disposed toward the **magistri**, **patricians**, and **household senators**..." <note>original: Λέων ὁ βασιλεὺς φιλοτιμότερόν πως πρὸς τοὺς μαγίστρους καὶ πατρικίους καὶ οἰκείους συγκλητικούς διακείμενος</note>, by which he makes it clear that the magisterial dignity was one common to and aiding the republic by its counsels, just as the patrician and senatorial ranks were. — GOAR.

vol. II, p. 245, line 3. ***exempt from equalization***] <note>original: ἀνεξίσωτος — anexisōtos</note>: According to Suidas <note>a 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedic lexicon</note> and modern Greeks, an **exisōtēs** <note>original: ἐξισωτής</note> is a censor and tax-collector; according to Blastares <note>Matthew Blastares, a 14th-century monk and legal scholar</note>, he is one who divides lands and fields equally among neighboring owners, and who fixes the measure of the tribute to be paid to the prince after weighing the wealth and possessions of each individual. Cassiodorus <note>Variae, book 6, formula 6</note> calls such a person a "proportional-adjuster of taxes" [peraequatorem vectigalium] in the royal city. However, an **anexisōtos** is one who is subject to no such tax-collector or adjuster. — GOAR.

vol. II, p. 249, line 8. ***Hagiopolite***] <note>original: Hagiopolita — "Citizen of the Holy City"</note>: In this and similar writers, just as the "Royal City" stands for Constantinople, so also the "Holy City" <note>original: urbs sancta</note> is often used as a circumlocution <note>original: κατὰ περίφρασιν</note> for Jerusalem, which you will easily notice. And it is probable that "Hagiopolite" should be understood as "the Jerusalemite." — XYL.

[Same page], line 11. ***of the Harmonians***] <note>original: Harmonianorum</note>: Zonaras <note>Joannes Zonaras, a 12th-century Byzantine chronicler</note> does not have "Harmonians" [ἁρμονιανῶν] as our author does, but "Armenians" [ἀρμενιανῶν]. From this passage, it appears that the right of designating and electing the Patriarch of Constantinople by vote belonged to the Bishop of Heraclea. He is the **protothronos** <note>original: πρωτόθρονος — "first-throned"</note>, holding the chief place in the assembly, such as (I believe) our **deans** [decani] are. — XYL.

[Same page], line 12. ***and following on his heels, Stephen***] <note>original: κατὰ πόδας δὲ Στέφανον — kata podas de Stephanon</note>: Xylander—whether as translator or scholiast—is mistaken here. He can be corrected in two ways. As a translator, in this manner: "Immediately [e vestigio] in his place, Leo designates and promotes his brother Stephen as Patriarch, because the Bishop of Heraclea at that time was not counted among the living..." Theophanes...
