<meta>This page continues the scholarly annotations by Jacques Goar and Wilhelm Xylander. While the previous page defined administrative titles and literary allusions, this page focuses on the ecclesiastical rights of the See of Caesarea, the building projects of Emperor Basil I, and the complex historical geography of "Lombardy" in Southern Italy as viewed by Byzantine sources.</meta>

<page-num>852</page-num>

<header>ANNOTATIONS BY XYLANDER AND GOAR</header>

*The bishop of the ancient primatial or more excellent see of Caesarea, and thus holding primacy among others, ordained and consecrated.* <note>original: "Caesareae primatialis antiquae..."</note> Truth refutes the error of the commentator <note>original: scholiastae</note>, for truth everywhere attributes the right of designating the Patriarch to the Emperor. However, the authority to actually consecrate him was reserved for the Bishop of Heraclea, because the See of Constantinople was originally subject to him. When that bishop died, the **first-throned** <note>original: πρωτόθρονος — prōtothronos, a title for the highest-ranking bishop under a patriarch</note> of the Diocese of Caesarea was substituted for this duty. For those who in ancient times, before the patriarchate was established, were **exarchs** <note>original: ἔξαρχοι — high-ranking governors or ecclesiastical deputies</note> and primates, are now called the "first-throned." — GOAR. <note>Jacques Goar, 1601–1653, a French Dominican scholar of Byzantine ritual</note>

vol. II, p. 252, line 18. **of the New Church** <note>original: τῆς νέας ἐκκλησίας — tēs neas ekklēsias</note>] This refers to the church built in the palace by the father Basil [I] in honor of Saint Nicholas and richly endowed, which was discussed on page 588. — GOAR.

ibid, line 22. *Angaeo*] Called "Hagios" by Zonaras. But truly, among the kings of the Franks who lived during that time, as far as I can find, none had such a son-in-law. I believe this requires further inquiry. These events certainly fall within the reign of the Emperor Charles the Fat <note>original: Caroli Crassi</note>, happening shortly before his death, when Berengar [of Friuli] was created King of Italy at Pavia, opposing the Emperor Arnulf. Perhaps this was the man called Hugh, Duke of Lombardy. But I have nothing certain, unless he is that Hugh, the son of King Lothair II of Lorraine by his mistress Waldrada (and grandson of Emperor Lothair I). It is established from history that at the very time Leo [VI] was recently made Emperor of Constantinople, this Hugh incited a rebellion against Emperor Charles the Fat on behalf of his brother-in-law, Godfrey, King of Frisia. Furthermore, it is well known that those subject to the Empire of Constantinople are called **Romans** by our author here and elsewhere, and he does not recognize the German Emperors as "Emperors" or "Romans." I have warned about this above; unless this is observed, many things will be understood absurdly—for instance, the accounts in the first year of Nicephorus Phocas concerning the Italians "liberated by the labor of the Romans" (for so he calls the people of Constantinople), etc. — XYL. <note>Wilhelm Xylander, 1532–1576, a German classical scholar</note> **Angaeon, the Duke of Lombardy** <note>original: Ἀγγαίων ὁ Λογγιβαρδίας δούξ</note>] The words of Constantine [VII Porphyrogenitus] in *On the Administration of the Empire*, chapter 27, fit well here: *it must be known that in ancient times all authority over Italy—namely Naples, Capua, Benevento, Salerno, Amalfi, Gaeta, and all of Lombardy (as he writes it)—was clearly held by the Romans [Byzantines].* <note>original: ἰστέον ὅτι ἐν τοῖς παλαιοῖς χρόνοις...</note> Therefore, this "Lombardy" was not the region of the Insubres [Northern Italy], but the region of Campania and Apulia [Southern Italy], discussed elsewhere, of which this Angaeon was a private prince. Indeed, it was not until the following age that the Greeks were entirely driven out of Italy by the Normans. The word **gambros** <note>original: γαμβρός</note> also signifies not only a son-in-law, but any relative by marriage on the wife's side. — GOAR.

vol. II, p. 253, line 4. **at the table** <note>original: ἐπὶ τῆς τραπέζης — epi tēs trapezēs</note>] Codinus, in chapter 7, number 21, shows that three officials served most closely at the Emperor’s table, of whom this man, the **Officer of the Table**, is the third. *First, the Grand Domestic stands near the Emperor; after him, the Domestic of the Table; and after him, the Officer of the Table.* <note>original: παρίσταται ππῶτος οὗτος δὴ ὁ μέγας δομέστικος...</note> The Grand Domestic stands nearest the Emperor (as a mark of honor); after him is the Domestic of the Table (who is to divide the food); and after him is the Prefect [or Officer] of the Table (who is to place the dishes upon the table). In number 33: *the Officer of the Table [takes] the small container of blessed bread...* <note>original: τὸ δέ γε παναγιάριον ὁ ἐπὶ τῆς τραπέζης λα- — the text cuts off mid-word</note>

It also clarifies that in Byzantine texts, "Lombardy" refers to Southern Italy and "Romans" refers to the Byzantines themselves.</summary>

<header>ANNOTATIONS.</header>

...[and] placing it [the dish] upon the table. According to Nicephorus Gregoras (Book 7), if he is to be believed, the leader of the Russians was honored by Constantine [the Great] with this duty of a **steward** <note>original Latin: *dapiferi* — a high court official responsible for serving food at a royal table</note>. — GOAR.

vol. II, p. 253, line 16. **Father of the Emperor** <note>original Greek: βασιλεοπάτορα — *basileopatōra*</note>] [Emperor] Marcianus had long ago bestowed that name upon Julius and Tatianus, brothers toward whom he was well-disposed: "If this happens by God's will, I will proclaim you as fathers." And a little later: "Having sent for Tatianus and Julius, he proclaimed them fathers." However, for them, this was an expression of goodwill and gratitude toward brothers, not a formal office or rank as it was for Zautzas <note>Stylianos Zautzas was a high official under Leo VI, for whom the rank of *Basileopator* was specifically created</note>. — GOAR.

vol. II, p. 255, line 3. The **Hungarians** <note>original: *Ungrorum*</note> mentioned in this passage (for they are clearly called so, as also by Zonaras, though others read *Ugros*) are undoubtedly those called Hungarians today. — XYLANDER. The translator here confuses the Turks with the Hungarians, whom the author distinguishes with the conjunction **and** <note>original Greek: καὶ</note>. Understand these to be the Scythians neighboring the Khazars, whose kinsmen subjected Persia to themselves during the reign of [Constantine IX] Monomachus. The author speaks of them at length, as does Constantine [Porphyrogenitus] in *On Administering the Empire*, chapter 38. — GOAR.

*ibid.*, line 12. **The Quaestor** <note>original: τὸν κοιαίστωρα — *ton koiaistōra*</note>] Concerning this official and how the office was administered in later times, see the *Graeco-Roman Law*, part 2, extensively. — GOAR.

*ibid.*, line 13. **Little Constantine** <note>original: Κωνσταντινάκιον — *Kōnstantinakion*</note>] A diminutive of Constantine, which in Latin would be *Constantinulus*. — GOAR.

vol. II, p. 258, line 9. *daughter of Babylon*] A curse taken, it seems, from Psalm 134 <note>modern numbering: Psalm 137:8. The text refers to the Babylonian captivity</note>. — XYLANDER.

*ibid.*, line 10. *epeicta*] **The Taskmaster** <note>original: ἐπείκτης — *epeiktēs*</note>. I did not fully grasp what this word signified, though if I were to guess, I would think it comes from the verb "to urge" <note>original: *epeigein*</note>; perhaps a driver of laborers. For it is indeed derived from "urging," but which people or things he urged, let others discover. Zonaras wrote *pektēn* <note>original: πήκτην</note>. But what is a *pektēs*? I hardly think it means a builder. Here I will freely set forth my conjecture in a matter of little or no importance, as it seems. The **pektis** <note>original: πηκτίς</note> is an instrument, either with many strings or otherwise producing a varied harmony; I learned this not so much from lexicons (which I do not trust blindly) as from Plato's *Republic*, Book 3. The words are: "Therefore, we shall not maintain builders of triangles, *pektides*, and all such instruments that are many-stringed and many-toned." Now, such was the license (or should I say audacity) of Cedrenus and writers of that ilk, that it was easy for them to name a singer or musician a *pektēs*. You will frequently find examples of this fault (for it is nothing but a fault) while reading them. What if, therefore, this *pektēs* was a musician, and specifically that same eunuch musician (whose name could easily have been derived from his art, just as the name "Copronymus" <note>literally "dung-named," a slur used against the Iconoclast Emperor Constantine V</note> was given to the Emperor and others, or to other great men from some action, or truly "to be called" used instead of "to be nicknamed" by a man who cared little for linguistic propriety) who provided the occasion for the Bulgarian war through his greed, relying on the favor he held with the Zautzas family? This would be all the easier if he were related to them by blood. I chose to note these things because I know that by applying such diligence, learned men have often healed the great wounds of good writers. In the meantime, I have changed nothing, so that if anyone knows that Epicta...

...so that he might speak more freely about what it is. I add this: the surname **Overseer** <note>original Latin: *epictae*</note> is placed below for Christophoros, the son of Andronikos, regarding Basil, the son of Romanos, who was oppressed by Duro. Concerning the privilege of Samonas <note>a prominent palace official of Arab origin under Leo VI</note> and all his accusers, I neither wish to inquire here, nor explain the nature of the matter by producing examples. **XYLANDER.** <term>Overseer</term> <note>original Greek: ἐπείκτης — *epeiktēs*; a taskmaster or one who urges others on</note>, who by another name is called an <term>Authority</term> <note>original Greek: ἐξουσιαστής — *exousiastēs*; a ruler or official with power</note>, about whom the author writes on page 442, as do we in the same place. Zonaras writes <term>pēktēs</term> <note>original Greek: πήκτης</note>, and Leo writes <term>epēktēs</term> <note>original Greek: ἐπήκτης</note>; both are in error. **GOAR.**

vol. II, p. 259, line 3. <term>those before the bedchamber</term> <note>original Greek: προκοίτων — *prokoitōn*</note>] Codinus writes that these are the <term>chamberlains of the bedchamber</term> <note>original Greek: παρακοιμωμένων τοῦ κοιτῶνος — *parakoimōmenōn tou koitōnos*</note>, the guards of the sacred bedchamber. **GOAR.**

*ibid. line 11.* <term>distribution for the soul</term> <note>original Greek: διανομὴν ψυχικῶν — *dianomēn psychikōn*</note>] I have translated this in a general sense as those things that are done after death by relatives for the salvation of the deceased’s soul. Perhaps it was some distribution of alms, which the word <term>distribution</term> <note>original Greek: διανομῆς — *dianomēs*</note> seems to suggest. And because it is not explicitly stated how Basil was related to Zoe, I have used a general term for the relationship, as is customary. Certainly, this passage seems to strongly support our conjecture regarding the musician mentioned here. **XYLANDER.** Xylander says: *so that the funeral rites might be completed.* More accurately: *so that he might distribute to the poor the alms left by the testament of his aunt Zoe.* For a <term>soul-gift</term> <note>original Greek: ψυχικόν — *psychikon*</note> is an act of almsgiving or any work of piety undertaken for the care of the soul. The word <term>distribution</term> also informs even the ignorant. **GOAR.**

*ibid. line 21.* <term>the Mystic</term> <note>original Greek: ὁ μυστικός — *ho mystikos*</note>] Meursius interprets this as a civil magistrate, *specifically a senator of the secret council; Junius calls him a secretary:* neither pleases me, though I do not entirely disagree with them. However, the office of the <term>Mystic</term> is far removed from the senatorial rank, being listed as a military role alongside other military offices by Codinus in chapter 2; it is devoted solely to military service, such as the <term>Mystic of the Schools</term> <note>original Greek: μυστικὸς τῶν σχολῶν — *mystikos tōn scholōn*; the "Schools" were elite palace guard units</note>. Likewise, his clothing mentioned in chapter 4, note 33, reflects nothing worthy of a senator; and if one seeks his function from the same Codinus, he says in chapter 5, note 41, that it is clear from the name. In a single word, the <term>Mystic of the Schools</term> is he who carries the secrets of the prince to the "Schools" of the bodyguards and the army; he who proclaims peace and order, acting as an ancient silentiary <note>a court official who maintained silence and order in the palace</note> among the modern guard units. The same official is ordered in the *Greek Law*, Book 2, Novel 3 of Manuel Comnenus and Novel 2 of Alexios Comnenus, to reconcile the ministers of the royal treasury on one side and the church on the other when they disagree over their rights: <note>original Greek: εἰδήσεως ἀκριβεστάτης διδομένης τῷ κατὰ τὴν ἡμέραν μυστικῷ, ὃς καὶ ὀφείλει καὶ ἄμφω οἰκονομεῖν — "the most accurate information being given to the Mystic of the day, who is obliged to manage both [royal and ecclesiastical rights]"</note>. If the treasury officials should violently demand anything from the church estates, <note>original Greek: παρὰ τοῦ κατὰ τὴν ἡμέραν μεγαλεπιφανεστάτου μυστικοῦ καταναγκαζόμενος εἰς τὴν ἐπενεχθεῖσαν τινὶ τῶν ὑφ᾽ ὑμᾶς κτήσεων βλάβην ἀποθεραπεύσουσιν αὐτῇ — "being compelled by the most illustrious Mystic of the day, they shall remedy the damage inflicted upon any of the possessions under you"</note>. **GOAR.**

*ibid. line 22.* <term>the formal invitations</term> <note>original Greek: τὰ κατὰ τύπον κλητώρια — *ta kata typon klētōria*</note>] It has often been observed in these writers that <term>types</term> <note>original Greek: τύπους — *typous*</note> are statutes, laws, etc. I believe these <term>klētōria</term> were solemn banquets or feasts at which the Emperor, the Empress, and the nobles were present. In the time of Justinian the Great, around his thirtieth year, mention is made of <term>twelve-day estates</term> <note>original Greek: κτητορίων δωδεκαημέρων — *ktētoriōn dōdekahēmerōn*</note>; comparing this passage, if you read it as <term>banquets</term> <note>original Greek: κλητορίων — *klētōriōn*</note>, they might be seen as banquets lasting twelve days.

# ANNOTATIONS.

Whoever is more familiar with this matter may correct or expand upon these notes. **XYLANDER.** See above in the section on Justinian. **GOAR.**

*vol. II, p. 259, line 23.* "**Anna**"] the daughter, in whose presence, as if she were the Empress <note>original Latin: *Augusta*</note>, the customary banquets were celebrated. **GOAR.**

*vol. II, p. 260, line 17. **from the platform***] <term>ambo</term> <note>original Greek: ἄμβωνος — *ambōnos*; also called a *lettner* or *porkirchen* in German</note>. This is an elevated part of the church, such as those seen supported by columns, attached to walls, or built high up in the entrance of the sanctuary <note>original Latin: *adytorum vestibulo*</note> to accommodate people within the churches. **XYLANDER.**

*vol. II, p. 261, line 7. **tetraodium***] This seems to have been a hymn consisting of four parts or songs. However, what that specific work by "Cyrus Cosmas" might be, others must determine. I have provided the words of the psalm from the common version. **XYLANDER.** A hymn consisting of four odes to be sung on Holy Saturday is found in the <term>Triodion</term> <note>a liturgical book containing the entire service for Great Lent and Holy Week</note>, and its nature is well known. **GOAR.**

*ibid. line 8. **Cosmas***] This was Cosmas of Maiuma, a bishop and the teacher of John of Damascus, as well as the author of several sacred hymns. The word <term>kyrou</term> <note>original Greek: κυροῦ</note> is a diminutive for <term>kyriou</term> <note>meaning "of the Lord" or "of the Master"</note>. The full word is granted to more distinguished men, the diminutive <term>kyros</term> <note>κυρός</note> to those of lower rank, and the abbreviated <term>kyr</term> <note>κῦρ</note> to the humble. **GOAR.**

*ibid. line 18. **unroofed***] <note>original Greek: ἀστεγὴς — *astegēs*</note> The Greeks punish second marriages with a light penance, subject third marriages to a heavier one, and utterly reject and condemn fourth marriages. For that reason, the Eastern Church never allowed this Zoe Carbonopsina <note>Zoe "with the Coal-Black Eyes," the fourth wife of Emperor Leo VI</note> to be admitted to the crowning of Empresses according to the custom. **GOAR.**

*vol. II, p. 262, line 7. **at Tripoli***] In Syria. **GOAR.**

*vol. II, p. 263, line 20. **he cut the tendons***] Specifically so that he might snatch away from the Emperor’s ministers the ease of pursuing and dragging him back from his flight. Moreover, the Greek text uses the word <term>hamstrung</term> <note>original Greek: ἠγκυλοκόπησεν — *ēnkylokopēsen*</note>, which I translated according to the general meaning. **XYLANDER.** It seems more likely that Samonas <note>a powerful court official of Arab descent</note> pierced the feet and hooves of the horses with hooks or sharp irons rather than cutting their tendons. For he wished to keep his flight secret, and the word <term>ankylopo</term> <note>related to bending or hooking</note> is unrelated to cutting. **GOAR.**

*vol. II, p. 265, line 6. **he was deposed***] By those who, as we mentioned before, judged the fourth marriage of Leo VI to be entirely illicit. **GOAR.**

*ibid. line 7. **because of this deed***] Namely, because he had taken four wives one after another; for that first woman, Zoe Zautza, his concubine, did not count against him. However, as for what a <term>mitatorium</term> <note>original Greek: μιτατώριον; vol. II, p. 265, line 9</note> is, I do not know. Something was said about <term>mitata</term> <note>lodgings or quarters</note> above. Perhaps it was a part of the temple, somewhat secular in nature, accessible even to those barred from the use of the sacred rites. I do not wish to argue here about what was done in the ancient church, since among the fickle Greeks something seems to have changed from time to time. Choniates mentions that *mitatum* was the name for a Saracen synagogue in the time of Isaac Angelos. But that is of little relevance here, except that the mention of this *mitatorium* occurs again. **XYLANDER.** The **mitatorium** is a small chamber at the side of the altar, in which a simple table—specifically bread and wine—was set out for singers weary from their labor. Following the very learned Allatius <note>Leone Allacci, a scholar of Greek liturgy</note> in his notes on the *Euchologion*, we believe the word should be read as <term>mensatorium</term> <note>from the Latin *mensa*, meaning "table"</note>. Furthermore, it was to this place—as one excluded from the sacred rites and excommunicated—

...regarded by the patriarch in such a way that, lest he should renounce his own rights or offend those holding the opposite view, the emperor would withdraw when he was about to offer prayers or participate in the sacred rites in whatever manner possible. **GOAR.**

*vol. II, p. 265, line 10.* <term>parakoimōmenon</term> <note>original Greek: παρακοιμώμενον</note>] I have translated this as "intimate bedchamberlain," referring to one who sleeps near the emperor; I would wish it translated this way elsewhere as well for the sake of clarity. **Galakrenōn** <note>original Greek: Γαλακρηνῶν</note> means "fountains of milk." **XYLANDER.**

*vol. II, p. 266, line 1.* <term>kata tauton</term> <note>original Greek: κατὰ ταυτόν</note>] means "simultaneously." However, I certainly do not think Emperor Leo intended this to mean having so many wives at the same time, but rather that after one died, another was taken. It appears he did exactly this, and for that reason was excommunicated by the patriarch as an ungodly man. Nevertheless, I did not wish to change anything. Zonaras <note>a 12th-century Byzantine historian</note> uses the phrase <term>kat’ auton</term> <note>original Greek: κατ’ αὑτόν</note>, meaning "according to his own" or "by his own example": that is, so that Leo’s fourth marriage would not only be considered no fault in Leo, but that others might be allowed to imitate the same without punishment. After the word <term>kēdestēn</term> <note>original Greek: κηδεστὴν</note>, I translated "relative by marriage," as I was unsure whether it referred to a son-in-law, a father-in-law, or some other relation. **XYLANDER.**

*vol. II, p. 267, line 22. **of the praetorium***] <note>original Greek: τοῦ πραιτωρίου — *tou praitōriou*</note>] A place where those guilty of crimes were held in prisons, as were the Saracens <note>a medieval term for Muslims</note> on account of their profane religion, as the author will narrate shortly. **GOAR.**

*vol. II, p. 270, line 17. **not unseen***] <note>original Greek: μὴ ἀθέατα — *mē atheata*</note>] Read this as "easily seen" <note>original Greek: εὐθέατα — *eutheata*</note>, for the sense seems to require it. I have taken **Megisto Coetonitae** as a proper name. Otherwise, it could be translated as "the Great Chamberlain." **XYLANDER.**

*vol. II, p. 271, line 15. **worldly clothing***] <note>original Greek: στολὴν κοσμικήν — *stolēn kosmikēn*</note>] What the Latin church calls "secular" clothing. **GOAR.**

*vol. II, p. 272, line 19.* <term>pittakion</term> <note>original Greek: πιττάκιον</note>] A paper, a small leaf of writing, especially made from "paper skin" or parchment. **GOAR.**

*vol. II, p. 273, line 13. **the customary address***] <note>original Greek: τὴν συνήθη προσηγορίαν — *tēn synēthē prosēgorian*</note>] This is the same address that Lucius Verus in the writings of Herodian, Julian in Marcellinus, Tiberius in Simocatta, and other emperors in other authors are read to have used when near death. **GOAR.**

*vol. II, p. 274, line 19. **silence having been made***] I believe this refers to an "edict," as it does elsewhere. **XYLANDER.** I believe it should be interpreted not as an edict or silence, but as a "council," as is the case elsewhere. **GOAR.**

*vol. II, p. 275, line 8.* <term>klērikos</term> <note>original Greek: κληρικός — "cleric"</note>] One who is enrolled in the clergy of a great church or any metropolitan see and is distinguished by ecclesiastical dignity or office is a *cleric*. From this comes the term "clerical offices" <note>original Greek: τὰ κληρικάτα ὀφφίκια — *ta klērikata ophphikia*</note> found in Balsamon’s letter from Basil to Amphilochius. **GOAR.**

*ibid. line 20.* <term>daiktōra</term> <note>original Greek: δαίκτωρα</note>] Liutprand <note>a 10th-century diplomat and historian</note> calls this man the "rector of the house" (Chapter 5, last section). **GOAR.**

*vol. II, p. 276, line 18.* <term>stoicheion</term> <note>original Greek: στοιχεῖον</note>] This is what he calls an object that, through the power of magical arts, governs the fortune of some human being. An example of this was the statue in the Xerolophos <note>a district in Constantinople</note> belonging to Romanos Lekapenos, which represented Simeon the Bulgarian; when its head was struck off, Simeon died. The poets have something very similar regarding the fatal brand of Meleager <note>a hero whose life was tied to a piece of wood</note>, and Apollonius in the *Argonautica* regarding the Hamadryad in the second book. Hence, magicians are called <term>stoicheiōmatikoi</term> <note>original Greek: στοιχειωματικοί</note>, who were thought to unite a certain power into objects for the purpose of performing something through specific signs and incantations. And the verb <term>stoicheiousthai</term> <note>original Greek: στοιχειοῦσθαι</note> means to set something in motion by magical arts. It is used in the passive voice below regarding that statue: "for this [statue] had been magically linked to him" <note>original Greek: ταύτην γὰρ αὐτῷ ἐστοιχειῶσθαι — *tautēn gar autō estoicheiōsthai*</note>.

->### ANNOTATIONS ###<-

...that this was fatal to him by some magic power, having been <term>magically bound</term> <note>original Greek: εἰς τὸν Συμεὼν ἐστοιχειῶσθαι</note> to Simeon. **XYLANDER.** The predominant position of the stars in any person’s life is an "element" <note>original Greek: στοιχεῖον (stoicheion); here referring to an astrological or talismanic force</note>: hence the word signifies the author of fortune, lot, fate, a guardian spirit, or a harmful or benevolent ghost. **GOAR.**

*vol. II, p. 278, line 23.* **first of the priests** <note>original Greek: πρώτου τῶν ἱερέων</note>] The "Archpriest" <note>original Greek: πρωτοιερεύς</note>, who is also called the "Head Priest" <note>original Greek: πρωτοπαπᾶς</note>, or the first of the priests, is the <term>archipresbyter</term>. In the Great Church <note>Hagia Sophia</note>, at the sacred tribunal of the altar (though not everywhere), he holds the second rank after the patriarch. Codinus. *Euchologium* <note>a liturgical book of the Eastern Orthodox Church</note>. **GOAR.**

*vol. II, p. 279, line 24.* **he proceeds to the circus**] And yet he was excluded from there, unless perhaps he entered by another gate, or—as I suspect—the author is speaking of a different circus. **XYLANDER.**

*vol. II, p. 280, line 4.* **by the rowers** <note>original Greek: ἐλατῶν</note>] So called because they drive the ships by rowing. Zonaras uses the term "seafaring men" <note>original Greek: πλωίμους</note>, which means the same thing: naval allies. **XYLANDER.** I do not believe these rowers were commoners or a haphazardly gathered mob; for just as the "companies" <note>original Greek: ἑταιρεῖαι</note> mentioned were elite troops of confederates, so too were these rowers accustomed to manning the Emperor’s <term>dromon</term> <note>a fast-sailing Byzantine warship</note>. Regarding these, Constantine Porphyrogenitus writes in *On Administering the Empire*, chapter 51, and our author says below on page 615: "if he has men who are obedient, noble, and fit to row the imperial trireme." **GOAR.**

*ibid., line 5.* The "arms" of the **chariot** <note>original Greek: ἅρματος</note> were turned: for they did not use chariots; the author turned this word into Greek, as I have noted previously. **XYLANDER.**

*ibid., line 18.* **Chaldian** <note>referring to a person from Chaldia</note>] An obscure and, I believe, false reading. **XYLANDER.** Chaldia is a portion of Armenia toward Syria. Thus, the word is only "false and obscure" to Xylander. **GOAR.**

*vol. II, p. 281, line 14.* **Eparch** <note>original Greek: ἔπαρχος; the Prefect of the City of Constantinople</note>] In later times, he was occupied with punishing crimes, which is why he had a residence assigned to him by virtue of his office in the prison for the accused within the praetorium. The author mentions this in several places. **GOAR.**

*ibid., line 18.* **of the Heifer in Chrysopolis** <note>original Greek: τῆς ἐν Χρυσοπόλει Δαμάλεως</note>] A place so named because of the stone heifer <note>original Greek: δάμαλιν</note> standing on a column across from it in Chrysopolis, on the Thracian Bosporus. The author mentions this shortly below on page 617. **GOAR.**

*vol. II, p. 282, line 21.* I have retained the Greek word <term>epirriptarium</term>, which seems to signify a hood or some other covering thrown over the head, from the word "to throw over" <note>original Greek: ἐπιρρίπτειν</note>. **XYLANDER.** It is a <term>mandyas</term> <note>a ceremonial cloak</note>, called a <term>pallium</term> by the Latins; it is to be thrown over <note>original Greek: ἐπιρριπτέον</note> all other garments. This is different from Xylander’s "hood," as is clear from Codinus, chapter 6, number 2. **GOAR.**

*ibid., line 22.* In the works of Zonaras, the opposite of this passage is read: namely, that this peace agreement fell apart; I consider this more probable and true. For soon after, without any mention of a violation of peace, he reports that Simeon overran Thrace. **XYLANDER.**

*vol. II, p. 283, line 18.* **to receive a prayer** <note>original Greek: λαβεῖν εὐχήν</note>] The Greeks did not undertake public offices or ministries without heavenly auspices and the prayers of the Church. Thus, when Constantius was announced as a Patrician by the Empress, he immediately went to the church to receive a prayer, in the manner of a consecration. This is found in the recently printed *Euchologium* regarding the promotion of a Patrician or a <term>Curopalates</term> <note>a high-ranking court title, literally "manager of the palace"</note>. **GOAR.**

<meta>This page continues the scholarly commentary by Wilhelm Xylander and Jacques Goar. Following the previous page's focus on maritime and priestly titles, this section examines specific Byzantine administrative offices, military ranks, and liturgical calendars. The scholars debate the interpretation of titles like the "Drungary of the Watch" and the "Turmarch," while also clarifying obscure Greek phrasing through references to classical authors like Euripides and other Byzantine historians like Zonaras and Constantine Porphyrogenitus.</meta>

858 XYLANDER AND GOAR

vol. II, p. 283, line 21. **he makes him the Drungary of the Watch**] I have repeated the verb **he appoints** <note>original Greek: προχειρίζεται</note> as a shared term <note>original Latin: ἀπὸ κοινοῦ (apo koinou)</note>, as I do not believe the office of a single **Commander of the Bodyguard** <note>original Greek: ἑταιρειάρχης (hetaireiarches)</note> was entrusted to two people, which the ambiguously placed words seem to suggest. **XYLANDER.**

*Same page, line 24.* **if he were distinguished with the honor of a patrician**] **honored as a patrician** <note>original Greek: πατρίκιος τιμηθείς</note>. Perhaps it should have been translated thus: "Bogas the patrician promises, etc.," so that he did not receive this rank as a reward for his work, but had already undertaken the matter as a patrician. It is an ambiguous passage. Moreover, I have not yet learned who that **Prince of Princes** <note>original Greek: ἄρχων ἀρχόντων (archon archonton)</note> is. **XYLANDER.**

vol. II, p. 285, line 12. **the Chief Priest of the Palace** <note>original Greek: ὁ πρωτοπαπᾶς τοῦ παλατίου</note>] The emperor had his own clergy in the palace, where there were various churches, such as those of St. Stephen, the Heavenly Hosts <note>original Latin: ducum caelestium</note>, Elisha, and others; the head of that clergy was the **Chief Priest of the Palace**. **GOAR.**

*Same page, line 17.* **of the Hikanatoi** <note>original Greek: τοῦ ἱκανάτου</note>] Named after a specific military unit <note>an elite regiment of the Byzantine army established in the 9th century</note>. The author mentions below: **the commander of the regiment of the Hikanatoi** <note>original Greek: τοῦ τάγματος ἄρχων τῶν ἱκανάτων</note>. **GOAR.**

vol. II, p. 291, line 2. **an unruly mob** <note>original Greek: ἀκόλαστος ὄχλος</note>] This alludes to a passage in Euripides, found in his play *Hecuba*. Garidas is the successor of John Leon, a surname which Zonaras also added here. **XYLANDER.**

vol. II, p. 293, line 13. **the third day of Galilee**] It is clear that the **Annunciation** <note>original Greek: εὐαγγελισμόν (euangelismon)</note> refers to the feast day commemorating the joyful news of the incarnation of Christ brought by the Angel Gabriel to the Virgin Mary. However, I do not know what this "Galilee" refers to, and it seems to be a mistake; in its place, the historian Zonaras has "Easter." **XYLANDER.** It refers to the third day of Easter week itself. Leo the Grammarian writes: **on the third day of Easter, called that of Galilee** <note>original Greek: τῇ τρίτῃ τοῦ πάσχα τῇ λεγομένῃ τῆς Γαλιλαίας</note>. In the same way, they call Sundays the **Sunday of Thomas, of the Prodigal [Son], of the Samaritan [Woman]**, etc., naming the Sunday after the Gospel readings regarding Thomas, the Prodigal, the Samaritan, and so on. **GOAR.**

*Same page, line 22.* That Romanos was so intent on crushing Leo, with whom he is said to have made a treaty shortly before, is clearly the result of new necessities being preferred over old ones. **"When a dearer thing came, the sorrowful one was out"** <note>original German: da liebers kam, war leiders aus; a proverb meaning new interests or loved ones displace old griefs or obligations</note>. For with Leo crushed, Romanos held both his son-in-law and the empire under his control. **XYLANDER.**

*Same place.* A **Golden Bull** <note>original Greek: χρυσόβουλλον (chrysobullon)</note> is a royal diploma or royal letters—sacred documents written in purple ink—with which the impression of the Imperial image is made with a **gold seal** <note>original Greek: βούλλᾳ (boulla)</note>. The author spoke above on pages 178 and 615 A of **securing it with a gold seal** <note>original Greek: διὰ σφραγῖδος χρυσῆς ἀσφαλίσασθαι</note>. **GOAR.**

vol. II, p. 294, line 11. He who is a **Turmarch** <note>original Greek: τουρμάρχης; a middle-ranking military commander</note> is also a **Merarch** <note>original Greek: μεράρχης</note>, a **Tagmatarch** <note>original Greek: ταγματάρχης</note>, and as Emperor Leo writes in *Tactics, Constitution 3*, **sometimes also a General** <note>original Greek: ποτὲ καὶ στρατηλάτης (strategelates)</note>. And as Constantine Porphyrogenitus says in *On the Themes, 1*: **those called Turmarchs were appointed to the service of the generals. Such a rank signifies one who has under him five hundred archers, three hundred targeteers, and one hundred light-armed scouts** <note>original Greek: οἱ δὲ λεγόμενοι τουρμάρχαι... δεξιολάβους ἑκατόν</note>. **GOAR.**

The commentator <note>Xylander</note> trifles here regarding machines and ballistas. **GOAR.**

This officer is called a *cornicularius* <note>adjutant</note> or *clavicularius* <note>key-bearer</note> by Pancirollus in the *Notitia of the Empire*, chapter 11; he is the head of a cohort guarding the prince. At the prince's command, as the one in charge of executing sentences on the guilty, he punishes whatever criminals the prince has condemned, while the prince watches. Codinus reports that in his time this was the duty of the Bardariotai, of whom he says: "from the belt of each of these hang leather thongs, which they call *manglabia* (as he writes it), that is, canes or rods, to scourge those worthy of being scourged." **Leo Grammaticus** writes: "he sends a manglabite (as he reads it), the Black-Theodore, to slay the monk with a sword." The Turks, having borrowed much from the Greeks, have a *manglabite* as a precursor in the presence of the emperor (*buiurdi* they call it in their own language), ready at his command to subject any guilty person to extreme punishments. Both, having spoken of peace, were feasted together quietly. **vol. II p. 313 line 6.** Greek architects call the *kosmitis* <note>original Greek: κοσμήτην; literally "the adorner"</note> the entire assembly of the entablature, composed of the cornice, the frieze, and the beam placed beneath it (the architrave), so called because it "adorns" <note>original Greek: κοσμεῖ</note> the columned building. Germanus, in his *Mystagogia*, places the *kosmitis* upon the "railings and breast-high walls" <note>original Greek: κιγλίσιν καὶ στήθεσι</note> or "small columns" <note>original Greek: κιονίοις</note>, which are the lattices and pillars separating the people from the altar. Constantine Porphyrogenitus <note>Emperor Constantine VII (r. 913–959), known for his writings on administration and ceremony</note> in *On the Administration of the Empire* follows the same description: *and in such a fortress there also stand thick columns having "kosmitas" above them.* **GOAR.**

**ibid. line 13.** *when he was unwilling* but] the passage is mutilated. I believe it should be completed thus: *since he was unwilling, the emperor, fearing to disturb him by force, asked etc.* In the margin the scribe noted <margin>Look at both the malice of the metropolitan and the "simplicity" of the archbishop.</margin> He calls it "simplicity" <note>original Greek: ἀπλαστίαν; meaning a lack of guile or being unformed</note>, I think, because the mind of Tryphon <note>Patriarch Tryphon of Constantinople (928–931)</note> was not so fashioned as to understand those arts. What if he meant to write "insatiability" <note>original Greek: ἀπληστίαν</note>, because he was not satisfied with the legitimate administration of the patriarchate? **XYLANDER.**

**vol. II p. 315 line 23.** *and together with the bridal crown*] the author indicates that Anna was married and announced as a partner in imperial honor at the same time, receiving the crowns of marriage and of the empire on one and the same day. **GOAR.**

**vol. II p. 319 line 9.** *Hugh, king of France*] No indeed, as the histories say, he was king of Italy. But in these matters, neither our author nor other writers of this sort were diligent. Understand this Constantine Porphyrogenitus to be not the son of Romanus, but the son of Leo—the one whom Romanus Lecapenus <note>Emperor Romanus I (r. 920–944)</note> imposed himself upon as a father-in-law, and after Constantine was reduced in rank and restricted, Romanus ruled almost alone with his own sons. The first of the "Born in the Purple" <note>original Latin: Porphyrogennetorum</note> mentioned is Copronymus <note>Emperor Constantine V</note>, named after a chamber of the palace called the *Porphyra* (perhaps because it was adorned with purple tapestries or curtains) in which he was born; and perhaps also the others were so called, as being legitimate emperors born in their proper place, in that room destined for childbearing. Our author expresses this regarding the son of Leo also below, in the first year of Nicephorus Phocas. You may best call Romanus (son of Constantine, grandson of Leo) "Romanus the Third," lest he be confused with the other Romanus (grandson of Romanus, son of Christophorus). The name of Hugh’s daughter is recorded as Bertha-Eudoxia. **XYLANDER.** He whom Constantine calls "the illustrious" in *On the Administration of the Empire* chapter 26, had Adelbert for a father and Bertha for a mother, and for a grandfather Lothair, the son of Louis the Pious. He was never king of "Greater France," to use Constantine’s words, but count of the province of Arles. Called by the Italians after Rudolph was expelled, he obtained the kingdom of Italy; hence he deserved to be called "King of Francia" <note>original Greek: ῥῆξ Φραγγίας</note> by the Greeks. His daughter Bertha, born of a concubine, was joined to Romanus, son of Constantine Porphyrogenitus, with Sigefred, Bishop of Parma, leading the bride...

# THE ANNOTATIONS OF XYLANDER AND GOAR

...sent his son to Constantinople, and she was afterwards known by the name of Eudoxia. **GOAR.**

**vol. II p. 319 line 13.** *demi*] <note>The Latin *demi* refers to the Greek *demoi* (δήμοι), usually meaning "people" or "districts."</note> that is, "districts": for this is how Cicero translated the Attic *demoi*. Otherwise, either *bathra* <note>original: βάθρα</note> signifies "feet," or *stethea* <note>original: στήθεα</note> signifies something other than the common meaning. **XYLANDER.** *demoi*] are the protruding faces of roof levels and stones from buildings—the eaves and the crowns of the wall—named *demoi* as they "look out over the people." We have said above that *bathra* are the stone platforms and seats arranged near the palace for receiving the emperor and for him to sit upon. *stethea* are small columns arranged in order and joined by a longer top-piece (an architrave), surrounded by lattices, enclosed barriers, and bars, or lower railings, which protect those within their inner space from the surrounding or rushing crowd. Germanus, in his *Mystagogia*, not far from the beginning, writes: <note>original Greek: τὰ κιόνια ἤτοι τὰ στήθεα διαχωρίζοντα τὸ βῆμα ἀπὸ τοῦ λοιποῦ ναοῦ, καὶ κάγκελλα.</note> "the small columns or breast-high walls that separate the sanctuary from the rest of the temple, and the railings." With these three words explained, the meaning of this sentence is clear: *violent blasts of wind arose, by whose force the eaves of the roof and walls fell and collapsed, crushing and wearing away the platforms and seats beneath them, as well as the railings.* Xylander, as if about to cause laughter from a stage, says: *a violent wind arose, and the falling things called "demoi" crushed the "chests" and "feet" of those who were below.* <note>Goar is mocking Xylander for translating the architectural terms "stethea" (railings) and "bathra" (platforms) literally as "chests" and "feet."</note> **GOAR.**

**vol. II p. 320 line 13.** The history of Eli from the beginning of the sacred Books of Samuel is very well known. And the narrative concerning the image of Edessa <note>The Mandylion, a famous relic of Christ’s face sent to King Abgar of Edessa.</note> is set out above, though differently than here. **XYLANDER.**

*ibid. line 14. Proten*] <note>original Greek: Πρώτην</note> An island in the Hellespont near Constantinople. **GOAR.**

**vol. II p. 324 line 11.** *the poet says*] the meaning is: just as one heat is more intense than another, so too the craftiness and effort of Stephen were hindered and rendered void by the greater shrewdness and zeal of Porphyrogenitus. <note>Referring to Emperor Constantine VII "Born in the Purple."</note> **XYLANDER.**

*ibid. line 23. Panormos island*] <note>original Greek: Πανόρμῳ νήσῳ</note> An island of the Hellespont. **GOAR.**

**vol. II p. 325 line 1.** *Terebinthos*] <note>original Greek: Τερεβίνθῳ</note> In the same Sea of Marmara. <note>original Latin: Propontide</note> **GOAR.**

**vol. II p. 328 line 2.** *by John*] <note>original Greek: ὑπὸ Ἰωάννου</note> By Emperor Otto, writes Curopalates, <note>A high Byzantine court title, here likely referring to the historian George Kedrenos or John Scylitzes.</note> with whom the truth of the history agrees. **GOAR.**

<meta>This page continues the scholarly annotations by Xylander and Goar on Byzantine history, focusing on specific vocabulary used by classical and medieval Greek authors, as well as identifying historical figures like Sayf al-Dawla and Pope John XII.</meta>

# ANNOTATIONS

I have taken the word *semantir* <note>original: σημαντῆρα</note> to mean "guardian," a term Homer uses to mean "shepherd" in the *Iliad* (Book 15, line 325): "herdsmen not being present" <note>original: σημάντορας οὐ παρέοντος</note>. Also, in the *Iliad* (Book 10, line 485), he mentions "unguarded sheep" <note>original: μῆλα ἀσήμαντα</note>, meaning those deprived of a shepherd. It is derived from *semainein* <note>original: σημαίνειν</note>, which means "to command" or "to order." In this sense, *semantor* <note>original: σημαντώρ</note> can also be understood at the beginning of the *Odyssey* (Book 17). However, what it signifies in this specific context, I leave as an obscure point. **XYLANDER.** Xylander did not recognize any specific meaning for *semantir*, even though it clearly resounds with the idea of a signal. It is actually a <term>semantron<note>original: crotalus</note> a wooden sounding board used in the Eastern Church instead of a bell</term>, a long, square, moderately thin piece of wood to be struck with a small mallet so that the sound may signal the faithful to come to church. There is also a *semantir* made of an iron plate, to be struck with a small iron rod at the church doors for the same purpose; Leo Allatius has written learnedly about this, as is his custom, in his book on the more recent Greek temples. Therefore, having seized this signal—whether made of wood or rather of the church's iron or bronze—"he warded off those who were entering," meaning *the valiant priest attacked, repelled, and drove back the Saracens who had entered the church.* **GOAR.**

*ibid. line 19. Since he did not persuade]* Xylander translates this as: "when he did not obtain admission." More truly: "when he did not persuade them to pardon his crime," that is, he did not obtain his request. **GOAR.**

*vol. II p. 331 line 1. He earned the favor of Leo]* In the text, it is written as if the gifts and honors from the emperor were given to the defeated Abu'l-Asayir <note>original: Apolasaerum</note>; I think this is absurd, and I have instead attributed it to the one whose efforts led to the enemy being captured and displayed in triumph. For the emperor was not accustomed to show any grace to those he triumphed over after treading on their necks; and if this had been done as a new precedent, the unusual nature of it would have been highly noteworthy. Now, Sayf al-Dawla <note>original: Chabdanus</note> was the Emir <note>original: ameras</note> of Aleppo <note>original: Chalepi</note>, as our author teaches in the third book of *Romanus*. **XYLANDER.**

*ibid. line 4. Chaleb]* Berroea of Syria, today called **Aleppo.** **GOAR.**

*ibid. line 14. those whom he had captured]* "He took them alive" <note>original: ἐζώγρησε</note>. The passage seems to be cut short. It appears these men were captured before this specific expedition. **XYLANDER.**

*vol. II p. 332 line 21. the fruits of cones]* Xylander saw in the Lexicon that *konos* <note>original: κῶνος</note> can mean a "turning post in a courtyard" or "the fruit of pines" (pine cones); he chose the turning post for the wrestling ground, but in his ignorance, he allowed the horses of Theophylact to eat the fruit of the pines. **GOAR.**

*ibid. Thasian]* elsewhere called *leptokarya*, meaning Pontic nuts or hazelnuts. **GOAR.**

*vol. II p. 333 line 20. Domestic of the Church]* The catalog of officials by Codinus passes over this official: our author shows a double "Domestic," one for the "right choir" and one for the "left choir," meaning the *primary singer of the right and left choirs*, over whom is placed another "Domestic of the Psalm-singers," and above them all the *Protopsaltes* (Chief Singer). See the *Euchologion*. **GOAR.**

*vol. II p. 335 line 5. of the Western Romans]* The Greeks, as successors to the Roman Empire, have boasted of being "Romans" <note>original: Ῥωμαίους</note> even to this day. However, they call the true Romans—that is, the Latins—by Cedrenus's term "Western Romans." **GOAR.**

*ibid. line 6. John, son of Alberic]* This is Pope John XII.

vol. II p. 335 line 13. *he took a fourth wife* <note>original: τὴν τετάρτην ἠγάγετο γυναῖκα</note>] regarding the legality of these marriages see Arcudius <note>Peter Arcudius, a 17th-century theologian who sought to reconcile Greek and Latin traditions</note> in Book 7 of *The Harmony*. **Goar.**

vol. II p. 339 line 17. *to receive a prayer from one of the priests* <note>original: εὐχὴν παρά τινος τῶν ἱερέων λαβεῖν</note>] among the Greeks, monks are consecrated by the hand of a priest after a long series of preceding prayers, regarding which see the *Euchologion* <note>The primary liturgical prayer book of the Eastern Orthodox Church</note>. Those prayers render the profession of the monks solemn. See also Balsamon <note>Theodore Balsamon, a prominent 12th-century commentator on Byzantine canon law</note>. **Goar.**

vol. II p. 340 line 12. *with palisades and stakes* <note>original: σταυρώμασι καὶ πασσάλοις</note>] specifically, stakes fixed into the ground and joined very tenaciously to one another with wooden nails: for a *stauroma* is a *stake.* Hesychius <note>A 5th-century lexicographer</note> says: *stauroi* <note>original: σταυροὶ</note> are stakes driven down, poles, and all upright timbers, so named from "standing" or from standing in the open air. Eustathius <note>A 12th-century scholar and archbishop</note> says: *skolopes* <note>original: σκόλοπες</note> are upright and sharp pieces of wood, which they also called *stauroi*. **Goar.**

vol. II p. 344 line 5. *they ate meat* <note>original: ἐκρεωφάγουν</note>] an unspeakable crime for Greek monks, even for those who are ill. **Goar.**

vol. II p. 345 line 1. *three years*] in the Greek text it is "13" <note>original: ιγ'</note>. But that this is false is shown not only by Zonaras <note>Joannes Zonaras, a 12th-century chronicler</note>, but much more certainly by the logic of the dates. For if you compare this year with the year noted for the death of Constantine his father, you will find an interval of no more than three years. **Xyl.**

vol. II p. 346 line 15. *Methymna*] above, it was stated that he was in exile at Mitylene; either this is an error of the scribe, or in the meantime Stephen was moved from Mitylene to Methymna. Both cities are on the island of Lesbos. **Xyl.**

vol. II p. 347 line 3. *cometopoli*] they are so named as if they were "chicks" (that is, sons) of the count <note>The Cometopuli were a Bulgarian dynasty</note>. **Xyl.** The word *polos* <note>original: πῶλος, meaning foal or chick</note>, in the common tongue *poulos* <note>original: ποῦλος</note>, when added to another word signifies both "son" and a certain diminutive quality. Thus *archontopoulon* means "son of a noble," *basilopoulon* means "son of a king" or "little king," and finally the author calls the "sons of the count" *kometopoulous*; and as he adds, "the children of the counts who were very powerful in Bulgaria." Below on p. 694: "being children of a count and for this reason named *kometopouloi*." **Goar.**

vol. II p. 349 line 9. *for he was not fit*] in the margin: "Such also was that old man Andronicus who recently seized power." <note>This marginal note likely compares the historical figure to Andronicus I Komnenos</note>. Well known are the verses of Lucan <note>A Roman poet whose *Pharsalia* was often quoted by medieval scholars</note> regarding the common people, through which Bringas <note>Joseph Bringas, a 10th-century eunuch official</note> acted contrary to his own misfortune: "a hungry populace knows not how to fear." **Xyl.**

vol. II p. 352 line 6. *penalties for those marrying a second time* <note>original: ἐπιτίμια δευτερογαμούντων</note>] monogamy is praised by the Greeks, bigamy is tolerated and penalized, trigamy (a third marriage) is hated, and tetragamy (a fourth marriage) is utterly forbidden. To what penalty is bigamy <note>original: διγαμία</note> subjected? To a two-year deprivation of the sacraments; regarding which see Nicephorus in the Canons, Basil, the *Euchologion*, and the Greek canon lawyers. If you ask the reason: they restrain and punish lack of self-control. **Goar.**

*ibid.* line 20. *protopapas* <note>original: πρωτοπαπᾶς</note>] the *archpriest of the palace churches.* Xylander speaks of him impressively, making him the prince of the palace prelates. He acts as a strenuous defender of the title of "pontiff." **Goar.**

### ANNOTATIONS. 865

vol. II p. 355 line 12. *Known to Dandulphus*] The calculation of dates and certain other conjectures move me to believe this is the man whom our historians call Rudolph, King of Burgundy and of Italy against Berengar. You will find these and many other things among other writers, though not by chance. **XYL.** I would believe *Pandulpho* is the better reading, a name more common among the Latins. Baronius, in the years 957 and 968, drawing from the *Chronicle of the Lombard Princes of Benevento*, mentions Pandulf, prince of Capua and Benevento, who was a contemporary of Constantine VIII, Nicephorus Phocas, and his successor John Tzimiskes; he was called the "King of Lombardy" <note>original: ῥῆγα Λογγιβαρδίας</note> by the author for this reason, as he was still waging wars against the Greeks. **GOAR.**

vol. II p. 359 line 1. *Long John* <note>original: Μακροϊωάννην</note>] John, so called because of the tallness of his body. **GOAR.**

vol. II p. 362 line 6. *May be seen*] Much is missing. The scribe wrote: "one leaf is missing, and so it is also in the copy." These things can be recovered somehow from Zonaras <note>Joannes Zonaras, a 12th-century Byzantine chronicler and theologian</note>: for otherwise our author is more detailed in many places. **XYL.** We have supplemented this from Scylitzes <note>John Scylitzes, an 11th-century historian whose "Synopsis of Histories" covers the years 811–1057</note>. **GOAR.**

vol. II p. 364 line 22. For Anabarza I would read Anazarba. And "Drizium" in Zonaras is Drizibium. After the gap, there is a list of cities which Nicephorus recovered from the Hagarenes <note>original: Agarenis; a term used for Arabs or Muslims, referring to their traditional descent from Hagar</note> in that war. **XYL.**

vol. II p. 365 line 13. *Commander of the camp* <note>original: στρατοπεδάρχην</note>] The official in charge of those who measure the camp; the chief surveyor. **GOAR.**

vol. II p. 368 line 7. *To Taxeidium*] It seems to have been a place where the accounts of taxes or payments were kept. **XYL.** A *taxeidion* <note>original: ταξείδιον</note> is a voyage or a journey to be completed by sea, by which subjects are burdened; they welcome the Emperor who arrives unexpectedly, win him over with gifts, nourish his retinue, and even follow him with presents when he departs, thus being deprived of their own necessities of life. What Xylander brings forward regarding the *taxidion* is ridiculous. **GOAR.**

ibid. line 15. *Immovable goods*] Immovable <note>original: ἀκινήτοις</note>. I will not hide that I used this word deliberately, as it retains an ambiguity. For both lands are "immovable goods," and whatever is considered in that category: yet I think this is understood more regarding the "eternal donations," as they call them, which bind an heir to perpetual succession; it is not obscure that the goods called "ecclesiastical" have been increased by such things. I believe that man [Emperor Nicephorus Phocas], great in war, did not want one emperor to prescribe to his successors how much they should be forced to cut from their own treasury for this or that monastery, because "one does not eat measured portions" <note>original: οὐ σιτεῖται μετρούμενα; a Greek proverb suggesting that vital needs or great endeavors cannot be strictly rationed</note>. Therefore, if anyone wished to bestow something, he thought it better for it to be done without prescription and for the present (once for all, as they say). For I hardly believe he forbade anyone from donating land, especially a private citizen. But he saw that the "sacrificers" <note>Xylander uses this term dismissively for the clergy/monks</note>, relying on perpetual revenues, lived luxuriously. The reader may follow what he wishes. In general, however, all those who defended and increased the state in war but did not enrich the "sacrificers" are poorly spoken of among this type of historian. **XYL.**

vol. II p. 369 line 11. *The tetarteron* <note>original: τεταρτηρόν</note>] Zonaras writes that he [Nicephorus Phocas] reduced it to a *tetarteron* from a *hexagion* <note>A standard unit of weight/currency</note> or *sextula* (for I read it as *hexagion*). Which George Cedrenus <note>An 11th-century historian</note> says thus in volume II...

I understand that the ratio of the later coin to the earlier one was that of a *bessis* <note>original: "bessis", a Roman term for two-thirds of a unit</note> to an *as* <note>original: "assem", a whole unit of weight</note>, so that the larger was one and a half times the smaller. For just as the <term>exagion</term> <note>original: ἐξάγιον; a standard weight or coin</note> seems to be named from the number 6, so the <term>tetarteron</term> <note>original: τεταρτηρόν; a lightweight gold coin introduced by Nicephorus Phocas</note> seems named from 4. For instance, if the old coin weighed 6 obols, the new one weighed 4 obols. He seems to have used the word "exodus" <note>original: ἔξοδον</note> for "expense" twice in this passage. **XYL.**

vol. II p. 370 line 4. *For as predicted*] The scribe not ineptly added: "And yet he should rather have stayed outside the palace continuously because of this" <note>original: καὶ μὴν ἔδει μᾶλλον αὐτὸν διὰ τοῦτο διηνεκῶς τοῦ παλατίου διάγειν ἐκτός</note>. **XYL.**

ibid. line 10. *For with the wall completed*] These remarks pertain to Nicephorus, and are poorly connected with what preceded. **XYL.**

vol. II p. 379 line 4. *Of whom this fifth one*] This can in no way be true, since both were born to their father Romanos II <note>Byzantine Emperor, 959–963</note> before their mother Theophano married Emperor Nicephorus Phocas. From the notes of Panvinius <note>Onofrio Panvinio, a 16th-century historian renowned for his accuracy in chronology</note>, a man by far the most diligent and skilled, you can discover that Basil II was about 14 and Constantine VIII about 12 years old at the time when they were admitted into the partnership of the empire by Zimisces <note>John I Tzimiskes</note>. Their stepfather had excluded them from this partnership either because of their age, or at least they had possessed nothing but the name of emperor. For at the end of the section on Basil, Zonaras <note>a 12th-century chronicler</note> says they even reigned alongside Phocas. The accounts read at the beginning of their reign, which are much more suitable than these, support Panvinius; they are found in our author and have Zonaras as a witness. **XYL.**

ibid. line 7. <term>proedros</term> <note>original: πρόεδρον; literally "one who sits in the first seat"</note>] His duty toward the citizens and the state was not unlike that of the city prefect: for in the anonymous lexicon of the Royal Library he is called "the leader of the state, the guide, and the first" <note>original: ὁ τῆς πολιτείας ἀρχηγός, ἡγεμὼν καὶ πρῶτος</note>. Unless you would prefer to say he was the chief of the councils, since Constantine, son of Romanos, immediately at the start of his reign created three <term>proedroi</term> at once: the Domestic of the Schools, the Protovestiarius, and the Drungarius. He could have called them not to increase their offices, but to invite them into the more secret administration of business; and once the dignity was made common, he established the chief among them as <term>protoproedros</term> <note>original: πρωτοπρόεδρον; "first among the proedroi"</note>, as Curopalates <note>referring to a high court official or the historian George Codinus</note> and the *Greco-Roman Law* <note>original: Ius GR</note> establish. **GOAR.**

vol. II p. 380 line 16. *And that the volume was torn* <note>original: διαρραγῆναι δὲ καὶ τὸν τόμον</note>] This exists in the second book of the *Greco-Roman Law*, in which, following the decree that revoked the <term>Novels</term> <note>Novellae Constitutiones; new laws or amendments</note> of Nicephorus, a more sacred Novel of Basil the Porphyrogenitus <note>Basil II</note> is subjoined. **GOAR.**

vol. II p. 391 line 16. *He had been a duke* <note>original: dux fuisset</note>] The family of the Ducas is noble in these histories. But here I do not doubt it is the name of an office <note>The Latin "dux" could mean the title "Duke" or simply "military leader/general"</note>. For I do not think the Ducas and Phocas families were the same. Both elsewhere and at the beginning of the reign of Basil, son of Romanos, you will find this word used for "general." And again, he calls Theophylact Botaniates, the prefect of Thessaloniki, a <term>douka</term> <note>original: δοῦκα</note>, though elsewhere he is called a "ruler" <note>original: ἄρχοντα</note> and "general" <note>original: στρατηγόν</note>. Likewise, there were <term>doukas</term> <note>original: δούκας</note> of Antioch and Iberia during the reign of Constantine's brother. Furthermore, the word "uncle" <note>original: θεῖος; theios</note> both here and elsewhere means a father’s brother: for Leo the <term>curopalates</term> (a term I have discussed elsewhere) was the brother of Emperor Nicephorus Phocas and the son of Bardas Phocas, whom the father, once he became emperor, had created Caesar. **XYL.**

# ANNOTATIONS

**vol. II p. 391 line 22.** *military cloak* <note>original: "paludamento"</note>] The term "over-cloak" <note>original: ἐφεστρὶς; a Greek outer garment</note> is used here, which was also placed above for the saddle cloth used to cover a horse. I have not found much precision in the use of these words by this writer, and so I have translated such things rather freely. Furthermore, regarding these passages, "the West" should several times be understood as Constantinople and the territories in Europe that still submitted to it, while "the East" refers to the Asian provinces, lest any unskillful reader dream of Italy here. As for the fact that Theodora, the wife of John Tzimiskes, is called the daughter of Constantine (son of Leo) and sister of Romanos III by Cedrenus <note>George Kedrenos, an 11th-century historian</note>, the same is found almost identically in Zonaras <note>John Zonaras, a 12th-century chronicler</note>. Panvinius <note>Onofrio Panvinio, a 16th-century historian</note>, following other authors (I believe), makes her the daughter of Romanos II by Theophano Anastasia, and thus the sister of Basil II and Constantine VIII. **XYL.**

**vol. II p. 395 line 23.** *having scattered those who were there* <note>original: "dissipatis qui ibi"</note>] The scribe wrote these words in the margin: "I wonder if the barbarians did not then have a sturdy spear, by which they could have prevented such a person from making the ascent" <note>original: θαυμάζω εἴπερ οὐκ ἦν τότε τοῖς βαρβάροις δόρυ στιβαρόν, δι᾽ οὗ τὸν τοιοῦτον ἂν ἐκώλυσαν τῆς ἀναβάσεως</note>. This seems relevant because these narratives are certainly thin; such great deeds ought to be described more diligently through their circumstances, lest they appear to be fictions and follies. For while historical faith leaves no doubt that the courage of a single man often stands and triumphs against many enemies, for one man to climb a wall in the manner described here, while many armed enemies are looking down from above, seems to be "among the impossible things" <note>original: τῶν ἀδυνάτων</note>. It is likely, as Zonaras seems to hint, that he held a section of the wall in a place empty of defenders, as did others; then, having made an attack on the guards and routed them, he provided the rest with the opportunity to ascend. The story told below regarding Basil and the blinding of Ibatzes is not much more skillfully constructed; there, the perpetrator of such a deed was able to calm a hostile, armed, and roaring multitude with a wave of his hand and soften them with a speech—a crowd that usually will not even listen to a magistrate once it is stirred up. **XYL.**

**vol. II p. 397 line 16.** *of the Holy Resurrection* <note>original: τῆς ἁγίας ἀναστάσεως</note>] This word is not written in full, but the mark "S" shows that it should be read not as "Anastasia" (the name), but as "Resurrection" <note>original: ἀναστάσεως</note>. Thus, I have taken it to mean the Resurrection of Christ from the dead, especially since shortly thereafter the feast day of St. George is mentioned, which is usually not far after Easter. Our author mentions a male Anastasius and a female Anastasia elsewhere above. **XYL.** The Temple of Anastasia also gained fame through the miracle of the Resurrection <note>original: ἀναστάσεως</note>: hence the interchangeable use of both words; here it is taken for the Resurrection of Christ. See the author on Valentinian the Younger, page 315. **GOAR.**

**vol. II p. 402 v. 22.** <term>Monoxyla</term> <note>original: Μονόξυλα; "single-wood"</note> These are small boats or skiffs, hollowed out from a single thick tree trunk, so light that they can even be carried on shoulders. "Regarding the Russians coming from Russia with their single-log boats to Constantinople," as Constantine Porphyrogenitus discusses at length in *On Administering the Empire*, chapter 9. **GOAR.**

**vol. II p. 405 line 22.** *the [leader] of the Cretans of the palace* <note>original: ὁ τῶν κρητῶν τοῦ βασιλείου</note>] Either "Basileios" is the surname Kurupas and the word "Emir" <note>original: ἀμηρᾶ</note> has been omitted, or "Basileios" denotes the Emir himself. I believe the former is true. And later, "Emir" is added concerning the same person, with the name omitted. **XYL.** Setting aside Xylander’s conjectures and corruptions, I interpret these words thus: *when Anemas had seen him at the palace...* **GOAR.**

<meta>This page continues Jacques Goar’s scholarly annotations on the Byzantine histories, specifically focusing on military titles, court offices, and the symbolic regalia of the emperors. It provides linguistic and historical context for terms found in the main text of volume II.</meta>

# ANNOTATIONS

**vol. II p. 411 line 2. of the noble victors <note>original: "τῶν καλλινίκων"</note>]** The Greeks venerate two saints named Theodore with special devotion: one known as the General <note>original: "στρατηλάτην"; Stratelates</note>, and the other as the Recruit <note>original: "τύρωνα"; Tyron</note>. They used to invoke both in wars as defenders and champions, calling them "noble victors" <note>original: "καλλίνικον"</note>, and they carried their images painted on their banners. Codinus, chapter 6, number 22. **GOAR.**

**vol. II p. 414 line 2. letters in the Roman style <note>original: "γράμματα Ῥωμαϊστί"</note>]** While I was recently staying in the East, a bronze coin of this sort came into my hands—which was later transferred to the de Thou Museum <note>original: "Museum Thuanum"; the famous library and cabinet of Jacques Auguste de Thou</note>. Its wording is indeed Greek, but the characters are Latin—the "letters in the Roman style"—and they appear in this form: *Jesus Christus basileus basileon* <note>"Jesus Christ, King of Kings"</note>. **GOAR.**

**vol. II p. 415 line 9. of the eunuch]** Specifically the chamberlain <term>parakoimomenos: literally "one who sleeps beside" the imperial bedchamber, often the most powerful official in the court</term>, as was the custom for a Eunuch. **GOAR.**

**vol. II p. 417 line 17. the overseer and supervisor of the East]** Such a man as the Master of Offices of the East described by the commentator on the *Notitia Imperii* <note>a document detailing the administrative organization of the late Roman Empire</note> in chapter 62. **GOAR.**

**vol. II p. 418 line 12. to the rank of the generals <note>original: "στρατηλατῶν"</note>]** Their troop was assembled from men so distinguished, noble, and brave in military glory that every single one of them was considered a *stratelates*, or "Master of the Soldiers." **GOAR.**

**vol. II p. 420 line 8. the whip]** Xylander interprets this as the emperors instructing the grooms with whips. However, Codinus describes a double scepter in chapter 17, number 35: namely, a cross and a staff. He says: "In the right hand he holds the cross, and in the left hand he holds a staff" <note>original: "νάρθηκα"; narthex</note>. Both are scepters, and as the anonymous Lexicon in the Royal Library (930) states, "a scepter is a royal rod." Symeon, the Metropolitan of Thessalonica, asserts that the emperor carries the cross as a "demonstration of piety," and then adds that he also receives a staff "not heavy or hard, but light and soft, signifying a discipline of gentleness, not of anger or destruction, nor one that crushes and obliterates." This is the "imperial whip" shown to Bardas in a dream. **GOAR.**

**ibid. line 17. the syncellus <note>original: "ὁ σύγκελλος"</note>]** I have already explained in the notes on page 1 that the *syncellus* was originally a priest, a spiritual father, and a companion who shared the living quarters of the Patriarch. Over the course of years, examples of several men who were promoted from the rank of *syncellus* to the patriarchal throne show that he was regarded not only as a companion of the cell and residence, but as the designated successor to the Patriarch. Our author himself testifies to this in clear words later on page 775. Now, since this Stephanus was neither a successor to the throne, nor a cell-mate of the Patriarch—seeing as he resided as a prelate in Nicomedia as was customary—how does he bear the name and dignity of a *syncellus*? The Greeks have always sought honors immoderately; they frequently desired the title of a dignity to be granted to them even when they were not performing the duties of the office. Thus, as the Empire declined, there were entire cohorts of "Masters" where there had once been only one during the press of business in more vigorous times. As is often repeated in Codinus: "but the office is not actually exercised." Therefore, when the Patriarch died and many sought succession to the throne, many also strove to nourish their hope with the title of *syncellus*, or at least a vain desire for the honor... <meta>The text cuts off at the end of the page at the word "cupi-"</meta>

# THE ANNOTATIONS OF XYLANDER AND GOAR

...rank. From this come the swarms of syncelli <term>syncellus: literally "one who lives in the same cell"; a high-ranking confidential advisor to a bishop or patriarch</term>, and the title of "syncellus" was granted to prelates removed from the patriarch's household who were never heirs to the see. From the very origin of this name, he was accustomed to offer prayers for the patriarch in public church assemblies for many years, and to pronounce those words from the sacred sanctuary during the solemnities of the Mass by which the people are summoned to pray for the patriarch. For this reason, he was required to be a priest and to concelebrate with the patriarch. He was the same person as the **protosyncellus** <term>protosyncellus: the "first" or chief syncellus</term> in the Great Church <note>Hagia Sophia</note>, who performed this duty as the most distinguished of the syncelli, and he was known as the **patriarchal syncellus**. The others, who performed this duty in private churches, were left in the general crowd of syncelli once the name became common. I add also the spiritual fathers for confessions who accompanied the emperor everywhere and stayed in the palace (the inner and more secret chamber of which was called the *kellion* <note>original: "κελλίον"; cell or private room</note> according to Codinus); these men, like those of the chancellery, were honored with the title of syncelli. Phranzes is a witness to this when describing the retinue of John <note>Emperor John VIII Palaeologus</note> setting out for the Council of Florence. He says there were present with him **his own priests** (distinct from the patriarchal ones) and the spiritual father **Gregory, the great protosyncellus**. He is called "great" here to distinguish him from the other protosyncellus of the patriarch. Add to these the things to be read below on page 723, sections B and C, lest the word "syncellus," unknown to most, should cause a doubt that has not been resolved by what has been said. **GOAR.**

**vol. II p. 422 line 6. mercenary Saracens <note>original: "μισθοφόροις Σαρακηνοῖς"</note>]** This refers to those who, after peace was settled with them, were numbered among the *hetaireiai* <term>hetaireiai: the imperial bodyguard "companies," often composed of foreign mercenaries</term> of which the author speaks. **GOAR.**

**ibid. line 21. *Lapara*]** Our manuscript clearly has it this way. In Zonaras it is read as *Lipara*, which is a much more elegant word and harmonizes better with both the etymology and the Greek language. Unless perhaps the Cappadocians said *laparon* <note>meaning soft or loose</note> for what other Greeks called *liparon* <note>meaning oily, shining, or sleek</note>. But also, "Licandum" is written there with an *iota* <note>i</note>, while here it is with a *upsilon* <note>y</note>. **XYL.**

**vol. II p. 424 line 2. the Attalians <note>original: "Ἀτταλεῖς"</note>]** From Attalia, a city of Pamphylia, just like Cibyra in Asia Minor, famous for its naval power. **GOAR.**

**ibid. line 4. *with that very leader*]** This passage in the Greek is confused and defective, at least in my judgment. I have learned this from what follows: that this Kurtikes led the fleet of Durus, and was defeated in a naval battle by the imperial general Theodore. However, I am not certain whether the Cibyratae stood for Durus, or whether (as I thought) Durus ordered them to be attacked by the Emperor's fleet when it had gone over to Durus. **XYL.**

**ibid. line 13. having received <note>original: "δεξάμενον"</note>]** The translator writes "having received" <note>original: "δεξάμενος"; nominative case</note>; I retain "having received" <note>original: "δεξάμενον"; accusative case</note>. For the author himself referred "the receiving" <note>original: "τὸ δεξάμενον"</note> to John, just as he did "the shouting" <note>original: "τὸ βεβοημένον"</note>. **GOAR.**

**ibid.** *Dipotamum* seems to be so called because it was situated between two rivers, or rather at the confluence of two streams. **XYL.**

**vol. II p. 437 line 5. Contostephanus <note>original: "Κοντοστέφανον"</note>]** For *kontos* <note>original: "κοντός"</note> signifies "small, moderate, or short" to the Greeks. **GOAR.**

**vol. II p. 438 line 5. of the sphere <note>original: "τῆς σφαίρας"</note>]** That is, of the *Trullus* <note>the dome; often referring to the Council in Trullo</note>. **GOAR.**

**ibid. line 11. *and of no account*]** <note>original: "μηδ’ ἐν καιρὸς λογισάμενος μοίρᾳ"; literally "not even considered in the portion of the moment"</note>. In the margin it is noted that this is a proverb. It is said in this way regarding Aga-

### ANNOTATIONS

Regarding Memnon in Homer, Achilles says: "I value him at the worth of a hair." <note>original: "τίω δέ μιν ἐν καρὸς αἴσῃ." This is a famous phrase from the Iliad signifying something of no value.</note> Here some read "within the brain" <note>original: "ἐγκαρός"</note> as a single word. But I do not wish to bring here the various explanations of this saying, as they can be sought from the scholiast <note>an ancient commentator on a text</note>, Eustathius, and others. **Xylander**

Volume II, page 439, line 12. *from the Eastern Turks* <note>original: "ἀπὸ τῶν ἑῴων Τούρκων"</note>] from which the author explains that the Turks were rendered as "Orientals" on page 768. **Goar**

Volume II, page 446, line 7. *seiromasta*] a *seira* <note>original: "σειρά"</note> is a rope. But what a *seiromastes* <note>original: "σειρομάστης"</note> might be, I do not know. I had almost translated it as a "whip." **Xylander**
What a *seiromastes* is, Hesychius <note>a 5th-century Greek lexicographer</note> teaches: "a type of spear." Suidas: "a type of javelin." Tzetzes: "a javelin." We read in Numbers 25 that Phinehas killed the Israelite and the harlot who were shamefully coupled together with a *seiromastes*; for which Aquila <note>a translator of the Old Testament into Greek</note> uses "pole," Symmachus "spear," and the Vulgate "dagger." An anonymous Lexicon already cited elsewhere calls it "a type of javelin or spear." **Goar**

Same page, line 10. Regarding what is said about the "cross and the winnowing fan" as a sort of proverb, I suspect it has this meaning: that among those people, the cross was held as the most precious and holy of things, while the winnowing fan was considered common and cheap. Therefore, he compared the brothers—the abusive one to the fan, and the modest one to the cross—because there is no religious restriction preventing both from being made from the same wood, as per the well-known divine sentiment of the prophet. **Xylander**
Xylander has captured the sense, but not the actual words of the proverb. For what is so cheap about a winnowing fan, or what is so foreign to the cross that it should hold the extreme opposite position when speaking of value? Yet it certainly holds that position if taken in the true sense of a "wooden shovel" <note>original: "batillo"</note> with which earth, rubble, and filth are usually moved or carried out. That this sense was held from of old is witnessed by the *Euchologium* <note>a primary prayer book of the Eastern Orthodox Church</note> in the office for the dead, where the priest, about to cast earth upon the corpse, is read to take up a "winnowing shovel" <note>original: "πτυόν"</note> and sprinkle the earth with it. Modern speakers pronounce it "ptyarion" or, more corruptly, "ptyari." Thus the anonymous Lexicon in the Royal Library defines "ptyon" as "ptyarion." **Goar**

Volume II, page 447, line 7. *being occupied in* <note>original: "ἐνασχολούμενοι"</note>] this word must be retained despite Xylander’s objection, and the version corrected in this way: *those who, being accustomed to and practiced in rebellions, given the opportunity, etc.* **Goar**

Same page, line 18. *by his brother David*] the word "brother" <note>original: "ἀδελφόν"</note> is missing: but both the context suggested this and Zonaras <note>a 12th-century Byzantine historian</note> has it. From this passage it appears that these petty kings, or lords of the regions neighboring the Romans <note>the Byzantines called themselves Romans</note>, are called <term>curopalatas: "guardian of the palace," a high-ranking Byzantine title often given to neighboring princes</term>, and above also mention was made somewhere of a "curopalates of Iberia" <note>an ancient kingdom in what is now Georgia</note>. **Xylander**

Volume II, page 448, line 17. *lest power multiply*] I think, rather than know, that this is the sense of the law by which the excessive power of private individuals was restrained, who were bringing even public goods into their own possession. This, I think, was "to increase in a mass of villages" <note>original: "ἐν ὁμάδι χωρίων αὐξάνεσθαι"</note>, continually adding some estates to others. We see that this Maleinus <note>a member of the powerful Maleinos family of Byzantine landholders</note> did this, and Tzimiscas <note>Emperor John I Tzimiskes</note> had noted it to his own misfortune in the case of Basil the chamberlain. If anyone brings forward a better explanation, we shall offer him not just a tuft of grass but a crown—not as to a victor, but as to one who has served well. **Xylander**
I, being one who intends to serve Xylander well (since he promises gratitude in his annotations), say that the Emperor ordained by this law—not as Xylander himself writes, *that the power of private individuals should bring public goods into their own possession while adding estates to others*—but rather that public magistrates, while performing their office, should not take the goods of private individuals even when given...
