<meta>This page continues the philological and historical commentary by Wilhelm Xylander and Jacques Goar on a Byzantine chronicle. The previous page discussed the meaning of "seiromastes" (a type of spear or javelin) and the "cross and winnowing fan" proverb. This page focuses on legal terms, titles of nobility, and specific historical events during the reign of Emperor Basil II.</meta>

->XYLANDER AND GOAR<-

...they might obtain property for themselves at a low price and from there easily amass and join one estate to another. Blastares <note>Matthew Blastares, a 14th-century monk who compiled a major collection of Byzantine laws</note>, in chapter 4 of the letter "A" <note>Byzantine legal codes were often organized alphabetically; here, under the letter Alpha</note>, refers to this from the civil laws regarding buying and selling <note>original: "περὶ ἀγορᾶς καὶ πράσεως"</note>: "A person holding office in a province cannot buy movable or immovable property in it, either by himself or through another, except from the public treasury. For he both loses the property and does not recover the price paid." **GOAR**

Volume II, page 451, line 16. *prevented by his death*] I do not doubt that this passage is defective. I conjecture the meaning was that the betrayal of Dyrrachium <note>a strategic coastal city in modern Albania, then a key Byzantine theme</note> did not succeed because of the premature death of Chryselius. But you might easily judge that Basil [II] had taken possession of it from what follows, as when Basil is said to have set out for the purpose of defending Dyrrachium from John, and was informed of the death of John, who was killed there, by the patrician Pegonita, etc. **XYLANDER**
Nothing here is defective or mutilated to one who perceives the sense: the condition was that if only he [Chryselius] were elevated to patrician honors, which same dignity his two sons would also obtain once he was snatched from the living. On this condition, Chryselius was betraying Dyrrachium to the emperor. **GOAR**

Same page, line 18. *the mute* <note>original: "ὁ βουβός"</note>] This is how the Greeks call the stammering and the mute. **GOAR**

Same page, line 21. *Pedias* signifies a "plain" <note>level ground</note>. But I suspected it might be a proper name. He calls *illustres* <note>original: "ἰλλουστρίους"</note> those who, as the empire declined, were usually called "illustrious men," just as they were called "respectable," "most distinguished," etc. The matter is well known, and our author himself added an explanation of the word. **XYLANDER**
I interpret *illustres* <note>original: "ἰλλούστριοι"</note> here as "nobles." The author supports this by following up and calling these illustrious men "those who have distinguished themselves in military commands" <note>original: "στρατηγικαῖς ἀρχαῖς διαπρέψαντας"</note>. This is supported by the Glosses on the *Basilika* <note>a massive 9th-century codification of Byzantine law</note>, which explain "illustrious" as "noble" <note>original: "εὐγενῆ"</note>. Blastares confirms this in chapter 17 of the letter "A," calling a noblewoman an *illustria* <note>original: "ἰλλούστριαν"</note>: "the noblewoman having legitimate and illegitimate children." **GOAR**

Volume II, page 454, line 2. *privatarii* <note>original: "πριβαταρίων"</note>] What this is, I have not yet learned. What if it were something similar to those called "prebendaries" <note>clergy receiving a stipend from church lands</note> today? Nor am I unaware that 'b' is often used for 'v,' so that you might read *privatarum* <note>referring to private property</note>, which is just as familiar to me. **XYLANDER**
Just as the emperor had a "count of private affairs" <note>the *comes rerum privatarum*</note> and a private treasury, later called the "prefect of the private treasury," so also the church had its own curators, defenders, stewards, and as the author says, *privatarii*, the overseers of the treasury. **GOAR**

Volume II, page 455, line 1. *Dormition of the Mother of God* <note>original: "κοίμησις τῆς Θεοτόκου"</note>] This seems to be the Assumption <note>the feast of Mary being taken into heaven</note>, unless it is something else: for I have nothing to affirm. See below in the history of Ibatzes for what might help in understanding this passage. *It was somewhat not unlike our church-consecration festivals.* **XYLANDER**

Same page, line 10. *ruler of Antioch* <note>original: "ἄρχοντα Ἀντιοχείας"</note>] Previously he had called him "Duke" <note>original: "δοῦκα"</note>. **GOAR**

Volume II, page 456, line 5. *Allelengyum* <note>a controversial tax policy enacted by Basil II, requiring the wealthy to pay the tax debts of the poor</note>] In the margin the scribe wrote: <margin>Oh, what a marvelous invention!</margin> <note>original: "ὢ τῆς θαυμαστῆς ἐπινοίας"</note>. If these words are correct as written, he seems to marvel at such a subtle method of exaction, by which satisfaction would be made even for those who were hindered by extreme poverty or lost property...

### ANNOTATIONS

...even so, the dead were unable to pay. But it is clear from the history of Justinian that Basil did not discover this. I will not deprive the reader of what he adds soon after, where the intercessors for the pontiff are said to have suffered a rejection: <note>original Latin: "etiam ita mortui solvere nequirent..."</note> "But my Emperor Isaac Angelus, without anyone asking, shook off many of the irrational burdens of the Roman land." <note>original Greek: "ἀλλ᾿ ὁ ἐμὸς βασιλεὺς Ἰσαάκιος ὁ ἄγγελος μηδενὸς παρακαλέσαντος πολλὰ τῶν παραλόγων βαρῶν τῆς Ῥωμαίων γῆς ἐξετίναξεν." Isaac II Angelos reigned 1185–1195 and was known for popular tax remissions.</note> **XYLANDER**

Volume II, page 459, line 13. *The Dema tower in the pass* <note>original: "Δέμα turris ἐν κλεισούρᾳ"</note>], in an enclosure or *wall* <note>original Latin: "muro"</note> erected between two rugged mountains, the approach to which is here called a "little key" <note>original Greek: "κλειδίον," referring to a strategic mountain pass or fort</note> in various places. **GOAR**

Volume II, page 462, line 14. *with golden letters* <note>original Greek: "χρυσίοις γράμμασι"</note>] that is, a *chrysobull* <note>original Greek: "χρυσοβούλλῳ"; an official decree from the Byzantine emperor with a gold seal attached</note>. **GOAR**

Volume II, page 464, line 6. *into Chazaria* <note>original Greek: "εἰς Χαζαρίαν"</note>] situated toward the land of the Alans and the Tanais <note>the Don River</note>. **GOAR**

In the same place, line 9. *who [married] the sister of Emperor Basil*] In the Greek, it says "brother" <note>original Greek: "ἀδελφοῦ"</note>, which strangely obscures the passage. Looking at the history, I have provided clarity. He is speaking of Vladimir, Prince of the Russians <note>Vladimir the Great, who converted to Christianity</note>, who, as Kedrenos showed above, had the sister of Emperor Basil as his wife. <note>Anna Porphyrogenita, whose marriage was a condition of Vladimir’s baptism.</note> **XYLANDER**

Volume II, page 466, line 12. *bexite* <note>original Greek: "βεξείτε"</note>] I believe this word means "flee." The circumstances a little earlier suggest this. **XYLANDER**
In Latin words, or rather Italian, *fugite o Caesar* <note>"Flee, O Caesar!"</note>, with the pronunciation proper to those same Italians. <note>This refers to a famous linguistic moment in 587 CE where a soldier shouted "Torna, torna, fratre," often cited as an early specimen of a Romance language / Balkan Latin.</note> **GOAR**

Volume II, page 468, line 9. *which city is the head*] The words do not cohere at all, and I have little doubt that the passage is mutilated. Regarding what it says of the city, I conjecture it to have been Strumpitza <note>modern Strumica in North Macedonia</note>. Moreover, I think he calls that region "Ionian" which overlooks the Adriatic Sea, due to its proximity. **XYLANDER**
The words do not cohere at all, says Xylander. Rather, the translator does not cohere with the author! Therefore, after these words, let "the city of Ochrid" <note>original Greek: "πόλις δὲ Ἀχρὶς"</note> be inserted as a parenthesis, the end of which is at "near the fortress of Elissos" <note>original Greek: "περὶ τὸ Εἰλισσὸν τὸ φρούριον"</note>: then nothing mutilated or obscure remains. "The city of Ochrid is the metropolis of all Bulgaria." <note>original Greek: "πόλις δὲ Ἀχρὶς μητρόπολίς ἐστι τῆς πάσης Βουλγαρίας."</note> This is that most famous Justiniana Prima, the homeland of Justinian, which was elevated above most other cities in both ecclesiastical and political matters. Concerning which, see Gregoras, Book 2; Justinian himself in the *Novellae* 2; Cuiacius’s notes on him; and all geographers. **GOAR**

Volume II, page 475, line 13. *with a golden crown* <note>original Greek: "στεφάνῳ χρυσῷ"</note>] This crown is the *victory crown* <note>original Greek: "τροπαιουχία," a crown of triumph</note> of Codinus, in the judgment of Coresius of Chios; an ornament of triumphant emperors. **GOAR**

Volume II, page 476, line 2. *being the first of the elders of the church in the palace* <note>original Greek: "πρῶτος ὢν τῶν πρεσβυτέρων τοῦ ἐν τοῖς βασιλείοις ναοῦ"</note>] whom the author previously called the *Chief Priest of the Palace* <note>original Greek: "πρωτοπαπᾶν τοῦ παλατίου"</note>; about whom I have already written abundantly. **GOAR**

Volume II, page 477, line 3. *of Abasgia* <note>original Greek: "Ἀβασγίας"</note>] A Scythian province in Asia, neighboring the Iberians <note>Caucasian Iberia, roughly modern Georgia</note>. **GOAR**

In the same place, line 5. *but two* <note>original Latin: "at 2"</note>] Something is missing before these words, namely the mention of Xiphias <note>Nikephoros Xiphias</note>, who joined himself as an ally in the rebellion of Phokas <note>Nikephoros Phokas Barytrachelos</note>; which the following text shows. Otherwise, the "they" <note>original Greek: "οἱ δέ"</note> and other plural forms cannot refer to Phokas alone. **XYLANDER**

<meta>This page continues the philological and historical commentary by Jacques Goar and Wilhelm Xylander on the works of George Kedrenos. The notes focus on administrative titles, geography of the islands near Constantinople, and specific textual corrections regarding the transition of power and court appointments in the Byzantine Empire.</meta>

# COMMENTARY BY XYLANDER AND GOAR

Volume II, page 478, line 1. **Protonotary** <note>original Greek: "πρωτονοτάριον"</note>] whom the *Register of Offices* <note>original Latin: "Notitia imperii"; a document from the late Roman Empire detailing administrative organization</note> calls the **chief of the notaries** <note>original Latin: "primicerium notariorum"</note>; concerning the insignia and privileges of this office, see Panciroli in his *Commentary*. **GOAR**

In the same place, line 2. **At the island of Antigone** <note>original Greek: "τῇ νήσῳ τοῦ Ἀντιγόνου"</note>] situated near Constantinople, between the islands of Prote and Plate <note>islands in the Princes' Islands chain in the Sea of Marmara</note>. **GOAR**

Volume II, page 479, line 7. **Being the Duke of Thessalonica** <note>original Greek: "δουκὸς ὄντος Θεσσαλονίκης"</note>] In these times, Thessalonica had a duke; as the empire's power decreased, the prestige of these titles was increased to compensate. **GOAR**

Volume II, page 483, line 6. Panciroli, in his *Notes on the Empire* (chapter 47), contends that this is the province of the **Bucellarians** <note>original: "Bucellariorum"; a military district or "Theme" in Asia Minor</note>. Rigaltius, in his *Tactical Lexicon*, denies this and suggests they were the managers, providers, and carriers of the **rations** <note>original: "Bucellarum," referring to the soldier's biscuit or hardtack</note>. I more willingly agree with the former: for the leaders of the armies used to assign Galatians and Gallogreeks to this duty; thus it happened that the grain ministers, the **Galatian Bucellarians**, seem to have given the name of their office to their homeland. **GOAR**

In the same place, line 9. **At the island of Oxeia** <note>original Greek: "Ὀξείᾳ νήσῳ"</note>] a small island in the Sea of Marmara <note>original Latin: "Propontidis"</note>. Plate is indeed the third island from Constantinople heading south in that same sea. **GOAR**

In the same place, line 16. **Of Zacharias** <note>original Greek: "Ζαχαρίας"</note>] Before the word "Zacharias," the letter *a* is written, and above it something not unlike the letter *ch*, with a grave accent. Perhaps the scribe intended to express the word **governor** <note>original Greek: "ἄρχοντα," transliterated "archonta"</note> with that mark, which I did not fully understand. It would then mean "To Zacharias the governor." I have omitted this in my translation. **XYLANDER**

Volume II, page 484, line 19. **Throughout the Armeniac region** <note>original Greek: "κατὰ τὸν Ἀρμενιακόν"</note>] Zonaras <note>a 12th-century Byzantine chronicler</note> records this as "in the **Theme** of the Armeniacs," that is, in the province of Armenia that was subject to the Romans. And thus, later on, "Armeniac" is used for the province of Armenia in the account of the plague under Romanos Argyros. **XYLANDER**

Volume II, page 485, line 10. **From the daughter of a patrician** <note>original Latin: "ex filia patricii"</note>] A name has been lost here: in Zonaras, the name is Alypius. He also calls Argyros "Argyropoulos," which is to say, the son of Argyros: in the same way that "Comitopouloi" was used above for the sons of the Bulgarian Count. Regarding the death of Constantine VIII, the scribe added, not without reason: "You did well, Constantine, by departing so quickly from among men"; for those who live as he did bring nothing but the greatest evils to the state. **XYLANDER**

In the same place, line 17. **He is hallowed** <note>original Greek: "ἱερολογεῖται"</note>] He is joined together by the **sacred nuptial blessing**. **GOAR**

Volume II, page 486, line 13. **The blood-relative of the patriarch** <note>original Latin: "consanguineum patriarchae"; original Greek: "ὁμαίμονα"</note>] This word is usually used by these writers to mean "brother," just as Virgil said "Sleep, the **blood-relative of Death**," mirroring Homer’s "there he met Sleep, the **brother of Death**." For the word "renewed" <note>original Greek: "ἐκαίνησε"</note>, I have read "emptied" <note>original Greek: "ἐκένωσε"</note>, following the general sense of the passage. Whether **Zostica** is a proper name, or (as I suspect) refers to the office of the **Girded Lady** <note>original: "Zostae"; referring to the "Zoste Patrikia," the highest court title for women</note>, is unclear. **XYLANDER**

Volume II, page 487, line 11. The **synthronos** <note>original Greek: "σύνθρονος"</note> is a series of seats against the wall in a curve around the altar; if you like, a row of seats in the choir where the bishop sits with his priests, or the patriarch with his bishops. Thus the *Prayer Book* <note>original: "Euchologium"</note> calls it the **consession** and the **sharing of the same throne**. In this place, the *syncelli* <note>advisors/cell-mates of a bishop</note> (as well as certain **chosen** <note>original Greek: "ἔκκριτοι"</note> deacons, who were clerics or officials of the Great Church, about whom the *Graeco-Roman Law* speaks abundantly) not only hold a seat...

# ANNOTATIONS. 875

But they also attempted with all their desires, force, and influence to seize precedence over other priests and bishops (imitating the Roman cardinals who, in regard to this privilege of honor, are ranked above bishops). See the mentioned volume of *Greek Law*, the section on the **Chartophylax** <note>The archivist and registrar of the Great Church in Constantinople</note>, and in the *Novels* <note>New laws issued by an emperor</note> of Alexius Comnenus. **GOAR**.

Vol. II, p. 488, line 3. **To Mount Athos** <note>original Greek: "τῷ ὄρει τῷ Ἄθῳ"</note>] named the **Holy Mountain** <note>original Greek: "ἁγίου ὄρους"</note> in later centuries due to the astonishing number of monks and monasteries located there. **GOAR**.

In the same place, line 7. **Petrion** <note>original Greek: "Πετρίον"</note>] a monastery. **GOAR**.

Vol. II, p. 494, line 12. **Telouch** <note>original Greek: "Τελούχ"</note>] a region and city near Mount Taurus. Ortelius <note>Abraham Ortelius, the 16th-century cartographer</note> citing Curopalates <note>A high-ranking Byzantine court official and historian</note>. **GOAR**.

Vol. II, p. 495, line 3. **Of Mistheia** <note>original Greek: "Μισθείας"</note>] a city in Galatia. **GOAR**.

In the same place, line 13. **General-autocrat** <note>original Greek: "στρατηγὸν αὐτοκράτορα"</note>] the commander and supreme leader of the army. Synesius in his oration *On Kingship*: "make yourselves autocrats." For "autocrat" is a title of generalship that implies the authority to do all things. Both Iphicrates and Pericles sailed from Athens as **generals-autocrat**. **GOAR**.

Vol. II, p. 497, line 15. **Capitals of the columns** <note>original Latin: "capita columnarum"</note>] this passage is not of the highest importance and is somewhat obscure. I translated **column-capitals** <note>original Greek: "κιονόκρανα"</note> as "capitals of the columns," **plaster** <note>original Greek: "χρίσμα"</note> as "incrustation" or "plasterwork," and **painted** <note>original Greek: "ὑλογραφικόν"</note> as "painted with colors." I have not followed the literal meaning of the words too anxiously, nor would I claim to have understood everything perfectly. **XYLANDER**. I interpret **the plaster of the wall** <note>original Greek: "τὸ τοῦ τείχου χρίσμα"</note> as the face of the wall coated with silver leaf in a painterly manner, for "plaster" <note>original: "chriama"</note> belongs to painters, not silversmiths; nor does anyone record the Church of Blachernae <note>A famous imperial shrine to the Virgin Mary in Constantinople</note> being covered in silver plates. **GOAR**.

Vol. II, p. 498, line 17. **To the bishop Peritheorius** <note>original Latin: "episcopo Peritheorio"</note>] or "of Peritheorium." For the word is ambiguous as to whether it is the name of a place or a man. **XYLANDER**. It is the name of a city, not a man, according to Ortelius. Therefore, it should be translated as **the bishop of Peritheorium**. **GOAR**.

In the same place, line 20. That detail concerning the brother of Emperor Michael is not without reason suspected. I see no other conclusion to draw than that he was the brother of Michael the Paphlagonian, who held the empire after this Romanus; you should understand the phrase **having reigned** <note>original Greek: "βεβασιλευκότος"</note> in respect to the author’s perspective, not that of Romanus, as I have expressed. **XYLANDER**.

In the same place, line 22. **Thrown among the self-killers** <note>original Greek: "ῥιφεὶς μετὰ τῶν αὐτοφόνων"; likely referring to those who died by suicide or in fratricidal conflict</note>] in the hunt <note>original Greek: "ἐν τῷ κυνηγίῳ"</note>. Suidas <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note>. **GOAR**.

Vol. II, p. 499, line 18. **Honoriada** <note>original Greek: "Ὀνωριάδα"</note>] another Asian region in Pontus. Ortelius. **GOAR**.

Vol. II, p. 503, line 4. **Pegonites** <note>original Greek: "πηγονίτης"</note>] one whose chin is rather broad. **GOAR**.

Vol. II, p. 504, line 3. I interpret **channels** <note>original Greek: "ὁλκούς"</note> as underground conduits or even upright tubes in aqueducts for water brought from a distance; I interpret **castles** <note>original Greek: "καστέλλους"; referring to "castellum aquae" or distribution tanks</note> as the actual arches and bridges of the aqueducts over which the water flows. **GOAR**.

# NOTES BY XYLANDER AND GOAR. 876

Vol. II, p. 504, line 5. **Hospitals for the maimed** <note>original Greek: "λωβοτροφεῖα"</note>] Perhaps these are what we call leper colonies or lazarettos, in which lepers are maintained. It is common for the word **maiming** <note>original Greek: "λώβην"</note> to be used specifically for leprosy <note>original Latin: "κατ' ἐξοχήν"</note>, as I have noted elsewhere. **XYLANDER**.

*In the same place, line 14.* **The art of the charlatan** <note>original Greek: "ἀγυρτικὴν τέχνην"</note>] I truly do not understand this. For this John was a chamberlain, unless perhaps he had previously made a living as a traveling street-peddler. **XYLANDER**. These are the "circulators" or "itinerant physicians," known as **periodoi** <note>original Greek: "περιοδευταί"; literally "those who go around," referring to traveling healers</note>, who run here and there to offer cures, wandering about and carrying snakes and poisons; they promise to bring remedies for every kind of disease with a chattering swarm of words. It was from them that the emperor’s **hair-loss condition** <note>original Greek: "τριχόρροια"</note> originated. **GOAR**.

*In the same place, line 22.* I do not know what the office of the **Prefect of the Pantheon** was. It seems to be the guardianship of some temple. **XYLANDER**. The **Pantheotai** were military attendants, joined with the trumpeters around the emperor’s table. Their troop was called the **Pantheon**, according to the anonymous works of Rigaltius and Meursius <note>Nicolas Rigault and Johannes Meursius, 17th-century classical scholars</note>. **GOAR**.

Vol. II, p. 505, line 10. **The distribution** <note>original Greek: "τὴν διανομήν"</note>] This distribution of gifts or stipends—performed in his presence by the emperor’s own hand with solemn preparation on the Eve of Palms <note>Palm Sunday</note>—is described by Liutprand in Book 6 <note>Liutprand of Cremona, a 10th-century bishop and historian</note>. Balsamon <note>Theodore Balsamon, a 12th-century canonist</note> complains in a small work found in Book 7 of *Greco-Roman Law* that he earned nothing from it. **GOAR**.

*In the same place, line 13.* Regarding the death of Romanos, the scribe noted: <note>original Greek: "σημείωσαι δὲ ἐνταῦθα καὶ τὸ τοῦ θεολόγου λέγοντος “πῶς γὰρ σώσει ἡ ἀλλοτρία, ὃν ἡ ἰδία ἀπώλεσεν;”"</note> "Note here also the saying of the Theologian <note>Saint Gregory of Nazianzus</note>: 'For how shall a stranger's soul save him whom his own soul has destroyed?'" I do not see to what he refers or what it has to do with this matter. For Helena, the wife of Argyros, is certainly beyond blame; as much as was in her power, she voluntarily released her husband, preserved the marriage, and he owed both his eyes and his empire to her. But in this Romanos, it is apparent how much he is disapproved of by God, since his own ordinances are violated under whatever pretext of necessity. **XYLANDER**.

Vol. II, p. 506, line 1. **Of the Peribleptos** <note>original Greek: "τῆς περιβλέπτου"; meaning "The Admired" or "The Illustrious"</note>] Unless this is a proper name, which I do not think, the name of the holy woman in whose honor he founded the monastery is missing. But further down, in the section on Calaphates, mention is made of the **Monastery of the Peribleptos** <note>A famous Byzantine monastery in Constantinople</note>, not far from the Sigma <note>A C-shaped portico or district in Constantinople</note>. Furthermore, this Emperor Michael was a Paphlagonian; in the margin he has the epithets **sold for silver** <note>original Greek: "ἀργυροπράτου"</note> and **possessed by a demon** <note>original Greek: "δαιμονίῳ κατόχου"</note>, as Cedrenus later relates that he was occupied by an evil spirit. **XYLANDER**.

Vol. II, p. 508, line 20. **Of the Varangians** <note>original Latin: "Barangorum"</note>] It appears from Choniates <note>Niketas Choniates, the historian</note> that these were the bodyguards or attendants of the emperor in war, who carried double-axes. Hence, the scribe shows at the beginning of the *Stratiotikon* <note>A military treatise</note>—where they are mentioned—that he either does not know who they were or at least wants them to be explained. **XYLANDER**.

*In the same place, line 23.* **The man’s scimitar**] Was it her husband’s or the Varangian’s? **XYLANDER**.

Vol. II, p. 509, line 4. **Those who commit suicide**] I have translated it thus, because I do not think this condition was imposed on everyone who died a violent death. But that man had brought destruction upon himself. **XYLANDER**.

*In the same place, line 10.* **Not a dream, but a waking reality** <note>original Greek: "οὐκ ὄναρ ἀλλ᾽ ὕπαρ"</note>] From Homer’s *Odyssey*, Book 19, line 549. **XYLANDER**.

<meta>This page continues the philological and historical annotations on the Byzantine historical texts (specifically George Kedrenos). # ANNOTATIONS.

Vol. II, p. 512, line 1. **Fortified places** <note>original Greek: "κάστρα"</note>] The translator [renders this as] *citadels*. *Cities* is more appropriate; for the author very frequently calls cities **castra** <note>originally "κάστρα"; while this looks like the Latin for camp, in later Greek it often referred to a fortified city</note>. This is how Benevento, Capua, and Bari were referred to in previous sections. **GOAR.**

*In the same place, line 11. Aspracania*] Thus several times above. For here **Baspracania** <note>original Greek: "Βασπρακανία"</note> is read, or *Baaspracania*, the second being surely an error. Certainly in the history of Monomachos and in our author it is *Baspracan*, and in Zonaras it is called Media with the doubled 'a' as *Baaspracan*; and it is also read thus in Cedrenus hereafter, as *Baaspracania*. The **orphanotrophos** <note>original Greek: "ὀρφανοτρόφος"; the high official in charge of the Great Orphanage of Constantinople</note> is John, the emperor’s brother, as he was called above. **XYLANDER.**

Vol. II, p. 516, line 6. **The Mandylion** <note>original Greek: "μανδύλιον"</note>] Commonly called a **sudarium** <note>sweat-cloth</note> or **hand-towel**. The author recently called it the **holy shroud** <note>original Greek: "ἅγιον ἐκμαγεῖον"; literally "holy wiping-cloth," a reference to the Image of Edessa</note> on page 735. The anonymous Lexicon in the Royal Library defines **mandylion** as a **hand-cloth**. **GOAR.**

*In the same place, line 6. The Grand Domestic* <note>original Greek: "ὁ μέγας δομέστικος"</note>] This is read here for the first time in this author; under him served others **of the East, the West, and the Thracians** <note>original Greek: "τῶν ἀνατολικῶν, τῶν δυτικῶν καὶ τῶν Θρᾳκησίων"; referring to the regional commanders of the Byzantine army</note>. **GOAR.**

*In the same place, line 7.* **A letter** <note>original Greek: "ἐπιστολήν"</note>] An **autograph** <note>original Greek: "ἰδιόγραφον"; a document written in the sender's own hand</note>. The author says this in the same place. **GOAR.**

*In the same place, line 10.* **A prayer** <note>original Greek: "λιτήν"</note>] Xylander, in a heretical and ambiguous manner, renders this as *punishment*; clearly and in the Catholic sense, it is a **procession**. **GOAR.** <note>Goar frequently corrects Xylander's Protestant interpretations of liturgical Greek.</note>

Vol. II, p. 521, line 7. 47] Contrary to the reliability of the Greek manuscript (for it clearly has 40), I have written it this way, following the sequence of years and indeed of the **indictions** <note>a 15-year cycle used for dating and taxation</note>, as the reader will easily notice. **XYLANDER.**

*In the same place, line 14.* What the **aerikon** <note>original Greek: "ἀερικόν"</note> might be—which I have expressed literally as "pertaining to the air"—I do not understand, nor do I know what weight or currency this sign "2" denotes. **XYLANDER.** <note>The *aerikon* was a notorious and somewhat mysterious tax levied by Byzantine emperors.</note>

*In the same place, line 20.* **He was baptizing**] I do not think he was baptizing them himself, but rather that he was acting as a godfather <note>original Latin: "de sacro fonte suscipiebat"; literally "receiving from the sacred font"</note>, which he judged to be a work of no small piety, and by which he hoped to obtain healing from God. I thought it should be noted in passing that in this and the following section, there are very many things that do not quite agree between our author and Zonaras. But since both will now be in the hands of men [readers], it is not our place to crowd them onto these pages. **XYLANDER.**

Vol. II, p. 527, line 10. **To the Kral** <note>original Greek: "τῷ κράλῃ"</note>] Xylander [renders this as] *jurisdiction*; more truly, it is **to the king**. *Kral* in the Bulgarian language means **king**. **GOAR.**

Vol. II, p. 528, line 6. **Armaments** <note>original Greek: "ἅρματα"</note>] It now signifies **arms** [weapons], not **chariots**. **GOAR.**

Vol. II, p. 529, line 25. **Koutzomytes** <note>original Greek: "κουτζομύτης"</note>] **Flat-nosed**. **GOAR.**

Vol. II, p. 535, line 15. **Nobelissimos** <note>original Greek: "νωβελίσσιμον"</note>] In the time of Constantine the Great, there were three primary titles: Augustus, Caesar, and *Nobilissimus* [Most Noble]. The Augustus was the emperor; the Caesar was the successor to the empire; the *Nobilissimus* was cherished by the hope of eventually obtaining the name of Caesar. Hence, only the sons or primary relatives of the last emperors are read as being adorned with that title while the empire flourished. More on the *nobilissimus* can be found in Trivorius, *Apologetic Observations*, chapter 10. **GOAR.**

Vol. II, p. 536, line 21. **Report** <note>original Greek: "ἀναφορά"</note>] The translator renders this as a *relation* [report], because it is directed to the people. I might also call it a **decree, issued by the emperor**. It is more aptly rendered as a **book of apology and a proven defense of the deed**. **GOAR.**

# THE ANNOTATIONS OF XYLANDER AND GOAR

Vol. II, p. 537, line 7. **Cross-trampler** <note>original Latin: "stauropatam"</note>] From where he obtained this name, I do not quite follow. It sounds like "one who tramples the cross." But whether this was considered a specifically impious status here, I am not certain. **XYLANDER.** When a person is about to make a public oath, he touches **the precious wood, the venerable cross** <note>original Greek: "τὰ τίμια ξύλα, crucem venerandam"</note>; in private, he displays some cross, or forms one with his index fingers crossed, and kisses it while swearing by it. When confirming or promising something in writing, he places a cross at the top of the paper as a symbol of his oath, as discussed previously. Hence, any perjurer who pledges his faith by drawing or making a cross is considered not merely to have trampled his word, but the cross itself—to have scorned and spat upon it as a **cross-trampler** <note>original Greek: "σταυροπάτης"</note>. Leo the Grammarian says: *He treated with contempt the perjurers and cross-tramplers.* <note>original Greek: "ἐξουθένωσεν τοὺς ἐπιόρκους καὶ σταυροπάτας"</note> **GOAR.**

*In the same place, line 10.* **May his bones be dug up** <note>original Greek: "ἀνασκαφείη ὀστᾶ"</note>] This imprecation is often used elsewhere regarding the dead. For how can the bones of a living person be dug up? But evidently, this curse became so common that it was used against the living as well; in the same way, many of our own foolish people devote their tools and instruments to terrible curses when something fails to work or when they are harmed, curses which apply to them no more than poverty applies to a stone or damnation to hay. **XYLANDER.**

Vol. II, p. 538, line 20. **The Excubita** <note>original Greek: "τὰ Ἐξκούβιτα"</note>] *The place and station of the palace guards known as the Excubitors.* Codinus, in *On the Origins of Constantinople*, writes: *He built the palaces of Chalke and the Excubita.* <note>original Greek: "ἔκτισε τὰ παλάτια τῆς Χαλκῆς καὶ τῶν Ἐξκουβίτων"</note> However, elsewhere it signifies the guards themselves **of the palace, the palace guard, and the regiment of the Excubitors** <note>original Greek: "τοῦ παλατίου, τὴν παλατίου παραφυλακὴν καὶ τάγμα τῶν Ἐξκουβίτων"</note>, as Rufus and Constantine write; about which there is no difficulty. **GOAR.**

Vol. II, p. 539, line 15. **Antipascha** <note>original Greek: "Ἀντίπασχα"</note>] The day opposite Easter and the eighth day [the octave] is Antipascha, which is **Thomas Sunday** <note>original Greek: "κυριακὴ τοῦ Θωμᾶ"</note> from the Gospel reading; for us, it is the Sunday in White <note>Low Sunday</note>. **The third day** <note>original Greek: "ἡ τρίτη"</note> which follows is Tuesday. **GOAR.**

Vol. II, p. 541, line 21. **Katepano** <note>original Greek: "κατεπάνω"</note>] This word signifies "superior" or "above"; it appears he was a prefect of some matter or province. But what that was remains obscure. As for the **Argoclines** <note>original Greek: "ἀργοκλίνης"</note>, what kind of office it is: I find the name recorded in a list, but I do not understand the thing itself. What if there was a certain silver dining room, just as there was a golden one, of which he was the curator, a **silver-couch master** <note>original: "ἀργυροκλίνης"; Xylander is guessing a derivation from "argyros," meaning silver</note>? **XYLANDER.** An **Argo-clines** is a servant of the bed, or one who serves the prince when he is about to lie down late in bed, veiling him by drawing and spreading the bed-curtains all around; [the name comes] **from being idle around the bed** <note>original Greek: "παρὰ τοῦ ἀργεῖν ἀμφὶ τὴν κλίνην"</note>. **GOAR.**

Vol. II, p. 542, line 8. **Judge of the Greeks** <note>original Latin: "δικαστὴν Ἑλλήνων"; here "Greeks" refers to pagans or non-Christians</note>] One who judged disputes arising among the Saracens and other northern infidels, deciding them based on equity and what is good. He is distinguished from the camp judge in this: the latter administered the law to Christians serving the Emperor, while the former did so for all those outside the faith of Christ. One author mentions him; another, Codinus, lists him as the fifty-second among the officials. **GOAR.**

*In the same place, line 17.* **From the first priest of the New** <note>original Greek: "παρὰ τοῦ πρώτου πρεσβυτέρου τῆς νέας"</note>] Xylander ridiculously, and as he pleases, invents for himself priests in New Rome [Constantinople] from his own head. More reverently and truly: once the solemnity of the nuptial blessing was performed...

<summary>This page analyzes Byzantine terms related to legal oaths, court offices like the Excubitors and Argoclines, and ecclesiastical dates such as Antipascha. Jacques Goar provides corrective insights into the "Judge of the Greeks," clarifying that this official oversaw legal matters for non-Christian foreigners.</summary>

# ANNOTATIONS. 879

...authority by the archpriest of the **New Church** <note>original Greek: "ἡ νέα"</note>. This "New Church" was the one built in the palace by Emperor Basil, of which the author speaks on page 588 B. **GOAR.**

Vol. II, p. 545, line 13. Under the leadership of Arduin the Lombard, the Normans took possession of Apulia, and once it was divided among them, they sometimes became friends of the Greeks. See Leo of Ostia, 2.68. **GOAR.**

Vol. II, p. 546, line 13. **Phoiberaton** <note>original Greek: "φοιβεράτων"</note>] This error must be removed, by which "foeberati" and "foederati" <note>foreign allies under treaty</note> are thought to be the same. The latter are from every foreign nation; the former are from the subject Pisidians and Lycaonians, as this author explains. **GOAR.**

Vol. II, p. 548, line 21. **Sebastophoros** <note>original Greek: "σεβαστοφόρον"</note>] The Greek emperors rewarded the messenger who brought news of the empire being conferred with the title of *sebastophoros*, literally meaning one who "bore the dignity of the Augustus." The author illustrates the use of this custom in the case of Stephen, and indicates the reason for the title "sebastophoros" was because **he conveyed to him the good news of the empire** <note>original Greek: "τὰ τῆς βασιλείας εὐαγγέλια τούτῳ διεκομίσατο"</note>. Zonaras says it was because he had adorned him with the imperial insignia. **GOAR.**

Vol. II, p. 556, line 7. **Manai** <note>original Greek: "μάναι"</note>] Not **ladies** but **mothers**. **GOAR.**

Vol. II, p. 557, line 22. **his own war** <note>original Latin: "bello suas"</note>] I have placed an asterisk before these words: for the sentence seems to be mutilated. The meaning, however, was this: Cacicius <note>Gagik II, the last King of Bagratid Armenia</note> did not refuse to be a subject to the Romans, but he wished to do so on the condition that his paternal rule be left to him. **XYLANDER.** It is Xylander's sense that is mutilated here, not the text. The meaning is as follows: **even though he professed himself a subject (vassal), the emperor decided he must settle the matter with him by war.** Another might read it more clearly: **The emperor judged that war should be waged against one who, while confessing himself a servant, etc.** <note>original Greek: "τῷ δὲ δούλῳ μὲν ἀνομολογοῦντι πολεμητέον ἐδόκει τῷ βασιλεῖ"</note>, that is, **the emperor decided war must be declared against him, however much he professed to be a subject.** **GOAR.**

*In the same place, line 23.* **Bestes** is later called **Bestarches** <note>original Greek: "βεστάρχης"</note>, as if it were a title perhaps derived from some office: for Catacalo "The Burnt" is also called a **Bestes** below in the Median <note>Persian/Armenian</note> war. **XYLANDER.** I thought for a long time—as it pleased others, including Meursius—that the head of the wardrobe was called a **Bestarches** <note>deriving it from the Latin 'vestis' for garment</note>. But since this same Iasites was recently called **Bestes and appointed ruler of Iberia** <note>original Greek: "βέστης καὶ ἄρχων τῆς Ἰβηρίας προβεβλημένος"</note>, and further down on page 771 A we read of **Aaron, the ruler of the country** (that is, of Vaspurakan) **and a Bestes**, and immediately after we read of **the Bestes Catacalo of Ani and governor of Iberia**, I have abandoned my former opinion. I now judge that in the Iberian dialect and the custom of that region, a prince is called a **Bestes**, just as we read that the Bulgarians call their petty kings **chagan**, the Saracens call theirs **amir**, and the Serbs <note>original Latin: "Triballos"</note> call theirs **kral**. **GOAR.**

Vol. II, p. 558, line 20. **Choria** <note>original Greek: "χωρία"</note>] **Villages**. In the modern tongue, a *chorion* is a **village** <note>original Latin: "pagus"</note>. **GOAR.**

Vol. II, p. 559, line 17. **Servant** <note>original Latin: "servum"</note>] I do not believe that the "masters" <note>magistroi, a high court rank</note> were servants. I would read something else instead of **servant** <note>original Greek: "δοῦλον"</note>, perhaps **brother** <note>original Greek: "ἀδελφόν"</note> or something similar: for it is more likely that a brother, rather than a servant, was the "master" of Nicholas. **XYLANDER.** Retaining the author’s reading as sound, Xylander must be warned that the same person who is a "master" can also be a "servant." Is not a duke in some province a subject of the king and, as they say, a vassal? For the word **servant** <note>original Greek: "δοῦλος"</note> is used here not in the sense of a lowly slave, but in the sense of an honorary subject. To our point: Cacicius recently [offered] himself [to the] emperor...

# ANNOTATIONS OF XYLANDER AND GOAR

He professed to be a servant, that is, a subject, but with no other purpose than to claim for himself a permanent sovereignty over **Ani** <note>An Armenian city-capital</note> and **Iberia** <note>A kingdom in modern-day Georgia</note>. This same Constantine, having been promoted to the rank of **Magister** <note>a high-ranking senior administrative official</note> in the court of Constantinople, was able to be declared lord of a portion of **Alania** <note>a kingdom in the North Caucasus</note> by the emperor, while simultaneously serving as a subject or vassal under the same emperor in wars. **GOAR.**

Vol. II, p. 562, line 20. **Chrysopolis** <note>original Greek: "Χρυσόπολιν", literally "Golden City"</note>] Now called **Scutari** <note>Modern Üsküdar in Istanbul</note> by the Turks. It is incorrectly confused by some with Chalcedon, which is situated further down. **GOAR.**

Vol. II, p. 563, line 4. **The Holy Unmercenaries** <note>original Greek: "τῶν ἁγίων ἀναργύρων"</note>] These are Saints Cosmas and Damian, who practiced the medical arts out of charity, with no hope of payment. **GOAR.**

Vol. II, p. 564, line 20. **Strabomytis** <note>original Greek: "στραβομύτην"</note>] This means **with a twisted nose**. Nicknames derived from bodily defects are common among the Greeks. **GOAR.**

Vol. II, p. 568, line 16. **The wilderness of the Turks** <note>original Latin: "solitudinis Turcorum"</note>] This passage is undoubtedly flawed, although the reader can easily complete the sense. **Tragolipaces** is mentioned later as **Tangrolipaces** <note>The Seljuk Sultan Tughril Beg</note>. However, it is not unusual in this manuscript for the same word to be written differently a little further on. **XYL.**

Vol. II, p. 570, line 22. **The son of Leichudia** <note>original Latin: "Leichudiae filius"</note>] In Greek, **of Leichudia** <note>original Greek: "τῆς Λειχουδίας"</note>. A little above, mention was made of the deeds of Constantine Leichudes during the rebellion of Tornikios; now, why the feminine article **the** <note>original Greek: "τῆς"</note> is added, I do not know, unless I conjecture that he could have held this surname from some estate or jurisdiction of his. **XYL.** Not from a jurisdiction or estate, but from his mother; for the Greeks sometimes name sons after their mother if she is more distinguished and well-known. Here, Stephen is called **the son of Leichudia**; otherwise, according to Xylander, he would have to be asserted as the "son of an estate or jurisdiction." **GOAR.**

*Ibid.* <term>Paradynasteuon</term> <note>original Greek: "παραδυναστεύων"</note> is the name of a dignity or office, designating as it were a deputy and colleague of the emperor, who was also called a **Rector**. **XYL.**

Vol. II, p. 575, line 10. **A brother from another parent** <note>original Latin: "fratre ex altero parente"</note>] It is uncertain whether this means a brother born of the same womb or of a different mother—as if he were a brother who had "bloomed" from elsewhere, rather than a full brother. For this is what the word **half-brother** <note>original Greek: "ἑτεροθαλής", literally "differently-blooming"</note> sounds like. Such "little flowers" <note>metaphorical rhetorical flourishes</note> are not uncommon in the meadows of these writers; the same word is found in Zonaras, and again below regarding the brother of Alimus. **XYL.**

Vol. II, p. 578, line 23. **In the second indiction** <note>An indiction is a 15-year tax cycle used for dating</note>] Specifically in the Year of the World 6557 <note>approximately 1049 AD</note>, since the indiction changes according to the years, and returns to the same number in a fifteen-year circuit. It is established from previous sections that the eleventh indiction was the year [10]51, and the twelfth was the year [10]52, as well as from what is said below concerning the rule of Empress Theodora and many other things. Thus the rebellion of Tornikios, which was said to have fallen in the first indiction, was in the year 6556 according to our reckoning <note>approximately 1047-1048 AD</note>. I wanted to note this for the sake of the less experienced. **XYL.**

Vol. II, p. 589, line 17. **Triaditza** <note>original Greek: "Τριάδιτζαν"</note>] Formerly called **Sardica** <note>Modern Sofia, Bulgaria</note>. **GOAR.**

Vol. II, p. 596, line 14. **Not far from Adrianople**] The sense certainly requires this, unless I am quite mistaken, as is clear enough from what follows. Therefore, in the Greek, instead of **and very far** <note>original Greek: "καὶ πάνυ πόρρω"</note>, it should read **and not very far** <note>original Greek: "καὶ οὐ πάνυ πόρρω"</note>. Similarly, in the account of the burial of Emperor Monomachus, instead of **attaining** <note>original Greek: "τυχούσης"</note>, I read **not attaining** <note>original Greek: "οὐ τυχούσης"</note>. **XYL.**

Vol. II, p. 597, line 16. **Francopulum**] Just as the Bulgarians were previously called **Comitopuli** <note>sons of the Count</note>, I conclude that this man was of Frankish descent <note>literally "son of a Frank"</note>.

**The Frank** <note>original Latin: "Francigenam"</note>, who perhaps served for pay with a certain troop of Frankish cavalry under **Monomachus** <note>Emperor Constantine IX Monomachos, r. 1042–1055</note>, just as **Arduin** did under Michael as mentioned above. Indeed, it is said below that the Franks served as soldiers in Iberia; and in the *Stratioticon* <note>A military handbook or treatise</note> it is clearly shown who that **Erbebius** <note>Hervé Frankopoulos, a famous Frankish mercenary general</note> was. **XYL.**

Vol. II, p. 598, line 3. *escaped by flight*] Here in the manuscript, almost an entire page was blank. There is missing, I conjecture, a description of the failed battle of **Nicephorus the Rector** against the **Pechenegs** <note>A nomadic Turkic people</note>, and the subsequent attack by some of the Pechenegs and their raid right up to **Byzantium** <note>Constantinople</note> itself, as well as the manner in which **Kegen** <note>A Pecheneg chieftain who defected to the Byzantines</note> was sent out from the city. But here **Zonaras** <note>A 12th-century Byzantine chronicler</note> cannot help us to know anything for certain, as he scarcely touched upon this long and varied history. **XYL.** We have filled this gap from the historian **Skylitzes**. **GOAR.**

Vol. II, p. 603, line 22. **The Follower** <note>original Greek: "ὁ ἀκόλουθος", *ho akolouthos*</note>] **Codinus** in *On Offices*, chapter 5: "The *akolouthos* is found to be the leader of the **Varangians** <note>The elite Viking/Anglo-Saxon bodyguard of the Emperor</note>; he follows the Emperor in front of them. For this very reason, he is called the *akolouthos* [The Follower]." **GOAR.**

Vol. II, p. 604, line 24. *indictions 4 and 5* <note>An "indiction" is a 15-year cycle used for dating in the Roman and Byzantine empires</note>] In the text, it says 14 and 5. But I think that is a mistake, nor do I admit such a large gap between these and the previous events; I say that the 5 is correct, and that the "iota" <note>the Greek numeral for 10</note> was added to the "delta" <note>the numeral for 4</note> by error. Why say more? A little later, mention is finally made of the 7th and 8th indictions. **XYL.**

Vol. II, p. 610, line 11. **The Presiding One** <note>original Greek: "ὁ πρωτεύων", *ho proteuon*</note>] Who is also the **Great Lord** <note>original Greek: "μέγας ἄρχων", *megas archon*</note>. For among the lords and the governors—the presiding officers and rectors of the provinces—one person was designated by the Emperor to be hailed as the *proteuon* or *megas archon* as a mark of honor. **Coresius**. **GOAR.**

Vol. II, p. 614, line 14. **The Strategeion** <note>original Greek: "Στρατήγιον", the headquarters of the military commander</note>] This is a place in the fifth region of the city. **Pancirollus** <note>A 16th-century legal scholar</note> believes it to be the praetorian camp, in which, because Michael had perhaps played there, the citizens made an allusion to it. **GOAR.**

Same page, line 17. *heads not with letters*] I still do not understand this passage, and in interpreting it, I do not want to claim I have touched the truth or that anyone else has reached a false conclusion. **XYL.** I do not suspect that **letter** <note>original Greek: "γράμμα", *gramma*</note> refers to a head-covering that had the form of a hat or a cap shading the head in one single way, but rather that it was a band or fillet twisted according to each person's whim, after the fashion of a **Turkish head-covering** <note>Likely referring to a turban</note>. For it was made of linen, as the author suggests, and because it was decorated with various colors, it obtained the name of "letter" <note>likely referring to embroidered patterns that resemble writing</note>; but that which was woven of fine linen with various purple lines was called **greatly-lettered** <note>original Greek: "μεγαλόγραμμον", *megalogrammon*</note> by the Emperor's command. Furthermore, the Greeks call any variety of colors, flowers, stars, and figures on garments "letters." The frequently praised anonymous Lexicon, under the entry **wearer of a worn cloak** <note>original Greek: "τριβωνοφόρος"</note>, says: "one who wears a robe having marks like letters." **GOAR.** **Salmasius** <note>Claude Saumaise, a 17th-century scholar</note>, in his notes on Vopiscus, p. 406, col. 2, following Meursius's Glossary under the word **margellon** <note>a type of border or pearl decoration</note>, reads it as "decorated with a pearl-border." **FABROTUS.**

Same page, line 20. *fast scribes*] I think these correspond to our **notaries** <note>original Latin: "librarios"</note>. **XYL.**

Same page, line 23. **to distribute annually at the time of Easter**] I cannot restrain my pen from transcribing the words of **Liutprand** <note>Liutprand of Cremona, a 10th-century diplomat and historian who visited Constantinople</note> from Book 6. In that...

# XYLANDER AND GOAR

**He says** <note>This passage quotes Liutprand of Cremona, a 10th-century bishop and diplomat who described the Byzantine court</note> that in the week before **Palm Sunday** <note>original Greek: "Baïophoros," meaning the palm-bearing week</note>, which we call the week of the palm branches, the Emperor carries out a distribution of gold coins to the soldiers as well as to those established in various offices. This is where the name **rogas** <note>original Greek: "rogas"; a term for the annual salaries or ceremonial donatives distributed by the Emperor</note> comes from, given according to the merit of each person's office. Because the Emperor wanted me to be present for this distribution, he commanded me to come. 

A table was set out, ten cubits in length and four in width, which held the coins gathered in small chests, with the amounts written on the outside of the chests according to what was to be given to each person. They then entered before the Emperor, not in a confused mass but in order, according to the voice of the caller who read out the names of the men written down according to the dignity of their office. 

The first to be called was the **Rector of the House** <note>The *Rector Domus*, a high-ranking court official</note>, for whom the coins were placed not in his hands but upon his shoulders, along with four **scaramangis** <note>original: "scaramangis"; these were long, ornate tunics or caftans worn by the Byzantine elite</note>. After him, the **Domestic of the Schools** <note>The commander of the elite palace guards</note> and the **Accountant of the Fleet** <note>original Greek: "logariastes tes ploias"</note> were called, one of whom was in charge of the soldiers and the other of the sailors. These men, being of equal rank, received an equal number of coins and tunics, but because the weight was so great, they did not carry them on their shoulders but dragged them behind themselves with labor, with others helping them. 

After these, twenty-four **Masters** <note>Magistri</note> were admitted, to each of whom were distributed twenty-four pounds of gold coins, along with tunics. The order of the **Patricians** <note>A high honorary title</note> followed behind them, and each was presented with twelve pounds of coins and one tunic. After these, an immense crowd of **Protospatharians** <note>literally "First Sword-bearers"</note>, **Candidates**, and clients of that sort were called. King **Theodoric** <note>The Ostrogothic King of Italy</note> writes about receiving an annual gift in the Roman custom in **Cassiodorus**’s *Variae*, Book 5, Letters 26 and 27. **Balsamon** <note>Theodore Balsamon, a famous 12th-century jurist</note> laments in his *Greek Law*, Book 7, page 471, that this custom had become obsolete by his time. **GOAR.**

Vol. II, p. 615, line 6. The nickname **Uranius** was also used above. **XYL.**

Vol. II, p. 625, line 13. **military muster** <note>original Greek: "adnoumion"</note>] What this word is, or what thing it signifies, I have not yet learned. **XYL.** 

The **adnoumion** is a description or roll-call of the soldiers to be made by the tribunes, the leader of the army, or sometimes by the Emperor himself. The person who officially attended to this was the **Great Muster-master** <note>original Greek: "ho megas adnoumiastes"; translated in the text as the "Great Counter"</note>, whose duties the Emperor is performing here himself. **GOAR.**

Ibid. line 19. *domestic troops*] In Greek: *oikeious*. These were perhaps those who were enrolled and served from that specific province. However, I understand the "foreign" troops to be two Gallic units and one Russian unit; the author himself calls them "from the nations." 

A little later, it follows that before the **Comnenians** <note>Supporters of the future Emperor Isaac I Komnenos during the revolt of 1057</note> fought with the imperial forces, mutual conversations were held between them and they took turns soliciting each other to defect. A scribe noted, not without reason, that this was out of place for military encounters. His words are: **"these things are unsuited to the conversations of soldiers."** Indeed, it seems much more just to criticize such things than that famous dialogue between **Glaucus and Diomedes** <note>A reference to Homer’s *Iliad*, where two enemies stop to exchange armor after discovering their families are linked by hospitality</note>. 

But we make an end of annotating here. Let the reader seek the rest from the reading and comparison of other writers; for we neither wished nor were able to pursue everything. And whatever else we have concerning the affairs of the **Constantinopolitan** empire, we shall provide in its own time (God willing).

# ANNOTATIONS

We will publish these findings gradually <note>original Latin: "lente"</note>, so that we might reduce the labor of searching and investigating for both the learned and the unlearned alike, and propose several things that have escaped our notice until now. **Xyl.** <note>Wilhelm Xylander (1532–1576), a German humanist scholar and translator of Byzantine texts</note>

Volume II, page 629, line 7. *Doting* <note>original Greek: "κρονόληρον" (kronolēron); literally "senile like Cronus," referring to a person whose mind has failed due to old age</note>, as if you were to call an old man doting in his brain or reason. I refer the term *the doting one* <note>original Greek: "τὸν κρονόληρον"</note> back to Xylander. **Goar.** <note>Jacques Goar (1601–1653), a French Dominican monk and renowned scholar of the Byzantine liturgy</note>

Volume II, page 632, line 18. **Constantine Psellus, the Supreme of the Philosophers** <note>original Greek: "Κωνσταντῖνος ὁ Ψελλὸς τῶν φιλοσόφων ὁ ὕπατος" (Konstantinos ho Psellos tōn philosophōn ho hypatos)</note>] The exquisite name of <term>Psellus</term><note>Michael Constantine Psellus, a 11th-century polymath and high official</note>, by which he is called *Supreme of the Philosophers* (that is, *most high* <note>original Greek: "ὑπέρτατος" (hypertatos)</note>), was given not only from merit but from his official duty. Although the office would not be granted except by merit, it is listed in the twenty-ninth place among the palace ranks in Book 2 of the *Graeco-Roman Law* <note>A collection of Byzantine legal codes</note>. This office was also held by Theodore, the Patriarch of Constantinople, about whom more is said at the end of the same book. **Goar.**

Volume II, page 635, line 16. **Double cloak** <note>original Greek: "διπλοΐδα" (diploïda)</note>] This refers to the <term>phelonion</term><note>original Greek: "φελώνιον"; a liturgical vestment similar to a Western chasuble</note>, which is the priestly cloak that surrounds the entire body of the priest on all sides. **Goar.**

Volume II, page 636, line 12. **The one who is second in the Church** <note>original Greek: "τοῦ τῆς ἐκκλησίας δευτερεύοντος" (tou tēs ekklēsias deutereuontos)</note>] This refers specifically to the <term>protopapas</term><note>The "chief priest" or head of the secular clergy in a cathedral</note>, who holds the second rank in all matters after the Patriarch. See the works of Codinus and the *Euchologion* <note>The prayer book of the Eastern Orthodox Church</note>. **Goar.**

Volume II, page 638, line 2. **The ambo** <note>original Greek: "τοῦ ἄμβωνος" (tou ambōnos)</note>] Concerning this, one should read the entire 17th chapter of Codinus <note>George Codinus, an author associated with Byzantine court ceremonies and offices</note>. **Goar.**

*Ibid.*, line 3. **The Autocrat Emperor** <note>original Greek: "βασιλεὺς αὐτοκράτωρ" (basileus autokratōr)</note>] An Emperor holding supreme power is distinct from one who is an *autocratic general* <note>original Greek: "στρατηγὸς αὐτοκράτωρ" (stratēgos autokratōr)</note>, just as a prince differs from a subject, or a king from a leader of an army. **Goar.**

Lest some should complain about the memory of Xylander being unjustly cast aside if his annotations had been cut away or his interpretation entirely replaced, I have praised your opinion—which I myself approve—in this edition and reprinting of Cedrenus, most distinguished **Fabrot** <note>Charles Annibal Fabrot (1580–1659), a French jurist and scholar of Byzantine law</note>; and I subscribe to that which has already been praised. Those who toil most diligently for the public good do not wish for any labors undertaken for that same public good to be deprived of their due praise, even if they met with an unfortunate outcome. Just as the state tolerates offspring that are almost like monsters so that the natural piety of human feeling is not violated, so too do those born for the public good preserve, bring forth, and set out the fruits of nightly vigils for others—even if they are otherwise tasteless—lest fastidious men reject them as if they were too delicate. These fruits may not be sweet, but they will at least be pleasing to some. No matter how bitter they were, they were ordered to become sweet by our art: through your industry they have now for the most part been softened, refined, and rendered no less sweet than they are pleasing. I would boast that I have brought help to the work undertaken; by my own efforts, I have provided light. **Goar.**

# JACQUES GOAR
## ON JOHN CUROPALATES
### NOTES.

**Volume II, page 641, line 10.** *having completely alienated him from the empire* <note>original Greek: "ἀλλοτριώσας τούτου παντάπασι τὴν βασιλείαν"</note>] Shall I praise the religious devotion or the power over the Church claimed for themselves by the Greek Emperors, and shall I mention certain rites brought from the Church into the palace? They were clothed in the **sakkos** and the **mandya** <note>The *sakkos* is a tunic-like vestment worn by bishops; the *mandya* is a ceremonial cloak</note>; the former is the ornament of the highest pontiffs during the performance of sacred rites, while the latter—as is clear from the writings of *Symeon of Thessalonica*—is the primary distinction of the readers. The cross served as their scepter, and in the later centuries, the royal inner chamber was called a *kellion* <note>original Greek: "κελλίον"; a small cell, typically for a monk</note>. Moreover, they constantly carried in their hand the <term>akakia</term> <note>original Greek: "ἐν ἀκακίᾳ" (en akakia); literally "guilelessness," a purple silk roll or pouch containing earth to symbolize human mortality</note>, a small bag filled with earth, by which they modeled for themselves a perpetual contemplation of impending death, much like monks. They even joined the procession of sacred gifts to the altar alongside priests and deacons, as if they had been admitted into the choir of readers. I will remain silent regarding the ecclesiastical canons they established; the *Graeco-Roman Law*, *Codinus*, and the author at the end of this history record that bishoprics were changed into metropolises by imperial edicts. Furthermore, they promoted patriarchs by invoking the name of the Most Holy Trinity and signing them with the cross; they burned incense at the altar; and from that same altar, they solemnly blessed the people with the **tricerion** <note>A three-branched candlestick symbolizing the Trinity, usually reserved for bishops</note> in the manner of high priests, as *Balsamon* testifies in his commentary on Canon 69 of the Council of Trullo. This type of legal right was also extended to courtiers and **civilian officials** <note>original Greek: "πολιτικοὺς ἄρχοντας" (politikous archontas)</note>; for in Book 4 of the *Graeco-Roman Law*, we read that a certain *Pothus*, a <term>protospatharios</term> <note>A high-ranking court title, literally "first sword-bearer"</note>, also served as the administrator of the Great Church, and another *Theodosius*, also a protospatharios, held the supreme care of the properties dedicated to monasteries—which our author here understands by the title of *the administration and the care and protection of the sacred treasures* <note>original Greek: "τῆς οἰκονομίας καὶ τῆς τῶν ἱερῶν κειμηλίων προνοίας καὶ προστασίας"</note>. Nevertheless, the author reports that the Emperor *Comnenus* later abstained from handing this power over to secular officials; for *Synesius* wrote beautifully in Letter 57: *To join political virtue with the priesthood is to weave together things that cannot be spun together* <note>original Greek: "πολιτικὴν ἀρετὴν ἱερωσύνῃ συνάπτειν τὸ κλώθειν ἐστὶ τὰ ἀσύγλωστα"</note>. **GOAR.**

**Volume II, page 643, line 12.** *Allow me, I created you* <note>original Greek: "ἐῶ σὲ ἔκτισα" (eō se ektisa)</note>] The Greek usage of speech is full of proverbs, which they call *myths*. In this instance, I judge the particle *eō* <note>Allow</note> to be a corruption, since even unrefined country folk pronounce the word *ego* <note>I</note> perfectly, except for those with a lisp. The particle *hina* or *na* is sometimes used, as it is here, as a marker of the future tense. The verb *chalo* commonly means *I ruin, corrupt, destroy, or cast down*. **GOAR.**

**Volume II, page 644, line 1.** **The Varangians** <note>original Greek: "Βαράγγους" (Varangous)</note>] *Gretser*, in his commentary on *Codinus*, writes that "Varangians" is as if you were to say "Franks" <note>original Greek: "Φράγγοι" (Phrangoi)</note>. But *Gretser* is practically guessing when he judges that the English (who were auxiliaries to the Greeks and the Emperor’s bodyguard, either earning the position through valor or being summoned by an embassy sent for that purpose) were called "Varangians" as if they were "Franks." For is not any Westerner—be they French, Italian, or German—called a "Frank" by the Greeks? Why then would an Englishman be called a "Varangian" as if he were a "Frank"? From

<meta>This page continues Jacques Goar’s commentary on Byzantine courtly and ecclesiastical customs. # JACQUES GOAR
## NOTES.

I have learned from the dictionary of Matthew Paris, the historian of the English, that *baranagium* or *barnagium* (which is also *baronagium*) refers to the senate and assembly of the kingdom’s peers, commonly called a parliament. From the nobility of this term, the English mercenaries of the Greeks—following the Greek fashion for a vain desire for titles—fashioned and adapted for themselves the name **Varangians** <note>original: "Βαράγγων" (Barangōn)</note> at the Court of Constantinople. Furthermore, Codinus does not hide the fact that the Varangians were English, even depicting them as speaking in **English** <note>original: "Ἰγγλινιστί" (Inglinisti)</note>. See page 723, section B. **GOAR.**

*The same, line 16.* [**formed into the shape of a cross** <note>original: "σταυροειδῶς σχηματισθεῖσα"</note>] The hand of a bishop or priest is shaped into a cross; when the thumb is placed over the <term>medicinal finger</term> <note>The "digitus medicus" is the fourth finger or ring finger</note>, a cross is formed from both. The remaining fingers stay extended, and all together they represent the first letters of these words: **Jesus Christ Conquers** <note>original: "Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς νικᾷ" (Iēsous Christos nika)</note>. Specifically, the little finger held straight represents the **I**, the middle finger and thumb crossed represent the **X**, and the middle and index fingers slightly separated represent the **N**. These things are explained by Symeon of Thessalonica and Malaxus, whom I discuss elsewhere. **GOAR.**

*The same, line 17.* [**proclaiming peace to the people** <note>original: "ἐπιφωνοῦντι τῷ λαῷ τὴν εἰρήνην"</note>] This refers to the peace invoked from heaven by the bishop with the words **"Peace be with you"** <note>original: "εἰρήνη ὑμῖν" (eirēnē hymin)</note> for those requesting a blessing. **GOAR.**

*Volume II, page 645, line 2.* [**Guardian of Rights** <note>original: "δικαιωμάτων φύλαξ" (dikaiōmatōn phylax)</note>] Later writers call those goods that fall to someone by law **rights** <note>original: "δικαιώματα" (dikaiōmata)</note>, not just the law or justice itself. Therefore, among these same writers, the "Guardian of Rights" is what we would call a defender of royal rights, who is also a royal procurator. **GOAR.**

*Volume II, page 650, line 1.* [**Catherine, renamed Helena in the monastic life** <note>original: "Αἰκατερίνης ἐν τῷ μοναχικῷ Ἐλένης μετονομασθείσης"</note>] Besides their family and national names, the Greeks have names of **honor, piety, and fortune**. The first are given to anyone at baptism; the latter are devised from chance occurrences, such as those found in Cedrenus like *Kontostephanos* (Short-crown), *Strabomytes* (Squint-nose), or *Argyros* (Silvery), given because of a short stature, a curved nose, or a brightness of character. Finally, the middle type (names of piety) are used in monasteries. These are not chosen by chance or merely by whim, but are made specific to monks according to a law observing both piety and honor. This is done either if the names suggest holiness, or if they at least match the baptismal names in their initial letters. From this you can learn why Andronicus the Elder, upon becoming a monk, was called **Antonius** (according to Gregoras, book 9); why John Cantacuzenus took the name **Joasaph**; why George Phranzes was called **Gregory** and his wife Elena called **Eupraxia**; and finally, why the Empress Catherine was called **Helena**—if not from the agreement of the first letter, then at least from the similarity in sound. **GOAR.**

*The same, line 7.* [**abbot** <note>original: "καθηγουμένου" (kathēgoumenou)</note>] A *hegoumenos* is any superior of a monastery; a *kathegoumenos* is one who is also adorned with sacred orders; and a *prohegoumenos* is a former superior. **GOAR.**

*Volume II, page 651, line 10.* The difference between **popular** <note>original: "δημοτικόν" (dēmotikon)</note> and **common** <note>original: "κοινόν" (koinon)</note> is the same as that between organized guilds or factions and the unorganized masses. **GOAR.**

*The same, line 17.* [**the memory of the holy Great-Martyr George** <note>original: "τῆς τοῦ ἁγίου μεγαλομάρτυρος Γεωργίου μνήμης"</note>] Concerning this, and the trust the emperors placed in the saint, see Codinus chapter 15, note 9 and chapter 17, note 50. **GOAR.**

*Volume II, page 652, line 16.* [**concerning the body, he was disciplined** <note>original: "περὶ τὸ σῶμα ἦτον κολαστικός"</note>] *body*...

<summary>Jacques Goar explains the etymological link between the English "Baronage" and the Byzantine "Varangian Guard," as well as the symbolic gestures of liturgical blessings. He also outlines the naming conventions for Byzantine royals and monks, where names were often changed to a pious alternative starting with the same letter.</summary>

# JACQUES GOAR

*...accustomed to taming and subduing himself through austerities, but sluggish and dull regarding anything else.* **GOAR.**

*Volume 2, page 653, line 24.* The historian Cedrenus says that the title **Sultan** <note>original: "Sultani"</note> signifies <term>Almighty and King of Kings</term> <note>original: "παντοκράτορα καὶ βασιλέα βασιλέων" (pantokratora kai basilea basileon)</note>. Among the Turks, it is now commonly used to mean "lord"; their prince holds this name <term>preeminently</term> <note>original: "κατ' ἐξοχήν" (kat' exochen)</note> as the sole and greatest lord. So says Leunclavius. **GOAR.**

*Volume 2, page 654, line 9.* [**sklysmos** <note>original: "σκλυσμόν"</note>] I read this as <term>deluge</term> <note>original: "κατακλυσμόν" (kataklysmon)</note>, a word which modern writers often use to interpret a massive storm of business or affairs. **GOAR.**

*The same, line 16.* [**boats made from a single trunk** <note>original: "λέμβοις αὐτοπρέμνοις" (lembois autopremnois)</note>] Cedrenus and Constantine Porphyrogenitus, in *On the Administration of the Empire*, call these <term>monoxyla</term> <note>original: "μονόξυλα"; literally "single-wood" boats or dugout canoes</note>. **GOAR.**

*Volume 2, page 665, line 7.* [**on the birthday of the Savior** <note>original: "τοῖς γενεθλίοις τοῦ σωτῆρος" (tois genethliois tou soteros)</note>] The day on which everyone among the Greeks is welcomed with gifts <note>Goar refers here to the tradition of gift-giving on Christmas</note>. **GOAR.**

*Volume 2, page 672, line 20.* [**they simulated** <note>original: "ἀφωμοιώσαντο" (aphomoiosanto)</note>] They represent war through light skirmishes. Or perhaps the word is <term>they performed the rites</term> <note>original: "ἀφωσιώσαντο" (aphosiosanto)</note>, meaning they only took a small taste or a preliminary omen of the battle. **GOAR.**

*Volume 2, page 673, line 24.* [**the rank of the Schools** <note>original: "τὸ τῶν σχολῶν τάγμα" (to ton scholon tagma)</note>] I understand this to mean a legion of native guards, whose various troops were formerly called "Schools." The "Federated" troops <note>Latin: "foederati"</note>, who composed a distinct military service among the Praetorians, are not considered included in this group. **GOAR.**

*Volume 2, page 683, line 9.* [**and judgment** <note>original: "κρίσιν δέ" (krisin de)</note>] The Emperor performed a duty for which a <term>Judge of the Camp</term> <note>original: "κριτὴς τοῦ φοσσάτου" (krites tou phossatou)</note> is recorded as being established in the writings of Codinus, chapter 15, number 72. **GOAR.**

*Volume 2, page 686, line 22.* [**the caverns of the chasm** <note>original: "τὰς τοῦ χάσματος σήραγγας" (tas tou chasmatos seranggas)</note>] I neither demand nor beg for faith in Apocryphal writings. However, I will briefly relate what the Greeks tell in the 18th Sermon of the *Thesaurus*—a lectionary regularly read in their churches—so that the author’s text does not remain obscure or unexplained. 

In the city of Chonae in Phrygia, they say, water was kept that had been blessed by the hand and prayers of John the Apostle; through the sprinkling of this water, heavenly and angelic power was never lacking for the performing of miracles. Moved by the frequency of these signs, a certain Archippus of Hierapolis built a church at the water, dedicated in the name of Michael, the prince of the heavenly host. The pagans, being hostile to the Christian religion and name, attempted to destroy it by diverting the river Chryses through it. Heavenly power mocked their attempt and expectations, and drove the course of the river in the opposite direction. 

Ignoring the miracle, the pagans persisted even more stubbornly in their undertaking; they diverted the rivers Cuphus and Lycocas from elsewhere and drove them into the church. The building would have already collapsed under the flood of waters, had not Michael, the leader of the heavenly ranks, appeared equipped with a spear. He struck a rock and excavated a massive void within it, capable of absorbing such a great mass of water. Thus, the plunging and low whirlpools of the rivers entered the subterranean caves—**the caverns of the chasm**—and, being much steeper than the church's foundations (as if terrified by the sanctity of the place), they emerged into the neighboring fields where a channel was provided, gliding toward the sea in an undisturbed course. <term>Because of this very miracle</term> <note>original: "ἀπὸ αὐτὸ τὸ θαῦμα" (apo auto to thauma)</note>, they write, <term>the place was named Chonae, though it was first named Colossae</term> <note>original: "ὠνομάσθη ὁ τόπος Χῶναι, ἀμὴ πρῶτα ὠνομάζετο Κωλασσαί"</note>. It was called the miracle of Chonae (which is to say, "the Funnels") at the place of Colossae...

<summary>This page features Jacques Goar’s scholarly notes on Byzantine terminology, including the definition of "Sultan" and various military ranks. The most significant portion recounts the "Miracle at Chonae," explaining how the city of Colossae was renamed after the Archangel Michael saved a church by opening a chasm to swallow a diverted river.</summary>

# ANNOTATIONS

### Page 887

...who was called upon first and gave the name. Those who have seen both with their own eyes report that the monastery built over the <term>chasm</term> <note>original: "voragini"; referring to the miraculous opening of the earth at Chonae</note> still exists, and that the city of Chonae was named <term>Michael</term> <note>original: "Μιχαὴλ Χώναις" (Michael Chonais)</note> because of him. **GOAR.**

*Volume 2, page 689, line 11.* [**about to strip** <note>original: "ἀποδύσουσα" (apodysousa)</note>] I read this as **about to pay back** <note>original: "ἀποτίσουσα" (apotisousa)</note>, and I interpret it as someone about to fulfill a vow for a safe journey, or perhaps being received for a final conversation before departure. One should recall what was written above regarding the <term>farewell address</term> <note>original: "περὶ συντακτηρίου" (peri syntakteriou)</note>. **GOAR.**

*Volume 2, page 690, line 7.* [**imperial saddlecloths and bridles** <note>original: "ἐφεστρίδες βασιλικαὶ καὶ χαλινά" (ephestrides basilikai kai chalina)</note>] Both of these are purple; the latter are also fringed with a golden border, and for that reason, they are far more noble than the rest. See Codinus, Cedrenus on Basil the Macedonian, and Gregoras, Book 9. **GOAR.**

*The same, line 11.* [**of the bridge called Zompos** <note>original: "τῆς Ζόμπου λεγομένης γεφύρας" (tes Zompou legomenes gephyras)</note>] This is the bridge constructed by Justinian, called elsewhere the **Five-Bridge** <note>original: "Πενταγέφυρος" (Pentagephyros)</note> in the writings of Cedrenus. The common people called it **Zompos**, using an appellative rather than a proper name; for *Zompos* signifies **humpbacked** <note>original: "gibbosum"</note>, and it is considered a fitting epithet for a very convex bridge. We have mentioned the Sangarius River in our notes on Cedrenus. **GOAR.**

*Volume 2, page 691, line 4.* [**cold spring** <note>original: "κρύαν πηγήν" (kryan pegen)</note>] Modern Greeks call springs of colder or chillier water <term>kryas pegas</term>, and we know of several by this name on the islands of Chios and Tinos. **GOAR.**

*Volume 2, page 696, line 11.* [**he gave them a cross** <note>original: "σταυρὸν αὐτοῖς ἐπιδέδωκεν" (stauron autois epidedoken)</note>] A note on page 527 of Cedrenus explains how a cross depicted on a document serves as a pledge of given faith and a symbol of an oath. **GOAR.**

*The same, line 19.* [**the most victorious symbol** <note>original: "τὸ νικητικώτατον σύμβολον" (to niketikotaton symbolon)</note>] The author means nothing less than a weapon pertaining to victory, but specifically the **Cross**, of which he speaks, by whose power all enemies are subdued. Since the time of Constantine, who once beheld it surrounded by the words **In this sign, conquer** <note>original: "ἐν τούτῳ νίκα" (en touto nika)</note>, emperors have been accustomed to raise it upon their standards as the symbol of victory. **GOAR.**

*Volume 2, page 700, line 6.* [**trampling, as is the custom** <note>original: "πατήσας ὥσπερ ἔθος" (patesas hosper ethos)</note>] Among the Persians—from whom this Sultan descends—it was a familiar practice to trample defeated enemies underfoot. From this custom, their King Shapur <note>original: "Sapores"</note> reduced the Emperor Valerian to such a miserable necessity that, bent down like a slave, he provided a step with his own neck for the king as he was about to mount his horse. (Caelius, *Ancient Readings*, 18.18). Justinian II, imitating the Persians, was led by a wild heat of vengeance to trample Leontius and Apsimar under his feet for a considerable time before they were beheaded by his order. (Cedrenus, in his *Life*). In these same provinces and with similar ferocity, the more recent Tamerlane, whenever he mounted his horse, used the necks of the prostrate Bayezid <note>original: "Baiazetis"</note> as a footstool. (Dubravius, Book 25). The Norman chronicles in the life of Robert I report that defeated enemies, with a saddle laid upon them, were once trodden upon by the Franks and Normans. **GOAR.**

*Volume 2, page 700, line 16.* The adage **as far as words and salt** <note>original: "μέχρι λόγων καὶ ἁλῶν" (mechri logon kai halon)</note> denotes a fellowship of secrets and living together granted to a friend. Plutarch, in his *Symposium*, once used the phrase "to the point of salt and cumin." Even today, the Turks praise the "partnership of salt." **GOAR.**

<summary>This page contains scholarly commentary by Jacques Goar on Byzantine history, focusing on the miracle of Michael at Chonae, the architectural details of Justinian's "Humpbacked" bridge, and the symbolic importance of the Cross. It also provides a grim historical overview of the custom of "trampling" defeated rulers, drawing parallels between Persian, Byzantine, and Mongol leaders.</summary>
