# THE ANNOTATIONS OF JACQUES GOAR

### Page 888

*Volume 2, page 701, line 12.* [**The Master of Petitions** <note>original: "ὁ ἐπὶ τῶν δεήσεων" (ho epi ton deeseon)</note>] Regarding this office, Codinus writes in chapter 5, number 65: *He receives the petitions of those asking for help and those who have been wronged, while the Emperor is passing by on horseback.* Cassiodorus, in his *Variae* (6.17), calls the official performing this duty a **referendary** <note>original: "referendarium"</note> and explains his duties at great length. Procopius says in a few words that he is the one who explains the prayers of the supplicants to the prince and manages his responses. Pancirollus, in his *Notes on the Empire* (chapter 18), claims he should be called a **regendary** <note>original: "regendarium"</note>. However, the official described by Cassiodorus in *Variae* (book 11) is far removed from the other, being a military official compared to a civil one. **GOAR.**

*In the same place, line 21.* [**The Sultanic robe** <note>original: "Σουλτανικῆς στολῆς" (Soultanikes stoles)</note>] When Muslims wish to follow someone with affection or honor, they adorn them with their own clothes—except for the head-covering. Hence, the Emperor, distinguished by this **Sultanic** <note>original: "Sultanica"</note> (that is, royal and Saracen) garment, returns to his own people. **GOAR.**

*Volume 2, page 704, line 6.* [**through those villages and lands** <note>original: "δι’ ἐκείνων τῶν κωμῶν καὶ τῶν χωρῶν" (di’ ekeinon ton komon kai ton choron)</note>] I interpret this to mean he was making his way through those villages and cities. For among modern Greeks, the word <term>chora</term> <note>original: "χώρα" (chora)</note> is used to mean **city**. **GOAR.**

*In the same place, line 13.* [**of the high priests** <note>original: "τῶν ἀρχιερέων" (ton archiereon)</note>] To me, these words mean: "the bishops offered no help, though they had been sent to obtain a promise for his safety and well-being." **GOAR.**

*Volume 2, page 705, line 5.* [**nothing blasphemous or ill-omened** <note>original: "οὐδὲν βλάσφημον ἢ ἀπόφημον" (ouden blasphemon e apophemon)</note>] In these desperate circumstances, this is the highest praise for the unfortunate prince: that he rejected tragic complaints and the elegiac speech so frequently used by the Greeks when tossed by adverse fate. Instead, he turned himself toward the decrees of divine providence—not merely to praise them, but to accept them. For modern Greeks say that **to give thanks** <note>original: "τὸ εὐχαριστεῖν" (to eucharistein)</note> means to be **contented**, just as a man who has been fully satisfied is called **thankful** <note>original: "εὐχαριστημένον" (eucharistemenon)</note>. Nevertheless, one who is oppressed by calamities and calls God to mind often sighs with the words, **Glory to you, O God** <note>original: "δόξα σοι ὁ θεός" (doxa soi ho theos)</note>; thus, "giving thanks" is clearly understood in that sense. **GOAR.**

*Volume 2, page 706, line 1.* [**Nicephoritzes** <note>original: "Νικηφορίτζην" (Nikephoritzen)</note>] There is a type of diminutive used by modern Greeks seen in this name, **Nicephoritzes**, instead of **Nicephorus**. Cedrenus has similar names, such as **Theophilitzes**, **Diakonitzes**, and so on. Another type ends in **-akios**; for instance, **Basilakios**, whose name is actually **Basileios** (Basil). A third type is composed from the word for "colt" or "son" <note>original: "πῶλος" (polos)</note> and another word: thus Cedrenus wrote **Kometopoulos**, and the author on the following page (852) wrote **Longibardopoulos**, meaning the "son of a Lombard," or if I may say so, a **little Lombard**. **GOAR.**

*In the same place, line 4.* [**of a secretary** <note>original: "σεκρεταρίου" (sekretariou)</note>] Meursius wants this to be the same as the **asecretis** <note>original: "τὸν ἀσηκρῆτις" (ton asekretis)</note>, who is more frequently considered a judge. But since this person is described as **having served the father of Michael**, he should be identified as the prince's private secretary rather than a judge whose work is devoted to the people. **GOAR.**

*Volume 2, page 714, line 12.* [**foundax** <note>original: "φούνδακα" (phoundaka)</note>] This refers to a table for business or banking, or a money-lender's workshop. It is called this from the Italian *fundaco*, derived **from the fund** <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ φούνδου" (apo tou phoundou)</note>—that is, from a sum of money—a word known to Greek legal experts. **GOAR.**

*Volume 2, page 720, line 5.* [**the Frank, Robert** <note>original: "Φράγγον Ῥουμπέρτον" (Phrangon Roumperton)</note>] This refers to **Robert Guiscar-** <note>Goar likely refers to the Norman adventurer Robert Guiscard, a major figure in Byzantine-Norman conflicts.</note>

# ANNOTATIONS

### Page 889

...he understands the famous Duke of the Normans <note>Likely referring to Robert Guiscard (c. 1015–1085), the Norman adventurer who conquered Southern Italy and Sicily.</note>, who liberated Campania, Calabria, Apulia, and Sicily from the tyranny of the Saracens, Greeks, and Italians. This is discussed at length by Pandolfo Collenuccio, Leo of Ostia, Fazello, and the *Norman Annals*. **GOAR.**

*In the same place, line 7. Longibardia* <note>original: "ἡ Λογγιβαρδία"</note>] that is, Apulia and the adjacent provinces, which were the last territories ruled by the Greeks in Italy. Recall the note on page 577 C. **GOAR.**

*Volume 2, page 725, line 4. Produce* <note>original: "γεννημάτων" (gennematon)</note>] The *Euchologion* <note>The primary liturgical service book of the Eastern Orthodox Church, containing the rituals for the sacraments and various blessings.</note> and *Greek Law* use the term **produce** <note>original: "γεννήματα"</note> to refer primarily to legumes and whatever is sown. **GOAR.**

*In the same place, line 23. Resources* <note>original: "τοὺς βίους" (tous bious)</note>] More recent interpreters translate **life** <note>original: "βίον"</note> not merely as a lifespan, but also as the **wealth, craft, and means** by which one lives. It is clear that these are meant here, given the condemnation of the emperor’s greed. **GOAR.**

*Volume 2, page 727, line 17. The Immortals* <note>original: "ἀθανάτους" (athanatous)</note>] Just as among the ancient Roman legions there were titles like "The Victorious," "The Pious," "The Thunderer," or "The Fortunate," or perhaps the **Magnanimous** <note>original: "τῶν μεγαθύμων"</note> based on some past event (as mentioned in the *Register of Offices* <note>original: "Imperii Notitia," a document from late antiquity detailing the administrative organization of the Eastern and Western Roman Empires.</note>), so this regiment—vainly promising itself immortality in battle even as the Empire aged and verged toward death—was so named. **GOAR.**

*Volume 2, page 733, line 5. Of the Caliph* <note>original: "τοῦ Χαλιφᾶ"</note>] Kedrenos, in his account of Monomachus (p. 775), calls the "Seriph" the second after the Caliph, as the successor to his dignity. Leunclavius, in his *Onomasticon*, interprets the term **Caliph** <note>original: "Calipham" or "Halife"</note> as a **vicar, lieutenant, heir, or successor**. He states: *'Halife Lullahe' means the vicar of God, acting in God's stead on earth. 'Halife Muhamedum' means the heir of Muhammad, the successor of Muhammad. This is what the ancient kings of the Hagarenes* <note>A historical term for Muslims, referring to the tradition of descent from Hagar.</note> *called themselves. This was the title Shah Ismail sought to hold. Finally, the princes of the Turks adorn themselves with this same title.* **GOAR.**

*In the same place, line 14. Among the urban and common people* <note>original: "ὅσον ἐν ἀστικοῖς καὶ δημοτικοῖς"</note>] I explain this as follows: those who flocked together from the common populace or from the leaders of the districts, guilds, and political factions; for it was stated in the notes on Kedrenos that **demotikous** <note>original: "δημοτικούς"</note> signifies such people. **GOAR.**

*In the same place, line 17. Inaugural rites* <note>original: "ἐπιβατηρίων" (epibaterion)</note>] **First attempts, the inauguration of a work, the dedication of an action, beginnings, as well as happy omens** are called **inaugural rites** <note>original: "ἐπιβατήρια"</note>. Kedrenos wrote an **inaugural prayer** <note>original: "ἐπιβατήριον εὐχήν"</note> following the first emperor to be inaugurated with auspicious vows. Synesius also writes in *Letter 57*: *Thus the city welcomed us with such bitter inaugural rites.* Here, the **inaugural rites of the Annunciation** are the sacred beginnings and auspices of the Feast of the Annunciation. **GOAR.**

*Volume 2, page 734, line 7. On the Sabbath* <note>original: "τῷ σαββάτῳ"</note>] Among the Greeks, that Sabbath is the vigil of Palm Sunday <note>Commonly known as Lazarus Saturday, celebrating the resurrection of Lazarus.</note>. **GOAR.**

*In the same place, line 8. It is celebrated* <note>original: "ἑορτάζεται"</note>] Among the **Feasts of the Lord** <note>original: "δεσποτικὰς ἑορτάς"</note>, the Eastern Church numbers the raising of Lazarus from the dead, commonly called **Lazarus Day** <note>original: "Λαζάρου τὴν ἡμέραν"</note>. **GOAR.**

*Volume 2, page 735, line 1. Great Tuesday* <note>original: "τὴν μεγάλην τρίτην"</note>] The third day of Holy Week; for all the days of that week are called **Great** by the Greeks.

# ANNOTATIONS BY JACQUES GOAR

### Page 890

Zonaras <note>Joannes Zonaras (12th century), a high-ranking Byzantine official and monk who wrote a comprehensive history of the world.</note> writing on Constantine, the son of Leo the Wise: **on the holy day of Great Thursday.** <note>original Greek: "κατὰ τὴν ἱερὰν τῆς μεγάλης πέμπτης ἡμέραν" (kata ten hieran tes megales pemptes hemeran). This refers to Maundy Thursday in the liturgical calendar.</note> **GOAR.**

**Volume 2, page 736, line 8. Element** <note>original: "στοιχεῖον" (stoicheion)</note>] This is an ambiguous word. It has been noted in multiple places regarding Cedrenus <note>George Kedrenos, an 11th-century historian.</note> that it refers not only to a physical element or a letter of the alphabet, but rather to **fate, lot, prophecy, a guardian spirit, the power of portending, or an omen.** Since the author never writes "the 'N' element" <note>original: "τὸ ν στοιχεῖον"</note> but rather "the element of 'N'" <note>original: "στοιχεῖον τοῦ ν"</note>, I conclude it should be understood in the latter sense rather than the former. His meaning is as follows: those who superstitiously observed the initial letters of the names **Nicephorus** and **Bryennius** <note>Nicephorus III Botaniates and his rival, the general Nicephorus Bryennius the Elder, who both vied for the throne in the late 1070s.</note> as they struggled for the empire, claimed that the fatal omen in the letter **N** prevailed over the fate of **B**. They believed the spirit and fate tied to the **N** was "straight," like the lines of the letter itself, whereas the **B** was an unlucky omen because of its two "humps" <note>original: "gibbos"</note> twisted away from a straight line. Furthermore, it is remarkable how much the Greeks attended to superstitious prophecies as the Empire declined, so much so that even emperors and nobles could not restrain themselves from them; Cedrenus, Nicetas <note>Nicetas Choniates (c. 1155–1217), a Byzantine civil servant and historian.</note>, and Gregoras <note>Nicephorus Gregoras (c. 1295–1360), a scholar and historian.</note> mention this frequently. **GOAR.**

**Volume 2, page 738, line 14. All-Holy** <note>original: "πανάγιον" (panagion)</note>] Greek monks call one another **holy** <note>original: "ἁγίους" (hagious)</note>, just as Latin monks call each other **brothers** <note>original: "fratres"</note>. Consequently, they addressed this man as "All-Holy," as if he were shining with a special degree of sanctity. To us, these Greek titles seem like "monsters of honor" <note>Goar likely means these titles feel excessively grand or strange to a Western ear.</note>. **GOAR.**

**Volume 2, page 741, line 1. Fountain** <note>original: "βρύσις" (brysis)</note>] Today, the common Greeks generally call a spring or fountain a **brysis** or **bryse**. Thus, the "Fountain of Basilacius" <note>Nicephorus Basilacius, a general who rebelled in 1078. After his defeat, he was blinded.</note> was the name given to the place where the blood burst forth from his gouged-out eyes. **GOAR.**

**Volume 2, page 742, line 15. His statue** <note>original: "ἡ στήλη αὐτοῦ" (he stele autou)</note>] Meaning his statue. **GOAR.**

**Volume 2, page 744, line 3. Concerning the money belonging to the Empress** <note>original: "περὶ τῶν τῇ βασιλίδι διαφερόντων χρημάτων" (peri ton te basilidi diapheronton chrematon)</note>] If these words do not prove that he was the <term>Logothete of the Treasury</term> <note>The *Logothetes tou genikou* was the official in charge of the general tax and the state treasury.</note>, then one might as well go looking for a second sun in a clear sky at high noon <note>A Latin idiom meaning the fact is "blindingly obvious."</note>. **GOAR.**

<meta>This page transitions from the historical annotations of Jacques Goar to a philological glossary compiled by Charles Annibal Fabrot. While Goar’s work focused on the context of the events in Cedrenus's history, Fabrot provides a lexicon—a "Glossarium"—to explain the difficult Greek vocabulary and administrative terminology used by the historian, often drawing parallels between Greek and Latin legal or ecclesiastical traditions.</meta>

# FABROT'S GLOSSARY
## OR THE INTERPRETATION OF OBSCURE WORDS
### IN CEDRENUS.

**Abbas, abbadion** <note>original Greek: Ἀββᾶς, ἀββάδιον</note> abbot or abba, father. <note>From the Latin *pater*.</note> Novella 123. Jeremiah, Patriarch of Constantinople, in his second response to the Lutheran theologians of Tübingen regarding monastic life: <note>original Greek: "οὓς ἀββάδας καὶ ἀρχιμανδρίτας ἡ τάξις ὠνόμασεν" (ous abbadas kai archimandritas he taxis onomasen)</note> **"those whom the church order named abbots and archimandrites."** <term>Archimandrite: a high-ranking official in the Eastern Church who supervises several monasteries.</term> St. Benedict, in his *Harmony of the Rules*, chapter 34: **"who is also the superior [maior] of the monastery."** From this we get **abbatia** <note>original Greek: ἀββατία</note>, meaning paternity. The Council of Meaux, canon 10: **"let such an abbey [abbatia], which in the Latin name is called 'paternity,' be fundamentally removed."** From this, used with contempt, comes **abbadion** <note>original Greek: ἀββάδιον</note> or "little abbot." Stylianos writing to Pope Stephen (found in the Acts of the 8th Council of Constantinople): **"he associated with a certain ignoble and obscure little abbot [abbadion], who was both a conjurer and a magician."** A previous translator rendered this as: *“he had joined to himself a certain obscure and ignoble little abbot, moreover a trickster and a mage.”*

**Abēnai** <note>original Greek: ἀβῆναι</note> reins. <note>A Greek transliteration of the Latin *habenae*.</note> Theophanes writes: <note>original Greek: "δι’ ἀβηνῶν μαστιγῶσαι" (di’ abenon mastigosai)</note> **"to scourge with reins."** Anastasius the Librarian, in an unpublished ecclesiastical history: **"to strike with a rein or a rod."** Cited in the Laws (Digest, on the Silanian Decree of the Senate): **"to an underage person."** In the Glosses of Cyril: *lōros* <note>original Greek: λῶρος</note> is defined as **"rein"** (written as *havena* for *habena*). Also: *himas* <note>original Greek: ἱμάς</note> is **"rein."**

**Adnoumion** <note>original Greek: ἀδνούμιον</note> a levy, census, or enrollment of soldiers. <note>Derived from the Latin *ad nomen*, "to the name" or roll call.</note> Constantine [Porphyrogenitus] in his *Tactics*: <note>original Greek: "ἁρμόζει δὲ καὶ εἰς τὸν καιρὸν τῆς ῥόγας καὶ τοῦ ἀδνουμίου ἀδνουμιάζεσθαι καὶ ἀπογράφεσθαι" (harmozei de kai eis ton kairon tes rogas kai tou adnoumiou adnoumiazesthai kai apographesthai)</note> **"it is also fitting at the time of the distribution of pay and the muster [adnoumion] for the troops to be mustered and enrolled."** Leo the Wise in his *Tactics*, constitution 9, section 4: **"if ever necessity calls for this to be done for the sake of a muster."** See also the lexicons of Suidas, Phavorinus, and the Glosses on the *Basilica* <note>a collection of Byzantine laws</note>.

**Aerikon** <note>original Greek: ἀερικόν</note> a tribute or tax for the "aerial spirit." <note>The *aerikon* was a notorious and often arbitrary Byzantine tax; the name suggests something collected "from the air."</note> The legal scholar Cuiacius notes this. Leo the Wise in his *Tactics*, chapter 20, section 71: <note>original Greek: "ἀρκεῖ γὰρ αὐτοῖς τελεῖν τούς τε δημοσίους φόρους καὶ τὰ ἐπικείμενα αὐτοῖς ἀερικά, καὶ μηδὲν πλέον καταβαρεῖσθαι" (arkei gar autois telein tous te demosion phorous kai ta epikeimena autois aerika...)</note> **"for it is enough for them to pay the public taxes and the 'air-taxes' imposed on them, and not to be weighed down any further."** This is a passage that a previous translator did not understand. It seems to agree with the interpretation of Procopius in his *Secret History* [Anecdota], as a type of tribute demanded over and above the usual set rule [canon].

**Athanatoi** <note>original Greek: ἀθάνατοι</note> the **"Immortals,"** as they were called among the Persians. <note>An elite military unit in the Byzantine Empire, modeled after the ancient Persian guard.</note> Procopius, in his *History of the Persian War*, page 22: <note>original Greek: "μόνον δὲ τὸν τῶν ἀθανάτων λεγόμενον λόχον ἡσυχῇ μένειν ἕως αὐτὸς σημήνῃ ἐκέλευσεν" (monon de ton ton athanaton legomenon lochon hesyche menein eos autos semene ekeleusen)</note> **"he ordered only the battalion of those called the 'Immortals' to remain quiet until he himself gave the signal."** See also the historian Socrates Scholasticus (Church History 7.20), the orations of Themistius, and Athenaeus.

<summary>This page contains a scholarly glossary by Charles Annibal Fabrot defining Byzantine Greek terms—ranging from monastic titles like "Abbot" to military and tax terms like "Adnoumion" and "Aerikon"—using historical and legal citations.</summary>
<keywords>Fabrot, George Kedrenos, Byzantine administration, Abbas, Aerikon, military muster, Immortals, tax history, monasticism, etymology</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Fabrot’s philological glossary for the works of the historian Cedrenus. Following the previous page's discussion of ecclesiastical titles like "Abbot," Fabrot here moves into terms regarding specific monastic orders, civil rebellion, and everyday Byzantine life, such as currency exchange and transportation.</meta>

# FABROT'S GLOSSARY

**The Sleepless Ones** <note>original Greek: ἀκοίμητοι (*akoimētoi*)</note> *sleepless monks*. <note>The Acoemetae were a class of monks who celebrated the divine office without interruption, day and night, by dividing into choirs that relieved one another.</note> *The Series of the Bishops of Byzantium*, Greek Law, page 298: **"and a monk from the Sleepless Ones."** Council of Florence, page 723, edition R: **"in the monastery of the Sleepless Ones."** Theophanes: **"a monk from the monastery of the Sleepless Ones."** Nicephorus Callistus 15:23: **"having established monks there from the monastery of the Sleepless Ones."** Letter 141 of Theodoret is addressed to **"Marcellus, archimandrite of the Sleepless Ones,"** and their monastery is called *Acoemetense* in Latin. Victor in his *Chronicle*: **"Primasius is also relegated to the Acoemetense monastery."** Pope John in a letter to Justinian: **"who was from the Cumitense monastery."** Cujas correctly emended this to **"from the Acumitense."** The same Victor: **"by the monks of the Achimitensian monasteries."** Read this as *Acumitensium* or *Acoemetensium*.

**Follower** <note>original Greek: ἀκόλουθος (*akolouthos*)</note> see **Varangians** <note>original Greek: βάραγγοι (*barangoi*)</note>. <note>The Akolouthos, or "Follower," was a high-ranking court official, often the commander of the Varangian Guard who followed the Emperor.</note>

**Rebellion** <note>original Greek: ἀνταρσία (*antarsia*)</note>. Theophanes writing on Phocas: **"for he heard of a rebellion being planned in Africa against Phocas,"** <note>original Latin: *meditatam adversus Phocam rebellionem*</note>. **Rebel** <note>original Greek: ἀντάρτης (*antartēs*)</note> *one who affects a tyranny.* The same Theophanes on Maurice: **"and the tyrant sent out Alexander, his co-rebel."** <note>original Greek: συναντάρτης (*synantartēs*)</note> A *co-rebel* is an accomplice and participant in a rebellion, translated as *correbellis* by Anastasius the Librarian. Theodore Metochites: **"for which things they accused him of being a rebel."**

**Exchange** <note>original Greek: ἀλλάγιον (*allagion*)</note> or **change** <note>original Greek: ἀλλαγή (*allagē*)</note>, the **exchange of money**. Even today among the Greeks, *allagō* <note>original Greek: ἀλλάγω</note> means **I exchange**.

**Mutual Guarantee** <note>original Greek: ἀλληλέγγυον (*allelengyon*)</note>. See **Zonaras on Basil**, and the **New Constitution of Basil regarding the mutual guarantee of those paying the same tax**, and **Meursius**. <term>Allelengyon: a controversial tax policy introduced by Emperor Basil II, requiring the wealthy to pay the tax debts of their poorer neighbors.</term>

**Horse** <note>original Greek: ἄλογον (*alogon*)</note> *horse, beast of burden*. <note>Literally "irrational [being]," the term replaced the classical "hippos" in common Greek usage.</note> Leo’s *Tactics*, chapter 10, section 5: **"to manage their horses."** Theophanes on Heraclius: **"many of his horses were destroyed."** Nicetas Choniates in *Manuel Comnenus*, book 2: **"loading the spoils onto the horses,"** and regarding the events after the destruction of the city: **"others, mounting the women they had violated onto the horses."** The *Basilica* <note>The Byzantine legal code</note> on law 17 of the Digest concerning the petition of inheritance. Today also among Greeks, *alogon* is **a horse**. In the same way, the Latins used the word *animal* <note>meaning "living creature"</note> for a horse. Julius Firmicus, *Mathesis* book 3, chapter 7: **"those placed in charge of the royal animals [horses]."** The Salic Law, title 19: **"If anyone burns a stable with animals [horses] or a hayloft."** Theodore Studite, in a letter to Plato: **"sitting upon animals [horses], we entered the city."** <note>original Greek: ἀλόγοις (*alogois*)</note>.

**Ambo** <note>original Greek: ἄμβων (*ambōn*)</note> *ambo, pulpit, rostrum*. The *Annals of Fulda*: **"he ascended the ambo in the Basilica of St. Peter, having placed the Gospel upon his head."** Anastasius the Librarian in his *Ecclesiastical History*: **"they anathematized the Council of Chalcedon from atop the ambo."** Council of Laodicea, canon 15: **"those ascending the ambo."** Synod of Constantinople 7, act 1: **"before the most holy ambo of the temple of the most holy Great Church named Sophia [Hagia Sophia]."** Basil on the *Life of Saint Thecla*, Theophanes on Justinian. Nicephorus Callistus 14:10: **"this was placed under the ambo, which is the platform of the readers."**

**Emirate, Emir, to be an Emir** <note>original Greek: ἀμηράδης, ἀμηρᾶς, ἀμηρεύειν (*amēradēs, amēras, amēreuein*)</note>. <note>Byzantine transliterations of the Arabic "Amir."</note> Zonaras: **of Tarsus**...

<summary>This page defines various Byzantine terms, ranging from the "Sleepless Monks" (Acoemetae) and civil rebellion to the linguistic evolution of the word for "horse." It highlights how classical Greek terms shifted into medieval administrative, ecclesiastical, and everyday vocabulary.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Fabrot’s philological glossary for the Byzantine historian Cedrenus, moving from terms related to monasticism and rebellion into administrative, military, and liturgical vocabulary. It maintains the alphabetical sequence of Greek terms starting with alpha.</meta>

-> # GLOSSARY <-

**Emir** <note>original: ἀμηρᾶς (*amēras*)</note>. Latin: *amiras*, *amiraeus*. To act as an emir: **to rule as an emir** <note>original: ἀμηρεύειν (*amēreuein*)</note>. Theophanes, in his history of the Emperor Heraclius: **"the one serving as their emir."** <note>This term was used by Byzantine writers to refer to Arab leaders or commanders.</note>

**Annona** <note>original: ἀννώνα (*annōna*)</note>. The *Legal Glosses* state: **"Annona signifies a provision, a market, and the annual distribution."** Meursius believed the word for **"market"** <note>original: ἀγοράν (*agoran*)</note> should be read as **"stipend"** <note>original: ῥόγαν (*rogan*)</note>, but nothing should be changed: for **"market"** also refers to types of grain provisions, as Casaubon observes in his notes on the first book of Polybius. **"Annona"** also signifies salaries, customs, stipends, food rations, payments, and rewards which are distributed to soldiers, magistrates, or others. <note>The *annona* was originally the Roman grain dole, but evolved into a general term for state-supplied provisions or the taxes used to pay for them.</note> *Novella* 130, chapter 1. Theophilus on the final section regarding military wills. Macarius, *Homily* 26. Vegetius, book 2, chapter 7. Saint Ambrose, letter 27 from book 5. An uncertain author—or perhaps John of Constantinople—in his *Homilies on Matthew*, 51 and 53. Gregory the Great, book 1, letter 20. Anastasius the Librarian, in his *Ecclesiastical History*: *Macedonius, however, ordered a certain Acholius—who had drawn a sword against him at the instigation of his enemies—to receive monthly provisions [annonas].* See the *Basilica* at book 2 of the Code *on partners* and the Greek interpretation of book 19 of the Digest *on witnesses*.

**To Encamp** <note>original: ἀπληκεύειν (*aplēkeuein*)</note>. To pitch camp, to measure out a camp. <note>Derived from the Latin *applicare*.</note> Leo the Wise, *Tactics*, chapter 9, section 37: **"and to safely encamp there."** Theophanes, in his history of Justinian: **"as they were encamping shortly before reaching the city."** From this comes the term for **camps** <note>original: ἄπληκτα (*aplēkta*)</note>. Leo, in the aforementioned chapter 9, section 54. Onosander, *The General*, chapter 9: **"concerning the frequent changing of the camps."**

**Apokreos** <note>original: ἀπόκρεως (*apokreōs*)</note>. The forty days, or the farewell to meat <note>Latin: *carnisprivium*</note>. <note>Apokreos is the Eastern Orthodox equivalent of Carnival or Shrove-tide, specifically the week before Great Lent begins, during which meat is given up.</note> See Filesacus on *Lent*, page 447, and Scorsus on the 15th Homily of Theophanes Cerameus. Nicephorus Gregoras, book 8: **"for it was the season of Apokreos."**

**Apocrisiarius** <note>original: ἀποκρισιάριος (*apokrisiarios*)</note>. <note>An *apocrisiarius* was a high-ranking diplomatic representative or legate, often acting as a permanent ambassador for a Patriarch or the Pope at the Imperial court.</note> Isidore of Pelusium, letter 144, book 4: **"having learned through the imperial legate."** Sixth Synod of Constantinople, act 1: **"the most holy legate Theodore."** The *Menologium* for July: **"legate of the Church of Alexandria."** Latinized as *apocrisiarius* or *apocrisarius*. Facundus of Hermiane, book 4: *from Stephen, deacon and legate [apocrisario] of the Roman church.* Deacon Ferrandus to Anatolius: *the legate of Eutyches,* **"the legate of Eutyches"** <note>original: ἀποκρισάριος τοῦ Εὐτυχοῦς</note>. Council of Chalcedon, act 1. From this comes the term for the office of the legate <note>Latin: *apocrisariatus*</note>. Humbert, *Against the Slanders of the Greeks*: *at the time of his office as legate.* An old translator of the Sixth Synod of Constantinople interprets the term for **"legate's office"** <note>original: ἀποκρισιάριον</note> as *responsalem* <note>meaning a representative or one who delivers responses</note>. Facundus, in the aforementioned book 4: *the representative [responsalem] of the Roman church.* Aimoinus, book 3, chapter 66: *through the representatives [responsales] of Fredegund.* Anastasius the Librarian, in his *Ecclesiastical History*: *the representatives [responsales] of Felix the Roman meeting...* and shortly after: *Felix, however, having discovered what had been done by his legates [apocrisiariis].* Others translate it as "one making responses." Gregory the Great, book 7, letter 5: *our deacon, who was making responses [acting as representative] at his court.* Theophanes: **"the one who delivers the imperial responses."** A "response" is **"apokrisis"** <note>original: ἀπόκρισις</note> in the *Novels* of Justinian. The *Alexandrian Chronicle*: **"and to tell the response to the emperor."** Saint Benedict, abbot of Aniane, in his *Concordance of Rules*, chapter 58: *brothers who are sent for any response.* Therefore, an *apocrisiarius* is a legate of the church, or of princes, or even of a private individual.

**Armament** <note>original: ἀρμάμεντον (*armamenton*)</note>. An armory or arsenal <note>Latin: *armamentum*</note>. Theophanes: **"and he deposited the armament there."** Anastasius the Librarian, in his *Ecclesiastical History*, translates it thus: *and there...*

It illustrates how Latin legal and military vocabulary was absorbed and adapted into Greek during the later Roman and early Byzantine periods.</summary>

--- Page 904 ---
<meta>This page continues Fabrot’s philological glossary for the historian Cedrenus. The previous page discussed military and administrative terms starting with the letter alpha; this page focuses on the evolution of words for weaponry and the titles of high-ranking imperial secretaries.</meta>

-> # FABROT’S GLOSSARY <-

...**established an armament**. **Armory** <note>original: *armamentarium*, ὁπλοθήκη (*hoplothēkē*)</note>. <gloss>Glosses of Cyril: **armory** <note>original: ὁπλοθήκη</note> is an **armory** <note>original: *armamentarium*</note>.</gloss> Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews* book 9, chapter 7: **"And Jehoiada, having opened the armory in the temple..."** Rufinus of Aquileia translates it thus: ***meanwhile Jehoiada, opening the armory***. Add *Novella* 81, chapter 1. Theophanes in his account of Maurice. *Sometimes* **armament** <note>original: ἀρμάμεντον (*armamenton*)</note> is understood as **the weapons themselves**. Leo the Wise, *Tactics* chapter 6, § 28: **"other wagons carrying the armament of each unit of soldiers."** Constantine Porphyrogenitus, *Tactics*: **"and have other wagons carrying the armament."**

**Weapons** <note>original: ἅρματα (*harmata*)</note>. **Arms** <note>original: *arma*</note>. Leo, *Tactics* chapter 19, § 13: **"let them have weapons."** Constantine in his *Tactics*: **"wearing weapons."** Codinus, *On Offices*: **"whether concerning horses or weapons"**, *sive de equis sive de armis*. Also: **"those lacking horses or some weapons"**, *qui equis aut armis nonnullis careant*. Achmes uses this in his *Interpretation of Dreams*, chapters 24, 54, 69, and 156. Thomas Magister: **"The word 'arms' [hopla] refers not only to common weapons [harmata]."** <note>In classical Greek, *harmata* meant chariots, but in the Byzantine era, it became the standard word for weapons, influenced by the Latin *arma*.</note> Legal Glosses: **"'Weapon' [harma] also signifies an 'arm' [hoplon]."** The later Greeks, therefore, used the singular **weapon** <note>original: τὸ ἅρμα</note> and the plural **weapons** <note>original: τὰ ἅρματα</note>. Harmenopulus book 1, title 26, § 12: **"he who stole another’s weapon"**, *qui aliena arma subripuit*. Alexios Rhartouros: **"the strong weapon."** Also: **"it is the greatest weapon against adversaries."** Manuel Moschopulus: **"'Harma' in the singular means a four-horse chariot, but 'harmata' in the plural means weapons."** <note>Moschopulus is a grammarian attempting to maintain classical distinctions against the evolving language of his time.</note> The grammarian is mistaken who denies that **weapon** in the singular can signify **arms**. Eustathius on the *Iliad*, book 2: **"the word 'harma' is also used for a weapon, and this is a Roman usage"** <note>By "Roman," Eustathius refers to the Latin-speaking ancestors of the Byzantine "Romans."</note>. Nikephoros Blemmydes, *Epitome of Logic*, chapter 8: **"the word 'harma' refers to weapons according to the custom of the Romans."** Just as writers of a more recent age used these Greek forms, so too did late Latinity use the word *arma* as a singular or collective. Dositheus Magister in his *Glosses*: ***unarmed, without weapon*** <note>original: *inermis sine arma*</note>. Laws of the Lombards, title 42: ***when he has caused a wound with an arrow or any weapon*** <note>original: *qualibet arma*</note>. From this comes **the armed** <note>original: ἀρμάτοι (*armatoi*)</note> in the books of the *Basilica* and Cedrenus, meaning **armed men** <note>original: *armati*</note>. George of Alexandria in his *Life of Chrysostom*: **"For we do this neither by our own power, nor by the might of horsemen and royal weapons and the multitude of an army."** And **to arm** <note>original: ἀρματοῦν (*armatoun*)</note>. Council of Florence, page 567 of the R. edition: **"that he might provide twenty galleys, armed at all expense."** Alexios Rhartouros, *Doctrine on Holy and Great Friday*, and **unarmed** <note>original: ἐξαρμάτος (*exarmatos*)</note>. *The Precious Crown* [glossary]: **"unarmed, without a breastplate"**, *exarmatus, inermis*.

**Secretariat** <note>original: ἀσηκρητεῖον (*asēkrēteion*)</note>. **A private office** <note>original: *secretarium*</note>. 8th Ecumenical Council, act 4: **"thus they also confessed yesterday in the offices of the secretary."** It seems it should be read as "secretariats" <note>original: ἀσηκρητεῖα</note>: for the translator rendered it as ***in the secretariats***. However, there were various **offices** <note>original: *secretaria*</note>, about which see the entry for **secretum** <note>original: σέκρετον</note>.

**Secretary** <note>original: ἀσηκρήτης (*asēkrētēs*)</note>. Legal Glosses: **"A secretary is the scribe of secret matters"**, *a secretis, a secreta, secretorum notarius*. Procopius, *Persian Wars*, book 2: **"For it happened that the Emperor Justinian had sent John the son of Rufinus and Julian the secretary of secret matters as ambassadors to Chosroes; the Romans call this dignity 'asekretes,' for they have the custom of calling secret things 'secreta'."** The same author in his *Secret History*, page 63 at the end: **"But for those called secretaries, the dignity was not limited to writing the emperor's secret matters, for whom the..."** <note>The text here breaks off mid-sentence.</note>

<summary>This page analyzes the Byzantine evolution of military and administrative terms, specifically how the word for "chariot" (harma) shifted to mean "weapon" under Latin influence, and defines the high-level bureaucratic role of the "asekrētēs" or imperial secretary.</summary>

<keywords>armory, armamentarium, weapons, harmata, asekretes, secretariat, Byzantine administration, philology, Procopius, Leo the Wise, military terminology</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the glossary of administrative and ecclesiastical terms. The previous page ended while discussing the term for an imperial secretary (asecretis), which is a Greek transliteration of the Latin phrase 'a secretis'.</meta>

-> # GLOSSARY <-

...had been appointed. Nicephorus the Patriarch in his *Short History*: **"They proclaimed Artemios as Emperor; he was the secretary of Philippicus, whom they call *asecretis* in the tongue of the Italians [Latin]."** <note>original: ἀσηκρήτης (*asēkrētēs*)</note>. Sixth Synod of Constantinople, Act 2: **"Paul, the most magnificent *asecretis* and royal secretary, said..."** and Act 4: **"Of Diogenes, the most magnificent *asecretis* and royal secretary."** Second Synod of Nicaea, Act 2: **"royal *asecretis*."** Nicephorus, Archbishop of Constantinople, in a letter to Pope Leo: <note>original: *cum igitur aetatem virilem attigissem...*</note> **"When I had reached man's estate and left my youth behind, being occupied in the royal courts, I practiced a certain kind of military service—one not without effort and application, but which is performed by means of hands and pens. For I was among the imperial writers. We know it is a word of the Latin language; they are accustomed to call them *asecretis*."** Landulphus Sagax, book 17: **"Phocas therefore sent Theodorus, the *asecretis*."** The first of this rank is called the **Chief *Asecretis*** <note>original: πρωτοασηκρήτης (*prōtoasēkrētēs*)</note>, or **"First among the Secretaries"** according to Anastasius the Librarian. See the entry for **Chief *Asecretis***.

**Silver** <note>original: ἄσημον (*asēmon*)</note>. **Silver, even when stamped or coined.** Georgius Alexandrinus in the *Life of the Blessed Chrysostom*: **"He gave the gold to the poor and those in need, but the silver he distributed among the churches."** Today the Greeks say *asēmi* for **silver** and *asēmenion* for **silvery** or **made of silver**. Cyril, Patriarch of Constantinople, in his work *Against the Jews*: **"where he had a head of gold, but the hands and chest were silvery."**

**Monastery** <note>original: ἀσκητήριον (*askētērion*)</note>. **A place of asceticism.** Julian the Ancestor, *Novella* 66. Papias: **"An *assisterium* is a monastery in Greek, used for *asceterium* or *asciterium*, as the manuscript codices of Julian have it."** Greek *Menologion* [Calendar of Saints] for March: **"After my passing, this house shall become a monastery for venerable women."** Nicephorus Callistus, book 9, chapter 14: **"who elsewhere—namely, among the Athenians—held his place of exercise [asceterium]."** From this comes the word **Ascetic** <note>original: ἀσκητής (*askētēs*)</note> found in Saint Basil. Theophylactus on Luke chapter 11: **"For the Pharisees seemed like ascetics, set apart from others."** From this comes **Fellow-Ascetic** <note>original: συνασκητής (*synaskētēs*)</note> in Curopalates, page 817, and **Female Ascetic** <note>original: ἀσκήτρια (*askētria*)</note> or **nun**, Julian *Novella* 53. It is derived from **exercise** <note>original: ἄσκησις (*askēsis*)</note>: **for ascetics (or monks) and female ascetics (or nuns) exercise themselves in every kind of piety.**

**Assarion** <note>original: ἀσσάριον (*assarion*)</note>. **A small coin, the *as*.** See the Glossary: an ***as*** is an *assarion* or an *obol*. And an ***assarium*** is an *assarion* or a *nummus*. Cleopatra, in her work *On Weights and Measures*: **"the ounce is called an Italian *tetrassarion* [four assaria]."** Papias: **"The *assarium* is a coin, the *as*, or a type of denarius."**

**Augusta** <note>original: Αὐγοῦστα</note>. **The Empress, wife of the Augustus.** Achmes, *Interpretation of Dreams*, chapter 125. Simocatta, book 8, chapter 13. *The Basilica*, book 1, title 6, chapter 1: **"The Emperor is not subject to the laws, but the Augusta is subject to them."** Theodoret, Letter 138: **"To the most pious and God-loving Augusta."**

**Augustaeum** <note>original: Αὐγουσταιών (*Augustaiōn*)</note>. **The Augustaeum.** *Description of the City of Constantinople*: **"The Augustaeum, the Capitol, the Mint."** Pachymeres, book 9: **"Filling the courtyard of the Augustaeum."** This refers to the **palace of Constantinople**.

**Augustal Prefect** <note>original: Αὐγουστάλιος (*Augustalios*)</note>. **Augustalis.** Paulus, book 35, § 3. For these reasons, he was also the **Prefect of Egypt**. *The Basilica*: **"The Augustalis of Alexandria."** Justinian, *Novella* 23: **"He shall have as an auditor the Augustal..."**

-> # FABROT’S GLOSSARY <-

...[the Gospel]. **Julian to the Augustal Prefect.** <note>The *Augustal* was the high-ranking Roman governor of Egypt.</note> Synesius, Epistle 29 and the end of 105. Isidore of Pelusium, 3.50. Nicephorus Callistus, 10.11. Photius, *Library*, page 259 of the Greek-Latin edition. Theophylact Simocatta, *History of Maurice*, 8.13. John Moschus, *The Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 207: **"from the rank of the Augustal."** Theophanes, Homily 46: **"A Duke of Egypt is ordained, and an Augustal."**

**Lord** <note>original: αὐθέντης (*authentēs*)</note>, meaning **master** <note>Latin: *dominus*</note>. Used by John Cantacuzenus, page 756. Papias: **"authentes: lord, author."** From this comes **authority** <note>original: αὐθεντεία (*authentia*)</note>. Thomas Magister says: **"The word *authentia* is not found in any of the approved orators used for the name of 'dominion'."** John Moschus, *The Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 79: **"He gave the key of the chest to the master."** Alexius Rharturus: **"and your Lordship."** Also, the verb **to rule** <note>original: αὐθεντεῖν</note> and the adverb **authoritatively** <note>original: αὐθεντικῶς</note>. Hesychius: **"To rule means to exercise power."** Codinus in the *Excerpts*: **"The Latins entering the Great Palace authoritatively [by their own right]."** Cyril, Patriarch of Constantinople: **"Sir, that is to say, Lord."** And in Laonicus Chalcondyles, **Great Lord** <note>original: μέγας αὐθέντης (*megas authentēs*)</note>, which refers to **"the Grand Seigneur"** <note>The common European title for the Ottoman Sultan.</note>. Regarding the Empress Sophia Augusta, Anastasius says in his *Ecclesiastical History*: **"Having summoned the money-lenders and the notaries, Sophia Augusta ordered the debt bonds and ledgers to be brought forth. Having read them, she took the ledgers and gave them to the debtors and returned them to their masters."** Cedrenus uses the word **masters** <note>original: αὐθένταις</note>.

**Palms** <note>original: βαΐα (*baïa*)</note>. **Gifts usually given annually by the emperor or patriarch before Palm Sunday, from which they get their name: for a *baïs* or *baïon* is a palm branch.** John, chapter 12. Porphyry, *On Abstinence from Animal Food*. See the homily of Epiphanius **On the Palms**. Dorotheus, Teaching 15: **"with palms."** From this comes **Palm-bearer** <note>original: βαϊοφόρος</note>. Georgius Logotheta in his *Chronicle*: **"He hastened to reach the bridal chamber before the Feast of Palm-bearing."** Which is also called **"the day of palms."** Metaphrastes, *Life of Cyriacus*: **"until the day of palms arrived."** This distribution was not done only once. Theophanes, writing on Apsimar: **"And he stepped on their necks until the end of the first palm-distribution."** <note>Referring to the public humiliation of rivals by Emperor Tiberius III (Apsimar).</note> Cedrenus says almost the same thing in so many words. However, see the later notes for page 446, column B.

**Guardian** <note>original: βαΐουλος (*baïoulos*), from the Latin *baiulus*</note>. The commentator on Sophocles' *Ajax the Whip-Bearer*: **"A tutor and physical trainer, the one called a *baïoulos*."** Balsamon, *Greeko-Roman Law*, page 472: **"We name the physical trainers *baïouloi*."** Theophanes: **"Emperor Theodosius made Antiochus—the Chamberlain and Patrician—his *bagilos* [guardian]."** Thus in manuscript R: but read it as ***baïoulon***. An anonymous author in the *Frankish Annals*: **"King Charles [Charlemagne] with his sons and army returned peacefully to Francia, and sent his son Louis to rule in Aquitaine, placing over him the guardian Arnold, and decently and orderly appointing other ministers suitable for the protection of a child."** *The Miscellaneous History*, book 23: **"which struck and shaved all the captured men of the Emperor, together with John the Protospatharius and his own guardian [baiulus]."** Fredegar the Scholar in his *Chronicle*: **"A certain Otto, son of Bero the domestic, who had been the guardian of Sigebert since his youth."** Aimoin, *Deeds of the Franks*, 4.38: **"The guardian of King Sigebert. A guardian [baiulus] is a tutor or preceptor."**

...advisor, ruler, *governor*. From this comes *baiulatio* <note>original: baiulatio, the office or jurisdiction of a guardian or tutor</note>. Aimoinus, *History*, Book 5, chapter 39: *committing to the guardianship.*

**bandon** <note>original: βάνδον</note>, a banner, flag, or military standard. Pope Hadrian, in an Epistle to Charlemagne the Great: *the Neapolitans looking up to the Greeks themselves with banners and standards.* Anastasius the Librarian, in his *Ecclesiastical History*: *he sent this Hisam in honor of his son and to terrify the emperors, with imperial and fitting honor, with troops and banners <note>The Latin text has "blandis," which the editor notes should be read as "bandis"</note> and scepters to Jerusalem.* Procopius, *On the Vandalic War*, Book 2, page 123: *Entrusting to John the Armenian the shield-bearers and the standard, which the Romans call a **bandon**.* Leo the Tactician, chapter 12, section 62: *the **banda**, that is to say, the standards.* Constantine, in the *Tactics*: *each unit ought to have its own **bandon**.* A commentator on the first *Invective* of Saint Gregory Nazianzen: *the password is the sign and symbol of the army which they call a **bandon**.* **bandora**, a cohort of soldiers, or a detachment <note>original: scara, a mobile, elite military unit in the Frankish tradition</note>. *Acts of the Life of Pope Alexander*, 3: *the standard-bearers ran together with their banners.* Radevicus, 2.66: *with standards and banners preceding, they led him to the palace.* *History of Wamba, King of Toledo*: *that he had approached with the standards of the banners.* Benno the Cardinal, *On the Life of Hildebrand*, Book 1: *and all the soldiers carrying banners.* Anastasius, in his life of Pope Hadrian: *they received him with **bandora**.* From this comes **bandophoroi** <note>original: βανδοφόροι, standard-bearers</note>. Procopius, same location, Book 2, page 134: *the other man, accustomed to carry the general’s standard in the battle-lines, whom the Romans call a **bandophoros**.* Leo the Tactician, chapter 4, section 14: *And a **bandophoros** is the one who carries the sign of the **bandon**.* **Standard-bearers, banner-bearers, also called dragon-bearers <note>original: draconarii; late Roman standards often took the shape of a dragon wind-sock</note>.** The *Roman Order*: *then the dragon-bearer soldiers, that is, those who carry the standards.* Theodoret, Epistle 59: *Patrouinos the dragon-bearer brings this.* See also Epistle 133. **Bandon** also signifies a troop, a detachment, or a wedge of soldiers. *Legal Glosses*: *a military crowd, which the Romans call a **bandon**.* The author of the *Life of Charlemagne* in the *Frankish Annals*: *The lord Charlemagne camped with the Franks at that same place, and sent his detachment.* And on page 19: *arriving at the place of Ingelheim, he sent four detachments.* Finally, **bandon** signifies victory, if we follow Stephanus of Byzantium regarding the city **Alabanda**. *Among the Romans,* he says, *they call victory a **bandon**.*

**Varangians** <note>original: βάραγγοι; the elite personal bodyguard of the Byzantine Emperor</note>, "protectors" according to Cujas, or "ax-bearers." Regarding these, see Codinus, *On the Offices of the Palace*: *to the chiliarch [commander of a thousand] of the 9th cohort of Varangians.* John Cantacuzenus, 1.41: *the Varangians, so called as those who carry axes.* Greek commentators on the Digest, Book 3, section 5, *On the Cornelian Law regarding assassins*: *if a senatorial Varangian kills another senatorial Varangian.* Astrampsychus, in his *Pythagorean Table*, mentions Varangians, magnates, and high officials. These were Celts <note>In Byzantine usage, 'Celt' often broadly referred to Western Europeans, including Norsemen or Normans</note>, as Scylitzes writes in the margin of Cedrenus, page 792, or English, according to Codinus. Their leader is the **Akolouthos** <note>original: ἀκόλουθος, meaning 'The Follower', the commander of the Varangian Guard</note>, as has already been noted.

**bardoukion** <note>original: βαρδούκιον</note>, a staff, javelin, spear, or a weapon that can be thrown. Constantine, in the *Tactics*: *axes, maces <note>original: βαρδούκια</note>, and clubs.*

**basileus** <note>original: βασιλεύς</note>, king, emperor, referring to the king of the present time. <meta>catchword: Zo-</meta>

**and basilis** <note>original: βασιλίς</note> used for *Augusta* (Empress). The same author in the same book says: "the multitude raging against the empress." This is how the Byzantine writers were accustomed to call the emperor. **Annals of the Franks:** "In their own custom, that is, in the Greek language, they sang praises to him, calling him emperor and *basileus*." <note>original Latin: more suo, id est Graeca lingua, laudes ei dixerunt, imperatorem eum et basileum appellantes</note> Almost the same words are used by the author of the *Life of Charlemagne the Great*, by Einhard in his *Deeds of Charlemagne*, and in the **Annals of Fulda.** They called other rulers *rhegas* <note>original: ῥῆγας; a Greek transliteration of the Latin "rex" (king)</note> out of contempt, such as the *rhega* of Francia. See **Liutprand in the Embassy.**

**vergion** <note>original: βεργίον</note>, a rod or staff. **Anastasius the Librarian** in his *Ecclesiastical History*: "he drove them back against the Bulgarians who were armed with slings and rods and were blaspheming." **Leo the Tactician**, chapter 7, § 3: "with shields and rods." And § 18: "handing out rods or canes instead of swords, or reeds instead of spears." **Constantine in the Tactics**: "let them also carry shields and rods." **Menologium** <note>A church calendar of saints' lives</note> for March: "The old man therefore wove fifteen rods <note>The manuscript spelling is 'ouergias'</note> with much labor until the ninth hour."

**bestiarites** <note>original: βεστιαρίτης</note>, see *protovestiarios* <note>A high-ranking court official in charge of the imperial wardrobe</note>.

**vigla** <note>original: βίγλα</note>, a watch or guard post. **Eustathius on the Iliad, book 2**: "He calls the lookout point what is commonly called a *vigla*." **Theophanes**: "having closed the gates of the walls and established guard posts." **Leo the Tactician**, chapter 11, § 9: "to have guard posts on the outside," and chapter 17, § 54: "so that there may be an accurate watch and safety for the rest." From this comes **viglatōr** <note>original: βιγλάτωρ</note>, a watchman or sentry. The same **Leo**, chapter 14, § 16: "with a few watchmen." And **vigleuein** <note>original: βιγλεύειν</note>, to keep watch: **Leo**, same chapter, § 13: "being obliged to keep watch." And the same chapter 17, § 102: "because of those who were keeping watch in every way." Or **viglizein** <note>original: βιγλίζειν</note>, to keep watch: **Constantine in the Tactics**, page 38: "for the purpose of them keeping watch," and on the following page: "so that the cavalry might go ahead and keep watch."

**vixillationes** <note>original: βιξιλλατίωνες</note>, vexillations, cavalry wings. **Glosses of Cyril**: *vixillatio*, a cavalry detachment. Concerning these detachments, see **Vegetius** and **Cujas on the last law of the Code** regarding those who were discharged before completing their military service.

**bisextos** <note>original: βίσεξτος</note>, a leap year. **Anastasius of Antioch**: "when the four-year period of the so-called *bisextos* completes the movement into a full day." **Manuscript Glossary of the most illustrious Chancellor Pierre Séguier**: "leap year: the cycle of a four-year period."

**blattion** <note>original: βλαττίον</note>, purple silk. **Bishop Solomon**:
> "This would have been sweeter to all than talents of silver and gold,
> than silk or gems, purple cloths, or ivory."
**Constantine on the Administration of the Empire**: "such as purple silks." A silk cloth. **Fortunatus**, book 2, poem 3:
> "Whose silk was born with snow-white threads of purple."

**boukellarios** <note>original: βουκελλάριος</note>, a *bucellarius* <note>A private soldier or bodyguard typically in the service of a general or the emperor</note>. **Legal Glosses**: *boukellarios*, one who is sent and brings someone. Also: *boukellarios*, a soldier in service. **Greek Book 60 of the Basilika**: "Those who remain in service as soldiers are called *boukellarioi*. From the name *bouka* <note>original: βούκα</note>, which is bread, they were called *boukellarioi* as those who eat someone's bread for the very purpose of remaining in his service." *Bucellarii* are called stationary soldiers. # GLOSSARY. 899

**Bucellarians** <note>original: bucellarii</note>, those who eat the bread of another in order to serve him. Therefore, the **bucellarians** are bodyguards, protectors, attendants, satellites, squires, followers, and domestic servants of the nobility or the prince. They are also called clients. **Papias** <note>A 10th-century lexicographer</note> writes: "a client is a *bucellarius*." They were also called parasites <note>In the classical sense: those who eat at the table of another</note>. **Aldhelm** in *The Praise of Virginity*: "seeing such great wonders, Claudius the tribune was amazed, and being pricked in his heart, he believed in the Son of God along with seventy soldiers and his whole household and domestic clientele, together with his parasites and companions." <note>original Latin: haec tanta prodigia cernens Claudius tribunus obstupuit, et corde compunctus cum septuaginta militibus et omni familia et vernacula clientela una cum parasitis et sodalibus credidit in dei filium</note> And in the same work: "by his own parasites and domestic clients." <note>original Latin: a propriis parasitis et domesticis clientibus</note> On the theme of the Bucellarians, see **Constantine Porphyrogenitus** <note>Byzantine Emperor and author</note> in *On the Themes of the East*, theme 6, and his *On Administering the Empire*, chapter 51, and **George Codinus** <note>referred to here as Curopalates</note>, page 839.

**boukinator** <note>original: βουκινάτωρ; a trumpeter</note>, a herald or trumpeter. **Theophanes**: "two brothers, lovers of Christ, residing in Tripoli, sons of a trumpeter." <note>original Greek: δύο ἀδελφοί τινες φιλόχριστοι ἐν Τριπόλει καταμένοντες, υἱοὶ βουκινάτορος</note> **Scholia on the Epitome of the Holy Canons**, title 2, section 2: "under the Patriarch Theodosius, a royal trumpeter was baptized." <note>original Greek: ἐπὶ τοῦ πατριάρχου Θεοδοσίου βουκινάτωρ βασιλικὸς βαπτισθείς</note> Derived from the *buccina* or *tuba* <note>trumpet</note>, which the later Greeks called a *boukinon*. **Suidas** <note>A 10th-century Greek encyclopedia</note>: "to practice the voice is to cultivate a beautiful sound, and a *phonasikon* is a trumpet." <note>original Greek: φωνασκεῖν εὐφωνίαν ἀσκεῖν, καὶ φωνασικὸν βούκινον</note> **Glossary of Cyril**: "a trumpet is a *salpinx*, a *litua*, or a *buccinum*." <note>original: σάλπιξ tuba, litua, buccinum</note> Although there is some difference between a *buccina* and a *tuba*.

**bouneuron** <note>original: βούνευρον; literally "ox-sinew"</note>. **Theophanes** writing on Emperor Phocas: "whom the tyrant killed by scourging him with ox-whips." <note>original Greek: ὃν ὁ τύραννος βουνεύροις μαστίξων ἀνεῖλεν</note> And elsewhere: "he ordered him to be struck with a hundred lashes of the ox-whip." <note>original Greek: ἀνὰ ρ' βουνεύρων ἐκέλευσε τύπτεσθαι</note> The **Menologium** for March: "while the holy martyr was ruthlessly cut to pieces for many hours with ox-whips." <note>original Greek: τοῦ ἁγίου μάρτυρος ἐπὶ πολλὰς τὰς ὥρας τοῖς βουνεύροις ἀνηλεῶς συγκοπτομένου</note> **Simeon Metaphrastes** in his account of Sergius and Bacchus: "And he handed Sergius over to a very secure prison, repaying him thus for his service, but he ordered Bacchus to be stretched out tightly by four men and flayed with raw ox-whips." <note>original Greek: καὶ τὸν μὲν Σέργιον ἀσφαλεστάτῃ φρουρᾷ παρεδίδου... τὸν Βάκχον δὲ διὰ τεσσάρων ἰσχυρῶς ἐκταθέντα βουνεύροις ὠμοῖς ἐκέλευε καταξαίνεσθαι</note> **Constantine Manasses**: "he blackened his flesh with raw ox-whips." <note>original Greek: ὠμοῖς βουνεύροις τὰς αὐτοῦ καταμελαίνει σάρκας</note> Also: "he tortured his bright flesh with raw ox-whips." The **Martyrology of Usuard**, October 7th: "whose Bacchus was beaten for so long with raw sinews <note>ox-whips</note> until, with his whole body torn apart, he gave up his spirit in confession." <note>original Latin: quorum Bacchus tam diu est nervis crudis caesus quoadusque totus corpore discissus in confessione emitteret spiritum</note>

**brachionion** <note>original: βραχιόνιον</note>, armlets or bracelets. **Achmetes** <note>author of a book on dreams</note>, chapter 127, *On Dreams*: "if he sees that he received gold armlets." <note>original Greek: ἐὰν ἴδῃ ὅτι βραχιώνια ἔλαβε χρυσᾶ</note>

**galea** or **galaia** <note>original: γαλέα / γαλαία</note>, a trireme or **galley**. **Leo the Tactician**, chapter 19, § 10. **galiatza** <note>original: γαλιάτζα</note> in the *Council of Florence*, page 567, edited by R., a **galleass** <note>a large, heavy galley</note>.

**genikon** <note>original: γενικόν</note>, the public treasury. The official in charge of this was called the *Logothete* of the Genikon <note>equivalent to a Minister of Finance</note>. **Nicephorus Gregoras**, book 7. **Codinus** in *On Offices* records that learned men call the same office *genikon* based on this passage from **Suidas**: "He appointed John as leader of the war, a deacon of the Great Church and an accountant of taxes, whom they call the *Genikos*." <note>original Greek: Ἰωάννην ἐφίστησιν ἡγεμόνα τοῦ πολέμου διάκονον τῆς μεγάλης ἐκκλησίας καὶ λογιστὴν τῶν φόρων, ὃν γενικὸν καλοῦσι</note> I have doubts about this: for **Nicephorus** in his *Short History* writes of the same John: "He appointed as leader over these John, a deacon of the Great Church and an accountant of public taxes, whom custom knows to call the *Logothete* of the Genikon." <note>original Greek: τούτοις ἡγεμόνα ἐφίστησιν Ἰωάννην διάκονον τῆς μεγάλης ἐκκλησίας καὶ τῶν δημοσίων φόρων λογιστήν, ὃν λογοθέτην γενικὸν οἶδε καλεῖν ἡ συνήθεια</note> And so perhaps it should be read in the same author on page 115: "accountant of public [taxes], whom the common folk [call] Logothete..."

<summary>This page defines various Byzantine terms, including the 'bucellarii' (private guards), 'buccinator' (trumpeter), and 'genikon' (the public treasury). It provides numerous historical and hagiographical citations to illustrate how these terms were used in practice, particularly regarding military equipment and administrative titles.</summary>
<keywords>bucellarii, bodyguards, trumpeter, ox-whip, torture, jewelry, galley, treasury, Logothete, Byzantine administration</keywords>

<meta>This page transitions from administrative titles starting with the letter G (gamma) to those starting with D (delta), focusing on high-ranking financial officers, court attendants, and tax systems of the Byzantine Empire.</meta>

# FABROTUS <note>Charles Annibal Fabrot was a 17th-century French jurist known for his editions of Byzantine legal texts.</note> 900

...they call, unless you take *publica* <note>original: δημόσια (demosia)</note> to mean taxes. *Theophanes in the Life of Constantine:* "Theodotos the monk and **General Logothete**." <note>The General Logothete was essentially the Minister of Finance; original Greek: τὸν τε Θεόδωτον τὸν μοναχὸν καὶ γενικὸν λογοθέτην</note> Hence the phrase **from the general offices** <note>original: ἀπὸ γενικῶν (apo genikon)</note>, referring to one who has held that office. *John Skylitzes at the beginning of his history:* "Of Emperor Nikephoros, who was **from the general offices**." <note>original Greek: Νικηφόρου βασιλέως τοῦ ἀπὸ γενικῶν</note> *The Old Chronology:* "Nikephoros, the one **from the general offices**." <note>original Greek: Νικηφόρος ὁ ἀπὸ γενικῶν</note> *The same words appear in the 8th Synod, page 348 of the Roman edition.*

**Petitions, the Master of Petitions** <note>original: δεήσεις, ὁ ἐπὶ τῶν δεήσεων (deeseis, ho epi ton deeseon)</note>. A master of petitions or legal appeals. *George of Alexandria in the Life of Saint Chrysostom:* "Having given the **petitions** to the emperor." <note>original Greek: δοὺς τὰς δεήσεις τῷ βασιλεῖ</note> *A Greek manuscript author cited by the most learned Allatius in his second dissertation on Church books:* "Of John, Master and **Official over Petitions**." <note>original Greek: Ἰωάννου μαγίστρου καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν δεήσεων</note> I shall discuss the *referendarius* and *regendarius* <note>Two other types of officials who handled petitions and reports</note> in the *Legal Glossary*.

**Deans** <note>original: δεκανοί (dekanoi)</note>. Deans. See the title in the *Justinian Code* regarding deans. *Blessed Chrysostom in his commentary on Paul's Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 7, homily 13, page 505 of the English edition:* "And they occupy the place of the so-called **deans** in the palaces." <note>original Greek: καὶ τῶν λεγομένων δεκανῶν τόπον ἐπέχοντες ἐν τοῖς βασιλείοις εἰσί</note> *Flotilda in her Visions:* "And she heard a voice saying that these were the archdeacons, provosts, judges, elders, and **deans**." *Blessed Ambrose, book 5, letter 35: "Because they were sending **deans** from the palace to the Portian basilica."*

**Informer, to inform** <note>original: δηλάτωρ, δηλατορεύειν (delator, delatoreuein)</note>. An informer or denouncer. *Ulpian, in his commentary on the speech against Timocrates*, interprets the term "the one who brings forward" <note>original: τὸν προσαγωγέα</note> as an **informer**. *Theodoret, letter 43:* "And having undertaken the work of an **informer**." <note>original Greek: καὶ δηλάτωρος ἔργον δεξάμενος</note> He also uses this in letter 45. *George of Alexandria in the Life of Saint Chrysostom:* "It happened that through some devilish envy, this unfortunate widow was **denounced** to the ears of Emperor Theodosius." <note>original Greek: ἔτυχε δὲ κατά τινα φθόνον διαβολικὸν δηλατορευθῆναι ταύτην τὴν ἄωρον χήραν εἰς τὰς ἀκοὰς Θεοδοσίου τοῦ βασιλέως</note>

**Steward** <note>original: διαιτάριος (diaitarios)</note>. A hall-warden or servant of the living quarters. *The Glossary of Philoxenus:* hall-warden <note>original Latin: atriensis</note> is a **steward** or **master of the quarters**. *Theophanes:* "A certain Eutychianos, the first of the **stewards**." <note>original Greek: Εὐτυχιανὸς δέ τις πρῶτος τῶν διαιταρίων</note> *An old inscription, page 576, entry 7: "Steward of the Augustan house." And in the history of Heraclius:* "Many of the **stewards** of the palace were also arrested." <note>original Greek: ἐκρατήθησαν δὲ καὶ ἐκ τῶν διαιταρίων τοῦ παλατίου πολλοί</note> *The Menology for July 30th:* "He is carried away by the **stewards** of the Great Palace." <note>original Greek: ὑπὸ τῶν διαιταρίων τοῦ μεγάλου παλατίου ἀποκομίζεται</note> *The Martyrology of Notker: "Who, since he was the **zaetarius** <note>A phonetic misspelling of diaetarios</note> of the palace..."* (using *zaetarius* for *diaetarius*, just as *zabolus* is used for *diabolus* [devil] in Phoebadius's work against the Arians, and in Gildas the Wise).

**Dikerton** <note>original: δικέρατον; literally "two keratia"</note>. A tax instituted by Leo the Iconoclast for the purpose of repairing the old walls. See, however, Constantine Manasses, page 93, regarding Nikephoros. Theophanes also mentions this below under the entry for **administrator**. *Anastasius the Librarian in his Ecclesiastical History:* "But the emperor addressed the people, saying, 'You are not able to rebuild the walls, but we command the administrators, and they shall exact by rule every year one silver coin, which the empire having received, rebuilt the walls; and thus the custom was established of giving **two silver pieces** <note>original Latin: binas siliquas; siliqua is the Latin equivalent of the Greek keration</note> to the administrators.'"

**Dictator** <note>original: δικτάτωρ</note>. A dictator. *Polybius page 237 d, 238 c. Diodorus Siculus page 127 at the end of volume 2, and page 919. Also Paeanius's translation of Eutropius, page 67.*

**Administrator** <note>original: διοικητής (dioiketes)</note>. A tax collector or public official. *Theophanes:* "From then on, the custom prevailed of giving the **dikerton** tax to the **administrators**." <note>original Greek: ἐντεῦθεν οὖν ἐπεκράτησεν ἡ συνήθεια διδεῖν τὰ δικέρατα τοῖς διοικηταῖς</note> Anastasius translates this as "administrator" in the passage cited above. *Pope Hadrian in a letter to Charlemagne: "Two envoys of the Greeks," he says...*

<summary>This page defines various Byzantine administrative and court titles, including financial logothetes, palace deans, and the specific "dikerton" tax used to maintain city walls. It emphasizes the etymology and historical usage of these terms across Greek and Latin sources.</summary>
<keywords>Logothete, Master of Petitions, Dekanoi, Delator, Diaitarios, Dikerton, Dioiketes, Byzantine administration, taxation, palace officials</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the glossary of Byzantine administrative and ecclesiastical titles, specifically focusing on terms beginning with the letter Delta, such as diptychs, domestics, dukes, and drungaries.</meta>

# GLOSSARY 901

*...the emperor's sword-bearers with the administrator <note>original: dioecete</note>, who in Latin is called the arranger <note>original: dispositor</note>.*

**Diptychs** <note>original: δίπτυχα (diptycha)</note>. In these were inscribed the names of the bishops. Constantine Pogonatus in a letter to Pope Domnus (found in volume 3 of the Greek Councils, page 7, Roman edition): "to cast out the most blessed Vitalian from the **diptychs**." <note>original: ἐκ τῶν διπτύχων; removal from the diptychs was a form of excommunication where a name was no longer read during the liturgy</note> The Synod of Mopsuestia, the acts of which are found in the 5th Synod, act 5: "The name of the elder Theodore was removed from the **diptychs**." <note>original: Theodori antiqui nomen eiectum est diptychis</note> Facundus of Hermiane in book 4: "I recognized the name of John written in the **sacred diptychs**." <note>original: sacris diptychis</note> The same author calls it the "catalogue of bishops" in book 8: "that Bishop Atticus should order his name to be removed from the **catalogue of bishops**." <note>original: ex catalogo episcoporum</note> Saint Cyril refers to it as the "**priestly catalogue**" <note>original: ἱερατικὸν κατάλογον</note> in a letter to Atticus found in Nicephorus Callistus, 14.26. Saint Chrysostom calls it the "**book of bishops**" <note>original: βίβλον ἐπισκόπων</note> in letter 125. They were called diptychs because they were double-folding tablets; on one side the names of the living were written, and on the other, the names of those who had died. Georgius of Alexandria, in his *Life of Chrysostom*, understands this as a "**two-leaved writing tablet**" <note>original: γραμματεῖον δίθυρον</note>: "And John, taking a **diptych**, wrote to Epiphanius," meaning the double tablets on which Chrysostom wrote his letter.

**Domestic of the Church** <note>original: δομέστικος τῆς ἐκκλησίας</note>. An official of the church. See the *Liturgy of Orders*, part 7, regarding the consecration of a bishop, and Meursius under this entry. **Domestic of the Schools**, **military leader**, **prefect**; the Domestic of the Schools <note>The Domestic of the Schools was one of the highest military ranks in the Byzantine Empire, commanding the elite guard units</note>. Constantine Manasses writes:
-> This man appointed Bardas Phokas as military leader, <-
-> whom the Romans would call the Domestic of the Schools. <-
The *Historia Miscella*, book 22: "Antonius, patrician and **domestic of the schools**." <note>original: scholarum domesticum</note> We shall discuss the various "Domestics" further in the *Legal Glossary*.

**Duke** <note>original: δούξ (doux)</note>. A leader, a commander of soldiers, a commander of the military registers, or a camp prefect. Legal glosses: "A **duke** is a leader." <note>original: δούξ ἡγεμών</note> Constantine, *On the Themes*, book 1: "under a **duke** and leader." Procopius, *Persian Wars*, book 1: "but no commander of the Roman soldiers, whom they call a **duke**." <note>original: δοῦκα</note> And in *On Buildings*: "Having established there a commander of the military registers, whom they call a **duke**." <note>original: δοῦκα</note> Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, 9.5: "the **camp prefect** whom the Romans address as a **duke**." <note>original: στρατοπεδάρχης ὃν δοῦκα</note> John Kantakouzenos, book 4: "When Chios was held—as we have related—unjustly by the Genoese during a truce, the Emperor sent word to its ruler, who is locally addressed as a **duke**." <note>original: δοῦκα</note> Nicephorus Callistus, 7.26. Harmenopoulos, book 1.16, last section: "Any audacity against a **duke** or the commander of the soldier brings capital punishment." Arrius Menander, in book 6 *On Military Matters*, had said: "against a **duke** <note>original: ducem</note> or governor." See the *Glosses of the Basilica*.

**Drungary** <note>original: δρουγγάριος (droungarios)</note>. A commander of a *drungus* <note>A military unit, typically a battalion-sized division of a 'turma'</note>, a tribune, or the commander of a single squadron. Legal glosses: "A **drungary** is a **chiliarch**" <note>A commander of a thousand men; original: χιλίαρχος</note>. Also: "the ancients called the commander of one division or squadron a **drungary**." An old inscription: "To Gregoras, royal squire and former **drungary**." Page 1161, 2. There were several types, among whom some were "**Great**" <note>original: μεγάλοι</note>, such as the prefect of naval affairs, the **drungary of the fleet**, called by Cedrenus the **drungary of the naval force**, the commander of the fleet. Anna Comnena, *Alexiad*, book 3.

<summary>This page defines key Byzantine titles including 'diptycha' (liturgical tablets), 'domesticus' (civil and military officials), 'doux' (military commanders/dukes), and 'droungarios' (naval and land battalion commanders).</summary>
<keywords>diptychs, domesticus, domestic of the schools, doux, duke, droungarios, drungary, Byzantine military ranks, ecclesiastical terminology, Constantine Phokas, Chios</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical glossary of Byzantine terms, moving from naval and military ranks like the drungarius to religious terms such as encaenia (dedications) and enkleistos (enclosed monks).</meta>

# FABROT 902

Nicetas Paphlago in the *Life of Patriarch Ignatius of Constantinople*: "the **drungary** <note>a high-ranking military or naval officer</note> of the imperial fleet." <note>original: ὁ τοῦ βασιλικοῦ στόλου δρουγγάριος</note> The "**drungary of the navy**" in Constantine Manasses and the "**drungary of the watch**" <note>original: δρουγγάριος τῆς βίγλης; Latin: drungarius vigiliae</note>. Constantine Manasses writes: "for he was the drungary of the watch, as the Romans would say." <note>original: βίγλας γὰρ ἦν δρουγγάριος, εἴποιεν ἂν Ῥωμαῖοι</note> The *Miscellaneous History*, book 24: "*and many **protospatharii** <note>literally "first sword-bearers," a high court rank</note> and **spatharii** <note>sword-bearers</note> and the **domestic of the palace guards** <note>the commander of the imperial guards</note> and the **leader of the ranks**, or **imperial drungary of the watch**.*" It is read more correctly in Anastasius the Librarian’s *Ecclesiastical History*: "*and even the **leader of the ranks** and the **domestic of the palace guards** or **drungary of the watch**.*" Regarding the **drungary of the Cibyrrhaeots** <note>the commander of a major naval district in southern Asia Minor</note>, see Cedrenus in the section on Leontius, Nicephorus in his *Historical Brief*, and Theophanes. See also the *Glossary of the Basilika* <note>The Basilika was a massive 9th-century collection of Byzantine laws</note>.

**drungos, drungisti.** <note>original: δροῦγγος, δρουγγιστί</note> A **drungos** is a mass or "globe" of soldiers. Leo the Wise's *Tactics*, chapter 13, section 3: "by **drungoi** and by **turmae** <note>military divisions or squadrons</note>." Vegetius, book 3, chapter 16: "*a leader ought to know against which **drungoi**, that is, masses of the enemy [he fights].*" This is the reading in the ancient manuscript of the most illustrious Nicolas Fabri. From this, the word is used for a "mass of monks" in Blessed Chrysostom's 14th letter: "**a drungos of monks**." <note>original: δροῦγγος μοναζόντων</note> For it is necessary to speak thus and to show their madness by the very word. From this comes **drungisti**. Leo's *Tactics*, chapter 18, section 144: "suddenly leaping out also in what is called **drungos-style**." <note>original: δρουγγιστί</note> This means: *immediately, in a mass.*

**hebdomon.** <note>original: ἕβδομον</note> Nicephorus in his *Historical Brief*: "and barely reaching the field before the city which they call the **Seventh**." Also: "near the seaside place called the **Seventh**." It refers to the **seventh mile-marker** <note>a famous suburb of Constantinople located seven Roman miles from the city center, often used for military gatherings and imperial coronations</note>.

**encaenia.** <note>original: ἐγκαίνια</note> Dedication or renewal ceremonies. Isidore, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, book 1, chapter 35: "*whenever anything new has been dedicated, it is called **encaenia**.*" Nicephorus Callistus, 8.3 and 18. The Scholiast of Euripides on *Orestes*: "**encaenia** is that which is in a state of renewal." Theophanes: "the **dedication** of the Holy Apostles took place." Marcellinus the Count in his *Chronicle*: "*The **dedications** of the baths, as they are called, were performed.*" Anastasius the Librarian in his *Ecclesiastical History*: "*In the month of June, the **dedication** of the Holy Apostles was performed at Constantinople, and the **relics** <note>original: lipsana</note> of the apostles Andrew, Luke, and Timothy were stored there; and Bishop Mennas passed by with the holy relics, sitting in a golden imperial carriage decorated with precious stones, holding three chests of the Holy Apostles on his knees, and thus he celebrated the **dedication**.*" From this comes the verb **to dedicate** <note>original: encaeniare</note>. Blessed Augustine, tractate 48 on John.

**enkleistos.** <note>original: ἔγκλειστος</note> A monk, **enclosed**, or **recluded** <note>refers to an ascetic who lived permanently locked inside a small cell</note>. Theophanes in the section on Justinian: "an **enclosed monk** of the same monastery." And in the section on Constantine Copronymus: "so that all the monks, both the **enclosed** and the **column-dwellers** <note>original: κιονίτας (kionitas) or stylites</note>." Anastasius the Librarian translates this as "*the **enclosed** and the **column-dwellers***": for you will always find *inclausum* written for *incluso* in his work. Theodore of Hermopolis, book 7, title 8, explaining these words of the law from the *Digest* (2.4.2) "*nor those who, on account of the religion of a place, cannot move themselves from there,*" says: "nor," he says, "those who are unable to depart from it due to the religion of the place, namely **enclosed monks** or **church-wardens** <note>original: προσμοναρίους (prosmonarious)</note>." John Moschus, *The Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 50: "he told us about the Abbot George the **enclosed**." Theodore the Studite, *Catechesis* 38: "*first a **pillar-dweller** <note>original: stylita</note>, and then made an **enclosed one**.*" <note>original: clusius</note> And in the testament of the same, Livineius...

<summary>This page defines Byzantine military and administrative ranks like the 'drungary' and explores the religious terminology of 'encaenia' (dedications) and 'enkleistos' (enclosed monks). It cites various historical sources to show how these Greek terms were adapted into Latin and used in the imperial court and church.</summary>
<keywords>drungarius, drungus, military ranks, encaenia, church dedication, relics, enkleistos, stylite, enclosed monks, Byzantine administration</keywords>
