<meta>This page continues the alphabetical glossary of Byzantine terms from page 902, focusing on ecclesiastical and administrative titles, including "ekdikos" (church defender) and "exarchos" (commander), as well as theological edicts like the "Henotikon."</meta>

# GLOSSARY

<page-num>903</page-num>

translates *clusium*, in Greek **enkleiston** <note>original: ἔγκλειστον</note>, for one who is enclosed. Peter Damian, in letter 19 of book 1: *in the letter sent to the lord Therson, the **recluse** <note>original Latin: inclusum</note>.* Fredegar the Scholastic in his *Chronicle*: *Sigebert, the **recluse** <note>original Latin: reclusum</note> of the basilica of Saint Dionysius the martyr.* From this comes **enkleisterion** <note>original: ἐγκλειστήριον</note> for a monastery. John Moschus in the *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 69: "in which part the **enclosure** <note>original: ἐγκλειστήριον</note> of the elder was located." The term *clusa* is used for the same thing by Marianus Scotus in book 3.

**ekdikos** <note>original: ἔκδικος; a legal representative</note>, a **defender of the church** or of church cases. The Second Synod of Nicaea, act 4: "the **defender** <note>original: ἔκδικος</note> of the most holy church of God." The Council of Constantinople under Menna, act 1: "the most devout notaries and **defenders** <note>original: ἐκδίκους</note> of the same apostolic throne of Old Rome who had arrived here." Pope Hormisdas, letter 36: *We took care to send Paulinus, a **defender** <note>original Latin: defensorem</note> of the Roman church, with the present writings.* Anastasius the Librarian in his *Ecclesiastical History*: *A certain Paul, one of the **defenders** <note>original Latin: defensorum</note> of the church.* These are mentioned in the *Code of Canons of the African Church*. There were four of them, who were also called **ecclesiekdikoi** <note>original: ἐκκλησιέκδικοι; church-defenders</note>, as seen in Justinian's *Novels* 56, chapter 1, and edition 13, chapter 10. The Council of Constantinople under Menna, act 2: "John, the most God-fearing priest and **church-defender** <note>original: ἐκκλησιέκδικος</note> of the most holy Great Church, said..." The primary one was called the **protekdikos** <note>original: πρωτέκδικος; "chief defender"</note>. The Council of Florence, session 25: "but also from among the clergy, the Great **Chartophylax** <note>archivist</note> and the **chief defender**." Theodore Balsamon <note>a famous 12th-century canon lawyer</note> refers to canon 85 of the Synod of Carthage, and the same author refers to a **protekdikian book** <note>original: πρωτεκδικικὸν βιβλίον</note> regarding canon 78 of the same Synod.

**henotikon** <note>original: ἑνωτικόν</note>, an edict for the **union** of the churches, authored by Emperor Zeno. The Sixth Synod of Constantinople, act 10: "We accept and praise the orthodox confession of the **Letter of Union** <note>original: ἑνωτικοῦ γράμματος</note> which the Emperor Zeno of most serene memory issued." Theophanes the Confessor: "Macedonius, being wrongly persuaded, signed the **Henotikon** of Zeno." Anastasius the Librarian in his *Ecclesiastical History*: *Then Zeno also issued the **enotesium** <note>original: enotesium; so written in the manuscript</note>, which some say was dictated by Acacius of Constantinople.* However, it is later written as *enotico*, and even *enotitium* in following passages. It appears in Evagrius Scholasticus, book 3, chapter 14.

**exarchos** <note>original: ἔξαρχος</note>, a leader or commander. Constantine Porphyrogenitus, *On the Themes*, chapter 12: "for he was the **exarch** <note>commander</note> of the imperial rank of those called **excubitors** <note>the elite imperial palace guards</note>." I do not know if it should be read as *exarchos*; however, the royal manuscript does not change it. What if you read it as **archon** <note>ruler/leader</note>, as used in Cedrenus: "the **leader** <note>original: ἄρχων</note> of the rank of the excubitors"? **Exarchs of the factions** <note>original: ἔξαρχοι τῶν φατριῶν</note> were the leaders of the political/chariot-racing factions. The *Basilika* <note>the Byzantine law code</note>, in the interpretation of law 16 of the Digest *on appeals*. Anastasius the Librarian translates this as *exarchum* in his *Ecclesiastical History*.

**exerketos** <note>original: ἐξέρκετος</note>, meaning **army** <note>original Latin: exercitus</note>. Legal Glosses: "*exikto* means army." It should be read as *exerkitos*.

**exisotes** <note>original: ἐξισωτής</note>, an **equalizer** or assessor. Thus in the final law of the Code *on censuses*: "both censor and equalizer." Eustathius, in his work *On Chronological Intervals*, interprets the **assessor** <note>original Latin: peraequatorem</note> as an **exisotes**. He was so called because he would correct the census books and divide the burden of taxes among the citizens fairly, taking the census into account. Saint Basil the Great, letter 259: "through our most venerable brother Hellenius, who is **assessing** <note>original: ἐξισοῦντος</note> Nazianzus," and letter 263: "we sent to the most venerable—"

# FABROT'S GLOSSARY

...to his most dear brother Leontius, the **exisotēs** <note>original: ἐξισωτής; an official responsible for equalizing tax assessments</note> of Nicaea; and in letter 278: "so that he might be released from the care of the equalization." This office is nearly the same as the **peræquator** <note>original Latin: peræquator; an equalizer or assessor</note> and the inspector. Regarding the office of inspection, Theodoret writes in letter 43: "and to command that the inspection which has often taken place be confirmed," and in letter 44: "for the inspection having occurred at that time." These were censors who define the tax assessment based on the proportion of what each person possesses. The *Glossary of Philoxenus* defines the **censitor** <note>original Latin: censitor; tax assessor</note> as a registrar or an estimator <note>original: ἀπογραφεύς, τιμητής</note>. See the letters of Saint Basil numbers 304, 352, 353, and 426, and Gregory of Nazianzus's oration concerning Julius the tax assessor.

**exkoubita** <note>original: ἐξκούβιτα</note> for the **excubitors** <note>original Latin: excubitoribus; palace guards</note> or the sentry watches. The *Glossary of Cyril* defines "wakefulness" <note>original: ἀγρυπνία</note> as a watch (*excubitum*). Likewise: a watch is an all-night vigil <note>original: παννυχίς</note>. Nicephorus Callistus in book 17, chapter 40: "being the Count of the **Excubitors** <note>original: ἐξκουβίτων</note>." Anastasius the Librarian in his *Ecclesiastical History*: *but the people of the Scholares <note>elite guards</note> and the **Excubitors**.* From this comes the **excubitorium** <note>original Latin: excubitorium</note> or guardhouse. Anastasius the Librarian in the *Collectanea*: *and they led him into the custody of the guardhouse.*

**exkoubitōr** <note>original: ἐξκουβίτωρ</note>, an **excubitor** <note>original Latin: excubitor; a sentry or imperial guard</note>. Procopius in his *Vandalic War*, book 2: "who led the Excubitors; for thus the Romans call the guards." George of Alexandria in the *Life of the Blessed Chrysostom*: "the queen sends two **Excubitors** <note>original: ἐκσκουβίτωρας</note>." Metaphrastes, for the month of September: "a certain soldier named John among those called **Excubitors**." The *Alexandrian Chronicle*: "the army of **Excubitors** guarding the palace." Emperor Maurice in a letter to Pope Gregory: *in which everyone said your beatitude sent soldiers to them with one tribune and one **excubitor**.* See the notes on the *Basilica* glosses.

**epeiktēs** <note>original: ἐπείκτης; a taskmaster or driver</note>. From an old glossary of the most illustrious Lord Pierre Séguier, Chancellor of France: an *epeiktēs* is a diligent man who urges workers to hurry. See the Index under the word **protomastōr** <note>original: πρωτομάστωρ; master builder</note>. Theophanes writes: "he built the so-called triclinium <note>dining hall</note> of Justinian and the surrounding walls of the palace, and appointed Stephen as the **overseer** <note>original: ἐπείκτην</note>." See the notes of Father Goar on pages 41, 42, and 598 b.

**episkopos** <note>original: ἐπίσκοπος; bishop</note>, a particular shepherd. Barlaam in *On the Primacy of the Pope*, chapter 3: "but the particular shepherds they named **bishops**." A Latin-Greek glossary defines **pastor** <note>shepherd</note> as a bishop. Theophanes Cerameus in sermon 47 calls him the "leader of the flock of rational sheep." Saint Ambrose in *On the Dignity of the Priesthood* says: *a bishop is a priest of the first order, the first priest*. From this comes **episkopē** <note>original: ἐπισκοπή</note> for the office of the bishop (episcopate). Justinian's *Novel* 123, chapter 1. Basil, a deacon of the Council of Ephesus, part 1. Gregory the Priest in the *Life of Gregory the Theologian*: "requesting the **bishopric** <note>original: ἐπισκοπήν</note> of the royal city." Theophanes: "wishing to appoint a certain archimandrite Eutyches, who was of the same mind as himself, to the **bishopric**." Anastasius the Librarian in his *Ecclesiastical History*: *they sent the deposition through the **bishop's office** <note>original Latin: per episcopem</note>.* The term **episcopium** is used for the same thing. King Charles III in a letter to the bishops of his kingdom: *he sought the **bishopric** <note>original Latin: episcopium</note> of the church of Tongeren.* Additionally, *episcopium* refers to the house of the bishop, as in the Synod of Ponthion, canon 12. Anastasius in the *Exile of Saint Martin*: *to be led around the entire **bishop's residence** <note>original Latin: episcopium</note>.*

**Heptaskalon** <note>original: ἑπτάσκαλον; "Seven Landings"</note>, a place in Constantinople named from its seven landings; for a **skala** <note>original: σκάλα</note> is a ladder or a pier. Moschopulus in his *Scholia*: a *klimax* <note>staircase</note> is what is commonly called a *skala*.

<summary>This page defines Byzantine administrative, military, and ecclesiastical titles, specifically tax assessors (exisotēs), imperial guards (excubitors), overseers (epeiktēs), and bishops (episkopos), providing citations from historical and legal texts.</summary>
<keywords>exisotēs, excubitor, episkopos, Heptaskalon, epeiktēs, tax assessment, Byzantine military, ecclesiastical hierarchy, Constantinople geography</keywords>

# GLOSSARY

Suidas: **anaboleus** <note>original: ἀναβολεὺς; a mounting block or stirrup</note> and that which is called a **skala** <note>original: σκάλα; literally a ladder or staircase</note> among the Romans. *The Precious Crown*: **skala** <note>original: σκάλα</note> means a ladder or steps. See Procopius, *Vandalic War*, book 2, page 148.

**hetaireia**, **hetaireiarches**. A cohort that consisted of war allies and confederates. The commander of this was the **hetaireiarches** <note>original: ἑταιρειάρχης; leader of the "companions"</note>, or as Cedrenus says, the **ruler of the companionship** <note>original: ἑταιρείας ἄρχων</note>. There were, however, as Meursius observes, many such "companionships," of which one was called **the Great** <note>original: ἡ μεγάλη</note>, and its overseer was the **Great Hetaireiarches**; regarding whom Constantine Manasses, George Logothete, and Nicetas write.

**zibene** <note>original: ζιβήνη</note>, a hunting spear. *Glossary of Philoxenus*: a hunting spear <note>original Latin: venabulum</note> is a **zibene**. It is also explained this way in the *Glossary of Cyril*.

**zoste** <note>original: ζωστή; literally "girdled"</note>, a type of rank or dignity. Codinus in the *Excerpts*: "and the **zostai** <note>high-ranking court ladies</note> and the patricians and the provosts processed forward." See the later notes.

**hegoumenos** <note>original: ἡγούμενος</note>, a leader, a superior, the head of a monastery, a prefect, or a provost. Saint Athanasius in a manuscript paraphrase of Psalm 67, at verse 26: "the leaders went before, the **hegoumenoi of the monks**." The Second Council of Nicaea, act 1: "Sabbas, the most devout **hegoumenos** <note>abbot</note> of the Monastery of Stoudios." Anastasius the Librarian translates this as "the **hegumenus** of the Studite monastery." The same Anastasius the Librarian in his *Ecclesiastical History*: "Peter the **Eugemenus** of Saint Sabas. Read: **hegumenus**." The Council of Nicaea, in act 1, translates **hegoumenos** as "provost." John Moschus in the *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 95: "he was the **hegoumenos** of the community of Abazanos." Palladius, *Lausiac History*, chapter 76: "an **hegoumenos** over a large brotherhood." From this comes **hegoumeneia**, the office of leadership or prefecture. The 8th Ecumenical Council, canon 4: "those promoted by him to the **hegoumeneia**."

**thema**, **thematikoi**. A province. Cedrenus: "through the Roman **themata**," meaning from the Roman provinces. Anastasius the Librarian in his *Ecclesiastical History*: "living as much in the royal city as in the **themata** <note>the administrative military districts of the Byzantine Empire</note>." Theodore of Hermopolis on Digest book 6, section 8, concerning the office of the governor: "the leaders sent into the provinces, that is, into the **themata**." From this comes **thematikos**, meaning provincial; as in the same Theodore of Hermopolis, book 9, title 1. Sometimes **thema** signifies a legion. An old Glossary under the title *On Military Service*: "a legion is a **taxis** or a **thema**." From this comes **thematikoi**, meaning legionary soldiers. Cedrenus: "the **thematikoi** having been gathered," meaning the **thematic** soldiers. Anastasius the Librarian in his *Ecclesiastical History*: "he was proclaimed Emperor by all the **themata** situated beyond the sea." *Miscellaneous History*, book 22: "and when he had run to the **thema** of the Orientals, of which Lacinus was the praetor." Concerning this **thema**, see Constantine Porphyrogenitus, *On the Themes*, book 1. And shortly after: "Artabasdus, however, was proclaimed Emperor by the **themata**." And in the same place: "Constantine arrived at Chrysopolis with two **thematic** soldiers." And book 24: "to the wives of the **thematic** soldiers who had been in Bulgaria, he gave five talents of gold." Codinus in the *Excerpts*, from the *Chronicle of Constantinople*: "he wrote also to the generals and governors and dukes and to all those who were leaders of all the royal **themata** of the East and West, North and South." **Cavalry themata** <note>original: καβαλλαρικὰ θέματα</note> in Cedrenus are cavalry forces; called a "cavalry troop" by Herodian.

<summary>This page defines Byzantine Greek terms related to military organization (themata, hetaireia), court titles (zoste), and monastic leadership (hegoumenos). It explains how the empire was divided into provinces called "themes" and defines the various ranks associated with these military and civil districts.</summary>

# FABROT'S GLOSSARY

**idikton** <note>original: ἴδικτον</note> *edictum* <note>An official proclamation or decree issued by a sovereign or high official.</note>. Cedrenus: "An **idikton** is issued." Legal Glossary: "**idiktis**, meaning decrees." Theophanes in the life of Heraclius: "The so-called **idikton** is issued." Pope Agatho in an epistle to Constantine, Heraclius, and Tiberius (found in the 6th Council of Constantinople, Act 4): "The writing of the heretic Apollinarius against Diodorus, regarding what was set down in the **idiktos** <note>original: ἠδίκτῳ</note> of the orthodox faith by the Emperor Justinian of blessed memory." Nicephorus Callistus, book 17, chapter 29: "He writes what is called in the Roman tongue an **idikton** <note>original: ἤδικτον</note>."

**hikanaton** <note>original: ἱκανάτον</note> *the name of a cohort*. The 8th Ecumenical Council, Act 1: "**Domestic** <note>a military commander</note> of the **Hikanatoi**." The Menologium <note>a church calendar of saints' lives</note> for July 1st: "He appointed him as the **Domestic** of the **Hikanatoi**." See also Constantine Porphyrogenitus, *On the Themes*, book 1, chapter 5. <note>The Hikanatoi, or "The Able Ones," were an elite regiment of the Byzantine imperial guard founded in the 9th century.</note>

**illoustrios** <note>original: ἰλλούστριος</note> *illustris* <note>literally "Illustrious," a high-ranking title in the later Roman Empire.</note>. Arrian, *Epictetus*, book 3, final chapter. Nicephorus Callistus, 17.14: "A certain **illoustrios** rank." Psellus in the *Synopsis*, verse 1255. Victor in his work on the African persecutions, speaking to Theophilus; and see Cuiacius on the Code, book 12, title 1.

**indiktion, indiktos** <note>original: ἰνδικτίων, ἴνδικτος</note> *indictio* <note>An "Indiction" was a 15-year cycle used in the Roman and Byzantine Empires to date documents, originally based on a cycle of tax assessments.</note>. Gregory of Tauromenium in his *Oration on the Indiction*: "There exists a beginning of the chronological cycle, called **indikta** in the Roman tongue." Others attribute this to Theophanes Cerameus, Archbishop of Tauromenium. Saint Maximus in the *Ecclesiastical Computation*, chapter 33. Isaac the Monk in the *Computation*, chapter 1: "The **indiktos**, which is also called **indiktion** and **epinemesis** <note>original: ἐπινέμησις; an allotment or assessment</note>." 

*However, it is more accurate to say that an 'indiction' is named from the declarations of taxes; since these were annual, years began to be numbered by indictions, as the greatest interpreter of law teaches on the title of the Code regarding indictions. For indictions are taxes. Blessed Augustine, in his commentary on Psalm 49, says: "Because he wished to be our king and wished us to be his province, he declares a tax [indictio] upon us. Let us hear his indictions, and let the poor man not tremble under the indiction of God." See also Ciaconius on Cassian.*

**kaballarika, kaballarios, kaballikeuein** <note>original: καβαλλαρικά, καβαλλάριος, καβαλλικεύειν</note>. "Cavalry themes" <note>thematic regions designated for horse-mounted troops</note> in Cedrenus and Theophanes. *A cavalry army*: **kaballarika stratos** <note>original: καβαλλαρικὸς στρατός</note>. Constantine, in the Council of Florence: "And the **kaballarioi** <note>horsemen</note> who were in front came forward." Theophanes in his account of Heraclius: "The Persian **kaballarioi**." John Moschus in the *Limonarion*, chapter 72. From this comes **kaballikeuein** <note>to ride a horse</note>. Theophanes in the life of Theodosius: "And through those means, we **rode** <note>original: ἐκαβαλλικεύσαμεν</note>." Constantine in the *Tactics*: "For these small horses often preserve men from great dangers, and through them, those who **ride** <note>original: καβαλλικεύοντας</note> them." The same author in *On the Administration of the Empire*, chapter 15: "But they do not **ride** <note>original: καβαλλικεύουσι</note> horses." Achmes, chapter 235: "If someone sees that he has **ridden** <note>original: ἐκαβαλλίκευσε</note> a mule." A manuscript Glossary: "He **rides** [kaballikeuei], he dismounts the horse." Actuarius uses the term in his book *On the Composition of Drugs*. 

*In the same way, more recent Latin writers used "caballare" or "caballicare" to mean to ride a horse. In the Salic Law, title 26: "And he rode [caballaverit] it (the horse)." In the Lombard Law, title 105, section 17: "If anyone shall mount another's horse and ride [caballicaverit] only within the neighborhood." The Monk of Saint Gall in book 1 of the Deeds of Charlemagne: "Riding [caballicans] through this field." This comes from 'caballus': though the Latins seem to use this word for a common or inferior horse. Blessed Jerome in his epistle to Heliodorus: "And immediately let us see arrows give way to pikes, caps to helmets, and work-horses [caballos] to noble steeds [equis]."*

<summary>This page defines Byzantine terms for official edicts, elite military units, and social ranks, while providing an extensive etymological study of the word for "riding" and its evolution from Latin to Greek.</summary>
<keywords>edictum, Hikanatoi, illustris, indiction, cavalry, kaballarios, Byzantine military, Roman law, etymology, horse riding</keywords>

-># GLOSSARY<-

**Kaisar** <note>original: Καῖσαρ</note>. Caesar; one designated for imperial power, a successor to the empire. Eutropius, book 10: *He created two Caesars,* and shortly after: *he was created emperor.* Also in the same book: *At that time, Constantius alone was prince and Augustus in the Roman Empire.* As time progressed, however, a distinction arose between a *despotes* <note>Lord or Despot</note>, a *sebastokrator* <note>Venerable Ruler</note>, and a **Kaisar**. See Codinus, *On Offices*.

**kalandai** <note>original: καλάνδαι</note>. The Calends <note>the first day of the month in the Roman calendar</note>. An interpreter of the Canons of the African Church: "On the eighth day before the **kalandai** of June" <note>May 25th</note>. Legal Glossaries: "**kalandai** are the first days of each individual month." The Glossaries of Cyril: "**kalandai** means calends." See Plutarch’s *Life of Galba*.

**kaligion** <note>original: καλίγιον</note>. A shoe. **kaliga** <note>original: καλίγα</note> is mentioned by Modestinus in book 10 of *On the Excuse of Tutors*. The Greeks [commenting] on Law 2 of the Digest regarding those marked with infamy: "For a **kaliga** is a shoe." From this comes **kaligarios**, meaning a shoemaker. The Glosses on the *Basilica* <note>a 9th-century code of Byzantine law</note> regarding the Aquilian Law, book 5: "A certain **kaligarios**." Julius Firmicus Maternus, *Mathesis*, book 3, chapter 12: *leather-dressers or shoemakers.* And book 4, chapter 7: *he will produce skinners, tanners, and shoemakers.*

**kalligraphos** <note>original: καλλίγραφος</note>. A calligrapher. See Anastasius the Librarian in his *Ecclesiastical History*, and see the later notes. An uncertain author in Suidas: "Having provided him with seven shorthand writers and even more **calligraphers**."

**kamelaukion** <note>original: καμελαύκιον</note>. A head covering, a brimmed hat, or a cap. Hero, in his *Excerpts*: "Wrapping himself in an Arcadian **kamelaukion**." Theophanes, in his life of Justinian: "And his garments along with the jewel-encrusted **kamelaukion**." Leo the Wise, *Tactics*, chapter 19, section 42: "The so-called **kamelaukion** was raised upon a spear." Constantine Porphyrogenitus, *On the Administration of the Empire*: "The crowns which you call **kamelaukia**." The lexicon of Stephanus, quoted by Fronto Ducaeus in volume 6 of Chrysostom: "The *kidaris* <note>turban</note>, the *korybantion*, and the *pilos* <note>felt cap</note> are types of **kamelaukion**, which is also understood as a tiara." In Latin, it is called *camelaucus*, *calamaucus*, or *camilaucium*. Anastasius in his *Ecclesiastical History*: *Having entered into war with Totila, the most powerful king of the Goths, he overcame him and took Rome, killed Totila, and sent his blood-stained garments along with his **camilaucium** (so in the manuscript), adorned with precious stones, to Constantinople.* The *Historia Miscellanea*, book 22: *And Habdalas ordered their beards to be shaved and **calamauci** to be made of one cubit and a half.* In handwritten books, one reads *amelaucos* or *camelaucos*. The Glosses of Isidore of Seville: *brimmed **calamauci**.* Also: *a **calamaucus** cap.* Josephus in the *Antiquities of the Jews* <term>archaiolo.</term> <note>original: ἀρχαιολο. (archaiologia)</note>, book 3, chapter 8: "Upon the head he wears a cap without a point." Rufinus of Aquileia translates this: *Upon the head he carries a cap in the manner of a small calamacus or helmet.* One should read *calamauci*, as in Bede, who uses almost the same words. Anastasius in the *Lives of the Popes* (regarding Constantine): *The Apostolic Pontiff with a caumelaugus, as he was accustomed to go forth in Rome.* One should read *calamauco*, or preferably, *camelauco*. A manuscript glossary says: *camelaucus, a garment of the Pope.* Papias says the same in so many words. And Bonaventura Vulcanius read it thus in Isidore's Glosses.

**kamisia** <note>original: καμισία</note>. A shirt, an undergarment, or a tunic. Victor of Vita, *History of the Vandal Persecution in Africa*, book 1: *From the altar cloths—oh, the wickedness!—they made for themselves **shirts** and breeches.* Anastasius the Librarian in his *Ecclesiastical History*: Chalba-

It traces how these Latin administrative and everyday words were integrated into Greek legal and ecclesiastical texts.</summary>

...many shirts <note>original: "camisias multas"</note>. *Alcuin, On Divine Offices: the linen tunic was an inner garment, which we call a camisa or a "supparum." Papias: the alba, a priestly garment of tight linen, is called a camisium. See the same author under "poderis" [a long robe]. From this comes the word* **hypokamison** <note>original: ὑποκάμισον; an undershirt</note>. *Cyril of Constantinople, Against the Jews, book 2, question 1. Codinus in the Excerpts. Moschus, chapter 186.*

**kampos** <note>original: κάμπος</note>. *A field or plain <note>Latin: campus</note>. Leo, Tactics, chapter 7, section 30:* "do not ride forcefully in the **kampos**."

**kandidatoi** <note>original: κανδιδᾶτοι</note>. *A class of soldiers whose physical strength and spirit recommended them; they were among the prince's bodyguards. Saint Jerome, in his Life of Hilarion: "a candidate of the Emperor Constantius." Emperor Michael, in a letter to Emperor Louis: "and therefore we have deemed it right to send to your Glory Theodore our chief sword-bearer [protospatharios] and Leo our **kandidatos**." The Acts of Sutri under King Henry: "the Pope sent to meet him at the Mountain of Joy, which is also called the Mountain of Marius, the porters, the candle-bearers, the **kandidatoi**, the defenders, and the grooms." Luitprand, European Affairs, book 3, chapter 5: "After these, an immense crowd is called forth: of chief sword-bearers, sword-bearers, and **kandidatoi**." Procopius mentions these in book 3 of the Gothic War. John Moschus, chapter 185:* "The God-loving and friend-to-the-poor Maria, the mother of Lord Paul the **kandidatos**, related to us." *Nicephorus of Constantinople, in his Short History:* "The rank which it is the Roman custom to call **kandidatos**."

**kanikleion** <note>original: κανίκλειον</note>. *Cedrenus: the honor of the **kanikleion**, a high office <note>The office of the keeper of the imperial inkstand</note>. Synod 8, volume 3 of the Councils, page 413, Rome edition:* "As written by Christopher, chief secretary and official over the **kanikleion**." *John Cantacuzenus, book 4, chapter 40:* "sending Angelos, the official over the **kanikleion**, as an ambassador to the Emperor." *Chronicle of Constantinople:* "through Nikephoros Aliatos, the official of the **kanikleion**." *The Latin form is "caniclinus." See Meursius, Vossius on Faults of Speech, and Alemannus on Procopius' Secret History, page 19.*

**kanon** <note>original: κανών</note>. *That which one ought to do according to a rule. Moschus, chapter 98:* "never performing my **kanon** <note>the prescribed daily rule of prayer</note>, I let my mind wander toward the earth." *Also a psalm or song accustomed to be sung on fixed days; and the divine office. See Meursius' Glossary and the notes of Hugues Ménard on the Concord of Rules, chapter 55, section 3.*

**kapnikon** <note>original: καπνικόν</note>. *A hearth tax <note>literally "smoke tax"</note>. See Theophanes regarding Nikephoros the Logothete.*

**kardarichas** <note>original: καρδαρίχας</note>. *Cedrenus. Anastasius the Librarian calls this "cardariga" in his Ecclesiastical History: "cardarigas," he says, "is not a proper name, but a very high rank among the Persians." From Theophanes.*

**kastellion** <note>original: καστέλλιον</note>. *A castle or fort <note>Latin: castellum</note>. Constantine Porphyrogenitus, On the Themes, book 1, theme 9:* "they surrendered the **kastellia** there." *Theophanes:* "they released them from the **kastellion**." *John Moschus, The Spiritual Meadow, chapter 167. The Synod of Florence:* "at the **kastelli** of Francoli." *John Cantacuzenus, book 4, chapter 40:* "they plundered the so-called **kastellion**."

**kastron** <note>original: κάστρον</note>. *A castle, a fortification, a place protected by walls. Suidas:* "**kastron** means a fortress." *Achmes, chapter 283:* "either a field or a **kastron**." *Theophanes: "According to this custom, the Persians [call] the place named Betzakidi a* **ka-** <note>the text breaks here for the catchword of the next page</note>

# GLOSSARY

...captured the fortress <note>original Greek: στρον παρελαβον, likely the end of κάστρον παρελαβον</note>. *But it is also well known that* **kastra** <note>castles/forts</note> *is used to refer to towns. Justinian, Novella 128, chapter 20:* "in the cities or rather the fortresses" <note>original: ἐν ταῖς πόλεσιν ἤτοι κάστροις</note>. *An ancient interpreter: "in cities or in castles." Understand this as "or in towns." Finally,* **kastron** *means an encampment <note>original: παρεμβολή</note> or a castle. A manuscript Glossary says:* "An encampment is a tent, a castle, a military camp." *A Greek-Latin Glossary:* "An encampment <note>παρεμβολὴ</note> is a phalanx or a castle." *Legal glosses:* "A castle, that is, a fortified camp <note>original: κάστρον ἤγουν φοσσάτον</note>." *I shall discuss* **fossaton** <note>a term for a camp or a ditch</note> *being used for a military camp in that entry, God willing.*

**katepanos** <note>a high-ranking military commander or provincial governor; the origin of the word "captain"</note>. *See Curopalates page 843 and Meursius on that word.*

**kellion, kelle, kelliotai.** *A small cell. Saint Athanasius, Apology 2:* "being sick in his cell and lying down." *Simeon Metaphrastes in the Life of Abramius:* "he is found in the said cell, having no one living with him." *The Menologium for the month of March:* "having closed the door of the cell." *This word is used by Saint Basil, Palladius in the Lausiac History, and Dorotheus in his fourth teaching:* "and they shook out their mats in front of my cell." *John Moschus, The Spiritual Meadow, chapter 46 at the end. Nicephorus, book 11, chapter 38:* "There is another place about seventy stades distant, well-suited for practicing philosophy <note>meaning monastic life</note>, which is called 'The Cells' <note>Kellia</note>, because the dwellings of the monks are not in a community but are scattered." *Theophanes also uses* **kelle**, *a cell. Simeon Metaphrastes in the Life of Pelagia:* "and indeed Pelagia, standing at the cell, knocked and called out." *Antiochus in the Pandects; George of Alexandria in the Life of the Blessed Chrysostom:* "having plundered the cells." *From this come the* **kelliotai** <note>cell-dwellers or hermits</note>. *Laonicus Chalcondyles calls them 'cellulani' from the cell in which they were enclosed.*

**kentenarion** *a centenarium <note>a Roman and Byzantine unit of weight and money, specifically 100 pounds of gold</note>, a quantity of money. George of Alexandria in the Life of Saint Chrysostom:* "having demanded a centenarium from Paulicius." *Codinus in the Excerpts:* "552 centenaria of gold were paid out." *Nicephorus Callistus, book 15, chapter 27:* "on which fleet the report is that he spent one thousand two hundred centenaria of gold." *Theophanes; the historian Candidus in Photius; John Moschus in the Meadow; Eustathius on the Iliad, book 2; Anastasius the Librarian in the Ecclesiastical History: "and he gives him fifty centenaria of gold." So it is in the manuscript. See the Greek interpretation of law 60 of the Digest regarding dotal law.*

**kenterion, kentyrion, kentourion.** *A centurion. Alexius Rhartes, teaching on Holy and Great Friday:* "they bring back the thief, the centurion." *It is written both as* **kentyrion** *and* **kentourion**. *Greek interpreter on the Basilika <note>a collection of laws</note>, book 48, title 3:* "the centurion prevented it." *The Basilika in the same place uses* **hekatontarchos** <note>the standard Greek term for centurion, literally 'leader of a hundred'</note>. *Theophylact on Mark chapter 15:* "the centurion, that is, the leader of a hundred; for the Romans call a hundred 'centum'." *See Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, book 7, chapter 15; Nicephorus Callistus, book 6, chapter 13.*

**keration** *a siliqua <note>the seed of the carob tree, used as a small weight and the name of a small coin; 1/24th of a gold solidus</note>. Constantine in the Agricultural Laws:* "one keration, that is, twelve follis." *See under 'phollis'.*

**kephalition** *a capitation <note>a poll tax or head tax</note>. Theophylact in the Commentary on the Epistle of Paul to the Romans, chapter 13:* "Give the tax to whom the tax is due, namely the so-called poll tax; and the tribute to whom the tribute is due, namely the contribution for the land." *These exact words exist in Oecumenius' commentary on the same epistle, chapter 18.*

<summary>This page defines various Byzantine administrative, monastic, and financial terms, including the transition of "kastron" from a military camp to a town, the nature of monastic "cells," and the units of currency like the gold centenarium and the keration coin.</summary>
<keywords>kastron, katepanos, kelliotai, monasticism, kentenarion, currency, centurion, keration, poll tax, Byzantine law</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical glossary of Byzantine Greek and legal terms, following the previous page's discussion of "kastron" (fortress/town). This section covers terms starting with the letter Kappa (Κ), specifically relating to trades, infrastructure, military geography, and church hierarchy.</meta>

<page-num>910</page-num>

# FABROT'S GLOSSARY

**keroularios** <note>original Greek: κηρουλάριος</note> candle-maker, **keropoles** <note>original Greek: κηροπώλης</note> wax-seller. Anastasius the Librarian in his *Ecclesiastical History*: "There was a certain candle-maker in the marketplace <note>forum</note>, wealthy from his own labors." <note>original Latin: cerularius quidam erat in foro, ex laboribus suis locuples</note>

**kinsterna** <note>original Greek: κινστέρνα</note> cistern. Leo the Tactician, chapter 15: "If they have drinkable water from a cistern." <note>original Greek: ἐὰν δὲ ἀπὸ κινστέρναϚ ἔχουσι πόσιμον ὕδωρ</note>. Suidas [The Suda] uses this in three places, as does Hero in *On Measures*. Zonaras in his commentary on the Councils, page 581.

**kleisourai** <note>original Greek: κλεισοῦραι</note> mountain passes <note>clusurae</note>, narrow entrances that do not accommodate a large number of people. By these, enemies were shut out. Procopius in *On Justinian's Buildings*, page 32: "And he walled up the narrow passages in the region, which they have been accustomed to call *kleisourai*." <note>original Greek: καὶ τοὺς ἐν τῇ χώρᾳ στενωποὺς ἐτειχίσατο, οὕσπερ κλεισούρας καλεῖν νενομίκασιν</note>. Stephanus in his commentary on Aristotle’s *Rhetoric* (which has not yet been published): "Those called *kleisourai* in common parlance among many." <note>original Greek: τὰς ἰδιωτικῶς παρὰ πολλοῖς λεγομένας κλεισούρας</note>. Eustathius on the *Iliad*, Book 2: "Where he speaks of the narrowings of a road, it is the same as saying *kleisourai* and straits." <note>original Greek: ὅπου ξυνοχὰς λέγει ὁδοῦ, ταυτὸν δὲ εἰπεῖν κλεισούρας καὶ στενότητας</note>. Codinus in the *Excerpts*: "He was blinded in the mountain pass." It is used by Leo in his *Tactics*, Constantine [Porphyrogenitus] in *On Administering the Empire*, Theophanes, and others. Latin writers use the terms *clusuras*, *clausuras*, *clusas*, and *claustra*. Cassiodorus, *Variae*, Book 2, Letter 5: "We command that the 60 soldiers stationed continuously in the Augustan passes <note>clusuris</note> be provided with their grain rations." For so it is read in the ancient manuscript; they used *cludo* for *claudo* <note>to shut or close</note> interchangeably, as in Law 226 of the Digest *On the Meaning of Words*, it is read as "he is shut in" <note>clusus est</note> in the Florentine edition. Regarding the term *clausuris*, the author of the *Miscellany*, Book 18: "They held the passes <note>clausuras</note> which lead into Persia." Egica, King of the Goths, in the 17th Council of Toledo: "The inhabitants are known to exist within the enclosures <note>clausuras</note>." Regarding *clusis*, Anastasius the Librarian in his *Life of Stephen III*: "To guard the Franks' own passes <note>clusas</note>." Hincmar, Letter 5, chapter 6: "But Aistulphus, puffed up with pride against the Franks, who had come to guard their own passes according to the command of Pippin." Luitprand, Book 1, chapter 2: "For it was separated from us by certain very difficult obstructions, which the common people call *clusas*." Nothing should be changed here, nor in Book 5, chapter 8. Regarding *claustra*, Cicero in *Against Verres*, Book 7: "Those who had often shut out our armies—we did not think the barriers <note>claustra</note> of the place should be entrusted to them." He uses it with the same meaning elsewhere. Jordanes, *History of the Goths*, chapter 32: "Valia, King of the Goths, met him at the barriers <note>claustra</note> of the Pyrenees with no less preparation for war." From *kleisourai* comes **kleisouriarches** <note>original Greek: κλεισουράρχης</note>, a commander of a mountain pass. Theophanes: "Gregory the Cappadocian, who also became a *kleisouriarches*." The author of the *Miscellany*, Book 19: "And Gregory the Cappadocian, who had been a *clusuriarches*." A prefect of a mountain pass.

**kleros, klerikoi, klerosis.** <note>original Greek: κλῆρος, κληρικοί, κλήρωσις</note> The clergy, sacred order, sacred college—a general term for all who are dedicated to divine ministry. Saint Jerome to Nepotian: "A cleric," he says, "is one who serves the Church of Christ." Saint Augustine on Psalm 67: "Adorned with the ranks of ecclesiastical ministry." The *Great Etymological Dictionary*: "*Klēros* is the name for the body <note>systema</note> of deacons and priests." <note>original Greek: κλῆρος λέγεται σύστημα τῶν διακόνων καὶ πρεσβυτέρων</note>. Oecumenius in his commentary on the First Epistle of Peter, chapter 7: "He calls the holy body the *klēros*, just as we do now." <note>original Greek: κλῆρον δὲ τὸ ἱερὸν σύστημα καλεῖ, ὥσπερ καὶ νῦν ἡμεῖς</note>. Saint Chrysostom, *Homily on Saint John the Apostle*: "Consider again the multitudes of the churches, the clergy <note>klēros</note>." Sometimes *klēros* is understood as all who are under a bishop. Saint Basil, Letter 52:

<vocab>κηρουλάριος, κινστέρνα, κλεισοῦραι, κλῆρος, cerularius, clusurae, clerus, Fabroti, Anastasius, Procopius, Cicero, Hieronymus, Augustinus, Chrysostomus</vocab>

It also begins a detailed theological and linguistic exploration of the term 'clergy' (kleros) using Patristic sources.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical glossary of Byzantine terms, moving from the previous page's discussion of mountain passes (kleisourai) into administrative and ecclesiastical titles beginning with the letter Kappa (Κ), specifically focusing on the clergy, the office of the quaestor, and various types of "counts" or imperial officials.</meta>

<page-num>911</page-num>

# GLOSSARY. 911

...and now from the sacred fullness, the clergy under you. <note>original Greek: καὶ νῦν δὲ ἀπὸ τοῦ ἱεροῦ πληρώματος, τοῦ ὑπό σε κλήρου</note> Paulinus, in his 28th letter to Victricius: "We have known you to be of the clergy, body, and spirit of your holiness." <note>original Latin: de sanctitatis tuae clero et corpore et spiritu esse cognovimus</note> **clerics** <note>term for ordained members of the church</note> <term>κληρικοί</term>. Nicephorus, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 7, Chapter 42: "Those providing service to the most holy religion, whom they are accustomed to name clerics." <note>original Greek: ὑπηρεσίαν τῇ ἁγιωτάτῃ θρησκείᾳ παρέχοντας, οὕσπερ κληρικοὺς ἐπονομάζειν εἰώθασιν</note> According to Meursius <note>Johannes Meursius, a 17th-century scholar of Greek culture</note>, the clergy in the Eastern Empire was fourfold. Regarding the "cleric of the prince," the 8th Ecumenical Council, Act 7, states: "The representatives spoke through Damian, the imperial cleric who translated into Greek." <note>original Greek: οἱ τοποτηρηταὶ εἶπον διὰ τοῦ ἐξελληνίζοντος Δαμιανοῦ βασιλικοῦ κληρικοῦ</note> Hincmar, in his 3rd letter, chapter 26, also mentions the clergy of the palace. From this comes the "archbishop of the sacred palace," and in the preface to the Council of Mainz, the "archchaplain of the sacred palace," as noted by Ademarus in his *Life of Louis the Pious*. Finally, the term "clericatus" <note>the state of being a cleric</note> appears in the *Code of Canons of the African Church*, page 283. Clerics are contrasted with the laity. Clement of Rome, in his first letter to the Corinthians: "The lay person is bound by lay ordinances." <note>original Greek: ὁ λαϊκὸς ἄνθρωπος τοῖς λαϊκοῖς προστάγμασι δέδοται</note> Theophanes writes: "Many clerics, monks, and devout laymen." <note>original Greek: πολλοί τε κληρικοὶ καὶ μονασταὶ καὶ εὐλαβεῖς λαϊκοί</note>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<term>κοιαίστωρ</term> **quaestor** <note>a high-ranking legal and financial official in the Roman and Byzantine systems</note>. Constantinus Manasses: "A quaestor by rank." <note>original Greek: κοιαίστωρ τὴν ἀξίαν</note> Basilius in his *Grammar*: "The dignity of quaestor." <note>original Greek: κοιαίστωρ τὸ ἀξίωμα</note> Nicephorus of Constantinople, in his *Brief History*: "Kosmas, who held the dignity they call 'kuaistor'." <note>original Greek: Κοσμᾶν τὴν ἀξίαν ἣν δὴ κυαίστωρα καλοῦσι</note> Gregory Nazianzen in his 10th Oration: "He stayed in Bithynia, administering an office that was not far removed from the emperor. This office was to manage the emperor's money and to have charge of the treasures. For it is from this post that the emperor begins a person's promotion to the higher offices." <note>original Greek: διέτριβε μὲν ἐν τῇ Βιθυνῶν, τὴν οὐ πολλοστὴν ἀπὸ βασιλέως διέπων ἀρχήν. ἡ δὲ ἦν ταμιεύειν βασιλεῖ τὰ χρήματα καὶ τῶν θησαυρῶν ἔχειν τὴν ἐπιμέλειαν. ἐντεῦθεν γὰρ αὐτῷ τὰς μείζους ἀρχὰς βασιλεὺς προοιμιάζεται</note> Similarly, among the Romans, the quaestorship was the first step in the ladder of honors.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<term>κόμης</term> **count** <note>from the Latin 'comes,' meaning companion; used here as a high-ranking title</note>. Of the imperial stable, of the East, of the excubitors <note>bodyguards</note>, of the federates <note>allied troops</note>, of the court. "Of the imperial stable" refers to the **count of the sacred stable** <note>original Latin: comes sacri stabuli</note>, as seen in Gruter’s *Ancient Inscriptions*, page 412. Manasses calls him the "overseer of the horses" <note>original Greek: φροντιστής τῶν ἵππων</note>, the one in charge of the royal horses, otherwise known as the **count of the stable** <note>original Greek: κόμης τοῦ σταύλου</note>. Theophanes uses the phrase "count of the imperial stables." The word *staulos* or *staulon* refers to a **stable** <note>original Latin: stabulum</note>. Eustathius, commenting on Book 24 of the *Odyssey*, notes: "Among the Attic writers, a *klesion* is a place for wagons and yokes; the Romans call this a *staulon* from the word for standing." <note>original Greek: παρὰ μέντοι Ἀττικοῖς τὸ κλήσιον ἁμαξῶν καὶ ζευγῶν ἐστὶ δεκτικόν, ὃ λέγεται τοὺς Ῥωμαίους παρὰ τὴν στάσιν σταῦλον καλεῖν</note> Theophanes writes: "And reaching the horses in the stables (so the manuscript, read as *staulois*) of Stauricius, etc." This role is equivalent to **the Grand Equerry** <note>original French: le grand escuier</note>. **Count of the East** <note>original Latin: comes Orientis</note>, mentioned by Cedrenus, Theophanes, Julius Pollux in his *Chronicle*, and Nicephorus of Constantinople. He was the count of the dawn <note>the East</note>, under whom were the fifteen provinces of the East, according to Zosimus, Book 5. **Count of the excubitors** <note>original Latin: comes excubitorum</note>, or "count of the school of excubitors." **Count of the imperial bodyguard** <note>original Latin: comes imperialis excubiti</note>. The 6th Synod of Constantinople, Act 14. Theophylactus Simocatta, in his *History of Maurice*, Book 3, Chapter 11: "He happened to be the leader of the emperor's bodyguards and shield-bearers, whom the Romans customarily call the 'count of the excubitors' in their usual tongue." <note>original Greek: ἡγεμὼν δ᾿ οὗτος ἐτύγχανεν ὢν τῶν τοῦ βασιλέως σωματοφυλάκων καὶ ὑπασπιστῶν, ὃν κόμητα ἐξκουβιτόρων τῇ συνήθει φωνῇ ἔθος Ῥωμαίοις καλεῖν</note> This is the count and provost of the attendants and the prince's protector. **Count of the federates** <note>original Latin: comes foederatorum</note>, the *tourmarches* <note>commander of a military division</note> of the rank of the federates, according to Zonaras. Others call him the "leader of the federates." See below under **foederati**. **Count of the court** <note>original Latin: comes cortis</note>, or prefect of the cohort. The Glosses state: "prefect of the cohort" is *epar-* [prefect]... <column-break/>

<vocab>κληρικοί, clerici, κοιαίστωρ, quaestor, κόμης, comes sacri stabuli, comes Orientis, comes excubitorum, comes foederatorum</vocab>

<summary>This page defines high-ranking Byzantine religious and civil titles, including the clergy (clericus), the quaestor (a financial and legal official), and various "counts" (comes) who managed the imperial stables, Eastern provinces, and elite bodyguard units.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical glossary of Byzantine administrative and courtly titles, moving from the general discussion of "counts" (komites) to specific variants like the "son of a count," tax systems (commercium), the imperial "court" or "cohort" (korte), and the officials of the bedchamber (cubicularii).</meta>

<page-num>912</page-num>

# FABROT'S GLOSSARY

...commander of the court. <note>original Greek: χος τῆς κόρτις</note> Leo the Wise, *Tactica*, chapter 4, section 10: "A **count** is the leader of one regiment or band." <note>original Greek: κόμης δέ ἐστιν ὁ τοῦ ἑνὸς τάγματος ἤτοι βάνδου ἀφηγούμενος. A 'bandon' was a Byzantine military unit of about 200–400 men.</note> Glossary of Law: "A count is the ruler of one *korte* <note>court or cohort</note>, to whom even centurions are subject." <note>original Greek: κόμης ὁ μιᾶς κόρτης ἄρχων, ᾧ καὶ ἑκατοντάρχαι ὑποτάττονται</note>

**komitopoulos** <note>original Greek: κομητόπουλος</note> "son of a count." Similarly, we see "Umbertopoulos" <note>son of Humbert</note> in the writings of Anna Comnena, page 412, and "iatropoulos" <note>son of a doctor</note> in Pachymeres. Also, Harmenopulus <note>son of an Armenian</note>.

**kommerkion** <note>original Greek: κομμέρκιον</note> commerce, or a tax. Cedrenus: "He eased the taxes of Abydos and Hierum." <note>original Greek: τῆς Ἀβύδου καὶ τοῦ Ἱεροῦ τὰ κομμέρκια ἐκούφισε</note> The same is found in Theophanes. Anastasius the Librarian, in his *Ecclesiastical History*, translates it thus: *He relieved the so-called taxes of Abydos and Hierum.* <note>original Latin: Abydi ac Hieri ea quae dicuntur commercia relevavit</note> The same Anastasius writes: *while they paid twelve pounds of gold, and at the same time the customary taxes.* <note>original Latin: cum auri librarum duodecim persolverent, simul et consueta commercia</note> Theophanes: "He relieved the tax of the fair by 100 pounds of gold." <note>original Greek: τὸ κουμέρκιν τοῦ πανηγυρίου ρ' λιτρῶν χρυσίου ἐκούφισεν</note> Constantine Porphyrogenitus, *On the Administration of the Empire*: "He also has vast tax revenue from such business dealings." <note>original Greek: ἔχει δὲ καὶ κομμέρκιον ἐκ τῶν τοιούτων πραγματειῶν ἄπειρον</note>

**korte** <note>original Greek: κόρτη</note> **cohort**. A hall, the court of a prince, or a tent. **komes kortes**: "count of the cohort"—see above under **komes**. Polybius, Book 11: "Three units (this regiment of infantry is called a *cortis* among the Romans)." <note>original Greek: τρεῖς σπείρας (τοῦτο δὲ καλεῖται τὸ σύνταγμα τῶν πεζῶν παρὰ Ῥωμαίοις κόρτις)</note> It is rendered as *konorta* by the Greek interpreters of the *Basilika* <note>the code of Byzantine law</note> in the second law of the title "On those who are marked with infamy." Theophanes: "All the imperial service and the **court** went out." <note>original Greek: ἐξῆλθε πᾶσα ἡ βασιλικὴ ὑπουργία καὶ ἡ κόρτη</note> He also says: "They also took the baggage, money, horses, and the **court** along with all the imperial service." <note>original Greek: ἐπήρασι δὲ καὶ τὸ τοῦλδον χρήματά τε καὶ ἵππους καὶ τὴν κόρτην μετὰ πάσης τῆς βασιλικῆς ὑπουργίας</note> Anastasius the Librarian translates it this way: *The Bulgarians also took away the baggage, money, horses, and the court tapestry along with all the royal equipment.* <note>original Latin: abstulerunt autem Vulgares etiam sarcinam, pecuniam, equos et aulaeam una cum universo regio apparatu</note> Thus it appears in two manuscript codices. I do not know if this is a sufficient correction, or if he should have written *aulam* <note>court</note>. Therefore, the word *korte* in Cedrenus, page 472b, does not mean a cohort; for Cedrenus and Theophanes are speaking of the same thing. Unless you prefer, with Father Goar, to interpret *korte* there as the "tent of the prince."

**koubikularea, koubikoularios**. **chambermaid**, **chamberlain**. <note>original Greek: κουβικλάρεα, κουβικουλάριος</note> George of Alexandria, in the *Life of the Blessed Chrysostom*: "The Queen also stood before the doors of the church with all her retinue and the **chamberlains** and her rank." <note>original Greek: παρέστη καὶ ἡ βασίλισσα πρὸ θυρῶν τῆς ἐκκλησίας μετὰ πάσης αὐτῆς τῆς φαντασίας καὶ τῶν κουβικουλαρίων καὶ τῆς τάξεως</note> John Malalas: "Theodosius the Younger loved the chamberlain Chrysaphius with great affection." <note>original Greek: Θεοδόσιος ὁ μικρὸς ἐφίλει ἔρωτι Χρυσάφιον τὸν κουβικουλάριον</note> See also the Synod of Constantinople, Act 7; Nicephorus Callistus; the *Alexandrian Chronicle*; and Nicephorus of Constantinople. A chamberlain (cubicularius) is named from the bedchamber (cubiculum), also called a *koitonites*, *prokoitos*, or *katakoimites* <note>various Greek terms for those in charge of the sleeping quarters</note>. A "chamberlain of the sacred palace" is mentioned in the *Chronicle of Marcellinus*. There were, however, many palace chamberlains; and he who presided over them was called the "count of the chamberlains." In the 8th Council of Toledo, Odoacer, the count of the chamberlains, signs his name. See Cujas on Title 5, Law 12 of the Code, and our Glossary to Julian.

**kouboukleion, koubouklion**. **chamber** or **bedroom**. <note>original Greek: κουβούκλειον, κουβούκλιον</note> Blessed Chrysostom, in his *Homily on Repentance*: "As if he were locked in some chamber." <note>original Greek: ὡς ἔν τινι κουβουκλείῳ ἀποκέκλεισται</note> Codinus, in his *Excerpts*: "Having locked the chamber in front of them again." <note>original Greek: κλειδώσας πάλιν ἔμπροσθεν αὐτῶν τὸ κουβούκλιον</note> *Alexandrian Chronicle*, page 90: "She being in the chamber." <note>original Greek: οὖσαν αὐτὴν ἐν κουβουκλείῳ</note> John Moschus, *The Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 129: "Come into the chamber." <note>original Greek: ἐλθὲ εἰς τὸ κουβούκλειον</note> Saint Maximus, chapter 84, century 2: "There followed the memory of gold, and the memory of the purse, and the chest, and the..."

<summary>This page defines Byzantine administrative and court terms including the military "count," the "commercium" tax, and the "korte" (court or cohort). It also details the roles of palace chamberlains and provides linguistic origins for the term "bedroom" or "chamber" (cubiculum).</summary>

This page moves into maritime terms, imperial household officials, and military terminology related to raiding.</meta>

<page-num>913</page-num>

# GLOSSARIUM.

<note>original: GLOSSARIUM. This is a glossary of terms found in Byzantine Greek texts, often explaining words borrowed from Latin or other languages.</note>

**Of the bedchamber.** <note>original Greek: κουβουκλείου (kouboukleiou)</note> Here it refers to a vessel or utensil <note>original Greek: σκεύριον (skeurion)</note>, which is a chest. The Roman jurist Ulpian, in the Digest, Book 1, Section 41, under the title "on deposits," mentions: "if a chest is sealed." The *Basilica* <note>a massive 9th-century collection of Byzantine laws</note> translates this as: "a sealed vessel." <note>original Greek: ἐσφραγισμένον σκεύριον</note>

**koumparia.** <note>original Greek: κουμπάρια</note> Large ships. Constantine Porphyrogenitus, *On the Themes*, Book 2, Chapter 11: "a fleet of 36 **koumparia**." <note>original Greek: στόλος λϛ' κομπαρίων</note> Leo the Wise, in his *Tactica*, Chapter 18, Section 140: "by means of those ships of theirs called **koumbaria**." <note>original Greek: διὰ τῶν παρ' αὐτοῖς πλοίων τῶν λεγομένων κουμβαρίων</note> This is a Saracen <note>Arabic</note> word according to Leo (Chapters 18 and 19), Constantine, and the historian Zonaras. However, the Latins used the word *cumba* or *comba* <note>a small boat or skiff</note>. An Arabic-Latin glossary defines *lembus* as a short boat, also called a *caupulus*, a *cumba*, or a *lintris*. The *Glossary of Cyril* defines a *skaphe* <note>skiff</note> as a small boat, or a *comba*.

**curator.** <note>original Greek: κουράτωρ</note> "Having killed four **curators** of the neighboring rulers." <note>original Greek: τέσσαρας ἀρχόντων γειτόνων κουράτωρας ἀποκτείναντα</note> Who were these curators of the princes? They were certainly men of primary dignity. Were they perhaps the curators of the "divine" or imperial household? Theophanes, writing about Emperor Maurice, mentions: "the **curator** of the imperial houses." <note>original Greek: κουράτωρ τῶν βασιλικῶν οἴκων</note> The Sixth Council of Constantinople, Act 1, mentions: "the **curator** of the imperial House of Hormisdas." <note>original Greek: κουράτωρος τοῦ βασιλικοῦ τοῦ Ὁρμίσδου οἴκου</note> There was also a "curator of the emperor," <note>original Greek: κουράτωρ τοῦ βασιλέως</note> who is now called a *logothete* <note>a high-ranking administrative official, often a finance minister</note>, as Constantine Harmenopulus states in his *Manual of Law*, Book 6, Title 1, Section 5. *Kourator* is also used for the guardian of a youth, and *kouratoreia* for the office of guardianship.

**curatorship.** <note>original Greek: κουρατωρεία</note> A curatorial office. Theophanes writes: "He ordered that the finer of the buildings be taken into the imperial **curatorship**." <note>original Greek: τὰ δὲ κρείττονα τῶν κτισμάτων εἰς τὴν βασιλικὴν κουρατωρείαν αἴρεσθαι ἐκέλευε</note> Anastasius the Librarian, in his *Ecclesiastical History*, translates: *Furthermore, he ordered that whatever was better among the items should be brought to the royal curatorship.* <note>original Latin: ceterum quaeque meliora erant in rebus in regiam curatoriam deferri iubebat</note> See the later notes of Father Goar, page 44, column 2, section d.

**curopalates.** <note>original Greek: κουροπαλάτης</note> The one who cared for the palace, to whom the care of the palace was entrusted. Nicetas Paphlago, in his *Life of Ignatius* (found in volume 3 of the *Councils*, edited by R.): "For Bardas, making the Roman empire subject to himself, was first made **curopalates**, etc." <note>original Greek: Βάρδας μὲν γὰρ ἐφ' ἑαυτὸν τὴν Ῥωμαϊκὴν ἀρχὴν ὑποποιούμενος πρῶτον μὲν κουροπαλάτης</note> The power of the **curopalates** was the highest after the emperor. Nicephorus, in his *Short History*: "Heraclius held Theodore, his own brother, in the first rank of authority after the emperor; those around the palace were accustomed to call him **curopalates**." <note>original Greek: Ἡράκλειος δὲ Θεόδωρον τὸν ἑαυτοῦ ἀδελφὸν τὴν μετά βασιλέα πρώτην ἀρχὴν κεκτημένον, κουροπαλάτην δὲ αὐτὸν οἱ περὶ τὰ βασίλεια καλεῖν εἰώθασι</note> It is incorrectly called *curopalatus*. Liutprand of Cremona, in his *Report of his Embassy*: *I was led into the presence of his brother Leo, the curopalates and logothete.* <note>original Latin: ante fratris eius Leonis curopalati et logothetae praesentiam sum deductus</note> Even more incorrectly, *curapalatius*. Pope Vigilius, in an encyclical letter to the whole church, mentions: *Justinian the ex-consul and curapalatii.* <note>original Latin: Iustinianum exconsulem et curapalatii</note> It appears as *curopalasius* in the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, chapter 7. Among the Latins, it was first called "the care of the palace" (*cura palatii*), as seen in the Code of Justinian. From this comes the term *excura palatii* <note>formerly of the palace care</note> in the historian Ammianus Marcellinus, book 22.

**raid, plunder, to raid.** <note>original Greek: κοῦρσον (kourson), κούρσευμα (kourseuma), κουρσεύειν (kourseuein)</note> An incursion or booty. Constantine, in his *Tactica*: "Do not allow the soldiers to go out into the enemy land in a disorderly fashion for **raids**." <note>original Greek: μὴ ἀφίῃς τοὺς στρατιώτας εἰς τὴν πολεμίαν γῆν ἵνα ἀτάκτως ἐκβαίνωσιν εἰς κοῦρσα</note> Also: "For indeed, the soldiers go out for **raids** and other incursions, taking their pack-animals with them." <note>original Greek: καὶ γὰρ εἰς μὲν τὰ κοῦρσα καὶ τὰς ἄλλας ἐπιδρομὰς ἔρχουσιν οἱ στρατιῶται τὰ συρτὰ μετ' αὐτῶν</note> Also **plunder** <note>original Greek: κούρσευμα</note>. Astrampsychus, in his *Pythagorean Table*: "It signifies captivity and **plunder**." <note>original Greek: δηλοῖ αἰχμαλωσίαν καὶ κούρσευμα</note> Hence **to raid** <note>original Greek: κουρσεύειν</note> meaning to seize booty. Constantine, in his *Tactica*: "For having **raided** Syria and secured many captives and much plunder." <note>original Greek: κουρσεύσας γὰρ τὴν Συρίαν καὶ κρατήσας αἰχμαλωσίαν καὶ πραῖδαν πολλήν</note> Theophanes, regarding Emperor Heraclius: "**raiding** and plundering." <note>original Greek: κουρσεύων καὶ πραιδεύων</note> See below: **coursors** <note>skirmishers or raiders</note>.

<summary>This page defines several Byzantine administrative, naval, and military terms, focusing on the evolution of titles like "curator" and "curopalates" and the origin of the word for "raid" (kourson).</summary>
<keywords>curopalates, curator, logothete, koumparia, Byzantine navy, military raids, imperial household, legal terminology, Theophanes, Constantine Porphyrogenitus</keywords>

<page-num>914</page-num>

<header>FABROT</header>

**Runners** <note>Greek: κούρσωρες (*koursores*); Latin: *cursores*</note>. Suidas <note>a 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> says: "Young man [*koure*], in the Roman tongue, means 'run'; hence the 'runners'." The "divine runner" <note>Greek: θεῖος κούρσωρ (*theios koursor*)</note> refers to the emperor's messenger. Caesarius, in *Dialogue 2*, response 107 B, and John Chrysostom—or rather the author of the homily *On the Just and Blessed Job* found in volume 6 of Chrysostom’s works—states: "how they send the swift ones, called *koursores* in the Roman <note>Latin</note> tongue." Philostorgius, in *Ecclesiastical History*, book 2, mentions: "and she was caught again committing adultery with one of the runners." Libanius also understands this to mean a messenger in his *23rd Oration*: "then neither the boy arrived, nor those whose business it is to run." It is also mentioned by Petronius in *Ancient Inscriptions*, page 600, line 15, and by Firmicus. Lupus the Abbot, in his final letter, writes: *"Until we arrive, our runner shall fulfill the role of a poor man among you."* Peter of Blois, in *Letter 41*: *"I have sent various runners ahead in every direction as scouts of our routes."* Adventius, Bishop of Metz, writing to Pope Nicholas: *"Nevertheless, amidst these troubles, we were barely able to direct one runner—namely, the religious priest Theodoric—to your Mercy by a shortcut, carrying these present letters."* Paulinus, in *Letter 24*: *"That we may praise Cardamas, the Lord’s runner, by the examples of the swift men of old recorded in the divine law."* Therefore, "runner" is taken to mean a servant, whom the Greeks today call an *oulakis* and the French call a *laquais* <note>a lackey or footman</note>. Laonikos Chalkokondyles says: "these heralds are called *oulakides*." It can also refer to a courier or someone we send to deliver something. The term *procursor* <note>forerunner</note> in the *Miscellany History* and the ecclesiastical history of Anastasius the Librarian is, I believe, the **protokoursor** <note>Greek: πρωτοκούρσωρ</note>, the "chief of the runners." Furthermore, **koursores** is the name given to soldiers who carry out raids during wartime. See Leo the Wise, *Tactica*, chapter 7, section 36.

**The Block** <note>Greek: κοῦπος (*koupos*); Latin: *cippus*</note>. An ancient lexicon from the Royal Library defines it as: "the *koupos* is a gaming board <note>specifically for a game like chess or backgammon</note>, or a place of punishment for slaves." Others explain it as a "foot-shackle" <note>Greek: ποδοκάκη (*podokake*)</note>. Simeon Metaphrastes explains what these foot-shackles are in his life of Lucian: "And they forced both his feet into the shackle (which is a long wooden torture device), pulling them through four holes, which is the most severe form of this punishment."

**Hunting Arena** <note>Greek: κυνήγιον (*kynegion*)</note>. A place in which the hunting of wild beasts was exhibited for the pleasure of the people. From this comes the term **beast-fighting hunters** <note>Greek: κυνηγοὶ θηριομάχοι (*kynegoi theriomachoi*)</note> in the Legal Glosses, which refers to "beast-fighters" <note>Latin: *bestiarii*</note>; I shall speak more fully of them in that section. Punishments were occasionally carried out on defendants in such places. Nicephorus, in his *Short History*, writes: "He sent him out to have his head cut off in the place called the *Kynegion*." Likewise: "He ordered his head to be cut off in the city’s *Kynegion*."

**The Lord's Day** <note>Greek: κυριακή (*kyriake*), κυριακόν (*kyriakon*)</note>. "One of the Sabbaths" <note>Greek: μία σαββάτων (*mia sabbaton*)</note>, meaning the Lord’s day [Sunday]. Saint Gregory of Nyssa, in *To Those Who Resent Censures*, asks: "With what eyes do you look upon the Lord's Day, you who have dishonored the Sabbath?" See also Saint Gregory of Nazianzus, *Oration 19*, and Nicephorus Callistus, book 7, chapter 46. "One of the Sabbaths" is the Lord's Day, the first day of the week. Oecumenius, commenting on *1 Corinthians*, chapter 9, says: "He calls the Lord’s Day 'one of the Sabbaths'." Theophylactus, on *Luke*, chapter 18, notes: "They called the first day of the week—the day we call the Lord's Day—'one of the Sabbaths'."

<summary>This page defines Byzantine terms for messengers (koursores), punishment devices (koupos), the public hunting arenas used for executions (kynegion), and the theological terminology for Sunday (kyriake).</summary>
<keywords>koursores, messengers, raids, koupos, stocks, torture, kynegion, arena, executions, kyriake, Sunday, Sabbath, Byzantine law, etymology</keywords>

<page-num>915</page-num>

<header>GLOSSARY.</header>

See the same author at chapter 24 regarding **The Great Lord’s Day** <note>original: ἡ μεγάλη κυριακή (*hē megalē kyriakē*)</note> in Cedrenus <note>an 11th-century Byzantine historian</note>; this refers to the day of Easter. Likewise, in the same author on page 295, **Lord’s house** <note>original: κυριακή (*kyriakē*) or κυριακόν (*kyriakon*)</note> refers to a temple or church. See also Nicephorus Callistus, book 7, chapter 38; Cyril’s *Catechism*, page 494 of the quarto edition; the *Alexandrian Chronicle*, page 660. Saint Athanasius in the *Life of Anthony*: "immediately going out of the church." Simeon Metaphrastes in the *Martyrdom of Cyprian*: "he arrives at the church." See Zonaras on Canon 74 of the 6th Synod in Trullo. Walafridus Strabo, in *On Ecclesiastical Matters*, chapter 7, writes: "Just as the house of God is called a 'Basilica'—that is, a 'royal house' from the word for king—so it is also called *kyriaka*—that is, the 'Lord’s house' from the word for Lord." Add Aimoin’s *History of the Franks*, book 2, chapter 11.

**Lord, Master, Sir** <note>original: κυρός, κύρ, κῦρις (*kyros, kyr, kyris*)</note>. Meaning 'lord' <note>Latin: *dominus*</note>. Used in the title of the work of **Lord Cedrenus**. Joseph, Bishop of Methone, thus titled his defense against the pamphlet of Mark, Metropolitan of Ephesus: "A defense against the pamphlet of **Lord Mark Eugenikos**, Metropolitan of Ephesus." Council of Chalcedon, Act 1: "we ask that **Lord Mamas** also speak." The old translator renders this: *we supplicate that Master Mamas may speak.* Synod of Constantinople, Act 14: "**Lord Constantine**." The old translator: *Master Constantine.* And shortly after: "I gave these things to the **Lord Constantine** himself." Council of Chalcedon, Act 1: "The transaction took place in the presence of **Lord Thalassius**, **Lord Eusebius**, and the Silentiary <note>a court official who maintained order and silence in the palace</note>."

**Codex, Small Book** <note>original: κῶδιξ, κωδίκιον (*kōdix, kōdikion*)</note>. A codex or manuscript. Saint John Chrysostom, in his *Homily on the Savior’s Birthday*: "and in the ancient public **codices** kept at Rome." Theophanes: "The Emperor Anastasius saw in a vision a terrifying man carrying a **codex**." Pachymeres: "The **small book** of the church was brought forward as evidence." Sixth Synod of Constantinople, Act 5: "Let the aforementioned **codices** be received." The old translator renders this: *let the predicted codices be received.* In Act 7, the old translator renders it as *codicillum* <note>a small codex or letter</note>, and in Act 13 as *polyptychum* <note>a multi-leaved register or ledger</note>.

**Laterculum** <note>original: λατέρκουλον (*laterkoulon*)</note>. A register or list. Cedrenus explains what a *laterculum* is on page 169. Theodoret, in *Questions on the Book of Kings*, Question 40: "I believe it is called a *plinthion* <note>literally a small brick</note>, which external writers call a *plaision* <note>a frame</note>. This is a type of military formation having a square shape." See Cujas on the title of the Code regarding the "proximate of the sacred bureaus," law 13; on Novel 8; and on the office of the Quaestor in the *Paratitla* of the Code.

**Legacy** <note>original: λεγάτον (*legaton*)</note>. A bequest or legacy. Mentioned by Suidas. It occurs frequently in the *Basilica* <note>the 9th-century code of Byzantine law</note>. Council of Florence, Session 3: "Just as he left to them a sort of **legacy** and inheritance."

**Litter** <note>original: λεκτίκιον (*lektikion*)</note>. A *lectica* <note>a portable bed or litter</note>. *Menologium* for August 2: "placing the holy relic in a **litter** upon a donkey." The Greeks refer this to law 60, paragraph 8, of the *Digest* <note>a collection of Roman legal juristic writings</note>.

**Lessa** <note>original: λέσσα (*lessa*)</note>. See the work of Meursius <note>Johannes Meursius, a scholar of Greek antiquity</note>.

**Libellensis** <note>original: λιβελλίσιος (*libellissios*)</note>. One who writes petitions or legal briefs <note>from the Latin *libellus*, meaning a small book or petition</note>. Novel 20, chapter 9. Refers to one who drafts petitions, mentioned in the law "By this law" in the Code concerning the "proximate of the sacred bureaus," and law 3 of the Code regarding the Senate. Julian the *Antecessor* <note>a 6th-century law professor</note> in the *Novel regarding the assistant to the Quaestor*. See the commentary on Theophilus regarding bail.

<summary>This page defines ecclesiastical and administrative terms, focusing on the etymology of church buildings (kyriakon), honorific titles for officials (kyros), and various legal documents or military formations like the laterculum.</summary>
<keywords>kyriakon, church, kyros, lord, codex, laterculum, legacy, litter, libellensis, Byzantine law, ecclesiastical history</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical glossary of Byzantine Greek and legal terms. The previous page (915) discussed the terms for "Lord" (Kyros) and "Church" (Kyriaka). # FABROTUS

**Petition** <note>original: λίβελλος (*libellos*); Latin: *libellus*</note>. Phavorinus <note>a 16th-century lexicographer</note>. The Third Act of the Sixth Synod of Constantinople: "two petitions were found in it." And in Act 4, the **petition of faith** of Pyrrhus is praised. Theophanes, in his account of Emperor Heraclius, writes: "and having delivered a petition of orthodoxy to the Pope." In the letters of Saint John Chrysostom to Pope Innocent, we find "petitions of accusation" <note>original: λίβελλοι κατηγοριῶν (*libelloi katēgoriōn*)</note>, or legal indictments.

**Passage** <note>original: λόγγος (*longos*); Latin: *locus angustus*</note>. A narrow place. See Meursius <note>Johannes Meursius, a Dutch scholar of Greek antiquities</note> on this word.

**Logothete** <term>logothete: a high-ranking administrative official in the Byzantine Empire, roughly equivalent to a Secretary of State or a Minister</term>. There were several types. The **General Logothete** <note>original: γενικὸς λογοθέτης (*genikos logothetēs*)</note>, whom we discussed above under the entry for "General." See Procopius’s *Secret History*, pages 81 and 104, and the notes there. Nicephorus Gregoras, Book 8: "Theodore Metochites, the Logothete of the General Treasury." The **Logothete of the Household** <note>original: ὁ τῶν οἰκειακῶν (*ho tōn oikeiakōn*)</note>. George Pachymeres mentions: "the Great Logothete of the Household." The **Logothete of the Course** <note>original: ὁ τοῦ δρόμου (*ho tou dromou*)</note>, who managed the public post and foreign affairs. Constantine Porphyrogenitus, *On Administering the Empire*, chapter 32. Theophanes, in his account of Constantine: "among whom the leaders were Constantine the Patrician, who became Logothete of the Course." The **Military Logothete**: Sixth Synod of Constantinople, Act 1, mentions a "military logothete"; Seventh Synod, Act 1, mentions "John, the imperial Usher <note>original: ὀστιάριος (*ostiarios*)</note> and Logothete of the military treasury." Anastasius the Librarian <note>9th-century historian</note> translates this as: *John, imperial usher and logothete of the imperial treasury.* Another translator renders it as: *John, royal usher and quaestor of the military treasury.* Codinus, in his work *On Offices*, mentions the **Logothete of the Herds** <note>who managed imperial horse and livestock farms</note>. Finally, the **Logothete of the Secrets** <note>original: ὁ τῶν σεκρέτων λογοθέτης</note>, mentioned by Nicetas, who was also called the **Great Logothete**. Nicephorus Gregoras, Book 6: "Muzalon the Great Logothete." Today, this office is equivalent to a **chancellor**. Papias <note>an 11th-century lexicographer</note> notes: "the logothete announces the emperor’s edict abroad to the people." See the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, chapter 68.

**Cuirass** <note>original: λωρίκιον, λουρίκιον (*lōrikion, lourikion*)</note>. Emperor Leo’s *Tactica*, chapter 15, section 9: "those who do not have cuirasses." Constantine’s *Tactica*: "let the cuirasses have leather cases." A manuscript glossary under the word "weapons" <note>original: ὅπλα (*hopla*)</note> states: "the breastplate is the iron shirt, which is the *lourikion*." Legal glossaries define it as: "a mantle, a garment, the cuirass." Laonikos Chalkokondyles, Book 9: "making excellent cuirasses." Theophanes, in his account of Heraclius: "they took their cuirasses." In the *Precious Crown* <note>a Greek-Latin dictionary</note>: "a jacket, a *louriki*." From this comes the term **armored men** <note>original: λωρικάτοι (*lōrikatoi*)</note>. Mentioned by Leo in the section cited above. In Theophanes’ account of Justinian, they are called *lourikatoi*, and in his account of Theodosius, *lōrikatoi*.

**Thong** <note>original: λώριον (*lōrion*); Latin: *lorum*</note>. A leather strap. See Meursius.

**Strap** <note>original: λῶρος (*lōros*); Latin: *lorum*</note>. An ancient commentator on Homer’s *Iliad*, Book 3, defines it as: "a strap, a lorum." Eustathius, commenting on *Iliad* Book 2: "the *telamon* is now a wide strap <note>original: λῶρος (*lōros*)</note> by which the shield was carried." Macarius, in *Homily 32*: "he tortures him with thongs." A commentator on Euripides's *Hippolytus*: "charioteers are accustomed to fasten the straps to the rim of the chariot." Theodore Metochites, in his *Roman History*: "the back is scourged with woven thongs; for such is the scourge <note>original: φραγγέλιον (*phrangelion*)</note>." A manuscript glossary from the collection of the most illustrious Chancellor of France, Pierre Séguier, states: "the *amphōriskos* is the strap." See the *Greek Breviary*, pages 365 and 517, part 2. The Greeks used both the forms *lōros* and *lōron*, just as the Latins used *lorus* and *lorum*. Cyril’s Glossary: "a strap: a bridle, a lorum, a thong."

**To Magarize** <note>original: μαγαρίζειν (*magarizein*)</note>. To profess the Islamic faith <note>original: "Mahometan impietacy"; this was a medieval polemical term for converting to Islam</note>. Theophanes: "and to speak to a certain *magaritēs* <note>a convert or Muslim</note>." Anastasius the Librarian, in his *Ecclesiastical History*: "and he said to a certain Cosmas standing near him, a Roman refugee and a *magarita*." The same author notes: "Umar the Saracen was killed—"

<meta>catchword: rum (completing "Saracenorum")</meta>

<summary>This page defines Byzantine administrative, military, and religious terms, most notably providing an extensive breakdown of the various types of Logothetes (imperial officials) and descriptions of Roman/Byzantine armor and leatherwork.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical glossary of Greek and Latin terms used in Byzantine administration and history. The previous page (915) discussed legal petitions and administrative offices like the Logothete. This page moves into the letter Mu (μ), specifically examining military siege engines and the rank of the Magistrianoi.</meta>

### GLOSSARY

...leader, by a certain Persian apostate named Margarita <note>original: *margarita*; likely a name or title meaning "pearl."</note>. See *Miscellaneous History*, book 19.

**μάγγανον** *Mangonel, war machine.* <term>mangonel: a type of catapult or siege engine used to hurl stones</term> The Philoxenus Glossaries define it as: a *ballista* <note>original: *ballistra*; a heavy missile launcher</note>, a sling, or a war engine. The commentator on Thucydides says: "the *balanos* <note>an iron bolt or pin</note> is the iron piece thrown into the lever, which we call a *manganon*." The same commentator on Aristophanes' *Assemblywomen* says the same. Papias <note>an 11th-century lexicographer</note> writes: *a siege engine is called whatever is twisted with the greatest force, as it is commonly called a mangonel.* Abbo, in his poem *On the Siege of Paris*, book 2:

> They build mangonels with equally long paired timbers, 
> as they are called in the common tongue, 
> with which they hurl massive stones, or by throwing them, 
> they crush the lowly tents of the savage people.

*Miscellaneous History*, book 20: "placing heavy crossbow-engines and large and clever machines on the towers." However, Anastasius the Librarian <note>a 9th-century scholar and translator</note> records it thus in his *Ecclesiastical History*: "placing heavy crossbow-engines and mangonels in the towers." Therefore, read "mangonels" in the *Miscellaneous History*, or if you prefer, *manganas*: for they also used the term *manganas*. In the *Passion of Saint Tyemo*: "at the constructed machine, which they commonly call a *mangona*." Read *manganam*. The former is more likely: for the written manuscripts have *mangana*, as Canisius notes in his various studies; and in the old manuscript of Anastasius, from whom the author of the *Miscellaneous History* borrowed, it is read that way. From this comes **μαγγανάρῐος**, one who builds mangonels, a **manganarius**. Leo the Tactician <note>Emperor Leo VI, known for his military treatises</note>, chapter 15, section 35: "through the ingenuity of the accompanying engine-makers." *Miscellaneous History*, book 17: "He strove to kill Basas, the city's engine-maker." Read it thus: for Theophanes uses the word *manganarios*. Indeed, Anastasius also uses it in his history, as well as the term **μαγγανικόν** <note>the mechanical apparatus itself</note>. Cedrenus writes: "he was struck by a stone from the engine." Theophanes, writing on Justinian the Younger: "having delivered to him for the siege a battering ram, mangonels, and every kind of city-taker tower" <note>original: ἑλέπολιν (*helepolis*); a massive mobile siege tower</note>.

**μαγιστεριανός, μαγιστριανός.** *Magistrian, an agent in affairs, an official of the Master of Offices.* <term>Master of Offices: one of the most senior administrative officials in the Roman and Byzantine Empires, overseeing the civil service and state security</term> In the letters of Isidore of Pelusium, letter 229, addressed to Leontius the Magistrian. The Second Council of Nicaea, Act 1, from the *Life of Saint Sabas*: "with the magistrians and officials still present and listening." Anastasius the Librarian: "with the magistrians present." Theophanes: "Julian the magistrian with the sacred imperial decree." Anastasius in his *Ecclesiastical History*: "Julian the magistrian with the sacred decree." Emperor Constantine, in a letter to Arius at the end (found in Gelasius of Cyzicus's account of the Council of Nicaea): "through the magistrians Syncletius and Gaudentius." It is used by Constantine Porphyrogenitus in *On Administering the Empire*, and in Palladius’s *Lausiac History*, chapter 149. It occurs often in the Council of Ephesus. Bishop Agapitus, in a letter to Emperor Leo (found in the third part of the Council of Chalcedon): "lest any impediment be made for Eudoxius, a devoted man and a magistrian." Mark the Deacon, quoted by the eminent Cardinal Baronius: "meanwhile, while the place was being purified, a magistrian arrived bringing imperial letters from the ever-memorable Eudoxia." The *Short History of the Eutychianists*: "he directs magistrians throughout the whole..."

<summary>This page defines the "manganon" (a siege engine or mangonel) and the "magistrianus" (a high-ranking administrative official), providing numerous citations from Byzantine historians, church councils, and poets.</summary>
<keywords>manganon, mangonel, siege engine, manganarius, magistrianus, Master of Offices, military technology, Byzantine administration, Theophanes, Anastasius the Librarian</keywords>
