<meta>This page continues the alphabetical glossary of Byzantine administrative and legal terms. The previous page (915/916) discussed military hardware such as "manganons" (siege engines). This page (918) moves into the civil and courtly administration, specifically focusing on the "Magistrianoi" (agents of the Master of Offices) and the rank of "Magister" itself.</meta>

->FABROTUS<-

The East. Anastasius the Librarian in his work on Hormisdas: *with soldiers and magisterians* <note>original Latin: *cum militibus et magistrianis*</note>. The Acts of Abercius in the same work by Baronius: *We sent Valerian and Basian, magisterians of our divine offices* <note>original Latin: *Valerianum et Basianum magisterianos divinorum nostrorum officiorum misimus*</note>. In other versions, it is read as "masters." The former reading is confirmed by Simeon Metaphrastes in his life of Abercius: *ordering that Valerios and Basianos, the magisterians, be immediately prepared* <note>original Greek: καὶ Οὐαλέριον καὶ Βασιανὸν μαγιστριανοὺς εὐθὺς εὐτρεπισθῆναι κελεύσας</note>, and a little later: *We sent Valerios and Basianos, the magisterians of our divine offices* <note>original Greek: Οὐαλέριον καὶ Βασιανὸν μαγιστριανοὺς τῶν θείων ἡμῶν ὀφφικίων ἐπέμψαμεν</note>. This is how it is read in two manuscripts. Marcellinus Comes and Victor mention them in their Chronicles. Regarding the *agent in affairs* <term>agent in affairs: from the Latin "agens in rebus," these were a class of imperial messengers who also served as inspectors and secret police</term>, see Ammianus Marcellinus. The Glosses of Philoxenus state: *agent in affairs* <note>original Latin: *agens in rebus*</note> is a *magistrianus* <note>original Greek: μαγιστριανός</note>. In the Council of Chalcedon, act 1: *Constantine the devoted magisterian* <note>original Greek: Κωνσταντῖνος ὁ καθωσιωμένος μαγιστριανός</note>. An old translator renders this as *agent in affairs*. And on page 76 at the end of the same work: *Veronicianus the magisterian* <note>original Greek: Βερονικιανὸς μαγιστριανός</note>, translated as *magistrianus*. As in act 3, page 229 d. Leo the Great, in letter 70 to Marcian Augustus: *that he should immediately send Nectarius, an agent in affairs, to Alexandria*. Lucifer of Cagliari, in a letter to Florentius, the Master of Offices: *handed over to Bonosus, the agent in affairs, to be delivered*. In the 5th Synod: *I am called Comitas, an agent in affairs*. Anastasius in his life of Liberius: *then authority was sent through Catulinus, the agent in affairs*. Add also Saint Augustine’s *Confessions*, book 8, chapter 6 and book 9, chapter 8; and Saint Ambrose’s letter to Marcellina and *On Duties*, book 3. Saint Athanasius, in his *Apology to the Emperor Constantine*: *Antiochus and Evagrius, agents of the silk* <note>original Greek: ἀγεντισηρίκους; likely a corruption of "agentes in rebus"</note>. The translator renders this as *prefects of the silks*. But other manuscripts have *agent-seribous*, that is, *agents in affairs* <note>original Latin: *agentes in rebus*</note>. See the notes of Fronton du Duc on Chrysostom’s 13th homily to the people of Antioch. An old translator of Justinian's *Novel* 17, chapter 4, translates *magistrianon* as *magisterianum*, and in *Novel* 124, chapter 3. However, Julian in *Novel* 21, chapter 1, uses *agent in affairs*, and in *Novel* 122, chapter 2, *magistrianum*. Theodoret in letter 79 calls him a *general-official* <note>original Greek: στρατηλατιανὸν</note>, but in letter 136, a *magisterian*. They were called "agents in affairs" because they serve in active affairs and in practice. They were, I say, as I have stated, magisterians, the officials of the Master of Offices, concerning which see below under *Master* <note>original Greek: μάγιστρος</note>.

**μάγιστρος, μαγιστερία, μαγιστέριον.** *Master, Mastership, Office of the Master.* Master of the divine or courtly offices <note>original Latin: *magister divinorum seu aulicorum officiorum*</note>, *master of the divine offices* <note>original Greek: μάγιστρος τῶν θείων ὀφφικίων</note>, Council of Chalcedon, act 1. Master of the sacred offices: Sixth Synod of Constantinople, act 1, *master of the imperial offices* <note>original Greek: μάγιστρῳ τῶν βασιλικῶν ὀφφικίων</note>. Master of the palace. Saint Athanasius, *Apology to Emperor Constantine*: *Palladius, the former master of the palace* <note>original Greek: Παλλάδιος ὁ γενόμενος τοῦ παλατίου μάγιστρος</note>. Among the letters of Saint Basil, 84, 329, and 416 are addressed to *Sophronius the Master*. Stephanus of Byzantium, in his work *On Cities*, under the entry for *akonai*: *differing however from the most praiseworthy patrician and the all-wise master Peter* <note>referring to Peter the Patrician, a 6th-century official</note>. See Saint Chrysostom’s 17th homily to the people of Antioch and the notes. The Greeks interpret the Master as the *leader of the ranks in the court* <note>original Greek: ἡγεμόνα τῶν ἐν τῇ αὐλῇ τάξεων</note>. Suidas: *Rufinus, a Celt by birth, was appointed master of the ranks in the court*, from Zosimus, page 773. Others define the office of the Master more strictly, such as Procopius of Gaza in his commentary on 1 Kings, chapter 3: *this man was the same as the one now called Master among the Romans, leading the troops guarding the Emperor*. Agathias, book 4: *For while Barazes was counted among the captains, the other was of those in the...*

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical glossary of Byzantine administrative and legal terms. The previous page (918) concluded with the "magistrianoi" (agents of the Master of Offices). # GLOSSARIUM.

...led the court of the King of the Lazi <note>The Lazi were a people of the Caucasus (modern Georgia) who were often clients or allies of the Byzantine Empire</note>. The name of his office was "Magister." *Theodoret of Cyrus, Questions on the Second Book of Kings, question 40:* **The official now called "Magister" among the Romans has been entrusted with the command of those infantrymen around the emperor, I mean the shield-bearers and spear-bearers** <note>original Greek: ὁ νῦν παρὰ Ῥωμαίοις μάγιστρος ὀνομαζόμενος τῶν περὶ τὸν βασιλέα πεζαιτέρων, ἀσπιδηφόρων φημὶ καὶ δορυφόρων, τὴν ἡγεμονίαν πεπίστευται</note>, specifically because he presided over the prince’s attendants. Synesius in his *On Providence* calls him the **overseer of the spear-bearers** <note>original Greek: ἐπιστάτην δορυφόρων</note>, the one placed in charge of the praetorian soldiers. The honor of the Magister was great, and it was even bestowed upon those joined by blood to the Emperor. *Constantine Manasses:*

->**one of the brilliant and renowned men,**<-
->**being of the Emperor's kin, held the rank of Magister.**<-

The **dignity of the Master** <note>original Latin: magistri dignitas</note> was called *magisteria* or *magisterion*. *Legal Glosses:* **a prominent office, perhaps the magisterium** <note>original Greek: περιὸν ἀρχή, ἴσως μαγιστέριον</note>. *Theophanes:* **he removes Longinus from the magisterium** <note>original Greek: παύει τὸν Λογγῖνον τοῦ μαγιστερίου</note>. As found in Sidonius, **palatine and military masterships** <note>original Latin: magisteria palatina et militaria, Book 1, Letter 3</note> and in the single law of the *Codex of Justinian* regarding the Quaestor and the Master of Offices: **or by an effective mastership** <note>original Latin: aut efficaci magisterio</note>. Claude Saumaise <note>A 17th-century French classical scholar</note>, in his notes on Trebellius Pollio, page 293, reads it as *magisteria*. However, the authority of Jacques Cujas <note>A 16th-century French legal humanist</note> is stronger for me, as he retains *magisterio* in the same law. *Sulpicius Severus, Dialogue 3, chapter 15: the officials of the mastership having been sent to meet them.* <note>original Latin: missis obviam magisterii officialibus</note>. Likewise, **to perform the mastership** <note>original Latin: magisterio fungi</note> is found in *Suetonius, Life of Domitian*. I do not see why the dignity of the "Master" should be called *magisteria* while that of other masters is called *magisterium*. Cujas considers the "Master of Offices" <term>Master of Offices: Magister Officiorum, one of the most powerful administrative officials in the late Roman and Byzantine Empire, overseeing the civil service and palace security</term> to be similar to the official called in France the **Provost of the Household** <note>original French: prévost de l'hostel</note>, in his notes on Law 3 of the Code regarding the Provost of the Sacred Bedchamber; see also his *Paratitla* on the Code under the title "Of the Office of the Master of Offices." One who has served in that dignity is called *apo magistrōn*, meaning "from the Masters" <note>This title was used for retired officials, similar to "Emeritus"</note>. *Council of Chalcedon, Act 1*; *Theodoret*, Letter 110. They also used the form **maistōr**, as in *Theodoret, Letter 140*, addressed to **Maistor Bigkomalos**. *Theophanes: Illos the maistor.* *George Kodinos in the Origins of Constantinople: and he gave centenaria to the people through the generalship of the Master.* <note>original Greek: καὶ ἔδωκε κεντηνάρια τῷ λαῷ διὰ στρατηγίου μαγίστρου</note>. In the copy owned by the illustrious Nicolas-Claude Fabri de Peiresc, it is read as *maistrou*. *The Basilica <note>A 9th-century collection of Byzantine laws</note>, Book 7, Section 1: the maistor of his own ship.* <note>original Greek: μαΐστορα τοῦ ἰδίου πλοίου</note>. It should be read this way, as in the Royal Manuscript of the *Synopsis*, and not *magistōra*, as it appears in the manuscript of the *Basilica*.

**μαγκίπειον, μάγκιψ.** (Mankipeion, Mankips). A **bakery** <note>original Latin: pistrinum</note>. *Alexandrian Chronicle, page 786: and he built bakeries inside the palace.* <note>original Greek: ἔκτισε δὲ ἔνδον τοῦ παλατίου μαγκίπεια</note>. *Nicephorus Callistus, 12.22.* Where Ulpian says in one place **he cast him into the bakery**, the Greeks translate it as **I provide in the mankipion** <note>original Greek: ἐν μαγκιπίῳ παράσχω</note>. *Life of John the Almsgiver, chapter 21: and an animal carrying fine flour from the bakery for his own lunch.* From this, **mankips** refers to a baker. *Legal Glosses: a mankips is the craftsman of common bread.* <note>original Greek: μάγκιψ ὁ τεχνίτης τοῦ δημώδους ἄρτου</note>. *Ulpian in law 13, final section, on Usufruct: if he should lease a stable for a bakery.* <note>original Latin: si stabulum pistrino locaverit</note>. *The Basilica: nor the stable to a mankips.* <note>original Greek: οὔτε μάγκιπι τὸ στάϐλον</note>. See Cujas, *On the Prescription of Different Times*, chapter 13.

**μαγκλαϐίτης.** (Manklabites). A **manklabion** is a **leather strap** or **whip** <note>original Latin: lorum, flagellum</note>. *Theodore of Hermopolis, Book 7, title 8: striking him with whips or rods.* <note>original Greek: τύψας αὐτὸν μαγκλαϐίοις ἢ ῥάϐδοις</note>. *Achmes, chapter 249.* *Astrampsychus in the Pythagorean Quarry: it signifies murders, beheadings, and the cutting off of hands and feet, and whip-lashes.* <note>original Greek: δηλοῖ δὲ καὶ φόνους καὶ κοπὰς κεφαλῶν καὶ χειρῶν καὶ ποδῶν καὶ μαγκλάϐια</note>. From this comes the **manklabites** <term>manklabites: a member of the imperial bodyguard who carried a whip (manklabion) as a badge of office and to clear the way for the emperor</term>. *George Logothetes in his Chronicle:*

<vocab>μαγίστρος (magistros - Master), μαγιστερία (magisteria - office of Master), μαΐστωρ (maistor - Master/teacher), μαγκίπειον (mankipeion - bakery), μάγκιψ (mankips - baker), μαγκλαϐίτης (manklabites - whip-bearing guard), μαγκλάϐιον (manklabion - whip/strap), pistrinum (bakery), lorum (leather strap), flagellum (whip), magisterium (mastership), magisterio officialibus (officials of the mastership)</vocab>

<summary>This page defines the high-ranking office of "Magister" (Master), tracing its evolution from a military guard commander to an elite court title often held by imperial relatives. It also covers more mundane terms like "mankips" (baker) and the "manklabites" guards, named for the whips they carried.</summary>

# FABROT'S GLOSSARY

...and the *manklabites* <note>original: μαγκλαβίτην; an imperial bodyguard who carried a "manglabion" or whip/club</note> Nicholas. *Regarding whom see Meursius and the most learned Vossius in "On the Faults of Speech."*

**<term>μακελλεῖον</term> (makelleion), <term>λεωμακέλλιον</term> (leomakellion).** A meat market or slaughterhouse <note>original Latin: macellum, laniatorium</note>. From this comes **<term>μακελλάρης</term> (makellarēs)** and **<term>μακελλάριος</term> (makellarios)**, meaning a butcher. Astrampsychus in the *Pythagorean Stone-cutter*: **it shows the man to be a butcher and a cook.** *Makellos* is the same as *makelleion*. Xiphilinus in his *Life of Nero*: **the market for delicacies, named the *makellon*.** From this comes **<term>λεωμακέλλιον</term>** in the works of Cedrenus. See Meursius under the entry **<term>μάκελλος</term>**.

**<term>μάνα</term> (mana).** Mother. See Meursius and the very learned Vossius in *On the Faults of Speech*, book 3, chapter 24. **"Ma" is the mother according to the address of an infant** <note>original Greek: μᾶ ἡ μήτηρ κατὰ βρέφους προσφώνησιν</note>, as noted by Eustathius in his commentary on the *Iliad*, book 5. See also the *Etymologicum* under the entry for "all" (*pas*).

**<term>μάνδρα</term> (mandra), <term>μανδρίτης</term> (mandritēs), <term>ἀρχιμανδρίτης</term> (archimandritēs).** A monastery <note>literally a "sheepfold" or enclosed pen; later used for the enclosure of a monastic community</note>. George of Alexandria in the *Life of the Blessed Chrysostom*: **those whom he was snatching while alive in his own monastery.** Also: **to proceed diligently to the monastery of the father.** Mentioned by Dorotheus in *Doctrine 23*, Nicephorus Callistus (14.51), and Simeon Metaphrastes: **into this newly-built monastery of yours.** Alcuin in *Epistle 27*: **the ranks of the heavenly sheepfold.** Albinus in book 2 of the *Life of Saint Willibrord*: **Therefore the watchman circles the sheepfolds with this protection.** From this comes **<term>μανδρίτης</term>** <note>a monk</note>. Council of Constantinople under Menna, act 5. Ermenoldus in the *Life of Saint Sola*: **monks coming from different places.** And **<term>ἀρχιμανδρίτης</term>** <note>Archimandrite; a superior over several monasteries or a high-ranking abbot</note>. Synod of Constantinople 7, act 1: **of the most reverent archimandrites, superiors, and monks.** Avitus of Vienne in *Epistle 2*: **He was placed in charge of a large multitude of monks; the Eastern bishops call the persons of this office archimandrites.** Defined as the **leader of monks** by the ancient interpreter of the Council of Chalcedon.

**<term>μανδύλιον</term> (mandylion).** A cloth or napkin <note>original Latin: mantile</note>. Mentioned in the *Etymologicum*. Alexius Rharturus in his final *Doctrine*: **the cloth for the eyes.** See Meursius’s *Glossary*.

**<term>μανίκιον</term> (manikion).** A sleeve <note>original Latin: manica</note>. Theophanes in the *Life of Theodosius*: **they dipped the sleeves of their right hands.** Constantine in the *Tactics*, page 15: **it is necessary for them to have very wide tunics and wide sleeves.** The Legal Glosses interpret this as a **handle** or **hilt**. We shall speak of that in its proper place.

**<term>μάππα</term> (mappa), <term>μαππάριος</term> (mapparios).** A napkin or cloth. Concerning the *mappa*, see those who have written about the Circus <note>the cloth was dropped to signal the start of a race</note>, and Vossius, a man by far the most learned, in *On the Faults of Speech*, chapter 4. Marcellinus Comes in his *Chronicle*: **at least one and the last cloth was denied to the raging people.** From this comes **<term>μαππάριος</term>**, the official who threw the *mappa* in the Circus.

**<term>μαργελόγραμμον</term> (margelogrammon).** Thus Salmasius reads in his notes on Vopiscus, page 406, column 2, following Meursius in his *Glossary* under **<term>μάργελλον</term>** <note>likely referring to a garment with a decorated border or "margella"</note>. See also the later notes, page 57.

**<term>ματρικάριος</term> (matrikarios). <term>ξυλουργός</term> (xylourgos),** a woodworker or carpenter.

**<term>ματρίκιον</term> (matrikion).** A register or roll <note>original Latin: matricula</note>. The Canons of the Church of Africa: **the register and archive of Numidia.** Zonaras on canon 93 of the Council of Carthage: **a certain census or list...**

# GLOSSARY. 921

**...for this is the <term>ματρίκιον</term> (matrikion)** <note>original: matrikion; a register or original record-book</note>. The Greeks in Book 22 of the *Basilika*, Title 4, regarding Novel 73, chapter 8: **"a comparison of writings is made both from the codex and from the *matrikion*."**

**<term>μάτριξ</term> (matrix).** Latin: *matrix* <note>a list, register, or source</note>. The Greeks, commenting on the *Code of Justinian* regarding witnesses (Book 4, Law 15): **"such as an *isokodix* [equal copy] or a *matrix*."** In the *Latin-Greek Glossary*: **"*matrix* is a mark of names."** In the *Legal Glossaries*: **"*matrikes* are census records and copies."** Tertullian in *On Flight in Persecution*: **"when in the *matrices* [registers] of the beneficiaries and officials, etc."** See the notes on the *Canons of the African Church*, page 46, and Zonaras on Canon 36 of the Synod of Carthage. From this comes **<term>ματρικουλάριοι</term> (matrikoularioi)** <note>matricularii</note>, that is, those enrolled in the *matricula* <note>a register, often specifically the list of the poor supported by a church</note>. Aldhelm, in *The Praise of Virginity*: **"But they bestowed all their inheritance and the glory of their ornaments—as much the hair-parting pins and the leg-bracelets as the scent-bottles of nard and the trinkets hanging from the neck with gem-bearing crescents—with lavish generosity as alms for the maimed and those on the church-register [matricularii],"** that is, the needy. On the various types of registers (*matriculae*), see Vossius’s *On the Faults of Speech*.

**<term>ματρωνίκιον</term> (matronikion).** A *matroneum* <note>the area in a church reserved for women, usually a gallery</note>. See Meursius.

**<term>μέταξα</term> (metaxa).** Silk <note>also called *sericum*</note>. Laonicus Chalcondyles, Book 4: **"this land nurtures silk, producing the most beautiful kind."** See also the *Dream Interpretation* of Achmet, chapter 222; Procopius in the *Secret History*, page 111; Zonaras on the *Councils*, page 231; Nicephorus Callistus, volume 2, page 787; and Cujas on Law 10 of the *Code* regarding murex-fishers.

**<term>μιλιαρίσιον</term> (miliarision).** A *miliarense*, a type of coin, the twelfth part of a *solidus* <note>the standard gold coin</note>. Constantine Porphyrogenitus in *On the Administration of the Empire*: **"another ten pounds of *miliarisia*."** George Syncellus: **"And taking the vessels of the churches, he struck coins and *miliarisia*."** See also Moschus in the *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 185; Nicephorus Callistus, volume 2, page 838; Codinus in the *Origins of Constantinople*, page 79; the *Menologion* for March; and Theophanes in the entry for Heraclius. Cedrenus derives the name from *militia* [military service]. Hero, in *On Weights*: **"the silver *miliarision*, which is also a military gift; for *militia* is military service."**

**<term>μῖσος</term> (misos).** Cedrenus interprets this as a "prize" or "reward" <note>athlon</note>. In the *Greek-Latin Glossaries*: **"prize [athlon]: *missum*."**

**<term>μισσίκιος</term> (missikios).** Latin: *missicius*; one who has obtained a discharge after completing his military service. I have discussed this in my notes on Theophilus.

**<term>μιτατώριον</term> (mitatorion).** See the later notes on page 51, column 2. Learned men doubt the true reading. I advise, however, that it is read consistently in Leo the Grammarian: **"he found him in the place where he was praying, in the *mitatorion*."** And **"as far as the *mitatorikion*."** This is the reading in the Royal manuscript instead of *mitatoriou* <note>The mitatorion was a private reception room or changing room used by the Emperor in the Hagia Sophia or the Palace</note>.

**<term>μοδίολος</term> (modiolos).** See the same author, page 45 b. <note>A small measure, a diminutive of *modios*</note>.

**<term>μοναχός</term> (monachos), <term>μονάζων</term> (monazon), <term>μοναστήρ</term> (monaster). <term>καλόγηρος</term> (kalogeros).** A monk. In the *Greek-Latin Glossaries*: **"*monachos*: solitary, single, a monk."** Rutilius in his *Itinerary*, Book 1:

->*They call themselves monks by a name of Greek origin,*<-
->*Because they wish to live alone with no witness to their lives.*<-

Hence the "profession of singularity" in Canon *Propositum* 10, question 3. Zosimus, page 800: **"The church was now occupied by those called mona—"** <note>The text cuts off here at the end of the page</note>.

<summary>This page defines Byzantine terms for official registers (matrix), luxury goods like silk (metaxa), and currency (miliarision). It also introduces ecclesiastical terms for women's church galleries and the etymology of the word 'monk'.</summary>
<keywords>matrikion, matrix, silk, miliarision, currency, monasticism, Byzantine law, official registers</keywords>

# FABROTI # 922

...**monks** <note>original: χῶν, the ending of μοναχῶν</note>. Epiphanius in *Physiology*, chapter 22. The same is called **<term>μονάζων</term> (monazōn)** <note>one who lives alone; a solitary</note>. Macarius in *Homily 38, B*. Chrysostom in *Epistle 14*. 

**<term>μοναστής</term> (monastēs)** <note>a monk</note>. Gregory the Presbyter in the *Life of Gregory the Theologian*: **"choosing to be a monk instead of a worldly man and propertyless instead of wealthy."** 

**<term>καλόγηρος</term> (kalogeros)** <note>literally "good old man," a common term for a monk</note>. John Moschus in the *Spiritual Meadow*, chapters 27 and 45. In French, *beau père* <note>literally "fine father," used respectfully for monks</note>. 

**<term>μονάστρια ζωή</term> (monastria zōē)**, a solitary life, mentioned by Constantine Manasses. 

**<term>μονάστρια</term> (monastria)**, a nun. Manasses writes: **"and they appoint her a nun."**

**<term>μονή</term> (monē)**, a monastery. Nicephorus Gregoras, Book 3: **"who happened to be near his own monastery."** Simeon Metaphrastes in the *Life of Hilarion*: **"to those arriving at the monastery of Anthony."** Suidas regarding Justinian Rhinotmetos: **"a monk of the monastery of Kallistratos,"** and in the same place: **"the abbot of the monastery of Florus."** Cedrenus simply says: **"the abbot of Florus."** From this comes **<term>μονήδριον</term> (monēdrion)**, a small monastery. Nicephorus Gregoras, Book 4.

**<term>μονοστράτηγος</term> (monostratēgos)** <note>a single general or commander-in-chief</note>. Page 444 a. *monostrategus*. Anastasius the Librarian in his *Ecclesiastical History*: **"He busied himself with transferring the empire to his own father, whom he also made *monostratēgos*."** Thus two manuscripts write *monostrate-gum*, as elsewhere in the same author.

**<term>μονόξυλα</term> (monoxyla)**, small boats or skiffs carved from single logs <note>dugout canoes</note>. Vegetius, *On Military Affairs*, Book 2, last chapter. The *Alexandrian Chronicle*, pages 900 and 904. Nicephorus of Constantinople in the *Short History*. *Greek-Latin Glossary*: **"*monoxylon*: a skiff."** Zosimus, Book 4: **"The barbarians, embarking the peak of their force onto a multitude of dugouts, drew them up."**

**<term>μονοπώλειον</term> (monopōleion)**, a monopoly. Curopalates, page 850. See the title in the *Code of Justinian* regarding monopolies.

**<term>μουλικὸν ζῷον</term> (moulikon zōon)**, **<term>μοῦλα</term> (moula)**, **<term>μουλίων</term> (mouliōn)**. Theophanes in the *Life of Constantine*. Anastasius the Librarian uses "mule-like animal," just as *moula* appears in the *Basilika* <note>Byzantine law code</note> for a female mule. Alexander Trallianus, Book 1, chapter 15: **"It [the seizure] will cease if you fumigate with the hairs of a donkey and a mule."** And *mouliōn* for a muleteer. *Basilika*, at Book 60, Title 7 of the Digests, and elsewhere.

**<term>μυστικοί</term> (mystikoi)** <note>secretaries or confidential advisors, often a high Byzantine court rank</note>. John Cantacuzenus, Book 3, chapter 97: **"to the *mystikos* Kinnamos and Asanes the *panhypersebastos*."** Nicephorus Gregoras, Book 8: **"Whence he was captured by the trickery of a monk who was a *mystikos*."** See the later notes, page 51. Balsamon on the *Councils*, page 520 d.

**<term>νάρθηξ</term> (narthēx)**, a narthex <note>the enclosed porch or entrance area of a church</note>. Regarding the narthex, whether it was inside or outside the church, see the most learned dissertation of Leo Allatius, *On the Narthex and the Temples of the Greeks*, page 110 of the Paris edition.

**<term>νοτάριος</term> (notarios)**, a notary; one who writes with "notes" or shorthand abbreviations of letters. St. Basil, *Epistle 178*, addressed to a notary: **"Words have a winged nature. For this reason, they require signs [shorthand], so that while they are in flight, the writer may catch their speed."** St. Athanasius, *Epistle to the Solitaries*: **"For neither was a soldier present, nor were palace officials or notaries sent out."** Blessed Chrysostom, *Epistle 1* to Innocent: **"And the most God-beloved Emperor sent notaries for this purpose."** This term occurs everywhere, such as in the 6th Synod of Constantinople, Acts 2 and 3; in Theophanes; in Codinus’s *Excerpts*; and the translator of the *Canons of the African Church* and the books of the *Basilika*: **"Let the notaries also enter, whom the order requires for reciting or taking down [records]."** In the chapter titled "The Order for Celebrating a Council..."

<summary>This page defines Byzantine Greek terms ranging from monastic titles (monastēs, monē) and maritime vessels (monoxyla) to administrative roles (mystikos, notarios), including a notable quote from St. Basil on the necessity of shorthand for capturing "winged words."</summary>

# GLOSSARY. 923 #

...council, before the Council of Elvira. In the school of notaries, the one who holds the first place is called the **<term>primicerius</term> of the notaries** <note>literally "the first on the wax [tablet]"—the head of the department</note>. Prosper writes in his *Chronicle*: **"John, formerly the chief of notaries, seized the throne though he had no legal right to it."** <note>original Latin: *nullo iure debitum Ioannes ex primicerio notariorum regnum sumit.*</note> At the Council of Chalcedon, session 3: **"Aetius, the archdeacon and chief of notaries, said..."** <note>original Greek: Ἀέτιος ἀρχιδιάκονος καὶ πριμικήριος νοταρίων εἶπε.</note> See also under **<term>protonotarios</term>** <note>first notary</note>. One who has completed this office is called **<term>ho apo notarion</term>** <note>one formerly among the notaries</note>, according to Theophanes. See also Cujas on the title of the Code regarding the *primicerius* and *secundarius* <note>the first and second in rank</note>, and Meursius under this word.

**<term>νούμερα</term> (noumera)**: numbers, or cohorts <note>military units</note>. Theophylactus, commenting on the Acts of the Apostles, chapter 10, says: **"a 'speira' [cohort] is what we now call a 'noumeron' [unit],"** following Saint Chrysostom’s 22nd homily on Acts. The *Menologium* <note>a church calendar with lives of saints</note> for July 8th records: **"so that the soldiers, seeing those of the two units along with the two tribunes, Nicostratus and Antiochus, believed in Christ."** And on the 14th: **"serving in the units under the tribune Claudius."** Theodorus in the *Basilica* <note>a collection of Byzantine laws</note>, Book 45, Title 1: **"when a soldier dies without a will and has no heir, his property is given to his own unit."** <note>original Greek: τῷ ἰδίῳ νουμέρῳ</note> Constantius had stated in Book 2 of the Code regarding the inheritance of decurions that his belongings should go to the *vexillatio* <note>a cavalry detachment</note> in which he served. The *Basilica* says: **"he is inherited by his own rank."** <note>original Greek: ἐκ τοῦ τάγματος αὐτοῦ</note> An interlinear gloss notes: **"from the system."** <note>original Greek: ἐκ τοῦ συστήματος; here meaning the military organization</note> Therefore, "number" or *noumeron*, detachment, rank, and system are all understood as the same thing here. The word "numbers" appears in law books and other authors. An ancient inscription reads: **"on account of the return of the unit."** Another: **"a unit of common soldiers."** Others call them "arithmoi" <note>the Greek word for numbers</note>. Theophanes writes concerning Justinian: **"he also gave him four units from the General of the East."**

**<term>νωβελίσσιμος</term> (nōbelissimos)**: most noble <note>a high-ranking title in the Byzantine court</note>. Curopalates, page 863, sections c and d. The sons and brothers of the Emperor, and those joined by close kinship, were honored with this dignity; they were granted a share of the imperial majesty, for they used a crown and wore a golden **<term>chlamys</term>** <note>a formal cloak</note>. Theophanes writes regarding Constantine Copronymus: **"Making Niketas, his youngest brother, a *belissimos*, he placed upon him a golden cloak and the crown."** One should read this as **<term>nōbelissimos</term>**. Anastasius the Librarian translates this in his *Ecclesiastical History* as: **"and making Niketas, their youngest brother, a *novelissimus*, he placed upon him both a golden cloak and a crown."** This is how it is read in two manuscripts instead of "making him most noble." Regarding the same Niketas, Nicephorus of Constantinople writes at the end of his *Short History*: **"and Niketas as *nōbellissimos*."** In the manuscript of Theophanes regarding Leo, it is also mistakenly read as **"and with three *belisēmois*"** instead of **"with three *nōbelissimoi*."** Philostorgius in his *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 8: **"The Emperor Jovian, departing for Constantinople and arriving in Ancyra, declared the other of his sons, Varronianus—who was still quite young—to be 'most illustrious,' which among the Romans has the power of the *nōbellissimos*."** See the same author in Book 12.

**<term>οἰκουμενικός</term> (oikoumenikos)**: ecumenical <note>universal</note>. Regarding the title of "Ecumenical," see what we have said in the notes on Balsamon's collection of ecclesiastical constitutions.

**<term>ὄρνα</term> (orna)**: for "ornamentation" <note>decoration</note>. Papias: **"a 'limbus' [border] is what we call an ornamentation, which surrounds the edge of garments, or is woven from gold thread and sewn onto the furthest part of the clothing."**

**<term>ὀρφανοτρόφος</term> (orphanotrophos)**: an orphan-warden, a guardian of wards or youths...

# FABROT'S GLOSSARY. 924 #

...tutor or curator, who supports and educates orphans or young people deprived of their parents. Nicephorus in his *Chronicle* writes: **"Acacius, priest and <term>orphanotrophos</term>"** <note>original Greek: Ἀκάτιος πρεσβύτερος καὶ ὀρφανοτρόφος; an official in charge of an orphanage, often a position of high state importance in Constantinople</note>.

**ὀφφίκιον (offikion)**: *duty, office, or official position.* <note>original Latin: *officium*</note>. Eustathius in his commentary on the *Iliad*, Book 40: **"For a Greek man does not double the aspirated consonants, once the <term>officium</term> [grammatical function] is removed."** The Sixth Synod in Trullo, Canon 7: **"those holding ecclesiastical offices."** <note>original Greek: ὀφφίκια ἐκκλησιαστικὰ ἔχοντας</note>. Balsamon writes: **"of an ecclesiastical office, that is, a dignity,"** and a little later: **"offices are called <term>archontikia</term>."** <note>original Greek: ἀρχοντίκια; minor administrative posts or lordships</note>. See the same author on Canon 34 of the Synod of Carthage, and Zonaras on the Councils, page 420. Nicephorus Callistus, Book 14, Chapter 39: **"the first office."**

**ὀψίκιον, ὀψικεύειν (opsikion, opsikeuein)**: *attendance, retinue, or the emperor’s bodyguard.* <note>original Latin: *obsequium, obsicium*</note>. This term occurs often in the writings of Theophanes. George of Alexandria, in his *Life of the Blessed Chrysostom*: **"A great rank followed him as he went out, not only as his retinue [opsikion], but because they were eager and desiring to be hearers of his wisdom."** In the *Life of Saint John the Almsgiver*, Chapter 26: **"And behold, a certain royal chamberlain, having with him others of the divine retinue,"** <note>original Greek: θείου ὀψικίου; 'divine' here refers to the imperial court</note>. Anastasius the Librarian, in his *Ecclesiastical History*: **"having taken with him those who were of the retinue [obsicii]."** Also: **"Maria, the wife of Leo, was crowned Empress in the triclinium [dining hall], and she proceeded alone with a solemn retinue [obsequio]."** The commander over this unit was called the **<term>Comes Opsikii</term>** <note>original Greek: κόμης ὀψικίου; Count of the Opsikion. The Opsikion was originally the elite imperial guard but became one of the largest administrative districts, or 'Themes,' in the Byzantine Empire</note>, as seen in Theophanes. The Synod of Constantinople 7, Act 1: **"Theophylactus, Count of the royal retinue [opsikion] protected by God."** Anastasius the Librarian translates this as: **"The Count of the imperial office [officii] to be preserved by God."** However, one should read 'retinue' [*obsequii*] or rather *obsicii*: he uses both. The same Anastasius, in his *Ecclesiastical History*, says: **"Bachurius, the first patrician and Count of the retinue [obsequii], was killed."** So it is in the manuscript; read *obsequii*. And in the *Collection on the Exile of Saint Martin*: **"he sends his secretary and certain men from his retinue [obsequio]."** Gregory II, in his letter to Leo the Isaurian: **"For Nexeuxios was then the Count of the Procession."** The translator renders this as 'Count of the Retinue' [*comes obsequii*], unless it was Gregory himself who wrote in Latin. Nicephorus, in his *Short History*, mentions: **"of the so-called royal retinue [opsikion]."** From this comes the verb *opsikeuein*, meaning to attend, to accompany, or to provide service. Theophanes: **"he was attended [opsikeueto] as a man of consular rank."** Council of Florence, Session 16: **"They all went out attending [opsikeuontes] the Patriarch."**

**ὀψώνιον (opsonion)**: *provisions, wages, daily allowance, or salary.* <note>original Latin: *obsonium, stipendium, diarium, salarium*</note>. Polybius: **"by the payment of wages."** This is cited in the manuscript *Selection on Virtue and Vice*. Greek-Latin Glossary: **"opsonion: provisions, daily allowance."** Saint Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 9: **"Be content with your own wages, you soldiers, and demand nothing beyond what is ordered. These things John, the great herald of truth and the voice preceding the Word, commands you along with us. What does he mean by 'wages'? Clearly the imperial grain allowance and the gifts that belong by law to those in high positions."** Saint Chrysostom, Homily 23 on the Second Epistle to the Corinthians: **"For when he says 'wages,' he means the necessary food."** Theophylactus, on Paul's Epistle to the Romans, Chapter 6: **"<term>Opsonion</term> is the name for the grain allowance given to soldiers by the emperor."** Oecumenius, on the same epistle, Chapter 8: **"Opsonion is what the imperial gift is called."** Nicetas...

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical glossary of Byzantine terms, following the previous page's discussion of the "opsikion" (imperial retinue). This section covers terms related to military wages, diplomatic tributes, the imperial palace, and high-ranking court officials like the "parakoimomenos."</meta>

# GLOSSARY #

**ὀψώνιον (opsonion)**. Nicetas Choniates, in the *Life of Manuel Comnenus*, Book 7: **"that wages be provided to those in military service."** <note>original Greek: ὀψώνια τοῖς στρατευμένοις παρέχεσθαι; *opsonion* originally referred to a soldier's food rations or the money to buy them</note>. The *Basilica* [legal code] in Book 17, Title of Mandates, interprets the Latin *salarium* [salary] as **"opsonion."** See also Book 13, Title 1, Chapter 18, Section 2. From this comes **ὀψωνάτωρ (opsonator)**, meaning a wage-earner or mercenary, as seen in Athenaeus, page 171. However, *opsonion* is also used to refer to a period of military service, as in the first sentence of Book 3 of the *Grammar* of Dositheus.

**πάκτον (pakton)**, **πακτοῦν (paktoun)**. *A pact, treaty, or tribute.* <note>original Latin: *pactum, tributum*</note>. Constantine Porphyrogenitus in *On Administering the Empire*: **"not being able to provide such a tribute."** <note>original Greek: μὴ δύνασθαι παρέχειν τὸ τοιοῦτον πάκτον</note>. Theophanes: **"promising to also provide annual tributes to the emperor."** The *Menologium* of Augustus, August 17: **"But when Emperor Leo proposed giving them tributes, they also demanded to station guards in the city."** From this, the verb **πακτοῦν (paktoun)** appears very frequently in the writings of Cedrenus and the Greek legal interpreters; it means to make a pact or to "pact," which is a barbarous form <note>meaning a non-classical, medieval invention</note>.

**παλάτιον (palation)**. *A palace.* <note>original Latin: *palatium*</note>. The Scholiast on Oppian’s *Halieutica*, Book 10: **"the 'megaron' is the palace."** It is used by Diodorus Siculus, page 228; Arrian in the *Discourses of Epictetus*, 4.1; Saint Athanasius in the *Epistle to the Solitaries* and the *Life of Saint Anthony*; Saint John Chrysostom in his Liturgy; Macarius in Homily 15; Saint Basil in the inscription of Epistle 308; and Gregory Thaumaturgus in a sermon on the Annunciation of the Virgin Mary. Also, Cyril in an epistle to the clergy and Lampon (which appears in the Fifth Synod, Collection 5): **"a certain man of the distinguished soldiers serving in the palace."** <note>original Greek: ἀνήρ τις τῶν ἐπισήμων στρατευομένων ἐν παλατίῳ</note>. See Eustathius on Dionysius, page 49.

**πάπας (papas)**, **παππᾶς (pappas)**. *Pope or father.* <note>original Latin: *papa, pater*</note>. Constantine Manasses in his *Chronicle*:
> This Constans, the sinister one, afflicted with perpetual exile
> Martin, the bishop of Elder Rome;
> The tongue of the Romans knows how to call him **"papas."**
Eustathius, in his commentary on the *Iliad*, Book 5: **"papas in the tongue of the Romans signifies father."** It occurs throughout the Greek councils, in the works of Saint Basil, and others. Add also Constantine’s *On the Themes*, 2.10. **παππᾶς (pappas)** appears in the Council of Chalcedon, Act 1: **"the father [pappas] Eutyches,"** who is elsewhere called an **<term>archimandrite</term>** <note>an abbot or head of a monastery</note> in the same text.

**παππίας (pappias)**. *Father.* Eustathius on the *Iliad*, Book 5: **"Every word spoken as a single syllable as a child's greeting, as the ancients say—just as 'ma' is mother—becomes 'papas' and 'pappias' by doubling the sounds."** It was also a title of dignity in the court of Constantinople. Anastasius the Librarian, in his *Ecclesiastical History*: **"But in the middle of the week of fasting, Jacob the <term>protospatharius</term> and <term>papias</term> was arrested."** <note>A *papias* was a high-ranking official, the "concierge" or warden of the Great Palace; a *protospatharius* was a high military-judicial rank</note>. See Meursius.

**παπυλεών (papyleon)**. *A butterfly, tent, or tabernacle.* <note>original Latin: *papilio* (meaning both butterfly and a military tent, likely due to the shape of its flaps)</note>. Modestus, in his work on military terms; Vegetius, Book 1, Chapter 3. The *Alexandrian Chronicle*, page 626: **"under the pavilion."** <note>original Greek: ὑπὸ τὸν παπιλεῶνα</note>.

**παρακοιμώμενος (parakoimomenos)**. *An attendant, or "one who sleeps beside [the imperial bed]."* <note>original Latin: *accubitor*</note>. Constantine Manasses: **"a bed-companion and guardian of the royal bed."** Constantine Porphyrogenitus in *On Administering the Empire*: **"the current house of Basil the parakoimomenos."** Liutprand [of Cremona] in his account of his embassy: **"there sat with him for your debate, according to their tradition, most wise men, powerful in Attic eloquence: Basil the parakoimomenos, the <term>protoasecretis</term> [chief secretary], the <term>protovestiarius</term> [master of the wardrobe], and two masters."** And later: **"Basilius parakimomenos instead of paracoemomenos."** Anastasius the Librarian, in his *Ecclesiastical History*: "with a loud voice..."

<vocab>ὀψώνιον, πάκτον, παλάτιον, πάπας, παππᾶς, παππίας, παπυλεών, παρακοιμώμενος, Manuel Comnenus, Constantinus Manasses, Eustathius, Anastasius Bibliothecarius, Liutprandus, pactum, palatium, papa, paracoemomenus</vocab>

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical glossary of Byzantine terms, moving from "opsonion" (wages) and "pakton" (treaty/tribute) to terms beginning with "para-" and "patri-," focusing on court titles, ecclesiastical administration, and military equipment.</meta>

# FABROT #

**ad paracoemumenum (concerning the grand chamberlain).** This is how it is read in two manuscripts. It is a title of great dignity: **"The chamberlain, a thing of great importance to the Romans,"** as Constantine Manasses says <note>original Greek: παράκοιτος, πρᾶγμα Ῥωμαίοις μέγα; the "parakoimomenos" was the chief palace official who literally "slept beside" the emperor's bedchamber</note>. See Meursius.

**παραμήριον (paramerion)**. A dagger or short sword worn at the thigh. Cedrenus writes: **"With the paramerion he cut off his head."** The author of the *Miscella* says: **"He cut off his head with the dagger with which he was girded."** <note>original Latin: pugione quo erat accinctus caput eius amputavit</note>. The Glosses of Cyril define it: **"the paramerion is a sword,"** or a short blade <note>original Latin: sica</note>. It is used by Leo and Constantine in the *Tactica*. The Council of Chalcedon, Action 11: **"having bared his dagger."**

**παραπόρτια (paraportia)**. Small gates or postern gates. This term appears frequently in the works of Anastasius the Librarian. The Glosses of Cyril call it a **"small portal."** Leo's *Tactica*, Chapter 15, Section 4: **"to the small gates of the city."** Theophanes: **"at the upper postern gate of Kallinike."**

**παρασκευή (paraskeue)**. Friday. Eustathius in *On Chronological Intervals*, Chapter 4: **"The Great Preparation"** <note>original Greek: μεγάλη παρασκευή</note>; in Cedrenus, this refers to **"Good Friday."** <note>original French: le grand vendredi</note>. Why it is called the "Preparation" is explained by Theodore Metochites in his *Roman History*, page 33 and following, by John of Damascus in his *Oration on the Sabbath*, and by Michael Glycas. <note>In the Christian calendar, Friday is the "day of preparation" for the Sabbath</note>.

**παραφοσσατεύειν (paraphossateuein)**. To set up camp nearby.

**παροικία (paroikia)**. A parish. The bishop of the parish of Ephesus is mentioned in Cedrenus, page 247, column C. It is very common for "parish" <note>paroecia or parrochia</note> to be used in place of "diocese."

**πατριάρχης, πατριαρχεῖον (patriarches, patriarcheion)**. Patriarch. From this comes "Patriarchate," the house of the Patriarch. The Sixth Synod of Constantinople, Action 4: **"Anastasius, priest and monk of the chapels of the holy Patriarchate here."** The ancient interpreter translates this as: **"the venerable patriarchate."** <note>original Latin: venerabilis patriarchii</note>. I discuss the Roman Pontiff and the Patriarch of Constantinople in my notes on the *Collection of Ecclesiastical Constitutions*, the author of which is Balsamon, who was previously unknown.

**πατρίκιος (patrikios)**. Patrician. After the time of Augustus, these were the primary citizens. John Tzetzes in the *Chiliads*, Book 1, History 34: **"Theophilus the proconsul, patrician, and quaestor."** The Greek *Menologium* for August: **"not only of noble birth, but also famous for his patrician authority."** He is called the **"father of the emperor or the empire."** Constantine Manasses: **"He made him father and protector of the empire."** Priscus in the *Excerpts on Embassies*: **"And Nomos, who had held the honor of Master and was enrolled among the patricians with him—those indeed who have ascended to all the highest offices."** See also Sozomen, Book 8, Chapter 7, and Nicephorus Callistus, Book 13, Chapter 1.

**πατρικιότης (patrikiotes)**. The dignity of the patriciate. Constantine Porphyrogenitus in *On Administering the Empire*: **"and he was promoted by him to the rank of patrician."**

**πατριμόνιον (patrimonion)**. Patrimony. Theophanes, writing on Emperor Leo: **"The so-called 'patrimonies' of the holy and supreme Apostles who are honored in Old Rome—which had long been paid to the churches, amounting to 57 talents of gold—he ordered to be paid to the public treasury."** See the *Glosses on the Basilica*.

**πῖνα (pina)**. Hunger. See Meursius. Others write it as **πεῖνα (peina)**, such as the author of the *Lexicon of Barbarous Greek*.

**πινάκιον (pinakion)**. A small tablet or platter. George Kodinos (Curopalates), page 850, column D. See Meursius.

**πινσός (pinsos)**. A stone pillar, or a man-made mound. Theophanes in...

It highlights the linguistic shift where "parish" and "diocese" were often used interchangeably in the medieval Greek context.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the glossary of Byzantine Greek and Latin terms, moving from the previous page's discussion of religious "preparations" to architectural, legal, and military vocabulary beginning with the letters P-I and P-O.</meta>

# GLOSSARY #

**In the time of Justinian:** "They stripped the **pillars** <note>original Greek: πινσοὺς (pinsous); these are the structural piers or supports</note> that supported the **dome** <note>original Greek: τροῦλλον (troullon), likely referring to the great dome of the Hagia Sophia</note>, and because of this, they failed to provide support. Later, the most pious Emperor, having seen this, raised other pillars, and the dome was supported." Codinus in the *Excerpts* writes: "The word of the angel came to the boy on the right side of the **pillar**." Also: "Then they decorated it with mosaics and lined it with vertical marble, both on the **pillars** and in the porticoes." The *Seguerian Glossary* defines it: "**pillar** means the wall."

**πιττάκια (pittakia)**. The *Glosses of Cyril* define it: "**petition** or **brief**." <note>original Latin: pittacium, brevis</note>. Lampridius writes in his life of Alexander Severus: "**he read through all the petitions**." <note>original Latin: perlegebat cuncta pittacia</note>. Julian in the law code <note>Digest 4.8.49.1</note> says: "the arbiter may order the litigants to be present either through a messenger or by **letter**." Harmenopoulos, Book 1, 4, 64: "through a letter or a **petition**." Scaevola in the law code <note>Digest 2.14.47.1</note> says: "if any **document** issued by you remained with me." The *Basilica* <note>a collection of Byzantine laws</note> states: "If a **document** of yours is found with me, let it be invalid." This does not mean just any letter, but a short one. The *Glosses of Isidore* state: "**a pittacium is a brief and modest letter**." At the Second Council of Nicaea, Action 4: "Instead of books, they showed us **small tablets**."

**ποιναλίζειν (poinalizein)**. **To punish** or **inflict a penalty**. <note>original Latin: poena afficere</note>. See the works of Meursius.

**πολυκανδήλα (polykandela), κανδήλα (kandela), κανδήλαβρον (kandelabron)**. **Chandeliers** or **lamps**, literally "carrying many candles." Anastasius the Librarian in his *Ecclesiastical History* writes: "Having borrowed money from the venerable houses, and being constrained by poverty, he even took the **many-candled lamps** <note>original Latin: multas candelas ferentia</note> of the Great Church, as well as other serving vessels." Theophanes, writing about the Emperor Heraclius, says: "I took the **lamps** and other liturgical vessels of the Great Church." The manuscript says this, but I believe it should be read as **many-candled lamps** (polykandela). For the word **lamp** (kandela) is "Greek-barbarous" for the Latin *candela*. Gregory the Great, in a dialogue translated into Greek by Pope Saint Zachary, says: "When evening came, he extinguished all the **lamps**." This word occurs often there. Eustathius, in his commentary on the *Odyssey*, Book 7, notes: "The use of the **lamp** is found there, as in the phrase 'buy a **lamp** for an assarion' <note>a small Roman coin</note>, that is, purchase it." The Greeks, in their notes on the laws regarding manumission in a will, say: "On the condition that they light a **lamp** at my tomb every other month." See also John Moschus in the *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 105. And the word **candelabrum** (kandelabron) is used for a lamp-stand in the *Basilica*, Book 15, Title 4, Chapter 6.

**πόρτα (porta)**. **Gate**. Leo in the *Tactica*, Chapter 11, Section 19: "at the **gates** of the camp." Constantine Porphyrogenitus in *On the Administration of the Empire*: "They opened the **gates** and received them with great joy. But as soon as they entered, those men seized the **gates**." Found also in the *Alexandrian Chronicle*, page 900, and Zonaras in his notes on the Councils, page 582. The Greek *Menologium* for the month of October says: "And they were buried at the Melandesia **Gate**." Theophanes, writing about Justinian, says: "They guarded all the **gates** of the wall."

**πόρτος (portos)**. **Port** or **harbor**. Nicephorus Callistus, Book 13, Chapter 35: "The **Port** of Rome is a very great shipyard."

**πραιδεύειν (praideuein), πραιδα (praida)**. **To plunder** or **to take booty**. From the *Excerpts of the History of John Malalas*: "And many Christians were killed by the city mobs whom they happened upon, and they were **plundered**." Theophanes writes: "And he came **plundering** as far as Byzantium." In the Council of Constantinople under Menas, Action 5: "all..."

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical glossary of administrative and legal terms used in the Byzantine Empire and late antiquity, moving from terms related to plunder and "praeda" to the official titles of "praepositus" (superintendents) and the various meanings of "praetorium" (headquarters or courtrooms).</meta>

->FABROTUS<-

...pillaged the churches. Leo the Tactician, Chapter 17, Section 35. Constantine the Tactician, page 25. From this comes **praida** <note>original Latin: praeda</note> meaning "booty." John Moschus in the *Spiritual Meadow*, Chapter 155: "He has taken the **booty** <note>original Greek: τὴν πραῖδαν (tēn praidan)</note>." Saint Athanasius in the *Epistle to the Africans*: "He gave the church over to **plunder** <note>original Latin: predam</note>." However, the written manuscripts use the Greek spelling *praidan*. See the *Nomicon Glossary* under that entry.

**πραιπόσιτος** (praipósitos) — **Superintendent** <note>original Latin: praepositus</note>. Basil in his *Grammar* states: "The **superintendent** is a rank." The application of the term "superintendent" is extremely broad. Ammianus Marcellinus mentions a superintendent of the bedchamber, of the factory, of the Martensian soldiers, of the mint, and of the Tyrian weaving-house. Regarding the "superintendent of the bedchamber," there is a title in Book 12 of the *Code*. Philostorgius in his *Church History* (11.4) writes: "Having risen to the honor of the **superintendent**." There was also a superintendent of the chamberlains <note>servants of the royal bedchamber</note>. Theophanes writes: "**superintendent of the chamberlains**." Regarding the "superintendent of labors," there is a title in Book 12 of the *Code*, as well as a "superintendent of the palace." Marcellinus in his *Chronicle* and an anonymous author of the *Life of Saint Athanasius* write: "And having corrupted the **superintendent** in the royal palace." John Malalas writes: "And the **superintendent of his palace**, Rhodanus, a man who was powerful and wealthy, and who managed the palace as the chief high-eunuch and was held in great honor." Simeon Metaphrastes (writing for the month of September regarding Eudoxius and Romulus) calls this official the "**superintendent of the court**." There was also a superintendent of the treasuries. Saint Basil in Letter 264 says: "I also wrote to your piety through the vicar of Thrace, by means of a certain **superintendent of the treasuries** at Philippopolis." There were also superintendents of soldiers, mentioned in the *Digest* on military matters (Book 3 and Book 6). Rufus in the *Military Laws* states: "If any soldier lays hands on his own **superintendent**, let him be punished by death." I will speak more fully on this in my notes on Julianus Antecessor and the *Nomicon Glossary*.

**πραιτώριον** (praitōrion) — **Praetorium** <note>original Latin: praetorium</note>. This term stands for a courtroom of judges, or the residence of a praetor <note>a high-ranking magistrate</note>, or of princes, or of those who hold any civil power. It can also refer to a place of custody or a location where defendants were detained. Its use for a courtroom is frequently observed. Regarding the residence of a praetor, Nicephorus in his *Historical Compendium* writes: "He goes up to the **praetorium**." Regarding the palace of a prince, Saint Chrysostom in his *Homily on the Epistle to the Philippians* (Chapter 1, Homily 2) says: "In the whole **praetorium**; for at that time they called the royal palaces by this name." Theophylact says in the same context: "Of the **praetorium**, that is, the royal palaces." There exists an Epigram by Paul the Silentiary (Anthology, Book 4): "On the great **praetorium**." Constantine, in *On the Themes* (Theme 1, Chapter 14) regarding the island of Samos, writes: "The general of the theme chose the city of Smyrna itself as his **praetorium** <note>meaning his official headquarters</note>." Regarding the praetorium as a place where prisoners are kept, the Greek *Menologium* for April states: "And having placed shackles on him as if on some criminal, he shut him up in the **praetorium**." George of Alexandria in his *Life of Chrysostom* writes: "The magistrate, taking the monks, dressed them in clothes and led them away to the **praetorium**."

**πριβατάριον** (pribatarion) — **Private treasury official**. Just as, says a very learned man in a later note, the Emperor had a prefect of the private treasury whom they called the **Count of the Privates** <note>original Greek: κόμητα πριβάτων (komēta pribatōn)</note>, as seen in Saint Basil (Letters 415 and 423) and the Council of Chalcedon (Act 1): "**Count of the Divine Privates**," about whom I have spoken elsewhere; so too the Church has its own **privateers** <note>meaning officials of the private treasury</note> or overseers of the storehouse.

<summary>This page defines three major Byzantine administrative terms: the superintendent (praepositus), the official headquarters or prison (praetorium), and the private treasury official (privatarius), citing various historical and ecclesiastical sources.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical glossary of administrative and legal titles from late antiquity and the Byzantine Empire, moving from terms like "praepositus" (superintendent) to specific ranks such as "primicerius" (chief of a department) and "proedros" (president or prelate).</meta>

### GLOSSARY.

**πριμμικήριος, πριμικήριος** (**primmikērios**) — **Chief** <note>original Latin: *primicerius*</note>. The first of any order, body, or guild, such as the notaries. The Sixth Synod of Constantinople, Act 9: "**Chief** of the most god-fearing notaries <note>original Greek: πριμικήριος τῶν θεοσεβεστάτων νοταρίων</note>." It is also written this way in the Council of Florence. The Council of Ephesus, Part 2: "Peter, presbyter of Alexandria and **chief** <note>original Greek: πριμμικήριος</note> of the notaries, said..." Nicephorus Callistus, Book 15, Chapter 30. Usuardus in the *Martyrology* for the month of May: "*the former of whom was the provost of the bedchamber of Emperor Decius, the other the **chief** <note>original Latin: primicerius</note>*." There were also ecclesiastical chiefs, such as the **chief of the school of singers** <note>original Latin: primicerius scholae cantorum</note>. Cardinal Benno, in his *Life of Hildebrand*, Book 1: "**Chief** of the Apostolic See." Pope John, Letter 7 to all the Gauls and Germans. Pope Nicholas, Letter to Hincmar of Reims. Alcuin, Letter 25: "**Chief of the chapel**." Anastasius, in his work on the exile of Saint Martin: "*because in the absence of the bishop, the archdeacon, the archpriest, and the **chief** represent the person of the bishop*." **The dean** <note>original French: le doyen</note>. Regarding the office of the ecclesiastical chief, see the letter of Isidore the Younger, Bishop of Seville, to Leudefred, Bishop of Córdoba, in the works of Loaysa in the notes to the 8th Council of Toledo. He who holds the second place or rank is the **second-in-command** <note>original Latin: *secundicerius*</note>. Anastasius: "*they ran with some others to the aforementioned gate, and with them was Demetrius the **second-in-command***." Council of Constantinople under Menas, Act 1: "**Second-in-command** of the notaries <note>original Greek: νοταρίων σεκουνδοκήριος</note>." The *Menologium* <note>a church calendar of saints</note>: "Bacchus the **second-in-command**." See Book 12 of the *Code*, Title 7.

**πρόεδρος** (**proedros**) — **President, prelate, or overseer** <note>original Latin: *praeses, praesul, antistes*</note>. There were both ecclesiastical and palace **presidents**. Regarding the ecclesiastical ones, the Sixth Synod of Constantinople, Act 12: "Of the **president** of the city of Alexandria." An old interpreter translates this as "overseer" <note>original Latin: antistitem</note>. And Act 13: "Of Sergius, the former **prelate** <note>original Latin: Sergii quondam praesulis</note>." Petrus Siculus addresses his history "to the **president** or archbishop of Bulgaria." From this comes the term **first-president** <note>original Greek: πρωτοπρόεδρος (protoproedros)</note>. John Curopalates, page 839 b.

**προέλευσις** (**proeleusis**) — **Procession or parade** <note>original Latin: *processio, pompa*</note>. Eustathius on the *Iliad*, Book 1: "It should be known that among the writers after Homer, the word 'to send' <note>original Greek: πέμπειν</note> also meant to set out triumphantly, from which a 'triumph' is a parade <note>original Greek: πομπὴ</note>, which common speech calls a **procession** <note>original Greek: προέλευσιν</note>." See Meursius.

**πρόκενσος** (**prokensos**) — **Procession** <note>original Latin: *processus*</note>. Regarding the procession of a prince, the *Chronicle of Alexandria*: "In the **procession** of the seventh <note>meaning the seventh district or milestone</note>." Council of Constantinople under Menas, Act 3: "It being a **royal procession**." Marcellinus Comes in his *Chronicle*: "*at this time while Theodosius celebrates a **procession** to the public granaries*." Also: "*With Emperor Anastasius passing his time in **processions***."

**πρόοικος** (**prooikos**) — **Steward or Master of the House** <note>original Latin: *maior domus*</note>. This is how Anastasius the Librarian interprets it in his *Ecclesiastical History*. Also known as the prefect of the palace, prince of the palace, or **sub-regent** <note>original Latin: subregulus</note>. Ursinus, in his *Deeds of Saint Leodegar*: "*so that all might rejoice to have Childeric as king and Leodegar as prefect of the palace. And the same Ebroin, restored by King Theoderic to his former status and made **major-domo** <note>original Latin: maior domus</note>, began to think about taking revenge on his enemies, who remembered him holding the rank of **sub-regent**, that is, the major-domo or prince of the palace*." See Paul Warnefrid <note>Paul the Deacon</note> on the *Deeds of the Lombards*, Book 6, Chapter 16.

<meta>catchword: Georg. Cedrenus tom. II.</meta>

<page-num>930</page-num>
# FABROTUS

**προτίκτωρ** (**protiktōr**) — **Protector**. Protectors are **bodyguards** <note>original Greek: σωματοφύλακες</note> or soldiers chosen for the protection of the prince, who guard the prince's side. Regarding these, see Procopius in his *Secret History*, page 108. Simeon Metaphrastes, writing in October on the life of Saint Demetrius, says: "When Minucianus the **protector** <note>original Greek: προτίκτωρος</note> had assisted in the slaughter." Also, the work *Sophia* <note>likely referring to a hagiography or imperial text</note> states: "Immediately, therefore, having given way to irrational anger, he sent out those whom the rank knows to call **protectors** <note>original Greek: προτίκτωρας</note> to bring those women." Paulinus of Nola, in Letter 37 to a soldier of the age, writes: "*Then in this military service you are accustomed to hope for this promotion in duty, so that you might be made protectors.*"

**πρωτασηκρήτης** (**prōtasēkrētēs**), **πρωτοασηκρήτης** (**prōtoasēkrētēs**) — **Chief Secretary** <note>original Latin: primus a secretis</note>, or **First Secretary**. Nicetas Paphlago, in the *Life of Ignatius*, says: "Photius, being both a Protospatharios <note>a high court rank</note> and a **Chief Secretary** <note>original Greek: πρωτασηκρήτην</note>." Codinus, in the *Origins of Constantinople*, writes: "As Plutarch, the **Chief Secretary**, says." In the handwritten manuscript of the late and most illustrious man Nicolas-Claude Fabri de Peiresc <note>original Greek: τοῦ μακαρίτου Nicolai Fabricii</note>, the term is written **Chief Secretary** <note>original Greek: πρωτασηκρήτης</note>. Nicephorus Gregoras, Book 8: "The daughter of Neocaesareites the **Chief Secretary**." The term **First Secretary** is also found in Theodore of Hermopolis’s notes on the 41st law of the *Rules of Law*. The collection of Anastasius the Librarian <note>a 9th-century scholar and translator</note> in the *Hypomnesticum* states: "*Indeed, even Theodore, the chief secretary of the prefect of the praetorium of Constantinople, told me this before.*"

**πρωτεύων** (**prōteuōn**) — **Primate** or **Leading Citizen**. Letter 421 of Saint Basil is addressed to a **leading citizen** <note>original Greek: πρωτεύοντι</note>. There also exist letters from Theodoret addressed to a **leading citizen**, namely Letters 15 and 33. They translate this term as "primate."

**πρωτοβεστιάριος** (**prōtobestiarios**) — **First Prefect of the Wardrobe** <note>original Latin: primus praefectus vestiarii</note>. For later Greeks, the word **garment** <note>original Greek: βέστιον or βέστης</note> refers to clothing <note>original Latin: vestis</note>. The manuscript of the *Basilica Glosses* defines **garments** <note>original Greek: βέστια</note> as "clothes." Julius Pollux, in a previously unpublished *Chronicle*, says: "setting aside wine, meat, and **garments** <note>original Greek: βέστια</note>." From this comes the term **wardrobe keeper** <note>original Greek: βεστιαρίτης</note> in the works of Cedrenus, or **keeper of the robes** <note>original Greek: βεστήτωρ</note>. Theophanes, in the *Royal Codex*, writes: "the **keepers of the robes** lost the king’s crown." George Pachymeres uses the phrase "the one presiding over the **wardrobe**." Additionally, **wardrobe** <note>original Greek: βεστιάριον</note> is used for clothing in the 4th law of the Digest concerning legacies of food and provisions. The word "wardrobe" appears in other legal contexts as well. Astrampsychus, in his *Pythagorean Lot-casting*, writes: "it signifies a deposit for the trade of a great deal of **clothing** <note>original Greek: βεστιαρίου</note>." The term **wardrobe** is also accepted as the place where clothes are stored. The continuator of Theophanes, in the life of Theophilus, says: "which is called even today the **wardrobe** <note>original Greek: βεστιάριον</note> of the stored silk robes." Similarly: "which is now the **wardrobe** of the Augusta <note>the Empress</note>." Hence, we find the "imperial wardrobe" in William of Tyre’s second book of the *History of the Crusades*. An old interpreter of the homilies on Matthew (ascribed to Blessed Chrysostom, or perhaps John of Jerusalem), on Chapter 23, Verse 14, says: "*For just as the master of the house does not have his pantry or his **wardrobe** open to everyone.*" Finally, a **wardrobe official** <note>original Latin: vestiarius</note> is one who is in charge of clothing, as explained by an old manuscript glossary. Papias says the same. The same interpreter of John of Jerusalem’s homilies says: "*If you require your **wardrobe official** to be diligent and your pantry’s key-bearer to be faithful to you.*" Michael Cerularius, in a letter to Peter, Bishop of Antioch, writes: "which the **wardrobe official** <note>original Greek: βεστιάριος</note> received from the emperor and reported." He had written it in Greek as *ho bestiarios*. Peter the Deacon, in the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, Book 4, Chapter 21, writes: "Pandulph the **wardrobe official**, rising up, said..." The "imperial wardrobe official" is also mentioned by William of Tyre...

It traces the evolution of these terms from military and domestic service into significant administrative and state offices.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical glossary of Byzantine court titles and administrative offices, specifically moving through titles prefixed with "proto-" (chief or first), such as the chief of the wardrobe, chief messenger, and chief notary.</meta>

<page-num>931</page-num>
<header>GLOSSARY. 931</header>

...in the sacred war 2. The same term, **vesterarius** <note>original Latin: vesterarius; a wardrobe keeper</note>, is used in chapter 8 of the Council of Ponthion and in a certain letter of Pope John VIII. Thus, the **first prefect of the wardrobe**, as has already been said, was called the **protobestiarios** <note>original Greek: πρωτοβεστιάριος</note>. Anna Comnena in the *Alexiad*, Book 3, writes: "both a protosabastos and a **protobestiarios**." This is also found in the writings of Cedrenus. Constantine Porphyrogenitus, in *On the Themes*, Book 1, chapter 12, says: "Theodosius, the **protobestiarios** of my blessed father." It appears in John Cantacuzene 1.43, and Laonicus Chalcondyles, Book 9. An anonymous author in the *Life of Emperor Basil* writes: "whom Procopius, the emperor's **protobestiarios**, led." George Acropolites, on page 3 of the Royal edition, says: "he honored this man as **protobestiarios**." There was another official called the **bestiarites** <note>original Greek: βεστιάριτης; a member of the wardrobe guard</note>, whom Cedrenus mentions on page 375. The leader of these was called the **protobestiarites** <note>original Greek: πρωτοβεστιάριτης</note>, about whom Codinus writes in *On Offices*. John Cantacuzene, Book 4, chapter 19: "leaving Diplovatatzes the **protobestiarites** as governor in Beroea." George Logotheta, in the *Chronicle of Constantinople*, says: "and Angelos John as protostrator, and Karyanites as **protobestiarites**." Nicephorus Gregoras, Book 6, mentions: "Livadarios the **protobestiarites**."

**πρωτομανδάτωρ** (**prōtomandatōr**) — **Chief Messenger**, the first of the messengers <note>original Latin: primus mandatorum</note>. A **mandator** <note>original Greek: μανδάτωρ</note> was a type of official. The Second Council of Nicaea records: "The illustrious imperial **messenger** <note>original Greek: μανδάτωρ</note>, having entered, said..." Constantine Porphyrogenitus, in the *Tactica*, writes: "**messengers** who are vigilant and swift." Theophanes, in the section on Justinian, says: "I do not know who this **messenger** is." The *Legal Glosses* explain who the messengers are: "**messengers** are those who swiftly convey the commands <note>original Greek: τὰ μανδάτα</note> from the magistrates to the soldiers." I shall speak more of these in that entry.

**πρωτονοτάριος** (**prōtonotarios**) — **Chief Notary**, the first of the notaries or the *primicerius* <note>a title for the head of a department</note> of the notaries. The Council of Chalcedon, Action 1, states: "John, a priest and **first of the notaries** <note>original Greek: πρῶτος τῶν νοταρίων</note>, spoke." An ancient interpreter translates this as: "John the priest and **chief of the notaries** <note>original Latin: primicerius notariorum</note> said." See the entry above for **primicerius**. Pope Hadrian, in a letter to Charlemagne, writes: "Rado, your most beloved **protonotary**." It is defined as the "foremost of the imperial secretaries" by Nicephorus in the *Short History*. See also Paul the Deacon's *History of the Lombards*, 4.34.

**πρωτοπάπας** (**prōtopapas**) — **Chief Priest**, the first priest after the patriarch. Balsamon, commenting on Apostolic Canon 59, writes: "perhaps a chorepiscopos <note>a rural bishop</note> who has been promoted, or a **chief priest** <note>original Greek: πρωτοπάπαν</note>." And on Canon 8 of the Council of Antioch: "the priests in the country districts, namely the **chief priests** <note>original Greek: πρωτοπαπάδας</note>." And on Canon 10: "priests or **chief priests** and chorepiscopoi." See the works of Meursius.

**πρωτοσπαθάριος** (**prōtospatharios**) — **Chief Sword-bearer**, the first of the sword-bearers <note>original Latin: spatharii</note>, who carried the emperor's sword. Among the letters of Photius, one exists addressed to "Theophilus the **protospatharios**." I shall discuss this further in the *Glosses on the Basilica* <note>the Basilica was a major 9th-century law code</note>.

**πρωτοστράτωρ** (**prōtostratōr**) — **Chief Groom**, the first of the imperial grooms <note>original Latin: stratores</note>, according to Anastasius in the *Ecclesiastical History*. Nicephorus Gregoras, Book 7, writes: "who had later received from the emperor the staff <note>a symbol of office</note> of the **protostrator**." Theophanes says: "Rufinus, the **protostrator** of the Opsikion <note>a military district or theme</note>, entered." See below under **strator**.

**πρωτοσύμβουλος** (**prōtosymbolos**) — **Chief Counselor**. Used by Anastasius the Librarian. Cedrenus provides an explanation for this term.

**ῥαίκτωρ** (**rhaiktōr**) — **Rector**, a type of high-ranking dignity. See the works of Meursius. [Continued in the] Menolo—

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical glossary of Byzantine Greek terms, specifically those derived from or corresponding to Latin administrative and legal vocabulary. It transitions from the end of a discussion on "rectors" into entries for "region," "king," and "military pay."</meta>

<page-num>932</page-num>
<header>FABROT</header>

...Greek [Menologium] August 31: "for in that night [the Saint] appeared to the **rector** <note>original Greek: ῥαίκτωρι; a governor or high official</note> and to a certain youth belonging to the **rector**." See later notes. Peter Walafrid also mentions the **rector** <note>original Latin: rectoris</note> of the place in *The Deeds of Ludwig*, Book 6, chapter 24.

**ῥεγεών** (**regiōn**) — **region** <note>original Latin: regio</note>. Eustathius on the *Odyssey*, book 8: "according to the **regions** <note>original Greek: ῥεγεῶνας</note> used by many, or the Cretan troops, or even according to the Attic districts." Council of Chalcedon, Act 13: "and that which was previously a **region** <note>original Greek: ῥεγεὼν</note> later became a city again." Gregory the Great, in a certain dialogue translated into Greek by Pope Zachary: "in the city of the Romans, in the **region** <note>original Greek: ῥεγεῶνι</note> called Subura."

**ῥήξ, ῥῆγας** (**rhēx, rhēgas**) — **king** <note>original Latin: rex</note>. Ecumenical Synod 8, Act 3: "and having sent word secretly to the **king** <note>original Greek: ῥῆγα</note>." Nicetas the Paphlagonian in the *Life of Ignatius, Patriarch of Constantinople*: "winning over the **king** <note>original Greek: ῥῆγα</note> of Francia, Louis <note>likely Louis II of Italy</note>, and his wife Ingelberga with magnificent gifts." Gregory the Great in the dialogue translated into Greek by Pope Zachary: "Hermenigild the **king** <note>original Greek: ῥὴξ</note>, being the son of Leovigild, the **king** <note>original Greek: ῥηγὸς</note> of the Visigoth nation." John Cantacuzene, Book 4: "**King** <note>original Greek: ῥήξ</note> Charles." It is also used by Theophanes, Constantine VII in *On the Themes*, chapter 11, and Codinus in his *Excerpts*. They also used the form **rhēgas** <note>original Greek: ῥηγάς</note>. Synod of Florence: "both the great lords and **kings** <note>original Greek: ῥηγάδες</note> and dukes."

**ῥόγα, ῥογεύειν, ῥογάτορες** (**rhoga, rhogeuein, rhogatores**) — **pay**, **stipend**, or **bounty** <note>original Latin: roga, stipendium, donativum</note>, which was paid out to soldiers, the people, or the clergy by the emperor, the Roman pope, or the Patriarch of Constantinople. Anna Comnena in the *Alexiad*, Book 3: "both with gifts of immovable property and increases in **stipends** <note>original Greek: ῥογῶν</note> and additional payments." Julius Pollux in his *Chronicle*: "distributing a **bounty** <note>original Greek: ῥόγαν</note> of money to the army." George of Alexandria in the *Life of Saint Chrysostom*: "Your Excellency knows how much expense the imperial court incurs for the **stipends** <note>original Greek: ῥόγας</note> of the camps." Constantine, *On the Administration of the Empire*, pages 137 and 140, and in the *Tactics*, page 16. Anastasius the Librarian in his *Ecclesiastical History*: "*the army, deprived of its pay, deserted*" <note>original Latin: exercitum roga privatum deseruit</note>. The same author in the *Lives of the Popes*, regarding Pope Deusdedit: "*the pay having been given to the soldiers, peace was made*" <note>original Latin: data roga militibus pax facta est</note>. And in the *Ecclesiastical History*: "*while the pay was being distributed to the people by the Strumon river*" <note>original Latin: dum roga penes Strumonem amnem populo distribueretur</note>. The same Anastasius in the *Lives of the Popes*: "*but here he greatly increased the pay—that is, the stipend—for his clergy, especially in the presbytery*" <note>original Latin: hic vero rogam, stipendium scilicet, clero suo in presbyterio maxime ampliavit</note>. And regarding Boniface V: "*he loved the clergy and gave a full payment to his clergy*" <note>original Latin: hic clerum amavit, rogam integram clero suo dedit</note>. A commentator on the *Synopsis of the Basilica* <note>a 10th-century legal manual</note>: "those things belonging to the military savings are called *castrensia* or private property. These are whatever things are given from **pay** <note>original Greek: ῥόγας</note> to a certain cleric or a **chartulary** <note>original Greek: χαρτουλαρίῳ; an administrative official or archivist</note> who is in service." From this comes **rhogeuein**, which means **to pay out** <note>original Latin: erogare</note>, *New Constitutions* 130, chapter 1. Theophanes: "**having paid out** <note>original Greek: ῥογεύσας</note> money." And **rhogatores** means **paymasters** <note>original Latin: erogatores</note>; the *Synopsis of the Basilica*, Book 57, title 4, calls them *rogatarii*. Papias: "*a rogatarius is a petitioner or a distributor*" <note>original Latin: rogatarius petitor, distributor</note>. If this is true, a *rogatarius* is both one who asks and one who pays out. Or they are **paymasters** <note>original Latin: erogatarii</note>. The Council of Ponthion, chapter 14: "*ecclesiastical paymasters and almoners*" <note>original Latin: erogatarii et eleemosynarii ecclesiastici</note>. Greeks today still use these same words; and the *Greek-Latin Lexicon*: **rhoga** means **stipend** or **salary**. **rhogemenos** means **salaried**. **rhogeueuo** means **I pay wages**.

**ῥούσσιον** (**rhoussion**) — **russet** or **red** <note>original Latin: russeum</note>. This word appears in a Greek commentator on Oppian, page 18.

<summary>This page defines Byzantine terms for administrative districts (regiōn), foreign kings (rhēx), and the system of state salaries and clerical stipends (rhoga). It highlights the linguistic exchange between Latin and Greek in the late Roman and Byzantine bureaucratic systems.</summary>
