--- Page 943 ---
<meta>This page continues the alphabetical glossary of Greek and Latin administrative terms used in the Byzantine Empire, moving from the geographical concept of "Romania" to officials like the "Sakellarios" and imperial documents known as "Sakra."</meta>

<page-num>933</page-num>
<header>GLOSSARY</header>

**Ῥωμανία (Romania)** — the Roman Empire or the Empire of Constantinople <note>The inhabitants of the Byzantine Empire referred to themselves as Romans and their land as Romania</note>. Mentioned by Epiphanius in Book 2 of the *Panarion*, and in Heresy 66. Theophanes, in his account of Emperor Heraclius, writes: "the captivity of all Romania" <note>original Greek: πάσης Ῥωμανίας αἰχμαλωσία</note>. "Great Romania" is mentioned by Astrampsychus in his *Pythagorean Calculation*.

**σακελλάριος (sakellarios)** — a treasurer, keeper of money, or official in charge of the treasury <note>original Latin: sacellarius</note>. A commentator on Gregory Nazianzen’s first *Invective* notes: "**Sakellion** is a Roman word signifying a place for guarding money; hence they call the treasurer and guardian of the money a **sakellarios**." Patriarch Nicephorus, in his *History of Constantinople*, defines him as: "the treasurer of the imperial funds." You might not be wrong to translate **sakellarios** as coming from *sacellus* or *sacculus* <note>Latin for "little bag" or "purse"</note>. A *sacellus* or *sacculus* is indeed a pouch or a small money-bag. Petronius writes: "*where would the pimps get their living if they did not cast into the crowd either little boxes or little purses ringing with bronze, as if they were hooks?*" Paulus, in the *Comparison of Mosaic and Roman Laws*, Title 10, writes: "*if I shall have deposited a small bag <note>original Latin: sacellum</note> or silver.*" However, in the *Sentences*, Book 2, Title 12, it is published as "*if a small purse <note>original Latin: sacculum</note>*," and similarly in Law 29 of the *Title on Deposits*. A manuscript glossary states: "*saccus and sacculus: a pouch, a treasury.*" The Glosses of Cyril state: "a purse: *sacculus*, *sacculum* <note>original Greek: βαλλάντιον</note>." Excerpts from ancient glosses on the title *Concerning Clothing* state: "*saccellum*: a small pouch <note>original Greek: μαρσίππιον</note>." The Legal Glosses state: "pouch, bag, sack, purse <note>original Greek: μάρσιππος, σάκκος, θυλάκιον, βαλλάντιον</note>." A Greek translator of Law 3, paragraph *if more*, in the Digest *On the status of freedmen*, writes: "whether he gave the twenty coins all together in a small bag <note>original Greek: ἐν σακκούλῳ</note>." There were both ecclesiastical and imperial treasurers. Nicephorus Callistus, 18.44. Patriarch Nicephorus in his *Chronograph*: "Thomas, a deacon of the same church and a **sakellarios**." These exact words appear in Theophanes’ account of Phocas. Nicetas the Paphlagonian in the *Life of Ignatius*: "For how shall we pass over the affair of Lydus the **sakellarios**?" The Sixth Synod of Constantinople, Act 12: "the imperial **sakellarios**." The inscription of Letter 50 by Photius: "To John, patrician and **sakellarios** in charge of the post-horses <note>original Greek: κατὰ τοὺς ἀγγαρίους; referring to the imperial courier system</note>." The Roman Council, Act 1: "*Theophanes, regional notary and **sacellarius**, read it out.*" Anastasius, in the *Collation of Saint Maximus*: "*who had been the **sacellarius** of Peter, formerly the governor of Numidia.*" Josephus in *Antiquities* 12.2 mentions: "to the royal bankers." Rufinus translates this as "to the royal **sacellarii**." This official was also called "the one over the purse" <note>original Greek: ὁ ἐπὶ τῆς σακέλλης</note>, as found in Theodorus of Hermopolis regarding Law 99 of the Digest *On the Signification of Words*.

**σάκρα (sakra)** — an imperial letter or decree <note>from the Latin 'sacra', meaning 'sacred'</note>. Constantine Pogonatus, in a letter prefixed to the Sixth Synod of Constantinople, writes: "But Justin, having sent **sakrai** everywhere." The Seventh Synod, Act 1: "our good masters ordered a precious and worshipful **sakra** to be sent." Anastasius translates this as "*sacram*." The Menologium for August 2: "having signaled to her father through letters and received an imperial **sakra**." Theophanes: "when the **sakrai** of the Empress Verina arrived." Menander Protector, in *On Embassies*: "when the treaties reached their conclusion, the so-called **sakrai** were exchanged." See also Menander, page 114. Nicephorus Callistus, 14.33. The *Alexandrian Chronicle* says: "having sent divine **sakrai**." Vegetius, Book 2, chapter 7, writes: "*a higher tribune is appointed by the judgment of the emperor through a sacred <note>original Latin: sacram</note> letter.*" However, the word *sacram* is missing in some manuscript codices, as it is in Modestus’s *Military Vocabulary*. I would prefer to retain *sacram* and remove the word "letter." Saint Augustine mentions this in his book *To the Donatists*.

<summary>This page defines three significant Byzantine terms: "Romania" (the Empire), the "Sakellarios" (a high-ranking financial official or treasurer), and the "Sakra" (a sacred imperial decree or official communication).</summary>

<keywords>Romania, Sakellarios, Treasurer, Sakra, Imperial Decree, Byzantine Administration, Etymology, Roman Empire, Financial Officials, Legal Terminology</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the exploration of Byzantine legal and administrative terminology, moving from "Sakra" (imperial decrees) to technical terms for weapons and, most extensively, the various meanings of "Sekreton" or "Secretarium," referring to private council chambers and court offices.</meta>

# FABROT

Following the *Collation*, chapter 31: "They carried the sacred imperial letters <note>original Latin: *sacras*</note> of many emperors, but we carried only the gospels." From the *Short History of the Eutychianists* <note>a 5th-century Christian sect</note>: "Because the official brought the emperor’s sacred letter against Bishop John, the Pope was suspended from the confirmation of that bishopric."

**σαξιμοδέξιμον (saximodeximon)** — <note>A technical term likely referring to a legal hand-shake or a ritualized oath-taking</note>. See Meursius <note>Johannes Meursius, a 17th-century Dutch scholar of Greek antiquities</note>.

**σειρομάστης (seiromastes)** — *a spear, weapon, lance, or dagger.* See Meursius. Moschopoulos <note>a 14th-century Byzantine grammarian</note> explains it differently in his work *On Syntax*: "a *seira* is a chain, from which comes *seiromastes*" <note>implying a hooked spear or a probing tool used to search for hidden items</note>.

**σέκρετον, σεκρετάριον (sekreton, sekretarion)** — *a private chamber, a secretariat, or a council room.* Both Greeks and Latins used these terms interchangeably. For instance, in Book 15 of Ammianus Marcellinus, he speaks of a "judicial *secretum*, that is, a *secretarium*." Theophylactus Simocatta, in his *History of Maurice*, Book 8, Chapter 8, writes: "He withdrew from what the Romans call the *sekreton*." In the *Basilica* <note>a major 9th-century Byzantine law code</note>, Book 60, Title 33, Chapter 29: "They enter into the *sekreton*." The glosses on that passage state: "into the secretariat of the court." See also the Council of Constantinople under Menna, Acts 1 and 5. A *secretum* or *secretarium* was the place in which the cases of the accused were weighed. In the *Passion of Saint Cyprian*: "In the *secretarium*, Paternus the proconsul said to Bishop Cyprian..." John of Jerusalem describes the form of a trial elegantly in his commentary on Matthew, chapter 25, verse 31:

> "A judge about to hear criminal cases places his tribunal in a high place in public; he sets the imperial banners around himself; before his eyes, he places a small tablet <note>original Latin: *calliculam*</note> on the table, from which he might write the death or life of men with three fingers. On this side and that, officials stand in order; in the middle of the **secretarium**, horrible types of punishments are placed, which are a torment not only to suffer but even to see. Torturers stand ready nearby, more cruel in their appearance than in their hands. The whole face of the judgment is clothed in the terror of a certain display; and when the criminal persons have been brought into the middle, they are unnerved by the terrible sight of the judgment itself even before the judge's interrogation."

I also read of the "secretariat of the senate." An ancient inscription reads: SECRETARIAT OF THE MOST NOBLE SENATE, where the acts of the senate were kept. There was also a "secretariat of the praetorium" <note>the headquarters of a governor or commander</note> mentioned in a petition found in Saint Augustine, Book 3, *Against Cresconius the Grammarian*, Chapter 56, and in Severus Sulpitius’s *Life of Saint Martin*, Dialogue 2. Theophanes, in his account of Emperor Phocas, writes: "They set fire to the praetorium, and burned the *sekreton* and the prisons." This is also called the "praetorian secretariat" in Cassiodorus, Book 11, Letter 36. 

There was also the "secretariat of the Palace." The Sixth Synod of Constantinople, Act 1, mentions: "in the *sekreton* of the divine palace, the so-called Trullus <note>a domed hall in the Great Palace of Constantinople</note>." And Act 7: "the *sekreton* of the Trullus." There was also a "prince's secretariat." Saint Maximus says in his dispute with Pyrrhus: "in the imperial *sekreton*." See also Balsamon on Canon 34 of the Sixth Synod in Trullo. Meursius observes from a decree of Alexius Comnenus and from Cedrenus that there were various types of *secreta*, namely for private and public affairs. Look to him for more; for I am not in the habit of merely copying the writings of others. There were also *secretaria* in churches. The Synod of Carthage, Canon 36: "in the *sekreton* of the church of Restituta," and likewise: "in the *sekreton* of the church of Peace." George of Alexandria, in the *Life of Saint Chrysostom*, says: "explaining matters to the crowds not only in the church, but also sitting in the *sekreton* and in the bishop's residence." The Council of Rome, Act 1: "what therefore..."

<summary>This page defines and provides historical context for the terms "saximodeximon," "seiromastes," and "sekreton," detailing the use of private chambers (secretariats) in judicial, imperial, and ecclesiastical settings.</summary>
<keywords>sekreton, secretarium, judicial process, imperial palace, Trullus, Meursius, trial description, Byzantine law, church architecture, secretariat</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the term "secretarium" (a private chamber or office), specifically focusing on its use in church councils and patriarchal residences. It then transitions to titles like "secretarius" and terms for seating or saddles, such as "sella."</meta>

# GLOSSARY

"...did you demand to enter our secretariat again?" <note>original Latin: *denuo secretaria nostra ingredi postulasti?*</note> The Council of Saragossa <note>a church council in Spain held in 380 AD</note>: "With the bishops residing in the secretariat at Saragossa." <note>original Latin: *Caesaraugustae in secretario residentibus episcopis*</note> That is, in the secretariat of the bishop’s residence. The Council of Chalcedon <note>a major 4th-century ecumenical council</note>, Act 1: "in the secretariat of the bishopric" <note>original Greek: ἐν τῷ σηκρήτῳ τοῦ ἐπισκοπείου</note>. The patriarchs also had secretariats, which were likewise of two types: the "great" and the "lesser." The Second Council of Nicaea, Act 1: "Peter, the most devout reader and notary of the venerable patriarchal secretariat, holding [the document] in his hands, read it." <note>original Greek: Πέτρος ὁ εὐλαβέστατος ἀναγνώστης καὶ νοτάριος τοῦ εὐαγοῦς πατριαρχικοῦ σεκρέτου ἔχων ἐπὶ χεῖρας ἀνέγνω</note>. Anastasius the Librarian <note>a 9th-century scholar and translator</note> in his *Ecclesiastical History*: "He erased the icons made of mosaic that belonged to the lesser patriarchal secretariat, and took down the images of the great secretariat, which were carved from wood." <note>original Latin: *iconas ex musio factas, quae patriarchii secreti minoris erant, erasit, et imagines magni secreti, quae sculptae ex ligno erant, deposuit*</note>. In these rooms were kept the sacred vessels and church books, episcopal and patriarchal legal rights, and synodal decrees—just as in other secretariats one finds the private or public legal instruments of princes, imperial constitutions, and "golden bulls" <note>decrees issued by Byzantine emperors with a golden seal</note>. The Second Council of Braga, Canon 41: "It is not permitted for anyone to touch the sacred items, except for a subdeacon or acolyte to touch the Lord’s vessels in the secretariat." <note>original Latin: *non liceat quemlibet ministeria tangere, nisi subdiacono aut acolytho in secretario tangere vasa dominica*</note>. Paulinus, in Letter 12 to Severus: "In the two secretariats which I mentioned above as being over the apse, these verses indicate the duties of each."

->to the right of the apse<-
->*This is the place where the venerable stores are kept, and from which*<-
->*the nourishing splendor of the sacred service is brought forth.*<-
->to the left of the same<-
->*If a holy desire to meditate on the law holds anyone,*<-
->*sitting here he may focus on the sacred books.*<-

I also find *secretarium* used to mean an "action" or a "session." The Sixth Synod of Constantinople, page 192: "the future session" <note>original Latin: *futurum secretarium*</note>. The end of Act 1 of the Roman Council: "the coming session" <note>original Latin: *venturum secretarium*</note>. And Act 2: "the past session." They were called *secretaria* because business was handled there secretly and inwardly. Saint Augustine alludes to this in his 23rd tractate on the Gospel of John: "as if in a treasury, as if in a certain secretariat and inner sanctuary." <note>original Latin: *quasi in thesauro, quasi in secretario quodam et penetrali interiore*</note>. See the commentaries of Balsamon on Canons 9 and 12 of the 7th Synod and Canon 34 of the 6th Synod in Trullo, Zonaras on the Councils, and Nicephorus Callistus.

**σεκρετάριος (sekretarios)** — Curopalates <note>a high court official title</note>, page 839: "a secretary in charge of secrets" <note>original Latin: *secretarius a secretis*</note>. Nicephorus Callistus, Book 15: "Constantine the secretary." Council of Chalcedon, Act 1: "Secretary of the divine consistory" <note>the emperor's advisory council</note>. See also Cujas on the title in the Code regarding the *primicerius* <note>the head of a department</note>.

**σέλλα, σελλίον (sella, sellion)** — *a seat or saddle.* Constantine, in his *Tactics*: "let the saddles have thick saddle-cloths." <note>original Greek: ἐχέτωσαν δὲ καὶ αἱ σέλλαι ἐπισέλλια δασέα</note>. Eustathius <note>a 12th-century scholar</note> on the *Iliad*, Book 7: "Among later writers, the word for a chariot seat [diphros] is found used for what is more commonly called a *sella* [a saddle or seat]." And on the *Odyssey*, Book 1: "a pack-saddle, which means a *sella* and a burden." The *Glosses of Cyril*: "*sella*, a seat." Suidas <note>a 10th-century Greek encyclopedia</note> under the entry "from seats": "for seats are called *sellai*." From this comes *sellarios*. The same author says: "a race-horse is a lone horse, and the one carried upon it is the *sellarios*, a horseman" <note>original Latin: *eques*</note>. Eustathius on the *Iliad*, Book 15: "the term for riding a race-horse is derived from *keles* [a fast horse], which indicates an unyoked horse, and according to some, a horse with a single head-ornament, which..." <note>the text breaks off here</note>

<summary>This page defines "secretarium" as both a physical chamber for storing sacred items and records and as a term for a formal council session. It also introduces Byzantine terms for administrative secretaries and equipment for horses and seating, such as saddles.</summary>
<keywords>secretarium, church councils, archives, patriarchal residence, secretary, sella, saddle, administrative titles, Byzantine law, church architecture</keywords>

--- Page 946 ---
<meta>This page continues the alphabetical glossary of Greco-Roman and Byzantine terms. The previous entry concluded the discussion on the "secretarium" (a private council chamber or office) and began exploring terms related to "sella" (seats or saddles).</meta>

# FABROTUS

Now, they say, he is called a **sellarios** <note>original Greek: σελλάριος; a maker of seats or saddles</note>. They also used the term **sellion** <note>original Greek: σελλίον; a small seat or stool</note>. Eustathius <note>a 12th-century scholar and archbishop</note> in his commentary on the *Iliad*, Book 2, writes: "For a *selma* is a seat, from which the word *sellion* seems to be derived." The Scholiast <note>ancient commentator</note> on Aristophanes’ *The Assemblywomen* writes: "carrying either the stool [*sellion*] or the seat." Varinus <note>a Renaissance lexicographer</note> notes: "a folding stool, a *sellion*." The term **sellarios** also appears in Achmes’ *Interpretation of Dreams*, chapters 14 and 262.

**Senaton** <note>original Greek: σενάτον</note>, **senator** <note>original Greek: σενάτωρ</note>, from the Latin *senatus* <note>the Roman Senate</note>. Codinus <note>a Byzantine official and writer</note> in his *Excerpts*: "opposite the Senate house." Hesychius of Miletus, writing on Constantinople, says: "In addition to these, he also built houses for the High Council [*synkletos*], naming them *senata* <note>original Greek: σενάτα; the Senate houses</note>." And for **senator**, Priscus in his *Excerpts on Embassies* writes: "that a senator should go on an embassy." Paeanius, the Greek translator of Eutropius, notes: "calling them *senators* according to the language of the Italians, since they call old men *senes*."

**Signon** <note>original Greek: σίγνον</note>, **signophoros** <note>original Greek: σιγνοφόρος</note>, from the Latin *signum* <note>a sign or military standard</note> and *vexillum* <note>a flag-like banner</note>. St. Proclus in his ninth oration: "[He] knows no gold-plated chariots, no teams of six mules, nor the rest of the pageantry that temporary kings are accustomed to display in their processions—no weapons, no shields, no military standards [*signa*]." Paeanius, the translator of Eutropius, at the end of Book 1, writes: "And the military signs [*signa*], which they had taken from the Romans in the previous battle—the Romans call them *signa*—taking them all back." Theophylact in his commentary on the *Acts of the Apostles*, chapter 21, asks: "What is meant by 'Away with him!'? It is what they say among us according to Roman custom; wrap him in the standards [*signa*]." <note>Theophylact is interpreting the Roman soldiers' arrest of St. Paul through contemporary military jargon.</note> Oecumenius writes the same in his commentary on *Acts*, chapter 32; both took this from St. John Chrysostom's 46th homily on *Acts*. In the work of Gelasius of Cyzicus, Book 1 of the *Acts of the Council of Nicaea*, the heading of chapter 5 is: "Concerning the military standard [*signon*]," etc. See also the *Alexandrian Chronicle*, page 780. However, **signon** is also used for a small statue [*andriantarion*], as in Horace’s "movable statue" <note>original Latin: *mobile signum*</note>. An old inscription in Gruter, page 86, line 8, reads: "He dedicated the silver statue [*signon*] with all its ornaments." From this comes **signophoros**, a standard-bearer [*vexillarius*]. See Johannes Tzetzes, page 481, verse 9 and following.

**Sikarios** <note>original Greek: σικάριος</note>, from the Latin *sicarius* <note>an assassin or "dagger-man"</note>. St. John Chrysostom in his 46th homily on the *Acts of the Apostles*: "Some say the *sicarii* were a certain tribe of bandits, so named for the swords they carried, which the Romans call *sicae* <note>short, curved daggers</note>."

**Silentiarios** <note>original Greek: σιλεντιάριος</note>, from the Latin *silentiarius* <note>a "Silentiary," a high-ranking court official responsible for maintaining order and silence in the imperial palace</note>. Philostorgius in his *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 7, section 7, writes: "seeing one of the so-called Silentiaries emitting a flame of fire from his mouth." Theophylact Simocatta in his *History of the Emperor Maurice*, Book 8, chapter 9: "He had been adorned with the troops of a Silentiary." George of Alexandria in his *Life of Chrysostom*: "and he revealed it to him through a certain Silentiary." The Silentiaries were protectors of the Prince <note>the Emperor</note>, stationed in the inner bedchamber. The claim made by Zonaras <note>a 12th-century historian</note>—that the office of Silentiary was among the lowliest—is of doubtful truth. Indeed, a Silentiary is called "most wonderful" <note>original Greek: θαυμασιώτατος</note> in the *Acts of the Council of Chalcedon*, Act 1, pages 77 and 116. Dorotheus in his 23rd *Teaching* writes: "Just as in the palace there are great and illustrious ranks—consider the Senate, the Patricians, the Generals, the Prefects, and the Silentiaries; for these are highly valued ranks." See Alemanus’s notes on Procopius’s *Secret History*, Meursius’s *Glossary*, Cujas on the *Codex*, title 16, and Vossius’s *On the Vices of Speech*. The first of this order, the *primicerius* of the Silentiaries...

<summary>This page defines Byzantine and Roman terms related to seats (sellarios), the Senate (senaton), military standards (signon), assassins (sikarios), and the elite court officials known as Silentiaries (silentiarios).</summary>
<keywords>sellarios, senate, senator, signum, military standards, sicarius, assassin, silentiarius, Byzantine court, Roman law, Greek lexicon</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical glossary of Greco-Roman and Byzantine terms. The previous page ended with an entry on military or court titles beginning with "S."</meta>

# GLOSSARY

...he was called [the first-ranking official], the **primikērios of the silentaries** <note>original Greek: πριμμικήριος τῶν σιλεντιαρίων; the "Silentaries" were high-ranking court officials responsible for maintaining order and silence in the imperial palace</note>, as seen in the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon (Act 11) and in Agathias (Book 5): "Who truly held the primary position among the overseers of the silence around the emperor." <note>original Greek: ὃς δὴ τὰ πρῶτα τελῶν ἐν τοῖς τῆς ἀμφὶ τὸν βασιλέα σιγῆς ἐπιστάταις</note>

**skamnos** <note>original Greek: σκάμνος</note> *scamnum* <note>a bench or stool</note>. **skamnalia** <note>original Greek: σκαμνάλια; small benches</note> from the Council of Constantinople (Act 5): "that certain small benches should be purchased." <note>original Greek: ὠνηθῆναί τινα σκαμνάλια</note>

**skaramangion** <note>original Greek: σκαραμάγγιον</note> *scaramangium* or *scaramangis*. Luitprand, in *European Affairs* (Book 6, Chapter 5), writes: "with two *scaramangia*" <note>original Latin: cum scaramangis duobus</note>. It is a garment suitable for warding off the rain, as the very learned men Leunclavius (in his *Turkish Laws*) and Vossius (in *On the Faults of Speech*, Book 2, Chapter 17) believe. However, they should consider whether a silk *skaramangion*, which Achmes mentions in Chapter 158, would be truly suitable for warding off the injuries of the weather. See the *Glossary of the Basilika* <note>a 9th-century code of Byzantine law</note> under **polli** <note>original Greek: πόλλι</note>.

**skeuophylax** <note>original Greek: σκευοφύλαξ</note> *guardian of the sacred vessels*. The one who held higher dignity than the rest was called **the Great** <note>original Greek: ὁ μέγας</note>. From the Council of Florence: "the Great Skeuophylax Xanthopoulos." <note>original Greek: ὁ μέγας σκευοφύλαξ ὁ Ξανθόπουλος</note> Moreover, the place in which the sacred vessels were kept was called the **skeuophylakion** <note>original Greek: σκευοφυλάκιον; a sacristy or treasury</note>. The Sixth Synod of Constantinople states: "being the authentic book of the sacristy." <note>original Greek: τὸ αὐθεντικὸν βιβλίον τοῦ σκευοφυλακίου ὑπάρχον</note> Anastasius the Librarian, in his *Ecclesiastical History*, translates this as "the repository of vessels." <note>original Latin: vasorum custodiarium</note>

**skorpiōn** <note>original Greek: σκορπίων</note> *scorpio* <note>a scorpion, but also a type of knotted, painful whip</note>. In the Third Book of Kings <note>modern 1 Kings</note>, Chapter 12: "but I will discipline you with scorpions." <note>original Greek: ἐγὼ δὲ παιδεύσω ὑμᾶς ἐν σκορπίοις</note> Jerome translates this as: "but I will beat you with scorpions." <note>original Latin: ego autem caedam vos scorpionibus</note> In the writings of Cedrenus, it reads "with a scorpion" <note>singular</note>. The *Martyrology of Usuard* for the month of July says: "having suffered the rack, the sinews, clubs, flames, and scorpions." <note>original Latin: eculeum, nervos, fustes, flammas scorpionesque perpessi</note> And for November 8: "first sent into prison, they were then most severely beaten with scorpions." To be beaten with scorpions is more severe than being beaten with whips. Suger, the Abbot of Saint-Denis, in his book on the life of Louis the Fat <note>Louis VI of France</note>, writes: "but those whom the father [disciplined] with whips, the son, more wicked than his father, beat with scorpions." The *Martyrology of Hrabanus* says: "they were ordered to be raised on the rack, stretched with sinews, and beaten with clubs and scorpions." Innocent III, in *On the Contempt of the World* (Book 1, Chapter 27), writes: "they are tortured by tigers and scourged with scorpions."

**skutarion** <note>original Greek: σκουτάριον</note> *scutum* <note>a shield</note>. Constantine [Porphyrogenitus], in *On the Themes* (1:13), writes: "in which the small shield of the Great Martyr Theodore is hung." <note>original Greek: ἐν ᾗ τὸ σκουτάριον τοῦ μεγαλομάρτυρος Θεοδώρου ἀποκρέμαται</note> The commentator [Scholiast] on Oppian says: "the *skutarion* is a shield [sakos], named after the Sakae people who first discovered it." <note>original Greek: σάκος τὸ σκουτάριον, ἀπὸ τῶν πρώτως εὑρόντων αὐτὸ Σακῶν</note> Theodorus Hermopolites (Book 7, Title 11) writes: "a small tablet or a small shield." <note>original Greek: πινακίδιον ἢ σκουτάριον</note> Theophanes says: "he was carrying a small shield." <note>original Greek: ἐβάσταζε σκουτάριν μικρόν</note> The *Corona Pretiosa* dictionary translates *scudo* as **skutarē**. Furthermore, a **skutarios** <note>original Greek: σκουτάριος</note> is a *scutarius* <note>a shield-bearer or a member of the imperial guard</note>. Marcus Antoninus uses this in the first book of his life <note>Meditations</note>, though the most learned men prefer the form *skoutarios*. See Suidas under the entry **Prasianos**. St. Jerome, at the end of his *Chronicle*, writes: "This man was a tribune of the shield-bearers [*scutarii*] from Pannonia, etc." Simeon Metaphrastes, in his life of Hilarion, says: "a certain shield-bearer, when he was being tortured in the Basilica of Saint Peter." Julius Firmicus, in *Mathesis* (Book 3, Chapter 14), says: "it will make them shield-bearers, or protectors of emperors, or those who preserve the safety of princes by their own watch." See the notes on Cantacuzenus, page 995. They also used the term **skoutaratoi** <note>original Greek: σκουταράτους; shield-bearing soldiers</note>. Leo [the Wise], in his *Tactics* (Chapter 9, Section 74), writes: "those of the heavy infantry, that is, the shield-bearers." <note>original Greek: τὰς δὲ τῶν ὁπλιτῶν ἤγουν σκουτάτων</note> Constantine, in his *Tactics* (page 6), says: "and first, the shield-bearers." From this comes the verb **skouteuein** <note>original Greek: σκουτεύειν</note>, meaning *to defend with a shield*. Leo, in the aforementioned Chapter 9 (Section 49), says: "and to be shielded, as it were, by them." <note>original Greek: καὶ ὑπ᾽ αὐτῶν ὡσανεὶ σκουτεύεσθαι</note> Add also Section 64. Regarding the *scutarii* <note>shield-bearers</note>, see Ammianus Marcellinus and the *Legal Glossary*.

<summary>This page defines various Byzantine and late Roman terms related to court offices (Silentaries), furniture (skamnos), clothing (skaramangion), church roles (skeuophylax), and military equipment or punishments (scorpions and shields).</summary>
<keywords>Silentaries, skaramangion, skeuophylax, scorpions, punishment, skutarion, shields, scutarii, Byzantine military, sacristan</keywords>

--- Page 948 ---
<meta>This page continues an alphabetical glossary of Greek terms and their Latin equivalents, primarily focusing on Byzantine court titles, military equipment, and ecclesiastical vocabulary beginning with the letter "S."</meta>

### FROM FABROTUS

**soubla, soublion** <note>original Greek: σοῦβλα, σουβλίον</note> *an awl or a spit*. <note>original Latin: subula, veru</note> Suidas says: "a *soubla* is a spit or a small skewer." <note>original Greek: ὀβελὸς καὶ ὀβελίσκος ἡ σοῦβλα</note> Nicephorus Callistus (7.44) writes: "he thrust skewers through the hidden passage," <note>original Greek: κατὰ τοῦ κρυφίου πόρου σούβλας εἰσώθει</note> and (10.7): "there were some who pierced these men with skewers and spits." <note>original Greek: ἦσαν δ’ οἳ καὶ ὀβελίσκοις σούβλαις τούτους διέπειρον</note> The *Menologium* <note>a church calendar with biographies of saints</note> for March 22nd: "he ordered him to be pierced with red-hot spits." <note>original Greek: ὁ δὲ πυρωθείσαις σούβλαις κατακεντῆσαι αὐτὸν ἐκέλευσε</note> And for June 13th: "their ears are pierced with red-hot iron skewers." **soublion** <note>original Greek: σουβλίον</note> is the same thing. Leo the Wise in his *Tactica* (chapter 20, § 80) lists: "except for an iron skewer and a cup." <note>original Greek: πλὴν σουβλίου σιδηροῦ καὶ ποτηρίου</note> Eustathius, in his commentary on the *Odyssey* (Book 10), says that Aelius Dionysius considers the word for "patching" <note>original Greek: τὸ δὲ ἠπήσασθαι</note> to be entirely foreign/barbaric; however, common usage agrees with Dionysius, where "to pierce with an awl" is called "to patch." <note>original Greek: τὸ σουβλίῳ τρυπᾶν ἠπᾶν λέγεται</note> Also, in his commentary on the *Iliad* (Book 1): "*pempobolon* <note>a five-pronged fork</note> is an Aeolic word signifying a five-fingered cooking tool, or as a common person might say, a **penta-soublon** <note>original Greek: πεντάσουβλον; a five-spitted tool</note>." In the *Corona Pretiosa* <note>a medieval Greek-Latin dictionary</note>: *soublē* <note>original Greek: σουβλή</note> means "a spit." In the Legal Glossaries: *souglarion* <note>original Greek: σουγλάριον</note> means "a tool kit," perhaps meant as *soublarion* <note>original Greek: σουβλάριον; a case for awls</note>.

**soultanos** <note>original Greek: σουλτάνος</note> *Sultan*. <note>original Latin: sultanus</note> Nicephorus Gregoras, *History* (Book 3): "unless someone among those related by blood to the Sultan..." <note>original Greek: εἰ μή τις τῶν τῷ Σουλτὰν κατὰ γένος προσηκόντων</note>

**spatharios** <note>original Greek: σπαθάριος</note> *a sword-bearer; an attendant who carries a broadsword or blade*. <note>original Latin: spatharius, satelles qui spatham seu ensem gestaret</note> Theodoretus, in Letter 110: "as he received letters from both the most magnificent *spatharios* and the most illustrious former Master of Offices." <note>original Greek: ὡς ἐδέξατο γράμματα καὶ τοῦ μεγαλοπρεπεστάτου σπαθαρίου καὶ τοῦ ἐνδοξοτάτου ἀπὸ μαγίστρων</note> Theophanes mentions: "the *spatharios* of the Master." Procopius of Gaza, in his commentary on Genesis (Chapter 39): "The Chief Cook, namely an attendant and as it were a *spatharios*." <note>original Latin: archimagirus scilicet satelles et quasi spatharius</note> Bishop Idatius writes in his *Chronicle*: "And with him, through his *spatharios*, some honored men were secretly let in and slaughtered." <note>original Latin: et cum ipso per spatharium eius aliqui singulariter intromissi iugulantur honorati</note> Rufinus of Aquileia in *Lives of the Fathers* (Book 2, n. 59): "just as the emperor's *spatharios* always stands by him armed." <note>original Latin: quemadmodum imperatoris spatharius semper illi assistit armatus</note> The *Brief History of the Eutychians*: "When Eutyches saw his faction was being pressured, he sought the protection of the Emperor through Chrysaphius, the *spatharios* of Theodosius." <note>original Latin: cum partes suas Eutyches videret urgeri, per Chrysaphium spatharium Theodosii praesidium principis expetivit</note>

**spathē** <note>original Greek: σπάθη</note> *a broadsword*. <note>original Latin: spatha</note> They more frequently use the diminutive **spathion** <note>original Greek: σπαθίον</note>. Constantine Porphyrogenitus, *Tactica* (p. 4): "with their swords," and (p. 10): "sharpened and polished swords." <note>original Greek: σπαθία ἠκονημένα καὶ σεσαμιωμένα</note> Theophanes: "having bared his sword." From this comes the verb **spathizein** <note>original Greek: σπαθίζειν; to strike with a sword</note>. The *Menologium* for June 18th: "that Saint Theodoulos be struck with a sword and thus their heads were cut off." <note>original Greek: τὸν ἅγιον Θεόδουλον σπαθίζεσθαι καὶ οὕτω τὰς κεφαλὰς αὐτῶν ἐκτμηθῆναι</note> However, *spathē* is a purely Greek word. See Julius Pollux (10.31). Theodorus Prodromus, in his *Praise to the Emperor John Komnenos*: "Already I see the imperial sword lying near your necks, terribly sharpened." <note>original Greek: ἤδη κειμένην θεωρῶ πρὸς τοῖς ὑμῶν τραχήλοις τὴν σπάθην τὴν βασιλικὴν δεινῶς ἠκονισμένην</note>

**sporta** <note>original Greek: σπόρτα</note> *a basket*. <note>original Latin: sporta</note> Greek-Latin Glossaries: *spyris* <note>original Greek: σπυρὶς</note> is a *sporta*, a small wicker basket or box. From this comes **sportoula** <note>original Greek: σπόρτουλα</note>, or "gifts given in a basket," as found in the Legal Glossary, meaning **sportulae** <note>fees or small gift-baskets given to officials</note>. Council of Chalcedon (Act 10): "Bishop Daniel receiving a *sportoula*." See *Novella* 82 <note>a law of Justinian</note>.

**stichēra** <note>original Greek: στιχηρά</note> *certain hymns or chants in the church*. <note>original Latin: cantica certa in ecclesia</note> See Meursius. Codinus, in the *Excerpts*: "She, being most wise, composed and set to music both canons and *stichēra*." <note>This likely refers to the poetess Kassia</note>

**stratēgos** <note>original Greek: στρατηγός</note> *a general or military governor*. Anastasius, in his *Ecclesiastical History*: "Anatolius, the **stratēgos** of the East." <note>original Latin: Anatolium Orientis stratigon</note> See Bonaventura Vulcanius's notes on Constantine's *On the Themes* (Book 1).

<vocab>soubla, soultanos, spatharios, spathē, sporta, stichēra, stratēgos</vocab>

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical glossary of Byzantine Greek terms, specifically focusing on military and ecclesiastical titles under the letter Sigma (Σ). It moves from military tools like skewers to high-ranking administrative and church positions.</meta>

# GLOSSARIUM.

**stratelates.** <note>original Greek: στρατηλάτης; literally, "leader of an army"</note> The *Glosses of Cyril*: *stratelates, master of soldiers.* <note>original Latin: magister militum</note> Julian the Antecessor also translates it this way in *Novella 125, chapter 1*. From the Council of Constantinople under Menas: "Many years to Vitalian the **stratelates**!" <note>original Greek: Βιταλιανοῦ στρατηλάτου πολλὰ τὰ ἔτη</note> The interpreter renders this as: "Many years for Vitalian the **stratelates**." <note>original Latin: Vitaliani stratelatis multi anni</note> A handwritten glossary defines it: **stratelates**, a leader, a commander of an army. <note>original Greek: στρατηλάτης, ἡγεμών, ἄρχων στρατοῦ</note> See also Zosimus (Book 2, p. 688), Eusebius in *Ecclesiastical History* (7.32), and Theodore Lector (Book 1). Damascius, in the *Photian Excerpts* (p. 572), writes: "After these things, the great **stratelates** of the East <note>the commander-in-chief of the eastern frontier</note> made an attempt." Saint Athanasius, in his *Letter to the Solitaries*: "Sebastian the **stratelates** with the local provosts and military authorities." <note>original Greek: ὁ μὲν στρατηλάτης Σεβαστιανὸς τοῖς κατὰ τόπον πραιποσίτοις καὶ στρατιωτικαῖς ἐξουσίαις</note> See also Dorotheus, *Instruction 23*.

**stratopedarches.** <note>original Greek: στρατοπεδάρχης; literally, "commander of the camp" or "master of the camp"</note> Mentioned by George Logothetes in his *Chronicle*. In the *Menologium* <note>a liturgical book of saints' lives</note> for the month of March: "The wife of a certain **stratopedarches** named Pantile." <note>original Greek: Παντίλης ὀνομαζομένης γαμετῆς στρατοπεδάρχου τινός</note> There were, however, several of these officers, and *among them was the **Great [Stratopedarches]**.* <note>original Greek: ὁ μέγας</note> Pachymeres writes: "He also chose Synadenos and the **Great Stratopedarches**." From this title comes **stratopedarchiai** <note>military districts or commands</note>. Theodore Prodromus (found in the Royal Library), in his *Panegyric to the Emperor John Komnenos*: "And again battles and an army and **stratopedarchiai**." <note>original Greek: καὶ πάλιν μάχαι καὶ στρατὸς καὶ στρατοπεδαρχίαι</note> See Meursius and the later notes on page 656.

**strator.** <note>original Greek: στράτωρ; a groom or equerry responsible for the Emperor's horses</note> The *Onomasticon* <note>a dictionary of names and terms</note> defines it as: *strator, an assistant who helps one mount a horse.* <note>original Greek: ἀναβολεύς</note> Leo the Wise in his *Tactica* (chapter 14, § 81): "And one **strator** and one **spatharios** <note>a sword-bearer or palace guard</note>." George Pachymeres: "Either cooks or **strators**." Theophanes: "With certain **spatharioi** and **strators** and other imperial men." Papias: *stratores, those who arrange the royal saddle.* Saint Augustine, in his *Second Sermon on the New [Converts]*: "He had placed three **strators** on the chariots." Gunther of Pairis, in his *Ligurinus* (Book 2):

> *The **strator** was indeed from the common people, nor was his name*
> *widely known; he served for a modest wage in the camp.*

See Vossius on the *Vices of Speech* (1.7, p. 33), and Cujas on *Book 12 of the Code, Title 24*, and the annotations to Paul the Deacon (Book 2, chapter 9).

**syncellus.** <note>original Greek: σύγκελλος; literally, "living in the same cell"</note> Cedrenus (p. 775): *the syncellus is the designated successor to the patriarch.* The Second Council of Nicaea: "When the **syncelloi** of the patriarchs there were present." <note>original Greek: συγκέλλων γενομένων τῶν ἐκεῖσε πατριαρχῶν</note> And in Act 7: "The patriarchal **syncellus**." The *History of George the Monk* is inscribed as: "The composition of George, the most devout monk and **syncellus** to Tarasios, the most holy Bishop of Constantinople." He was so named because he lived with the patriarch and stayed, as it were, in the same cell. The Council of Chalcedon (Act 3): "Nevertheless, even among the witnesses produced by me, who were his **syncelloi** and were brought forward," <note>original Greek: συγκέλλων αὐτοῦ ὄντων καὶ παραφερομένων</note> *nevertheless, through the witnesses named by me, appointed as his **syncelloi**, who until now seem to live and remain with him.* See the same work, page 239 in the Roman edition. William of Tyre, in his *History of the Holy War* (Book 14, chapter 12): "And since it was necessary for the same patriarch to have, besides the aforementioned metropolitans, familiar suffragans whom the Greeks call **cancellos** [chancellors]. They correct this in the margin to **syncellos**." I do not know if they would be more correctly read as *concellos*, *concellanos*, or *concellaneos* <note>Latin variations of "cell-mate"</note>. There were several of them, of whom the first was called the **protosyncellus** <note>the chief syncellus</note>. See above under that word.

<summary>This page defines high-ranking Byzantine military and ecclesiastical titles, including the Commander-in-Chief (stratelates), the Camp Master (stratopedarches), the imperial groom (strator), and the Patriarchal advisor or "cell-mate" (syncellus).</summary>
<keywords>stratelates, magister militum, stratopedarches, strator, equerry, syncellus, protosyncellus, Byzantine titles, church hierarchy, military ranks</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical glossary of Byzantine terms, moving from military titles to geographical locations and professional roles like the imperial guards and legal advocates.</meta>

# FABROTUS

**Sycae.** <note>original Greek: Συκαί; literally, "The Figs"</note> Sycae. Cedrenus writes: "He docked at **Sycae**." <note>original Greek: προσώρμησεν ἐν Συκαῖς</note> Anastasius the Librarian, in his *Ecclesiastical History*: "And he landed opposite the city in **Sycae**." <note>original Latin: et applicuit ex adverso civitatis in Sycis</note> Nicephorus in his *Chronography*: "He established another church by the sea at the place called **Sycae**, naming the building Peace." <note>original Greek: οὗτος ἑτέραν ἐκκλησίαν ἀνίστησιν ἐν παραθαλασσίῳ τῷ ἐπιλεγομένῳ Συκαῖς, Εἰρήνην τὸν οἶκον ἐπονομάσας; Sycae was the district across the Golden Horn from Constantinople, later known as Galata.</note>

**synteknoi.** <note>original Greek: σύντεκνοι; "co-parents" or spiritual sponsors/godparents</note> See the *Glossary of Meursius*.

**scholarii.** <note>original Greek: σχολάριοι</note> Scholarians, scholars, or cohorts of soldiers who were assigned to the guard of the palace. Procopius (Book 8) writes: "The companies for the guard of the palace, which they call *scholae* <note>meaning 'schools' or elite units</note>." <note>original Greek: οἱ περὶ τῆς τοῦ παλατίου φυλακῆς λόχοι, οὕσπερ σχολὰς ὀνομάζουσι</note> And in the *Secret History*: "Other soldiers, no fewer than three thousand five hundred, were established from the beginning for the guard of the palace; these they call **scholarii**." <note>original Greek: ἕτεροι στρατιῶται οὐχ ἥσσους ἢ πεντακόσιοι καὶ τρισχίλιοι τὰ ἐξ ἀρχῆς ἐπὶ φυλακῇ τοῦ παλατίου κατέστησαν, οὕσπερ σχολαρίους καλοῦσι</note> The *Alexandrian Chronicle*: "And the area along with the portico of the **scholarii**, the protectors, and the candidates was burned." <note>original Greek: καὶ ἐκαύθη τὸ μετὰ τοῦ πορτίκου τῶν σχολαρίων καὶ προτηκτόρων καὶ κανδιδάτων; these were all specific ranks of the imperial guard.</note> The Seventh Council of Constantinople: "The emperors and the people of the regiments—**scholarii**, excubitors, and the rest of the troops serving in the royal city—having entered." <note>original Greek: εἰσελθόντων οὖν τῶν βασιλέων καὶ τοῦ λαοῦ τῶν ταγμάτων, σχολαρίων, ἐξκουβιτόρων τε καὶ τῶν λοιπῶν στρατευμάτων τῶν στρατευομένων ἐν τῇ βασιλίδι πόλει</note> Anastasius translates this as **scholarii**. In the same way, Marcellinus Comes writes in his *Chronicle*: "A rustic count of the **scholarii**." <note>original Latin: rusticus comes scholariorum</note> Elsewhere they are called *scholares*, as in the third act of the Council of Chalcedon. Sulpitius Severus, in his *Life of Saint Martin* (chapter 1): "He himself followed the armed military in his youth among the **scholar** wings <note>cavalry units</note> under King Constantius, and then served under Julian Caesar." <note>original Latin: ipse armatam militiam in adolescentia secutus inter scholares alas sub rege Constantio, deinde sub Iuliano Caesare militavit</note> This can also be read throughout the Theodosian and Justinian Codes and in other authors. They were called *scholares* from the military *scholae* (schools/units), of which there were several. Malchus says of the embassies (page 76): "And all the *scholae*." <note>original Greek: καὶ τὰς σχολὰς ἁπάσας</note> Theophanes, in his section on Justinian: "The *scholae*, the protectors, and the *arithmoi* <note>regiments</note>." <note>original Greek: αἱ σχολαὶ καὶ οἱ προτήκτορες καὶ οἱ ἀριθμοί</note> See Meursius in his *Glossary* and Valesius on Marcellinus (Book 14, page 32).

**scholasticus.** <note>original Greek: σχολαστικός</note> A scholastic, a patron of legal causes <note>a lawyer or advocate</note>. Saint Basil, in *Epistle 242*: "If a certain **scholasticus** practices some law, he has public courts and laws." <note>original Greek: εἰ δέ τινα δίκην γυμνάζει ὁ σχολαστικὸς ὁ δεῖνα ἔχει δικαστήρια δημόσια καὶ νόμους</note> Anastasius Sinaita, in the *Guide* (Question 3): "That a certain **scholasticus** cursed much." <note>original Greek: ὅτι τις σχολαστικὸς πολλὰ κατηράσατο</note> John of Jerusalem, in his *Homily 24 on Matthew*: "So that while the apostles are accused and while they respond, the truth of Christ may be preached in every judgment hall, the treachery of the Jews may be shown, and the mystery of piety may be revealed to the nations who believe unto salvation. But the apostles, hearing that they were commanded to stand before kings and judges, might perhaps say to Christ: 'You yourself know that in those judgments, **scholastici** <note>lawyers</note> preside.'" <note>original Latin: ut dum apostoli accusantur... tu ipse scis quia in illorum iudiciis scholastici praesunt</note> Usuard, in his *Martyrology* (February 6): "In whose confession a certain **scholasticus** named Theophilus was converted." <note>original Latin: in cuius confessione quidam Theophilus scholasticus conversus</note> In the *Acts of Dorothea*, which contains her passion, he is called an *advocatus* (advocate). Theophanes writes: "Eusebius, a certain **scholasticus** of the Empress of Constantinople." <note>original Greek: Εὐσέβιός τις σχολαστικὸς τῆς βασιλείσης Κωνσταντινουπόλεως</note> In a manuscript of Cedrenus, it is read as "of the Queen/Empress" <note>original Greek: τῆς βασιλίσσης</note>. Francis Pithou, in the *Glossary of Julian the Antecessor* under the word *Basilica*, read it as "of the basilica" or "royal." <note>original Greek/Latin: βασιλικῆς, basilicae</note> Anastasius the Librarian, in his *Ecclesiastical History*, translates it thus: "A certain Eusebius, **scholasticus** of the Empress of Constantinople." Therefore, he was an advocate of the royal city, or the ruling <note>original Greek: βασιλευούσης</note> Constan—

It cites numerous historical sources, including Procopius and Saint Basil, to illustrate how these terms evolved in military and civil contexts.</summary>

# GLOSSARY

...tinople, as in the Council of Chalcedon and elsewhere. See our *Glossary to Julian*.

**solea** <note>original Greek: σωλέα</note>. Solea. Codinus in the *Excerpts*: "and the precious **solea** and the multi-colored floor." <note>original Greek: καὶ τὴν πολυτίμητον σωλέαν καὶ τὸν πολυποίκιλον πάτον; the 'solea' was a raised walkway or platform in Byzantine churches that extended from the sanctuary into the main body of the church.</note> See the notes to Cantacuzenus page 994 and Allatius’s *On the more recent temples of the Greeks*, page 171 and following.

**tabla** <note>original Greek: τάβλα</note>. From the Latin *tabula*, a board or table. Nicephorus Callistus (4.25): "a prophet plays with **boards** and dice." <note>original Greek: προφήτης ταύλαις καὶ κύβοις παίζει</note> The Council of Elvira, canon 79: "If any of the faithful plays at dice, that is, the **board**." <note>original Latin: si quis fidelis alea, id est tabula, luserit</note> Hence *tablizein* <note>original Greek: ταβλίζειν</note>, to play at the board. *Tablissare* in Diomedes the Grammarian. Isaac Porphyrogenitus in his *Character of Palamedes*: "by whom playing at the **board**, that is dicing, was first invented." <note>original Greek: ᾧ δὴ πρώτως τὸ ταυλίζειν ἤτοι κυβεύειν ἐξεύρηται</note> And soon after: "he defined the **board**." <note>original Greek: ὡρίσατο τὴν ταῦλαν</note> Astrampsychus in the *Pythagorean Table*: "He has fellowship with his wife and beardless children, with eunuchs and games and chess and **board-games**." <note>original Greek: ἔχει κοινωνίαν πρὸς γυναῖκα καὶ παῖδας ἀγενείους, πρὸς εὐνούχους καὶ παίγνια καὶ ζατρίκια καὶ ταυλία</note> Also: "both chess and the **board**." <note>original Greek: καὶ ζατρίκην καὶ ταύλην</note> They wrote it as *tabla*, *taule*, and *taulion*.

**tablia**, **rhousia** <note>original Greek: τάβλια, ῥούσια</note>. Scarlet garments, having **boards** or circles of red, with purple studs. *Rhoussion* <note>original Greek: ῥούσσιον</note> means red.

**taktika** <note>original Greek: τακτικά</note>. Books on military matters. Saint Chrysostom, in Homily 3 on Paul's Epistle to the Thessalonians: "with the teachers who teach them **military tactics**." <note>original Greek: μετὰ τῶν διδασκάλων τῶν τὰ τακτικὰ διδασκόντων αὐτούς</note> Saint Gregory of Nyssa in his *Catechetical Oration* 35: "Just as those who are trained in **tactics** are led toward experience in heavy weaponry, through which those being instructed see rhythmic and armed movement." <note>original Greek: ὥσπερ γὰρ παρὰ τῶν πεπαιδευμένων τὰ τακτικὰ πρὸς τὴν ὁπλιτικὴν ἐμπειρίαν ἀνάγονται, δι’ ὧν βλέπουσιν οἱ πρὸς τὴν εὔρυθμόν τε καὶ ἔνοπλον κίνησιν παιδευόμενοι</note> Theophanes Cerameus, Homily 41: "those who teach **military tactics**." <note>original Greek: οἱ τὰ τακτικὰ ἐκπαιδεύοντες</note>

**taxation** <note>original Greek: ταξατίων</note>. From the Latin *taxatio*; meaning a garrison or protection. Theophanes in his life of Constantine: "And from his own army they established a **garrison** in it." <note>original Greek: καὶ ἐκ τοῦ οἰκείου στρατοῦ ταξατίωνα ἐν αὐτῇ κατέστησαν</note> Anastasius the Librarian in his *Ecclesiastical History*: "fearing the battle and the **garrison**, they caused an uproar." <note>original Latin: quod formidantes praelium et taxationem tumultuarent</note> And *taxati* <note>original Greek: ταξάτοι</note> were garrisoned soldiers. The same Anastasius: "He sent **garrisoned soldiers** from the Obsician district." <note>original Latin: misit taxatos ex themate obsicio</note> Theophanes in his life of Theodosius: "One thousand **garrisoned soldiers** with their commander entered there." <note>original Greek: χίλιοι ταξάτοι σὺν αὐτῷ τούρμαρχοι ἐκεῖ εἰσῆλθον</note>

**taxeidion**, **taxideuein** <note>original Greek: ταξείδιον, ταξιδεύειν</note>. Meursius interprets this as a "garrison." However, later notes on page 658 say otherwise. The *Basilica* <note>the major collection of Byzantine laws</note>, Book 10, Title 33: "One who is living on **campaign**," that is, "who is occupied in a military expedition." <note>original Greek: ὁ ἐν ταξειδίῳ διάγων; original Latin: qui in expeditione occupatus est</note> The final law in the Code *On the Restitution of Soldiers*. It seems **campaign** should be understood this way in Constantine's *Tactics*, page 22: "if a soldier is sent to his home during days of leisure, when there is no **campaign**." <note>original Greek: ἐὰν ἀπολυθῇ στρατιώτης εἰς τὸν οἶκον αὐτοῦ εἰς ἡμέρας εὐκαιρίας, ὅτε οὐκ ἔστι ταξείδιον</note> And to **go on campaign** on page 13: "whether the army is about to winter somewhere, or to **go on campaign**." <note>original Greek: ἄν τε παραχειμάσαι μέλλῃ που τὸ φοσσάτον, ἄν τε ταξιδεῦσαι</note> Achmes in his *Interpretation of Dreams*, chapter 15: "If he has a journey of **campaign**, he will be robbed." <note>original Greek: ἐὰν ἔχει ὁδὸν ταξειδίου, λῃστευθήσεται</note>

**titlos** <note>original Greek: τίτλος</note>. From the Latin *titulus*; a title. Legal Glosses: "**Title**, chapter, cause, inscription." <note>original Greek: τίτλος, κεφάλαιον, αἰτία, ἐπιγραφή</note> Hence "to title" (*titloun*). George of Alexandria in his *Life of Chrysostom*: "the suburb to be **titled** <note>officially marked or designated</note> with the imperial names." <note>original Greek: τιτλωθῆναι τὸ προάστειον τοῖς βασιλικοῖς</note>

**topoteretes** <note>original Greek: τοποτηρητής</note>. A legate, vicar, one acting in place of another, or a "place-keeper." Theophanes: "And the **deputies** of Pope Leo." <note>original Greek: καὶ οἱ μὲν τοποτηρηταὶ τοῦ πάπα Λέοντος</note> The translator of the canons of the African Church: "**deputy** of the church of Rome," that is, "legate of the Roman church." <note>original Greek: τοποτηρητὴ τῆς ἐκκλησίας Ῥώμης; original Latin: legato ecclesiae Romanae</note> And *topoteresia* means a legation (ibid., page 161). The Sixth Synod of Constantinople, Act 1: "**deputy** of the count of the imperial guards." <note>original Greek: τοποτηρητοῦ τοῦ κόμητος τοῦ βασιλικοῦ ἐξκουβίτου</note> An old translator: "and acting in the place of the imperial co-"

It highlights how Latin administrative and military terms like 'taxatio' and 'titulus' were absorbed and adapted into the Greek-speaking Byzantine world.</summary>

# FABROT

...of the gentle guard. And in the same place: **deputy** <note>original Greek: τοποτηρητοῦ; *topoteretes*, literally "place-keeper"</note> **of the throne of the great city of the Alexandrians.** An ancient interpreter translates this as: *place-keeper of the see of the great Alexandrian city.* <note>original Latin: loci servatore sedis magnae Alexandrinae civitatis</note> Anastasius the Librarian translates it the same way in the second Council of Nicaea, act 3. The same author in his *Ecclesiastical History* writes: *Then Dioscorus said: "And we all agree to this." And the deputies of Pope Leo of Rome, seeing the onset of Dioscorus...* The second Council of Soissons, act 1: *Sigloardus came, serving as the deputy of the archdeacon of the church of Reims.* See also Julian the Legal Scholar in Novels 124 and 125, and Emperor Constantine Porphyrogenitus in *On the Administration of the Empire*, page 182. Also John Moschus in the *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 19, 186 at the end; John Zonaras on the Councils, pages 384 and 410; and Balsamon, pages 591d and 630d.

**touldon** <note>original Greek: τοῦλδον</note> **The baggage and equipment of an army.** Legal Glosses: **touldos** <note>original Greek: τοῦλδος</note> refers to the pack-animals that carry the baggage of the enemy. Also: **touldos** is the baggage and every necessity of the soldiers, that is, both the servants and the pack-animals, and whatever else is dragged along for the service of the camp. <note>original Greek: φωσσάτου; *fossaton*, a term for a fortified camp</note> This term refers to the beasts of burden carrying all the equipment, furniture, or bundles of the soldiers; it seems to be taken from Leo VI’s *Tactics*, chapter 10, section 7. The second gloss is taken from the same Leo, chapter 4, section 29. Vegetius (Book 3, chapter 6) says: *the baggage, pack-animals, camp-servants, and vehicles should be placed in the middle.* Constantine the Tactician (page 32) writes: "The whole **baggage train**, the army servants, the pack-animals, and all the equipment ought to travel in the middle of the battle ranks." <note>original Greek: τὸ δὲ τοῦλδον ὅλον</note> Theophanes in his history of Emperor Maurice: "He broke through the Persian phalanx and captured the **baggage train**," and in the same work: "Since a great capture was made among them, they also took the **baggage train**." This word appears in Harmenopulus (Book 2, 6, final section), if we follow the correction of Cujas rather than the writing of two old manuscripts which I compared with the published editions. Moreover, the baggage was traditionally placed in the center. Vegetius (as cited above). Philo Judaeus in *The Life of Moses*, Book 1: "Having stationed the elderly, the women, and the children in the middle, so that they might have protection from those on either side, in case a crowd of enemies should attack from behind." Procopius in the *Vandalic War* (Book 1, page 102 and Book 2, page 123). Onosander in *The General*, chapter 6: "as booty." Agathias (Book 1, page 20): "And taking the plunder into the middle."

**tourmarches** <note>original Greek: τουρμάρχης</note> **A commander of a squadron, a turmarch.** Zonaras in his account of Leo the Armenian: "the **turmarch** of the unit of the Federates." In a certain *Novel* of Constantine Porphyrogenitus: "announced by the **turmarch**." See also the same Constantine in *On the Themes*, Book 1, theme 1 at the end. In the *Miscellaneous History*, Book 23: *He captured those who had been defeated and killed Andronicus the spatharios <note>a high-ranking palace official</note> and Theophilus the **turmarch**.* The word comes from *tourma* <note>a military division or squadron</note>. Constantine (Theme 5, Book 1 of *On the Themes*): "honored neither with *tourmai* nor *droungoi*." <note>divisions of the Byzantine army</note>

**tribunalion** <note>original Greek: τριβουνάλιον</note> **A tribunal or platform.** Anastasius the Librarian in the *Ecclesiastical History*. Nicephorus of Constantinople in his *Short History*: "in the **tribunal** called the Nineteen Couches," <note>original Greek: δεκαεννέα ἀκκουβίτων; the 'Nineteen Couches' was a famous ceremonial dining hall in the Great Palace of Constantinople used for imperial banquets</note> translated as: *in the tribunal which is called of the nineteen couches.* Philostorgius in his *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 11: "in the so-called **tribunal**..."

# GLOSSARY

...he was cut down with swords right at the king's feet. <note>original Greek: λίῳ, πρὸς αὐτοῖς τοῖς τοῦ βασιλέως ποσί, ταῖς μαχαίραις κατεκόψατο</note> *Alexandrian Chronicle*, page 676.

**tribunus** <note>Greek: τριβοῦνος; a military officer, originally a "tribune" in the Roman system</note> **tribune.** *Glosses of Cyril:* **tribunus** <note>original Greek: τριβοῦνος</note> is a tribune. *Manuscript Glossary:* a front-rank tribune. <note>original Greek: πρωτοστάτης τριβοῦνος</note> St. John Chrysostom, *Epistle 14*: "Upon hearing this, the tribune, taking the soldiers he had, went out." Theophanes: "Valentinian, being at that time a tribune of the unit called the *Cornuti* <note>a prestigious Roman auxiliary unit</note>." *Council of Chalcedon*, act 1: "and the most illustrious tribune, notary, and referendary <note>a high-ranking official who presented petitions to the emperor</note> shall inform [the court]." It speaks here of the tribune and notary of the prince. And St. Basil, *Epistle 208* to Emperor Julian: "your distinguished tribune." Add also Isidore of Pelusium, book 1, epistle 186 and book 2, epistle 291; Theodore Lector in his *Historical Excerpts*; and Harmenopoulos, book 4, last title, section 28, where the term *legatarii* <note>usually meaning those receiving a legacy or inheritance</note> is used for *legati* <note>ambassadors or envoys</note>, as it is also used in the St. Gall manuscript, book 2, regarding the deeds of Charlemagne: *the legatarii of the King of the Africans*; and in a certain letter directed to the Frankish legates by the clergy of Italy. See the annotations of the most learned man Henri Valois <note>Latin: Henrici Valesii</note> on Ammianus Marcellinus, book 17, page 140.

**trisagion** <note>Greek: τρισάγιον; literally "thrice holy," a standard hymn in the liturgy</note> **trisagion.** To those things observed by Meursius in his *Glossary*, add Andrew of Caesarea on the *Apocalypse*, page 5, among the works of Chrysostom published by Commelinus; the *Greek Menologium* for September 5; Nicephorus Callistus 15.28 and 18.51; Theophanes; and Antiochus, *Homily 130*. See the latter on page 1246 of volume 1 of the earlier Greek-Latin Library edition.

**trullus** <note>Greek: τροῦλλος or τροῦλος; a dome or cupola, often referring to a specific domed hall in the imperial palace</note> **dome.** Theophanes regarding Justinian: "They worked upon the piers <note>original Latin/Greek-derived: πινσοὺς; the structural supports</note> that were carrying the dome, and because of this they did not hold. Finally, the most pious emperor, seeing this, raised other piers, and the dome was supported." Likewise: "the dome of the church of Edessa." See Evagrius 4.31, and the later notes at page 386 a and b; and Allatius, *On the Temples of the Modern Greeks*, page 159 of the Paris edition. See also under **sekreton** <note>Greek: σέκρετον; a private chamber or council room</note>.

**typus** <note>Greek: τύπος; literally a "type" or "form," but in a legal context, an imperial edict or decree</note> **type, form, edict.** Pope Martin in his *Epistle to Amandus, Bishop of Utrecht*: "he persuaded our most merciful prince to create an imperial edict <note>original Latin: imperialem typum</note> with sacrilegious daring, full of all treachery." Anastasius the Librarian in his *Ecclesiastical History*: "Basiliscus, however, sent this man to Alexandria with edicts <note>original Latin: typis</note> against the council." And shortly after: "Furthermore, Basiliscus rejected the Council of Chalcedon by a general edict." The same author: "The emperor promulgated a form <note>a law or regulation</note> concerning bishops, administrators, orphanage directors, and hospital managers, that they should not possess inheritances except those they were proved to have held before they were promoted, concerning which they could have also issued a will." See volume 3 of St. Basil, page 70 of the Notes.

**hypante** <note>Greek: ὑπαντή; literally "meeting" or "encounter"</note> **The Meeting.** Thietmar, book 5: "There then the venerable Tagmo on the 4th Nones of February, that is, the *Hypante* <note>original Greek: ὑπαντὴ</note> of the Lord, that is, the meeting with Just Simeon, etc." <note>This refers to the Feast of the Presentation of Christ in the Temple, celebrated on February 2nd, commemorating the meeting between the infant Jesus and Simeon.</note> See Meursius.

**hypatia** <note>Greek: ὑπατία</note>, **hypateuein** <note>Greek: ὑπατεύειν</note>. **Consulship, to be consul.** At the beginning of their magistracy, consuls used to scatter *hypatia* <note>consular coins or small gifts</note> or money among the people. Marcellinus Comes in his *Chronicle*: "Emperor Marcian established by his decrees that those who wished to become consuls should scatter no copper money among the people." Or...

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical glossary of Greek and Latin terms found in Byzantine legal and historical texts, specifically focusing on terms starting with the Greek letter Phi (Φ). It transitions from the previous discussion of military ranks like "tribunus" to administrative and ecclesiastical vocabulary.</meta>

# FABROTI <note>Charles Annibal Fabrot (1580–1659) was a French legal scholar famous for his editions of Byzantine law.</note>

**princes.** <note>Latin: *principes*; referring to emperors or high leaders.</note> Theophanes says of Justinian: "the emperor gave a consulship, and he gave so much money as no one of the emperors who held the consulship had ever given." <note>original Greek: ἔδωκεν ὁ βασιλεὺς ὑπατίαν, καὶ τοσαῦτα ἔδωκε χρήματα ὅσα οὐδεὶς βασιλέων ὑπατεύσας</note> Likewise: "he held a consulship and threw much money [to the people]." <note>original Greek: ἐποίησε δὲ ὑπατίαν καὶ ἔρριψε χρήματα πολλά</note> Anastasius the Librarian in his *Ecclesiastical History*: *lavishly displaying the consulship.* <note>Latin: iactans liberaliter hypatiam; "hypatia" is the Greek term for consulship.</note> I have discussed this under Theophilus, the final section on the division of things.

**to falsify** <note>Greek: φαλσεύειν (*phalseuein*)</note> to forge, to adulterate.

**family** <note>Greek: φαμιλία (*familia*)</note> household or family. Achmes, chapters 79, 104, 299. Theophanes in the entry for Maurice: "we take their families captive." <note>original Greek: αἰχμαλωτίζομεν τὰς φαμιλίας αὐτῶν</note>

**factory-men.** <note>Greek: φαυρικίσιοι (*phabrikisioi*)</note> Cedrenus explains this on page 168: that is, those who make weapons in the public factories, which are called *phabrixi*. <note>original Greek: φάβριξι</note> St. Athanasius in his *Letter to the Solitaries*: "from the place there called the *fabrica* [factory]." <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τῆς ἐκεῖ καλουμένης φάβρικος</note>

**phelonion** <note>Greek: φελόνις, φελόνιον; a liturgical vestment</note> a priest's garment, also called a chasuble or *planeta*, as most learned men record. From the messenger of Patriarch Ignatius of Constantinople to Pope Nicholas: "garments, phelonia, and pectorals." <note>original Greek: ἱμάτιά τε καὶ φελώνια καὶ ἐγκόλπια; an "egkolpion" is a pectoral medallion worn by bishops</note> Blessed Chrysostom, commenting on St. Paul’s second epistle to Timothy, chapter 4: <note>The text says chapter 5, but the reference is likely 2 Timothy 4:13</note> "he means a garment here, though some say it refers to a book-chest where the books were kept." <note>original Greek: ἱμάτιον ἐνταῦθα λέγει, ὥς τινές φασι, τὸ γλωσσόκομον, ἔνθα τὰ βιβλία ἔκειτο</note> Those who interpret the *phelone* as a *glossokomon* or small chest for books are mistaken. See Suidas under the entries *phainoles* and *phenoles*; Balsamon in his *Commentary on the Councils*, page 622a; Hugo Menard in the *Sacramentary of St. Gregory the Great*, page 318; Meursius in his *Greeko-Barbarian Glossary*; and especially the *Archieratikon* <note>a liturgical book for bishops</note> of Isaac Habert—who, because of his integrity of life, singular piety, and supreme knowledge of both divine and human affairs, deserved to be promoted to the first order of the priesthood—pages 23 and 38.

**banner** <note>Greek: φλαμούλιον, φλάμουλον (*phlamoulion, phlamoulon*)</note> a standard or flag. Theophanes: "and having passed the banners." <note>original Greek: καὶ ἐπεράσασα τά τε φλάμουλα</note> Leo the Tactician, chapter 12, section 54: "at the time of battle, the spears should not have banners." <note>original Greek: ἐν δὲ τῷ καιρῷ τῆς μάχης φλάμουλα κοντάρια μὴ ἐχέτωσαν</note> and chapter 19, section 40: "there should be a sign standing on your ship, whether it be a *bandon* or a *phlamoulon*." <note>original Greek: εἶναι δὲ σημεῖον ἱστάμενον ἐν τῷ σῷ δρόμονι, εἴτε βάνδον εἴτε φλάμουλον; a "dromon" was a type of Byzantine galley</note> Legal Glosses: "a *phlamoulon* is a standard." Likewise: **standard-bearers** <note>Greek: φλαμβουλάριοι; likely a variation of *phlamoularioi*</note> those from the tip of whose spears hang purple rags. This appears as *phlampouron* in the author of the *Precious Crown*, and "Royal Banner" <note>original Greek: βασιλικόν φλάμπουρον</note> in Nicolaus Rigaltius' *Glossary of Mixed Greek*, page 201. Modestus (found in manuscripts of Tullius on military matters) regarding military vocabulary: *because of the sails, that is, the banners.* <note>Latin: quia velis, hoc est flamulis</note> This is how it is read in those same manuscripts, and how it should be read in Vegetius, book 2, chapter 1, not as "little flames" <note>Latin: flammeolis</note> as some learned men thought should be restored.

**foederati** <note>Greek: φοιδερᾶτοι; "federated" allies or mercenary troops</note> allies by treaty. Procopius in the *Gothic War*, page 324: "and those called *foederati* (for the Romans called them so then in the Latin language, indicating, I believe, that the Goths had not been defeated by them in war, but had become allies based on certain treaties)." <note>original Greek: καὶ φοιδερᾶτοι ἐπικληθέντες...</note> The Latin call treaties in war *foedera*, as I have previously shown in the first book of the *Vandal War*, page 106. See the *Legal Glossary* under *foederati*, and the notes of Jacques Sirmond on Sidonius Apollinaris, page 30.

**follis** <note>Greek: φόλλις; a low-value Roman/Byzantine coin</note> a follis. Basilius in his *Grammar*: "a *follis* is an obol." <note>original Greek: φόλλις ὁ ὀβολός; an obol was a small unit of currency</note>

# GLOSSARY

**follis** <note>original: φόλλις; originally a leather bag, it came to mean a bag of coins and eventually a specific copper coin in the Byzantine system.</note> Eustathius, commenting on the *Iliad*, Book 1: "they made the obols <note>small coins</note> which are called *folles*." Hero, in *On Weights*: "125 silver obols fill [the value]." This is the reading in the Royal Codex. Other copies have: "the *follis* fills [the value of] 125 silver pieces." What if we read: "the obol, or *follis*?" Excerpts from Epiphanius, *On Measures and Weights*: "three purses, which is also a *phole* <note>variant of follis</note> of 250 denarii, makes 312 pounds," and a little later: "a *phole* or purse has two and a half silver pieces, 250 denarii, [and] 50 pounds." <note>The arithmetic in these ancient metrological texts varies wildly between manuscript traditions.</note> Thus it is read in the R. copy: let the learned weigh the evidence. An old inscription: *he shall pay a thousand folles as a penalty.* In the *Acts of Cirta* by Numatius Felix: "He said to Nundinarius and Victor: 'Do you know that the *folles* were received from Lucilla?'" Saint Augustine, in his 40th sermon *To the New Converts*: "for a certain thing, which is truly said to have happened, a man who was not wealthy, but yet rich with the fat of charity even from a slender means, when he had sold a *solidus* <note>a gold coin</note>, as is customary, for a hundred *folles*, he ordered the price of the *solidus* to be distributed to the poor." Some *folles* were bronze, others were silver. On the value of both, see Sirmondus regarding the said 40th sermon. See also Procopius's *Secret History* page 111, Achmes chapter 237, Moschus's *Spiritual Meadow* chapter 134, Scaliger *On Matters of Currency* page 60, and Vossius *On the Vices of Speech* book 3, chapter 12, page 431 under the entry *Folleralis*.

**phoros** <note>original: φόρος</note> a forum or marketplace. The Emperor Marcus [Aurelius], in a letter to the Senate found in Justin's *Apology 2*: "and I command this my decree to be posted in the **Forum of Trajan** so that it may be read." <note>original Greek: καὶ κελεύω τοῦτό μου τὸ διάταγμα ἐν τῷ φόρῳ τοῦ Τραϊανοῦ προτεθῆναι πρὸς τὸ δύνασθαι ἀναγινώσκεσθαι</note> It is worth noting what Theophylact writes in his commentary on the *Acts of the Apostles*, chapter 28, that *images of the princes <note>emperors</note> are called foroi*: "as until now the images of the emperors are addressed as *phoroi*." <note>original Greek: ὡς μέχρι νῦν αἱ τῶν βασιλέων εἰκόνες φόροι προσαγορεύονται</note> Oecumenius says the same in *Acts*, chapter 39.

**fossaton** <note>original: φοσσᾶτον</note>, **fossatikos** <note>original: φοσσατικῶς</note>, a ditch-fortified camp, or an army. Blessed Chrysostom, in his 23rd homily on the *Epistle to the Ephesians*: "the present life is a kind of road and a military campaign, and as one might say, what is called among them a *fossaton* <note>army/camp</note>; one will not seek grand buildings. For who, tell me, even if he be very wealthy, would choose to build grand houses in what is called a *fossaton*? Not one; for he would be a laughingstock, and he would be building for his enemies and drawing them toward himself. So if we are sober, the present life differs not at all from a military campaign and a *fossaton*." See the last law in the Code *On the Restitution of Soldiers* and law 21 § 1 of the Digest, as well as the commentaries in the *Basilica* <note>a 9th-century code of Byzantine law</note>. I discussed this in my notes on Theophilus regarding military wills. The Synod of Constantinople 7: "that the nation of the Agarenes <note>Arabs/Saracens, traditionally descended from Hagar</note> goes out as an army [*fossatikos*]." <note>original Greek: ὅτι τὸ ἔθνος Ἀγαρηνῶν φοσσατικῶς ἐξέρχεται</note> Anastasius translates it thus: *that the nation of the Agarenes had gone out in a hostile manner.*

**phoulkizein** <note>original: φουλκίζειν</note>. "He executed [him] on the gallows [*ephoulkise*] and beheaded [him]" <note>original: δι’ Ἀδάμαντος ἐφούλκισε καὶ ἀπεκεφάλισε</note> page 385 b. Write it thus. Theophanes, however, says "he hanged some [*ephourkise*], and beheaded others." <note>original Greek: τοὺς μὲν ἐφούρκισε, τοὺς δὲ ἀπεκεφάλισε</note> Anastasius the Librarian in his *Ecclesiastical History* translates it as: *some he suspended, others he beheaded.* Therefore, those who think *phourkizein* and *phoulkizein* are different things are mistaken: for both are used for "hanging on a gallows" <note>Latin: furca</note> or "subjecting to the gallows." Theophanes: "two fell from the gallows [*phourka*]; they were hung again, and fell again." See Suidas.

<meta>catchword: Georg. Cedrenus tom. II.</meta>

# FABROT’S GLOSSARY

**fork** <note>original: φου̃ρκα; a term often used for a gallows or a specific agricultural tool</note>. Mentioned by John Moschus in *The Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 72, and by Alexius Rharturus in his penultimate teaching.

**oven** <note>original: φου̃ρνος; Latin: furnus</note>. Eustathius, commenting on the *Iliad*, Book 16 <note>designated as π</note>: "Observe the ancient use of the term *traktos* <note>a type of rolled dough</note> for bread. In such a context, he also uses the more common term *phournos*, from which he records the derived name *phournikios* bread, just as bread from a *klibanos* <note>a portable ceramic oven</note> is called *klibanikios*." John Moschus, *The Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 184: "to cast the loaves into the oven." It is also used by Achmes in chapter 159.

**paper-tax** <note>original: χαρτιατικόν; Latin: chartiaticum</note>. The *chartiaticum* is a fee paid for the issuance of official documents. Cujas, *Observations* 4.18. Theophanes: "and on account of the paper-tax, two *keratia* <note>carats, or small silver/copper coins</note> each." Anastasius the Librarian, in his *Ecclesiastical History*: *and to provide two siliquae <note>a small silver coin</note> for the sake of the paper-tax.*

**chelandion** <note>original: χελάνδιον; a type of swift galley or warship used by the Byzantine navy</note>, a type of vessel. Theophanes, in the section on Emperor Theodosius: "many *chelandia* departing from the city brought supplies." Anastasius in the *Ecclesiastical History*: *a fleet of two thousand chelandia against Bulgaria; and he himself entered in the red chelandia. And a little later: he died in a chelandion.*

**golden bull** <note>original: χρυσόβουλλον; Latin: aurea bulla</note>. Pachymeres: "a golden-bulled word" <note>referring to an imperial decree or Chrysobull</note>. Also: "secured with a golden bull." For a *boulla* is a seal. *Menologion* for August 31: "having a seal by means of a golden bull." The Emperors Romanus and Constantine in a certain diploma: *We decree and grant power to the abbot of the house itself through our present kind chrysobull and seal, etc.* In Greek it was *chrysobullon*. Saint Agobard, *On the Insolence of the Jews*: *commands signed in your name with golden seals.* Liutprand of Cremona in his *Embassy to Nicephorus Phocas, Emperor of Constantinople*: *With these things said and finished, they gave me a chrysobullion—that is, a letter written and signed in gold—to be brought to you; though in my opinion, it was not worthy of you. They also took other letters signed in silver.* From this comes the term **to seal** <note>Latin: bullare</note>. *Life of Saint John the Almsgiver*: *a sealed document* <note>original: pittakion bullatum</note>. And **to unseal** <note>Latin: disbullare</note>. Sixth Council of Constantinople, act 15.

**gold-writer** <note>original: χρυσογράφος; Latin: auriscriptor</note>. <note>A scribe specialized in using gold ink for imperial documents.</note>

**soul-offering** <note>original: ψυχικόν; Latin: eleemosyna</note>, alms. A medieval Greek author in the historical narrative about Belisarius: "give me again a lord’s *psychikon*, an obol <note>a small coin</note>." <note>This refers to charity given for the benefit of one's soul.</note>

**omophorion** <note>original: ὠμοφόριον; Latin: pallium</note>, the stole or vestment of archbishops. George of Alexandria in his *Life of Chrysostom*: "and he wrapped the *omophorion* around the neck of Ammonius, a man of his own age, with his own hands." Sixth Council of Constantinople, act 8: "let him be stripped of the *omophorion* placed around him." An old translator: *let him be stripped of the pallium placed around him.* See Isidore of Pelusium, book 1, epistle 136. **To wear an omophorion** <note>original: ὠμοφορει̃ν</note>. See canon 14 of the Eighth Council of Constantinople.

**granary** <note>original: ὠρει̃ον; Latin: horreum</note>. I mentioned this in my notes on Theophilus. Hence **granary-keeper** <note>original: ὀρειάριος</note>: "The granary-keeper is sued," or *legal action must be taken against the granary-keeper.* The *Basilika* <note>Byzantine law code</note> regarding book 4 of the *Digest*, *On the Production of Property*.

<vocab>φου̃ρνος, χαρτιατικόν, χελάνδιον, χρυσόβουλλον, ψυχικόν, ὠμοφόριον, ὠρει̃ον</vocab>

### HISTORICAL INDEX. 1008

[Romanos IV Diogenes] <note>The name is carried over from the previous page.</note> leads a weak army against the Sultan II, 868, 2 and following; his speech II, 693, 14; captured by the Sultan and released II, 699, 9 and following. <note>Romanos IV was the Byzantine emperor defeated and captured by the Seljuk Turks at the Battle of Manzikert in 1071.</note>
**Roussel the Frank** <note>original Latin: "Ruselius Latinus"; referring to Roussel de Bailleul, a Norman mercenary who attempted to carve out his own principality in Asia Minor</note>, commander of the army, is captured by the Turks II, 708, 6; 711, 18; 713, 17; 730, 5. His death II, 743, 16.
**Salerno**, the largest city of Calabria II, 721, 2.
**Samuch**, a Turk II, 653, 11.
**Samuel Alousianos**, a Bulgarian *court official* <term>bestarches: a high-ranking Byzantine court title, originally associated with the imperial wardrobe but later a general honorary rank</term> II, 678, 21.
**The Sangarius River** <note>A major river in Asia Minor, known today as the Sakarya</note> II, 690, 10.
**Sardices Diogenes**, a general sent into exile II, 663, 16 and following. <note>This likely refers to Nikephoros Diogenes, son of Romanos IV; "Sardices" may be a textual corruption or a specific epithet.</note>
**Saronites** II, 717, 10 and following. <note>A member of the Saronites family, a prominent Byzantine clan.</note>
**The city of Skopje** conquered II, 717, 17.
**The people of Scribona** II, 721, 22. <note>Referring to the inhabitants of Scribla, a Norman stronghold in southern Italy.</note>
**Sebastia** <note>Modern-day Sivas in Turkey; a vital military hub in the 11th century</note> II, 670, 3; 671, 9.
**Selte** II, 646, 2.
**The Monastery of St. Sergius** II, 718, 14.
**Mount Sophon** II, 710, 21.
**Straboromanos**, a governor <note>original Latin: "praeses"</note> II, 735, 15; 743, 20 and following.
**The army commander** <term>stratopedarches: a high military rank, literally meaning "the master of the camp" or "commander of the plains"</term> II, 648, 18.
**Tame**, leader of the Uzes II, 695, 5. <note>The Uzes were a Turkic people who invaded the Balkans in 1064.</note>
